It should be said early that this game is not for everyone, but if you like this type of genre, then Dominions 4 is definitely worth it in my book.
The mechanics are mostly about overall strategic movements around the world map, and army compositions, and axcept for a pre-battle plan, there is no way to control your units in combat.
To start, you design your god, who will then command your chosen nation in the fight for the thrones of succesion, and ultimately the title of Pentakrator, the sole remaining and most powerful god in the world.
The goal is to expand your "empire", which means conquering land and spreading your dominion, and claiming the victory points around the map to crown yourself victor. Dominion is basically your chosen gods influence, and will give provinces modifiers based on how you designed your god.
Conquering land is vital for securing enough resources and gold to build an ever bigger army. Enemies will usually not be far away, and on multiple fronts. Smart decision making will often decide the outcome of your games.
As you gain land, send skilled mages into them to search for magic sites. Magical sites will provide gems, which are mostly used for spellcasting (combat) and rituals (world map spells). Having a high gem income can a lot of times be the edge needed to subdue enemy nations.
Personally, i prefer less micro intensive strategy games, which is why i like this game so much. The god aspect is very well thought through, and there is tons of variety in gods and magic, which is the ultimate charm of the game.

This game is pretty amazing. Even now, years after its release, Illwinter continues to update it. Just a few days ago, one of these updates added and entirely new faction to the game. That kind of dedication to their game impresses me, and I appreciate it a lot as a player.
Dominions 4 is a pretty complicated and difficult-to-learn strategy game. That complication comes mostly from the sheer depth of the game's mechanics, and a lack of an in-game tutorial. You'll probably need to read the manual (which is linked here on the store page) to learn the proper way to play. I'd recommend skimming over it even if you haven't bought the game yet, as it can probably give you a pretty good idea of what you're buying.
The gameplay focuses heavily on the use of magic and the managing of your dominion - dominion measures the population's belief in you, and their willingness to worship you as their god. One method of victory involves spreading your dominion across the entire map, eliminating all belief in other gods through fanatical preaching and construction of temples.
The community still seems pretty active, and you can probably find people to play with on the forums - along with user-made content like maps and mods(including player-made factions).
As far as fantasy-themed grand strategy games go, I haven't played very many... but I'd hazard a guess that Dominions is by far the most deep and varied one, with 83 factions, almost 400 craftable and equipable artifacts, and like a zillion spells (I actually have no idea how many there are, since almost every faction has faction-specific spells). It's definitely worth your time, and I'd say it's worth your money as well.

This game, while having it's quirks and limitations is actually a very good football club director simulator. I say director, because there's very little management in the traditional sense. It focuses more on the business side of things, while keeping a level of simple, distilled gameplay akin to that of the DOS games of old (Football Limited jumps out as an example).
The game only features the German leagues, and quite unrealistically too, as there are 8 divisions down to what is known IRL as the Kreisliga (aka City Leagues) but strangely, the game features a completely 1 to 1 linear structure, not the pyramid football fans are used to.
The match engine is almost non-existent, with opaque number crunching happening behind the scenes and small highlights appearing every chance or goal, but nevertheless it's solid enough to make the business side of things fun. One gripe I have is that the engine seems to make a big deal of underestimation, where if you have a vastly superior team, your team has a chance of completely being swept aside, although I have noticed that upping the win bonus to about 5000 euros and higher offsets this somewhat, while also giving you an edge in closer matches.
The facilities building feature is great, you get to pick what parts of your stadium and grounds you want to upgrade, and it gives you a birds eye view of the area, where you can slowly build the crown jewel of your footballing empire. Of course, it's mostly in 2D but it's a nice touch anyway. Adding crowd capacity is easy, as is upgrading them from standing room, to seating with roofs. VIP boxes are also a part of the game, and you can even add catering, TV systems and service.
The transfer market is quite iffy though, you can only buy players in January and July, with no ability to offer in the off-period and get them when the window starts. The negotiations are simple and to the point, as the game will tell you how close you are to them closing negotiations by shrinking their happiness bar. Contracts are pretty much the same.
You may obtain sponsors, usually a main sponsor with bonuss based on wins, matches, promotiona and avoiding relegation, and as of update 1.42 you can get other sponsors which just pay a certain fee every month. Also of note is merchandisng, which you must stock for an entire season before July 15th or risk not being eble to sell anything. It's an exciting system which is certainly more fun than checking every so often to restock on a permanent basis.
You may buy player insurance which pays you when players get injured, I personally haven't used it, but it's a nice touch. You may also speculate on the share market, which I haven't done either. Also of note is socking money away as ban investment and getting it back a 1 to 7 years later with interest. The longer the term, the higher the interest rate.
Actually setting the formations is a chore that is confusing as hell, which is why I say it's more of a business simlator, it's so deep in business but lacking in actual management. No tactics to speak of, but I guess that's what makes the game so simple and fun. Usually, I just hire an assistanr manager to do both training and squad picking.
There's a plethora of stats screens in this game, which is a nice touch. I also love the found a club mode, reminds me a lot of the days when I played FIFA Manager religiously, back when it was actually good.
Anyway, I guess I should close this review now, so let me outline the pros and cons.
PROS:
* Good football club business sim
* Stadium and ground building is nice
* Financial options are plentiful
* Plenty of stats
* You can hire staff to do the actual football stuff
CONS:
* The actual football side of things is sorely lacking
* The transfer market is confusing and restrictive
* Formations are hard, especially with no tactics
* 30 dollars/euros/pounds is a bit much, prices aren't currency converted either.
OVERALL:
A good game for the tycoon guys out there with an interest in football. If you like football management games but find Football Manager too hard and complex, this could be good for you. If you're a diehard football manager, keep playing FM, you might not like this. If you love both tycoon games and football, you'll love this game.
Absolute waste of money. I am very disappointed.

Club Manager 2015 takes you into the back-end of how a football team is run; from selecting the right players to taking your team to glory; to the actual running of the club; and even right down to designing the stadium.
As you start, you will be run through a few helpful screens which will give you the basics of how to use the interface. Unfortunately, this will happen every time you start the game; making you click ‘Next’ often, just so that you can get to the main title screen.
Once you do start though, the game begins to take shape as something well worth playing. As you click on ‘New Game’ you are given the option to name your player; decide on how many players you would like to have in the game; game difficulty; and whether you would like to use an existing club or found your own.
Founding your own club will make the game far more difficult because, unlike selecting a pre-existing club, you start with some money and that’s it. You have to do everything from build your stadium; to buying players; to competing in matches.
Unlike most football management games, CM15 lets you see everything that you can do with your club. You can manage your team by:
changing your squad layout;
defining the training parameters;
seeing who’s contract will be expiring soon;
whether or not you want to keep them;
buying new players; as well as
renting your own players out to other teams.
Managing the club gives you the opportunity to hire staff to help you to run the club.  It also provides the opportunity of checking your youth team’s status; and deciding how much you want to spend on their annual training.  You can also check your prestige and view the history of the club.
Once you get into the finer points of managing a club, your work includes building the stadium and raising finances.As an example, you can’t run a football club without some good revenue coming in and the one way to do this is to make sure that your stadium look pretty. CM15 gives you a view of the exterior of the stadium where you can build everything to help players enhance their skills and even build bus stops for the fans.
The interior of the club gives you the tools to build your stadiums stands; the floodlights and even the public toilets.  The better the appearance of the stadium, the more fans will come and watch your team.
You can also set ticket and merchandise pricing as well as purchase the merchandise yourself, as well as deciding on how much you want in your store at any one time.
Financing the club is also made quite easy. You can apply for credit; choose sponsors; adjust merchandise prices; and get investments, all of which will either make or break your club. You can even insure a valuable player.
You also have a manager’s pass which will warn you when there is something wrong anywhere in your club. This little tool is very helpful when you don’t want to look through every detail of the club simply to find a problem.
As you click ‘Next’ you will move up the calendar days until either a match day; match draw; or construction completion comes up, if a match day comes up you will be taken to the match screen where you will have to decide on the line-up or, alternatively, let your assistant coach choose the best line-up. You will then move to the pre-match screen. Here it is made easy for you to decide on how you want your team to perform and whether or not to give them a bonus if they win. Both are slide bars from ;do little; to ;play aggressively. You are then moved to the match screen where you can watch the time run up and adjust the speed of the game. You will also see what penalties are being given and a short cinematic of a goal either being scored or missed.
The matches could have been made a little more interactive as most of the time you are just watching the time run up. It would be better if there was more control of the team. For example; throughout the match the ability to give commands to players on how aggressive they should be with their attacks. Speeding the match up, just to finish it, is all you would want to do so that you can get back to running the club.
After hiring an assistant manager you can give him tasks to do but, the problem here, is that you can’t see what the tasks are because they are all over-lapping each other. The language in the game could use some work too, as every once in a while you will see misspelled words or badly placed grammar.
Overall, Big Blaze Games has developed quite an addictive game, even though some of the playability is a bit irritating.
Whether you are a casual gamer or a hardcore football fan, this game will keep you playing for hours. Even when you aren’t playing, you will be thinking of ways to improve the club’s standings.

The Castle Doctrine is a highly original video game filled with challenges for even the best chess players. The gameplay is split between two tasks: building defenses to protect your vault and your family, and raiding your neighbors' houses for money and tools. The layers of planning that a good home defense require are extensive, and numerous strategies exist for both creating and overcoming creative traps.
The economy of the game is intelligently designed- players begin with enough money to build basic traps and buy tools for raiding. The tools, in essence, are used for destroying traps- and the more expensive the tool, the better the traps it can break. Balancing your funds between upgrading your own security and breaking into others' houses is a challenge.
The tricky part comes when you have to test your defenses. Any defense you build must let someone (hypothetically) reach your vault without any tools. (It should be noted that it does not have to be possible to reach the family unarmed, so as long as there are no traps in their path, one could line the hallway to one's family with pit bulls.) Unfortunately, it is possible for someone's house to become impregnable when it is raided- mobile creatures (such as pit bulls) could end up in positions that guarantee that no one else gets through to the vault. In addition, a vault that has been raided becomes empty, and reaching it no longer grants the raider an escape. This is part of the risk inherent in robbery though: it's always possible that someone else has screwed things up for you to get their own share of the loot.
There is one major flaw in the game, however. When testing your own security to prove it can be breached, accidentally triggering a deadly trap kills you, forcing you to start over. You can test these traps with various devices that indicate electric current without harming you, but it can be a pain when you have to start fresh because of a small mistake in building your own house. This part of the game seems unnecessary, as it only punishes players who make dumb mistakes designing their defenses, and the punishment is death.
All things considered, The Castle Doctrine is a great game if you want a fun, challenging robbery sim that lets you play both sides.

The core mechanic of this game is essentially building and attempting puzzles; and that core is fantastic. I really enjoy planning and laying out my house, and (to a lesser extent) I like trying other peoples houses. Unfortunately this enjoyable part of the gameplay is surrounded by some really frustrating and boggling mechanics.
The permadeath means that once I've finished setting up my initial house I can't risk going out to rob others' houses as I'll probably quickly die thus wasting the time spent on my own house. So I build my house and leave it to be robbed by others and see how well I did. Unfortunately people will quickly turn up with a backpack full of tools and smash a path straight through my house. Once my house is inevetibly robbed I'll have no money left and will be unable to perform even basic repairs to my house, let alone improve my design. So I must go out and rob other houses or commit suicide (effectively equivalent options).
I really think this game would be much better if it removed the permadeath and a lot of the money mechanics, and instead focused more on the puzzle aspect perhaps including leaderboards and tallies for houses/thieves.

The concept and design of this game often cross into brilliant territory. I haven't had a game make me feel so clever in a while. I spent the first few hours of the game meticulously setting up my maze of traps that involved making some cats flip some switches that activate some electric floor panels behind any potential intruder. I found myself engrossed with the idea of trying to create something to outsmart another player. It worked... and worked again... yes I thought, this is marvelous.
Then someone cut down a wooden wall that led to my family, shot down my wife and brutally clubbed my children to death. Oh my. I wrote down his name with some idea of revenge planted in my head. Then I thought about it and realized this game was leading me down a dark path. I started working on my house again...
This isn't to say that I don't think the game has some issues with balance and some other areas. I find that you want to often save a fair amount of money on a new life to make yourself a nice juicy target for some burglar. This is odd I thought to myself... I want people to break into my house. Without them I'll have no income... unless I go out and rob other people. I tried to rob other people but I soon found that other people's deathtraps rely heavily on presenting you with so many paths you're bound to fail at some point or another. Without tools you'll have no way to escape from a deadly situation, but I spent most of my money on my house... and tools are expensive.
Essentially I found that the game presents you with a paradox of sorts. While it wants you to realize that being a robber or killing people in your house isn't a good thing, it doesn't really give you any other option. There is no honest living in this game, you either steal lives in self-defense or you go out and rob other people's houses.
Still though, through all of this I still would recommend this game. The thrill of trying to outwit other players is too satisfying of an experience. I'm not sure I've ever really played anything quite like it. It's tense and everything feels weighty. It's really something how this game creates such a cynical atmosphere.

Dominions 4 is an extremely deep 4x, with more "under the hood" than its competitors. The combat, unit choice, list of factions, spells to research and ways to command your units is all far and above what other games offer.
But it doesn't have much interest in teaching you how to play it, and the interface is functional at best. Someone sitting down with Civ 5 or Endless Legend could quickly enjoy intuitive and simple mechanics, while Dominions 4 is a struggle from the start.
The setting is very rich, with mythological and history-based factions ruled over by a God of your design competing to bcome the omnipotent divinity. Dominions 4 requires a lot of investment to understand what's going on, why it's happening, and what to do, but it's very rewarding once you do so. 70 hours in I am still learning new things- Axe-equipped infantry are more likely to lop off an enemy's arm in combat, giving him hideous penalties and generally ruining his day. How awesome is that? But the game is in no hurry to tell you about its many wonderful features and possibilities.
Finally, the multiplayer is much smoother than other 4xes i've played, moving along comparatively fast. It's possible to play out thirty turns in one sitting with multiple friends, and a great way to spend an evening.  Especially recommended to those who love history and mythology.

I'm a livestreamer who plays quite a bit of minecraft on stream - and I was hoping this would be a nice "middle ground" where minecraft fans could enjoy, but it would be different enough from minecraft to feel like a new game.  Barring the fact that I had a blue-screen mid stream (Crashes happen, although while streaming they are very painful).
** Issue #1 ** Significantly too short.  I finished the episode in 1:30.  That includes the time it took me to crash, restart, load up my stream, and resume playing and replay through from my last auto-save...  If the remaining episodes will be included free as part of the $22 I spent on this, then it may be worth the price, but having to wait to play a game in full when I was under the impression that it was a full game, not an "early release"...
** Issue #2 **  Not NEARLY enough time to make choices.  I sometimes clicked at the last second and it didn't register, or spent 2 seconds looking at chat to look back and realize I missed a decision point.  I guess the game is so short I can do it over...
** Issue #3 ** Besides dialogue, there was no other choice.  In fact, the "challenges" were button-mashing (PRESS Q A BUNCH OF TIMES REALLY FAST) or the occasional "DDR-Lite" where you have to press A, S, D, or W to avoid an attack.  At best it was an interactive cut-scene where I occasionally did button mashing.  Far cry from being able to freely build whatever I want in minecraft...
** Issue #4 ** I mis-clicked on character creation.  I couldn't go back, I couldn't undo, I was stuck with the character I selected.  I even tried the "go back a menu" and it wouldn't let me go back.  SO, when picking a character MAKE SURE YOU PICK THE ONE YOU WANT.
** What I actually Liked ** I didn't hate the experience, just had lots of issues.  The story was "OK" although the story tries to carve you out as a weak and uncool kid, which makes all the "I'm awesome and kickass" dialogue options seem extremely out of place (even though I chose them, because I'm awesome and kickass).  I DID want to continue playing.  When the credits rolled I was left with two feelings: "HOLY CRAP IT'S OVER, WTF, THIS WAS JUST BARELY AN HOUR" and "WHY IS THE NEXT EPISODE HERE"  But for $22 I could have bought an entire TV season of Doctor Who and had 12+ hours of entertainment, whereas I got 1 1/2 hours of entertainment here and a sore finger (from mashing the Q button, BTW - Telltale, you owe me a new Q button).
Overall - I'd say DO NOT BUY until all the episodes are out.  Unless you like playing the same game over and over and over, because thats the only way you'll get value out of this.

I got The Binding of Isaac in a humble bundle for $5 along with a bunch of other games. Before this game, I didn't know what a roguelike game was, but after playing many other games I have to say this is still my favorite. For the low price, it was definitely worth every penny. I wouldn't have minded paying more for it either.
I've beaten the game on normal mode with most of the characters, but there are always new bosses to defeat, new items to unlock, and the game is a lot more fun on hard mode once you've beaten it a few times. On hard mode there are even old bosses with new powers or attacks, making the gameplay different each time.
If you're okay with permadeath, I definitely recommend this game. There is always something new to unlock, and after putting a lot of hours into the game I still feel like there are more challenges to complete.
This game is so much fun that you'll want to unlock every item possible. Which eventually grants you the status as platinum god. you have to admit that sounds pretty freaking badass.

After abit of poking from friends (a big thank you too Yorkie & Griff) i decided to get past the basic graphics and give this a go.

there is no team work co-operation bargining trading guilds leagues ..... its just you, oh and the loving wife and kids. Who strangely dont seem to matter as much as your money when your robbed. I've watched many a UTube vid where father arrives home and the missus and kids have been brutely executed in all the glorious 8bit detail and he casualy walks past their corpses lamanting about the money he has just lost and thinking of how he can upgrade his security. Life goes on I guess.
The game is deceptively simple to learn but hard to master. I had a good understanding of what needed to be done within half an hour but then I found myself working on my house for the next 3 hours trying to get the right balance of false sense of security for anyone wishing to come into my welcoming home and death around every corner for said person once hes taken 10 steps. Then theres the carrot, sure you could spend your $2000.00 starting cash on everything barring the kitchen sink (please note there are actualy no kitchen sinks in the game at this time) but whos going to try and rob you if their risking death for 3 bucks. That $2000.00 start up money isn't looking as generous as it did 10 seconds ago is it.
Happy with my death house from hell with a nice little carrot of $638.00 I headed out to partake in the second part of the game robbing everyone else blind. So after taking 11 steps into my first house ready to rob the rich and give to the poor, namely me, I found my self well and truly screwed. All I can say Mr Francis Dukis' wont have to feed that pitbull for a week due to the abundance of my carcess it threw around the place.
I had just discoverd the joys of my first permadeath! House gone , Wife and Kids gone (probably went off and married pitbull Dukis') my money gone and 3 HOURS of REAL LIFE GONE!!!. So back i went to my new life and started all over vowing to never die again ... yea right.
Overall this game is very promising the concept is fantastic and dark. I would like to think they will expand the crimes you can commit with the end result a dystopian society like in the movie "The Purge". If you do not know what this movie is google is your friend.
No doubt there are a lot of traps and equipment to be added to the game but from what i've read the developers are extremily commited to the game wanting the finished product to give the best possible gaming experience to us, the guys who pay the bills.
If I had one grip it would be that there needs to be something implemented sooner than later so you actually care what happens to your family instead of them just being cannon fodder.
I feel the game is a solid 7 out of 10 at this stage of development.
So get past the 8bit graphics (I did) and buy this game you wont regret it, it is only going to improve from here.
Now if you'll excuse me I must go and have a meet and greet with my new family ....... goddamn permadeath.

This is neither a review praising or criticizing the game. This is a review that recounts my personal experience, my initial impression, and ultimately, whether or not it felt like the price was worth the value and content I received. If you agree with my thoughts, you should definitely get it. If you don't, maybe wait for an update that brings in what you want or keep looking for that perfect fighting game!
Incredibly entertaining game. In a marketplace where fighting games with flashy supers and comeback mechanics oversaturate the market, this bare basic Kung Fu arcade fighter brings an oddly refreshing aftertaste. There are no fancy mechanics. In return, you get a game that is about raw skill.
This game initially felt very slow and heavy. I guarantee everyone will experience the same feeling. The perfect way to describe the pace is exactly like how its advertised on the store page. It's designed to remind you of fight scenes you'd typically witness in movies. Everything starts very slow, but once you get a tempo, it becomes very fast. After all the punches and kicks fly around everywhere, it starts to settle down. Because of the post-defeat slow mo, it feels gratifying when you land that hit that knocks out your opponent! It's exactly how a movie would go. That last final hit when the hero defeats the villain is slowed down immensely so all can savor the moment, the impact, the realization.
Because this is a 4 button fighter (no light, medium or hard attacks/just left punch/kick and right punch/kick), combo strings are longer to compensate. However, even if you drop it, it feels satisfying knowing there's a high chance you will be able to master it.
Some modes I really wanted after playing a few hours are in highest to lowest expectations 1) tournament mode 2) challenges 3) trials
Online, more characters, more combos, and constant dev communication and support are already essentially guaranteed so there is no reason to put those on the wishlist.
Now I'm off to play some more!

Kings of Kung Fu is a love letter to Black Theater Saturdays and imported kung fu films. While I do find the game's character models to be very dated in appearance I'm by no means a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ and only care about gameplay.  I do really love the film grain and style of the game. As for the core game, it plays much better than I expected. Combos are easy to pull off and look very brutal. What I do have issue with is that the controller scheme doesn't allow use of analog sticks or to change button setup (they are backwards to me). Using the D-pad is an issue FOR ME, but maybe not for others. I found that trying to pull of moves with the D-pad was a hit or miss task for me most times. Luckily I own Xpadder and just mapped my own controller scheme, but hope that this will all be supported in game soon. The computer opponent A.I. is competent as any other fighting game when turned up a few extra difficulty levels. Characters are all recognizable to any martial arts film buff as are the stages they fight on. In a nutshell, for the price tag this game is very original and FUN and can only be better with friends. This is just an ALPHA. I can only imagine the content and features that this game will gain in the upcoming development period. Not perfect by any means, but so far so good in my opinion.  Especially considering this is a game that's been in development for less than a year using Unity3D.

A loving fighting game homage to the halcyon chop-socky era of kung fu cinema.  Cool character 'likenesses'(!), excellent animations and overall persentation for an Indie game.  The gameplay is fun and not too 'Mugen-y' (NB: It's not KoFXIII, but it's much better than the likes of Vanguard Princess and about on par with Skull Girls in its own right).  Kung Fu Kings is the tongue-in-cheek, kung fu glory days, knock-about fighter fans of the genre have been yearning for but the big fighter development houses have continually shied away from.  This game shows a lot of promise.  Definitely worth the meagre price for such a novel game and a project that should be supported by fans of this video game genre.

Man, a review huh. I wasn't expecting much from this game as I've bounced from 4x to wargames, and back again over time never really being that impressed. So let me write a quick love letter to this one, that I've been hopelessly addicted to over the past several days despite its flaws.
This game does not compromise on what it's supposed to be. It's a lovesong to the heydey of the past, and it's built without regard to any mosquito-like whining of the modern age. It never adapted except maybe to make controls easier, and it's so easy to love for it's somewhat rustic charm. If you played this sort of game in 1998, you will be well at home here.
It treats graphics as though they were petty things for lesser purveyors of the arts. Instead, each and every facet of the game is just rich with an 11 herbs-and-spices of flavor. Every "pretender" God is interesting to read about, as is each civilization. As far as I can tell, they're all derived from one collection of lore or another, but they're adapted in such a way as to be interesting. Do you want biblical fanfiction? Norse mythology? The Deku tree? There's something for everyone here, and none of it is compromised to plebs that tend to fill modern video game audiences.
Let me also mention the depth here. This game is so incredibly deep that many complain about it. As a caveat, the depth may not be entirely perfectly crafted. I feel there are some imbalances between the value of units, and the sheer amounts of spells makes it unreasonable to have a good grasp on what any given casters capabilities are. However, I kind of enjoy the "fog of war" this creates, and as my group of bros got this on sale, we're all kind of on the same curve.
DO BE AWARE. There are a LOT of things in this game that are never explicitly explained, and I absolutely recommend looking up a guide. I watched the first 5 videos in this guy's guide:
Things like garrisons, prophets, many facets of casting, even just creating your nation are not obvious or intuitive. You can totally crap your way through it, but it'd be easy to go a few hours and still be missing things.
(on a side note, there are no dedicated servers, you have to use a VLAN with port access, however it has been the most seamless experience I think I've ever had with this system, even flawlessly connecting overseas)
Multiplayer aside, this game is really great on single player as well. I pretty much immediately put in several hours.
There's just so much meat here, and the meat is delicious. I havn't had such a boner for a game in quite some time. So please accept my full-bellied sloppy♥♥♥♥♥♥♥soaked recommendation. Time to play for a few more hours.

I feel like I'm playing a very slightly retuned Dominions 3, but that's not a bad thing. Also, there are still no elves, and that's awesome.
Dominions 4 is a turn-based fantasy strategy game that is about 99.985% substance and .015% style. The graphics endearingly suck, and that will turn more than a few people away, but a thorough check under the hood will reveal one of the most complicated and rewarding strategy experiences out there. Though it doesn't share all the features you may expect in your typical modern turn-based strategy game, the ones that it does have are taken to levels so unbelievably high that other games lose sight of it from their big-budget pedestals.
If the music upon boot-up sounds familiar, you probably played Dominions 3. I think I've heard a few new tunes, but it seems that all the originals are back. Once again, retuned Dom3.
Diplomacy is nonexistant, so don't expect any non-aggression pacts or trade and research agreements with the AI or with your friends. Although a form of coop has been added, it has a certain wonkiness to it that makes it a little less enjoyable than simply making secret alliances with other human players. Backstab, backstab, bacsktab!
There are a ton of factions to choose from inside of 3 different ages of existence, all with many, many unit types serving many different purposes. I'm not going to try counting the number of unique units in this game, but it's definitely somewhere between holy crap and even more holy crap.
Did I mention that in spite off all this variety there are no elves? That's a breath of fresh freaking air.
The magic system is just as varied as the soldiers in your armies, and there are tons of spells ranging from useless to game-ending. Experimenting with magic and finding what works what needs a little adjustment, and what just accidentally killed your entire army is half the fun. Compile that with a single save file and you may develop a light case of paranoia. I did.
If magic is the potatoes of this game, then combat is the steak, and it probably runs a bit different than what you may be used to. It involves a lot of indirect control and tactical trial and error. I'll admit it took some getting used to, and you will often find yourself wondering how your 400-something close-combat soldiers were scared off by a dozen elephants, but unexpected catastrophic defeats are all part of the fun. Just like when your fate conspires against you and a stray arrow takes your necromancer out of a fight, leaving your horde of undead to mindlessly scratch their butts while they're picked to pieces. There's so much to go into and so many hilarious stories, but you'll have plenty of opportunities to make your own.
My biggest warning: If you played the ealier Dominions and could not get into the swing of it, don't expect this to change that wind's direction. It's more of the same, but the keyword here is 'more'. If it was more you wanted, it's what you got. And It was definitely what I wanted. Kudos!
Lastly, Illwinter does sell a printed manual from their website. It's not necessary for the game, but it's certainly helpful. Mine is buried with notes already.

Great strategy game. Don't be fooled by the seemingly complex nature of Dominions 4, at its heart it is a turned based strategy game about conquering thy neighbor with a light build aspect to the game. While there are only about five buildings you will choose from to construct, what makes the game so complex and interesting is the myriad of magic research, races, troop types, and crafting items you can make for your heroes. When these are coupled with a wide variety of customizable deities/wannabe gods vying for ascension, different victory conditions (research, a capture the flag like thrones of ascension, domination, etc.) as well as different Ages with different technology and magic, you get a very complex layered game. The ability to set battlefield formations for your troops and command types whereby you can march them into war and watch the battles play out (adjusting accordingly should your plans backfire) makes it even more interesting. It would be nice if the graphics were a bit sharper, but that said, the focus on gameplay is the winning jewel for this game and should be a great examples for devs. out there that are graphics oriented versus gameplay oriented.

Dominions 4: Thrones of Ascension
It's not you're average stratagy fantasy game, no. Most of the civilizations for example, are based on historical civilizations but are changed to suit a more mythological theme. Meaning, you wont be fighting elves, orcs and dwarfs, but rather giants and lizard men. And the use of priests and religious figures is also an almost prominent factor of the games main objective.
Story:
The god of all has vanished and in the abscence of this supreme being, many 'pretender gods' have risen to take the throne above all. These pretender gods will raise armies, and fight eachother in brutal combat to ensure claiming the throne for themselves. You play as one of these pretender gods. You must claim the thrones of ascension to accomplish the goal of winning the game, however, you can also just dominate the land with your mighty armies.
How it plays:
This game plays very much like a board game. You can see the map on a birds eye scale of the world and you can move different units to different settlements in a turn based manner where they can perform different tasks. Such as, spreading your dominion (being your influential power over different areas), killing off rebel forces in nearby areas or build temples, forts and castles for extra deffensive capabilities. This game can be delightfully tactical.
Units:
There are many different units in the game. Each civilisation often has their own unique ones. But your pretender god is the most powerful a lot of the time. You can take your pretender god into battle, and it can increase the fear of your enemies more than anything which makes them more likely to flee the battle. Which is what happens a lot of the time, usually not all enemies get killed, they eventually run away. But the pretender god can be good for ensuring success in risky battles. There are then more weaker tier units you can simply use as cannon fodder, because of how cheap they are, resource wise. And then there are more powerful infantry and calvalry and as well as more powerful archer units that can be made for more resources. Different settlements may also allow you to recruit different units you can't recruit anywhere else. You can also make scouts and priests. Priests can spread dominion and scouts can swiftly move through enemy territory with ease.
Customization:
As far as customization goes, you get to choose what kind of pretender god you would like. Different civilizations have different kinds of pretender gods available, and a lot look different in their own unique ways. Also all will have different stats and abilities, but those can not be customized. You simply choose a god, give your god a name and then you get to choose the game options which there are many, as well as many different maps to play on, making the game very replayable for most I imagine. Also game options include victory conditions, difficulty and number of AI, etc...
Graphics:
This is not a game made for good or even half decent graphic design. The graphics are not that great, but that shouldn't be a problem for any gamer with a reasonably decent imagination. You play the game and as you play you can see everything that's going on inside your head and that's pretty easy to get into, and fun. If you do not have a good enough imagination the game will probably feel empty or hollow.
Learning curve:
There is a big enough learning curve at first, but things start to click into place eventually and when they do, you'll be flying through this game. There is a tutorial in this game, but for me it was quite a poor one.
On a sad note:
Diplomacy system is almost non-existent. To declare war means to attack someone. And the AI can declare war on you without even havind to attack you straight away. No sort of trade involved either, (But that seems okay.) or any kind of peace treaty can be made from what I have seen so far. Once war is declared, it goes on till one kingdom falls to the hands of the other. I wish diplomacy played a bigger role in this game it would make things a little more interesting, but then again, there can only be one winner.
Verdict:
Tons of fun to play, if you have a good imagination and don't mind bad graphics.
Steep enough learning curve, with poor tutorial.
Can be very tactical, with vast amounts of units and civilizations and different abilities for each one.
It immerses you in the story and goal to ascend to the throne above all gods.
No good diplomacy system.
More could have been added on to the soundtrack I guess, but that's my opinion. Many might disagree there.
Loads of stats and information is given throughout the game on all main units and battles are done accuratly.
Good AI from what I have seen.
All in all, it's a good game.
It's worth your time,
and can have some very epic and memorable moments.

I had high hopes for this game, but upon release I found that they were swiftly crushed.
- The games movement mechanics are awkward, most of the times I left clicked to move, my character wouldn't stop if I clicked somewhere else or targeted a monster.
- The skills are pretty but the leveling of skills is confusing, their level just seems to grow with no noticeable change in stats.
- Like many others have stated, this game is pay-to-win, you can listen to npc conversations to get points for use in special shops, but you recieve so few points compared to prices of average shop items that you have to use real cash to purchase the ingame points. (Ex. one conversation gave 3 points / some shop items are in the 10k and 100k's)
- Your character levels up and you get ATK points, which can increase damage, critical, or speed. The value changes every time you level, and the increase for the selected value is always minimal, about a 0.30% boost to attack speed, or a 0.15% boost to critical chance, or a 1 point damage boost. For now, horribly unbalanced.
- Normal items like potions aren't too terribly expensive early on, but they do require a bit of grinding to get the coins.
- I'll be honest, I had a lot more fun jumping on roof tops and sitting on the ocean floor taking screenshots than doing the quests or grinding. Your character doesn't say anything, you get narrative text that says what "you" did. (EX. "You apologize and ask for any way to make it up to her.") More or less, the conversations are just silly, one guy says his toast was going naked without the Jam you brought him. (You're a true hero.)

Portal + Metroid (NES) = Out There Somewhere.
This was a great little game, and I would have loved to have seen it last longer.  It took me about 2 hours to beat the game, but there is a marginal amount of replayability if you push for acquiring all of the Steam achievements.
The game is 2D Metroid (NES) style and is very linear, with a few optional detours for special items if you feel up to it.  Each side-scrolling screen you pass into plays out as increasingly difficult Portal-type, platforming puzzles.  Near the 2/3 mark of the game, there were perhaps 2 screens that were difficult enough that I had to cave in and check a walkthrough for and when I found the answer, it was a slap-upside-the-head DERP answer I felt like I should have obviously known, but some spots do require some brain-power, which were refreshing.
*DISCLAIMER: Everyone and their dead dog needs to buy this game while it is only 19 cents to purchase!  That being said, although it is a ton of fun, I personally would not recommend it for the full $4.99 price tag due to the overall lack of bang for your buck.*

This game is everything I have ever wanted in a short, cheap Metroidvania puzzle platformer. Don't buy it for $5, but for $0.19 it's a steal. A very cool and not at all gimmicky teleport gun mechanic, controller support, and a campaign that takes 90-120 min if you don't know what you're doing, 60-90 min to 100% if you know what you're doing, and 15-25 min to speedrun if you know what you're doing. I've played through the game start to finish about 5-7 times and I still don't have all the achievements. The collectibles are extremely fun and there's only one that I had to look up where to find it (the 11th core). All in all, I recommend this game to any fan of Metroidvania games and puzzle platformers. My only complaint is that backtracking is severely limited, but it's OK because the game is so short. Great replayability, great value, great game. 9/10.

Polarity is a below-average Portal knock-off that is childishly easy, but only made difficult in that you can’t fully remap your keyboard and mouse.
Its unique premise is that you have red and blue “polarities”, with each color reflecting the other. How this works in the game is that if you have a blue laser fence up, you have to change to the blue polarity to get past. Alternately, if the floor is blue, change to red polarity so that you can walk on it. The only real challenges are when you have to flip back-and-forth between them quickly, such as when you’re jumping on alternating colors.
The whole thing looks and feels like a college project with dreadfully simple layout, mismatched layers that caused me to continually “trip” every time I walked over a line, and simple challenges. The game features jumps but because they’re not flush with the wall, I kept getting stuck on those too.
Definitely not worth $5, and really not worth the 90% discount that I got it at. You’d do better with just about any other title.

NieR:Automata is in contention for my favorite game ever played.
Straight off, if you are the kind of 'PC Master-race' person who finds a game unplayable unless it's 8k, 300fps and multimontor compatible, then the chances are you are never going to fully appreciate Nier - even if you suck up your pride and play it.
- (On a side note, I personally play with a controller and would highly dissuade from using a keyboard.)
I love the deep, complex story and meta outlook on human society, but even if that's not your thing, Nier still offers alot.  The game starts with an incredibly cinematic action sequence, that uses forced perspective in the best way possible, before dropping you into a compact, yet well filled and expansive city.  If the first 5 hours don't have you saying 'WTF' at least 20 times, then I must be unusual.  The bizarreness of the machines keeps you on your toes consistantly, and finishing the game is simply a way of demonstrating that you've just started (i.e. 3 unique playthroughs, 5 real endings, 21 joke endings and a whole host of secret quests and characters that, after 42 hours, I'm still a ways off finishing).
Trust me when I say that the experience of NieR:Automata will redefine your preconcept of what makes a game not just good, but phenominal.
(The only real shame is the lack of merch from Squenix! XD)

This game is incredibly good at making statements about and offering commentary on the human condition, on the meaning of life. It does this masterfully, and this game stands out remarkably for it.
Expect spoilers.
There's nothing wrong with the game's other elements, whether that be it's fun, outlandish combat or it's beautiful soundtrack -- but it's really the pointed way this game draws attention to its message that makes it so great.
When I talk about message, about commentary, I'm not talking about the story as its presented explictly either. The story, too, is used as a vehicle for presenting a certain idea. To that end, it does this well, but I'm not chiefly concerned or interested in the direct fate of the characters in it.
Why is this? Well, NieR's story and its characters are very much analogues for actual human beings, and the thematic concern of the story with 'the meaning of life' is most important. So what happens to the androids '2B and 9S' isn't my care or concern, it's: What does 2B and 9S's fate tell us about how the game answers the question 'what is the meaning of life?'.
As one of my favorite critics has said, we love stories because we see ourselves in them. And it is my belief that stories and telling stories find their rightful place in telling things about us, in reflecting our own image back to ourselves -- whether it be a simple or complex message. Whether philosophical, religious, political, entertaining or humorous, stories must do this, and it is with the content of their reflection, what image the stories show of us that I am most interested.
I'll note before I continue that I did of course get the true ending, went through all the main routes, etc.
What image does NieR:Automata reflect back? What does it say about the human condition, about the meaning of life? For a good many critics, the meaninglessness of the game's world, and the way the characters face it points to existentialist (and thus pessimist) conclusions.
Another critic I admire offered his own analysis, which he said came from a Marxist and Hegelian lens. He noted the way the machines in the game all pursue their goals, their purposes with singular commitment -- whether a 'father' machine, 'older sister' machine, a religious machine, a machine committed to speed or a machine committed to love.
All of them, he noted, commit themselves to their singular purpose absolutely, but they generally tend to explode or die after finding it. He posited that the machines, like humans, were alienated from their labor, they lacked purpose just as humans can't find purpose because they don't have meaningful work.
It's an interesting thesis and it offers some insights, but I don't agree with it, likely because I don't share Marx's beliefs.
As a Catholic, the context I bring to this work is altogether something else. About a week back a figure I admire was reflecting on Ecclesiastes. The story it contains is relevant to NieR's meaning. It's about a man who had seen and done it all, he had felt real love, he had good friends, he enjoyed great meals, sexual pleasure -- everything under the sun.
Yet, he described it as 'wind chasing wind'. None of it had ever permanently satisfied him or given his heart peace -- there was a longing, an aching for a meaning the world couldn't provide. For him, this wasn't depressing, it only meant his heart longed for God, for That which he can only glimpse in this world, but wants most deeply.
Such sentiments and conclusions are often the basis of 'arguments from desire' for God's existence, that the innate desire we feel for something more, for something beyond all we can have here on Earth points to God, for innate desires point to the existence of their objects in general.
It seems that the machines of NieR and our android characters and allies are engaged in a similar quest for meaning. The machines act out their singular purposes and find them wanting, the androids fight and fight quixotically and discover, eventually, the meaninglessness of their own existence, how they are disposable to the utmost. They seek meaning, they seek something *more* and do not find.
I do not think that the game's director, Yoko Taro, necessarily means for an existentialist or nihilist conclusion with this though. One of the more notable characters, fittingly named Pascal, expresses direct disdain for Nietzsche.
At the game's initial endpoint in The Tower, these discoveries of meaninglessness issue in a bloody and sad conclusion with our characters' deaths. At our true ending, wherein all hinges upon the actions of our two support pods, 042 and 153, we find a rather remarkable action of faith. They find that the expected conclusion: the death of all androids, has completed. Thus, they can continue with the next phase of their project with the construction of new combat models.
However, something in both pods rejects this, they too, can't find a satisfactory meaning in continuing to act out their function. Flatly, Pod 042 states, 'I have come to the conclusion that I cannot accept this resolution'. So, they decide to rebuild 2B, 9S, and A2. Importantly, one asks the other if the same events could play out again, if all this could come to naught. The same conclusions reached. Plainly, what if they still cannot find the meaning they so long for, that all long for?
Pod 042 replies, saying 'I cannot deny the possibility. However, the possibility of a different future also exists'.
Again, I cannot help as a Catholic but see a certain meaning in this. To rebuild the androids, with the same memories, with the same parts, knowing what will likely happen, what conclusions of meaninglessness it will likely issue in, to do it anyway -- what a beautiful act of faith that is!
It says: 'I see the meaninglessness in all that has been pursued and sought up to this point, and they could pursue them again and still find nothing -- but I believe there is 'something' more to be found despite that.
Understanding the machines, pods and androids as analogues for human beings once more, it says that we too act out our lives and find our activities and goals enjoyable, and yet wanting in the end, the longing in our hearts for that 'more' unsatisfied. Yet, we believe there is That which we cannot find.
I don't mean to argue that Yoko Taro is making an explicit 'argument from desire' for God's existence, absolutely not, only that the story grants a beautiful reflection of human faith in finding meaning and of that desire so innate to us.
While not explicit, I must thus tenuously posit that the essence of the game does represent a sort of subtle, implicit argument from desire. I think that's beautiful.
Thus, the story's conclusion issues in a final act of faith in finding some future meaning and not, as some others think, meaninglessness or in 'finding your own meaning'.
This game masterfully expresses its meanings and messages, and for that reason I wholly recommend it. I haven't done its other elements justice here (the soundtrack is one of the best in any game), only discussed that which stood out most to me.
Thanks for reading!

This game is really close to being great in my opinion, but as it currently stands, I can't really reccomend it.
The game suffers from a couple major problems in my opinion. The first is that the risk reward ratio of robbing a house generally just isn't worth it. If you really commit to trying to make it through a house, you are far more likely to die than you are to make it through, the survival rates on most the listed houses back this up. The fact that you will fail to rob the house is not the problem however, the problem is how harshly you are punished for failing. You lose everything, your house, your money, Everything, and have to start the game over from scratch. Because of this, nobody ever wants to try to rob anyone else once they have a decent amount of money and a house established. 99% of the people who try to rob you have just started a new character and have not yet invested any time in building their own defenses (you can tell they are brand new because they are only worth $200 bounty if they die to one of your traps). The strategy tends to be to spawn a new character, spend the starting $2000 on robbery gear, and try to rob a house that has around $10k and build your house with the money. After that you don't rob houses anymore and you just sit back and watch people try to rob you.
If the game were to make failure less punishing I think things could be a lot more interesting. I do think having permadeath in the game is probably a good idea because it leads to people building new traps and whatnot, but I don't think permadeath should be the punishment for your first failure.
I think that with each death players should have to pay an increasing sum of money, starting low but working up to large amounts, and if they can't pay then they suffer permanent death of their current character. Perhaps the amount increment would drop over time as well so you never reached a point where the cost was so high a character would never try to rob a house again.
I'm not sure my suggestion is the perfect solution, but I really do feel that the game would be considerably more fun if players other than brand new characters were trying to commit robberies as well.

Say your name is John Smith. You design the perfect house to the best of your abilities. You step out into the world, you die two steps in because you haven't figured out the dog movement AI yet. No-one even got to see your house.
Say you're John Smith XII. You design the same perfect house. You google saving layouts in this game and find nothing. So you painstakingly make the same house again so you can see how it does. Stealing at this point seems too great a risk at any stage unless you are Batman. Still, you are lured in by another player's clever design, and ofcourse die.
Say you're John Smith XXXIV. You build an even better house, using your very original clever design to lure people in. It works! People die and drop their cash for you! You find indescribable, truly divine joy as you laugh maniacally at the security tapes and truly know what it is to be an evil genius. And so you add another wing to your dungeon, now it is even more dangerous... Then some rich ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with 3-5k (a substantial amount) of cash comes and... he dies and drops it! The feeling is indescribable. Only now your vault is actually worth something and you can't go back in because it's currently being robbed. And it turns out, it was Batman. As soon as you get a bit of money in this game, Batman is going to come and get you, and maybe you could stop him if only you could have spent some of that 3-5k cash on a better house...
Say you're Phonix111186. You write a review which you're still not sure is positive or negative, but you're sure there are possible improvements implied. Then you go back for more. The truth is, Batman eventually comes for all of us, we all have to live with that eventuality. Perhaps one day, if I get really good at this, I could be Batman. But as Liam Neeson once said, "There is always a bigger Batman." There is no 100% completion.

The game's concept is very interesting, and is what drew me in at first. I bought this game expecting to build a fortress to defend my wife, and my money. Little did I realize that 95% of your time is spent building your fortress. Don't get me wrong, this is the most fun part of the game, building your house. But in the time that I've played, about an hour or so, I find myself not building new designs, but repeating the same design. Why? Because if you die to your own design, you have to start all over. Now, permadeath is great and all, but it's really frustrating to "test" your own home and be killed by some flaw you overlooked, and have to restart. From scratch. The game is tedious, frustrating and incredibley boring. I've spent no time even invading another house, because I was testing mine.
The worst thing about this game so far though, is that when you complete a test of your house, it immediately makes it available for people to rob. This means that if you were testing with lights and chihuahas, then you're basically screwed. So you lose a couple hundred bucks, right? No big deal. Wrong. Then you don't have enough money to put grates in your house. And since you will just repeatedly get robbed, have no other choice but to commit suicide.
Again, I stress, the concept is very interesting and would be a fantastic idea for a video game... Sadly, this game just doesn't hit the mark. I only reccomend this game if you have nothing better to spend $12 on.

NieR:Automata is in contention for my favorite game ever played.
Straight off, if you are the kind of 'PC Master-race' person who finds a game unplayable unless it's 8k, 300fps and multimontor compatible, then the chances are you are never going to fully appreciate Nier - even if you suck up your pride and play it.
- (On a side note, I personally play with a controller and would highly dissuade from using a keyboard.)
I love the deep, complex story and meta outlook on human society, but even if that's not your thing, Nier still offers alot.  The game starts with an incredibly cinematic action sequence, that uses forced perspective in the best way possible, before dropping you into a compact, yet well filled and expansive city.  If the first 5 hours don't have you saying 'WTF' at least 20 times, then I must be unusual.  The bizarreness of the machines keeps you on your toes consistantly, and finishing the game is simply a way of demonstrating that you've just started (i.e. 3 unique playthroughs, 5 real endings, 21 joke endings and a whole host of secret quests and characters that, after 42 hours, I'm still a ways off finishing).
Trust me when I say that the experience of NieR:Automata will redefine your preconcept of what makes a game not just good, but phenominal.
(The only real shame is the lack of merch from Squenix! XD)

This game is incredibly good at making statements about and offering commentary on the human condition, on the meaning of life. It does this masterfully, and this game stands out remarkably for it.
Expect spoilers.
There's nothing wrong with the game's other elements, whether that be it's fun, outlandish combat or it's beautiful soundtrack -- but it's really the pointed way this game draws attention to its message that makes it so great.
When I talk about message, about commentary, I'm not talking about the story as its presented explictly either. The story, too, is used as a vehicle for presenting a certain idea. To that end, it does this well, but I'm not chiefly concerned or interested in the direct fate of the characters in it.
Why is this? Well, NieR's story and its characters are very much analogues for actual human beings, and the thematic concern of the story with 'the meaning of life' is most important. So what happens to the androids '2B and 9S' isn't my care or concern, it's: What does 2B and 9S's fate tell us about how the game answers the question 'what is the meaning of life?'.
As one of my favorite critics has said, we love stories because we see ourselves in them. And it is my belief that stories and telling stories find their rightful place in telling things about us, in reflecting our own image back to ourselves -- whether it be a simple or complex message. Whether philosophical, religious, political, entertaining or humorous, stories must do this, and it is with the content of their reflection, what image the stories show of us that I am most interested.
I'll note before I continue that I did of course get the true ending, went through all the main routes, etc.
What image does NieR:Automata reflect back? What does it say about the human condition, about the meaning of life? For a good many critics, the meaninglessness of the game's world, and the way the characters face it points to existentialist (and thus pessimist) conclusions.
Another critic I admire offered his own analysis, which he said came from a Marxist and Hegelian lens. He noted the way the machines in the game all pursue their goals, their purposes with singular commitment -- whether a 'father' machine, 'older sister' machine, a religious machine, a machine committed to speed or a machine committed to love.
All of them, he noted, commit themselves to their singular purpose absolutely, but they generally tend to explode or die after finding it. He posited that the machines, like humans, were alienated from their labor, they lacked purpose just as humans can't find purpose because they don't have meaningful work.
It's an interesting thesis and it offers some insights, but I don't agree with it, likely because I don't share Marx's beliefs.
As a Catholic, the context I bring to this work is altogether something else. About a week back a figure I admire was reflecting on Ecclesiastes. The story it contains is relevant to NieR's meaning. It's about a man who had seen and done it all, he had felt real love, he had good friends, he enjoyed great meals, sexual pleasure -- everything under the sun.
Yet, he described it as 'wind chasing wind'. None of it had ever permanently satisfied him or given his heart peace -- there was a longing, an aching for a meaning the world couldn't provide. For him, this wasn't depressing, it only meant his heart longed for God, for That which he can only glimpse in this world, but wants most deeply.
Such sentiments and conclusions are often the basis of 'arguments from desire' for God's existence, that the innate desire we feel for something more, for something beyond all we can have here on Earth points to God, for innate desires point to the existence of their objects in general.
It seems that the machines of NieR and our android characters and allies are engaged in a similar quest for meaning. The machines act out their singular purposes and find them wanting, the androids fight and fight quixotically and discover, eventually, the meaninglessness of their own existence, how they are disposable to the utmost. They seek meaning, they seek something *more* and do not find.
I do not think that the game's director, Yoko Taro, necessarily means for an existentialist or nihilist conclusion with this though. One of the more notable characters, fittingly named Pascal, expresses direct disdain for Nietzsche.
At the game's initial endpoint in The Tower, these discoveries of meaninglessness issue in a bloody and sad conclusion with our characters' deaths. At our true ending, wherein all hinges upon the actions of our two support pods, 042 and 153, we find a rather remarkable action of faith. They find that the expected conclusion: the death of all androids, has completed. Thus, they can continue with the next phase of their project with the construction of new combat models.
However, something in both pods rejects this, they too, can't find a satisfactory meaning in continuing to act out their function. Flatly, Pod 042 states, 'I have come to the conclusion that I cannot accept this resolution'. So, they decide to rebuild 2B, 9S, and A2. Importantly, one asks the other if the same events could play out again, if all this could come to naught. The same conclusions reached. Plainly, what if they still cannot find the meaning they so long for, that all long for?
Pod 042 replies, saying 'I cannot deny the possibility. However, the possibility of a different future also exists'.
Again, I cannot help as a Catholic but see a certain meaning in this. To rebuild the androids, with the same memories, with the same parts, knowing what will likely happen, what conclusions of meaninglessness it will likely issue in, to do it anyway -- what a beautiful act of faith that is!
It says: 'I see the meaninglessness in all that has been pursued and sought up to this point, and they could pursue them again and still find nothing -- but I believe there is 'something' more to be found despite that.
Understanding the machines, pods and androids as analogues for human beings once more, it says that we too act out our lives and find our activities and goals enjoyable, and yet wanting in the end, the longing in our hearts for that 'more' unsatisfied. Yet, we believe there is That which we cannot find.
I don't mean to argue that Yoko Taro is making an explicit 'argument from desire' for God's existence, absolutely not, only that the story grants a beautiful reflection of human faith in finding meaning and of that desire so innate to us.
While not explicit, I must thus tenuously posit that the essence of the game does represent a sort of subtle, implicit argument from desire. I think that's beautiful.
Thus, the story's conclusion issues in a final act of faith in finding some future meaning and not, as some others think, meaninglessness or in 'finding your own meaning'.
This game masterfully expresses its meanings and messages, and for that reason I wholly recommend it. I haven't done its other elements justice here (the soundtrack is one of the best in any game), only discussed that which stood out most to me.
Thanks for reading!

I really wanted to enjoy this game, but I'm just unable to get past its flaws. It's a fun little puzzle game, with nice level design, but suffers from numerous issues that would lead me to avoid recommending it.
First off, this it's a really bad console port. The options are practically useless. I'm unable to change my controls, or adjust the visuals besides monitor resolution. The keyboard/mouse support isn't well implemented either.
To make this worse, around one third of the game is the multiplayer campaign, which isn't even playable. The game only supports local split-screen. It has absolutely no network support, not even over LAN. This effectively takes out a massive chunk of the game.
To top it all off, the game feels very clunky, and isn't terribly interesting either. You end up spending most of your time playing just trying to move around the stages, as opposed to actually solving the puzzles. This game could've been great, but because of the oversight of the developpers, it really doesn't feel like a complete game.

Dominions 4 is a Dungeon and Dragons guy's dream strategy game.
You play as a Demigod, which can be a Manticore, an Antlion, a Cyclops, a Mummy, a Gorgon, a Dragon, a wide variety of Lich types or even as Dagon, Scorpion King or the Sphinx (or about a hundred other options)
Your worshippers can be Lizardmen, Centaurs, Deep Ones, Ghosts, Troglodytes, Demons, Oni, Spider-Riders, Harpies, Hydras, Illithids (Mind Flayers), Minotaurs, Naga, Satyr, many many more. There are 82 playable races. Yes, eighty-two.
The magic system is rich and highly customizable, with zillions of interesting spells. You can play each race many different ways depending on your magic decisions (did I mention there's 82 races?). Also, you can cast spells that create Gelatinous Cubes.
If you ever enjoyed reading the Monster Manual, you will love this game,

I was told I do too many negative reviews.
So I decided that all of the games I own Dominons 4 is the most deserving of reccomendation.
Dominions 4 is a game made by two devs who have worked on every iteration of Dominions.
Unlike many games which release and then charge you for additional content Dominions 4 recieves patches for new nations and units, FOR ABSOLUTELY FREE.
-------------GAMEPLAY-------------------
The gameplay is a turned based military management, strategy and tactic based game.
You have a Pretender God, the choices available depend on your nation.
Your pretender God is basically a demi-god who is trying to become the only God for the world as the big G that came before dissapeared.
You can then modify your Pretender God with magic scales which is representative of the gods magical skill. These scales also determine bless amounts which are bonuses given to holy units, which each nation has.
There is also Dominion which given it shares the name with the game is one of the most important aspects. Dominion is the Pretender God's influence, without it your God will die and you will be subjected to other Gods dominion which brings a morale detriment for you and a postive boost for morale for your enemies.
You can take negative dominions traits like chaos or death or positive ones like magic or growth. Depending on the nation some will be postive for some while harmful to others, for example MA Ulm benefits from drain and Ermor benefits from Death.
Winning conditions can be point based, deathmatch or my favorite Thrones of Ascension which are thrones of varying power that have an effect on provinces, dominion and gems.
Magic is fueld by Gems and much be researched to be usable.
Some spells require no gems but only effect Fatigue while others do. There are spells which have in battle effect and spells which can be used on the map to summon units, or attack provinces.
----------------Setting----------------------
The setting of Dominions 4 is amazing, each Nation changes based on the age its in.
Some dissapear other change dramatically.
Xibalba goes from a nation of Bat people to a nation of Frog people who enslave the Bat people.
Rlyeh goes from a nation of mindfrying fish called Aboleths into Squid people loosely based on Lovercraft who summon horrors from beyond to use as BLESSED units.
Some nations like R'lyeh that I mentioned are sea based as they start in ocean provinces and all units are able to breathe underwater.
Nations have diffrent spells which all come with their own flavor text describing the spell and its origins and value to the people who cast it.
----------------Music & Sound-----------------
Do not expect an epic soundtrack, one song and one song only, that goes on forever.
Sounds are good not great but indicate what is going on and are quite good when using iron blizzard in masse and hearing enemy splat noises.
-------------------Maps------------------------
The game comes packaged with quite a few high quality maps, there is also the ability to make random maps however they don't look the greatest.
However the game does have a very simplified map creation tool, and quite a few maps have been made for DOM 4 or converted from Dom 3.
One of my favorite maps is called Valanis and is quite beautiful visually and mechanically.
----------------------Performance----------------------
The performance is sex.
On a crappy lenova laptop which I use for work mainly is able to run the game and with most graphical options turned off can simulate very large battles which is impressive seeing as my laptop lacks a seperate video card.
My rig at home is a monster but even with a toaster with mild specs the game will run wonderfully.
One of the best aspects of the game as I enjoy being able to take my work laptop up with me on trips and being able to play the game without lugging my Tower around with me.
I highly recommend Dominions 4 for anyone looking for a great Tactics and Strategy game with a fantasy flair.

If you buy the cheaper Dominions 3 and like it youre only going to end up buying this after a while anyway.

After hours of playing, I realized the biggest flaws of the game. First of all, it's extremely unbalanced and the starting money the game gives you is absolutely not enough. The game itself begins on a cool concept, but a tremendous amount of mistakes makes it barely playable. And even for the few people who will manage to play it correctly, it won't even be fun for a long time... Last but not least, the game is 15€ ! I know it's still not really high if you compare it to some high-priced games today, but those high-priced games at least can give some fun for more time ! With that money, you could buy much, much better games.
While the developers surely had tons of very interesting ideas, once those ideas went into the actual game, it all became a huge mess and surely isn't at all what the developers did intend to do. When I feel like a game disappointed me so much that I wish I never bought it, that's a pretty bad sign, because that's very rare. And I felt that with The Castle Doctrine. I just feel like I wasted money, that's how frustrated it makes me after hours of playing !
Also, usually, a lot of games have a single player mode. While this game directly states it's going to be multiplayer only, when a game doesn't have a single player mode, then the multiplayer one really has to be ace. Seeing how this one is flawed and frustrating (and not for good reasons), it doesn't justify spending "so much" (for a minimalistic game, I mean) money into it.
When I say it's not frustrating for the good reasons, let me explain. In a game like Dark Souls for instance, when you die, it's frustrating. While you lose your souls (the money and experience of the game, which is very important), you do not lose your whole character, meaning that there is an overall progression that can be hindered by those deaths if you are not careful enough, but at least, in addition of being frustrating, it's rewarding. In the Castle Doctrine, I never felt rewarded at any point, even after robbing a high-valued house successfully. Because I could barely make myself a decent defense (and seeing how many griefers there are in the game, it barely counts unless you are REALLY rich)
How to sum-up if you didn't felt like reading all of this ? Frustrating and not rewarding, boring, expensive for such a minimalistic game, and the game doesn't match up to the concept. Definitely, I couldn't recommend it to anyone. Watching videos of it and looking at the concept is just filling your head with illusions, seriously.
