I have played this game for 21 hours so far... I give it a 5/10. Please read on to find out why!
At first, the game starts out very cool. You're new to everything. There are a lot of tiles to play with. The best way to learn how to make something, is to venture into someone else's house and die. "Clever..." you think to yourself, "I'll use that trap!"
After awhile, you learn how things work, so you set off to create your own house. With $2000 starting cash, you don't have a lot to work with. You don't want to spend too much making your house, because the left over money will be what people see, and they won't bother to take the time to try and beat your security for a measly $250-$500.
Really, you only have $600-$800 to spend to make sure you attract burglars. Not much in fact. A guard dog costs you around $300. Electrical stuff is cheaper though.
If you decide to venture out and attack others, you can buy tools to help you. The tools let you bypass specific types of security measures. Run into a dog? Use one of your sleep-laden-dog treats. Be careful though, you only have as many as you purchased. And other things like that. Every trap component has a counter of some sort.
If you attack someone's house, and decide that their design is just something you won't beat, and you will die trying, you can leave through the front door. However, if you do so, you forfeit all items you purchased to help you break in successfully. If you happen to make it all the way to their safe, you get money, but that is money minus what you spent on tools to make it there. Generally, one way or another, attacking another player, who understands how the game works (which everyone does sooner or later) will end up costing you money because it is hard to break into a decent house without tools.
If you happen to become successful a few times, and have built yourself a little stash of money, or you're fortunate enough to have some people attack you and die trying, you will then have enough money to start building some really cool traps. The side-effect of building your own nice house though, you stop attacking others. You won't be looking to die turning some corner 10 seconds into a robbery and then have to start over completely.
When you're poor at the start, spend $1000 for tools, and attack a house with $3000. You will come away with more than you started, though it may take you 20 tries to do so. A  bit tedious. When you're rich, or you've built your house, never attack anyone again.
This game really has a lot of cool concepts.
1. Permadeath is really neat because it gives you a good risk-reward factor.
2. The traps and tiles you can place add a lot of variety and allow you to create some really cool things.
3. All houses are user-created
4. You get to solve puzzles, one section at a time (through fog-of-war, you only see what your character can see)
5. The more successful you are, the more you can build.
1. Expect to lose, lose, lose, and lose. There really is no way to win. You will die eventually, no way around it, unless you get so much money that you can build an entire fortress within your walls. But then at that point, there is no reason to even play the game any more. You don't want to risk venturing out and losing everything. Your money keeps growing because people want to get a piece of it.
2. You cannot build, what you want, how you want, until you have enough money to do so.
3. The risk of getting money at the start is very high.
4. All houses are user-created. This is generally a good thing. Player made content is fun. However, because of the high risk-reward of the core design of the game, you will see the same cheap and easily duplicated puzzles that without spending lots of money on tools to destroy the house itself, you can never beat.
5. There are some bad UI design flaws that hurt you. Want to review how someone attacked your house? You can do so, but while you are reviewing, others may attack you. If you have a lot of money in your house, it may be impossible for you to get in it to fix what others have broken, or even change the design. You cannot even look at your house while it is being broken into. I constantly have the problem of attack after attack without being able to get in my house and fix things.
6. No way to save/load your design. You can use an online builder to create and save a design, but you will be reconstructing it in the game piece-by-piece, no zooming in or out to get the big picture.
But this game executes these great concepts poorly. It may be that that all of these concepts are actually executed well by this game, but all of these concepts put together just do not work well.
The game gives you a great feeling at the start, it's a lot of fun to explore it all. But once you see how it all works, it's like discovering who the Wizard of Oz really is. You'll be handicapped at the start to try and make money so that you can design a cool intricate puzzle that in all reality, only you could ever solve on the first try.
So what is the point? Where is all the fun? It's not here. Once more people get tired of the game, and I honestly think they will, the game will fade. It's been stated by the creator it will never, ever, again be on sale. At a cheaper price than it is, say 75% off, lots of players could be introduced to it that would get a kick out of it for awhile, and give the die-hard-masochist fan base some fresh meat to play with, but without it.....dead game

This game has an amazing concept that is close to working, with a few problems. Imagine this, a game where you design base defenses and attack other player's defenses, and if you die (either on your own or the other players... yes you need to navigate your own defenses) you start completely over.
It's a really fun game, but the problem is how you get money, by having people attack your base or attacking other people. To be any degree of safe you need to buy items to go attack people, which costs money (that you don't have in the beginning). If your base gets raided you lose half your money and all your items (which consists of most of the money if you are killing people with your defenses). People will also attack you when you are logged off. The amount of items people will bring as well as their commitment to attacking is based on how much money you have, so you need a powerful enough defense to defend against the level of player willing to attack you. This takes constant monitoring because if you don't return to your house every so often, the money value will increase past the level of defenses and people will destroy your house and you will be worse than square one.
So I would only recommend this game if you want to constantly monitor and be wary of your house, as this escalation will continue even when you try to 'log out'. It was fun for a while, but after I realize there was no way to 'turn off' the game to take a break from it, you can't play this game unless you're willing to commit.
Here is an example of what the game plays like----------
This is how I got a really super powerful house, and how I lost it:
I got lucky and broke into several low level houses with a couple low level items, and got enough money to make a fairly powerful house. I sat this house at the ~3k value range (by spending all excess money on improvements) allowing people to continually die and upgrading every 30 minutes. You need to continually upgrade to keep the value lower and prevent people from breaking in with more items.
Once the house was powerful enough I sat it at the ~30k value range - people were now breaking in with a LOT of items, but my house could stand up to them! Well, after several hours of letting people break in and upgrading I logged out - thinking this would make my house inaccessible - and went to sleep. Later that day I logged in and found my house has reached  over 300k value (woah), but someone broke in and stole everything, leaving me with half my cash money which was around 3k gold (most the value was in items), and also having to fix all the destruction to my house (which stays when someone is successful). After fixing the problems I had 300 gold left, which does not attract anyone to break in and die.
Since I had no money to invest in items and noone was dying I tried raiding low level houses without items, but most of the ones I ran into were ones similar to mine, obviously a lot of money was sunk into them but they had very little cash reserves likely due to someone raiding them.
I ended up dying by accidentally walking to my own pit in my own house after trying to make my house easier to break into to tempt lower level players... time to start over.
-----
Every time I start to get the ball rolling I hit a random snag here or there: someone finds a way to break traps I didn't think about, I accidentally fall for a trap I think I'm being safe about, I accidentally die in my own house due to having to run my entire defenses every time I make a change, etc.
Each snag does make me a better player, but also makes me have to start over again... and without good luck (or maybe a friend who can go die in your house) getting that ball rolling is difficult.

I loved this game for about... an hour or so, because it was new and interesting, but playing it for 15 hours allowed me to see everything.
If you gear up, enter a house and leave through the same door you walked in, you lose all of your tools. Amazingly unrealistic there. A powered door cost $240, while the crowbar to circumvent that powered door costs $2400. Pricing is terrible in this game. Drugged/unconscious pit bulls will kill you if you step over them again.
The most common types of houses are:
Players creating intricate mazes that only they know the path for. Causing you to run through and commit to paths from the very beginning, only to find out after you've committed to several paths, that you actually took the wrong one. So you die, lose your house, and any tools you had go bye-bye.
Houses with multiple-multiple-multiple-multiple choice paths for you to choose. Also forcing you to commit with each turn, once again only to find out that you've gone down the wrong path. You die again, lose your house, and lose your tools.
Combination locks. !@#$ing EVERYWHERE!!! We're going to force you to commit(again) by passing this powered door, pressing this button and the powered door closes behind you. Then have you guess a 6-12 digit combination, ALL of which are sticky pressure plates which are surrounded by concrete and steel walls... everywhere. You're not getting out. You might as well suicide.
Entering a house(which has very little money as far as the list is concerned). The house seems cheap, being mostly wood and all. Force you to commit down a certain path only to find out a few steps later that there's steel and concrete everywhere. Well !@#$. This could be fixed by using smaller houses and the camera staying centered on your character.
When you see the same garbage everywhere, and everyone pretty much does the same thing just because it's 'that' effective... it kind of sucks the fun out of the game for everyone except for those watching the 'security tapes' and laughing their asses off at anyone attempting to rob them and dying.
Lack of the ability to save a layout in the game for a $1000-1500 layout that works until you get a little more money. The  inability to sell your current house objects once you've proved your house was 'fair'. The camera does not stay centered on your character and some people take advantage of this.
I'm sure everyone who buys a game expects a certain amount of fun to frustration ratio. This game has been %10 fun to %90 frustration.
The player-base is going to suffer hardcore with or without sales.
Why?
There are going to be players with a ton of money, and no one trying to rob them because you have no new players and you don't make the game fun enough to keep playing. Or simply because everyone is afraid to lose all of their high value stuff by dying. This will cause a stalemate in the game between any of the high value players.
If someone whom has a ton of money tries to rob someone and dies or someone actually manages to rob them, they're going to stop playing because they don't care to take the incredible amount of time and effort to build up their castle like they did previously.
But hey, what do I know. I'm just another guy with an opinion. I want my money back, and I want this game off of my Steam library just as much as Dogfighter.

If you're looking for a massively multiplayer online role playing game? I wouldn't waste my time and bandwidth.

I can only recommend this game at the price I got it at, $0.19. At that price, it's well worth it. At the price listed, it's really not.
The game throws you onto an alien world in a story that tries to be more than it is. If this game is part of a series, something would be explained, but on its own it is unremarkable. The big hook to the game is that you have a teleporting gun that allows you to warp to wherever you hit with the gun. You retain your momentum, so much like Portal you encounter some interesting puzzles. The puzzles are seldom difficult, with the only real difficulty coming from the imprescision you deal with. Occasionally you'll encounter something where you have to think in order to proceed, but I got through these by just shooting and somehow ending up where I needed to be.
There is a secondary weapon that damages enemies as well. It was a good choice to introduce this weapon, as it does introduce some variety in the gameplay. However, the weapon never quite "feels" right. It's hard to explain. Combat, for what there is of it, feels frustrating, especially when you fail later in the room and have to do it over again. Still, having the gun does add to the gameplay.
When you die, you respawn quickly. This is good since you will want to try again quickly, but sometimes it can lead to you dying 2 or 3 times in a row because you're still moving when you spawn. This futher compounds the difficulty of a particularly tough puzzle.
The game lasts about 45 minutes. I enjoyed most of my time with it, and there are some interesting obstacles introduced throughout, but I did find myself wishing things would get mixed up a little more towards the end, or just wanting the game to end.
Overall, there's a lot of potential here. The teleporter gun brings some neat ideas, and the environments are well built around the mechanic. And it's worth the price at 96% off. It's a nice little game, that shows that the developer has a lot of upward potential for their next games.

NieR:Automata is in contention for my favorite game ever played.
Straight off, if you are the kind of 'PC Master-race' person who finds a game unplayable unless it's 8k, 300fps and multimontor compatible, then the chances are you are never going to fully appreciate Nier - even if you suck up your pride and play it.
- (On a side note, I personally play with a controller and would highly dissuade from using a keyboard.)
I love the deep, complex story and meta outlook on human society, but even if that's not your thing, Nier still offers alot.  The game starts with an incredibly cinematic action sequence, that uses forced perspective in the best way possible, before dropping you into a compact, yet well filled and expansive city.  If the first 5 hours don't have you saying 'WTF' at least 20 times, then I must be unusual.  The bizarreness of the machines keeps you on your toes consistantly, and finishing the game is simply a way of demonstrating that you've just started (i.e. 3 unique playthroughs, 5 real endings, 21 joke endings and a whole host of secret quests and characters that, after 42 hours, I'm still a ways off finishing).
Trust me when I say that the experience of NieR:Automata will redefine your preconcept of what makes a game not just good, but phenominal.

This review is in reference to all episodes before "FINAL ROUND" and that episode itself:
It is KOF the anime. It isn't better or worse than a regular anime. It does a great job of retelling the classic KOF stories while keeping this interesting while also adding some necessary changes to ensure the series stays exciting and encorporates most classic KOF characters.
It is really good if you play KOF but have no idea why the characters are fighting and if you don't want to sit through blocks of text on wikis to know your favorite character.
However, as I have to point out, I have an unique taste for media so my review may not apply to you. If you like shows like TMNT(2012) or Steven Universe and you play the KOF games, you'll definitely like this. However, if you are trying to get into KOF with this and you haven't actually played the games or you have actual expectations when you go into watching animes, I don't think this is for you. Animation is stiff('Cause motion cature) and fight screens aren't that exciting. The fights consist of people just punching each other, punching a bunch of mideless dudes, and shouting names of iconic attacks to make their opponent die.
The story here is great! The characters don't feel stereotypical nor boring. I will admit some of the characters don't feel too important. In all the episodes I watched, I bet you would only care about your favorite character(mine is Benimeru), Terry Bogard, Geese Howard, Kyo, and maybe Angelina(I didn't care about her because she lacked a distinct or unique personality, but she is very relivant to the plot). Everyone else feels like they're just... there. The other characters don't feel like a waste of time though, as they do have very humorous moments. Especially Kensou, Daimon, Ryo... and BENIMERU.
Also, the anime will force you to get used to it's flaws. It's possible, but hard. Listening to those stock sound effects, awkward character models(when compared to the games. Characters look more generic and less cartoony), and episodes that feel like they waste your time are issues very apparent.
In the future, I hope character models get reworked to resemble how the KOF fighters appear in their games... sprite games. KOF 14 looks awful to me. I prefer how KOF13 protrayed characters in it's artwork.
I'd give this a 6.5/10. It is kinda below average, but it is KOF afterall! I hope characters involved with NESTS*(Kula... and K' and folks like that), cammeo characters, or even Takuma... 'cause who doesn't LOVE Takuma... show up.
I primarily watch this only for the humor and lore. Some of the scenes... intension or not... make me laugh so hard. Intensional jokes include Clark having a smoking problem, Kensou not understanding Chin's advice, Mai scolding Joe instead of Andy for seemily no reason(and Joe being aware of this), Angelina... almost getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm an awful person), Mai making Yuri feel envious of her-, and Benimeru's dialouge+existence. Some unintensional jokes consisent of Terry Bogurd having heavy similarities to Ryu, voice acting(despite being in Japanese, some lines feel completely destroyed), VFX being prettier than everything else, classic tv tropes, names of certain characters(Clark Still and Geese Howard were gold mines for joke. "Clark still has that on his birth certificate?" "Jeff Bogurd died! Shouldn't have been messing with the Geese." ), some stiff movements, Mortal Kombat similarities, and suggestive dialouge(some intensional, some not).
So just freakin' watch it. You read all of my crap for nothing actually. It's good. Just watch it, especially if you have a huge sense of humor.

Polarity is an interesting little puzzle game where your interaction with each object is determined by you or the object's polarity (Red or Blue). Those who have played Portal will feel at home in this game with it's familiar Aperture Science chamber design and art style. The game doesn't have a lot in terms of story, which is perfect for this game because it keeps the game moving smoothly. You won't be stopping to hear character dialogue or any of that other nonsense.
In general, the game feels very arcade styled. it moves fast enough to be interesting, but it's not fast enough to leave the player struggling to keep up with new mechanics.
I can say much about the multiplayer mode due it being LAN only. I did look around in some of the multiplayer gamemodes though.One of them is almost like a race to complete a certain puzzle, which would be a lot of fun if players could use Steam Multiplayer instead of being stuck with only LAN.
Overall, I found the game to be worth the price and I would reccomend it to anyone who is fan of Puzzle Games.

Familiar Rail Slave elements (resource management, mix of genres, 80s-style die and try again) but this time it's in a fixed world that you'll have to spend some time exploring before you're ready to try and do "winning runs". This seems to be by design - your gameplay time will be split up between the exploration phase (which isn't just trying stuff out but also learning where each of the colored tapes are!) and then the runs which can be a bit more frustrating to die. The gameplay is definitely the sort that seems really hard and slowly gets easier; my main complaint while playing was that the shmup combat seemed disproportionately hard to the hand-to-hand combat (with the former being what you get launched into for failing the latter) but over time I got good enough to find it fun too.
Like most rail slave stories there are some very interesting ideas but not that much in the way of resolution. Still a pretty interesting game. Price might seem a little high, this is a pseudo-vignette, but dev didn't have control over that so.
I guess my favorite part was meeting each person for the first time, sadly besides talking to them initially and giving them the tape there's not much else to them. The world of the game is very intriguing but because of that you won't really get too much of a feel for it, or unlock new places. But a small world to master is very 80s-gameplay-style, so that's how the game wanted to be.
My favorite RSG are Uriel's Chasm and Selfie. I guess I like FMV. So while this wasn't in my favorites of the dev, that's just my personal taste, still an interesting work and it and the rest of the dev's games really deserve some analysis.

So love this game.
I have a penchant for mythological structures and this game explores many aspects thereof. That aside though, it is a novel strategy game in its play and dynamics with an intensly diverse set of creatures and a fair breadth of spell effects (there are a ton of spells and overland spells [rituals] but many are variants on a similar theme, leaving still a lot of variation amidst a ton of spells).
As well, the coop function of having other players be your disciple was well executed and a great way to allow for a grander style of co-op playing.
In all, if you enjoy multiple dynamics in a conquering turn-based game then this is a great game to snag. I have played it so many ways with a wide mix of friends and enjoyed it every time and still find new things to marvel at.

This might be The best strategy game I have ever played. Can recommend to anyone looking for good strategy game with fantasy twist.
Amount of lore is epic - I have spent hours just reading manual and planning how to play with different nations, gods and dominions settings.
Game is complex but still easy to start; even if you can't remember all spell effects and such - usually everything makes sense. Casting storm makes it hard to fly in combat, or shoot arrows. Rain will cause more fatigue to casters using fire magic.
Moving in world map is turn based and battles are resolved automatically, you just set unit formations and script spells for mages (not necessery, AI does mostly good job). Watching these battles after each turn is probably best way to learn game mechanics.
You can see stats for all units and there are many. Units gets older and old age makes you more vulnerable to diseases and injuries. Off course this in not issue if your units are demons or undead. or lifeless.
I have played this since Dom III and AI is constantly getting better. It gives very good challenge, even though there are tactics it cannot counter well. There are many very different nations and tons of units, but game is still well balanced.
Micromanagement with end game and large maps can be issue, especially with blood nations. Much of this depends how you play. If you have lots of commanders with equipped items, supply chain managament can take time.

Geez....what can I say about Dominions 4? Let's start with the ingredient list:
1. A bunch of hand drawn cartoonish maps
2. Tons of tiny, simple pixel sprites
3. A battle animation sequence that looks like it comes from an overheated Nintendo in 1989
4. The best sountrack you'll ever hear in a PC game
5. Crack
Mix all these together and, oddly enough, you end up with one of the most satisfying strategy games I've ever experienced. Maybe it's the stunning amount of content, literally hundreds of spells, weapons, and items. There are tons of unique races, each with their own developed lore and play style. You create your own customized pretender god and lead your pixel hordes to world conquest, spreading your religion and snuffing out belief in any god other than you.
The game's learning curve seems intimidating. The tutorial requires you to read the manual while you play, which is weird and off-putting; but if you do it, you'll be proficiently navigating the interface in no time.
It's a storyteller's game that will spark your imagination, and occupy your thoughts long after you shut your computer off.

This is hands down the best strategy game I have ever played. I got started with gaming on Age of Empires 1 and Starcraft. RTS and turn based strategy games have been some of my favorite genre's for about 15 years.
Despite the fact that I've played one or two dozen such games extensively, nothing comes close to dominions 4.
Although this game isn't for everyone, as it focuses very clearly on only one aspect of what would make a standard 4X strategy game, it does that one part of gameplay better than anything else by miles.
What aspect is that? Combat. Everything revolves around crushing your oppenent in glorious combat, or erroding the his ability to fight with powerful magic. Dominions 4 has 78 unique nations. Although some nations keep their themes and gods through multiple ages slightly reducing diversity from what you might see with 78 totally different nations (the game has 3 "ages" it is played through, and many nations exist in multiple ages, but generally they transition to a different playstyle from age to age, with different mages and troops).
The sheer number of nations alone makes for an incredible degree of variety and depth, but you can also customize a 'pretender' , the demi-god ruler of your nation. This can make for vast differences in gameplay giving each nations 1-3+ viable strategies, not counting meta-strategies you might employ versus a group of players you know well.
We haven't even gotten to the good part yet though. The meat of the game is a powerful combat simulation engine that allows detailed troop formations, powerful magical spells, special monster units, and magical artifacts to be employed in battle. This provides enormous opportunities for you to turn the tide of battle with clever strategy and planning.
On top of that, supplies and research do play a role. You can base strategies around researching powerful magics quickly, securing vast amounts of gold to build a powerful mundane army around, or raiding your opponent until they can no longer support their forces.
Take a look at the hours I've put into this game. I'd say I'm intermediate skill level. I could play most any nation competently, although I haven't nearly played them all. You will always have more to try and learn in this game, and it's more than worth any price it's ever been on steam.

Update: I recently had an epic experience that I posted on the discussion board, and people said I should at it as a review. So here it is.
How Heroes are Made
Earlier tonight, one of the most epic occurences I have ever seen in a video game occured. Seeing that as a sign of a good game and also worth telling about, I decided to post here for your reading pleasure. Since it is only due to a confusing chain of events that this occured, I'm going to tell the full story from start to finish. Enjoy.
Recently I started a MA game with my friend. It was Agartha and Pangea (me and my friend) up against 6 other pairs ( Ermor and Arcosephale, Ashdod and Nazca, Tien Chi and Caelum, Eriu and Ulm, Asphodel and Vanarus, Sceleria and Man ). Settings were for a long enjoyable coop game against the AI, with story events, conquest all, clustered spawns, and common random events. To start, we are luckily positioned with the one sea as our northern border ( the map had full wraparound), and mountains close by. We expand quickly and have a nice lump of land before we begin having conflicts with our neighbors, Ermor to the west and Ashdod/Nazca to the south. Im forced to support my Pangean friend with large blocks of Agarthan infantry supported with living statues so we can push back the enemies to the south. During the delay, Ermor casts a global enchantment, Burden of Time. Realizing the issues with all of our units dying of old age, we immediatly leave a small border garrison and charge our resources at Ermor. The endless legion combined with the death 3 provinces causes massive attrition, wearing our armies down to nothing and resulting in the deaths of my top commanders, excpet for one, Ernst, the Cave Captain. He has already aged to 45 / 50 from the Global Enchantment, so I prepare a suicide battalion of my remaining elderly units to rush Ermor and slay their god to end the enchantment. In a long battle across Ermor, I manage to corner and kill him in their capital. In the mean time, I've also rushed my way into Blood Magic to unlock Boots of Youth, which Ernst gets at the ripe age of 49, 1 year before old age. The Encantment is dispelled, but most players without undead focus have been crippled from its effects. My researchers are all diseased and my armies crippled. Ernst and only a few other commanders were given boots in time, the rest being too wounded to salvage. I recruit new generals, one of which being Aripert. The game is peacful for a time, but soon Ashopdel begins attacking. Im ready. Aripert and Ernst lead a combined force of over 400 Agarthan infantry, supported by foul spawn and living statues. Ashopdel is crushed, but their ally Vanarus pushes me back, killing most of my army. My commanders retreat, and I get a story event at my capital. A band of adventurers has joined the cause. I put them to good use as supporting commanders and mages for Aripert and Ernst. I launch a new attack at Ashopdel and Vanarus, killing the former and sieging the latter. My ally in the meantime has been fighting the war from the opposite side, and we meet together at Vanarus's capital. I storm first, Ernst, Aripert, and adveturers as commanders, a a vangaurd of Agarthan Living Statues in the front, foul spawn on the flanks, and Agarthan infantry in the core. The battle is brutal, with the archer towers killing 2 of my 6 adventurers, and my force being hit with many spells. Inside the fort is Vanarus' God, the Son of Fenrir. My own commanders have reached hall of fame status with 4 EXP and a heroic ability each. The battle rages, and I notice the adventures have been casting Nature 2 spells Enlarge and Enrage on my commanders. Suddenly, my small Cave Captains Ernst and Aripert have turned into size 4 killing machines, but are unable to get into combat. Eventually, morale breaks in both sides, and the mages run off the fields. My statues and the enemy elementals collapse into dust, leaving our core infantry to fight. The Son of Fenrir enters combat with his wolves, decimating my men while their men are whittled away by my more tanky infantry. The core infantry of their side routes, but mine route aswell after slaying the wolve body guards of their pretender god. All thats left are Ernst and Aripert, leading the charge alone. Against a god. With 200 hp. and Regen. I prepare for the worst, and to my astonishment Ernst strikes their god down with his enchanted Sword of Swiftness, with Aripert supporting. Vanarus was knocked out of the game, and a basic Cave Captain recruiting for a suicide mission many years ago had slain a god.

If I had to describe the game in one sentence, it woudl be a mix between Dungeon Keeper, Minecraft, and Chess.
Don't get me wrong though, this is me simplifying it.
Everyone is a burglar. Everyone is trying to rob everyone else whilst trying to prevent it from happening to themselves. You start off with $2000 in which to boobytrap your house however you see fit using vicious dogs, pits, electrified floors, and more.  Once you're satisfied that your money - and family - are protected as well as they can be, you get to go and 'visit' other peoples', seeing if you can spot a weak link in their carefully constructed plans, cutting your way through with saws, or throwing drugged meat to dogs, but be careful. Everything is dangerous, should you step on electrified flooring, get shot, or fall down a pit, it's game over. Whilst you're out plundering to the bestof your ability, they get the chance to do the same to you. Should someone attempt to break into your house, you are able to watch their movements, to spot the weak points in your plan, improve upon it, and repeat.
The catch? While you are given tools to break into other houses, when testing your own, you aren't allowed any - and any mistake in testing could cost you your life.
It is fair to say that The Castle Doctrine is an unforgiving game, especially to new players, and (at time of writing) there are many improvements that need to be made, there is something adictive about it.
Some might question why I likened the game to the three that I did:
Minecraft - the wiring in this game is a lot like 'redstone', wiring up pressure plates to lower drawbridges, or to turn off some harmful device.
Dungeon Keeper - you are building a trap that other people have to plunder. The only difference is that this is harder, as you have to make all the traps yourself.
Chess - perhaps the most 'wrong' from the list, but I think it fits. The game is turn-based. For every move you make, the enemies in the house are allowed to do the same.
The game currently fails in a number of areas; wiring can be a bit of a nuscience, along with having to ditch all of your equipment after breaking into someones house, even if you don't steal anything.

I wanted so much to love this game, but I just can't in the current state. There simply not enough content to justify it being a full game at the moment. Maybe enough to be a DLC expansion for RS1; 6 maps and a supposedly decent amount of weapons, but most are variants that are either far inferior to another or weapons unusable in some maps. I should be able to use the Mosin Nagant in every map if I wanted to, or choose between either of the Northern LMGs.
The reality is that this is very different game from RS1 and extremely different from RO2, unfortunately for the worse. The vast majority of combat is relegated to your primary weapon now, as almost every player has an automatic weapon, making it almost impossible to get in close enough to use grenade or bayonet. This fundementaly changes the entire game. No longer are large, concentrated pushes organized by team leaders successful, or even attempted anymore.  The combat devolves into two entrenched teams firing at 100m at each other until a commander can end the stalemate with a napalm or artillery, allowing the attacking team to take the point unapposed; a stark contrast to the previous meta of artillery use, which was used to DENY area rather than ATTTACK it. It might be a different game from a predecessors, but different != fun.
Both Rising Storms are built on asymmetry, with a well equipped and technologically advanced American army facing off against an Asian army countering their inferiority in weaponry with ambush tactics and traps. RS2 however, amplifies the American advantage by a degree of 10 and decreases the Asian ability to counter. The American forces have 3 options for fire support, all on seperate timers. The helicopters have many counters on paper, but can be eliminated by simply flying low when AA is up, and high when the (incredibly difficult to use) RPGs are pointed skyward. For a force most notorious for the usage of traps, the Northen force's traps are absolute garbage in comparison to the Japanese's in RS1. Every Japanese had the ability to place explosive mines very quickly, while Northern rifleman must dig a single punji trap in an agonizingly lengthy amount of time. Some Northern troops can put down tripwire traps, but they are both very difficult to place in the terrain (although they have gotten better) and are far too easily spotted. Only one Nothern class can put down explosive mines, but there is maybe only 2 in a team.
Enough bashing. The ability to customize your character by leveling up is a very welcome change. No longer do you have to slog through dozens of hours to unlock a bayonet or a sling. The decision to give more troops smoke grenades was great and the ability to change ammunition types on shotguns and grenade launchers allows each of those weapons to be used differently. Maybe allow rifles to switch between soft/hollow point and FMJ? The $25 price point is very cheap compared to the majority of shooters on the market, especially AAA titles.
The fundemental problem of the game is that it IS Vietnam. A war fought primarily in small, brief engagements rarely fought in larger than company size where Southern strategy was to search and destroy the enemy rather than assault entrenched positions like the game is built around. This is compounded with the lack of content to create a mediocre game. In my opinion, Korea and a few more months of development would have been a much better decision.

I haven't played much of Special Edition myself (I have around 347 [logged] hours on the original release), but I'm writing this review for all versions of Skyrim, since the old edition seems to have disappeared from the store.
Skyrim is a classic title that remains strong six years after its release. It is still one of the most played games each day on Steam, and with good reason. It's got a beautifully crafted world to explore. It's got a fantastic soundtrack. It's got replayability. It's got a thriving modding community that produces everything from graphical improvements to new features to new continents.
If you have never played Skyrim, then you ought to. The sense of discovery you feel when rounding a corner in Skyrim's world -- small in area compared to the real world but rich with life and full of depth -- is unique. There are plenty of quests to busy yourself with for hours, each rewarding in its own way, and practically endless amounts of minor quests that may never be exhausted. Hundreds of unique locations, characters, items... even 470 readable books! The amount of detail is astounding and equal to that of previous Elder Scrolls games.
On top of that, the DLCs are true expansions that add new areas to the game and plenty more original content. In the realm of modding: there are "immersive" hardcore roleplaying and survival mods; there are graphical mods; there are wacky reskins and everything in between, totalling more extra content than could ever be produced by the developers.
But give the developers credit -- Skyrim is a complete game on its own. Though it has its quirks that come with age, Skyrim is an all-around good game that will be remembered as such for years to come.

This game is incredibly good at making statements about and offering commentary on the human condition, on the meaning of life. It does this masterfully, and this game stands out remarkably for it.
Expect spoilers.
There's nothing wrong with the game's other elements, whether that be it's fun, outlandish combat or it's beautiful soundtrack -- but it's really the pointed way this game draws attention to its message that makes it so great.
When I talk about message, about commentary, I'm not talking about the story as its presented explictly either. The story, too, is used as a vehicle for presenting a certain idea. To that end, it does this well, but I'm not chiefly concerned or interested in the direct fate of the characters in it.
Why is this? Well, NieR's story and its characters are very much analogues for actual human beings, and the thematic concern of the story with 'the meaning of life' is most important. So what happens to the androids '2B and 9S' isn't my care or concern, it's: What does 2B and 9S's fate tell us about how the game answers the question 'what is the meaning of life?'.
As one of my favorite critics has said, we love stories because we see ourselves in them. And it is my belief that stories and telling stories find their rightful place in telling things about us, in reflecting our own image back to ourselves -- whether it be a simple or complex message. Whether philosophical, religious, political, entertaining or humorous, stories must do this, and it is with the content of their reflection, what image the stories show of us that I am most interested.
I'll note before I continue that I did of course get the true ending, went through all the main routes, etc.
What image does NieR:Automata reflect back? What does it say about the human condition, about the meaning of life? For a good many critics, the meaninglessness of the game's world, and the way the characters face it points to existentialist (and thus pessimist) conclusions.
Another critic I admire offered his own analysis, which he said came from a Marxist and Hegelian lens. He noted the way the machines in the game all pursue their goals, their purposes with singular commitment -- whether a 'father' machine, 'older sister' machine, a religious machine, a machine committed to speed or a machine committed to love.
All of them, he noted, commit themselves to their singular purpose absolutely, but they generally tend to explode or die after finding it. He posited that the machines, like humans, were alienated from their labor, they lacked purpose just as humans can't find purpose because they don't have meaningful work.
It's an interesting thesis and it offers some insights, but I don't agree with it, likely because I don't share Marx's beliefs.
As a Catholic, the context I bring to this work is altogether something else. About a week back a figure I admire was reflecting on Ecclesiastes. The story it contains is relevant to NieR's meaning. It's about a man who had seen and done it all, he had felt real love, he had good friends, he enjoyed great meals, sexual pleasure -- everything under the sun.
Yet, he described it as 'wind chasing wind'. None of it had ever permanently satisfied him or given his heart peace -- there was a longing, an aching for a meaning the world couldn't provide. For him, this wasn't depressing, it only meant his heart longed for God, for That which he can only glimpse in this world, but wants most deeply.
Such sentiments and conclusions are often the basis of 'arguments from desire' for God's existence, that the innate desire we feel for something more, for something beyond all we can have here on Earth points to God, for innate desires point to the existence of their objects in general.
It seems that the machines of NieR and our android characters and allies are engaged in a similar quest for meaning. The machines act out their singular purposes and find them wanting, the androids fight and fight quixotically and discover, eventually, the meaninglessness of their own existence, how they are disposable to the utmost. They seek meaning, they seek something *more* and do not find.
I do not think that the game's director, Yoko Taro, necessarily means for an existentialist or nihilist conclusion with this though. One of the more notable characters, fittingly named Pascal, expresses direct disdain for Nietzsche.
At the game's initial endpoint in The Tower, these discoveries of meaninglessness issue in a bloody and sad conclusion with our characters' deaths. At our true ending, wherein all hinges upon the actions of our two support pods, 042 and 153, we find a rather remarkable action of faith. They find that the expected conclusion: the death of all androids, has completed. Thus, they can continue with the next phase of their project with the construction of new combat models.
However, something in both pods rejects this, they too, can't find a satisfactory meaning in continuing to act out their function. Flatly, Pod 042 states, 'I have come to the conclusion that I cannot accept this resolution'. So, they decide to rebuild 2B, 9S, and A2. Importantly, one asks the other if the same events could play out again, if all this could come to naught. The same conclusions reached. Plainly, what if they still cannot find the meaning they so long for, that all long for?
Pod 042 replies, saying 'I cannot deny the possibility. However, the possibility of a different future also exists'.
Again, I cannot help as a Catholic but see a certain meaning in this. To rebuild the androids, with the same memories, with the same parts, knowing what will likely happen, what conclusions of meaninglessness it will likely issue in, to do it anyway -- what a beautiful act of faith that is!
It says: 'I see the meaninglessness in all that has been pursued and sought up to this point, and they could pursue them again and still find nothing -- but I believe there is 'something' more to be found despite that.
Understanding the machines, pods and androids as analogues for human beings once more, it says that we too act out our lives and find our activities and goals enjoyable, and yet wanting in the end, the longing in our hearts for that 'more' unsatisfied. Yet, we believe there is That which we cannot find.
I don't mean to argue that Yoko Taro is making an explicit 'argument from desire' for God's existence, absolutely not, only that the story grants a beautiful reflection of human faith in finding meaning and of that desire so innate to us.
While not explicit, I must thus tenuously posit that the essence of the game does represent a sort of subtle, implicit argument from desire. I think that's beautiful.
Thus, the story's conclusion issues in a final act of faith in finding some future meaning and not, as some others think, meaninglessness or in 'finding your own meaning'.
This game masterfully expresses its meanings and messages, and for that reason I wholly recommend it. I haven't done its other elements justice here (the soundtrack is one of the best in any game), only discussed that which stood out most to me.
Thanks for reading!

This game was great! WAS. It's creative, feels good to play, and doesn't rely on money to start playing (because it's free). The characters are fresh, the maps are interesting, the abilities are decently balanced, there is almost nothing I can say that is not positive about this game. The fatal flaw is simply that this game suffers from the beta syndrome so many new exciting games suffer from. It started as a finished product, and then the developers decided to change it... over... and over... and over again. I liked this game a lot, and with every update I decided I would give it a good shot before deciding the update made the game play worse, but the truth is, every update makes the game play more dull. When you have a game with many characters, they tend to become less and less balanced over time, making it difficult for anyone to play a character that isn't in the meta. The skins are getting a little out of hand, I enjoy content in a game, but all of it is just paid cosmetics, making opening crates feel almost empty... Well, it would feel empty if it weren't for the fact that all of the ability upgrades and actually interesting mechanics in this game are tethered to micro-transactions. While you can technically own everything in the game just by playing for a long time, this would take thousands of hours, and it really does encourage you to buy things in order to enjoy them, there simply isn't enough gold and elixir for everything, at least not in an easily accessible fashion. The game is still fun, and it is definitely worth at least exploring because of the price (nothing), but it just isn't reaching its full potential. I recommend this game, but I can only rate it a 6/10, and that may be too generous.

A charming and fun (if highly derivative and overdone) stylized platformer with a retro art style and a snappy chiptune soundtrack. You may see this and think "ugh this style of game has been played literally to death" and you'd be right, but this deserves its due diligence for being a really clever little game.
I feel it's very much like an alternate-universe take on VVVVVV's gameplay mechanics; instead of a gravity flip you have a simple teleportation gun, kind of like an ultra-simplified Portal; you shoot a beam that sends you in a straight line to wherever it hits, which in theory sounds pretty lame, but the level design makes for some very tricky and mind-bending puzzle situations.
You'd be a fool to pass this up for 19 cents. Hell, even its full asking price of $4.99. A fun little romp for fans of the aforementioned VVVVVV and similar games.

Two downers come to mind though. One, said 8 year old was busy getting engrossed in the story and wasn't looking for those quick time events. Really, those damn things should be banned. On steam, the game has currently has 80% approval from people who just forked out at least $22.50 for it, and have only received 1/5 of their game so far. That's more like it, and I score the game 8/10 myself. I've found Steam's "User Reviews" percentages to be by far the most reliable measure of a game. Not 100% reliable, but far and away better than metacritic, and especially better than the metacritic user scores which are absolutely untrustworthy.
It's a good game, if you 1. like Minecraft, 2. like Telltale games, 3. didn't expect adult content in a 10+ game, 4. don't mind blocky minecraft-style animation. In other words, it's a good game for what it is. The game is very different from Minecraft, and very different from other recent Telltale games, so many people might be expectinf something else. Still, the game has received good reviews so far among the people who actually bought it.
There's no point giving a game a bad score because it's different from Skyrim, or Minecraft, or the Wolf Among Us. I wouldn't criticise a painting because it is not a sculpture or a radio-drama. For what it is, a kid-friendly interactive story (with more story than interaction), Minecraft: Story Mode Episode 1 is well done and very enjoyable. It's just what I expected, and I'm very happy with my purchase!

My actual play time is over a thousand hours as I have only recently registed it on Steam. There are three key problems with this game.
The first is that the game gets boring after a while. Yes, I'm talking about multiplayer. Initially, it is exciting learning how to outwit other human players -- raid and counter raid, various strategies, spells and their counters. After a while, though, there is a serious lack of variety. There are many spells, units and items in the game, but the reality is that over 90% of them are plain bad and you'll always be restricted by a very limited selection to what is feasible/competitive.
The second problem is a rather toxic community. For some reason, many people who play the game think that they are geniuses and have sky high egos. It can be really frustrating communicating with them especially if they know that they are wrong but just plain refuse to admit it. I guess that people who play this game are naturally more logical and hence think that they are smart.
The third is that many multiplayer games end up dead. It is difficult to find a game where everyone is playing competitively until the end. Most of the time, someone will give up and disappear halfway through the game, resulting in his neighbour becoming stronger. Some times, people refuse to attack the leader and let him run away with the game. Some times your starting location is bad, you have no chance. In any case, it gets really frustrating when people treat the game flippantly. Winning the game can be due to plain luck since many factors are outside of your control.

I've always liked strategy games, but not been a hard core player. I've played lots of board games though and in my opinion Dominions is like playing a very good board game. In a true 4X style you Expand, Explore, Exploit and then Exterminate. Playing Dominions solely against the AI is ok for learning the game, but the real fun begins when you start to play against other players IMO.
Pros:
- Tons of varied nations to play with very different game styles
- Cast spells, build armies, forge items, build castles,  plan and execute large scale wars, Dom 4 has it all!
- You'll get literally hundred, if not thousands, of hours of varied gameplay
- It's turn based, no stress and lots of time to carefully consider your strategy
Cons:
- It is kind of ugly (but it grows on you, after a while you actually start to like the blurry pixels, less is perhaps more?)
- The UI is clunky and sometimes unintuitive
- It takes a long time to learn and to become good at it you have invest several hours
- A lot of micro management and scripting in the late game sessions
- You typically want to check stats and strategices online, not necessarily a bad thing, but some info is just esothericly presented in the game when you actually would prefer to get hard stats (Like, if you spend a lot of valuable magic gems on summoning a demon lord, you would want to know if it is worth it or not, but the game doesn't really tell you until you actually have performed the summoning ritual)
All in all, when my friend first recommended it, I just glanced at the graphics and sniffed at it. But, over 300 play hours later, it is one of my favourite games ever. And yes, the graphic does grow on you.

An EXTREMELY over complicated 4X game based around ancient mythology, history, and H.P. Lovecraft. You start out the game by choosing a map, age, empire, and then making a god. The game consists of three playable ages that show the development of the playable empires. The early ages have Magical and Nonhuman factions in abundance, while the human factions of the time are just discovering Copper and Bronze. This age also has the greatest amount of Magic, but also the least organised casters. The second age is marked with Human factions beggining to subjigate the assorted nonhumans with weapons of Iron and Steel augmented by enchantment. This age has a moderate balance of Magic and Organised casters. The Third age is a time were Man has all but destroyed the magical wonders of past ages. Magic is nearly drained from the world, but well organised wizards make do with what is left. After you choose your age, you choose your empire, Then make your God. Your God making sets how you will spend the next several hours of your life in this game. You select an available Deity for your faction, then get to choosing how strong it is in magic and what bonuses you get in lands were you are believed in. Say you're faction has very good yet expensive troops, yet poor magical researchers and practitioners so you can't get any late game spells, you would make your god have a dominion that boosts production and can cast what you need to be cast. FINALLY you are in the game after setting a few end game goals and options, and the real complicated hell begins. I think im going to stop soon so I am going to make this as simple as possible to summarise what you do in the actual game. Your first play through will just be throwing bodies at other bodies till you win or lose. Though what makes the game fun is the magic. One magician with some magical items and gems can single handedly destroy a quarter of an army, but what makes it complicated is knowing the exact stats of those items, spells, and how much your caster can take before fainting. I think this is way to long already and if anybody reads this far then I'm sorry if this was a mess. If you want to take the time to learn about this game and such then by all means get it.

In a nutshell, a brilliant idea, but execution so awful it's obvious it's the developer's first attempt at making any manner of a game, with possibly little to no experience in the field of game development even in general.
For instance, it's entirely possible you spend a good 30-40 minutes wiring up a house to your liking for the very first time, and then you decide to test it out, because the game requires you to.
So, you of course test your traps, let's say the electrified floortrap to see what it does, whether it's some sort of humorous zapping animation or something else. What this actually does, is instantly kills you for good, and permanently deletes any of your previous effort on the house.
The game has no way of informing you about any of this, and the only way to find out is experimentation. There is no manual, there isn't even a wiki.
There are other glaring issues, such as the obvious design of going with a multiple choice lottery where only one of a 5 dozen switches opens the vault, and all the other are lethal. You obviously know which one to press, the chances of an invading player knowing this are neglibly small. Protecting the family is a pointless matter by design, as there are no reasonable ways to protect them whatsoever. Why? They require an entirely trapless (and doorless) way out of your house. There are 3 familymembers. There are no turrets or any sort of traps like that, and the dogs are a joke to dispose of.
Such a shame; the idea is worth developing for, but the execution is lacking on all grounds. Please do not waste your money or time with this.

The game is developed by Bumblebee Games and is quite the management sim. I’m typically not very good at sims because I have a horrible habit of getting my town destroyed or worse. But Villagers does something a little differently, which I like. The game has a campaign mode. It gets you used to how the mechanics work and at the same time, tests you when you’re under pressure, like time, limited resources or deadly animals. It plays a lot like how you’d imagine sim games would play. You have your play area, your villagers and your resources. It’s entirely up to you on how you figure out how to build and shape your town.
In Campaign, you play through the story of your villager, male or female. You have quests lined up for you that lay out what needs to be done when they need to be done. While this takes place, a story unfolds about your character in little cards the peek off to the right. You come across corrupt figures, assassins, and hungry villagers during your journey. Campaigns are pretty short and can end abruptly I found. This may or may not sit well with folks hoping to get longer game play out of each chapter you are tasked with.
In Freeplay, it’s exactly that; play how you want without the story mode. You pick your terrain and you’re off to start your journey and build your town how you see fit.
The A.I. does tend to get a little wonky. I found a few of my villagers clipping and getting stuck on trees when I needed fish. The trees were stumps also, so there was nothing there to hinder them. The Campaign ends when your village can’t sustain itself or you move on to the next chapter of your story. Each chapter is broken up into sections about your life as the bard tells it. Each chapter can be short as it introduces you to the core mechanics.
Controls are WASD to move the camera around to see more of the board and scope out resources or enemies. Q and E rotate the camera for better angles to watch your villagers build and roam about. R and T are used to tilt the camera up and down so you can better see what’s going on and mouse wheel is used to zoom in and out.
There are other keys that control every aspect of building to make the experience easier for players. Using the Left Mouse Button, you can also click on each villager, name them, see their spouses or what’s ailing them. Useful if you want to find out on a villager level how your town is doing.
In the upper left, you also have controls that speed up, slow down or pause time. Just in case you need an extra moment while you think of what to do next. Down along the bottom is where you'll find your build bar, or where you go to find the structures you can build to create your town. You will also find the Gathering action here. This will let you mine stone or gather wood for the various buildings that need them.
The upper right has your mini map, quest log and settings. Along the top is where you can keep track of your resources, gold and villagers.
The game is pretty to look at. It features a load of colorful characters you’ll meet throughout your journey. Even zoomed in at the closest point, the game still looks rich and vibrant. Characters are also nicely done and the landscapes with which you play on look fantastic.
Sounds are alright. Nothing that stands out but it also isn’t too loud or too out of place. It fits the time period and it’s very nice background music when you’re building either in Freemode or Campaign.

I've been an avid Minecraft player for a fair amount of time, and I've only been a Telltale fan for maybe two years. However, when the two come together to produce a game, I'm all ears.
Let me just say this: The game is NOT like Minecraft. Don't go into it expecting a lot of running around, fighting, building, all those Minecraft-y things. Go into it expecting a Telltale game, but with Minecraft elements, styles, and references. The game even makes one think back to their early days of playing Minecraft, which I found to be really nice. It's always a good thing to think back to the good old days.
I managed to completed this first episode in just over an hour and a half, which is fairly standard for most of the Telltale episodes I've played so far. It's not particularly hard, but it gives you a lot to think about. Just how do you want to go about doing this or that? How do you respond to somebody, and who do you choose to side with? It's the basic Telltale dialouge options, but with a Minecraft twist.
The game is actually fairly gorgeous. It's like applying shaders to Minecraft, and then using the world as a sort of engine to base the game in. Kinda like turning the world into a 3D model file, and using it to build an animation, like many people do on YouTube, but it's also like being on a server. Only there's a lack of 'looking 4 fac' and '1v1 me brah' in the chat. In other words, it's really nice.
The gameplay is standard Telltale-style stuff: Explore the scene, find items, and talk with people to advance the story. However, it adds some more Minecraft-related play into the mix. There's combat, which has you moving forwards or backwards, and has you timing your sword strikes to hit an enemy without taking a hit yourself (Fighting zombies in Minecraft comes to mind a LOT here). There is also a crafting mechanic, where you have to craft the right item for a given situation. I could be wrong, but there may be multiple solutions here or there. I've yet to test that theory.
In terms of characters, I like them all so far. Each one has their own personailty, as well as their own skills. They also have their own likes and dislikes, so it's important to keep in mind just how one character will react to certain dialouge options. The voice-acting is hit-or-miss in some places, but it wasn't half bad. Over time, I grew to actually find the voices suiting, and tones each of them used to be more natural.
Personally: I love this game so far. I'm excited to see where it takes me next. Which reminds me: This is only ONE story. Just like the other Telltale games, and just like Minecraft, nobody's stories will be alike, and each one is unique. If you are willing to approach this game with that mindset, then good. If not, and you want something more along the lines of Minecraft, then I would suggest either giving the game a chance, or just going back to Minecraft itself.
But, in summary:
This is a decent start to another Telltale title. Visuals are pleasing, the characters are interesting, and the game brings to mind one's own time spent in Minecraft. It's Telltale, but with several Minecraft-related features. And, most importantly, it's only ONE of the millions of stories out there.
I rate it: 8.5/10. A decent game, best enjoyed when marathoned with the other episodes, but has charm and makes any Minecrafter nostalgic.

This game was great! WAS. It's creative, feels good to play, and doesn't rely on money to start playing (because it's free). The characters are fresh, the maps are interesting, the abilities are decently balanced, there is almost nothing I can say that is not positive about this game. The fatal flaw is simply that this game suffers from the beta syndrome so many new exciting games suffer from. It started as a finished product, and then the developers decided to change it... over... and over... and over again. I liked this game a lot, and with every update I decided I would give it a good shot before deciding the update made the game play worse, but the truth is, every update makes the game play more dull. When you have a game with many characters, they tend to become less and less balanced over time, making it difficult for anyone to play a character that isn't in the meta. The skins are getting a little out of hand, I enjoy content in a game, but all of it is just paid cosmetics, making opening crates feel almost empty... Well, it would feel empty if it weren't for the fact that all of the ability upgrades and actually interesting mechanics in this game are tethered to micro-transactions. While you can technically own everything in the game just by playing for a long time, this would take thousands of hours, and it really does encourage you to buy things in order to enjoy them, there simply isn't enough gold and elixir for everything, at least not in an easily accessible fashion. The game is still fun, and it is definitely worth at least exploring because of the price (nothing), but it just isn't reaching its full potential. I recommend this game, but I can only rate it a 6/10, and that may be too generous.

An EXTREMELY over complicated 4X game based around ancient mythology, history, and H.P. Lovecraft. You start out the game by choosing a map, age, empire, and then making a god. The game consists of three playable ages that show the development of the playable empires. The early ages have Magical and Nonhuman factions in abundance, while the human factions of the time are just discovering Copper and Bronze. This age also has the greatest amount of Magic, but also the least organised casters. The second age is marked with Human factions beggining to subjigate the assorted nonhumans with weapons of Iron and Steel augmented by enchantment. This age has a moderate balance of Magic and Organised casters. The Third age is a time were Man has all but destroyed the magical wonders of past ages. Magic is nearly drained from the world, but well organised wizards make do with what is left. After you choose your age, you choose your empire, Then make your God. Your God making sets how you will spend the next several hours of your life in this game. You select an available Deity for your faction, then get to choosing how strong it is in magic and what bonuses you get in lands were you are believed in. Say you're faction has very good yet expensive troops, yet poor magical researchers and practitioners so you can't get any late game spells, you would make your god have a dominion that boosts production and can cast what you need to be cast. FINALLY you are in the game after setting a few end game goals and options, and the real complicated hell begins. I think im going to stop soon so I am going to make this as simple as possible to summarise what you do in the actual game. Your first play through will just be throwing bodies at other bodies till you win or lose. Though what makes the game fun is the magic. One magician with some magical items and gems can single handedly destroy a quarter of an army, but what makes it complicated is knowing the exact stats of those items, spells, and how much your caster can take before fainting. I think this is way to long already and if anybody reads this far then I'm sorry if this was a mess. If you want to take the time to learn about this game and such then by all means get it.

Don't get me wrong, it's an incredibly addictive game, just for all the wrong reasons. For example, my labyrinth of a house took a number of hours to make during the last day of the contest, which I HAD to do all in one sitting as leaving it alone half finished would have certainly lost me all of my resources while I was away. This wasn't the first house I'd fully decked out either, so if it weren't for the real money incentive, I wouldn't have even have got this far.
Then come Steam launch night, a new burst of enjoyment came from watching new players dying in my house and from some easy robberies on their new houses. However, that same night, albeit after I'd gone to bed and left my house alone for a few hours, one of the worst (but most well funded) robbers I've ever seen tore through every single cerebral trap in my home, along with most of the walls, doors, dogs and children just because he had 100 of every tool on hand.
After dying trying to salvage and repair the intricate maze that took so long to make with my funds now at zero... what's the motivation to start again? I mean, what's the point in making a masterpiece of a puzzle when someone is just going to set it on fire as soon as you go to sleep? Do yourself a favour and don't even try to make one in the first place.

You'll likely read a lot of comparisons between Villagers & Banished. And for good reason. Both are Medieval City-Builders and both sell around the €20 mark, with Banished selling at €18.99 and Villagers at €19.99.
There is no contest. Banished is highly regarded, while Villagers is an entirely underwhelming experience. A long-winded, convoluted and tedious story begins when your character, by virtue of their natural-born "City planning" skills, is tasked with building a village. Each mission serves as part-tutorial with new features and buildings added with each new settlement you move to. Invariably each mission involves setting up your town hall, and gathering resources before some deus ex machina prompts you and your village to move along to somewhere else.
The shortcomings don't just end with the story-line though, where Villagers really falls flat is the lack of depth and difficulty. There are very few specialist buildings and very little micromanagement involved. For some, this could be a plus, with Villagers definitely offering a more casual experience than Banished, but for myself, it falls short of what I look for in a city-builder.
In terms of presentation and UI, Villagers offers a fairly simple interface thanks to it's lack of depth and the graphics are OK. I would expect users to have few problems running Villagers, visually it offers nothing remarkable or demanding.
In short Villagers is an expensive, casual city-builder, with a poor story and unremarkable features. And being priced more than Banished results in a disappointing experience.

I am writing this as credits have just finished rolling after the last story mission of this game
I decided to buy and complete Saints Row 2 as I have a PS4 and wanted to give Saints Row IV re-elected a go, but wanted to finish SR2 and 3 first to understand the story and the characters
Firstly, I was slightly worried when reading many reviews saying the game ran at low fps, crashed a lot and generally was a poor port for many people, especially those on Windows 7 which I use.
I would like to say here that I never had any of those issues (apart from having the game crash twice in 18 hours of gameplay, which for an older game and a port from a console I will accept). I never even installed the Gentlemen of the Row mod, I just downloaded the game, launched it and it worked fine, no issues.
I think this is a very good game and given its 2008 release I think it holds up well. The graphics aren't perfect, but are acceptable and characters actually have a very individual look to them. There is a lot of mayhem, a lot of humour, and fantastic characters which I was actually interested in rather than the bland clones in most of modern games (Dying Light I'm looking at you).
I only really played the story missions, with several of the side missions, but most of the side missions I didn't play as I was keen to get to SR3. So if you look at it, it's 18 hours gameplay of the main missions and a few side missions, with very little exploring etc. done. If you are someone who likes to engage in the side missions (and some of them are really, really fun), explore a bit and collect the collectables then this is easily a 25+ hour game. I played on the normal difficulty as well which made it easier.
Sure, there are little glitches, namely in cutscenes characters often didn't really hold items such as a cigarette - they floated instead. My favourite was in a cutscene where some of the rival gangsters drive up in a car at high speed, but the cutscene showed an empty car and the driver and his steering wheel and the passenger next to him floating in air behind the car - somewhat hilarious really. The AI also more often than not proved itself to be... not  very intelligent. But none of this takes away the fact that this is a very fun game to play.
Before I tried SR I was told it was 'discount GTA', but it seems that it really isn't so bad after all. Perhaps an underrated series?
Anyway, time for SR3 the full package. I would definitely recommend Saints Row 2!
