I rarely post reviews, but I view recent news as such a shame and injustice that I had to speak up. Up until the time of this review, Stellaris has been advertised as having 3 types of FTL travel: warp, wormhole, and hyperlanes. Hyperlanes should be familiar if you have experienced most other 4X space strategy games such as Sins of a Solar Empire. At this time, the development team has announced that an upcoming patch will be
warp and wormholes, a huge distinguishing feature of Stellaris.
is the official announcement and forum reactions.
Why removing 2/3rds of the FTL is bad news:
. They promoted the game with the promise of 3 types of FTL. This was one of the things that intrigued me enough to buy it, and I even pitched this to a friend as one of its selling points.
. With such a massive core mechanic change this late into the core game (not an optional expansion or mode, the
), I can not trust this developer going forward. The game is not marked early access on Steam, so the player should not have to fear that existing core systems will get changed or removed like it's still in beta.
. Stellaris to me is as much a story-generating toolbox as it is a game, similar to another favorite game of mine, Rimworld. I always saw Stellaris as a dream game because its systems were uniquely suited to being both a simulator and a role-playing experience. No other game came close to offering this. Look at how perfect the Star Trek and Star Wars mods (New Horizons and a Galaxy Divided) work within Stellaris as it is - and these two universes use two fundamentally different types of FTL. Star Trek uses warp and Star Wars uses "hyperspace" which is closest to hyperlanes. In Stellaris, the options were limitless, and it seemed that the devs would only make the game bigger and better as time went on - not smaller and worse. Maybe one could argue that different types of FTL is unbalanced because one is functionally better than the other. Fine, then play with only one FTL type allowed to all factions at a time. Play a warp-only game for Star Trek, a hyperlanes only game for Star Wars, and a wormhole only game for Stargate (or whatever). This works for multiplayer balance as well - make a match where everyone uses the same type of FTL, and boom, it's balanced. Even the "messy" systems become less messy if you are only playing with one FTL type at a time. My point is, leave all the tools on the table, don't leave me with one tool to work with because I can't build as much with just one tool.
. I understand the desire for "galactic terrain" like nebulae and whatnot. I understand the desire for fleets of ships to make lines of battle and whatnot. I also understand that in reality, space is big and empty and 3-dimensional, and you could fly around nebulae and attack other ships from any direction. Even in fiction, in the Wrath of Khan, it wasn't like Khan had no choice but to go into the nebula, he willingly pursued Kirk into it. Of the plausible methods of distant space travel, none relies on invisible naturally (or precursor technology, yuck) space highways of travel, but even if it were, come on man. It's space. It's meant to be free, the ultimate frontier, not like being forced to drive on man-made roads - it's more like piloting on the wide free ocean. Many players see warfare as the weakest aspect of the game and it's a reasonable thing to try and improve, but I cannot agree with how they choose to do this: by making space warfare more like land warfare, if land warfare was restricted to roads. It's silly.
. Sure they gave their argument in their announcement post: keeping the other types of FTL would be messy. The fact that their thread has 250 pages of people disagreeing (at the time of this writing) shows that people don't exactly concur. Hell, even the "messy" solutions given in the original post sound far more interesting and fun than a restrictive hyperlane-only playstyle! Like, why not have the interdiction bubble cover all 3 types of FTL, forcing warp civs to use hyperlanes within the bubble? People aren't stupid, especially people who play grand strategy games, and I would give them the benefit of the doubt on being able to grasp new systems. The devs could have come up with systems that build upon what they have in a fun way if they only tried instead of dismissing it outright. People do like the game how it is, and want more of it, not less. Save massive changes for dumbed-down sequels, not mandatory updates (choosing not to update isn't a real solution). Build upon what you have, don't do things just because it makes your job easier. If they couldn't find a balance with 3 FTL types, I'm sure modders could have - but they have even taken that away from us! They could even have kept all 3 FTL types but segregated them into different modes, but instead it seems like the easiest path was taken to ease the burden on their shoulders - make it more like every other 4X space strategy game out there, because it's
. Yes, it's easier to handle things when you don't have to juggle rock, paper and scissors, but it's not nearly as fun when you have just rock.
. I prefer warp. If they announced that they were getting rid of every travel type but warp, I admit I wouldn't be as peeved as I am right now - but it would still be wrong, and anger the wormhole and hyperlane players. It would still be restricting. I like the idea that I can freshen up the replay value by playing as wormhole next time, or hyperlane, or warp - like it's a whole new game. I can't help but think that the current development team prefers hyperlanes and using static defenses, other playstyles be damned. They try and rationalize and justify the removal of the other two FTL types by saying how they couldn't achieve the goals they want (land-style warfare and terrain... in space) and that the removal of features will bring more features, but that's all it is - rationalization and justification. But hey, you can build still play worm-hole kinda (extra-long hyperlanes) and practically play warp still if you increase the number of hyperlanes (... sure). It's like if Adobe's developers didn't use some features of Photoshop, so in the latest patch they stripped filters and tools because they didn't like them personally and didn't feel like keeping them updated - customers that used those features would be rightfully livid.
. For many, this isn't just one change, it's writing on the wall: raw gameplay over all else. I don't see Paradox's strength as being a traditional game developer, I see it as being a role-playing simulation sandbox developer that lets you play out "what if?" scenarios (like what if Poland invaded Germany first in Hearts of Iron?). This focus on dumbing down systems and on multiplayer balance is troubling because it feels like they are changing focus to the more casual, to the e-sports and multiplayer streaming crowd, rather than on what many people bought the game for - role-playing their dream civilization in an open-ended and flexible simulation. It seems Paradox is stepping on the toes of the latter to please the former, and as a consumer I find broad changes like this without our input to be an uncaring and unfriendly act on their part. It's like if you signed a marriage contract and then your spouse started changing for the worse, and then started doing things without your input and stopped caring about how you feel, they just do whatever they want because that's how they like it and it makes their lives easier... but at least in that scenario, you can get a divorce.
TL;DR: this is not the game I married.

Handball is a fun sport to play. Dynamic, spectacular and with tactical elements. Handball 16 fails to completely capture the handball atmosphere, but it is still fun to play. You can choose from different plays and if you perfrom them correctly you are awarded with a slowmotion jump shot giving you more time to aim and making it easier to score. So personally I would defintely recommend this game to anybody interested in handball. You will need some time to get used to it, but it is the only handball game out there and I as I definetely want this series to continue it just makes sense to support it.

I’m going to recommend this game, but I’m going to caveat it with some big buts. And not the kind that one can not lie about. Villagers is fun, but it’s a bit derivative and doesn’t offer much in the way of fresh gameplay. Villagers is pretty, but it isn’t going to knock your socks off with its beauty (see Planetbase for another, pretty simulation/builder game). Villagers is entertaining, but not deeply engrossing like a truly complex or deeply engaging builder game.
All that being said, I’ve enjoyed my time with it, bugs and all (see the end of my second video below for seasons and people going a bit.. weird!). If you see this on sale, and love builder games like Banished, the Anno series, or Planetbase - well - consider picking this up. You’ll get ten or twenty hours out of it, and then you can move onto something else. As I put it in my vids, this game is good filler when you want to play games but don’t want to have to think too much.
In terms of gameplay it’s the typical indirect control you expect in base building games: You order trees to be cut down, rocks to be dug up, and buildings built and your minions go about doing it. There’s pleasant music to keep you company and some quite nice looking seasonal changes. The main challenges are getting food made, progressing up the tech tree, and keeping your people breeding so there are always fresh adults to work your fields and buildings. Yes - citizens become old and useless if you don’t keep them happy and breeding!
Unless you’re freeplaying there’s an entertaining (if a bit silly) story that you can play through that also doubles as a tutorial. It goes on a bit long for my taste, but there’s some fun to be had there. Free playing seems a little limited right now as it looks like only a couple of maps have all the resources you need and you really do need a lot of resources. Although you can trade for resources, that takes away stuff you will want to build with and can leave you waiting around for, literally, trees to grow if you are resource short. That can be a bit tiresome.
To summarize: This is a fun builder that with a couple of patches and a good price you should pick up if you’re a big fan of the genre. It isn’t a game you’re going to be dreaming about and plotting about while you’re at work or school, but it is fun if you accept these limitations and treat it for what it is - a good distraction and a bit of a chuckle.
Below are two videos I made showing off the freeplay mode. They should give you a good sense of the scope of the game and the general style of play.

Low-res puzzle platformers are almost literally a dime a dozen now but Out There Somewhere manages to stand apart by being polished and clever with its core mechanic. That mechanic is a teleport gun, which fires a bullet that teleports you to its point of impact. The teleport preserves your momentum as well, so if you start a jump right before you warp, you can essentially tele-walljump. Several puzzles make use of this and other neat physics tricks you can do with yourself, gradually nudging the difficulty up in a pleasant, inviting way that has you feeling clever and masterful by the end of the game. There's a little combat with enemies and a few secrets to hunt if you are so inclined, but it's a very short and sweet package... one playthrough will last you less than an hour. I certainly wish it was longer because it is very tight and fun for those 45 minutes, but what's there is more than worth playing. There's even some inklings of plot and some interaction with aliens as you traverse the odd little world, and neat opening and closing sequences that play like Gradius-style shooters. And if you really feel like sticking with it, there are a mess of oddly-grindy achievements to shoot for, though I wouldn't encourage it. Overall a great little experience for even the most jaded puzzle platformer player.

I've been a huge King of Fighters fan since I was 10, as I first played KOF '97 at a local fair in Mexico. I've long waited for a KOF anime adaptation series since growing up, playing nearly all of the games that came out in the US. Since after hearing that they planning to expand the marketing once they merged with a huge Chinese corporation, including an anime series and a new live-action film (hopefully that it's far better than the atrocity that came out in 2010), I got intrigued, though I never expected it to be shown in Steam for free, so that is a real treat.
My first impressions on seeing the very first trailer promoting this series was mixed. On one hand, I'm glad that they finally made a KOF series I've long waited for. However, my conflicted thoughts had me worried about how will it turn out; I did not expect it to be a whole CG animated series, which I was hoping that it would be the traditional 2D anime style to begin  with. Not to mention that the editing of the first trailer showed a little less of the entire KOF cast and focused more on the Fatal Fury cast, which I'm not entirely against, but got me to think that it would end up more like a Fatal Fury series. Thankfully, I thought wrong and they showed me more non-Fatal Fury characters in later trailers.
So after seeing the first episode, I'm actually very pleased. The first episode wasn't anything big, but that is the nature of it which they gave a good introduction and I know it will lead to larger scales of the story in further episodes. The pacing is fairly slow, but it gave me the right time to let it all sink in with the characters. Each characters are properly staying true to their source counterparts. And I pretty much like the storytelling they they suggested they started off at the important events of the Fatal Fury lore, since they also held the same name of the tournaments. Though I'm expecting that the Non-Fatal Fury characters played an important part in Terry-central saga for later episodes before we reached to the beginning of the Orochi saga.
The highlight of this episode was at the end of the episode, we see Terry's flashback of his tragic backstory, which I'm sure every Fatal Fury fans knew. It's pretty much exactly what you expect, with some creative liberties thrown in its origins.
One of my gripes is that while that I'm not entirely against the CG anime approach, the models of the characters looks a little off. They're not terrible per say, but I feel they could've looked better. At least the characters are nicely expessive and decently animated. However, knowing that the animation is made directly from China, it's slightly disorienting that the Japanese dub are not properly lip synced. But those are just minor shortcoming. The rest of what it can introduced is very servicable.
I don't think I could recommend this to anyone. Though, if you're a King of Fighters fan, be it casual or hardcore, I'm sure you'll like this fine, as have I, and I'm looking forward to where it will go next, hopefully up until the end of Orochi saga. :)

My favorite thing about this game is that you can ask your allies for help and they will help you.  It's what I expected from allies in every game that has had them since the first time I ever got a strategy game.  This is the first time it's ever happened.  I need food, my allies give me food.  I need money, my allies give me money.  I'm equally happy to help them out.  This is what diplomacy should be.  Not a mere cease fire while you deal with your enemies on your other borders.
Secondarily, I like that the game feels interesting throughout.  My game has been mostly peaceful, and yet there's always more to do.  I finished exploring and populating my portion of the galaxy, now I can work on forming the galactic federation.  Every time I think I might be getting to some boring part of the campaign where in Civ I'd just be pressing end turn, this game reveals new story and new challenges.
Finally, I like the art and music.  These don't really come across in the screen shots as well as they should.  The game is really quite gorgeous and it helps to give a sense of grandeur.

I playtested this game for free for a few hours.
There are many other FPS PvP games and military simulations out there, sometimes free-to-play, that I find much better than this game.
Negative aspects :
- In somewhat realitic military games, like ARMA and most others, it is sometimes difficult to spot the enemy: fair enough. But, in this game, the map decorations or objects feel cluttered and blinding, so you will often never see the other player killing you.  Again, it is normal in a PvP game to often not see who or where the fatal bullet came from, but it is really just a chaotic mess, annoying and not fun in this game.  Experienced players manage to adapt, find ways of hiding and sniping, but is it worth the time, energy and money to adapt to that quirky mess while there are better games instead?
- The map are not impressive in size nor in form.  The terrain objects often make it an unpleasant battlefield in my opinion; except for the vietnamese houses (which should not stop bullets anyhow).
- The progression of characters is some cosmetic little things here and there, which has no importance as you will probably never have time to see what the other players look like. :P
- I only saw a multiplayer mode with random servers : I did not notice any *explained* or immersive scenarios and any context given.
- In the demo I played, the tutorial was not a tutorial really, and there are no solo quests to get you into it (immersion).
- So it just feels like a very incomplete game that offers a bunch of random arenas with quirky terrain.
After trying it, I went back to Heroes & Generals and am considering ARMA 3.

Purchased this game when I found out you could design your own alien species. From appearance and biological traits to the societal construct and government system. From a pacifist, open border, paradise democracy to an imperial hedgemony focused on scientific research and militarisation. This is the best feature of Stellaris, designing your civilization to win your way.
But as for the negatives: there are only 3 ways of winning; federation alliance, domination (owning 60% of galaxy) or playing space Stalin (all species and nations being under your control or else...). The game victory conditions focus on either alliances or conquering/purging (this game has at least 5 different options for driving sentient beings to extinction, don't ask me why). Yet there are only 4 combat ship types. Planet combat consists of dropping army units on a planet and watch the icon circles turn red. The science section involves randomly pooled technologies and choosing the least useless tech. Space combat is 50% luck. The Ai cheats.
I could go on, but for me the civilization mechanics make it all worth it, they are the best developed of any 4X game. The Utopia dlc adds good content but It would be wise to get it on sale. Just make sure you purchase AFTER the Cherryh update, stellaris updates tend to change the game experience from scratch.
This game is great and I recommend it for 4X fans, but it is still a WIP.

Let me preface this by saying that I've played Saints Row 2-4, but not Gat Out of Hell or 1. This is, in my opinion, the best Saints Row game.
Saints Row 2 is a very different experience from 3 or 4, but one that I find more appealing. The game is much more difficult, and emphasizes doing side missions over getting more money. The way that you unlock abilities (what little abilities there are, at least) and unique weapons (Kobras for the win). Despite being a couple years old, the gameplay is still pretty solid, especially the driving. The missions range from very easy (Septic Avenger, Mayhem) to mind-numbingly difficult (DRUG TRAFFICKING). If there is a mission where you are partially dependent on an AI driver, you will have difficulty.
The graphics for this game are dependent on your set up. I am running on a toaster, so the graphics look terrible and the game can be chopppy. On a decent rig, this game looks almost as good as SR3 or SR4. You can enable motion blur and HDR, and all that jazz, but for me I run the game barebones to maximize FPS.
The gameplay of SR2 is fast-paced, and this can make it unforgiving at times, especially because the way you heal in the game is by going into the weapons selection menu and selecting a food item to eat. There is no pause of the game while you are in the menu unlike in 3 or 4, so there is a greater emphasis on finding cover. Driving very fast can be difficult because if you have slower reflexes like me, you will have trouble accounting for the slow reaction time of the game.
A note on Controllers: I played this game first with the keyboard and mouse (a fairly bland experience) and then played through with the Steam Controller. This is not the place to debate the merits of the Controller, but it works very well with this game. Making use of a Controller takes a little getting used to, but the game is much easier to play and the conrtrols are more intuitive.
This is a port of the console game, and as far as ports go it is truly terrible. When I first played this game, I hated it, because of how difficult it was and how hard it was for me to get into the poorly rendered cut scenes and the mediocre voice acting. But when I've come back to it, the richness of the game and the sheer magnitude of how many unique little occurrences there are to find is staggering to me. The game is just as goofy as SR3 or SR4, but it does so without using spoof weapons like the penetrator, it lets you explore those moments on your own.
Overall, though it can be frustrating, Saints Row 2 is a very satisfying experience, and you can tell that so much effort was put into making this game a wide variety of experiences and choices. The customization of the vehicles is something that I've never seen before, with how many different ways you can play. I think that this game represents the best from Volition, and I highly reccomend that anyone play this game, even if they don't like other Saints Row titles. Believe me, this gamem makes it worth it.

Pros:
->Really impressive storyline - it makes the campaign very enjoyable, but be warned it takes quite a bit of reading
-> Promising population mechanics, I really enjoy how the villagers can have families and it is fun to watch them interact with the village
-> Challenging gameplay with production chains that are affected by weather: if winter hits before your grain is done growing...ouch. Food is tough to gather, and so is stone and iron. Water is also a resource you need to watch. The villager reproduction rate also makes it challenging because losing one villager is enough to topple the whole system. Some people think that makes it too hard, I love it.
Cons:
-> The game is buggy. Villagers do not move into houses that lose a family, so you end up with a bunch of homeless people while there's perfectly good houses sitting around.
-> Farmers do not interact with the fields very well. As far as I can tell, the 'harvest fields prematurely' button doesn't even work.
-> I had a few cases where merchants stopped showing up, I would have to build a new port or warehouse to bring them back.
-> Limited help. There's not really a 'help' program in the game and there isn't a wiki yet. The campaign will teach you a lot, but I still don't know if it is possible to demolish a building or not.
Despite the bugs, I would still recommend this game! I've logged almost 7.5 hours so far and I'm still on the campaign. It's a good, challenging game that will take you time to get through. All of my cons are bugs, and I'm banking on most of the bugs being fixed by future updates.
Finally, if you're looking at this just because it is 'like Banished', buy it with a grain of salt. Both games have you building settlements from the ground up, but Villagers focuses more on the story/campaign and less on the sandbox mode.
Its a good game, but I still feel as though it is lacking in content, hopefully the devs will add more content over the next year

I've been hesitant to write a review for Dom4 because after nearly 35 hours, I still don't understand most of it. But I feel like I should write something for it to let others know about this game.
This game is big, complex, and it all makes sense. There are massive amounts of strategies and a lot of depth, with a detailed world that all factors into how factions play. There are a large amount of factions, all of which have their own units and their own backstories, and a large amount of mythological beings, potential gods, and random events that can potentially completely change your experience.
The game is a tale about pretender gods, all together trying to eliminate the others so that they become the one real god. As the player, you control one such pretender god - Fully customised to your own likings and their nation/faction. Expand, research, play to your nation's strength, build up a massive army, and try to conquer the world. The keyword here being TRY, because every other faction has a pretender god trying to do the exact same thing, and things will often not go as planned.
You do not personally control the tactical combat, you only control the large picture. The army movement, the research, and important people(Such as scouts, mages, and commanders).
It may be overwhelming, and with a 300 page manual it's certainly not an easy game, but you don't need to know the top tier strategies to understand what's going on. Even without understanding most of the game you can enjoy it, with the large amount of mythology, customisation, and detail involved, you can easily weave your own tales of what happens in the world.
As a side note, the interface needs a little bit of learning too, but things become clear if you take a step back and calmly read the buttons and try them out
After all this time, I still have moments where I meet entirely new things I haven't seen yet, so I can not tell you much about the great strategies that will let you win. But I can tell you that if you try hard enough, you can at least not get overrun by the AI most of the time, giving you all the time you need to learn more about the game, regroup, and fight back.
It's difficult to truly explain its appeal, but Dominions 4 has a massive amount of content out there, with a lot of lore and depth to it. If you can get into it you will be able to spend hours on it, and if you want to really get involved with it there is a decently sized community out there to play with and learn from, showing you even more of an already huge game

I playtested this game for free for a few hours.
There are many other FPS PvP games and military simulations out there, sometimes free-to-play, that I find much better than this game.
Negative aspects :
- In somewhat realitic military games, like ARMA and most others, it is sometimes difficult to spot the enemy: fair enough. But, in this game, the map decorations or objects feel cluttered and blinding, so you will often never see the other player killing you.  Again, it is normal in a PvP game to often not see who or where the fatal bullet came from, but it is really just a chaotic mess, annoying and not fun in this game.  Experienced players manage to adapt, find ways of hiding and sniping, but is it worth the time, energy and money to adapt to that quirky mess while there are better games instead?
- The map are not impressive in size nor in form.  The terrain objects often make it an unpleasant battlefield in my opinion; except for the vietnamese houses (which should not stop bullets anyhow).
- The progression of characters is some cosmetic little things here and there, which has no importance as you will probably never have time to see what the other players look like. :P
- I only saw a multiplayer mode with random servers : I did not notice any *explained* or immersive scenarios and any context given.
- In the demo I played, the tutorial was not a tutorial really, and there are no solo quests to get you into it (immersion).
- So it just feels like a very incomplete game that offers a bunch of random arenas with quirky terrain.
After trying it, I went back to Heroes & Generals and am considering ARMA 3.

Stellaris is one of my favorite grand strategy games. The level of customization in this game is awesome. You can customize pretty much everything, your race, governing ethos, battle ships, planets, etc. The aesthetic to this game is especially pleasing, you always feel as if you're discovering a new life form or some valuable treasure left by an ancient spacefaring civilisation.
My only gripe is that there isn't much strategy to the combat. The only strategy that you can do is choose where and when you attack something, the rest is already predetermined by the composition of your fleet and the size of your fleet.

I must say, I really enjoy this game. I have spent countless (not really, I just forget how much) hours playing this game. I have played around with the mods and simply played the vanilla and fell in love. Both versions are equally fun and enjoyable. It is an extremely indepth game ranging from planetary edicts, government reform, space explortion, war strategy, diplomacy, and so much more. If you find yourself bored and in need for a new game this might be for you. I also have played hundreds of hours playing civilization, so if you like that give this a try!

Keep in mind, I don't usually play strategy games of any sort.  They're not the sort of games I generally enjoy playing, as they have a tendency to become boring and repetitive very fast.
That being said, I adore Stellaris.  While the concept of space strategy isn't new, this one was the only one that drew me in.  There's a ton of content (with more being put out fairly often) and enough events and interesting encounters in the game to keep me hooked even ~300 hours in.  That's a bit low of a number in comparison for people who DO usually play these types of games, but for someone like me, that's a lot.
I put the disclaimer about my inexperience of strategy games to warn the fact that I cannot reasonably critique things such as the combat and military systems that people often complain about.  Personally, the level of micromanagement is fine for me, but for others it may not be - and that may be up to your personal preference.  Mostly, I enjoyed the exploration and colonization aspects of the game.  I enjoyed finding anomalies and event chains with interesting stories that could sometimes even change depending on what kind of empire you're running.  I enjoyed creating different empire types every time and experimenting with the huge amount of options the game offers.
Overall, there's a lot of fun to be had, and if you like strategy games, give it a try.  Perhaps think about it even if you don't - like I did!  You might be pleasantly surprised.

Saints row 2 is one of my favorite games of all time, and up until Saints Row 4 came out, it was my favorite of the series. I've played through it 3 times already, once on console and twice here on PC. I love the feeling of the Saints criminal empire growing, such as the way the main hideout gets renovated throughout the story, to the satisfaction of opening the map and seeing purple overtaking it as you take more and more of the city. While I liked the more goofy direction Saints Row 3 and 4 have taken, the serious story here is very compelling, and while naturally not as goofy as the later entries, has a good amount of humorous moments sprinkled in alongside some much darker moments. The shooting feels generally alright, though sometimes the aiming feels just slightly off in a way that is hard to describe. Driving is fun though it has issues (more on that shortly), and there are a ton of side activities that are fun in their own right that give you rewards, such as infinite ammo for a certain gun type, infinite sprinting, and so on, for finishing all levels of that particular activity, and the character creation, oh the character creation. SR2 still has the best character customization in the entire series, it lets you create exactly what your character looks like, all the way down to their walking animation! The clothing options seem unlimited, and you can layer your clothes, something that was lost in SR3 forward that I really wish would return. But despite all the positive things, this game isn't perfect. Not by a long shot. For starters, the pc port. This is easily the second worst port I have ever had the displeasure of dealing with (First worst being Assassins Creed 3, the only port that was so bad that it was literally unplayable for me). Performance is absolutely terrible, its always a bad sign when the next game in the series both looks better and performs (infinitely) better. Even if you have a powerful enough computer to get high framerate, whenever the game loads a new chunk of the city as you drive around, the game stutters for a second, and you can kiss all hope of driving precisely in that moment goodbye. It may not sound bad, but I was always crashing into everything because of the game stuttering, and while after a certain point you get used to stuttering and can minimize its effect on your driving, you can never fully adapt to it. Speaking of crashing, you better make your desktop background something good, because with this game, you will be seeing your desktop quite a bit. This game, being a bad port from console, is probably best played with controller (though there are tweaks if you prefer keyboard and mouse) but despite this, the game doesn't show controller prompts. If you are wary about using mods, then don't buy this game, because some of the issues listed above (lack of controller prompts, some bug fixes) can be fixed by using the Gentlemen of the Row mod...Yes, they managed to screw the port up so bad you need to use mods to make it more stable. Most of my issues with this game stem from the port, only one really comes from the game itself: how easy it is to get ragdolled. I once failed a mission because I got ragdolled, and the game decided that everytime my character got up, they were just going to fall right back to the ground, while two nearby police officers laid into me with shotguns. Two enemies aren't a threat in this game, not even a little bit, yet I still died because my character decided that the pavement was the most interesting thing he had ever seen and couldn't pull himself away from it, and even when the ragdoll effect isn't glitching out, it's still annoying to get ragdolled by some enemy ramming their car into you, then pull yourself back up only to get rammed again. I have died numerous times to this and it is the only real time that the deaths felt unfair, as once that first ragdoll happened, I wasn't able to do anything to stop it happening again. Aside from occasional occurances like that where you effectively get stunlocked to death by the ragdoll effect, I really don't have anything else to complain about. If you are willing to install a mod and save obsessively to avoid losing progress when the game inevitably crashes, you will find a lot to like about Saints Row 2...Just get it on sale or something, even at the discounted standard price of $10 the port is just so bad that it isn't worth it. If you have a low spec machine or are too wary of mods, just buy SR3 instead. It's not as good, but a whole lot more stable. Something to note, however is that some people have stated that a good amount of issues with the port simply don't show up on windows 8, the game supposedly runs better and crashes less on it. I don't know how true it is, but if you are running Windows 8, it's something to consider.

I'd like to preface this review with a question about books. What makes a work of fiction a "classic" which endures generations into the future? Any novel can tell a story. A good novel spins a fantastic world in which the reader can immerse themself, lose themselves, offering an escape from a reality much messier than we would like. But a great book, a classic, is not an escape. Throughout it's fictional world are constant threads of reality, which evolve and grow leaving the reader with a new perspective on society by the end. A classic book is not an
, but rather a
reality, which seeks to enthrall the reader with it's fantastic world even as it's evolving themes crystallize into a message about the only world which really matters in the end.
Nier: Automata is one of the first examples I've seen of this social commentary in the gaming medium. Yes, you get to beat up machines with giant weapons and elegant combos, yes, you can stare at 2B's butt, and yes, the graphics (did I mention the butt?) are pretty great, but Nier: Automata isn't about any of that. Through the unique medium of a game, Nier forces your agency, making
, not some character, responsible for the events which transpire. This makes ultimate message far more personally powerful than a novel or movie adaptation ever could. You start to see hints of this distinction when you notice all the bosses are named after great philosophers or when one of the main characters drops a line like
, but the more you are drawn in the more you begin to see the tangled threads of reality which form the foundation for the game. This game is not about some perpetual war on a desecrated, fictional planet, it's about purpose, meaning, and destiny in a world which is very, very real.
A good game will show you a game can be fun, enjoyable, even addicting. Nier: Automata shows you how a game can be something more: a narrative about society, about reality, about us. It won't change your life, but it
make you think. And that, from a game, is pretty remarkable.

Villagers is strategy simulation, and no it is not a City Builder as it is stated in game tags, because you can't progress from village to city/town.. mmkay?! :)
First to say something about Banished drama stated in other reviews, it may look like it at first glance, but Villagers are far away from it. Just from start and Story Mode, Villagers are diferent kind of game, it has useful and helpful missions as tutorials, awesome artwork, characters and nice story.
If you don't want to bother with story mode, you have FreePlay mode, where you can chose one of 6-7 fixed maps, and play until you die or got borred :D
Ressources system are well optimized and with great tutorial people who are new to this type of games won't have trouble to start it.
What I think it's special about this game, it has some personal touch, for example in FreeMode you will start with 10 villagers, they will get married, you watch them grow old, their kids married have their own families and your village expands, it is nice touch to watch how families mix one with another to prospere.
Graphic has nice and quality textures and models, nothing spectacular but it is enough to please everyones taste.

+ Graphic

Maybe dev's should release this as Early Access until they add more stuff in game.

First, to address the elephant in the room that is already spamming reviews. Yes, this game is quite similar to Banished, That certainly is not a bad thing to my mind, and not at all shocking considering how broad the godgame/city manager genre is. They both focus on a similar scenario and involve many of the same resources, buildings and issues. That is not to say, as some reviewers have suggested, that this a copy of Banished. It plays and feels quite distinctive and focuses much more strongly on presentation and storytelling and less on hardcore survival.
The game is your typical village management game. Each villager is fully simulated with a day/night activity cycle. No villagers are directly controlled but rather carry out duties as assigned
For the bad, In it's current state, there are rough spots, but nothing major.
Moving on to the good, I think there is a lot to like here and promise for more as the dev's polish the title.
Certainly not a "casual" title but far more approachable than most, this title has some potential to be a great village management game. It's fully playable and far more developed than some of the "other" comparable titles that languish in perma-early access.
Current state: 7/10

Graphics and animations flat out suck.  That out of the way, your mileage with the art style may vary.  If you don't like looking at the battles, you can simply look at the summaries to see how your army fared.
Apart from that, you have the deepest turn-based strategy game available, fourth generation and better than ever for what it offers.  Easily modifiable.  There are plenty of mods available if you know where to look (start at the Desura forums for this game).  If you don't have an imagination, this game probably isn't going to come through for your inner strategy geek.  Many of the pre-made maps are beautifully realized in a variety of art styles.
The game is easy to learn, but complex.  Certain civilizations will outperform and outclass others.  The worst civilizations are there to handicap better players so that they may play with their lesser skilled friends, or simply for the challenge.
There's multiplayer mode, which is the preferred way to play the game for many.  The AI isn't perfect for those who prefer single-player, but there are ways of meta-gaming if you want to challenge yourself solo.
I'd recommend this game for anyone who can see past the game's flaws.  Perhaps wait for a sale and put this on your wishlist, but know that this game doesn't go on sale often.  If you do go full price, know that you're supporting a good indie developer that provides support for their games years after they're released.

The game doesn't run smoothly on my 4 gb ram, 2nd gen i5 processor, and 2gb NVIDIA video card laptop, even with the video settings turned down. This is the result from poor game design as other higher-end MMORPG's like guild wars 2 run fine. The game feels unresponsive and clunky, the minimap icons jump around when you move, and the camera panning isn't alinged with the cursor speed, resulting in having to move your mouse back into position after you move the camera if your mouse sensitivity is any higher than default.
The game itself looks nice enough if you can get over the standard kawaii boob-showing female characters that always tend to come with these kind of games. There is a wide variety of classes to pick from, ranging from your standard healers, buffers, tanks and dps that are designed for late-game PvE to several classes that focus on either melee or ranged AoE attacks that are likely designed for taking on larger groups of monsters to maximize leveling speeds.
The microtransaction system seems to be very ariagames-like. You will get a daily reward consisting of xp boosts and the like that you can use fom lvl 20 and up, and if you require more than that, or other luxury items like extra fast mounts or armor upgrades (call this pay to win if you like), you will have to pay real money for this.

Cons

I sincerely wish I could afford to buy every one of my friends a copy of this game.
1. To give them a chance to experience what could be Platinum's best game yet
2. To give Yoko Taro all of my damn money.
So, yeah, Nier: Automata. Sequel to 2010's Nier, which was a spinoff of the Drakengard series. Announced during Square-Enix's bizarre E3 conference in 2015, this game went under the code name Nier: New Project until its full reveal at the Paris Games Week show later in the year. It was delayed from its initial release window of November 2016 to give the team more time to work on improving gameplay balance the overall quality. Finally releasing in March of 2017, it has gone on to sell well over a million copies, making it one of Platinum's best-selling titles.
I admit I didn't know much about the game until I noticed the demo available on the PS4 store. Seeing that it was a Platinum Games title, I kinda knew what I would be in for, and that I would likely enjoy it. I decided to give it a shot one night and, needless to say, I was more than impressed. I bought it for PC right around release and have been enjoying it since.
As I said before, if you know Platinum's style, you know what to expect from a game like this. Frantic combat, a varied and dynamic soundtrack, a brilliantly-crafted story with memorable characters, and epic boss fights. But seeing as this is a Yoko Taro game, it has just the right amount of "what the ♥♥♥♥?" sprinkled in. It's equal parts heartwarming, heart-rending, hilarious, and horrifying, sometimes within the span of a few minutes.
Now, there are a couple of things that I have to mention that keep this game from being 100% perfect in my eyes:
1. The PC port is bad. It's not terrible, and I've seen much worse, but it needs work. For a while, I and many others couldn't play it due to a bug in graphics drivers causing the game to crash just from swinging around 2B's weapon. This was eventually fixed with a future driver, but there are still lingering issues that can be at least duct-taped over with the Far mod. If you get this game on Steam, you NEED the Far mod. It fixes some issues with fullscreen resolution and with stuttering during cutscenes. There are also some misc options and tweaks.
2. The second playthrough was kind of a bummer, mostly because the character you play as is weak when it comes to combat and thus relies on a separate skill to take down enemies. Basically, you better hope you're good at twin-stick shooters. If you are, well, it just gets kinda tedious. But if you can make it through that second playthrough, are you ever in for a treat!
Other than that, I can highly recommend this game. My best suggestion is to go in as blind as possible and do as many of the sidequests as possible to get the best experience. Also, the DLC isn't all that essential, but it has some fun extras like outfits and hair dyes, and a special boss fight.

This game is the greatest thing ever done to precision platformers. And I honestly don't think that's hyperbole. As for why, read on.
The Sun and Moon has the genre down to a tee. The average length of a level is about 10-15 sec, but the game still manages to make the solution to every level as interesting to plan out as it is to execute.
On top of that it's completed-bronze-silver-gold system is balanced perfectly, so that "completed" seems like something you could reasonably accomplish, whereas everything beyond that is an intimidating challenge.
What more could you need? The controls are perfectly precise, the music and artstyle are obviously subjective, but both are simple, don't get in the way, and what little is done with them, is done very, very well.
This is a perfect game, and I'm very thankful for having had the chance to play it.

One of the best FPS games I played for a long time (after DOI of course), certainly the best PvP FPS done by Tripwire ever.
The sounds are very atmospheric, all guns have "kicking" sound, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sounding or painball guns. They all kill like they are supposed to. Although I'm not a fan of the heli's (as I can't really pilot one myself), I do think they are an awsome addition to this game along with 2 classes of them: Transport and Attack. Cosmetic progression is one of the bigger plusses of this game too, as there's no more high level player BS, all clothes make you unique, but at the same time they doesn't make you invisible or give you any advantage that would make the game unfair.
But I do have some problems with this game, some of the servers lag although I get normal ping, thus making piloting heli's impossible as there's huge delay between your actions (there's a pretty delay in your actions while piloting heli in normal servers too, so it's not that really big of a problem). Placing traps, digging tunnels and destroying them is too glitchy and tricky, I hope that get's fixed eventually. One of the biggest problems I see with this game is penetration: you simply can't penetrate more than few surfaces, so even if you're shooting with AKM through 2 fences made out of stick, the bullets won't go through which is a big letdown for me... Better particle effects when you shoot things would be great too, as the effect that we get now look like everything is made out of concrete.
Long Story Short: It has minor problems that don't really effect the game that much, but the experience after playing this game is solid as a rock. 9/10 must buy for any player, that likes realistic shooters.
PS: Will probably buy it sometime in near future, but for now, free weekend will do.

Bought this game the day it came out. I've come back to it over and over again as a fun game to just pick up and putz around with. Every game is just different enough to keep you engaged, and the customization of the races creates a wide variety of playstyles that you can tailor to your own preference. Without a doubt, would recommend this game.
Pros:
-Tons of customzation with your own race and the galactic map
-Updates, bug fixes, and new content are released regularly
-Truly challenging to win a game, but rewards clever strategy
-Lots of immersion with anomalies, special events, and interaction with other empires
-There is a very talented community of players adding mods to this game, and you can incorporate elements of just about any Sci-Fi verse into your gameplay. Want to be a Salarian? Fly a Star Destroyer? Done.
Cons:
-It can be difficult to ally yourself with AI Empires, as they very stringently stick to their ethos, even in the face of overwhelming enemies. This makes stopping Endgame Crises and Awakened Empires rather difficult
-The economy is rather simple, and only grows complex after you've expanded to a point where micro-management becomes somewhat difficult
I have been really happy with each of the expansions that have come out, and am super impressed with the developer's response to player feedback. Hands down, this is one of my best Steam purchases ever and the reason that I am writing my first review.

Its been a long time since I played this game, and not because I didn't enjoy it, but because this is a game best enjoyed with friends. It's not easy to pull together three other people and coordinate them perfectly, but on those times you can, this game becomes an amazing experience, and that is also the draw of the game.
I can't think of any other multiplayer experience that got me more emotionally invested than this game. It's easy to become lost in the moment and immersion as you battle other ships, and almost get into the character of your crew. The intensity of holding on for dear life as you desparately put out fires and hold the ship together with duct tape nails can certainly tease out rage, but more than that too. The damaging of components means that as you pilot the ship, it realistically begins to become crippled and loses mobility, and you have to compensate due to damaged motors or inactive guns. And speaking of guns, each one is unique and effective at different  things, and learning which gun does what, and what ammo to use with it at certain times is a skill in itself. And when you actually pull together and gun down an enemy ship, blowing it out of the sky, it's one of the best best feelings I've had in a video game.
My favourite ship was the Spire, and maybe one day, I can get my crew back together and InSPIRE them to glory once more.
Heh...
Anywho, my views and feelings might be outdated, but assuming the core gameplay is still the same, I'd recomend this game to anyone with a lot of time, friends and patience.

Keep in mind, I don't usually play strategy games of any sort.  They're not the sort of games I generally enjoy playing, as they have a tendency to become boring and repetitive very fast.
That being said, I adore Stellaris.  While the concept of space strategy isn't new, this one was the only one that drew me in.  There's a ton of content (with more being put out fairly often) and enough events and interesting encounters in the game to keep me hooked even ~300 hours in.  That's a bit low of a number in comparison for people who DO usually play these types of games, but for someone like me, that's a lot.
I put the disclaimer about my inexperience of strategy games to warn the fact that I cannot reasonably critique things such as the combat and military systems that people often complain about.  Personally, the level of micromanagement is fine for me, but for others it may not be - and that may be up to your personal preference.  Mostly, I enjoyed the exploration and colonization aspects of the game.  I enjoyed finding anomalies and event chains with interesting stories that could sometimes even change depending on what kind of empire you're running.  I enjoyed creating different empire types every time and experimenting with the huge amount of options the game offers.
Overall, there's a lot of fun to be had, and if you like strategy games, give it a try.  Perhaps think about it even if you don't - like I did!  You might be pleasantly surprised.

There is a lot of comparison between Villagers and Banished. The similarities are both there and not there. Seeming how they are both medeival builders there is always going to be similarities. Meanwhile most those spouting the similarities avoid the simple answer. Which would you rather play Banished or Villagers? Since I own both I would pick Banished even without mods.
So why the thumbs dumb?
1. Maps. The game does NOT have a random map generator. I mean seriously, that is the majority of the replay value of any sandbox builder game. There is no map editor either.
2. Production balance. After playing a while the production values of various buildings seem very wonky and unbalanced.
- Barn had animals that pretty much died of old age before producing enough offspring to keep the barn producing.
- Other production issues resolved.
3. Combat. They tried putting some form of combat into the game.  Wild animal attacks and raiders. Honestly never should have bothered. Neither raiders or wild animals actually killed any villagers so kinda not seeing the point in investing in guards. It looks like the raiders basically ran in stole some stuff and ran off with it.
4. No refilling jobs. Anyone who played Banished knows this one. If a villager dies their job should be automatically filled from the pool of available laborers. Not having that feature in this game made it annoying once your settlers start dying off and you miss filling their job.
5. Bugs. Quite a few have been fixed however still a couple big ones that can ruin a game through population aging and starvation.
The game is getting better, there has been work on it since release. It just aint quite there yet I would recommend people to buy it. However if I knew someone that bought it, I would not make fun of them for owning a crappy game. So almost a thumbs up.

A Banished free review, since I haven’t played it.
Villagers is pretty simple, yet not so simple at the same time. The game is set in medieval times and as such life is not great, you’re constantly raided, food shortages, harsh winters and you’re spread very thin as you try and get your village together. I wouldn’t call this a city builder, more like a simulation of medieval life.
The game is harsh, you play for hours for 2-3 babies to be born, and hopefully they can survive through the winter before their mother gets attacked by wild wolves. Resources are limited and with a very small starting population it’s hard to cover all the bases. You’ll be spending your first years with a dozen people, with those dozen people they need to be set roles that all need to be filled, someone die? Well that just means you’re going to have to have no baths this month. Have everyone in your turn working jobs and no one to be a guardsmen? Pray to god you don’t get raided.
Outside of the harsh setting the game itself doesn’t lend itself to being easy to play. Poor AI leads to a lot of wasted time and with poor explanations on a lot of the jobs a wasted opportunity. I’ve seen farmers for days straight just walk around my city as there are crops that need watering and picking. Sawmill worker, whose job is to plant and cut down trees, sleep in front of the town hall as there are no trees planted in my set area.
The game is rough, there’s no denying that but I did enjoy playing the game. I liked the idea of being put into a harsh setting where it wasn’t all big city lights or not handed to me on a plate. In saying that I felt my time could have been much more enjoyable with a few changes here and there. At the price point maybe it’s an avoid for now, check out a sale in the future and see kind of thing.
If you’re still undecided I have a playthrough on Villagers which probably explains the game positives and negatives better than I can.

Reviewed 2 weeks prior to initial release. Unfortunatly at this time a I can't recommend Villagers, it just needs a bit more work. I made a video review to better showcase the aesthetics and gameplay mechanics, if you prefer a written review you can find that below.
Villagers is a town building game by indie developer Bumblebee, it focuses on village expansion and resource collection while also trying to keep your citizens happy and well fed.
I’m reviewing this game in mid March 2016, about 2 weeks before the game is officially released on the 25th of March. Which technically makes this a pre-release review but I think we can safely assume there’s not going to be any major changes in such a short amount of time. I should also mention that the developer sent me a review code for this game, I’d like to think it hasn’t biased my opinions but I thought I should disclose it anyway. The current version number I’m reviewing is 1.003.
Aesthetics
First off, Villagers looks absolutely beautiful. There seems to be two ways you could go with this kind of genre, either a cartoon or a realistic aesthetic. The realistic style works really well here and looks very nice. It runs very nicely too, I don’t have the best gaming PC but I have everything cranked to ultra and I’ve had no problems with it whatsoever. The minimum requirements needed to run this game are very easily achievable.
The boarders in this game are fantastic; the maps are surrounded by an ‘old-timely’ grid reference which gives it the feel of a ‘live action’ ordinance survey map on the table of an inn. I’m not sure if that’s ever been done before but I’ve never seen it.  It addresses a sometimes overlooked aspect of RTS games – “What in particular defines that as the boarder?” and “Why is that side of the field more important than the other side?” It would be cool if the developers took this one step further and added big pints of beer in the background or rulers and a compass etc.
Gameplay
Villagers looks very similar to the game Banished. And I think that statement translates over to the gameplay as well. There are a lot of mechanics that are very similar to Banished and even when Banished was first released, people were saying “Hey this is a good game, but it’s going to take the modding community to make it into a great game”. Comparing the day one releases of Banished and Villagers, Villagers is a lot less ‘fleshed out’ and personally I think it’s the lesser of the two. On top of that Banished has had a 2 year lead with the modding community, which have helped to iron out any initial problems with the game and add a lot more content.
Villagers also has a problem with the pace of its gameplay, things seem to happen very slowly – especially at the start. This is the kind of game that you could set up and leave for 20 minutes or half an hour and when you come back you’ve made some nice progress. Admittedly I’ve never made a large village which I assume would help to speed up the gameplay to a more enjoyable pace. However at that point, due to the lack of content, you’ve probably built all the available buildings anyway. The most villagers I’ve ever had at once was about 20 but there are steam achievements that go all the way up to 100. Thankfully there’s the option to speed the gameplay up x10 but I don’t think that’s enough, perhaps x25 would help to remedy the initial slow pace of the game.
There are two main gameplay modes available; the first is freeplay which is pretty self-explanatory but I’ll touch on that later. The second is the campaign, which also doubles as the tutorial, so if you do buy this game I’d recommend you play the campaign first. I’m hesitant to call the campaign a glorified tutorial because the narrative is so strong. Personally I actually really enjoyed the campaign and I’d have to say hats off to the developer Bumblebee for making a really interesting narrative, especially in the genre of game where you are essentially just building a town over and over with different objectives. That’s not to say that everyone will enjoy it, I’m sure you can imagine there’s a huge about of writing needed to spin a good plot into a town building game, none of which is voice acted at all so there’s a lot of reading involved. The entire campaign has six levels and probably took me around 4-5 hours to complete, which is a testament to both the amount of reading involved and the slow pace of the gameplay. There’s a funny part early on in the campaign where it explains about the foresters’ lodge which can plant trees to be later harvested, technically those trees should take 20 or 30 years to grow which completely contradicts the narrative, but they just point at it and joke about and don’t even attempt to avoid it.
There are three main building materials in this game, wood and stone can be used for most buildings and iron is needed for more advanced buildings. There are also three main ways of getting these resources, the first is to just pillage the land of what’s lying around, you can get wood and stone this way but not iron. The second way to get resources is to build a structure, I’ve already mentioned the foresters lodge for wood but to extract stone and iron from your map you’re going to have to build a mine, which can only be built in a very specific location. I’m bringing this up because the freeplay maps are exactly the same as the 5 maps available in the campaign. Early on in the campaign when it hasn’t explained about mines yet, there’s no need for the maps to have the specific locations where you can build mines. Which means that if you go to play that map in freeplay, you’re limited to the third way of gathering resources which is through a merchant at the warehouse. Which is a shame because the first map of the campaign is probably my favourite, but the very limited method of resource collection makes the gameplay incredibly slow. There’s obviously an easy fix that the developers or modders can do, just add those mining areas to the initial maps and the maps will be much more enjoyable.
Summary
At the moment I don’t think I can recommend Villagers and I feel terrible for saying that because this game has been developed by a small indie company who have obviously put a lot of work into it. It just needs a little bit more work, there are some problems to address, some bugs to iron out and there’s definitely some more content to add.
I Hope you found this review helpful!

This game can be pretty enjoyable for a few hours, and it's somewhat memorable. I'll go over its notable aspects here.
The story is pretty much as basic as it can get, cliché even. However, I was satisfied with how they handled it in implementation. Whoever designed the story segments was well aware that nobody would care. Instead of shoving some bland exposition down your throat while you slump lifelessly over your keyboard and wonder if playing through this game is a commitment you're willing to make, it provides the story in short, quickly skippable (or quickly readable) lines of text. You can get through it in a few seconds, and you're not missing much if you ignore it entirely. The gist is that you're a spaceman on a foreign planet and need to kill some guy. Narrative gold.
The pixel art isn't bad. It's not anything special. It's not too repetitive. Sprites gel pretty well with each other, but tile sprites stick strictly to their square shape and corners aren't adorned in any way to reduce the jaggedness of such defined tiles. All of the main character's animations are so beautifully fluid, though, and the walking animation is adorable.
The music is pretty average. Sometimes it gets better, but it gets redundant and loses its charm as it loops. In the game's store page description, it throws around names such as Cave Story. If they're going to tote around a reference to a game like that, I think it's only fair to interpret that as a standard to hold their game to. It falls abysmically below this standard.
Controls feel fine and function as intended. Some precision is required, but it's not unforgiving.
This is the good bit. The game is based on traversing through puzzles using a simple mechanic: You can fire projectiles horizontally. When these projectiles impact something, you are teleported to the point of impact. Combine this with precision platforming and quick thinking, and you can pull off some neat stunts. New objects are introduced that add more depth to the puzzles. For example, there are colored beams that can destroy, obstruct, or even redirect your shots. These can be toggled by switches or obstructed by objects. I think the store page description's comparison of this game to Portal is actually pretty fair. While the mechanics and dimensionality are different, they require the same kind of problem solving and reflex. The teleportation gun is ineffective as a weapon, however, which brings us to...
At first, you have to avoid enemies entirely because you lack a means of removing them. At some point, your character aquires a new tool: a firearm. Now, the first thing you'd want to do is go out and start packing heat at anything that looks like it could accommodate a few bullets, but you'd soon find out that your shiny new baby isn't very empowering. There are only a few types of enemies. Some exist to serve as barriers in the puzzles, and your weapon is only a tool for removing them. The rest exist just so that there are enemies. They're usually not challenging or unique, but I suppose they do add some variance. You can collect hidden items to increase the number of hits you can take, but health isn't really something that needs to be managed. Other than the boss battle, the combat isn't explored past this.
I'd like to point out that the store page description also points to Super Metroid, and again interpret such a reference as justification to compare these games both ways. Again, it's not even a close comparison.
At the end, you have to utilize both your teleport gun and firearm to battle the main antagonist by moving around the room to dodge attacks and position yourself to have a clear shot. This part is actually quite well done, but I was not at all prepared for what came next. That's covered in...
Puzzles can be pretty creative. They're typically not too difficult, and checkpoints are generous enough to ensure that you're not getting frustrated about replaying the same sections. Puzzles frequently introduce new ways to utilize the tools that you already have, rarely feeling repetitive. If you're observant and think a little more to get to alternate paths, you can get rewarded with items, even if they're not always useful. The puzzles are overall satisfying and engaging.
The largest and ugliest flaw of this game is its length. When I reached the end, I was unsure if I was just misinterpreting what was going on. It was just so absurdly short. It was a decent ride, though.
Now, I'd like to explain how it pulls off this ending. In the last section, I mentioned a boss battle in which you use what you've gained to take out the main antagonist. After he's defeated, you get out of there, walk a screen or two, and then it slams into you so unnervingly hard. Suddenly, the quite enjoyable puzzle platformer I was playing now has me careening through space in my ship, toe to toe with another.
I am now suddenly playing a side-scrolling shoot 'em up sequence. There is no similar puzzle mechanic or anything. There's just dodging and mashing to spam bullets. I personally do not enjoy shmups. I barely play them, and when I do, they do not entertain me. I didn't know that I was in for this when I played through a puzzle-oriented "action platformer," as the store page describes it.
Anyway, maybe I just suck at these things, but I didn't have the motivation to power through that final boss battle. I got someone else to help me out with the mashing part, just for the sake of completion.

If you are a mythology buff like I am who also happens to enjoy games like those in Sid Meier's Civilization series (or Conversely Europa Universalis/Crusader Kings), as well as nigh on Dwarf fortress level learning curves, then this is the game for you.
- Preposterously deep (multiple ways to play an asthma attack inducing number of different races)
- Mouth wateringly creative (A million spells of varying effects and quality)
- The game really caters to the modding community. Lots of great stuff out there.
- Faithfully (pun intended) retains the mythological feel of the various ancient faiths the game portrays.
Let me emphasize. There is no mythological figure too obscure. There is no faith's boogeymen left unjustly translated without all their crazy weird abilities. From sorcerous glamours, to shape shifting wolves/snakes/dragons, to religion not spreading unless you sacrifice some father's daughter at the altar of good intentions.
However it's not without flaws.
- Civ 2 era graphics.
- It's not so much a learning curve as it is a learning cliff. With poisonous thorns growing up it and a pit of sharp legos below just waiting for your to fall.
- Some nations can be more than a little imbalanced (Poor EA R'lyeh comes to mind).
- Pretty pricey at 'half a Triple A game sans DLC'.
Bottom Line: If you've ever wanted to feel like a callous vindictive divine entity with absolutely no regard for the well being of your people beyond their immediate use for dying in your glorious name, then look no further than Doms4.
It's the authentic god experience.

You are a god, one of a pantheon of many.  The Pantokrator, your Zeus, has for whatever reason gone AWOL, so like any good subservient god, you and your entire pantheon try to usurp his throne in his absense in a divine battle royale to claim the world, inevitably tearing it apart in the process.
Underneath the simple, almost retro 2.5d graphics, the clunky user interface, and all of the strange idiosyncracies in this game lies an extremely deep and varied turn based strategy game.  You begin as a patron god of one about 50 nations, each with a rich history, backstory, and set of quirks, and through your loyal believers, you take out the other gods by converting his believers, running them down with their military might, or by claiming enough thrones of ascension on the map.  Along the way, you use diplomacy and magic to gain every advantage you can, right up to and including casting spells that bend reality in your favor.
This is the only game I have ever played where I've had armies of naked women fight on my behalf, made trees sing praises in my name, turned the earth into a desolate wasteland in like ten different ways, stole the sun out of the sky, been a sun with arms, befriended water, and made a knight that lives in a coat pocket that lives on a diet of lint.

The interface is not modern. The graphics are not modern. But none of that matters.
Tell me one other game where you can say "I'm playing the God King Magus of Rome, fielding hundreds of individual troops against the vile threat of an army of undead" Or "I'm playing as the literal word of god, burned into creation by the creator himself, leading armies of angels against an army of devils".
Not only do both of those situations happen in this game, but everything is still somehow well balanced. Armies can be completely different, but still end up having both interesting battles and strategy behind it all. With a level of attention to detail that no other game even comes close to.

The German kingdom of Ulm knew what had to be done. After several stinging defeats to the Giants, their once proud realm stood on the edge of defeat. To the southwest, Hochmeister Sangerhausen, the leader of the Black Templars had slowly but surely secured Roskva from the slavic heathens of Bogarus to the south.
Soon, these fools would see the light of Ulm. They would see the light of their true God. He knows if you are sleeping; he knows if you're awake; he knows if you've been bad or good, so be good for goodness sake.
For when you are bad, as these slavs had been in the eyes of our Lord, he will come for you.
He is KRAMPUS, THE GREAT HORNED ONE, TRUE SUCCESSOR TO THE PANTAKRATOR'S THRONE.
Unfortunately, His Great finds himself in dire straights against his Giant foes. The Kingdom, however, was far too few of infantry, after having lost so many grave Ulmers by the giant scum.
He knew what had to be done. "Commander," Krampus said, his voice deep and raspy, "gather every criminal you see. Then lead them in the front lines."

Strongly Avoid, this game was released half finished.  While it is largly stable and bug-free it is a mess on nearly every level in terms of strategic depth, Interface, AI and performance.  Any Civilization game would be a better investment as well as numerous much cheaper 4X games.
A year after release none of the half-baked systems have been fixed, instead Paradox releases 'updates' which add new half-baked mechanics of no originality and cosmetic DLC packages to nickel and dime us.
Space combat consists of huge blob fleets that engage each other with no tactical depth, ability to retreat or even tell why your winning or losing.  No viable defensive strategy exists other then having a bigger fleet and losing said fleet is basicly fatal.  Weapons and ship design are so poor that high tech ships are actually worse then low tech ones.
Planetary development is borring and tedious, no meaningfull specialization is possible on planets as their are only minerals, energy, food to collect and this are pooled globally.  Mineral and Energy arn't even meaningfully different as you require both to do build/maintaine everything, they could be combined into 1 resource with virtually no effect on the game.
As your Empire grows you are forced to turn over most of your planets to AI managment which is cripplingly stupid, the game admits as much when it give you the right to manage more of your own planets as a powerfull Bonus perk.  Enemy AI is likewise stupid but simply loaded up with free resources to make it competetive.
No Espionage system exists whatsoever, diplomacy is thin, no UN or galactic council like mechanism exists for diplomatic victory.  AI attitudes are skitzophrenic so no matter how generous you are allies always turn on you.  Techs are shallow in their effects, +1 to this +1 to that, nothing that makes the game feel different at any point.
Leaders are a pain to aquire, die rapidly and develop without any input from the player.  Government and Ethics have almost no effect on how you play the game even when at 'fanatical' levels.  AI will still hate you for having different ethics in a robotic and arbitrary way regardless of how your actually playing.
Paradox decided that RTS meand 'Real time story' as their are more narrative elements delivered via popups then their are strategy elements in the game.  The science vessel based exploratiof of 'anomalies' is almost fun the first hour of the game then gets tedious to discover +1 mineral on a planet for the 50th time.  Well more then HALF of all the post release DLC and updates are aimed at adding more story elements, fixing core cludge elements not so much.
And last but not least the recently announced removal of 2 of the games original 3 methods of FTL is a last straw.  Instead their will be only 'starlanes' thus one of the BULLET POINTED selling points of the game will be eviserated along with any hope that Paradox would fuffill the trust put in it to 'support' their product post release and actually finish the game.
