Ok, so having purchased the game this morning and played about 8 hours worth today here are things I've experienced and thoughts on the game.
For those who think this is a banished clone, to some degree it is.  Same concept, basically same building types also.  Better graphics for sure.
Campaign mode:  if your a reader and like lots of story line content then campaign mode will please you.  Personally I found the story dialog banter wanter to long and tedious.  Some story cut scenes required 20+ OK button clicks to get through it all before you get back to building.
Free Play Mode:  As expected a sandbox mode.  Where it lacks is that it only provides 5 different maps to choose from.  Unlike Banished where your world terrain is generated dyamically.  Once you try all 5 map scenarios returning to the game is repeat.  Not only is the world terrain the same for each map, so are the resources allocated to your game session.  So you will nothing new replaying a map.
Potential bugs I found:
After playing one free play map for about 3 hours at 5X time speed I STILL haven't progressed passed 20 villagers.  I've built just about all the types of building that could be built.  Half of them sit empty because by the time an infact grows to adult hood 1 or 2 of your working adults dies from one reason or another.  Usually natural causes.
Merchants arrived only 2 times within the first 30 minutes of game play.  Once I upgraded my fishing pier to level 2 not only did the trader boats that were passing by stop coming by completely so did the land merchants.  So Gold income has completed stopped.  Thankfully I purchased some livestock before that happened.
Speaking of livestock, I purchased two chickens and two pigs.  Chickens are supposed to reproduce rapidly but I have found the pigs repoduce more than the chickens and within the hour I have a barn full of pigs and no chickens because the shepard killed them all for no known reason.  I checked and had plenty of food so it wasnt due to food needs.
All my villagers complain early for wanting a bath, which by the way is maybe the most expensive building to erect resource wise.  With a quarry built on a a stone outcropping that contains 150 stone resources, once my total stored stone resources reaches 40 no more stone is mined from the quarry therefore never allowing me to build the bath which requires 70 stone in total.  I have a town hall that currently holds 0/15 stone resources, a warehouse that current holds 12/30 stone resources and the quarry itself which is maxed out storage wise with 32/32.  I have 3 warehouse workers allocated but noone ever moves the stone from the quarry to the warehouse or townhouse so the quarry just grinds to a halt.  This is a bug with AI I am very sure.
SO... first impressions are mixed.  If the developers continue forward with this release, adding omre free play scenarios or a dynamic worl generator that will do alot for game play longetivity.  Clearly there are bugs needing resolved.  Lastly the game is badly in need of some game balancing such as I pointed out previously, population increase TEDIOUSLY slow to the point of making the game almost not enjoyable once you've got around to building enough resources to support the 15 - 20 villagers you manage to expand to.  BTW.. thats a total of 20 villagers after 3 hours of game play and the free play mode starts you out with 10!
While 16.99 isn't a lot of money I found myself wondering if I my money would have been better spent on another less than 20 dollar game here on Steam.
All that said I am hoping for an looking forward to seeing if the developers continue to expand on it.

If you're a visual person, I made a video of my review, which can be found here:
Today we'll be checking out a brand new Medieval Village Building Simulator appropriately named, Villagers.  Villagers is a colorful new city builder/manager with a sense of humor.  I consider Villagers to be the Zack Morris of City Building Simulators, as it has absolutely no qualms with breaking the fourth wall and making fun of itself with a lot of light-hearted humor.  Everything from how exactly trees grow so fast to be harvested to the various menu options are discussed by the well drawn and colored characters that tell the story of a young city Builder, which is of course your Hero.
For the review we'll be looking at four basic categories, Gameplay, Sound, Look, and Polish.
The gameplay of Villagers is fairly intuitive.  The controls are responsive and simplistic, with the left mouse button often selecting whatever it is you are clicking on, and the right mouse button deselecting.  The tutorial is extremely thorough, to some, maybe even too much so, but it nonetheless does an excellent job at teaching one how to access various menus, construct buildings, assign villagers to various professions, and utilize the different resources found in the game.  The gameplay of Villagers can be quickened or slowed with the help of convenient fast forward and pause buttons, which are a very welcome part of the game.  The gameplay of Villagers is both fun and fulfilling, with enough variance due to the inclusion of a story mode as well as a free mode.  The only issue is that the story mode is extremely short, giving most players approximately 3-4 hours of gameplay.
8/10
The music, ambient background sounds, and various effects are one of Villagers greatest successes.  The effects utilized for accessing menus, making selections, and moving through options are perfect.  The music itself is rich, appropriate for the setting, and very tastefully done.  The ambient background sounds are good, with various cheers, coughs, crowded talking, as well as effects for the buildings and even the more obscure actions, such as the firing of a hunter's bow.
9/10.
The game is crisp and colorful.  The animations are smooth and the addition of various wardrobes dependent upon the profession is a welcome attention to detail.  The “map”, being represented as if it were a drawn cartographers map come to life on a tabletop is a fresh look at the very word itself.  The animations for the villagers are basic, stiff, and a bit repetitive, but still somewhat appropriate for the tasks that they complete in their daily routines.  The inclusion of snow accurately falling on horizontal surfaces during the winter, as well as the flash of lightning, the obscurity of fog, and the pelting of rain creates reasonably believable seasons.  The artwork of the game is professional and well drawn, with the coloring and shading done in an aesthetically pleasing manner.  All in all, the animations and artwork are not perfect, it is clear that effort went into producing a strong quality.
7/10.
The game suffers from great polish in some places, and a lack of polish in others.  Now, some of these issues may be fixed in time, but I'll mention them as they are now.  The name I had chosen for my character, although absurdly lengthy, could not at all fit in the placard upon which it was placed.  This caused the letters to flood over the sides, creating a very amateurish look.  The animations themselves, while appropriate in action as I said before, are not at all in the correct direction or area.  For instance, a hunter hunting a boar will fire an arrow to the right, but the boar to the left will die.  The various screens, options, clicking reticules etc are well done, and the script is mostly well written.  There was at least one area that I found where a portion of text in the story script was placed in the game twice, as if it was cut and pasted into the game two times.
6/10
Overall, Villagers is a solid Medieval Town Simulator for an Independent Developer style of game.  There are areas to improve, but the attention to detail and the eccentricity of the game is very welcome.
7.5/10

THIS IS NOT A BANISHED CLONE.
Villagers is a God Game. The similarities to Banished are minorly asthetic, and the characteristics that come with it being a god game.
Where Banished is a punishing and intense game that requires extreme dedication and time; Villagers gives you a bit more of a break and lets you discover things with a bit more time to breathe.
Also not included in Banished is the story mode you get with Villagers. Its great to discover how you've become the planner of your cities and why you are trying to protect your people. This is also a wonderful introduction to the mechanics of the game.
And various other differences arise as you play through the game. Most notable is dealing with merchants is done with coin, rather than a straight recource barter. This is nice because you can use what is at your disposal to pool one recource for trading with wandering merchants.
TL:DR  Villagers only looks a little like Banished and plays similarly due to them being connected through genre. There are many different and exciting things to discover within this game and should not be written off as just another clone.

Extremely high quality game.
- Very unique, team-based gameplay with enough roles that there's something for everyone.
- High skill ceiling, especially for captains.
- Entry skill isn't terribly high. As long as you can move and whack things, you can engineer. As long as you can point and click, you can gunner. There is more to it, though -- you don't spend 40 hours as Engineer if all you get to do is whack things, and I have spent 40 hours as Engineer.
- Devs are extremely polite and (as far as I can tell) well-intentioned.
- The community is extremely polite and will usually help you out if you ask.
A few points against buying:
- Playing solo is a non-option. If you can't work together, you will die together.
- There are few people, and the ones that stick around are really good (hence, skill ceiling). However, if you take a low-stress role, like not captain, you can still reliably win games. I usually don't consider player count, because considering it is the very reason games like these have a low player count.
If you do buy:
- Yes, you might need to make a firewall rule to actually connect.
- The window in Windows machines often times renders wierd, at least for me. Use "-screen-fullscreen 1" to fix this.
- Yes, you do need to make an account outside of Steam.
- There are extremely helpful tutorials that take 30 minutes. So about $5, if you're measuring it in time. Unfortunately they're buried behind a few menus. Find them. It is well worth your time.
- If you're fortunate enough to buy during a rush period (like a sale), the game will, by default, put you in your first ~25 matches against bots. You can and should override this (once you're comfortable with basic gameplay) by entering the "Match List" right underneath the "Play" button.
- Join the faction your friends joined. Otherwise, pick the one you like the most. It makes less difference than Pokemon GO's, if you're sticking with Online only.
- Take a look around the GUI. As of right now it's not welcoming, but it is practical (and, as with most things, you can get used to it.)
- Don't stare at broken systems, dangit. Fix something else.

Out There Somewhere is a 2014 platformer developed by unknown studio Miniboss. Another in a long line of Super Metroid lookalikes, it's enjoyed some success mainly due to being incredibly cheap.
But rather then simply riding on the coattails of Super Metroid (or Knytt, as it were), Out There Somewhere proves to be an enjoyable linear puzzle platformer, with a teleportation mechanic that features conservation of momentum similar to Portal (though the two have no real similarity beyond that).  It's no metroidvania by any stretch of the imagination - most of the "upgrades" are for an endgame effect that doesn't amount to much, and outside of that venture there's a total of 5 collectibles.
Instead of playing a retro pixel wannabe, I played a well-paced linear adventure, that nevertheless isn't perfect.
Most of the pacing is due to just how short it is - a playthrough won't run you longer than an hour (15 minutes if you know what you're doing) and the sheer lack of enemy variety becomes apparent on subsequent playthroughs. Add to that, that while the sprites are well designed and look quite nice on inspection (thankfully, not using the retro clause of pixel art to turn out subpar product) the very poorly handed tiling and lack of visual noise make the game's art look much more amateur than it really is.
This is most readily apparent during the intro and outro space battles. With a closer look, you can see the spaceships slowly rotating, the metal sheens and the sci fi aesthetic shining through, when taken as a whole it looks so empty and barren that you could mistake it for a first-year highschooler's Game Maker project.
These aren't particularly pressing issues; Out There Somewhere suffers from a lack of talking points. This isn't a particularly interesting game, and for all the secrets thrown into its linear world or the cool design of the protagonist, if this game hadn't gone for 20 cents then I wouldn't be recommending it. I wouldn't have even bought it. I've played Newgrounds games with more lasting value.
At $5, I wouldn't recommend it unless you're the type that goes for 100% completion. At the ridiculous sales price, I fully recommend Out There Somewhere as a snack-sized short romp to pace out the larger, more memorable videogames.

I love strategy games. LOVE THEM. My favourites from the last twenty years include (in order) Age of Wonders III, Zeus: Master of Olympus, Crusader Kings II, Seven Kingdoms II, and Warlords III. Strategy fans will know that that's a fairly ecclectic mix of strategy sub-genres. Well, three days after purchasing Dominions 4 I can safely say that it has a place somewhere near the top of my list. I can't stop playing this game.
I'd heard whispers about the Dominions series down through the years. Legend had it that it was the most hardcore of the hardcore. In all honesty its reputation was rather intimidating. The ancient sages were right: I was baffled for my first three games. However, don't think that it's a project to merely get into Dominions 4. It really isn't. The appropriate phrase is, "easy to learn, difficult to master." That's Dominions 4.
The supreme god who brought order to the universe has disappeared, leaving it to a bunch of pretender gods to fight it out for His former position. You are one of those pretenders. Your first decisions will include what faction you want to control, which age of time you wish to play in, what physical form you'll take in the world, and how your influence will impact the lands under your dominion. The depth behind these choices alone is awesome.
Once you've chosen one of the many pre-made maps (or generated a random one) and have customised the scenario settings to your liking, it's time to conquer the world one province at a time until you've claimed the required number of Thrones of Ascension. Though even the victory condition is customisable.
In the process of doing this you'll command mighty armies, raise glorious heroes, spread the truth of your holy word, cast powerful spells, quell uprisings, contend with the fickle hand of fate in the form of random events, forge magic items, manage the economics of your realm, and a whole load more. This truly is one of those games that makes it impossible for you to keep track of time while you're playing. You may think that the graphics are simplistic (and they are), but trust me, after five minutes I don't see pixels anymore. All I see are my Atlanteans (or "Atlantians" as these developers have it) emerging from the ocean to crush all before them. I can't remember the last game I played that was so immersive. Your expectations would be better adjusted by considering Dominions 4 a board game with animated battles.
One thing that made me hesitate to buy the game were the number of reviews (positive ones) that cast a negative light on the single-player. This concerned me since I never have any interest in multiplayer whatsoever and only buy games for solo play. I'm very glad I decided to take a risk because the AI is a worthy opponent even on "Normal" difficulty. Looking through the updates I can see that a lot of work has been done on the AI since the time of release which probably accounts for the earliest reviews complaining about it and my experience towards the end of 2015 being totally different.
By this point in my review you'll probably already know whether or not this is the game for you, but let me share some of the cool elements in Dominions 4. You can rename not only your pretender god, but also any of your commanders. The factions in the game (there's loads of them) are all totally unique and change depending on the age you choose to play in. Those factions are all based on mythology from around our world, meaning you can live out your Arthurian or Atlantean fantasies (you have them too, right?) Your heroes can get wounded, which may involve losing one or more limbs. Characters will age and can weaken as they get older before finally dying, however some species live longer than others. The combat is detailed to the point that each unit not only has specified methods of attack, but does particular types of damage too. You can fight on the ocean floor, and some factions are aquatic. The music is wonderful.
In conclusion, Dominions 4 is one of those games that you come away from with a thousand hilarious and tragic tales to tell. It's perfect for emergent storytelling. In terms of being a strategy game, yes it's highly complicated and very deep, but it doesn't put a brick wall in front of you. With each game you play you'll utilise the latest thing you've learned until at last you understand the dynamics in play. This discovery process doesn't make you groan at the prospect of facing it; it excites you and makes you want to learn more. You'll be thinking about potential strategies as you lie in bed at night. The fact that the entire Dominions series is created by just two guys (under the company name "Illwinter Game Design") makes all the great aspects of the game even more amazing.
On a final note: I've ordered the physical manual available from the game's website. Doing such a thing is unheard of for me, but Dominions 4 is so good it's worth it.

I sincerely wish I could afford to buy every one of my friends a copy of this game.
1. To give them a chance to experience what could be Platinum's best game yet
2. To give Yoko Taro all of my damn money.
So, yeah, Nier: Automata. Sequel to 2010's Nier, which was a spinoff of the Drakengard series. Announced during Square-Enix's bizarre E3 conference in 2015, this game went under the code name Nier: New Project until its full reveal at the Paris Games Week show later in the year. It was delayed from its initial release window of November 2016 to give the team more time to work on improving gameplay balance the overall quality. Finally releasing in March of 2017, it has gone on to sell well over a million copies, making it one of Platinum's best-selling titles.
I admit I didn't know much about the game until I noticed the demo available on the PS4 store. Seeing that it was a Platinum Games title, I kinda knew what I would be in for, and that I would likely enjoy it. I decided to give it a shot one night and, needless to say, I was more than impressed. I bought it for PC right around release and have been enjoying it since.
As I said before, if you know Platinum's style, you know what to expect from a game like this. Frantic combat, a varied and dynamic soundtrack, a brilliantly-crafted story with memorable characters, and epic boss fights. But seeing as this is a Yoko Taro game, it has just the right amount of "what the ♥♥♥♥?" sprinkled in. It's equal parts heartwarming, heart-rending, hilarious, and horrifying, sometimes within the span of a few minutes.
Now, there are a couple of things that I have to mention that keep this game from being 100% perfect in my eyes:
1. The PC port is bad. It's not terrible, and I've seen much worse, but it needs work. For a while, I and many others couldn't play it due to a bug in graphics drivers causing the game to crash just from swinging around 2B's weapon. This was eventually fixed with a future driver, but there are still lingering issues that can be at least duct-taped over with the Far mod. If you get this game on Steam, you NEED the Far mod. I am a Telltale games aholic and when I saw this game I had a bad feeling about it. Because minecraft seemed like possible the worst IP to make a story based game around. However, I decided to give it a chance as so far Telltales borderlands which I also thought was a bad IP for telltale so far has been done surprsingly well. However my fears were confirmed this time. This is by far the worst Telltale game made yet and has so far and is bad enough to be a embarissment to their company. This game compared to all the other IPs they have purchesed in the past is the most obvious cash grab and Telltale was unfortnatlly not able to make the IP work with their game play style this time.
There are many negatives about this game...
1. It has a very bland and predictable story line and charcters. In other games this would not be that big a deal however since telltale games are entierly story driven this really is a huge deal breaker.

2. You have much less controll over what your charcter does and what they say than other telltale games. You will see obvious traps ahead and want to prevent them but will have no means to do so or wish for your charecter to do or say something different and not have the option to do it much more often than any other telltale game.  I understand that most telltale choices are only giving you a veil of choice however the veil in this game is way to easy to see through.
3. The few big choices the game lets you make that actually make a bit of a difference are much easier and unimportant than the other telltale games. They do not make you have the feeling of regreting your choice as the other IPs have. Nor do they have me think about what choice to make and the possible consquences for at least a good 5 minates like some of the other IPs often do as the choices are not only easier but also seem less important.
4. The game makes occsional minor mistakes in which skin for differnet items you should have forgetting your past choices which if followed you should have a different skin for that item.
Currnetly I would only recommend this game under 2 conditions.
#1 You are one of the young zeolous minecraft fanatics and love anything that has anything to do with minecraft in which case you already purchased the game anyway so your pretty much only reading negative comments to defend it.
#2 You are like me a telltale junkie and have already purchased all the other telltale games including similar games that are not telltale like life is strange and are desperate as hell waiting for more, have good amount of free time and disposable income. Ok my biggest gripe with this game is the pacing, One minute you are overwhelmed with things to do and having a blast sending your science ship out to go research and discover new worlds and the next you are just sitting there staring at the screen with literally no user actions to make. Compare this to other E4x games like Civ 5, sins of a solar empire and even Empire at War (not really an E4X in the slightest). All of these games are able to keep you engaged in everything that is going on Civ 5 uses an entirely turn based setup to ensure that you always feel you need to be doing things. SOASE:R keeps players engaged via research, development, and later combat (although it may have its own minor downsides). EAW has a brilliant yet frustrating real time galaxy map that pauses the game and loads up a total war style battle scenario when you are attacked.
Stellaris has none of these. My past three attempts to get back into the game have gone like this
- Open stellaris
- Create a race (usually 0 - 30 min)
- Start game
- Begin by sending science ship to survey worlds
- wait
- micromanage capital world
- wait
- Design a new ship
- wait
- Starts getting bored
- wait

Strongly Avoid, this game was released half finished.  While it is largly stable and bug-free it is a mess on nearly every level in terms of strategic depth, Interface, AI and performance.  Any Civilization game would be a better investment as well as numerous much cheaper 4X games.
A year after release none of the half-baked systems have been fixed, instead Paradox releases 'updates' which add new half-baked mechanics of no originality and cosmetic DLC packages to nickel and dime us.
Space combat consists of huge blob fleets that engage each other with no tactical depth, ability to retreat or even tell why your winning or losing.  No viable defensive strategy exists other then having a bigger fleet and losing said fleet is basicly fatal.  Weapons and ship design are so poor that high tech ships are actually worse then low tech ones.
Planetary development is borring and tedious, no meaningfull specialization is possible on planets as their are only minerals, energy, food to collect and this are pooled globally.  Mineral and Energy arn't even meaningfully different as you require both to do build/maintaine everything, they could be combined into 1 resource with virtually no effect on the game.
As your Empire grows you are forced to turn over most of your planets to AI managment which is cripplingly stupid, the game admits as much when it give you the right to manage more of your own planets as a powerfull Bonus perk.  Enemy AI is likewise stupid but simply loaded up with free resources to make it competetive.
No Espionage system exists whatsoever, diplomacy is thin, no UN or galactic council like mechanism exists for diplomatic victory.  AI attitudes are skitzophrenic so no matter how generous you are allies always turn on you.  Techs are shallow in their effects, +1 to this +1 to that, nothing that makes the game feel different at any point.
Leaders are a pain to aquire, die rapidly and develop without any input from the player.  Government and Ethics have almost no effect on how you play the game even when at 'fanatical' levels.  AI will still hate you for having different ethics in a robotic and arbitrary way regardless of how your actually playing.
Paradox decided that RTS meand 'Real time story' as their are more narrative elements delivered via popups then their are strategy elements in the game.  The science vessel based exploratiof of 'anomalies' is almost fun the first hour of the game then gets tedious to discover +1 mineral on a planet for the 50th time.  Well more then HALF of all the post release DLC and updates are aimed at adding more story elements, fixing core cludge elements not so much.
And last but not least the recently announced removal of 2 of the games original 3 methods of FTL is a last straw.  Instead their will be only 'starlanes' thus one of the BULLET POINTED selling points of the game will be eviserated along with any hope that Paradox would fuffill the trust put in it to 'support' their product post release and actually finish the game.

Villagers is a bit technically incompetent, having quite a few stability issues, some performance issues and abysmal animations. These are offset some by the lovely crafted graphics for the various buildings and objects with great attention to detail.
Full review:
View the video for the best possible and most accurate impression & detailed information.
Summary:
While the games system are competent and work in nice cohesion between the gathering, trading, crafting and refining processes. There are a few flaws that mostly stem from the way the game has decided to create maps and allow for population growth.
See, population takes forever to increase and while much like banished - which this game is a, albeit less good, copy of for the most part - population (micro) management is what this game is all about, you have to make sure people get babies, and those babies grow up to get more babies so your old people can die and your town doesn’t starve and get murdered by bears.
All good right? Except that housing is a major investment initially, and you need to get quite a few, that take up a lot of space & take quite a bit of time to get children and they take time to grow up.
This is doubly made worse by the map design decisions where campaign maps are reused for the "sandbox" maps... but aren’t adapted to fit with a sandbox mode, meaning that resources those maps might not have in the campaign (such as stone quarries or iron mines) heavily restrict your gameplay should you want to play those maps in sandbox mode.
This, while SOMEWHAT combatted by the x10 speed, really isn't a solution. The slow growth and the issues with maps bring together to create a problem that the game simply can’t solve in its current form: You'll never have enough housing to grow enough people to maintain enough infrastructure (pharmacy, market, church, farms etc...), because you can’t gather those resources initially due to population limits, and "faster" doesn't help this seemingly perpetual cycle.
Also because people who have a task, often wait too long to get food and what and simply fall over and die of starvation when both their house, the warehouse and the barns have all the food they could want. Which then compounds your problems to grow more people.
Lastly, the game tries to distinguish itself from banished by having a campaign and being a bit more forgiving. Sadly, while the campaign story is pretty fun, it only lasts 6 missions and those combined have a total gameplay value of 4 or 5 hours, they are a glorified tutorial more than anything.
So combining all of this: PC Performance / stability issues, Population + Ai issues + map design issues as well as the very limited campaign, I simply cannot recommend this game in its current form, just get Banished, it’s the same …but better in every way. And has extensive modding support.

After selling a handfull of cards I got the game for just 20 cents. I've only played the single player mode, so all this is based only on that mode (no idea what co-op is like).
The game takes a few things from Portal and Antichamber as well.
The game mechanics, the launh pads, the blocks and the way blocks activate platforms is well known from Portal while the graphical style, the very simplistic, bold style with a thick black outline around certain objects looks pretty similar to Antichamber at times.
I found the puzzles to be pretty easy to complete. Near the end the puzzles actually became more challenging, but yeah, that was at the end. Definitely not on the same difficulty level as Portal's chambers in my opinion.
Having said that if you find Portal too challenging then this game might just be for you. Bare in mind though that you're going to want to play this for the puzzles and not for the story as there isn't much to it. Also if you're thinking about buying Portal but you're uncertain as to whether or not you'll like that kind of game then you may want to get this first given that it's quite similar in terms of gameplay and (at the moment) dirt cheap.
Summary: For 20 cents the game is more than worth it. It's not that difficult in my opinion and could definitely use some more levels and perhaps a bit less headbobbing, but still well worth it.

SHORT REVIEW INCOMING:
One of the best jump'n'runs I've ever played. Smooth controls, unique gameplay and tight visuals ensure you'll have a great time with THE SUN AND MOON. A perfect game in my opinion. It's even better than SUPER MEAT BOY. Go get it.

Quick explanation about the game: The Sun and Moon is a platformer where momentum is conserved but gravity is reversed, letting you fling yourself high into the air or deep beneath the surface and in order to complete a level, you must collect 3 scattered beads around the stage before being able to enter at the exit point which is portal. Having the basic explained let me tell you something right now: This game is a newborn legend that rests atop with with the other beasts of platforming that are Super Meat Boy and Dustforce. I was amazed with how well polished is the level design, one of the bests I've seen in awhile, and it shows from the beginning to the end.
You start simple with the first world, some spikes a ground, platforms, you get feeling of diving into the ground and of momentum. But as levels come there is always something new and refreshing, you may face yourself with fireballs that race through the screen, appearing-disappearing platforms ruled by a set time, appearing-disappearing platforms ruled by if you are pressing the button that lets you through solid material, flying spikes that patrol a certain area, and even in every world there is a homing boss that will chase you until you collect all the beads, that in this case are 5 instead of the regular 3, and reach the portal but, the boss is different with every world. He may leave some spikes as he goes or instead of going at a regular peace, it will fling itself into your direction from time to time, so yeah lot of variety and of the good one.
Even though you may simply describe this game as a platformer, the best way to describe it would be a puzzle platformer, or that's at least how I perceived it, having in mind I was always aiming in obtaining a Sun Medal (The best grade out of the 3 that are included in the game). Why the puzzle part you ask? Because of multiple reasons actually but mostly because of the scattered 3 beads in the stage, it makes you really think and ponder: Which is really the optimal path? Which bead should be the first I collect? And after that? Not every time the beads are set in a simple path, maybe they are too far apart or maybe some momentum may be of help in shaving those milliseconds to achieve that so grossly incandescent Sun Medal. And things keep stacking up. Should I jump from platform to platform? Or dive into the ground continuously? When should I start moving before the clock sets on? I need that platform to be on, or that fireball at that distance at least, or that flying spike to be at least in the right instead of the left.
And that is why so brilliant the level design, it makes you stop and watch the stage and think, but I really mean it when I say think. I even at times just took a walk through the stage (If it was big enough) and watch carefully everything I should be aware of to just start planning, yeah you read correctly, planning. And after that, your regular Dustforce or Super Meat Boy: Try, try, try, try, try until you succeed.
Another huge plus is the music, it's so relaxing and soothing it will make it will hinder the possibility of becoming angry. It's somewhat similar to Dustforce´s music, ambient electronic. And it gets better, The Sun and the Moon´s OST is like an evolving album, as you progress through worlds you start unlocking new tracks and every track feels like an upgrade from the last one, like an evolving experience. Good stuff, I've never seen any game doing that with its own soundtrack.
I liked this one more than Super Meat Boy but less than Dustforce. What can I say, Dustforce has an astounding skill ceiling that probably no platformer ever will be able to beat. But, still it's tons of fun and with that price tag of $6.99 USD it's pretty damn hard to say no. I spent 30 hours, getting the most Sun Medals I could, on it with zero idle time so the price is extremely fair for the 150+levels the game has but if you play it just for completing stages I guess the game could be beaten in 16-ish hours. If you are a platform lover, please don´t lose the opportunity to play it.

(At the time of this review I am NieR
100% of the game with one non main ending missing and a few data entries and thier quests left)   Review is 100% story spoiler free.
This game is so nice to get these days. We are flooded with these generic games that have all amalgamated into the same damn generic storys and structures. Story and character writers for most games coming out now seem to have forgotten how people think and interact. I swear that with each new release characters be they actual people, aliens, or whatever takes the stage are becoming more and more unrealistic in the sense of how they grow and how naturally they portray someone's personality.
With this game, however, you can instantly tell it was made with love and originality in mind. I had never heard of Yoko Taro before seeing this game pop up on steam but now i'm considering back tracking to his other games just off of how satisfied I was with this game. He is definatly the kind of game dev. who cares about how the whole thing comes together and he isn't afraid to have some fun and goofy stuff thrown in. He makes this game feel like it was made 20 years ago  when most games felt much more seperated from each other and told a story through a drawn out plot line that gave a nice sense of progression instead of just throwing the story in your face like most do now.
The number reviews I do are not going to be some IGN everyone who pays us money gets 10/10 it goes like               5-ok/average 6-solid 7-good 8-fantastic 9-nearing perfection 10-perfection (basically needs to resonate with someone so deeply that it is perfect in thier opinion it won't apply for everyone)
Story: 7.5/10, The story isn't a masterpiece but it sure beats the hell out of 90% of the stuff recently and has some nice twists and reveals. Good high and low points very nice dynamic mood swings most of the way through, may make people ask questions and think which is always plus points.
Soundtrack: 8.5/10, Not trying to be a braggy♥♥♥♥♥♥but I have played music for 8 years play 7 instruments all at high levels and study music as a hobby/passion. Soundtracks mean a lot to me and I feel they are never looked into as much as they should. I feel ashamed to say I haven't made myself familiar with the composer of the soundtrack but I will soon. There was a point when I left an area and liked the music so much that I went back and sat there for 5 minutes because I didn't want to stop listening. Out of all of them around 3 are so fitting and well made that they are in my top tracks from games. Much respect to the score writer absolute talent at making music that encompasses the scenes.
Characters: 8/10, A damn shame that a game with androids has more human feeling characters then some recent *Cough Mass Trash Andromeda *Cough games. Each character individually doesn't have a huge amount of time to go through growth but they make the most of it and you can see changes. The interaction between the main and supporting cast is very well done. Side note: I appreciated how though 2B and A2 are sexualized it was not as upfront as most other games do and turn their characters into sex objects which I thought very tasteful. (proud to not have the look up skirt achievement but not really kinda want to do it)
Combat: 7.5/10, This game didn't do anything new really with its combat mechanics. The game keeps it fresh with a bunch of weapons and pods that let you use special abilities. Where the combat really shines is the variety. This game is a hack and slash with abilities and then there are a bunch of projectiles like a bullet hell game. There are parts that are a true bullet hell top down and 360 degree which is a unique touch for an rpg and they are fairly frequent. The other part of the game with hacking felt like it could have been improved on but it could have been much more dry as well. It isn't a game that I would come back to for combat but the combat was more than good enough to get to that wonderful story. Bonus points for having nice polish animations like 2B's pirouette after holding down light attack with a large sword which is a fairly realistic weight/energy distribution move to handle the excess momentum generated by the attack.
Graphics/Setting: 7/10, (Minor setting spoilers) NieR has very nice character design on all its characters. I don't think I saw even one character that didn't seem to fit in. The general aesthetic of a deteriorated world with machines everywhere is portrayed very well. As far as character design adn aesthetic go it's more of an 8/10 but there are technical issues. The game was designed for ps4 so it is limited in that aspect and it affected the final product. I feel that the city area should have had more diverse building shapes and mabey some more distinction everything was the same rectangle with different heights. The other areas do better and have more diverse wreckage and scenery. NieR got a bad port and it needs fan patches to run best (look up FAR you need it for fullscreen). I was lucky enough to play on maxed settings and encounter few problems after installing FAR and tweaking stuff with nvidias software (there are guides for this aswell). It sucks that Japanese devs. in general don't care about their pc ports because there isn't much of a pc market in Japan so the games rarely get the attention they need.
Overall: 8.5/10 More and more games come out and try to over-hype themselves and seem much deeper than they really are. The level of care put into the development of the story and characters between those games and games like NieR is like looking at the detail between a teddy bear and a real life grizzly. The teddy bear is cute and more appealing and can hit a larger audience, its face value seems better but there isn't much underneath that fur except some filler. The grizzly on the other hand is a far more complex creature, you can see it breath and change before your eyes. You can see a grizzly has more under its fur, it has an entire body to be understood it has feelings of its own and can interact with you unlike the teddy bear which you can restuff with other filler and it has the same emotionless disposition. When a game like NieR comes along and can make people feel and think it may not make as much money as these big ticket sellers but true gamers care a lot more for one and in the end NieR and games of similar quality will end of being remembered and praised in years to come as the ones who cut above the generic cash grabs and told a story. They offered an experience through a medium because that is all games are, a medium. Just like a book or movie puts down a narritve so to does a game and in a more intimate way as well. I can see why Yoko Taro's games are cult classics and can't wait to see what he does next as well as check out his older works.
Thank you for reading my review I hope you consider buying the game.

It's pretty great, particularly on the writing on atmosphere front. Started off a bit barebones and limited, and has since expanded via a combination of free and paid DLC to be something unique - a playable sci-fi/space opera novel, with significant variability and replayability, given the radical difference in the various races and lifeforms.
In terms of the "doomstack" issue (winning the military version by creating larger numerical stacks than your opponents) - it is real, but not as bad as many other 4X games. Diplomacy works pretty well, for one thing, and economic and political constraints limit your expansion during the first two-thirds of the game, regardless of military size or advantage. But it does tend to happen, and it is the most frequent end game. I think the upcoming Cherryh update may address that to some degree, by allowing more effective fortification, but time shall tell. Either way, I have a high degree of confidence that problem will be corrected, since all of my other launch complaints have been addressed.

I came into this game expecting obnoxious memes from Youtubers saturating the entire thing.
Seems like Telltale has a golden touch - I never really was intrigued by any Minecraft setting. But here rather than taking Minecraft and tacking on some overdone Herobrine plot, they actually managed to do something with the story. They used Minecraft as a canvas for a fantasy tale while at the same time keeping many, MANY esoteric adventure game and fantasy game tropes out of it to make it accessable as possible.
Even better is, aside from the crafting system required to solve puzzles (which even has in-game recipes) you can go into this game with NO knowledge of Minecraft game mechanics and still come out enjoying it. I caught myself smiling like a loon several times.
A+

This game actually made me interested in Minecraft again. There goes my life for a few days. Anyways, they took a game that had a simple story and gave it a delicious, rich new one while remaining true to the design of the original game. It is smooth and, at least for me, gives a wonderful cinematic of the classic innovative game.
While beautiful, it does remain rather short at the moment. Still, games like Bioshock Infinite and Portal 2 were considered rather short but they had a wonderfully designed story and beautiful levels. Those are the games you can't put down and feel great afterwards for playing. Yes, they are going to add extra fees for the new episodes, but the cost pales to the content you receive for it. We should be happy the designers didn't stretch out the story just to add more game time.
Story mode, at least in it's current state, is definitely for the appreciator of cinema or story, and not for anyone looking to mash buttons to gain levels.

He had assembled an army of 80 men clad in the finest black steel, his own black armor was forged by the master smiths of Ulm, the two handed black halberd heavy enough to chop through even a knight and his horse. He strode forward with the weapon in hand, alone except for his thoughts when movement through his narrow eyeholes in his helmet drew his attention. A man clothed all in black stared at him, nodded and ran forward a longsword appearing in his hands.
Gawain parried the first blow with a sweep of his halberd and launched a furious blow diagonally downward catching the man across the legs as he attempted to dodge the blow. The man stumbled but still stood, blood poured from the massive gashes across his legs, crippled and limping the man could barely move and Gawain laughed as he stepped in close to deliver the final blow. The man, just barely staying on his feet slashed desperately at the young prince....and blade met flesh and tore through into open air only to bite into flesh and rip through again.
Gawain stared at the spurting bloody stumps where his hands and part of his forearms had been. The huge black halberd lay on the ground next to him his hands still clutched tightly around the handle. The young prince screamed as the pain assailed him and he tried to stumble backwards, away from the man with the blade but his eyes locked onto the blade the man was swinging and he could not bring himself to turn his back and die without seeing. No, the young prince would not die at all. Still screaming in pain but feeling anger flair in his chest Gawain hurled himself at the man with the sword and without a fist to swing found himself kicking with all his strength into the mans chin.
With a loud crack the man fell backwards and lay still. Gawain stared at the motionless body for a few seconds and stumbled away. His blood dripped onto the ground and he found himself feeling rather tired. In the distance he could hear the shouts of his men. Dully he thought they might've been drawn by the sounds of battle or his screams. Either way, they would find him soon. Sighing he sat down against a tree, and waited nothing in the world but exhaustion and pain.

I'd like to preface this review with a question about books. What makes a work of fiction a "classic" which endures generations into the future? Any novel can tell a story. A good novel spins a fantastic world in which the reader can immerse themself, lose themselves, offering an escape from a reality much messier than we would like. But a great book, a classic, is not an escape. Throughout it's fictional world are constant threads of reality, which evolve and grow leaving the reader with a new perspective on society by the end. A classic book is not an
, but rather a
reality, which seeks to enthrall the reader with it's fantastic world even as it's evolving themes crystallize into a message about the only world which really matters in the end.
Nier: Automata is one of the first examples I've seen of this social commentary in the gaming medium. Yes, you get to beat up machines with giant weapons and elegant combos, yes, you can stare at 2B's butt, and yes, the graphics (did I mention the butt?) are pretty great, but Nier: Automata isn't about any of that. Through the unique medium of a game, Nier forces your agency, making
, not some character, responsible for the events which transpire. This makes ultimate message far more personally powerful than a novel or movie adaptation ever could. You start to see hints of this distinction when you notice all the bosses are named after great philosophers or when one of the main characters drops a line like
, but the more you are drawn in the more you begin to see the tangled threads of reality which form the foundation for the game. This game is not about some perpetual war on a desecrated, fictional planet, it's about purpose, meaning, and destiny in a world which is very, very real.
A good game will show you a game can be fun, enjoyable, even addicting. Nier: Automata shows you how a game can be something more: a narrative about society, about reality, about us. It won't change your life, but it
make you think. And that, from a game, is pretty remarkable.

I sincerely wish I could afford to buy every one of my friends a copy of this game.
1. To give them a chance to experience what could be Platinum's best game yet
2. To give Yoko Taro all of my damn money.
So, yeah, Nier: Automata. Sequel to 2010's Nier, which was a spinoff of the Drakengard series. Announced during Square-Enix's bizarre E3 conference in 2015, this game went under the code name Nier: New Project until its full reveal at the Paris Games Week show later in the year. It was delayed from its initial release window of November 2016 to give the team more time to work on improving gameplay balance the overall quality. Finally releasing in March of 2017, it has gone on to sell well over a million copies, making it one of Platinum's best-selling titles.
I admit I didn't know much about the game until I noticed the demo available on the PS4 store. Seeing that it was a Platinum Games title, I kinda knew what I would be in for, and that I would likely enjoy it. I decided to give it a shot one night and, needless to say, I was more than impressed. I bought it for PC right around release and have been enjoying it since.
As I said before, if you know Platinum's style, you know what to expect from a game like this. Frantic combat, a varied and dynamic soundtrack, a brilliantly-crafted story with memorable characters, and epic boss fights. But seeing as this is a Yoko Taro game, it has just the right amount of "what the ♥♥♥♥?" sprinkled in. It's equal parts heartwarming, heart-rending, hilarious, and horrifying, sometimes within the span of a few minutes.
Now, there are a couple of things that I have to mention that keep this game from being 100% perfect in my eyes:
1. The PC port is bad. It's not terrible, and I've seen much worse, but it needs work. For a while, I and many others couldn't play it due to a bug in graphics drivers causing the game to crash just from swinging around 2B's weapon. This was eventually fixed with a future driver, but there are still lingering issues that can be at least duct-taped over with the Far mod. If you get this game on Steam, you NEED the Far mod. It fixes some issues with fullscreen resolution and with stuttering during cutscenes. There are also some misc options and tweaks.
2. The second playthrough was kind of a bummer, mostly because the character you play as is weak when it comes to combat and thus relies on a separate skill to take down enemies. Basically, you better hope you're good at twin-stick shooters. If you are, well, it just gets kinda tedious. But if you can make it through that second playthrough, are you ever in for a treat!
Other than that, I can highly recommend this game. My best suggestion is to go in as blind as possible and do as many of the sidequests as possible to get the best experience. Also, the DLC isn't all that essential, but it has some fun extras like outfits and hair dyes, and a special boss fight.

In terms of the "doomstack" issue (winning the military version by creating larger numerical stacks than your opponents) - it is real, but not as bad as many other 4X games. Diplomacy works pretty well, for one thing, and economic and political constraints limit your expansion during the first two-thirds of the game, regardless of military size or advantage. But it does tend to happen, and it is the most frequent end game. I think the upcoming Cherryh update may address that to some degree, by allowing more effective fortification, but time shall tell. Cradle of Rome is a challenging puzzle game with a simple premise, match three objects in a row to destroy the blocks. Where it becomes complicated however, is that each of these matches contributes to a pool of resources that you use as currency to buy more buildings between stages. Taken together, Cradle of Rome is both unique and refreshing and offers hours of puzzle fun for any casual gamer. I highly recommend this game.

So recently, the Saints Row Ultimate Franchise Pack was on sale, for about £12. Not a bad price, considering what I knew of the series. So I bought it, played it, and out of them all, this was the one that surprised me the most.
Some disagree on the positive outlook on this game, but that is their opinion. It may be an old game, with a 'not so great' port on PC, but it is totally worth the purchase. Even as a standalone, this game shines.
The Saints Row series had a lot of fans before hand, but popularity struck mostly at SR3. (That's when I first found out about it). It has the goofy side, in later titles, to avoid being called 'just another GTA clone'. But, even without the goofy, as in this game here, it is NOTHING like GTA.
Sure, you can hijack vehicles, shoot guns at anyone and run around the city at your free will. But, ask yourself, can you kill a bunch of bums by chucking them into their own shanties; take down a bunch of gangs and topple a whole city in ONE GAME?
No. No you can't.
This is why the game shines. The complete customisation, the actual living breathing city, the out of the ordinary storyline. Proper enjoyable and lovable characters. It shocks me how underrated it was to a wide range of people.
But, this is where I stop kissing SR2's♥♥♥♥♥and come clean.
The port, in my experience, isn't too bad. But it does have it's moments. For example, I tow a car and I'm suddenly driving like I'm on an ice skating rink. Going to forgive and forget, just to get rammed by the cop that was just chasing me, to get the wanted level back again. (not sure about the last one, might be in the game either way).
Various people recommend the 'Gentlemen of the Row' mod, which I am still trying to figure out how to install properly. From the looks of things, I would recommend it too, just for the sheer amount of new content.
Overall, this game is a must-buy. I really hope you don't have a shadow of a doubt about this game, because even though it's older, it's just plain amazing. (Even the graphics are still OK!)
And for the funny catagory, I'll never forget my first moment. Just completed the first mission, (not spoiling it, so I won't say what it is), and walked onto the street to hijack a car. I saw a cop run into a pimp, then pepper spray him, then proceed to beat him down. I walked into the fight, and proceeded to get destroyed by an oncoming army of pimps and cops. ONLY IN SAINTS ROW.

I have played Dominions since the original, and have always enjoyed it.  It is one of my favorites, and I come back to it every few months.  Each version has brought improvements, and 4 is the best so far.  I don't mind spending the money for the new versions, because supporting a durable indy developer is priceless.
There are numerous races to be played, and they are all very different.  There is a ton of replay value, just trying out new factions and learning their strengths and weaknesses.  It also makes you a better player, since those factions appear in other playthroughs as your rivals, and there is nothing like knowing your enemies intimately.
This very diversity of strategies leads to the game's major limitation: the AI opponent presents a very weak challenge.  It simply isn't built to compete at your level, so you will get to the point where playing against the computer is like playing against a young child: the only way to create a challenge is to let it cheat gratuitously.  Higher difficulty levels simply give the AI more and more bonuses, rather than kicking in more cleverness or sophistication.  I recognize that game AI is still a fantasy, but this is a fantasy game after all. ;)
I am confident that human players would provide that competition; however, I have never had the flexibility to commit to that kind of long social engagement.  I will continue to dream of a day when the computer opponent is as satisfying as a person.

Let me throw my hands up and say I've never played any of the previous titles. I openly admit that. What I want to know is how at no point in four renditions of this game have they introduced a way to manage buildings more effectively than one province at a time. It took me nearly 20 minutes to complete a turn, and then I realised this was on a small map. I can't even concieve of how long it would take to complete a single game, and not because of any kind of "gameplay", simply hours and hours of clicking the same thing in menus.
A building queue. That's all it would take. Let me queue up multiple buildings to be built, like you can with infantry. If I have 20 provinces, I have to go back and build every single building individually 20 times. Every castle, tower, walls, etc. I realized in my short time with this game I had spent about 50~60% of it not actually "playing". I was spending it clicking "build this". I could go into MSPaint, write the word "build this" and click it a few hundred thousand times and get pretty much the same experience.
The actual game? The infantry battles, the heroes, the actual "PLAYING" part? It's awesome. It was really fun! It's really in depth, a lot of tactics involved, and I loved it! But how does this game not have a better management system!? HOW?! How has not a single fan of this game told the developers "Hey you know what would be a good idea? The ability to queue up buildings." How can I possibly reccomend a game where I would completely cut out 50% of the "gameplay" if I could? It's horrendous. It's inhuman. I genuinely am concerned for anyone who plays this game regularly. How do you possibly do that for hours and hours on end?

Of all the strategy games I've played over the years, both turned-based and real-time, I don't think I've played any that are nearly as mechanically deep and complex as Dominions 4. Its negative aspects are relatively minor, especially to attentive players who prefer gameplay to pretty pictures.
So let's address those negatives, shall we? I see two complaints more than any other: the interface and the graphics.
In regard to the former, everything is labelled one way or another and any and every action you take during your turn can be changed or undone until such time as you click the "End Turn" button. For attentive players, the interface should be no problem after a few minutes of browsing and experimentation.
While I agree the graphics aren't pretty, I would argue that they don't need to be. As Dominions 4 is a turn-based strategy, there's no pressure to be able to identify everything immediately on sight. The graphics are sufficient in light of the type of game Dominions 4 is. Were it real-time, then I would agree entirely with the argument of sub-par graphics. As a bit of a tangeant, the game is a very small download, thanks in large part to the lesser graphics.
Dominions 4 has perhaps more positives than I can list, mostly in the form of its complex mechanics. While I would love to comment on them, I'm just trying to promote interest in the game, not write guides for it. Dominions 4 handles similarly to Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic, in that the map is divided into spaces (called Provinces) and armies are composed of commander units who lead squads of lesser soldiers. Assuming either series is of interest to you, I would suggest looking into this game as well.
TLDR: Dominions 4 is a turn-based strategy with many complex mechanics that appeal to people looking for thoughtful gameplay and strategy over simplicity and high-end graphics. I give it my highest recommendation.

Rising Storm 2 is near the sweet spot between authenticity and fun gameplay for a hardcore shooter. It's closer to it than any other FPS on the market (except previous games in the franchise). Enemies drop fast and so do you. However, you don't have to walk for long periods before seeing action.
Still, I would have liked it more if it was a little more on the "realism" side of the spectrum. For example, the guns in this game have a MOA approximately 10 times as large as in real life. This is a departure from previous games in the series where the weapons were realistically accurate. You can also sometimes shrug-off 1 hit without needing to bandage. I understand why these compromises were made but I don't approve of them.
The choppers are a ton of fun. Their handling feels just right. Not too simplistic - not DSC level. I appreciate the details like the instruments on the panels actually working.
The game doesn't have as much content as previous entries in the series but the devs are working on it. There are also custom maps made by the community in some servers already.
I absolutely recommend this game.

I have been on a 4x binge this past six months.  Endless Legend, Fallen Enchantress, Age of Wonders 3, Endless Space, Civ6, Masters of Orion, and now Stellaris.  I was hesitate to get it based on reviewers saying the combat was not the best, but I eventually gave in to the desire to try something new and a sale on Steam.  At first I was enthralled. The UI is great, the initial coolness of exploration and discovery.  How things unfold and it gains layers of depth as new mechanics come into play and you research new techs.  The tech tree mechanism of getting a draw of 3 options to research instead of a linear tech tree is brilliant.
Then you meet other AI races and the game falls apart.  How does it fall apart, combat mechanics.  For reasons I don't understand, the AI civs seem to always be able to create fleet power many times that of what you can muster.  I have read forums, watched you tube videos, spent hours reading the wiki.  Which by the way I should not have to do to understand how the game works.  Why is there no manual?  Once an AI civ decides they want to attack you, its over.  They come and steamroll you with their fleet many times larger than yours.  Once this starts, you can't come back. They may show up with a fleet that is 10K in strength versus your 3K fleet that you have been slowly building and developing for hours.  Your fleet is gone in literally seconds (unless you slow down the game speed, then you can watch it die a horrible death more slowly).  Once your main fleet is gone, you are toast.  You can start trying to build a replacement at other spaceports but you are starting from zero while the enemy has a massive fleet taking over your planets one by one.  Meanwhile they are sending a steady flow of additional ships just as fast, if not faster, than you are building your replacements.
If there is some setting, or trick, or way to have the game not progress this way, please tell me.  Until then, or they update  the combat mechanics of this game, I can't recommend it.
By the way, which of the 4x games have I played that have been the best before trying Stellaris?  Endless Legend is awesome.  They get a lot, and I mean a lot, right.  Endless Space is kinda boring.  Like a really small print graphical front end to an underlying spreadsheet of mechanics.  Fighting there is also very bland, at least you have a few card based mechanics to try and improve the results of the dice roll.  Master of Orion is great.  Wonderful graphics, easy UI, lots of character and tons of voice acting.  Very good production values.  Unfortunately, it is not that deep so you can get bored with it pretty quickly.  Combat actually has some tactical control however which is the ONLY 4x space game I have played that offers this.
If Stellaris developers can spend some time fixing the combat mechanics, there may be hope.  I will wait and see.

Excellent mastery-based platformer (like VVVVVV, Super Meat Boy, etc.) with a super innovative but intuitive movement mechanic that is fully explored and brilliantly utilized in the level design. Very simple pick up and play presentation makes it fun in short bursts, but trying to get the best time on each level provides a lot of depth and makes you really appreciate the mechanics and design even more.

So. This game. Is... I would put it in the "meh" category if Steam had that one, so this is a very light recommendation, but I think its main mechanic is interesting enough and it does enough with it to justify a recommendation, I did have a good bit of fun with this game after all.
That being said, I kinda wish this was a shorter $5 game. Instead of the 160 levels, give us 80 of them, pick out the better ones and give a more consistently enjoyable experience. This game really feels stretched out for content, in the end. There are some levels that toy with a few extra mechanics (time shifting blocks, blocks that pop in and out of existence when you hold the shift button, a few autoscroller-type things, basic stuff mostly) but the majority of the game is confined to making use of the main mechanic in a static environment. And there's only so much that can be done with that, I felt the game getting repetitive pretty early on and it didn't get more varied down the road.
There's also an uneven difficulty curve, I feel. Outside of the bonus world, I didn't find myself challenged too much by any particular world... but each world had a few levels way harder than anything around it. A lot of the boss levels also felt a bit unfair, having to pray that the boss would end up in around the same spot every time so that you could learn the level and complete it, and the final boss especially felt too long. There's a fair few levels requiring precision beyond what the game gives you, too. I feel like focusing on really precise movements in a physics-heavy game may not have been the best of ideas. But that's just me.
The main mechanic of the game is pretty interesting though and makes for some enjoyable platforming challenges. There's some levels about getting enough height via flying through blocks, other levels about trying to get down below via gravity and clever use of the main mechanic, and some just straight-up platformy levels. The extra mechanics occasionally thrown in also make things a bit more interesting; there's a few levels where you basically fly using the user-controlled blocks, and the boss of the 8th world has this very clever proximity thing going on, I really enjoyed that one especially. There's also plenty of replay value here; every level has three time challenges to meet. Personally I couldn't be bothered to even go for time challenges most of the time, ending up with very few sun medals and only a few dozen of the full-moon medals, though usually the half-moon medals aren't too hard to get. I spent around 7-8 hours just playing through all the levels once, so there's no shortage of content here, certainly, though honestly I would have preferred a bit less in the end xD
Overall it's a solid precision platformer, definitely unlike any other game I've played, but I feel the focus should've been on making a more compact and enjoyable experience rather than just throwing every level the developer made into the game and calling it done. I think it would've made this "okay" a pretty "great" one if there was a bit more polish to it.

Simple but challenging controls, a non-linear map layout, and a timer for speedrunning each level. A fresh take on the platformer genre thanks to its unique, physics-based diving mechanic.
The start is simple and straightforward but the game gradually becomes complex and challenging. Level design and pacing here are fantastic, testing a player's skill and problem solving while never feeling that a failed attempt is because of unfair or broken game mechanics. Completed levels unlock multiple new ones, allowing for a non-linear progression through the game, and each new quadrant unlocked adds a new color scheme, a new layer of music, and a new platforming mechanic for that area. For the 150 or so levels there are also record times for high score lovers and speedrunners alike.
This game will take a while to finish and even longer to beat the times. An addictive platformer that is really worth checking out.

This is a review of both the game and the PC port
The game:
Easily a MASTERPIECE, and without a doubt one of the best games of 2017.
Pros:
Story/Storytelling - Lots of plot twists and you will get the chance to see the story from different perspectives. It is a game that has a lot of philosophical concepts and will make you think outside of the game. I can't say more to avoid spoiling but I loved it.
Characters - At first you might think the characters are shallow and not that interesting, but as you start playing you realize why the characters are the way they are. Hell, even the bosses of this game have personality and motives for their actions. There is just one character in the game that I wished it was explained a bit better.
Gameplay - It is not a game like Bayonetta where you have dozens of different combos, it is more simplistic BUT is excellent as you would expect from a game from PlatinumGames. There is a huge selection of weapons and abilities you can choose so there are many different play styles to try out.
Graphics - They're alright, what you would expect from a modern game, but definitely not the best out there. I really love the animations during combat and the design of most of the bosses though. Maybe a nitpick from my side is that I got a bit tired of the overall color pallet in the game and the enemies, since most of the enemies are robots, and most robots have the same color I got tired of seeing the same type of enemies over and over again.
Soundtrack - One of the finest soundtracks you could find in gaming alongside the original Nier. If the game doesn't appeal you for some reason, I still recommend checking the soundtrack if you love music.
Voice Acting - I played with the English voices and I personally think that the voice actors did a fantastic job. You also have the option to play with japanese voices if you want to.
Cons:
-There is a hacking mechanic that you get halfway through the game that is OP but at the same time it gets tedious to use and it breaks the pacing of the game. I didn't mind the mini game but I wish it was used in more specific parts of the game or to be more balanced.
-The side quests can break the pacing of the game. Overall the story missions are heavily action oriented while the side quest are slower and can involve some fetch quests. However, the side quests do give a lot of back story to the main plot. What I recommend is to do as least quests as possible during your first playthough, and on new playthroughs complete all the side quests.
-Don't play this game expecting an open world. It has areas you can explore and side quests you can complete but it is not a huge map, and some of the spaces in between the areas can feel empty.
The port:
Mediocre at best. A lot of issues reported from the users that the developers keep ignoring. The development team instead of focusing the attention on fixing the issues and deliver a high quality port, they decide to release a DLC instead. Even with a High-end PC I experienced a couple of crashes and a few frame drops during some specific fights. I can see how these issues are more frequent for a Mid-Range PC.
Overall if you have a high-end PC I can recommend this game on Steam, otherwise I recommend it to play it on Playstation, but it's a game I recommend to anyone who calls himself a gamer.

Stellaris is a good Sci-Fi Grand Strategy game in which you create an alien race and empire (Or pick from a pre-made list, but honestly, making your own is SO much more fun), and essentially play a game of civilization (albeit much more in depth) in space.
With empires, you have things like
-Ethos (Are you an authoritarian dystopia? Egalatiarian Paradise? Militaristic Dictatorship? Religious Zealots?)
- Technology : You get a choice of three tech types, astrophysics, engineering, and biology, in which you get different techs randomly each time you finish researching one (You pick them from a group of "Cards" that you get after you finish, and those cards are random, but none will appear if you don't have the requisite tech)
-Ships : You can customize each and every unit your space navy employs, from your corvette to your carriers and battleships. Even the way they move through space is different, as each empire has Hyperlane, Wormhole, or Warp Drive (although in the next patch this will be changed to be hyperlane only, with wormhole and warp added as an extra tech you research later, due to the devs wanting to implement space terrain which will affect said travel, although wormholes will appear randomly, so you can still use them at the beginning if you are lucky)
-Edicts and Policies : These kind of allow you to determine how your empire behaves, such as it's war policy, how it treats robots, does it have slaves, what rights do said slaves have, etc.
-DLC : While I admit the DLC policy of Paradox is......well......not great (Seriously look at Europa Universalis and Crusader Kings 2, there are literally 50+ DLCs for them and counting), and Stellaris seems to be heading the way of both. If you do get this game, I'd recommend getting the Utopia DLC, it adds traditions (empire wide buffs that also add flavor to your empire, such as making a full on race of Psychics, or an alien species that turned themselves into robots, or genetic engineering masterminds, and Superstructures), in addition to Synthetic Dawn (Allows you to play fully robotic empires from start), with Leviathans (Enclaves you can get help from, in addition to gigantic "monster" like creatures in space that pose a heavy threat should you engage them but give massive rewards)
-Future Patches and Content : While I can't say much about this (Unlike some aliens, I'm not psychic), I can say that Paradox does release regular content updates, like the upcoming patch, and while this usually comes with DLC, the next one, for example, will not, and it does add new mechanics and reworks a bit (Namely the terrain of space, like having a nebula affect travel speed, in addition to reworking FTL types to have hyperlane as the only beginning choice while reworking Wormholes as a random occurence, but adding gateways in their place, and generally keeping Psionic Drive as is).
-Overall : 8/10, good space strategy game, although if you do buy it, get it on sale with the Utopia + Leviathans + Synthetic Dawn DLC. Really just Utopia imo, can't play without it.
-Also, you've GOT to try being a xenophobic expansionist empire, you never get tired of literally turning your enemies into lunch for your citizens (I'm not kidding it's an actual edict, try it for yourself)

Stellaris is a masterpiece 4X Galactic Empire simulator that I recommend without hestitation. This review is based on the current 1.8 build of the game. If you were a fan of the Master of Orion series this is the game you have been waiting for. Do not let the fact that it is technically "real time" discourage you as it plays more like a turn based game as it progresses slowly enough and allows "pausing," if you wish to enter commands.
As with many games from Paradox interactive the game evolves over time based on fan input. It is also extremely mod-able and has a very active modding community. It has a great randomized research system (similar to but better than MOO1) where you are randomly assigned research options so you have to prioritize and make due if your favorite technology does not show up right away.
This game heavily emphasizes the eXploration part of 4X in the early game as you start out exploring the galaxy. The game rewards you for surveying each star system you encounter. You then eXpand by finding planets suitable for your race's characteristics that have resources to justify the initial expense of building a colony. You can eXploit resources in inhabitable systems as well and even ecounter primitive civilations and deal with them in any manner you please (depending on the vast array of ethics and government choices you picked at startup) from everything to passive observation with non-interferencde for study, to enlightening them to become a space fairing civiliation (under your guidance of course) to conquering, enslaving, eXterminating, or even consuming them.
The game is not super beginner friendly given all the many ways to play and has a bit of a learning curve. For example you can build and modify robotic populations, genetically modify your own species or others, enslave or set a "caste system" or a varying hierarchy of rights for different species, etc. Many cool possiblities from an egalitarian democracy to an enslaving or exterminating empire.   Also, late in game some players will experience lag as fleets get very large. Additionally, while you can go to war with, trade with, ally with, or even start a federation with other AI empires, encounter powerful ancient galactic civilizations, and encounter one of 3 different "end game crisis" some will find the diplomatic options limited in the current build.
Worry not though, this game has had major updates and will continue to improve. Finally, some of you may have noticed a "protest" movement related to the changes to the starting options for your species FTL method. All I can say about this is that it shows the passion that these players have for the game and how much they love it and worry that it will change. It bears repeating that the game is highly moddable and the developers know what they are doing by making the more powerful FTL drive choices unlockable later in game whether than available to all players at start (after all, any player that knows what they are doing, will obviously pick the most powerful wormhole travel to start if that's an option).
I highly recommend this game.
