The first time I played after the tutorial was a singleplayer game, to get a feel for the games' mechanics. I played as R'lyeh (named for the city in which Cthulhu lies in deathless dreams) and zerg rushed everything unfortunate enough to be underwater. Then I turned my attention to the land. This is difficult as R'lyeh, as most units available to it can only survive underwater or with costly magic to allow them to breathe air or transport them in a bubble of water, and my enemies had fortified the coast at this point. So instead of raiding their ports the traditional way I summoned a bunch of sea trolls, which can survive both on land and underwater, and had them repeatedly throw themselves into suicide missions along a coastal region until the area was strewn with corpses. Then I marched the Eater of the Dead, a massive undead horror summoned from a nether realm that feeds on corpses to grow in power until it inevitably becomes too powerful for its summoner to control and breaks free, wreaking havoc indiscriminately, over to the battlefield and had it gorge itself. It broke free quickly and began rampaging, but this was all according to plan- I cast a spell to freeze the oceans over, so it could not get back down to my oceanic empire, yet was free to destroy all unfortunate enough to live above sea level. Sadly, I did not comprehend the importance of proselatyzing, so belief in me gradually ran out throughout the empire, until I had no divine dominion left and lost anyway.
Since then I have played as the lavamen of Abysia and created a second sun so there was eternal burning day, crippling the offencive of my cold-loving Niefelheim foes; As the Ashen Empire of Ermor, an undead post-apocalyptic Roman empire that spreads like an infection, turning the world into skeletons, and did the opposite, blotting out the sun and causing the entire world to age at an incredible rate (skeletons have great longevity, humans not so much); As Kailasa, an Indian-themed realm of reincarnating monkey gurus, I used the power of the stars to transform a demigod of mercy into a ruthless and indiscriminate killing machine, flying around the world with a shapeshifting dragon princess she once saved in tow and bringing destruction upon my enemies; As the amphibious subterranean civilisation of Agartha I broke an ancient seal, releasing mad gods upon the world; And so on- These are only the more prominent examples, stories many players are likely to experience because they align with each nation's strengths and lore.
Make no mistake, Dominions is only superficially yet another army-management turn-based wargame. In fact it is more of a game about great magical beings at war with each other, and the havoc they wreak in their strife for supremacy. Like certain other absurdly complex modern CRPGs with minimalistic graphics (the most prominent being Dwarf Fortress), Dominions has decent gameplay, but its real strength is in its equally complex and convoluted lore and the intriguing stories that come from it.
One of my favourite games, strongly recommend.

I love this game ...
That said There are 2 fundamental design flaws with it:
1. the graphics are horrible ... really really bad ... not not that bad worse far worse ... think 1980's low budget game then wind back your expectations. Good games (imo) arnt all about the graphics but they're bad enough to make it hard to play.
2. starting a game you are presented with a dizzying array of nations, gods and possible setups, the most complex part of the game is deciding on your setup - but you really have to understand the game quite well in order to do this, these choices are fundamental and important. There is no guidance in game that helps a new player, the 397 page pdf manual is little or no help (once you find it) googling 'dom4 nation setup' gives lots of forum postings by those who use so many acronyms they're illegible.
[e.g. EA Neif Monolith E9A1E6 D6 O3P3C3G1M3D0 - really didnt help me - though now I know the game better I can see is a helpful build suggestion]
In short you really have to put work in to get to the point where the game is anything more than a turn based terrirtory domino fall game of conquest.
Dominions 4 is however far more than that. Yes you can just pump troops out and spread your gods dominion by attacking and taking over all other gods territories but there is so much more here once you look. Research of spells & items to forge add a lot but other than being a wider available choice you get similar tech tree approaches in many other games.
Adding the divine to the game is a somewhat new, interesting and brilliant twist - the aim is not global military dominion but instead for your god to spread his dominion to the world, to spread belief in your god to the exclusion of all other gods. Belief can cross borders stepping right over a turtled mass of troops in a pinch point.
As a suggestion:
1. find the online pdf manual (linked in guides) play the 9 turn by rote guide to controls (found somewhere about 90 pages in interspersed with irrelevant and unhelpful history of how the game was made and waffle about the designers inspiration for the game.
2. Play a Late Age (LA) Nation called Man, dont worry about nation / god setup on a small map against any random land based nation, dont research anything / forge any items just work with longbowmen to get the feel of the game.
3. Play an Early Age (EA) Nation called Metlican. Google some setups but the one that works for me is :
Demilich (Imprisoned): Water 4 Death 9 Nature 9, Dominion 8 Order 3 Sloth 3 Heat 2 Growth 2 Misfortune 2 Drain 2
Set a commander to the spells Blessing / Divine Blessing and work with Jaguar Warriors.
Use these to learn the game to the point where you feel comfortable experimenting & understand the forum post acronyms you'll find from google.
I hope you enjoy the game as much as I have!

This game. This franchise. This madness!
Seriously, I love the Saints Row series. Mindless fun, destruction everywhere and completely over the top gameplay. Well, not so much in 2, but in the Third, the madness is cranked up a couple notches.
Having purchased this game in a bundle of Saints Row franchise, I sadly have to say that, although I greatly enjoy the franchise in general, having SR:tT next to this game is... suboptimal, I would say. I just love the madness of the third game so much that 2 seems a bit dull in comparison.
But it is by no means a bad game. Oh no. I already got a whiff of that madness Saints Row is known and loved for in the first two main missions (which by this point is all I have played). I might return to this game one day, but before that, I will wreck everything in the titles which followed this one.

It's just as well that this can be bought with the Saint's Row Ultimate Pack. Because as a standalone title, I can't really recommend this. Not now that there are many games that exceed it now.
Let's get the positives out of the way. Compared to SR3, the character customisation options was a broader package. Though the number of items is admittedly not that much larger than its successor, you were given far more wearable options. The general story of SR2 represents a form of balance for its time between its rival(GTA) that moved towards a more gritty, realistic setting, and its successor games (SR3 and 4), which essentially took the Cave Johnson approach and started throwing crap at the wall and seeing what sticks.
That's where the positive notes end though. As far as graphics go, it has aged horribly. The colours look dull and faded when they don't need to be, Lighting and shadows don't work like they're meant to-even for a game of its age, And the skin textures. Ugh....... Put it this way: The original Saint's Row was a better looking game in comparison. I wish I was making this up......
Now this wouldn't be so bad if the game was optimised effectively. It isn't. I run a nvidia GTX 770, and I can get a smoother framerate with SR3- a graphically superior game in every sense of the word, than I can here. I'd say you'd have to overkill big to get your unbroken 60fps, but I wouldn't be surprised if Titan Black cards can't iron out the jitters.
Finally, we have gameplay. While it was good for its time, it hasn't stood the test very well. With successor and rival games branching out in more advanced paths, you're left with this thing that lacks GTA's precision, and also lacks the fluidity of a game like Just Cause, or SR2's eventual successors. Any amount of time spent on the game will have you wishing you were playing something else.
If you must, get it with the Ultimate franchise pack if you ever feel you want that nostalgic kick at any point. But on its own, I can't recommend it for anything over 4 bucks. And even then, there are a tonne of indy games you could buy at that price......

Out There Somewhere is possibly one of the most challenging, unique and intriguing platformers you'll ever play, as it puts you in control of a little alien, stranded on an unknown planet after his ship has crashed as a result of a space battle between him and his nemesis, Grigori, who ended up on the same planet as you, changing the lives of the planet's inhabitants. With that being said, you'll soon be on your way to recover the core needed for your ship to function again and finish what you've started, but to do so you'll have to traverse a long way, filled with danger, friendly and foe aliens and plenty of secrets. While the intelligent life on the planet will mostly only complain about how Grigori has influenced their lives since his arrival, and occasionally open a door for you or give you a hint to where you should head next, the more barbaric enemies simply known as monsters will often stand between you and your next objective, forcing you to think up different strategy on the move. While the plot isn't the most unique one and it certainly doesn't have any twists along the way, it is pleasing to see how many different areas and secrets you can find along the way, some which will often lead to items that will make your journey easier, such as abandoned cores or ancient alien artifacts. There is a certain lack of character development when it comes to the intelligent aliens, which will only interact with you with the same line of dialogue, which in most cases doesn't make any sense.
As any platformer you'll want to play, gameplay is the key element for an unforgettable experience, and in this aspect, Out There Somewhere brings some interesting concepts to the table, such as the teleport gun which allows you to send a beam to any wall that will teleport you there once it reaches its destination. As that mechanic alone would soon run out of challenging situations, blue, red and green beams will make puzzles more difficult, as red beams will block your teleportation beam, blue beams will stop the gun's beam at their location, and green beams will send it upwards. Combing those simple mechanics with the machine gun that will allow you to shoot enemies in your path in addition to using the teleport gun creates situations that are challenging, yet fun to solve and think your way out of. Secrets are also an important part of the experience, as exploration is rewarded with items such as health upgrades or the machine gun upgrade that allows you to shoot faster, and looking for different alternatives out of a certain screen will often take you to a completely new one with a new challenge ahead. The most important thing is that the game allows you to play however you want to, as you can avoid shooting enemies completely, making your way forward using the teleport gun alone, or take your time, explore the world around you and make sure you collect everything along the way.
Out There Somewhere goes for an old school look, with simple, low resolution textures formed out of squares, and while that art style fits the concept of the game fairly well, the problem comes in the form of repetition using those textures, as each screen will look similar to the previous one, and even when you do reach an area that's meant to feel and look different such as Grigori's Tower, it still feels like the same square with a different color shade on top.
The audio quality is pretty cheap, which isn't necessarily a problem since there isn't much to hear aside from the effects that will only show up when you command them to. The soundtrack is okay for this time of game, but it does get boring pretty quickly, but since there isn't much else to hear aside from the background song, you could just mute it and play your own tunes.
It will probably take you around one hour to complete Out There Somewhere for the first time, but just as a note the game can be completed in less than 15 minutes, and the game even encourages you to do that as it has a specific achievement. You could play it a second time to earn all the achievements and see the secret areas you might have missed, but afterwards that's it.
Out There Somewhere is a cute, challenging adventure to spend your afternoon with, as long as you don't mind the fact that it will be over fairly soon, but for its low price and a possible secondary replay, it's worth a try.

This is a review of both the game and the PC port
The game:
Easily a MASTERPIECE, and without a doubt one of the best games of 2017.
Pros:
Story/Storytelling - Lots of plot twists and you will get the chance to see the story from different perspectives. It is a game that has a lot of philosophical concepts and will make you think outside of the game. I can't say more to avoid spoiling but I loved it.
Characters - At first you might think the characters are shallow and not that interesting, but as you start playing you realize why the characters are the way they are. Hell, even the bosses of this game have personality and motives for their actions. There is just one character in the game that I wished it was explained a bit better.
Gameplay - It is not a game like Bayonetta where you have dozens of different combos, it is more simplistic BUT is excellent as you would expect from a game from PlatinumGames. There is a huge selection of weapons and abilities you can choose so there are many different play styles to try out.
Graphics - They're alright, what you would expect from a modern game, but definitely not the best out there. I really love the animations during combat and the design of most of the bosses though. Maybe a nitpick from my side is that I got a bit tired of the overall color pallet in the game and the enemies, since most of the enemies are robots, and most robots have the same color I got tired of seeing the same type of enemies over and over again.
Soundtrack - One of the finest soundtracks you could find in gaming alongside the original Nier. If the game doesn't appeal you for some reason, I still recommend checking the soundtrack if you love music.
Voice Acting - I played with the English voices and I personally think that the voice actors did a fantastic job. You also have the option to play with japanese voices if you want to.
Cons:
-There is a hacking mechanic that you get halfway through the game that is OP but at the same time it gets tedious to use and it breaks the pacing of the game. I didn't mind the mini game but I wish it was used in more specific parts of the game or to be more balanced.
-The side quests can break the pacing of the game. Overall the story missions are heavily action oriented while the side quest are slower and can involve some fetch quests. However, the side quests do give a lot of back story to the main plot. What I recommend is to do as least quests as possible during your first playthough, and on new playthroughs complete all the side quests.
-Don't play this game expecting an open world. It has areas you can explore and side quests you can complete but it is not a huge map, and some of the spaces in between the areas can feel empty.
The port:
Mediocre at best. A lot of issues reported from the users that the developers keep ignoring. The development team instead of focusing the attention on fixing the issues and deliver a high quality port, they decide to release a DLC instead. Even with a High-end PC I experienced a couple of crashes and a few frame drops during some specific fights. I can see how these issues are more frequent for a Mid-Range PC.
Overall if you have a high-end PC I can recommend this game on Steam, otherwise I recommend it to play it on Playstation, but it's a game I recommend to anyone who calls himself a gamer.

It seems that, nowadays, there’s a new gamejam almost every month. And why the hell not? They’re a great opportunity for developers, amateur and professional alike, to flex their creative muscles within the confines of each jam’s chosen theme and time constraint. Ideas thought up in the heat of a gamejam can even make it to a full retail product, and join the likes of Surgeon simulator or Receiver. For Ludum Dare 29 all competitors created games to fit the theme “beneath the surface”, and now its winning game, The Sun and Moon, has graduated to a full Steam release.
First impressions are key, so you could be forgiven for thinking that The Sun and Moon‘s visual simplicity belies an even simpler game. You play as a small worm creature with the ability to dig underground, but in order to dig deep down you’ll need to leverage the power of gravity and your own weight. Whilst the game is mechanically simple, it’s the ways in which you’ll utilise them, to overcome the game’s puzzles, that provides variety.
Each quick-fire level has you collecting a number of gems, and you can make your way to the exit once you’ve picked them all up. Levels don’t last very long, with some being as brief as 8 seconds or less, but you’ll need to be quick and have some serious finger dexterity to become that masterful. A three-tier grading system is included to encourage/taunt you, and you’ll face a real challenge to even gain the lowest grade in some levels.
The game drops you in the shallow end to begin with, tasking you with only picking up gems, but the difficulty ramps up very quickly. Pretty soon you’ll be throwing yourself off platforms and stairs, trying to gain enough momentum to fire yourself to other, higher platforms. Each level has an ideal solution, and its up to you to figure it out. But even if you do manage to decode a level, you’ll still need to seamlessly weave every movment, dive and dodge together to get to the exit quickly enough for that top ranking.
The control scheme is, at least, on your side, and you’ll only need to use the directional keys alongside the shift button if you want to dive underground. Some levels may prove too difficult or demand some time to fully understand, luckily the overworld map has a branching structure that allows you to visit multiple different areas at once. Each new area brings its own challenges, but also a refreshing change of scenery, as well as an extra layer for the game’s chiptune soundtrack.
And about that soundtrack, it’s pleasant enough to keep your head bopping and feet tapping, whilst not breaking your concentration as you fail for the 20th time. It’ll even extend itself as you unlock new areas, adding new layers to the beat, making it more complex and diverse.
You probably already know if you’ll enjoy The Sun and Moon. Its excruciating difficulty and intense gameplay make it an acquired taste, only fit for those who can pick themselves up after repeated failure, only to continue playing.
It’s the very epitome of videogame masochism and punishes far more than it rewards – unless you can give it the ample time required to master its 150+ levels. It’s one of those games that really makes you work for your gratification, even if  only a fleeting sense of achievement. As much as we wish we were any good at The Sun and Moon, we just aren’t – as our ground teeth, pounded keyboard, and flipped desk will attest to. So if you don’t mind, we’ll be backseat gamers and watch someone else play it instead

The Sun & Moon is, without a doubt, one of the most innovative platform titles of this year. For its unique twist on the traditional style alone, gamers should consider adding it to their collection, with the simplicity of control and great audio sealing the deal.
Instead of being limited to the traditional gameplay directions (up, left, right), players can defy gravity and propel themselves downward into the ground in their ongoing quest to collect three shiny orbs and advance to the next level.
This unique mechanic is the definitive highlight of the game as a whole. Forcing players to rethink classic strategies of beating platform puzzles is no easy feat, but The Sun & Moon does so in a way that is simple to pick up, yet challenging to master. With over 150 levels of gameplay (ranging in difficulty from easy to what the developer describes as “brutally hard”), players will likely enjoy the fun dynamics this feature of the game creates.
The only objection casual players might have is the price, but if it is on sale, it's definitely worth the purchase!
Highly recommended!

This is an expanded and polished version of the game that won the 29th Ludum Dare game jam (48 hour version). The theme was Beneath the Surface, and the way the developer interpreted that theme was to implement a simple movement mechanic: the player can dive INTO the platforms, retaining momentum but with reversed gravity. The level designs really force the player to think and move in different ways, and they grow more challenging fairly quickly.
I recommend this game for anyone who likes platformers with unique movement mechanics and anyone who likes short, skill-based challenges (the game keeps track of the player's best time for each level).

The Sun and Moon is a lovely little game, kinda challenging and super addictive with tons of levels! As you can see the game won a Ludum Dare and was created by a single person - so huge props for that!
The goal of the game is pretty simple and straightforward : you play as a sun, that needs to gather 3 moons to orbit it and get enough mass to enter the wormhole and complete the level. It's not as simple as it sounds and needless to say - the game is unforgivable and you die instantly! The main game mechanic is pretty interesting - you can penetrate the "ground" and move inside it. Once you do that, your impulse remain, but the "ground" wants you out of it and creates a sort of anti-gravity to push you out. The mechanic is tricky and mastering it is of utmost importance in order to succeed. Not all levels are static with only spikes and endless drops, there are levels, where you are being chased by an unknown entity, that follows you around and destroys you on impact - so you need to be swift and decisive in your movements to kite it around.
There are highscores for each individual level, as the position is determined by the time you needed to complete it - the faster the better. Important the point out is, that the timer starts not when the level loads, but when you move for the first time - so you have time to look around and plan ahead.
The controls are really tight, there is a full controller support, but I personally did prefer my keyboard. The levels are not always straightforward and you need to plan and think about the optimal route, or try and test to see what is even possible and what not. The music is "ok"-ish, might get a little repetitive in the long run, but you can always disable it. The levels appear in the form similar to a graph tree leafs, so you can navigate around the level map and not necessary complete the levels in order, with the occasional block, requiring you to have a certain number of levels completed, before progressing.
The huge amount of levels and the challenging nature of the game, paired with per level leaderboards make this an easy recommendation!

username: The wide side of the Force
text:
If you are hesitating thinking this is an over-hyped weeb game I can tell you 100% it is not.
(At the time of this review I am NieR
100% of the game with one non main ending missing and a few data entries and thier quests left)   Review is 100% story spoiler free.
This game is so nice to get these days. We are flooded with these generic games that have all amalgamated into the same damn generic storys and structures. Story and character writers for most games coming out now seem to have forgotten how people think and interact. I swear that with each new release characters be they actual people, aliens, or whatever takes the stage are becoming more and more unrealistic in the sense of how they grow and how naturally they portray someone's personality.
With this game, however, you can instantly tell it was made with love and originality in mind. I had never heard of Yoko Taro before seeing this game pop up on steam but now i'm considering back tracking to his other games just off of how satisfied I was with this game. He is definatly the kind of game dev. who cares about how the whole thing comes together and he isn't afraid to have some fun and goofy stuff thrown in. He makes this game feel like it was made 20 years ago  when most games felt much more seperated from each other and told a story through a drawn out plot line that gave a nice sense of progression instead of just throwing the story in your face like most do now.
The number reviews I do are not going to be some IGN everyone who pays us money gets 10/10 it goes like               5-ok/average 6-solid 7-good 8-fantastic 9-nearing perfection 10-perfection (basically needs to resonate with someone so deeply that it is perfect in thier opinion it won't apply for everyone)
Story: 7.5/10, The story isn't a masterpiece but it sure beats the hell out of 90% of the stuff recently and has some nice twists and reveals. Good high and low points very nice dynamic mood swings most of the way through, may make people ask questions and think which is always plus points.
Soundtrack: 8.5/10, Not trying to be a braggy♥♥♥♥♥♥but I have played music for 8 years play 7 instruments all at high levels and study music as a hobby/passion. Soundtracks mean a lot to me and I feel they are never looked into as much as they should. I feel ashamed to say I haven't made myself familiar with the composer of the soundtrack but I will soon. There was a point when I left an area and liked the music so much that I went back and sat there for 5 minutes because I didn't want to stop listening. Out of all of them around 3 are so fitting and well made that they are in my top tracks from games. Much respect to the score writer absolute talent at making music that encompasses the scenes.
Characters: 8/10, A damn shame that a game with androids has more human feeling characters then some recent *Cough Mass Trash Andromeda *Cough games. Each character individually doesn't have a huge amount of time to go through growth but they make the most of it and you can see changes. The interaction between the main and supporting cast is very well done. Side note: I appreciated how though 2B and A2 are sexualized it was not as upfront as most other games do and turn their characters into sex objects which I thought very tasteful. (proud to not have the look up skirt achievement but not really kinda want to do it)
Combat: 7.5/10, This game didn't do anything new really with its combat mechanics. The game keeps it fresh with a bunch of weapons and pods that let you use special abilities. Where the combat really shines is the variety. This game is a hack and slash with abilities and then there are a bunch of projectiles like a bullet hell game. There are parts that are a true bullet hell top down and 360 degree which is a unique touch for an rpg and they are fairly frequent. The other part of the game with hacking felt like it could have been improved on but it could have been much more dry as well. It isn't a game that I would come back to for combat but the combat was more than good enough to get to that wonderful story. Bonus points for having nice polish animations like 2B's pirouette after holding down light attack with a large sword which is a fairly realistic weight/energy distribution move to handle the excess momentum generated by the attack.
Graphics/Setting: 7/10, (Minor setting spoilers) NieR has very nice character design on all its characters. I don't think I saw even one character that didn't seem to fit in. The general aesthetic of a deteriorated world with machines everywhere is portrayed very well. As far as character design adn aesthetic go it's more of an 8/10 but there are technical issues. The game was designed for ps4 so it is limited in that aspect and it affected the final product. I feel that the city area should have had more diverse building shapes and mabey some more distinction everything was the same rectangle with different heights. The other areas do better and have more diverse wreckage and scenery. NieR got a bad port and it needs fan patches to run best (look up FAR you need it for fullscreen). I was lucky enough to play on maxed settings and encounter few problems after installing FAR and tweaking stuff with nvidias software (there are guides for this aswell). It sucks that Japanese devs. in general don't care about their pc ports because there isn't much of a pc market in Japan so the games rarely get the attention they need.
Overall: 8.5/10 More and more games come out and try to over-hype themselves and seem much deeper than they really are. The level of care put into the development of the story and characters between those games and games like NieR is like looking at the detail between a teddy bear and a real life grizzly. The teddy bear is cute and more appealing and can hit a larger audience, its face value seems better but there isn't much underneath that fur except some filler. The grizzly on the other hand is a far more complex creature, you can see it breath and change before your eyes. You can see a grizzly has more under its fur, it has an entire body to be understood it has feelings of its own and can interact with you unlike the teddy bear which you can restuff with other filler and it has the same emotionless disposition. When a game like NieR comes along and can make people feel and think it may not make as much money as these big ticket sellers but true gamers care a lot more for one and in the end NieR and games of similar quality will end of being remembered and praised in years to come as the ones who cut above the generic cash grabs and told a story. They offered an experience through a medium because that is all games are, a medium. Just like a book or movie puts down a narritve so to does a game and in a more intimate way as well. I can see why Yoko Taro's games are cult classics and can't wait to see what he does next as well as check out his older works.
Thank you for reading my review I hope you consider buying the game.

This is a review of both the game and the PC port
The game:
Easily a MASTERPIECE, and without a doubt one of the best games of 2017.
Pros:
Story/Storytelling - Lots of plot twists and you will get the chance to see the story from different perspectives. It is a game that has a lot of philosophical concepts and will make you think outside of the game. I can't say more to avoid spoiling but I loved it.
Characters - At first you might think the characters are shallow and not that interesting, but as you start playing you realize why the characters are the way they are. Hell, even the bosses of this game have personality and motives for their actions. There is just one character in the game that I wished it was explained a bit better.
Gameplay - It is not a game like Bayonetta where you have dozens of different combos, it is more simplistic BUT is excellent as you would expect from a game from PlatinumGames. There is a huge selection of weapons and abilities you can choose so there are many different play styles to try out.
Graphics - They're alright, what you would expect from a modern game, but definitely not the best out there. I really love the animations during combat and the design of most of the bosses though. Maybe a nitpick from my side is that I got a bit tired of the overall color pallet in the game and the enemies, since most of the enemies are robots, and most robots have the same color I got tired of seeing the same type of enemies over and over again.
Soundtrack - One of the finest soundtracks you could find in gaming alongside the original Nier. If the game doesn't appeal you for some reason, I still recommend checking the soundtrack if you love music.
Voice Acting - I played with the English voices and I personally think that the voice actors did a fantastic job. You also have the option to play with japanese voices if you want to.
Cons:
-There is a hacking mechanic that you get halfway through the game that is OP but at the same time it gets tedious to use and it breaks the pacing of the game. I didn't mind the mini game but I wish it was used in more specific parts of the game or to be more balanced.
-The side quests can break the pacing of the game. Overall the story missions are heavily action oriented while the side quest are slower and can involve some fetch quests. However, the side quests do give a lot of back story to the main plot. What I recommend is to do as least quests as possible during your first playthough, and on new playthroughs complete all the side quests.
-Don't play this game expecting an open world. It has areas you can explore and side quests you can complete but it is not a huge map, and some of the spaces in between the areas can feel empty.
The port:
Mediocre at best. A lot of issues reported from the users that the developers keep ignoring. The development team instead of focusing the attention on fixing the issues and deliver a high quality port, they decide to release a DLC instead. Even with a High-end PC I experienced a couple of crashes and a few frame drops during some specific fights. I can see how these issues are more frequent for a Mid-Range PC.
Overall if you have a high-end PC I can recommend this game on Steam, otherwise I recommend it to play it on Playstation, but it's a game I recommend to anyone who calls himself a gamer.

TL;DR: It will hook you in the first 20 hours, then bore you to death the next 200.
Great artwork and soundtrack, nice species customization and exploration, but that's about it.  Beyond a certain point, there is just no reason to keep playing. After an exciting early game, I felt I was just kept busy by the tedious and pointless micromanagement.
- The tech tree is laughable, like, Laser lvl 1-5 which are all the same except a minor increase in damage.
- The exploration events are very atmospheric, at first, before you have seen them all.
- Making the game real-time is about the worst design decision I have ever seen in a game.
- There are no tactical space battles - you only throw your doomstack against the enemy's and wait for the outcome.
- Diplomacy is really important - but also really limited, which is a bad combination.
- Grave performance issues late game. Not only do the ridiculous large numbers of ships you have to produce force you to click the same buttons hundreds of times again, but they also take their toll on the CPU.
Funnily, the feature people complain most about is actually pretty good in my opinion: the "War Goals". It sort of joins diplomacy and war, which is pretty nice, and strategically relevant.
Still, the core concept of the game is: "micro-optimize a huge amount of small numbers to get one number (i.e. "fleet power") really high", which is about as lame as strategy gaming can get.
I didn't like "Sins of a Solar Empire" and "Endless Space" either, but they are both still better than this.

Reviewed during the Free Weekend event:
I can not recommand this game simply because I can't even play it. Many other players including myself keep running into a "Bug Splat Error Report" at the splash screen that prevents me from even getting into the menu. I have tried almost every suggestion by the community on how to fix this issue from setting the game to Windowed mode to deleting the config files, and logs in the Documents folder. So far nothing has fixed this error for more than a match, and then it goes right back to the same issue of "Bug Splat Error Report" after either a crash, or closing the game down myself. This has been a reported issue for several months now, and has shown no signs of being fixed at all with how slow updates to this game come out. With both of these issues I can see why the game has such a small playerbase, and this is why I do not recommand the game to anyone.
I highly suggest anyone who wants to buy this game to wait for Free Weekend, and try that as a demo to see if you can even get into the game for longer than just a handful of matches. So far I'm very glad I did not buy this game as I have not been able to even play it with my friends.

The Sun and Moon begins as what feels like your ordinary indie platformer, a crisp and clean minimalistic aesthetic accompanied by the nostalgic blips of an 8-bit soundtrack set the background for the seemingly straightforward gameplay involving moving and jumping your way to the exit. This familiar and direct-to-the point platformer feeling quickly and gradually transforms itself into something deeper, more complex and thought provoking as you are given the ability to slingshot yourself through solid walls to reach the previously unreachable orbs needed to exit the stage.
The action and the speed with which you break through each surface leading to your next goal are set to a pace that is addictive and constant, keeping you moving and diving through each cleverly placed obstacle at increasingly speedy times. Even when not rushing at full force for the objectives or trying to collect the little orbs The Sun and Moon is just a blast to relax and experiment with, watching the momentum change as you arc between solid obstacles at different angles.
The name The Sun and Moon itself seems to me like a metaphor for the opposing colors in the back and foreground, and the way your small round character transcends these two different realms as you bounce between jumping in the open air and sliding through the solid material of the ground as you phase into it. The visuals have a very simple and effective yet pleasantly abstract quality to them, the backgrounds in particular starting off looking like continents on some kind of extraterrestrial world map or more-so the dreamlike clusters of clouds amongst a green sky.
The Sun and Moon has a very progressive and rewarding structure to it. It lulls you into a false sense of safety, starting out in the most basic of ways with a challenge that is easy and all-too obvious. The music
bears a strikingly repetitive yet charming 8-bit tone and the map seems to be nothing more than a series of boxes connected by a line. These simplicities don't last long, though;
As you move on this all changes, the levels become large sprawling towers that you weave in and out of, carefully timing your momentum in order to land on a faraway platform. The music from the always incredible Dubmood grows and evolves as more adventurous compositions are layered into the mix and draw you into the expanding challenge. The map twists and conforms into complex shapes as it progresses, branching off into multiple paths of varying difficulty.
With loads of alternate stages locked behind hidden pathways on a huge almost metroidvania-like map, insane par times to challenge yourself with for each stage, and leaderboards to check your skills against the rest of the world the content here is enormous with 150 stages and plenty of replayability keeping you coming back to each one long after you've completed a basic run.
Rising from its roots as a Ludum Dare 29 gamejam under the fitting theme "Beneath the Surface", The Sun and Moon has come a long way and developer Daniel Linssen has turned what was a fantastic and simple concept with suprisingly deep mechanics into a content-rich package that is much sleeker, shinier, and polished than before. With its unique brand of platforming, progressively intensifying audiovisuals, and addictive map system this is must-buy status for anyone who enjoys the likes of The Floor is Jelly or VVVVVV.

Are you looking to buy any of Saints games? Here you will get some tips on which one's better. I recommend buying Franchise Pack because all three games are amazing! Review is SPOILERS FREE!
Graphics and Optimization.
Saints Row 2 runs at various framerate with spikes along the way at random moments. Overall it looks ok to me because of great details in cloth, characters models and surroundings.
Saints Row 3 looks like a game I would recommend to a person with the outdoors fear because it looks soo real. Maybe because I launched it right after SR2? The greatest thing is that this game runs much smoother than the previous one.
Saints Row 4 runs even better than SR3 when having the same engine. Amazing job, devs!
Game World
Saints Row 2 has many types of pedestrians scattered around depending on a location you're in. You can find students and goths at University, nurses and doctors at hospitals, bums at local hoods, jugglers on a beach and skaters in mall. Random citizens at diners use laptops, call their friends via phones, eat things and drink popsicles. The best thing about it is that all parts are connected to each other and interacting in different ways. Walking with a straight back katana holder stumbles across a policeman. After yelled curses they start to shoot in each other. Suddenly a driver decides that it's enough red lights on this street so he jammes a gas pedal on the floor and turns on a sidewalk where are the first two men are. On top of that is ability of all characters including the player's to use drinks and food and weed at any time.  All this makes exploration in this game is so amazing. Visiting the same place makes you recall different facts that you discovered. It makes exploration a rewarding system in which you always look up for something amazing around a corner. There are many different buildings you can enter and explore. Some of them are parts of missions and some are not. For me-this game's world is the best of GTA 1-4 and other saints row games because it's living and it's awesome.
Saints Row 3 looks the same at the first sign - the same pedestrians and random folks outside in parks, on piers and in shops. Their look is more casual like what you see in real life. Rarely you come across individuals such as a peeing old man and weird black man with a chicken commercial on a t-shirt underneath weird massive rags. Character's movement is slower and actions they make when something's happening around are slower as well. Overall it feels like the world has less energy in it. The same is about Steelport itself. Everything is sleepy and doesn't catch your eye like in SR2 or GTA Vice City.
Saints Row 4, however, is a different story. Weird virtual effects on buildings, water and citizens are catchy and interesting to explore. Everything implemented connects very well with the whole idea of a matrix world. The more you progress in the game the more weird everything becomes. It's easy to just jump from a roof to roof, then go explore that big glowing alien tower, then suddenly become interested in something red below you and finally find yourself doing that for hours. Since you're acting in Steelport again, it's always cool to find places that you remember and compare them in both games. Until the final mission you're stuck in the night.
Difficulty
Saints Row 2 is the hardest game of three. I can't say how many times I respawned in front of hospital. What makes it so hard? Firstly, there's no upgrades likein  the other two. You simply start and end with the same amount of health + bonuses from side quests. The game itself is much faster and random events occur all the time. It's way harder to fly helicopters. During shooting you want to hide behind something like trashcan. Does it make game more interesting? Yes!  It doesn't look hardcore but provides some challenge which for me is an essential thing for any game.
Saints Row 3 throws at you masses of enemies. A fight may start calmly but be warned! In a few seconds you'll be overwhelmed by enemies. They will send simple cars, then mutants and then brutes and everything times 10! The same thing is going on during missions. Also there are upgrades that help a lot especially when you hit a high level and become unvulnarable to bullets, car explosions and fire. Overall yes it's a hard game at the beginning and then it becomes easy.
Saints Row 4 has spawning aliens and robots and cars with cookies. It has upgrades as well that protect you from certain types of damage and increase health.The main difference from SR3 is an enemy spawnign rate which is much lower. The increased amout of danger levels all the way up to six means that you'll be dealing with various enemies as it grows and at the 6th it'll be a 1v1 fight agains a guard.
Driving, Cars and Driving Cars
Saints Row 2 has the most types of cars I've ever seen: all your normal and fancy defaults as well as busses, bulldozers, weird food vagons, limos, airport baggage carts, trailers, trucks, bikes.
Saints Row 3 appears to have a little bit less amount of 'normal' cars but definately has more weird cars developed mainly for combat and destruction. My favorite feature is drifting. Using cars such as Bootlegger and Churchill allows you to do long around the corners, 180 degrees and spin drifts. Everything about it feels and looks good!
Saints Row 4 is more about super jumps and running so it's not much to say about cars because they're more just of a things somewhere below. You use cars mainly during missions where using of superpowers are limited or disabled. The game still offers you some new fancy crazy vehicles.
Story
Saints Row 2 has three main scenarios each of them is a story of how a gang died. Missions vary in places and objectives and events. For example, sneak into a power plant and steal a radioactive barrel. Escape with it on a heli and mess up with an enemy boss by using it as a ... in a different way. Homie characters are developing during cutscenes.
Saints Row 3 has even more variety and characters and things. It's one big quest about restoring control over Steelport. Missions and sidequests come along.
Saints Row 4 has the most epic story that involves so many crazy and awesome ideas. That's where the creativity flows. Characters development uses connections to the previous games as well as explanations of past events. Although the game features only a couple new characters it keeps it on a high level.
Co-op mode
Saints Row 2 is running without Steam features such as Achievements and Steam Hud menu and Join Game options. If you're not playing with a friend in the same network you'll have to use a third party programm such as Evolve. However, connection is pretty smoove even though between me and my friend are 7.000 miles. The guest has all features that the host has except: no crew and homes costumization, can't buy property and no side quests progress will carry on in singleplayer and games with other folks online. The gameplay is pretty awesome where you drive around together and do missions and even control your roles in side quests.
Saints Row 3 has an easy to connect Steam support to all players - just start a game and right click on your friend and press 'invite'. You can do things together, you explore the city together, you do missions together. Everything is easy and works just fine. The guest cannot costumize crew or houses but is able to purchase property to recieve an hourly income.
Saints Row 4 has the same easy way to connect to each other. Co-op game still exist on missions and on some side quests however is almost dead during free roaming and collecting stuff. Players use super run and super jump but there's just no way to do it together or simultaniously. So the gameplay looks like this. You and your friends are doing things and sometimes start missions and do them together. After the missions they again move in different directions.
Have fun.

I'm not a big Minecrafter, I do get excited and play some once or twice a year. And this is the first time I've met with a Telltale product. I did not know what to expect but I could see good potential in the concept. Unfortunately it became a terrible disappointment pretty much from the first minute.
The plots are stupid, the conversations are boring. Overall the complexity of the story can make anyone above the age of 10 do self-harm after a couple of minutes. The whole flow of the game (interactive movie?) is painfully slow.
On the rare occasions when your character gets some freedom to act and not just talk crap you realise that the controls are horrible and the world is very linear. Otherwise it's just all talking and selecting your response in a timely manner. The later kills whatever immersion you may (not) have as you need to focus on picking your answer before the time is up, while the others are still talking. Speaking of which, dialog choices detemine the storyline and add dynamism to the gameplay. I can see how that could work, pity I can't force myself to replay the choices just to get a slightly different dumb version of the dialogs.
Not sure what's the intention with this product. It's not a good game as there's pretty much nothing to do in it. Action scenes require the pressing/smashing of one of the 5 control keys within given time. Not that too much action would be required, it's more about not missing those random moments - which again breaks immersion. Fights look awkward and unrealistic even in the standards of Minecraft.
It's not a good movie cause the lack of real plots and twists, at least ones that would get the attention of a 5th-grader or higher. Dialogs are poor and cheesy and everything's happening very slow. Could be al-right for kids, but the age range who could enjoy it the most may require parental guidance during some scenes.
It does not have stunning visuals... hey, it's Minecraft at its basics after all. And it does not have stunning acting either...
Overall it's some good money wasted with regrets in hindsight.
If you try to look past how cheesey it can be at times, it's actually quite enjoyable. I suggest looking up the first episode on youtube and watching at least a little before purchasing.

Episode 1 didn't disappoint, the story is amazing, the characters are awesome, and one of the best things about the game: theres a pig, I love the creature idea, I can't wait for the other episodes to be released, 10/10.

A few minor graphical glitches, and you can't remap your controls. Other than that, a really good game. Telltale is on point, and the characters and story are engaging. Looking forwards to the next episode.
With regards to some of the other reviews, I don't think I've ever seen so many people misunderstanding the central concepts of a game. Others have said it, but I'll say it again: This is not Minecraft, nor made by Mojang. It is a point-and-click adventure game with quick time events and a heavy emphasis on story. Minecraft: Story Mode is a very fun and quirky game, paying homage to the monstrously popular game, Minecraft. It captures the atomsphere, the scale and traits Minecraft had to offer, and the teams at Telltale Game's did a great job porting all that, in their own ways into their own game! You can really feel that they've had fun making this.
While this doesn't play out as a Minecraft game (with the lacking of mining, larger selection of crafting recipes and free roaming survival), this isn't what Telltale Game's was going for. They set out to create a story, that would have the feel of adventure and excitement of Minecraft.
Graphics are great, the characters are loveable, it does have the tendency to crash sometimes, however this can easily be fixed with a quick reboot, and the choses; much like from their previous titles, do make a diffence on how you play and adds in the replay vaule of seeing every possible choses that you may have missed. Sometimes the facial expressions on the characters can be a little bit weird, like squinting their eyes at times and having completely straight mouths, but these do not take away my attention to the bigger picture.
Telltale Game's did all they could to squeeze in loads of familiar touches to the game, to make a Minecraft gamer feel at home. With the textures on blocks, the redstone mechanics, the enemies and mobs and even the weapon condition (albeit, only one weapon has shown this)!
I look forward to future episodes being created for Minecraft: Story Mode, and it has given me some thoughts whether to try out some of their other titles. Unfortunately my wallet isn't so forgiving when it comes to making these decisions (Prohaps Christmas will come calling)!

isn't awful per se, and in fact it's quite playable and has very decent, high-quality, high-res graphics. But the lack of a coherent plot or backdrop makes the game rather aimless and kills motivation to press on.
You are given a random year in time (e.g. 1826, 1411, 2019, etc) and asked to find out what happened then that was of importance. Answers range from things like actual events (e.g. famous wars, stuff that was invented, etc) to fictitious occurrences (mostly for future dates).
This wouldn't have been bad if there were at least some
. But instead the player is just thrown into the game, with no proper introduction or anything, and just instructed to follow directions.
As I said, the graphics are quite good and pleasing to look at. However, instead of looking for objects, you look for things like double or single digits (e.g. "5", "41", "26", "13", etc) and alphabets (e.g. "J", "W", "H", etc) that are hidden in each scene. Every scene also has a "fantasy world" version - I had no idea what that was about, but essentially it is the same scene, except depicted in a surreal manner (e.g. feathers instead of sails for ships, and seashells as chairs and so on).
There was no explanation as to why you were searching for numbers and letters. Also, the "fantasy world" version of each scene was wasted potential, because once again, no reason was given as to how or why this fantasy world existed, and in the fantasy world, the items and searches were exactly the same format as in the non-fantasy world version. So what was the point of having this fantasy version then?
Well, of course right? This isn't very grating - you get pop-ups asking if you want to purchase in-game goods from time to time, but I'm sure players would be more inclined to spend money if they knew what the heck they were doing, and why they were doing it. I'm not about to pay for a treasure chest of stuff (which the game offered me), for instance, if I have no idea what it's for.
Download and play only if you're desperate to look at some nice scenes and perhaps complete some hidden object searches involving letters and numbers. Otherwise, don't bother.

Rising Storm 2:  Vietnam is a great modern edition to the RS/RO game line.  Play is very similar to RS/RO2 and controls will therefore seem very familiar to fans of the series.  It can be a trifle hard sometimes to identify enemy soldiers vs. your own troops, especially at longer ranges or in frantic in-your-face encounters so team kilings abound.  In many ways that is quite realistic so if that was the developers' plans, then well done.  If it isn't then it could use some tweaking if only to give ranters something less to rant about.  Sometimes I've had the team indicator not pop up until after I fired other times there wasn't one visible at all.  Graphics are vivid (and impressively well done) but sometimes the teams can look TOO much alike.  Of course SOME players get bent out of shape about the nearly inevitable TKing but it's just a (really good) game and someone is always going to forget that no matter what game they're playing.  The play is intense and realistic and the maps are impressive.  Recoil makes aiming a challenge on full auto (as it should) and encourages bracing your weapons (as it should) if precision is called for.  My only real complaint is that the lack of bots and single player vs. bot play greatly increases the learning curve for noobs and means that to play, you must deal with the seemingly inescapable mega-players who gripe constantly and demean others (you know those that forget it's ... just ... a ... game -- there's always one).  But, hey, while I REALLY hope they bring back bots I still love this game! :)  A LOT of research and thought obviously went into the weapons for their animations, pros/cons, and overall detail.  I was amazed to see the odd tracer round from "Spooky" (C130 gunship) go bouncing across the landscape as they sometime are wont to do in real life.  Amazing details like that make this one heck of a cool game.  Squad play and good communication is essential if you want to win.  If you join a game just for the fun of running around (or hunkering down) and killing enemies your side might not do as well.  But, hey, fun's fun, am I right? So, in conclusion, for a first person, online, mass participation war game with lots of realism and tons of fun, set in the Viet Nam era,  I don't think you'll find a better one.  You want this game.  Buy it.  Buy it now (then write a review asking for bots, heh-heh-heh).

For now, I am giving this game a good review as I await the dreaded update that is supposed to get rid of Wormhole and Warp FTL Travel Starter tech.
As it stands, I always felt that is what made this game unique, what kept me coming back, unlike Sins of a Solar Empire. It was the variety, the unexpectedness, the fact I had to adapt to different technology like Warp or Wormhole. Space is a 3D environment and I always felt Warp and Wormhole treated it as such.
Warp Travel is the slowest form of FTL travel, but allows your ships to travel to any star within a certain radius. It has a long cool down but has the greatest about of freedom when it comes to movement.
Hyperspace allows your ships to travel pretty quick to new stars, but only along hyperlanes. Cool down is alright, but restricts your movement to these hyperlanes, for good or bad.
Wormhole Travel (my favorite) is the most expensive and restrictive form of FTL travel. It requires you to build Wormhole generators in a system. It works as a focal point for your FTL Travel, as your ships must be in that system to travel to other systems. The Wormhole generator will open a wormhole from that system to another system within a certain radius. It does suffer a pretty glaring tactical weakness as if you lose your generator and there isnt another one within range of your fleet, your fleet is stranded until you can build a new one.
With the proposed update, Paradox is removing Wormhole Travel and Warp Travel, replacing them with naturally spawning wormholes that require technology to stabilize and use. They are also introducing Gates that allow travel between them, but they are naturally spawning and unable to be built as far as I know.
I forgot to mention this above, but there is a 4th option for FTL travel; late game tech Jump Drive. It allows instantanous travel from one system to another, similar to Warp but no travel time. Issue with this is it can bring the Unbidden and start a End-Game Crisis.
Thats all I am putting for now. If Paradox goes through with the update, I plan on switching this to a Not Recommend. As there are already options to restrict the different forms of FTL travel already, it just takes away from what makes this game unique and reduces it to space chokepoints, similar to Sins of the Solar Empire.

Having bought this in a pack of four games for next to nothing in the sale, I honestly feel like I'd have been happy to pay full price for this as the replay value is immense.
The Story itself is actually quite short, and can be fully completed in under twenty minutes after enough practice, but what it lacks in length it makes up for in pure, unbridled fun. It plays like how you'd imagine arcade games would be nowadays, it's smooth, simple, and some of the moves you have to pull off require a serious amount of precision, not to mention patience! The teleport mechanic is nothing short of genius. It's one button that sends out one projectile that puts you wherever it hits; Poundland's answer to a portal gun. However despite the simplicity, it still has so much depth as you end up having to string together jumps and multiple shots to overcome obstacles in some very challenging ways, not many of which are immediately apparant towards the end or for a few of the secrets.
That's another thing this game does well, collectibles. I went through my first playthrough taking roughly over an hour and I found a grand total of two collectibles. I didn't even know one type of collectible even existed until I saw an achievment for it! Without giving much away, there are some places that pure curiosity will take you on your second playthrough, using all your skills from the first, that will give you the best feeling of "Woah, I didn't even know that was in the game!" and then a feeling of "What the F*** do I do to get that?" and believe me you will try for anywhere between ten minutes to an entire afternoon to get that but you'll get it. And that feels so good. Behind all of this, is the brilliant and catchy soundtrack, which is stuck in my head forever at this point unfortunately!
In short, well worth the price and I'm still coming back for more from a game which can be beaten comfortably in roughly half an hour. Well done Miniboss, you have me hooked!

Paladins was at one point a promising game... countless patches later not so much. Instead of improving on it's initial game concept most of the development time was spent becoming that thing most people accused the game of: being a f2p Overwatch rip-off. Core gameplay mechanics were dropped (siege), cards trivilaized to "fake" customization, the TTK lowered and maps shrunken down. The developers seem to be perfectly content on becoming the casual friendly Overwatch which is a shame because just like with Tribes Ascend they had something good in their hands but managed to ruin it.
Things to note:
- The netcode sucks (or the servers).
- Queue times are long and MMR is a joke.
- General pub play nets you more bots than anything (which are not even visibly distinguished from regular palyers).
- Comptetitive Paladins is a joke. It's the same handful of players since the beginning and they would probably struggle to even reach Masters in Overwatch.
- Every patch adds more bugs the devs will never fix (and it has plenty of those).
- Hitboxes are crazy big and as blocky as the map design.
- Resources are quite sacre when starting out leaving you with a subpar champion roaster. Apparently the gold prices also never get readjusted for the post-steam release champions.
- Balancing is too difficult for the devs...
- Footsteps in this game make me manic... totally failed in the sound design there.

Reasons its awesome:
(perspective from co-op vs bot player)
The EOR LOADOUT GAME ENGINE is really Refined and Smooth. The PHYSICS are EXCELLENT and u get a real feel for the game after awhile.  It doesn't make me tired or dizzy after playing awhile like the VALVE engine and others and the Cartoony graphics are a fun pretty enviroment to play in.
The Audio is EXCELLENT and intuitive and the game play is a razer fast twitch play to a laid back and remote kill game so it covers a lot in a sandbox.
The latency is the best I have seen, and that generally averages 30-35ms.
So between the GAME ENGINE and LATENCY it Really Feels CUTTING Edge!
A lot of work has been done to balance the guns ahead of release and the more you dig in the RPG nature of Weaponcrafting and strategy of use, the more you enjoy.
The AI of the bots level up as you level and it is difficult to corral them unless all 4 team players are on the same page.
The Game rewards team work and assist as its more important to do collective damage than to be a RAMBO KILL Monger. Good team work really owns the day.
I have only seen vids/streams of the people vs people mode, but it would seem the same would carry over.
This really is a free to play game and not a PAY to WIN approach like so many others.
The only thing you purchase is cosmetics and the ability to double XP/blutes and a few slots.
The only advantage of double XP is that it cuts down the time in half to level up parts and guns, but you need experience to use each gun part per personal taste.
There are a few bugs like connection issues once in awhile and the matchmaking system isn't fully worked out.
There is also needed effort to improve the Player VS Bot experience such as being able to change the difficulty of the bots per your mood or team experience rather than it being automaticly done for you.

This is an update of my review after finishing 40 hours of the game. I have just killed a big boss and concluded the main game. I am about to start on 2 different DLCs of this game.
Now after 40 hours of this game, I have seen a number of shortcomings and bugs, and will try to write about them in this update, so that I present an accurate picture of the game.
Shortcoming of this game.
1. This game is an ABANDONWARE, like what many other  previous reviews have said. It was originally a Kickstarter game, where backers paid money directly to the developer to create this game and some DLCs. The developer got the money, created the game and 2 DLCs and left in February 2017. What this means is that currently there is no tech support of any kind, and there are many small bugs and irritating features which are not fixed. However, the game itself is still good enough to be played, and I have completed the main game. For the price of $6.99, I think it is definitely worth it for me.
2. My biggest complain about this game is the high monster encounter rate. However since the developer is gone and there is no tech support, I just have to bear with it to play this game.
3. There are also several game breaking bugs, like being trapped in a certain wall. However they can be avoided by reloading an earlier save and taking a different route for example. There are also minor glitches in several of the quest. However, I was able to finish the main game and all the quests after 40 hours of game play. I also read up on the forum about possible bugs and avoided them.
4. This game is unpolished as there are various spelling errors and small glitches that will never be fixed since the developer got the money and left. Arrh. It's irritating.
Strength of this game.
1. Excellent story. The story is really excellent, but is a bit on the dark side. It is the story that keep me playing despite all the glitches and bugs. The story just drive me to play 1 more hour and 1 more hour. I just have to find out what happen next. Also there are many dark twists to the game and that create suspense as well. I love that.
2. I love the combat mechanics, the various spells that have to be learn by discovery and not obtained automatically from leveling.
Overall, I will give this game a 70%, and would still recommend this game despite the fact that the developer abandon the game. It is interesting enough for me to finish the game, and I will look forward to playing the 2 DLCs. I will give another update after I spend more time in this game.

This was my original review after 10 hours.
I normally write reviews after I completely finished a game, or at least spend about 50 hours into the game.  However, this RPG Maker game is so much fun that I feel compelled to write about it after just 10 hours of gameplay. I am still really far from completing this game, but am impressed by the quality of the game to write about it comfortably.
What is really fun about this game is the preponderance of quests. Furthermore, many of the quests are proactively thrust upon you, instead of you making efforts to find them. For instance, when you enter a zone, the barkeeper's daughter will come running to you to tell you that her father have some key information for you and you should go to the bar immediately. That will start a quest. Another example would be that your fellow team member would initiate a conversation with you saying that she needs to visit her parents and that will lead you to a series of events which trapped you, leading to another quests. This is a game that keeps you on your toe all the time. There is no need to grind or wait for things to do. In fact, from the 10 hours that I played, I am flooded with so much quests that I am always behind. In the time that I take to solve a quest, 4 or 5 other would have sprung out on their own. Talking about an immersive gaming atmosphere, WOW !!!
The storyline is a bit on the dark side. You are teleported to a fairy tale universe with strange twists instead. Many of the childhood fairy tales that you used to know are presented in this game with strange alternate interpretations.
Visually, the graphics is stunningly beautiful and the gameworld is extremely detailed. I also like the samller (thinner) game font, and the high resolution display. The game also implement many useful features to make life easier. For example you can selectively chose which few quests you want to track and they will display key information on your game screen in the crispy small fonts. I also like the fact there there seems to be no upper limit to the number of quests that you can accept and keep open at any time. I will feel overwhelmed and pressured if I have to drop quests due to any kind of limitations. However, that does not happen in this game.
Another thing I love about this game is that your skills (called affinities in this game) are not automatically given to you when you level, like most other games.  Many of the skills, including spells that you can cast, are given to you as rewards for solving certain quests. This enable me to really appreciate each spell, and understand how difficult it was to acquire them.
One of the most fun things about old school rpg is called "chest scumming" and it is present in this game as well. When you come across a big chest, it will give you a key weapon or armor. The type of item in the chest is usually fixed, but that item will have variable statistic. For example a certain overcoat may increase your defence, agility and luck, but the actual increase is variable, and changes with each time you load the game. Normally, I would reload the game a few times until I feel satisfied with the item. As a completionist, this is something that I like and missed in many of the fast pace newer games.
Overall, this particular game does bring back happy memories of the old school rpg that I played many years ago, like Wizardry and Ultima. However, what is nice is also the excellent graphics and useful tools (like quest tracking, etc) that comes with the old school game :)
I highly recommend this game, and know that I will be spending many more "10 hours" in this game as well.

“Unhappy Ever After” is a RPG in a grim fairy world where well-known tales and characters (Alice, Hеnsel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood, etc.) were twisted by wicked minds of developers from Warped Tales. Beyond its parody to the fantasy “Unhappy Ever After” also aims to parody the real world drawing on situations that are all too prevalent in our society such as drug abuse, terrorism, and dirty politics.
“Unhappy Ever After” takes place in a dark fantasy land of Twelve Duchies where Emperor’s dictatorship is issued for legitimate power and mages’ resistance is called terrorism.
I’d rather say it’s a mature story that provides a unique perspective on children’s tales while addressing the difficult issues that plague modern society. I really liked the main story and the Twelve Duchies’ background written with subtle humor and usage such adult themes like cannibalism, vengeance, death, substance abuse.
Visually “Unhappy Ever After” is pretty impressive for a RPG Maker game. Game’s graphics and art style are very nice and immersive.
To my surprise developers did their best designing each area of the world beautiful looking (for a RPG Maker game). They tried to make each region (location) is unique and visually unlike other regions. Besides there’re different monsters in each region and every region has its own story and side-quests.
Sure there’re some problems in the game. Although the music is pretty good the sounds are repeating and annoying. There’s no load option in the menu and no in-game map. The developers didn’t hire any proof-readers so there’re some typos, misspelling and wrong items’ descriptions in the game. Every player can see glitches and bugs in the game (e.g. walking through walls, unreachable chests, unequipable items).
But the primary reason for me finally giving up the game after such a long time playing this game (over 8 hours) was a high rate of random encounters (battles with monsters unseen in the screen). ARGH! I couldn’t walk a few steps without starting a random battle! Random battles were
while traveling outside town!
And to double my frustration the enemies were auto-leveling up with my party’s level.
The game really needs a lot of polishing but for unknown reasons developers stopped communication with the community and correction the game in February, 2017.

______________________________________________________________
«Unhappy Ever After» - это RPG в мрачном сказочном мире, где хорошо известные сказки и персонажи (Алиса, Гензель и Гретель, Красная Шапочка и т. д.) были искажены испорченными разработчиками из Warped Tales (Извращенные Истории). Помимо пародии на фэнтези «Unhappy Ever After» также нацелена пародировать реальный мир, показывая ситуации, которые слишком распространены в нашем обществе, такие как злоупотребление наркотиками, терроризм и грязная политика.
Действие «Unhappy Ever After» происходит в стране темного фэнтези - Двенадцати Герцогствах, где диктатура Императора выдается за законную власть, а сопротивление магов называется терроризмом.
Я бы сказал, что это зрелая история, которая показывает детские сказки в уникальной перспективе, обращаясь к сложным проблемам, которые наносят ущерб современному обществу. Мне очень понравилась основная история и общий фон Двенадцати Герцогств, написанные с тонким юмором и использованием таких взрослых тем, как каннибализм, месть, смерть, злоупотребление психоактивными веществами.
Внешне “Unhappy Ever After” выглядит довольно впечатляюще для игры, сделанной при помощи RPG Maker. Графика и художественный стиль игры очень приятные и захватывающие.
К моему удивлению, разработчики старались изо всех сил, чтобы сделать каждую область мира красивой (для RPG Maker игры). Они попытались сделать каждый регион (локацию) уникальным и визуально непохожим на другие локации. Кроме того, в каждом регионе существуют разные монстры и у каждого региона есть свои история и побочные квесты.
Конечно, в игре есть некоторые проблемы. Хотя музыка очень хорошая, но звуки повторяются и раздражают. В меню нет опции загрузки и нет внутриигровой карты. Разработчики не нанимали корректоров, поэтому в игре есть опечатки, орфографические ошибки и неправильное описание вещей. Каждый игрок может увидеть глюки и баги в игре (например, прогулки сквозь стены, недосягаемые сундуки, неодеваемые вещи).
Но для меня главной причиной наконец-то забросить игру после столь долгого времени (более 8 часов), была высокая частота случайных встреч (битвы с монстрами, невидимые на экране). АРГХ! Я не мог пройти даже несколько шагов, чтобы не началась случайная битва! Случайные битвы были
во время путешествия за пределами города!
А для увеличения моего расстройства враги автоматически подравнивались с уровнем моей партии.
Игра действительно требует доделки, но по неизвестным причинам разработчики прекратили общение с игровым сообществом и исправление игры в феврале 2017 года.

Unhappy Ever After is an RPG that takes place in a fantasy fairy tale world. If you couldn't tell from the title, the game has a little dismal atmosphere (It kind of reminds me of the LISA games, in terms of atmosphere). If you're not a fan of dark comedy, you might not like it.
PROS:
- Nice artwork on the sprites and overworld maps. I love that there's a day/night cycle and that the sun rises/sets while you walk around.
- Battle Screens are clean , easy to understand, and the enemy design is creative.
- The game autosaves when you enter a new screen. You never lose any significant progress.
- The world building. I found myself sucked into the story upon reaching the first town.
- The characters are funny and multi-faceted.
- I love the atmosphere and the dark twists on standard fairytales
- Length. You get your money's worth. It took me 8 hours to get out of the first area because there was so much to do.
- Sidequests. Lots and lots of sidequests.
- It's not super easy, but not frustratingly difficult. I like that there's a difficulty slider that you can change at any time.
- You actually have to use your items. I have an issue with item hoarding when I play RPGs and end up never using the stuff in my invetory. Not the case here. Healing spots a rare, so you need to use your potions.
- I like the replayability factors. There's lots of alternate ways to finish the quests. You also have to choose what 3 affinities you want Sophia to focus on. So I already have an incentive to play the game again.
- The devs seem really nice, and actually listen to feedback.
- It's only $5.99!
CONS:
- There's no map. It'd be nice to have a map of some sort. I found myself getting lost a lot, and sometimes the directions are unclear to where you need to go.
- I've noticed some typos. It's nothing major, but it is a little distracting.
- It's hard to tell where you can/can't walk because of the scenery. Also NPCs will walk in front of me sometimes and prevent me from moving.
I give this game a 9/10. Definitely worth your money if you like RPGs.
