This is an edit of my earlier review.  Initially, the way the monsters leveled with you, along with the lack of gear, made the battles very long and tedious.  However, within days of posting my review, the developer has made several changes to the game that eliminate many of my negative comments. First, there is now a difficulty setting. Those who want the much more difficult battles, can have them, and those who want a bit less of a grind feel and a more casual experience can select the very easy or easy settings.  I've tried them out, and it's like a completely new game.  Even in very easy mode, the battles still require a bit of strategy and take a little time, but they are nowhere near the length they used to be. Monsters will be a lower level than you and do far less damage, which means the constant need for health items is also greatly diminished.
As for the game itself, beautiful graphics and environments.  There was a lot of thought and a lot of custom detail that went into this game, making it a delight. On top of that, the story revolves around a very dark and twisted fairy tale world. I love it, but, it might not be everyone's cup of tea. So far, the game delves into many dark topics and violence is a key element. It really is an amazing twist on something normally for children, and the dark side of fairy tale characters is delightful. Just a fair warning--don't grow too attached to anyone. I haven't finished the game yet, but anticipate more devastating loss, and I actually can't wait to see the twists and turns the story takes.
Another thing I really enjoy about the game is the way that abilities are set up for Sopie, the main character. No earning them by simply leveling, but rather you have to find certain things in order to gain new skills. On top of that, you have to make choices. There are six types of magic that Sophie can learn; however, to gain strength, three of those will have to be sacrificed.
As for your companions, their skills are called "affinities," something everyone in the fairy tale world has. This means that they will have an affinity for one thing or another, and nothing else. As far as I know, they don't gain any new skills as they level--whatever they have is it. This means that you often have to think through how best to defeat certain kinds of monsters based on the skills your companions have and on what the monsters' weaknesses are.
With the changes in place--and the fact the developer readily listens to feedback and implements regular changes and updates--I would definitely recommend this game. Especially if you like things a little more on the dark and twisted side.

For now, I am giving this game a good review as I await the dreaded update that is supposed to get rid of Wormhole and Warp FTL Travel Starter tech.
As it stands, I always felt that is what made this game unique, what kept me coming back, unlike Sins of a Solar Empire. It was the variety, the unexpectedness, the fact I had to adapt to different technology like Warp or Wormhole. Space is a 3D environment and I always felt Warp and Wormhole treated it as such.
Warp Travel is the slowest form of FTL travel, but allows your ships to travel to any star within a certain radius. It has a long cool down but has the greatest about of freedom when it comes to movement.
Hyperspace allows your ships to travel pretty quick to new stars, but only along hyperlanes. Cool down is alright, but restricts your movement to these hyperlanes, for good or bad.
Wormhole Travel (my favorite) is the most expensive and restrictive form of FTL travel. It requires you to build Wormhole generators in a system. It works as a focal point for your FTL Travel, as your ships must be in that system to travel to other systems. The Wormhole generator will open a wormhole from that system to another system within a certain radius. It does suffer a pretty glaring tactical weakness as if you lose your generator and there isnt another one within range of your fleet, your fleet is stranded until you can build a new one.
With the proposed update, Paradox is removing Wormhole Travel and Warp Travel, replacing them with naturally spawning wormholes that require technology to stabilize and use. They are also introducing Gates that allow travel between them, but they are naturally spawning and unable to be built as far as I know.
I forgot to mention this above, but there is a 4th option for FTL travel; late game tech Jump Drive. It allows instantanous travel from one system to another, similar to Warp but no travel time. Issue with this is it can bring the Unbidden and start a End-Game Crisis.
Thats all I am putting for now. If Paradox goes through with the update, I plan on switching this to a Not Recommend. As there are already options to restrict the different forms of FTL travel already, it just takes away from what makes this game unique and reduces it to space chokepoints, similar to Sins of the Solar Empire.

In essence Dominions 4 is a very enjoyable strategy game that offers a very unique concept and experience. I thoroughly recommend this game for those who enjoy turn based strategy games, and D&D players.
The game features well researched historical nations fighting alongisde their own mythologies, such as Japanese Ashigaru being supported by Tengu, or Viking raiders paired with dragons. These nations are led by your own custom god who radically changes the territory that he/she/it controls, wether by making it into a fertile and well ordered land or turning it into a disease ridden, unproductive region of unrest. Or your god can simply be a towering behemoth that smashes its opponents to pieces in battle. Both methods are completly viable. The final component is the deep magic system, with apocalyptically powerful spells and summonable creatures divided into different schools. Some nations have excellent soldiers but terrible mages, and vice versa. It is very rewarding to create your own deadly combinations of different nations, gods and magics; the amount of combinations is staggering. The game is still updated fairly often bringing more nations to the increasingly large roster. Furthermore, there are many mods to keep adding content to the game.
However, the game can be rather intimidating with a frankly inadequate tutorial, making a read of the manual essential. I had to lose several games before even starting to understand what was going on, and I'm still pretty bad at it. The graphics are certainly functional but they are not exactly good either. In singleplayer there really is no diplomacy to speak of, you are constantly at war with the other players - I think that the lack of diplomacy is the biggest issue the game has.
Ultimately, Dominions 4 is a great game that I greatly enjoy playing.

Dominions 4 is a turn-based strategy game similar to Risk but way more complicated. This game is not for everyone. It is a very good game but it requires patience, a lot of thought, and a whole lot of reading. The manual for the game is over 300 pages long. The graphics are very simple and not at all amazing, but it gives you the IDEA and you lets your imagination do the rest. If you like games like Risk, you will like this game.

This isn't a game for everyone.
The strategy game players already have their traits, but this game requires them to utilize their traits to the maximum.
Dominions 4 has so many different aspects, it'll probably take you a couple of new games to get adapted to the controls and different things you can do.
There is a huge amount of different startup settings you can use, and a huge amount of factions to choose from. Every faction is different - and I mean different not just cosmetically, but to the very essence. To give an example to show the contrast between the factions:
Late Age Agartha is a nation of cave-dwellers. Their version of cavalry rides cave drakes, their mages are skilled in earth and death magic. They also recieve a bonus to alchemy. Their best soldiers require a large amount of resources to produce. Since most of their soldiers have darkvision or are already blind, they don't get harmed from spells like Solar Eclipse and Darkness.
Late Age Lemuria is a land of the Undead (it's basically a fantasy counterpart of Ancient Rome which gets corrupted). The extent of your pretender god's dominion will always kill off the populace in provinces. You then use these dead bodies to bolster your army with spectral centurions, velites, and consuls  - not through training, but through summoning with spells. Thus, you have little use for gold or resources.
---
There are also many Pretender Gods to choose from. From a mere sculpture that has gained power through millenia of worship, to a divine burning glyph, from a titan of the sea, to a dragon. You can further customize your pretender by changing the effects of its dominion (the extent of its power), and its capabilities in magic.
Units differ wildly. Some are only recruitable in some regions, most are only available to a single nation. They have tons of attributes, a stat sheet, and commander/spellcaster/scout/priest units have an inventory for items.
The graphics are a bit of a shame, it's true. Most of the time, you won't even watch the battle replays, the random map generator creates ugly looking maps. However, the userbase (and potentially you will too), have created some lovely looking maps, worthy of Tolkien himself.
The gameplay is very complex. I don't like Let's Play videos, so I had to learn by myself. You'll need a bit of patience, some intuition, and curiosity to understand fully how it works.
But here's why this game is really worth playing: The storytelling.
The richness of the world and its backstory will pull you in. Every single unit type has a story. Every "hero" type character has the potential to be your favourite character in the game.
You will spend astral magic gems, month after month, empowering Sybil - your Oracle fountain pretender goddess. And you will craft the most powerful of items, to arm Eteonos - a 54 year old Strategos. Eteonos is 54 years old. His best years should be behind him, but he still fights with the vigour and heart of a young hoplite. A shaman you've recruited helped you put a spell over your dominion - where creatures of all kinds age slowly and every wound heals given time, even a lost eye or limb. Eteonos's stiffening joints move with ease, his reflexes and strength are active as ever. You don him with the arms and armor of the Warrior of Dawn, and you send him to the Arena, to fight other champions on your behalf, to bring honour on to your name, and win the prized Champion's Helmet.
Will he succeed? Wİll he fail? Who knows. What matters is your brain weaves together a story, and that story enhances the game greatly.

People have said a lot of things about Dom4, with the top ones being statements like "I'm sending my race of lavamen led by a sun with arms and bird wings against giant Jewish cannibal wizards led by a sentient blood fountain." They've also probably said things like "if you love spreadsheets, you'll love this game." Both of these statements hold truth. Here's what you'll find in the game
Pros:
- The largest variety of choices I've seen in any video game.
- Over twenty races, each radically different in a way that still tends to balance itself out.
- Three eras of play, each radically affecting said twenty races. Changes range from shifting their focus to turning them into different nations entirely.
- Weird and wonderful lore everywhere.
- A robust and well-crafted magic system.
-Most of the actual micromanagement is under the hood, and a lot of things can be automated, allowing you to spend your time on the more important stuff.
- It'll run on a potato.
Cons:
- Said choices are shoved in your face up front, and even with the handy tooltips, it's hard to get what they all mean.
- Unless you read the doorstopper of a manual, you will be confused. And even then, it takes experimentation to actually know what every number means.
- The wrong mistake at the wrong time can send your entire civilization kicking and screaming into the abyss.
- Multiplayer is plagued by a meta nearly as bad as DOTA 2.
- All that important stuff you micromanage? It's still a lot.
- It has the kind of graphics you'd expect from a potato.
Don't be scared by its price tag, either. It's 35 dollars, but it's already given me more replay value than nearly any game I've spent 60 bucks on, and it's definitely given me more content. But if you're really adamant about saving money, wait till a sale. You won't regret it.

It is a really big shame that Creation Club exists. In news, it overshadows what is an excellent remake. Moreover, you will find it more rewarding and better in quality to obtain mods from free sites. Learning how to manage mods, living through a game that had 250+ mods (@me in oldrim) and troubleshooting was a really relly big part of why I loved Skyrim so much to begin with.
A bit of backstory:
Way back in 2012 I got an xbox360 for Christmas and it came with a downloadable code for Skyrim (no DLC). I put it aside, not knowing what TES was and forgot about it. A year and a half later, I found it and decided to give it a shot. That was a difinitive moment in my life; I racked up over 500 hours, hit level 81 and actually purchased all of the DLC as it came out. It was the first game that I fell in love with.
Then, I built my PC.
I bought Skyrim: Legendary Edition right away, and logged over 1000 hours, doing more of the same from what I did on xbox, but this time with mods. Subsequently, I learned how to mod, and spent over double my playtime toubleshooting, and finding new styles, new visuals, etc. You can read my rull review of oldrim on it's storepage, but essentially I love it.
This brings us to SSE.
Because I bought Skyrim: Legendary Edition, Steam automatically gave me SSE (kudos to Bethesda for doing this, really smart). SSE, put simply, is just Skyrim 64-Bit based on DX11.
WHICH IS A REALLY BIG DEAL
Oldrim used a 32-Bit based DX9 engine: Okay, fine for last-gen consoles, doesnt really cut it for people who lived off of mods (like myself). If you're not really familiar with computer hardware, a 32-Bit architechure cannot take advantage of more than 4GB of RAM. This meant that if you were running very heavy mods, then that would fill up quickly, leading to stuttering, CTD's and much more. It was *possible* to work around this, but you would always be limited by the bottleneck of the game engine.
A 64-Bit Skyrim means that you can mod more intensively. For reasons beyond me, Bethesda did not remove the 255 plugin limit to your loadorder, but honestly this was never really a big deal because there are tools available for you to combine mods, and chances are, if you're running more than 255 plugins, you're well versed in modding already.
A DX11 based engine means that you are able to take full advantage of more than the ram limit on a GTX 970, allowing for smoother gameplay with higher testures/resolutions.
There are graphical improvements to SSE, but they are (imo) negligable, and you're probably just going to mod over them anyway (I certainly have). SSE delivers the same experience as oldirim on a new engine, which is a-okay for me.
TL;DR - Dont use the Bethesda mod marketplace/ Creation Club ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and SSE is just Skyrim 64-Bit, which is actually really ♥♥♥♥ing handy.

This is a deep turn-based strategy title that's about spreading you your deity’s religious power through conquest and proselytizing. It’s a fantasy title and has something like 10,000+ unique spells between the different factions.
Your deity’s avatar (pretender god) will appear at some point, which you preset. You pick the time period you want to start the game in, which will affect technology and available starting factions. You need a pretty hefty system to run it at max fps, there’s a lot of calculations that go on in the background. The graphics aren’t spectacular either way. Combat is hands off. You set the tactics and formations your commanders will use, as well as the dispositions of the units. Spying will help you know how to set your tactics. Proselytizing will give you advantages as the faith of the locals will change advantages. Watching post-combat reports and fact sheets will be hugely beneficial on how you change your tactics for the next conflict with that particular army. As you learn the game it becomes even deeper. The dev’s made it so it’s easy to make your own maps, and the community has uploaded quite a few between Dominions 3-4. The game does allow you to build up territories that you control. You can also search for places of power, which give you advantages. Research will allow you to have access to more powerful spells (and better craftables), which allow you to more fully utilize the power of your casters (individual units have caps on capabilities and with what kinds of spells they can utilize; it’s all part of the strategy).
I’ve enjoyed this title, and if you like strategy games this is a title you will like. It’s from a small dev team, which has a long heritage of solid strategy/tactical games. If you buy it from the dev’s website (or their publisher) you will get the DRM-free version as well as a steam key. Desura was also giving you a key if you had a license from the dev (I’m not sure if they still do or if Desura is a healthy company at this point).

Good, but not as good as I'd hoped.
After playing Metal Gear Rising, and Transformers: Devastation, I was prepared for a great game that I would want to play again, and again, and again. However, I've only played it for 7 hours and I can already tell that they traded substance for size. In Metal Gear Rising, there was never more than 30 seconds of running around until you got to a fun new fight, or something. That doesn't happen here, there are plenty of times where you have to run in a straight line for 5 minutes just to get to a fast travel point, so you can wait for a loading screen so finish, so you can run 5 more minutes to get to where you want to go. Admittedly this isn't a GAME BREAKING issue, but it's not exactly fun either. Throw in sub-par keyboard support and occasional crashes and you have a game that only succeeds in reminding you of better days.
Now the plot on the other hand was pretty good, not as good as Metal Gear Rising, but pretty good. There were a few, shall we say "odd" decisions here and there. Some of which were enough to break the immersion and make you think "What? Why would anyone put that in there?" but in an effort to not spoil anything I'm not gonna say exactly what those moments were.
Lastly, the save system hearkens back to the old days of classic JRPGs, because you have to go to a save-point, and there is NO auto-saving (Something that MGR and T:D DID have, IIRC.) Personally I didn't find this to be TOO bad, but it was definitely an inconvenience. I just thought I should mention it because there are plenty of people that DO think it makes the game unplayable in the discussions section.
Honestly I had such higher hopes for a Platinum Games product, but hey, you can’t win them all. Hopefully their next game can fix these issues.

This game isnt RO3, its RS2 (Rising Storm 2). If you've played Rising Storm 1 (which I can only assume the people who thumbs down didn't) then you'd know these are not the same games. The Rising Storm Series is more of a testement to aymmetrical combat than it is a "military simulator". In fact, it's not a military simulator at all (nor is RO2 for that matter), and if that's what you are looking for, ♥♥♥♥ing look elsewhere. Yes RO:2 had tanks and APC's, but the thing is is that Rising Storm:1 stripped these out when it first came out and never updated them in. Does that suck? Of course it does, but the ♥♥♥♥ing videogame is like 30 bucks what are you ♥♥♥♥♥ing about. Most negative reviews on here dont account for the price of the game and the predecessor that came before. This game is inline with the evolution of Rising Storm, it is progressing as the developers see fit and they just updated the game adding 2 new guns and another gun variant. Also why would you even want a campaign? The RO:2 campaign was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and if you think it was good your opinion just is not valid. Offline bots at the most; but this is a multiplayer game for purists. Free aim, minimal hud, lethal weapons and realistic recoil. This is what the game is about, not vehicles or campaigns or easy modes. Play Insurgency if you want that, but good luck finding a good Veitnam game; besides this one of course.
I made this review in part of the vehement responses from the so called "community". This game won't die, Rising Storm: 1 is still going strong for Christ's sake. I love this game because there just aren't games like this out there. If I had to talk about the improvements of this game I'd have to say accessibility is its strongest suit. This is one of the few "mil-sim/twitch shooters" I can pick up and just have a blast in, with friends or by myself. More so than Insurgency because of the massive maps and usually non-linear objectives, and more so than Battlefield 1 because of the brutal, tactical realism and one shot kills this game is so fond of. You also can't beat the Vietnam backdrop that so few games take advantage of. The removal of experience based weapon upgrades are nice and the cosmetic replacement is even nicer. With every click in the menus and options and upon observance of this games production value you can absolutely see the love that went into making this game.
All in all this is a one of a kind, Tripwire attention to detail, 'Nam romp that is waiting to be explored by more players. If you enjoy FPS shooters even a little bit, dont hesitate, It's a great little game that admittedly could use more players. Then again, I never struggle finding a full server (64 players) myself (I live in the U.S.).
Anyway, ♥♥♥♥ the haters this game is great. I needed to make this review because people have been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on this game for no reason.

Buyer beware: The game is very clearly unfinished in lots of ways. Consider 'Early Access' before purchasing.
The game is reminiscent of a more lite version of Grand Theft Auto, or more accurately for GMod players, DarkRP. Overall it seems to be quite a solid game, with the lo-fi graphics actually beneficial especially to lower end users who don't have very good computers. For only having a single developer it seems to have a quite good track record of updates, updating at what looks like once per month on average.
What impresses me more is the
for the game -- not because what it offers looks promising, but because progress is tracked well, and the goals seem very realistic instead of making over-ambitious promises. Don't get me wrong, ambition is good, but the developer seems to have a good idea of what's more important at this time.
Multiple times I found myself saying "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥that's cool" in response to multiple features, including being able to trade with bystanders, the fact that each of them have unique needs of their own, being able to intimidate NPCs, and the knockout/revival system.
Some things I'd like to see are the ability to rob apartments, so that there's a degree of having to defend your♥♥♥♥♥♥from players, or perhaps cops/rival gangs. I'd also like for police detection to be more complex, in that if there are no witnesses to a crime, the crime shouldn't be reported. Think Watch_Dogs style where you can spot civilians calling the police but you can put a stop to them. What else would be cool would be fluctuating prices of different objects, like weed suddenly booming on the drug market. Also make a different attachment slot for faces so I can wear hats with bandanas around my mouth.
My only complaints mostly concern the user interface. It looks janky and what one would expect a Unity product to look like. I also think the method of interaction is clunky (especially being bound to the middle mouse button by default) and that it could definitely user a better context menu. These however are not gamebreaking issues, and I can understand the developer not considering such things as a higher priority than addition of features to finish the game itself, and fixing bugs.
Overall a great project to keep your eyes on that offers a city RPG experience I haven't quite seen. (also it's $5. good luck beating that price tag)

Hey folks,
just for anyone here who’s interested… this is a list of things to keep in mind when it comes to Stellaris. I put this in as a positive review because after all, i’ve played this a couple times and still play it, but… ya. See below.
This is written from 1st-hand xp in Stellaris 1.8, including Utopia.
1. Failure in Stellaris is not an option.
In some situations Stellaris presents failure risk as a sort of… realistic (…? ahem) outcome. You’re well advised to not take this seriously.
Failure in certain situations can have consequences that lead to a game loss several hours later. Whenever Stellaris tries to make it look like, failing in a given game event is safe and normal to accept, don’t accept it. Reload and try until it works. You have been warned.
2. Setbacks in Stellaris are not an option.
You can’t rely on Stellaris to give you another chance once you lose a decisive conflict. Avoid setbacks like the plague. If you can’t avoid them, consider starting a new map.
Not doing so will likely end up in wasting hours of your valuable time and effort. It will also result in various extra ulcers, fantasies of violence against fluffy aliens, and hardware abuse. Putting your time and energy in a new map is likely to be more fun and less frustrating. You have been warned.
3. Lagging behind in Stellaris is not an option.
Don’t expect any of the perks you’re granted as a player to give you any kind of edge over an AI-controlled faction. If anyone is ahead of you and they’re not on your side, it will likely cost you the map. Teaming up with another faction may help but that has its risks as well, see below.
When in doubt, be smart and save yourself the effort. Just start a new map. Try to get ahead of everybody under all circumstances. You have been warned.
4. Nasty aliens in Stellaris are dead serious about it.
The openly hostile type will immediately go and prepare to storm your planets, destroy your ships, and swallow your whole space civilization as soon as they appear on your map.
It may take several hours for them to actually take a shot at you but they will, take that shot. It’s only a question of time. You have been warned.
5. Nice aliens in Stellaris are not, what they appear to be.
Instead of trying to run you over with some ridiculously large fleet and idiotically large guns, they make every effort to beat you to every planet, every resource, every option in Stellaris to prevent you from getting it yourself.
Nice guys are just as aggressive as the nasties, just less direct. Again, you have been warned.
6. Stellaris plays against you. Not with you.
The AI factions in this game are designed and fully capable of totally sidelining you in your own game, on your own galaxy map.
If given half a chance, they will reduce you to a largely helpless observer. You’ll be forced to watch these things while the game is mostly playing against itself. You’ll get kicked out on the next best chance. Whatever you might remember from other games –– this one doesn't care to keep you in. It much rather wants you out. A.S.A.P. You have been warned.
7. When in Stellaris, save often. Save very, very, very often.
Manage your own saves. Don’t rely on Stellaris autosaves, they’re all too often worthless when it comes to fixing serious challenges you run into.
Also keep the stuff you saved hours ago. Or yesterday. Or ages ago. Reload as soon as you suspect that anything on your map has just gone royally downhill. You have been warned.
8. Think ahead in Stellaris. Also, watch your back.
Obviously you can’t do that as a rookie. You haven’t even been there, so you can’t know what’s essential to do and to not do. You may be able to get yourself a fairly safe and easy scenario by cutting down on the heat level in the settings before you start a new map.
Then again, if you play on anything anywhere close to what the game offers as default, you won’t get an easy scenario. Don’t rely on quick fixing. Stellaris has a habit of quietly creeping up on you, then adding your ears, nose and scalp to its trophy collection.
Recommended, with caveats. Rookies watch out. You have been warned.

So I cannot reccomend this game, but let me explain, because this does not mean I think it's bad, nor do I even think it shouldn't be bought.
That said, It absolutley should not be bought at full price. Wait for a sale or a decent bundle, but do not pay full price.
So, let's start at the start. There's Workshop support, which is about critical- mods are very much required to really be able to enjoy the game, in my opinion. We'll touch on this more later, but after a couple of vanilla games, you're going to be browsing for something to give you some options, spice the game up a bit. Thankfully, the launcher makes enabling and disabling mods a breeze, so there's not too many issues there. It can get a bit fiddly for multiplayer, but it's not too big a deal. It also lets you enable and disable DLC at will- though why you'd disable anything is beyond me. For multiplayer, only the host has to have the DLC, that's nice too.
Race customization isn't super deep- nothing you really wouldn't expect. Homeworld class, couple biological traits, couple government ethics and traits, again, nothing out of the ordinary. there's a couple options that will change the way the game plays, like hive minds, but other than that, it's whatever. Pick your favorite sci-fi trope empire, and move on. The biggest option here on gameplay is the FTL choice, but that's being removed with 1.9, so whatever. No big deal, I guess?
Game setup is exactly what you'd expect- pick number of stars, maxing out at a pretty anemic 1000 (Very tiny galaxy.. but not too out of the ordinary, either) Number of fallen empires, number of AI species, that sort of deal. You can limit the game to only one kind of FTL, but that does kind of remove flavor- not that it matters anyway, since by the late game everyone has jump drives researched. Again, this is all being removed anyway, so grain of salt there.
Game play is... shockingly shallow, honestly. It plays more like an RTS than a 4x or a grand strategy. There's no appreciable civilian economy, anything you build basically goes straight to you. There's a tax called 'consumer goods' but that's honestly all it is- a 15/20% tax on all the minerals you bring in that you can't meaningfully affect without gimping yourself in other ways. It's honestly not that big a drag on your progress, everything considered, since by midgame you should be pumping out plenty of minerals and credits anyway.
There is some management of civilians on your planets- they'll get unhappy and riot and threaten to break away from the empire or gain new ethics that clash with yours, but it's not too big a deal unless you let it get really out of  hand. Despite the devs doing everything they can to nerf the bajesus out of your options, it's still fairly easy to keep unhappy pops under control. Early on this isn't a problem, and xenophobes and spiritualists get even more methods to control it, so, again, not a real big concern. There's no real planet management beyond what to build, and really the only choices you need to worry about are research, minerals, or energy. You'll have one off buildings you'll want to build in some cases- the unity or whatever producing unique is a gimme, for example- but generally, it's either mines, power plants, or farms.
You don't get to control all your planets past a certain point. Basically, in an effort to 'reduce micromanagement', after a certain point  you have to start putting planets into 'sectors'. this is a fancy way of saying, build tall, not wide, cos the devs punish you for trying to build wide. You'll lose at least 25% of the output of a sector, and generally the AI managing them is dumber than a brick. There's mods to remove this, get them.
Exploration is, again, nothing too ground breaking. Occasionally your science ship can stumble across an anomaly or something, which may give you a bonus, may cause problems, up to and including loss of your ship or scientist. Early game, this can be a big blow, but later on you honestly probably couldn't possibly care less. Some of the event chains are really strong early game, some of them are pretty strong for the entire game- the precursor chains, for example, are good to finish off ASAP- but they're nothing game-breaking. Usually.
The exception to this is the cosmic horrors or levithans or whatever. There's a few of them, all of them don't like you, and all of them can and will annihilate your explorers without a problem. Most of them are a match for fleets up till the mid to late game. The reward for defeating them varies incredibly, but most of them are very lacklustre. The enigmatic fortress is probably the best, since at least it gives you a tangible benefit.
The ship designer isn't too deep or complex- certainly nothing we haven't seen before. Pick a hull, pick the weapons, support systems, generators, put them in slots, done. Later ships get various hull component options with different weapon and support slots- very similar, in fact, to sword of the stars. If you're familiar with SoTS ship design, Stellaris ship design isn't going to be too different for you. Civilian ships are a single hull type, as are army transports, so there's not a while lot of options involving them. "Civilian" Ships in this case being explorers (Science ships), constructors, and colony ships. There's no civilian shipping or anything, no freighters besides the army transports, nothing like that. Just warships and the aforementioned noncombatants.
Diplomacy is... I'd call it effectively nonexistant, but that's wrong. It's just exceedingly shallow. There are certain groups that will never engage in diplomacy (Fanatical purgers, for example) or only engage in it to insult you or make demands (Fallen empires). All empires hate warmongers, full stop, and if you conquer planets, it's gonna give everyone an opinion malus towards you. Doesn't matter anyway, wars are pretty, you guessed it, shallow, and it's honestly not hard to beat a large group of smaller empires. You can try to make friends, but ultimatley they're gonna end up hating you if you take out one too many threats.
Warfare sucks. Basically, here's how it works: ball your entire fleet up into one massive stack, find the other guy's massive stack, bash them togther. Loser loses the war- it takes way, way too long to build any kind of meaningful force to recover from a loss in the fleet battle. Accurate? Perhaps- certainly Mahanian- but not much fun, honestly. There's no strategy involved in it. Once you win (if you win), you bombard their planets with impunity, since there's no planetside fortification or surface to orbit weaponry, invade, and when you win the invasion,  that's it. move on to the next planet. Wash/rinse/repeat till you win.
Defensive stations exist, but are very weak, especially in the later game, and very difficult to use. The devs apparently decided in space, no one defends, so there's a limit around each station in which you cannot build another station. While this isn't too uncommon a concept, it also basically means you have to be very careful with spacing and placement of defensive stations to get any kind of use out of them. This is supposed to be the focus of the upcoming DLC, so this may be edited later.
The late game 'crisis' is pretty meh. This isn't to say they're not dangerous- even for a very militaristic late game empire, they're dangerous. It's just that they're nothing that can't be dealt with, especially with a little thought. Basically, your options are hideous xenoform bugs from beyond the dark edge of the galaxy, invaders from another dimension, and AI uprisings. Of them, the AI uprising is the easiest to aviod, and the bugs are the 'default' one, if neither of the other two pop. They all have very high fleet strength, and there's usually a lot of them, but if your fleet's big enough, it really doesn't matter. And if they blunder into a fallen empire, well, that ends that, usually.
It's like a Civ game, but in space, and 100x more detailed. Very good.

OK now hide the mission objectives behind some of those blank walls so that the player can't find them. No, not the red and blue "polarity" walls, that would seem like you're trying to design a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥puzzle. This is the best fantasy turn based strategy game I have played. It also works very well on Linux and MAC. The graphics are cheesy at first but they really grow on you and actually add flavor to the game. The fact is that this game is for true strategy game lovers and not so much for those who play games just for the whiz bang flashy graphics and ooooh shiny effects. If you love true depth in a strategy game which also has a thriving multiplayer community to boot, this game is it for its genre. The only other games which come close to matching the depth and breadth of this game is EU4 and CK2, which are different genres.

While not the prettiest game to ever grace a monitor, there is so much content here it's hard to not recommend if you like deep, complex strategy games. The learning curve is somewhat steep, but if you don't mind watching a few basic tutorials and/or gameplay videos, and doing a bit of research, you'll be in for a ride with Dominions 4. I'm actually a bit sad I've rediscovered this game after initially being overwhelmed, as I see it devouring my free time in the near future. Few games can boast having such a wealth of options, tactics, maps, and units, and the AI seems happy to pile armies on you and make things interesting if not difficult. Throw in multiplayer, which I've yet to try, and you have a huge heap of game here. Highly recommended, can't wait to get back to it.

I know that (a lot of) people have problems with running the PC port smoothly, even if the fan-made patch was applied, but I did not face these difficulties, so I dare to not let this affect my review. I admit that it is unforgivable to have fans fix issues with the game, but the (fixed) game was so breathtaking, I am willing to forgive this.
Story-wise this is probably the best game I have ever played so far. A complex plot with enganging characters you grow to love so much. Almost every cutscene gave me goosebumps and overwhelmed me with emotions, as did the ending(s).
I'm not much of a graphic fanatic, so I rarely ever care about it, but in some scenes, you just had to appreciate the beautiful scenery. Overall, it was quite pretty as well.
A really strong point of this game is the diversity in gameplay. Most of the time, it's a typical hack & slash RPG (which I'm totally a fan of), but you also get some well-made shoot 'em up sequences as well as a hacking minigame. The different playable characters also have different fighting styles. It makes fighting never boring.
The most rememberable part of the game (at least to me) is the music, though. The soundtrack was absolutely beautiful. It suited the scenes perfectly and really pulled at your heartstrings at some moments (dat ending title). The voice-acting is extremely well done, too. Personally, I friggin' loved the Japanese voices.
Overall, I am very very satisfied with the game and can really recommend it (as long as you can forgive the aforementioned performance issue), even at full price. The DLC is a sweet extra, but not really necessary. In fact, only the new outfit for A2 was actually an improvement, imo. The rest was just eye-candy.
On a last note, the multiple language support is a huge plus as well, especially when you can finally utilize your Japanese knowledge in a game for once!

I see there are massive thumbs down trending in the reviews. For my money ($17), I can't complain too much.
Yes, there are some bugs. Yes, the community is small. Yes the performance could improve. Yes there are a$$holes.
But these are not reasons I can not find the game worth playing.
There is work being done and the devs do listen. I've seen the changes since closed beta wave 1. While the release version was unimpressive and I thought they could have waited a month or two,  they have definitely fixed most things that have been major issues since. They just need to tighten their testing standards.
There is a support plan in place at the very least, fixes and content is being added slowly but surely, and not simply left to be the same state since release like some people pretend is worth complaining about at this point.
People need to realize what genre this game is. It is not AAA pricetag. It is not pure arcade, it is not pure simulation, it is a bit of both. It is Vietnam, not WW2. That means different weapons and general gameplay tactics and map designs.  If you like WW2 and simpler weapons and their involved tactics instead, then go play that.  I might be playing something different if I had the money to blow on some 60$ AAA game, but I don't, and I don't find many games that do multiplayer hardcore action this accessible and interesting at this price.
A lot of people complain about lack of content, yet forget the previous games did not have any more content on release as they do now. The custom maps made by the community then got adopted as official maps as part of contests. There are many custom map servers to play on so this illusion that you're only stuck with the stock maps is a lie.
Other than that, I can understand having issue with disabled primary weapons for US team in physical tunnels. I'm also not much of a fan of the spawn tunnel system as I find it extra work that often gets erased anyway. And the return to combat area zones seem a bit more obtrusive than previous games.
If there's any major issue afoot that I find ultimately troublesome is the use of UE3 vs UE4, as it is the primary reason that there are as many glitches and limitations as there are. But apparently those things are complicated when dumping the funds to get a new engine is involved.

This one has elements of greatness, but so far (7 hours in) seems to fall short in several ways.  Fighting is both repetitive and boring as you'll rarely find weapon upgrades and your supporting characters abilities are relatively benign (especially Gretel's).  That and after 10 levels, both the supporting characters still have access to only the first of their “Affinities/Abilities.”  The problem I have is that the game never lets you gain much of an advantage over mobs as they level with you without limits (I've leveled my main character to level 12 and the mobs in the first area have adjusted to be at my level consistently).  This pretty much takes away the incentive of fighting mobs/grinding to gain an advantage entirely--that and the fact that you'll struggle to find equipment upgrades which have even a slight impact to your characters' stats.
Additionally, there seems to be many bugs impacting optimization (FPS lags happen often) and many more affecting items and quests (Some items not equip-able, some quests crash the game or aren't always complete-able, etc.).  I guess what I’m trying to say is that there is little feeling of character progress so far, and after 7 hours and a dozen quests completed, I would like to see more than I have—which is very little if any.
Another issue I have is the consistent lack of an effective way to heal my party.  The game relies mainly on healing stones to top off your characters’ HP/MP and so far I’ve found ONE…near the first town of Driftsburg.  This means what money you scrape together will be largely spent on restorative items purchased in town.  Mobs drop items frequently, but many of those items are not guaranteed to produce their stated effect (i.e. Healing slime has only a 33% chance to heal your characters for 75 HP…by level 12 you’ll have over a 1000) so they’re not a reliable source of mid-dungeon party restoration by any stretch of the imagination.
On a positive note, the game offers a fairly fresh story with decent writing, albeit a bit macabre and dark (the game’s title should allude to this though).  I believe this to be the primary reason for me wanting to continue playing.  If you’re sensitive to adult themes (i.e. cannibalism, homosexuality, substance abuse, etc.) you may want to reconsider buying this one, because you’ll see some of that within minutes of playing.  Also the artwork is unique, though I’ve seen the same mobs simply rendered in different color pallets and reused to fit different local areas already and I’m only in the first town of the game.
My final verdict on this one is that I WANT to like this game enough to recommend it, but it unfortunately suffers from a lack of reward and character progression, balancing issues or some elusive combination of both.  Fighting seems dull and could use some polish—some additional abilities for the supporting cast of characters would be a great start (I get tired of simply attacking with a basic attack with the cat and Gretel in nearly every battle because they have nothing else of import to choose from).  Perhaps this observation changes and the game picks up exponentially as I continue through the story, but I’ve seen no hint of this being the case and there’s VERY little information available from the community on what to expect going forward.
Lastly, the Dev seems to be making semi-regular updates and implementing bug fixes so that’s a good start.  Though I’m not holding my breath for any major game changes at this point…When I log a few more hours and get a bit further into the story line, I’ll update this review.  Until then I would go with a thumbs down unless the things I’ve pointed out in this review don’t scare or bother you.

In this world, everyone (except Sophia) has lost the ability to read but instead have special magical powers called Affinities.  There is an evil cannibal Witch, an emperor who kidnaps children to serve in his army, drug dealers who take advantage of the common folk, monsters roaming around in the wild, and much more. Sophia has to find a way to get back to London to escape this dark and scary world as soon as possible before something terrible happens.
I am completely sucked into the world and story of this game.  The negatives are very quickly overshadowed by the great graphics, music, story, and world.  I would recommend this to anyone looking for a great and affordable RPG experience.  For around $6.00, I think this one deserves a spot in any RPG fan’s library.

I honestly have nothing to complain about. The game is beautiful to look at, and the music creates a chilling atmosphere that suits the world perfectly. I was initially conflicted with how fast the game starts (we only see Sophia in London for about a minute), but I now love the choice; just like Sophia, we are thrown into this world, and the story quickly becomes dark. What I did not anticipate was how open-ended the game was. Choices range from simple conversation options, to whether someone is killed. It encourages a replay, especially because I genuinely regret how I did some things. As far as combat goes, it starts off simple, but quickly becomes challenging. Early enemies drop plenty of healing items, but they have a low chance to actually do anything. It's quite unique, and forces even the most frugal player to spend money on reliable recovery.
The only problems I have found are that some item collectables are blocked and cannot be picked up (such as one in the Middle Terrace in Driftburgh). That and rain seriously started to lag the game, but after refreshing, it ran perfectly smoothly.
Overall, Unhappy Ever After is amazing. Everything about it makes me want to find out how it ends, and in particular, I can't wait to find the Emperor. I am so happy to have found this on Kickstarter.

This is my first review and I just HAD to write one for this game!
In short, it's an excellent example of what can be acheived with the RPGmaker engine. It has some flaws, but I'm able to overlook them thus far.
A lot of love and care has been put into the environment of the game. Pleasant music, weather effects, day/night system that isn't annoying, and best of all, well done balancing on battles.
The story, while I won't give away too much, is actually captivating despite the fact that it piggybacks on the tale of Hansel and Gretel. It's not childish, at all. There is a lot of social/political plot work that adds feeling to the game.
For the first time in a while, I actually feel like I can't get overpowered in a game. It forces you to manage your supplies and use all of your abilities strategically to get the most out of exploration. There are moments where I want to keep exploring but I know I need to rush back to a healing totem. Don't let that discourage you though, it's a pleasant experience I think, even for a seasoned gamer/rpg fan. Lots and lots and lots of side quests handed to you early on. There is even a nice tracker on the side of the screen to help you keep track.
I really love how the devs guide you through what to do by story telling. I love the chat options that you get with the characters in your party (similar to the Tales series) that expands upon their character backgrounds. You have multiple options to resolve quests differently using your own morality as a guide. This means the game might have replayability.
Things to note: A couple glitchy incidents, not game breaking, occured. After turning in a side quest the characters sprite split and appeared disconnected.
You occasionally have the option to talk to a character or fight them...you can accidentally select fight very easily :(
There are some passability issues, like shimmer spots that can't be reached because of furniture/foliage placement. This could be intentional, like a teaser, or there's a secret to get them but I have yet to figure it out. Also, as far as passability, there are places you can accidentally walk, like over roofs or on top of objects that you normally can't. Still though, not game breaking. I will most certainly report if there is a particularly bad error though.
One more thing...in the first city you cannot enter the shop at night time. The game has a way of telling you this but it wasn't clear to me at first. I played through a couple dungeons without the pleasure of reupping my supplies :3 Hard mode for a while there I guess!
For the small price point, you really can't pass this game up!

Really nice-looking, sometimes clever, yet very grindy and rage-producing Pay-to-Win PvE/PvP Multiplayer King's Bounty game. It was made by the same Katauri studio, which resurrected King's Bounty title in the first place. If you familiar with some of those King's Bounty games, you'll feel yourself like at home at the start.
But, but, but... the farther you go, the more you need dozens and hundreds of gaming friends on the Facebook, along you, to continue playing. Why? Firstly, friends are to send you some little, yet useful gifts, which you are need to strengthen up your army. And even with that help, you'll be grinding helplessly for missing ingredients. Secondly, some quests supposing that you're going to beat some tough enemies, which can be done only with help of friends.
Why I'm talking about Facebook friends so much? For it's not the game FROM Facebook. It still runs ON Facebook, and Steam there acting just as middleman. If you don't have Facebook account or if your account is made not for gaming (like you don't want to invite hundreds of unknown people just to play along them) - you can start the game, but certainly you will not succeed in King's Bounty Legions.
So don't start. It is just another grindfest, where you can't play like you want it, but need to wait until some hero's "energy" replenishes, which takes hours of real time. You can't get very far in it without supplement of at least 10-20 constantly playing facebook "friends". And you'll need hundreds of hours to achieve same things as normal game will give you in 10 hours...
Mark 5/10. Time-wasting facebook grindfest game. There are so many more "free-to-play" games on the market, that are much better in terms of gameplay, even if they might not look so gorgeous as "Legions". And there are original single-player King's Bounty games, which are good. Just not mess with "Legions", it's a bad idea, that will turn you down after some time.

I'm going to summarize my time spent playing this game.
I started out in a rainstorm looking at the protagonist. The camera zoomed in and crashed into his head a la Goldeneye 64. After the AI walked into the building for me, I was in control. My objectives told me that I was to go to my office. I sprinted to the third floor. I say sprinted, but running in this game is the speed of slow walking and walking is the speed of an elderly person recovering from hip surgery.
Upon reaching my office, I picked up a paper from the desk and spent the next 5 minutes walking around the office trying to figure out how to fax it to the client. Eventually, I figured out that I wasn't standing in the exact place I needed to be while clicking the fax machine and it wasn't registering.
With that objective complete, I went to make some coffee. Coffee machines function as save points. However, in order to save, you must watch the coffee brew in real time. It's great standing in one spot for 30 seconds, unable to move, while a fresh, hot cuppa joe brews for you. As I was about to take a sip, I heard a scream from the second floor. What could be wrong?
I plodded to the second floor and stepped through a door, wandering the hall full of pitch dark offices, searching for what made the sound. Oh no! A spooky witch! Oh, it's gone. Back to walking. I'm getting tired. I'd better go drink some soda. Oh, the door is locked and I can't get back to the vending machines. I spent the next 10 minutes searching random desk drawers, each step slower than the last until I finally passed out from exhaustion and died. Fantastic.

No doubt, this game ranks close to Dwarf Fortress in terms of complexity.  That being said, it can be a really wild ride.  The basic premise is that the Pantokrator (the Overgod, think Aao if you know Forgotten Realms), has vanshied.  This leaves the lesser gods, demi-gods, demon lords, elemental kings, and even powerful "mortal" beings struggling to become the new Overgod.  The game focuses on recruiting armies and researching powerful magic to push back your opponents and become the only remaining God.  The mechanics can take a bit of getting used to (think along the lines of Risk, but with more depth from the various unit types and magic) but there are plenty of guids and manuals available, as well as an active fan base that is very helpful when it comes to questions.
Also, all mechanics aside, you can play as frost giants led by the very physical embodiment of Winter itself against an undead Roman Empire led by a horror from the Void outside of reality.  Why the f**k wouldn't you want to try that?  Buy this game, be a Pretender God, and claim your rightful destiny.

Dominions takes that, strips away the civilization citybuilding aspect, and just goes for a full-on fantasy wargame.  Mages, spells, monsters, commanders, magic items... Turns are simultaneous, so combat is handled through an interesting scripting system where you can give a single generic command to each unit of troops, as well as up to five specific commands to each commander (important for your mages in particular).
PBEM Multiplayer is where the game is at, though-- the AI just has a terrible time doing more than making hordes and sending suicidal waves at you.  A pretty active modding community, as well.

Over 4000 hours spent on that game. Most of that was only being online to monitor my alliance chat, but you can guess I played a lot. Do I recommend the game? In it's current state, hell no!  Why? Here are some reasons:
Nival never showed even a tenth of an ounce of respect for their customers. People tried so hard to communicate with them, working on new ideas and sugestions about how to implement them in a way that the game would thrive instead of dying like it has been over the last 12-18 months.
I played this game so much and wanted it to get better. Instead, they implemented a stamina mechanic that totally makes the game unplayable for newcomers. This totally killed the community as old players were quitting faster than new "regular" players coming in.
About 24 months ago, when I started playing, it was a decent F2P. The P2W was there but you could still (slowly) progress without paying. Then, maybe 18 months or so ago, they implemented the stamina, which was not too much of a hassle for me as I had so many creatures I could use. But then, people started quitting. Others tried to open dialogue with Nival to improve the game. Nival gently told us to f**k off by deleting our forum posts. The message was clear : we don't give a s**t about what's going on and what you think. We are in charge and we will shamelessly ask you for money so you can replenish your troops stamina, troops which for some are only obtainable by spending in game currency or PVPing (but PVP matchmaking is broken anyway!). So basically, pay for troops, then pay to play with them if you are unlucky enough to have more than only a few minute for your play session.
But most of all, pay for gems that we will take forever to send you. I once bought gems that they took over 2 weeks to deliver to my account. After the 10th of 12th day, I asked them for a refund, and their answer was that I was too late, according to their policy, to be eligible for a refund. I am being told that I am late when I waited over 10 days for something that should have been delivered instantly?
Honestly, I don't know if it's the game itself that sucks, or the team behind it that can't seem to get their s**it together, but there's definately something fishy going on.

Other than that, this game has really shined where it counts; the gameplay is wonderful, the weapons feel like they have oomph behind them, the soundtrack is increadible, the director has taken an interesting approach with camera angle switching I've never seen done before which works well with this genre, and the story has a good structure and is not overly cliché.
Regardless of any shortcomings, Yoko Taru truly captured my heart with this game and I've been left with a void in my heart after completing all the endings.
Personally, my game of the year 2017.

Good, but not as good as I'd hoped.
After playing Metal Gear Rising, and Transformers: Devastation, I was prepared for a great game that I would want to play again, and again, and again. However, I've only played it for 7 hours and I can already tell that they traded substance for size. In Metal Gear Rising, there was never more than 30 seconds of running around until you got to a fun new fight, or something. That doesn't happen here, there are plenty of times where you have to run in a straight line for 5 minutes just to get to a fast travel point, so you can wait for a loading screen so finish, so you can run 5 more minutes to get to where you want to go. Admittedly this isn't a GAME BREAKING issue, but it's not exactly fun either. Throw in sub-par keyboard support and occasional crashes and you have a game that only succeeds in reminding you of better days.
Now the plot on the other hand was pretty good, not as good as Metal Gear Rising, but pretty good. There were a few, shall we say "odd" decisions here and there. Some of which were enough to break the immersion and make you think "What? Why would anyone put that in there?" but in an effort to not spoil anything I'm not gonna say exactly what those moments were.
Lastly, the save system hearkens back to the old days of classic JRPGs, because you have to go to a save-point, and there is NO auto-saving (Something that MGR and T:D DID have, IIRC.) Personally I didn't find this to be TOO bad, but it was definitely an inconvenience. I just thought I should mention it because there are plenty of people that DO think it makes the game unplayable in the discussions section.
Honestly I had such higher hopes for a Platinum Games product, but hey, you can’t win them all. Hopefully their next game can fix these issues.

Nier Automata is a wild and crazy and unique ride. It is incredibly beautiful and wonderfully animated. 1. there are five major endings to the game, and you progress through them linearly so you are not actually replaying the game to get different endings.

3. Don't bother grinding. Its not necessary. Trust me.

Polarity is a frequent target of outlandishly-good Steam sales. In theory, it goes for five dollars - already a low-risk investment - but in practice, you can generally pay more for a stale gumball than a copy of Polarity. I thought about typing this entire review without one reference to Portal, but the comparison is unavoidable. As a first-person puzzle-platformer that achieves diversity in level design without throwing too many game mechanics into the mix, Polarity succeeds in many of the same ways that Portal did, albeit on a much smaller scope. But to consider Polarity a decent poor-man's Portal is to do it a disservice. By utilizing a mechanic that is less visually jarring, Polarity makes similar gameplay more accessible for casual gamers, and while it is an easy play-through for most gamers, it provides solid and balanced entertainment throughout.
I don't think the premise can be laid out any more clearly than in the first sentence of the game: "You are a hacker." Lucky you. Supposedly, you travel a mainframe seeking out protected data for the agency that hired you, but a more-salient way to look at the objective is "Pick up the green glowy things and get to the end of the level." Each level has three bits of data, and while you can move on without collecting all three, the game does acknowledge 100% completion. Generally speaking, the data aren't too hidden, but it is worth it to explore the big, open rooms that comprise most of the game world to see what you can find.
In Portal, you used the titular portals to play with basic physics to complete levels. In Polarity, the concept is much simpler: you switch yourself between two color "poles," red and blue. The levels contain structures made of red and blue light. When your polarity matches, you phase right through the object; when your polarity does not match, it is as solid to you as the room itself. Alternatively, if the object is a laser and your polarity does not match, you die. Challenges sometimes require changing polarities while in motion, and even while in free-fall, so that you pass through one object but not another.
The levels also include red and blue Not-Companion Cubes. (I am a masterful and original comedian. Nobody has ever made that observation before.) These cubes are subject to the same rules of polarity that you are, and they can also power platforms and other machines when placed in circles with outlines of matching color. You are not able to directly change the polarity of a given cube, but there are green windows through which you can launch the cubes to change them. Occasionally, you will come to obstacles which you can pass through, but which your cube cannot.
The gameplay is incredibly smooth, and the sense of size and scope is nice. For levels that are largely wide-open rooms without too many moving bits, I was worried that after a time they would feel bland and empty, but instead I often had a sense of awe, looking to platforms three stories up that I knew I could find a way to. I did, however, want more from the cubes. In most cases, the cube was simply a proxy for a button or switch, and I felt like more could have been done with switching the polarity of individual cubes, or getting a single cube to help you in multiple ways.
Ultimately, the game is a success, providing a short journey through a world that needs little explanation, gives adequate time to learn the mechanics, and increases the challenge as you go. By the end, it is perhaps a bit too short and a bit too easy, but even if you breeze through all of its main and bonus levels, it provides entertainment along the way. Well worth the five-dollar price point - and if you find it at a discount, do not hesitate.

I picked this up with 3 other games for $1.49 total, not knowing what to expect (despite having positive reviews) I was pleasantly surprised with all the games but especially with Polarity. In polarity you find yourself switching polarity to get through/over red and blue "gates" and throwing/dropping red and blue cubes to power up devices in order to get to the end of the level while also searching for Data Fragments to unlock bonus levels.
Polarity is a simple, well-executed concept that makes the player feel good when they solve each puzzle. The game is casual friendly with it's level checkpoints, no real way to die and no enemies (at least in the levels I've played).
The game could be better with a level editor, steam workshop and leaderboards to encourage players to replay levels, the cubes also sometimes don't do what you want while you are carrying them by seeming to bug out on rare occasions.
I highly recommend this for fans of puzzle games and even the casual gamer looking for a new challenge but still want a relaxing game.

Its interesting with the direction they're going: focusing on a more natural universe that is populated by advanced races, beyond advanced races, primitive, and enough backstory about long LONG gone races to fill a book.
You get this feel that you're part of this grand story, and that feeling really does stay with you no matter how many play throughs (3 so far, none to finish).
But what they really are lacking, is a thorough rewrite of combat, invasion, and the need for a little more divergance in R&D.
What's more, they've focused all their efforts on trying to shoe-horn tactics into the game w/o putting time into fixing combat.  THey're doing this by removing a VERY unique feature--the three modes of travel--to force space lanes into the game.  This'll, in their minds, create more predictabaility and help the ailing AI. The gameplay wasn't bad at first. But when I tried to play as Sparta on meduim difficulty, I found the campaign forces you to play in a very precise way. AND be lucky with the RNG. Otherwise, you're going to lose every major challenge. Worse still, said required strategy makes a major shift roughly halfway through the campaign. It goes from forcing you to focus on military strength to forcing you to focus on economic strength. And this shift happens in a very short amount of time. It seems too short to make it feasible without plenty of special favors from the RNG.
What would've made this better is if each major challenge had at least two different ways to beat them. That would've provided some flexibility in strategy.
Oh, and did I mention you only get to play as either Athens or Sparta? It's not like a player can choose between many factions to fit their own playstyle. Granted, each of these two factions gets to choose between six perks at the start. But those perks make little difference. The campaign requirements are still too constricting and unfair.
And while I'm griping about poor gameplay balance, I'll also mention the "overpopulation" mechanic in the late parts of the campaign. Even on easy mode, it becomes way too cumbersome. It feels like a hastily tacked-on way to increase end-game difficulty.
Overall, not a good strategy game. Even for it's price range, I don't reccomend it, at least not without a major patch. But I doubt that will happen, considering the developer has already released another similar strategy game called Predynastic Egypt. Having only played that later game's demo, I can only hope it's gameplay is more flexible and better balanced than Marble Age.

TL;DR 5/10 A 1-track forced development of a civilization. Turn-based exponential clicker game.
5/10?  That is not great. Why am I still recommending it?  Well--I enjoyed myself for what it was.
As another reviewer warned before I played, this game plays like a clicker game, except turn-based.  Like all clicker games, the game goes through obscene levels of growth.  The result is that all of the action and growth that were done previously are quickly made irrelevant by the present state of growth.
The first time I played, I layed out a carefully managed plan of my resources.  Timed events occurred expecting me to be at a certain level of the growth curve.  I failed most of the challenging event (invading civilizations) because I thought that I could play the game at my own pace.  Since I conceded each of these overly unfair wars, none of my people died, and I was allowed to continue with a 40% reduction rate of some resource.  So, I lasted through half the game until the Huns came in and utterly wiped me out even with conceding the war.  During this first playthrough at my own managed pace, the game would feel sorry for me at certain checkpoints.  At least 8 different times, the game simply said, "Your neighbors are progressing well; so you benefit from the collective prosperity. Here is a reward of XX population, XX money, XX culture, XX army."  Literally 4 huge boosts to my present inventories of resources to try to level the playing field for where the game expected me to be.
Like other clicker games, your own army is irrelevant (when playing Athens, not Sparta). They participate, grow, and die in wars--but they are only meaningful as 5% of your army strength.  Your power comes from allying with neighbors and using their armies (20% of them) through treaty.  So, often, your army is your least important resource.  (The booster %bonuses to your army are very important, because they apply to your allied army)
Since it is a clicker game but turn-based, growth is mandatory at a certain time pace.  You must grow your population as fast as possible.  You keep them fed, while boosting 4 other resources--Production, Culture, Gold, with Army mostly irrelevant.  The only way to grow those resources is by allocating your population to each of the various tasks, fully changable each turn.
The second playthrough, I knew and could anticipate the non-random pre-timed events.  You shift your population into growing whichever resource is more important for the temporary challenge of the time.
The Production resource will purchase booster Buildings for your civilation layed out in a progressive tree of choices (along with a maintence fee to manage from your Gold resource.)  Culture will purchase boosters from a progressive Technology tree.  Both trees are mostly an illusion of choice.  You cannot purchase anything other than 2 or 3 options, and you are forced to purchase the other options soon afterwards.  Especially in the Technology tree, you are not allowed to purchase a more important technology from a different branch of study--the game forces you to purchase the remaining options first from earlier availability.  So, your only choice is what exact order of purchasing do you make in a forced, linear consumption track.
Many random events occur over the course of the 280-330 turn game.  "Here are some free armies."  "Here is some free culture."  "A city was poisoned; XX population die."  In a progressive game, these one time events are manageable and mostly shrugged off as a 1-3 turn delay.  However, I just hit mid-game the Starvation problem again.  You must have your farmers keep up with your growing population; yet because of the controlled expansion of farmers by the purchased Technology and Buildings, they can be maxed out.  So, my population got slightly ahead, with no ability to increase my farmers yet.  So, a few people die off and the population returns to an equilibrium of sustainability, right? WRONG !!  No joke--0.05% 100/200K of my people starved.  So, the game presents 3 punishments:  Give up some Culture growth for 10 turns, Spend an exhorbant amount of your Gold balance, OR murder 30% of your population.  OK--fine.  I took the Culture punishment.  However, next turn, the same problem is still there with no ability to rectify the food with increased farmers.  Again, 96/200K of my people die.  The game forces one of the remaining 2 choices of punishment.  So, after a few turns, the game forces you to murder 30% of your population because 0.05% were dying.
This kind of absurdity is the norm for this flawed game.  Well, I suppose it is similar to real life.  In RL, you planned and managed your resources, got an education, worked hard at a vocation.  Guess what?  Today, a truck hit you OR you got fingernail cancer.  You may not be dead, but which crippling result will you now manage for the rest of your life?
Grow your civilization along the path that the game expected, not much deviation is allowed.  Do this, and you will win the full achievements.  Almost.  Now do it one more time with the other Home city. (Athens or Sparta)
FATAL FLAWS:
#1 When conquering a city, you must beat them 3 times.  However, after each fight your armies lose an appropriate number in the fight.  However, for the target city, their armies magically respawn instantly.  Did they enlist more from the population?  -9M population, +16K army.
#2 When trading, other bonuses stack onto your commodity trades.  Unfortunately, this means that it makes sense to ONLY BUY when trading.  The bonuses do not boost your return of gold when selling.
Pay no more than $1.25 on sale for this.

Many people seem to be complaining about Marble Age being a "glorified Flash game". Well, it really quite literally is, considering that is the technology it uses (and you can find an earlier position in the series on those Flash games websites like Kongregate). But this isn't really a problem. In fact, The Binding of Isaac was a Flash game, too, and so what?
No, the problem with this game lies in its mechanics. The simplicity, combined with cute graphics, pretty nice music, and semi-educational content would have actually made it a great little title, but Marble Age's convoluted and unpredictable gameplay is what ruins everything about it.
To put it short, I have never seen a game this unbalanced. The progression of numbers (e.g. resources being required, your city's population etc.) is exponential, like in so many browser-based MMO strategies and other titles. But it is also so variable. Rather than being a smooth increase, it jumps all over the place. At one point you're suffocating, your city can't grow anymore, your tech research ground to a halt and you're passing turn after turn just to regain some military power. Then, you complete a goal and suddenly you have twice as much population as you had a moment ago, tons of new resources and several free technology levels. This pattern repeats from time to time, though you never really see it coming. It means that all the strategy goes to trash since the real way to progress is to fulfill whatever goals you have (or count on a lucky random event). What you're trying to do otherwise just doesn't matter.
In fact, the whole game is built in such a way that there is an invisible path you're supposed to be following. You don't quite know where it is, so you'll always stumble a bit. Stray too far from it and you reach a place you can't get out of. Manage to stay on track and the whole game becomes really easy. This is actually quite extreme — you can essentially lose a game if you do one thing wrong in the early stages, for instance.
(Here I'll note this isn't about following historical events or simply playing in an optimal way. The game is just constructed in such a manner that you have to make arbitrary decisions at right moments to be able to win.)
To be fair, the game does try to rescue you if you stray, giving you gifts through random events, but this only exposes the gameplay's faults even more — if the only way for me to get back on track is to accept those gifts, which are just enormous, then this just shows how big the difference between the "right" play and the "wrong" play is, even though what is right and wrong is decided arbitrarily.
It might seem like I'm complaining a lot about this subject but that really is something that ruins Marble Age for me. The game has more flaws than that (maybe I'll list some in the comments) but this is what makes it an unplayable rather than flawed title. Stay away from it unless you like gameplay that's about trying to guess what the developers intended for you to do at any particular stage.

The game has a board game style and deep systems.  The various factions are diverse and customizable.  The basic premise is amusing and the overall flow of the game seems well designed.
Where the problem for me lies is the combat.   Battles are automated and the player can view the results as a replay after they occur.  After spending a fair amount of time in several games as differently designed factions setting up squads, I can say that I have no clue what does or doesn't work.  My strong armies were defeated by what seemed to be weaker ones with ease.  Parsing the combat logs didn't help me figure things out.  I read the actual game manual, which is quite interesting in and of itself, but it didn't seem to help with this.
The in game combat probably would have worked better as a turn based, player-controlled system.  I think perhaps the developers avoided that as they wanted a board game style that didn't get bogged down with combat.  The result is that, without extensive forum-diving, the average player will end up simply building large armies and throwing them around with no preconception of what will be effective.
On the other hand, the game developer continually updates the game and there are avid players from whom one might receive help.  If the game were about half its current price of 34.99 USD, I would recommend it.
