I am going to write a review here because this game really doesn't deserve all the hate.
I have been a Telltale game ever since The Walking Dead Season 1. Telltale has proven to be good at making games with great stories and endearing characters, I have my doubts about Minecraft: Story Mode, but this game show that Telltale is still able to create a good solid story with good supporting characters.
This game isn't for everyone. Minecraft fans will be dissapointed that this isn't like Minecraft where you can build stuff. This is a game, where you are main character and you decide how you want to talk to the characters around you in a setting that Minecraft fans would be familiar with. Even if you aren't a Minecraft fan like me, it isn't neccesary to be one to understand the story.
I personally enjoy my time playing the first episode and I am excited for episode 2. Definitely, not a bad game, if you like a good story and good characters.
UPDATE:
Alright, have my opinion changed over time? Well, sorta. While Minecraft Story Mode doesn't live up to the same esteem and glory like their previous games, I have to admit that the story becomes better over time. It is still simple compared to the more mature games from Telltale, it does becomes more serious over time and it makes you invested.
One of the things that I like about this game is the crafting and more involving combat. The combat while very simple, feels very engaging compared to previous Telltale Games. And the crafting of items feel like you are personally interacting with the world.
The dialogue isn't the best and some are indeed cheesy. But I enjoy the game for what it is. An adventure game in the Minecraft world. I am looking forward to Episode 5 and the three adition episodes of this game.

This is an awesome game. Sad part, there is not a lot of people online. It takes me a minute or two to find a match. I always end up seeing the same people. More people need to start playing it.
The game is free. It runs off of microtransactions. You can buy coins to upgrade weapons faster, but you don't have to do it. You already earn currency in game called "Blutes". You use them to buy parts for your guns. The possibilities are endless. You can change every aspect of any gun. You can make a laser machine gun that sets people on fire.
There are casual and competitive matches, just like Counter Strike. The game modes are awesome! There is capture the flag but with hammers, king of the hill (secure as many flags as possible) and a lot more. The maps are pretty big and awesome. This isn't like a Call of Duty game where you stay in the same building for minutes at a time. In this game, you are running all over the map. You run really fast, jump high, and do long barrel rolls. So the mobility of your character is very high.
I like that you can edit guns that you have already made, and also rename them. That way you don't have to keep buying weapon slots, you can just change up the ones you have for the first few games, until you have some more. You get them as you level up.
The game is 3rd person, so if you are using a controller, like I am, it takes some getting used to. Today was my first day with the controller, and I have played a few games with it. Loadout works the best out of all of them with the controller. It makes the game more enjoyable. You can still use a keyboard and mouse, I still go with that once in a while. The response time is quicker with a mouse. It really makes a difference though.
Like I said, the characters are very mobile, so it is your best choice to use the mouse, that way you can aim at them faster while they jump around.
Anyways, this game is awesome, it's free, and the matches are long, if you enjoy that. You won't be disappointed.

Combat is weak, in an effort to make it better they're removing two of the three FTL types. The problem is the combat is weak because it comes down to "my huge fleet" versus "their huge fleet". Their "solution" to weak combat is to reduce the number of places the AI and the player can maneuver their fleets by having Hyperlanes (space roads) only, creating established pathways that you can or cannot go. The goal is apparently to enable doomstacks to fight each other more quickly than they would. Instead of adding anything interesting like having certain systems naturally have massive gravity wells that make having large fleets difficult, space weather that could be potentially dangerous if you put all your ships in one place, secret asteroid bases from which you can attack invading fleets or basically anything that would make combat actually kind of fun the solution they came up with is to just make it so you get to your doomstack fighting their doomstack as fast as possible.
Needless to say this will only make it so the AI can't flee from your superior fleet as easily, it will not actually make combat fun- it will only ensure the tediousness of the current system is reduced by reducing the overall time you spend at war.

TLDR: Great Sci-Fi 4X with tons of replayability and customization. Definitely worth a buy.
Stellaris represents an enjoyable mix of science fiction and empire building the likes of Sins of a Solar Empire mashed up with the Civilization series. Prior to playing Stellaris, I was not a fan of the myriad 4X science fiction games such as the Master of Orion series. However, Stellaris just clicked for me. I find it to be the best example of the symbiosis of micro and macro management in the science fiction X4 theatre. I could go on and on about the mechanics of the games or the ways that research, politics, war, and territory interact in interesting ways, but I just want to hit some of the overarching themes I have observed in my 180 hours of play time.
The game is in some respects the most fun as you are just starting out as the possibilities feel endless. At the same time, it is terribly frustrating in the beginning because of the necessary slow pace as things start to gear up. Interestingly, I find that the game is not so much about the victory screen, but more about seeing what random possibilities come to fruition. This has been echoed by other reviewers and rings quite true for me. Sadly, it also means that the middle to end game can get quite tedious.
I appreciate that achievements may only be earned on Ironman mode. It has saved me from the natural inclination to save before a war, see how it pans out, and then load a previous save if things don’t work out. That mechanic in itself gives each game much more gravitas. The victories mean much more because noting was guaranteed.
Also, I would like to say that Paradox does a great job continuing development of the game and providing both free and paid content.

Would have given Stellaris a positive review for being an aspirational, if somewhat flawed, entry into the annals of space strategy games.  But the developers, apparently keen to tilt at windmills, have announced that they will be removing any asymmetry of movement or unique flavor you might have from being able to choose one of the three possible FTL methods.  As of the next major patch, you will have only one choice. This is being done after over a year and a half since release, effectively removing a key feature - freedom of movement - which (had it not been present) might have caused me not to buy the game.  I didn't buy this game to get an Endless Space rehash with a slightly different PoV.
Now, this major aspect of replayability and strategy is being flattened out, those options being removed, and forcing the player into playing a version of space chutes and ladders like Endless Space, the failed MoO3, the recent MoO (non)re-start, and so many other generic node-and-lane strategy games.
This is done to "enhance" strategic choices - but one wonders how making war gameplay predictable and reducing it to a series of forts-in-space while taking away player agency in terms of movement and counter-play enhances anything.  The game already has an issue with doomstack fleets.  Now, you won't even have the option of decentralization and mobility as an option to counter them when (not if) they come.  Battles will be two large blunt objects smacking into each other, like in the days of the Napoleonic wars.  Ask yourself... does that belong in a space game?  My answer is a resounding "no."
Why is this "tilting at windmills?" Still unaddressed, over a year later, is any kind of compelling trade, espionage, or diplomacy mechanic.  The game is shallow in these elements.  You would think that a "grand strategy" title involving galacitc empires would have some semblance of depth in these categories.  Stellaris doesn't.  It does not even have a Victory Condition which isn't in the "conquer/subdue most of the galaxy" vein.
I bought Stellaris with high hopes of adding another great space strategy title to my long list of games going back to the late 90's and early 2000's.  Over a year and many DLC later, it looks like I am going to be disappointed yet again.
If you enjoy trying to build the "Maginot line" in space, letting terrain (in space no less) defend you more than your own intuition, planning, reaction and agency, this might be an entertaining title for you.  But beware... they may just decide to remove more key features you enjoy down the road.
If the developers decide to rescind their current development direction and priorities, I would be happy to amend this review.

Here are two lines from a recent update:
*Max number of commanders increased 9990 -> 20000
*Max number of units increased 160000 -> 250000
The graphics may be less than appealing, but this game has serious heart and heritage. Quality updates continue to trickle in, and I'm more than glad some of my money went to help the devs, and the future of Dominions.
For a "real" review, I'll talk about how the game plays. For each turn, you: 1. create new units or commanders and assign troops to those commanders 2. decide if you want to build any structures (temple, science-research, and castle/fortress/fortifications, basically) 3. assign new magic-school research, if needed 4. issue move orders, if any 5. End Turn. I mention this because I know, at first glance, Dominions 4 seems like it might be one of those "Cool concept, but too complicated to play!" kind of games, when it is not..
The game is nowhere near shallow, despite the above statement. Each faction (spanning through three different eras of time) has many tricks and strategies, some obvious and some downright devious, and "learning" a faction is quite challenging.. Adapting to your opponents strategy is also serious business..
There is no "diplomacy" here.. If Pangaea has a massive army of elite Shark Tribe warriors supported with massive underwater behemoths, well.. There is no "playing nice" :) Your goal is to conquer, one way or another..
Anyway, I'm sure there are far better reviews than mine, so I'll quit rambling. Just wanted to show my support and toss another vertically-inclined thumb into the mix ;)

This game very nearly got a "NO" from me, due solely to its cost. It is good, but it is by no means worth as much as they are charging for it. I decided against that, however, because how much money a player is willing to throw around will vary greatly from one to the next, and I want this review to be based solely on the experience of playing the game, rather than on the experience of buying it.
The game is very complex, and you will probably have to play several times before you are even aware of all of the options available to you during play. There are many factions to choose from, and some of them play quite differently from others. I have probably spent as many hours reading the 400+ page manual as I have browsing through the character creation screens, designing "pretender gods". If you saw the screenshots, and didnt lose interest immediately, then you very likely are the kind of player who can set aside graphics for depth of content, and this game will reward your attitude.
If I were to seek to complain, two things would come to mind. ONE: the user interface could really use some work. There are many icons which can be clicked which give absolutely no indication of it, and many things you would think were interactable which serve no function at all. It is very easy to lose track of an army or leader, and then discover him again 40 turns later, only to realize hes gone to waste all that time. And TWO: much of the depth of this game is merely superficial. Many units are near carbon copies of others, only a single stat apart, and once you throw them both into a battle, you wont see any difference. You can research volumes of spells, and build hundreds of items, but most of these things will "come out in wash", as they say, proving to be mere distractions when it comes right down to it... although I certainly enjoyed being distracted, as such.
If you get a boner looking through pages and pages of stats and lore, while micromanaging every tiny aspect of a massive and complex empire, than you are going to love the hell out of Dominions 4. If you want to learn to play a game you spent 40 bucks on, in less than 10 hours, then you will hate it. Its worth a second look if its on sale, but I have a hard time recommending this at full price... not when Age of Wonders 3 is only 5 bucks more, and is easily just as deep but with far better graphics and combat mechanics, to boot.

Amazing game, worth way more than 20 cents. I think the 5 dollars is a reasonable price. It's fun albeit short, and plays smoothly. You should beat it in approximately 1 and a half hours on your first playthrough, but if you try to get all the achievements you'll be playing for a lot longer. Developers: make a sequel. I really enjoy this style, especially since the actual Metroid series isn't doing so great at the moment, this made me feel a bit of that feeling again, of exploration, adventure and space.The platforming is certainly different, but reminds me a bit of shinesparking, especially the really difficult sections.
I personally haven't played cave story so I can't compare it to that, and I feel like the only thing really taken from portal was the teleport gun, so as far as I'm concerned, if you like metroid then certainly get this game. This games only downfall was its length, and I would happily play more like this.
One of the best aspects they used from Metroid was sequence breaking. This is when you speed run and find ways to skip certain sections of the game (kinda neat how one of the achievements is exactly this, Shortcut) or have an item earlier in the game than you are supposed to (Daredevil). Finding out these things on your own, is what makes this game like metroid.
One let down I felt was the text. Now I understand how complicated the portal gun is, and that the text is mostly necessary, but I felt that I didn't connect to the maini character as well. Super Metroid is a classic example of a game that needs almost no text, in fact the only text is at the beginning to explain what happened in the previous two games. But this is only a minor complaint, and a tip for the Devs if you are planning to make a sequel.
Nonetheless, this game is very enjoyable, and I'd just like to say thank you for helping me connect with Metroid again. To everyone else, I highly recommend this game, especially for the price it is right now.

My thoughts on Minecraft: Story Mode - A Telltale Games Series
Been a while since I’ve done one of these, but it’s been a while since I actually finished a game.
As many others, I did in fact enjoy Minecraft in the early days. I’ve grown tired of it, and have no desire to play it again in the near future. But all the hate Minecraft/Mojang is getting these days sickens me, especially since that hate rubs over to this game which is not the same thing at all. Judging a game after another game which is not even made by the same people, just using assets from it is simply wrong IMO.
With that aside, as usual, Telltale spared no expense in the writing SO FAR. I have come to conclusion that it’s not fair to judge the story until it’s all been released. That is the case for a lot of Telltale stories I’m following, But I have to say this one is a good one so far.
Gameplay-wise, this plays out like any recent Telltale game, which is just fine by me. And the game also borrows things like the crafting menu from the original Minecraft, which makes an old MC player feel familiar.
The graphics also looks a little better than Minecraft IMO, but that might be that it’s been ages since I played it. It might look better these days. It actually looks closer to many Minecraft animations on Youtube, which I don’t really have a problem with. I think it actually adds a lot to the storytelling side of it, I know I wouldn’t been as immersed into the story if the game looked like Minecraft did 2 years ago…
As usual I tried to keep it as spoiler free as possible. And I conclusion, I look forward to see where this is heading. Also I’m looking forward to the season finales on both Telltale's Borderlands and GoT games this month, which I enjoy very much so far.
And on another note, This is probably mo own fault, but Steam did not give me any of the archievements this time -_-*

Combat is weak, in an effort to make it better they're removing two of the three FTL types. The problem is the combat is weak because it comes down to "my huge fleet" versus "their huge fleet". Their "solution" to weak combat is to reduce the number of places the AI and the player can maneuver their fleets by having Hyperlanes (space roads) only, creating established pathways that you can or cannot go. The goal is apparently to enable doomstacks to fight each other more quickly than they would. Instead of adding anything interesting like having certain systems naturally have massive gravity wells that make having large fleets difficult, space weather that could be potentially dangerous if you put all your ships in one place, secret asteroid bases from which you can attack invading fleets or basically anything that would make combat actually kind of fun the solution they came up with is to just make it so you get to your doomstack fighting their doomstack as fast as possible.
Needless to say this will only make it so the AI can't flee from your superior fleet as easily, it will not actually make combat fun- it will only ensure the tediousness of the current system is reduced by reducing the overall time you spend at war.

TLDR: Great Sci-Fi 4X with tons of replayability and customization. Definitely worth a buy.
Stellaris represents an enjoyable mix of science fiction and empire building the likes of Sins of a Solar Empire mashed up with the Civilization series. Prior to playing Stellaris, I was not a fan of the myriad 4X science fiction games such as the Master of Orion series. However, Stellaris just clicked for me. I find it to be the best example of the symbiosis of micro and macro management in the science fiction X4 theatre. I could go on and on about the mechanics of the games or the ways that research, politics, war, and territory interact in interesting ways, but I just want to hit some of the overarching themes I have observed in my 180 hours of play time.
The game is in some respects the most fun as you are just starting out as the possibilities feel endless. At the same time, it is terribly frustrating in the beginning because of the necessary slow pace as things start to gear up. Interestingly, I find that the game is not so much about the victory screen, but more about seeing what random possibilities come to fruition. This has been echoed by other reviewers and rings quite true for me. Sadly, it also means that the middle to end game can get quite tedious.
I appreciate that achievements may only be earned on Ironman mode. It has saved me from the natural inclination to save before a war, see how it pans out, and then load a previous save if things don’t work out. That mechanic in itself gives each game much more gravitas. The victories mean much more because noting was guaranteed.
Also, I would like to say that Paradox does a great job continuing development of the game and providing both free and paid content.

Would have given Stellaris a positive review for being an aspirational, if somewhat flawed, entry into the annals of space strategy games.  But the developers, apparently keen to tilt at windmills, have announced that they will be removing any asymmetry of movement or unique flavor you might have from being able to choose one of the three possible FTL methods.  As of the next major patch, you will have only one choice. This is being done after over a year and a half since release, effectively removing a key feature - freedom of movement - which (had it not been present) might have caused me not to buy the game.  I didn't buy this game to get an Endless Space rehash with a slightly different PoV.
Now, this major aspect of replayability and strategy is being flattened out, those options being removed, and forcing the player into playing a version of space chutes and ladders like Endless Space, the failed MoO3, the recent MoO (non)re-start, and so many other generic node-and-lane strategy games.
This is done to "enhance" strategic choices - but one wonders how making war gameplay predictable and reducing it to a series of forts-in-space while taking away player agency in terms of movement and counter-play enhances anything.  The game already has an issue with doomstack fleets.  Now, you won't even have the option of decentralization and mobility as an option to counter them when (not if) they come.  Battles will be two large blunt objects smacking into each other, like in the days of the Napoleonic wars.  Ask yourself... does that belong in a space game?  My answer is a resounding "no."
Why is this "tilting at windmills?" Still unaddressed, over a year later, is any kind of compelling trade, espionage, or diplomacy mechanic.  The game is shallow in these elements.  You would think that a "grand strategy" title involving galacitc empires would have some semblance of depth in these categories.  Stellaris doesn't.  It does not even have a Victory Condition which isn't in the "conquer/subdue most of the galaxy" vein.
I bought Stellaris with high hopes of adding another great space strategy title to my long list of games going back to the late 90's and early 2000's.  Over a year and many DLC later, it looks like I am going to be disappointed yet again.
If you enjoy trying to build the "Maginot line" in space, letting terrain (in space no less) defend you more than your own intuition, planning, reaction and agency, this might be an entertaining title for you.  But beware... they may just decide to remove more key features you enjoy down the road.
If the developers decide to rescind their current development direction and priorities, I would be happy to amend this review.

What is the best part of gaming?
If you answered "moving sliders”, rejoice!
Who needs all those AAA graphical or sound settings screen: with this nifty little game, I can move sliders around all-day long, without having to worry about ruining the planet too much as it won't be taxing my GPU or CPU in any way.
I always thought trying to compute the best frames/second by moving sliders was too taxing for my brain. Problem solved: there is next to zero thinking required in this slider-moving feast.
Let's move my sliders, here comes a breakthrough! I can increase the number above one of my sliders tenfold and move those sliders again, but wait! A bad event! One of my slider has been set back to zero: I will have to move the others around next turn, until everything gets back in order and I get the next upgrade which will increase the numbers above one my sliders tenfold! Unless it is a bad event that set back one of the sliders to zero!
And I am sparing you the excitement of having to move some of the sliders (which scale crazily high) to the exact pixel they need to be, or else you'll have to cope with big letters pop-ups telling you are doing it wrong.
That's another theme of this
game: it loves to tell the player how much he is wrong. And what better way to do that than by throwing in predetermined events the player can't do anything about the first time around? Please, enjoy reading the big old dialogue box telling you what you should have been doing all that time, 'doh!'.
...
In short: unsatisfying and predictable.

When I saw this game I thought I hit the jackpot, really poor graphics with really great reviews.  There seemed to be awesome depth, with tons of units, races, leaders, status modifiers, spells, and victory conditions.  My first game I picked a magic heavy leader with a race balanced between magic and combat.  I left faith at the wayside and pursued magic early on.  Magic is very costly to develop, and gives very little back, not to mention the high cost when you do use it.  I switched to being combat heavy and did well, though I was still trying to grasp all the nuances of battle (it has tons of options, but is ultimately autocalced).  the enemy had a delayed start, and when they did come unto the scene I beat them at every turn, though my casualties got higher with each battle.  As I started to clinch my victory I suddenly lost.  I was out faithed, and my leader suddenly died due to such.  so for my second game I sat down and tried to figure out a better approach.  I realized that just by dumping all my points into faith, and picking a race that had good priests I would win without having to win many battles, or develop any magic.  I picked a combat heavy leader, but maxed out faith, and picked the race with the best priests.  Early on I was too aggressive and suffered a lot of losses.  In the end I was a push over in every area, except faith (which i was being very innefficiant at), and I won easily.
The problem is that faith is cheap and easy, and there is no way to remove it as a victory condition.  Have a low faith side, and end up dead quick.  Have a High faith side and almost auto win.  Don't get me wrong, the faith mechanics other than your leader insta dying are great.  In fact most aspects of this game is great, however all of it means nothing due to the current death by faith mechanic.  balancing all enemies to have the same faith is the only way to actually use the majority of the game's mechanics, which is easiest to do via multiplayer with humans.
EDIT: After the patches it is now seems somewhat balanced better, though the AI can't really keep up with all but the newest players (doesn't handle faith well and tends to end up killing itself off) so I can't really recomend the game for singleplayer use. Mulitplayer on the other hand would probably work out alright.

Isaac and his Mother lived alone in a small house on a hill.
Isaac kept to himself, drawing pictures and playing with his toys,
as his Mom watched Christian broadcasts on the television.
Life was simple, and they were both happy.
That was, until the day Isaac's Mom heard a voice, from above.
"Your son has become corrupted by sin! He needs to be saved!"
"I will do my best to save him, my Lord," Isaac's Mother replied,
rushing into Isaac's room, removing all that was evil from his life.
Again, the voice called to her:
"Isaac's soul is still corrupt! He needs to be cut off from all that is evil,
and confess his sins!"
"I will follow your instructions, Lord! I have faith in thee!" Isaac's Mother
replied, as she locked Isaac away in his room, away from all the evils of the world.
One last time, Isaac's mom heard the voice of God calling to her:
"You have done as I've asked, but I still question your devotion to me!
To prove your faith, I will ask one more thing of you."
"Yes lord. Anything!" Isaac's mother begged.
"To prove your love and devotion, I require a sacrifice.
Your son, Isaac, will be this sacrifice.
Go into his room, and end his life, as an offering to me to prove you love me above all else."
"Yes, Lord," she replied, grabbing a butcher's knife from the kitchen.
Isaac, watching through a crack in his door, trembled in fear.
Scrambling around his room to find a hiding place, he noticed a trap door to the Basement, hidden under his rug.
Without hesitation, he flung open the hatch, just as his mother burst through his door,
and threw himself down, into the unknown depths below.
And thus begins one of the best games I've ever played, on Steam or otherwise.
In this game you play as Isaac (or one of 6 other characters who may or may not also be Isaac in different costumes, depending on your interpretation of the endings) and go through randomized floors of the Basement (and the caves, and depths, and maybe even beyond!), collecting all sorts of weird/gross powerups to eventually face-off your Mother.
Even if you've played Rebirth, I'd recommend you pick this up, if only just to see where it all began.
It doesn't run perfectly (since it was programmed in Flash it's capped at 30FPS, but if you're on a toaster like me, that might be more than you get on rebirth!
The soundtrack is superb (and personally better than rebirth's soundtrack IMO), and the graphics just kind of work (it looks like it's all part of Isaac's drawings, which according to the first ending, it is)
Pros:
-Harder than Rebirth (due to mechanics changes and a lack of SUPER op items that aren't extremely rare to compensate for their power)
-10/10 soundtrack (even just opening it up today i found myself subconsiously humming the title screen music!)
-Spooky, but in a good way (ie subtlety, and not hamfisted jumpscares)
-Replayability (especially with the new "Eternal Edition" update, I still haven't been able to beat some of those new bosses)
Neutral:
-Different styled boss fights than Rebirth (while Rebirth has a lot of bullet hell-type fights, BoI has more mechanical fights, for example, instead of shooting bullet hell patterns like in Rebirth, the 'true' final boss will shoot at you only when you shoot, matching your fire rate, and some bosses like Carrion Queen are more about dodging the ground hazards while making sure to hit her weak point. Some people may prefer it, some may not, it's mostly a matter of personal preference)
Cons:
-Fewer item synergies than Rebirth (Brimstone doesn't really synergize with anything aside from generic tear effects, Mom's Knife SORTA works with Spoon Bender and other similar effects i can't remember the name of in that the knife sorta wiggles in the direction of enemies, but mostly just keeps its same trajectory)
-Lower framerate
-No controller support (unless you use Joy2Key)
One thing to keep in mind if you havent played it before, is that Wrath of the Lamb actually makes the game harder (by giving you a random chance to get alternate, harder versions of floors, and various curses that can help/hinder you), so if you're playing for the first time, you may not want to get the DLC right away, at least not until you've beaten the game a few times to unlock stuff.
Also, you won't want hard mode on unless you're experienced with this game.
Normal mode in this is equivalent to hard mode in Rebirth, so it's already decently hard.
Overall i definitely recommend this, you basically have no excuse not to pick this up if it's on sale because the price gets pretty low, and if you're like me you'll probably end up with a ton of time in this game (ignore my steam played stats, a lot of my progress was offline or using SpiderMod/Community Remix mod, which is why i'm missing a few achievements and still have platinum god)

So where do i start?
Right, how i know of this game.
this one day i was just browsing the internet when i saw picture of this hot blindfolded chick with a nice♥♥♥♥♥ i believe this is how it went for most people, noticing 2B, and then instantly decided to buy and play this game without regard of whether this game is just clickbait and its entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥ so yeah...bought the game without a second thought, and i was not disappointed.
i know this game is a sequel to the original Nier which no one plays really, but turns out, the two games makes sense no matter its viewed together or individualy. The producers did a great job to attract audiences who have never played the first game and it still appealed to them.
So, hopping into the game. and boom, bullet hell jet fighter game. Wat? turns out, this game is designed to fit several genres of gameplay into one single game. Just the first 30 mins, i was introduced to a bullet hell, hack and slash, platforming, top down shooter game that actually made sense when mashed together. it was not only in the introduction, this happens throughout the entire game.
Then, we were introduced to the characters, 2B, whom we thought is just all about fan service. Turns out, shes not only that, shes this badass android who kills everything, She appears cold at first, but became more likeable as time goes on. this is a very good example of character development and as times goes on, we witness the growth of characters, becoming someone they should have been in the first place.
As you play on, you notice the beautiful music that plays in the background. Every soundtrack is an absolute masterpiece, fitiing its designated location well, givng the suitable felling to the location. this is very important that you are immeresed into the environment around you. Even when i'm not playing, i notice myself singing the tunes to myself from time to time, its so beautiful you cant hardly get it out of your head.
The story strikes to me as being kinda generic, just a bunch of androids trying to liberate from machines that is gaining their own consciousness, so nothing too special.
The fighting is superb. Every move you do, different weapons you use, different pod programs you use, different upgrade chips you use, affects the flow and fighting style you fight when facing your enemies, this provides you with numerous combinations you can try out. When fighting stuff, be it the normal enemies or the bosses, its fluid and it makes sense, but most importantly, its fun.
And after hours of just doing the main questline, you did it, you beat the final boss, and its done, finished.
All these is what i concluded of Ending A
Indeed, you have just experrienced about 1/26 of the whole gaming experience, there are 5 main endings, and 21 joke endings. As you have noticed, i have played around 20 hours or so and have finsihed the main 5 endings, this is about how long it takes for the whole main questline to be done.
After A, there is B, and C, and D, and E.
And if i am to write anything more about these endings, the review will be too long, and too much spoilers, all you have to know is this. a lot of things ive written above will be changed when you continue on, and its for the better. which is great.
To conclude, this is my experience playing Nier Automata, one of the best games i've played so far, and one that impacted me the most. But remeber this is only the experience of one who have never played side quests becuase of the main storyline. so please dont follow in my footsteps, theres still a lot to discover.

In addition to the aforementioned player character bait-and-switch, the PC port for this game is awful. It runs fine, and controls well with an Xbox controller, but I could hardly ever get the game to run "okay" without extensive mods, and tweaking of the game, and I have a pretty good PC. Plus it will crash frequently, and you can't play in proper full screen without a mod. If you have a PS4, get it for that, unless the PC version is cheaper.
Lastly, this probably isn't as important, but this game lacks the staple of most Platinum titles, such as in
and
, that being the little grade you get at the end of the combat segment. This doesn't change gameplay too much, but with that gone, there's nothing to stop you from loading 2B up with all variety of auto-heal upgrades, and basically make your character invincible, whereas in the preciously mentioned titles would knock your score down significantly if you had to use a healing item.
That being said, I'd recommend it if you're okay with your play character changing a lot, like other Platinum titles, and you'd like to put up with the PC port problems.

I love this game, or better - I loved until some Wiz decided to remove the best and most unique feature of it: the choice between different FTL methods for each civ.

Fundamentally, I feel like the almost 18 months of post-release support and DLC (which I've duly purchased) has shown that Wiz or whoever is in charge of design, either doesn't really understand the core problems that stop Stellaris being a 'grand' strategy game, or don't have even the foggiest notion of how to try fix them.
Even at release, the early game was enchanting. The rush toward expansion, exploring using Science ships, maneuvering around enemy empires, but as soon as you hit the mid-game and expansion via colonisation dries up, the game bogs down. Diplomacy is still not really functional. War and combat are pointless exercises in having the biggest doomstack whereby a single battle at the very start of a war inevitably determines the outcome, but you still have to spend the next hour (or two, or three!) mindlessly shuttling armies around for...no real reason. Why are armies even in the game? No-one invades until planetary defenses are down so armies are rather pointless.
Sector AI has improved, but buildings on planets actually add nothing to the game. There was no reason to have that feature in the first place, and it still remains pointless busywork. There are no great trade offs, there are no real decisions to make, just click after click after click.
I played EU2 constantly for years. I still enjoyed EU3 and I found EU4 to be a breath of fresh air. I've gotten thousands of hours from other Paradox games, so this review isn't an attempt to belittle them or anything like that. I just think that the developers of this game were far out of their depth and there are so very many design decisions that show that (to name but one, copying the FTL mechanics from Sword of the Stars without copying the specific mechanics that made them so important and memorable in SOTS).
Is it worth buying? You'll probably get 20-40 hours out of enjoying early gameplay several times, but it isn't as if there is a dearth of excellent strategy games out there waiting for your precious time (including EU4 or HoI4)
P.S. I've bought many DLC at full price with not a quibble, but I have found Paradox's DLC policy on Stellaris to be a little galling. YMMV though.

Sure, this game is just a flash game, but that doesn´t mean it´s a bad game for Steam. The controls work fine so i don´t see why i should judge the game for it´s port.
The gameplay is what really caught me. You´re just sliding some sliders to assign your workers but the level of depth behind it is pretty amazing. Seeing if you can´t get that building one turn earlier or defeat the incoming enemy wave this time, there is more strategy to it than it might seem at first glance. I enjoyed boardgames with this mechanic so i had no problem to love the polished version of it in this game.
That said tho, beating the game is hard and will take multiple tries to finally do so. Luckily a decent variety of starting perks and two different factions give a nice replayability.
Onto the bad parts then. This point would usually mean i don´t recommend the game as i hate the word: random. There are some random elements that might or might not happen on which your success is based. Now as i think no game should have randomness in it, why am i still recommending it?
Becuase those things felt miner and are not what i took from the game.
If you´re looking for a casual game to spend some hours on to finally beat and then set aside, i really had fun trying to figure out what comes next and how i could improve my play...

While certainly lacking in the presentation department with it's very dated graphics, Dom4 more than makes up for it in it's charm. The game lets you take mythological lore from around the world and pit it in wars for ultimate domination. You will see Titans warring against undead legionares, yomi fighting against valkeries, and lich kings unleashing death on the men of Avalon.
To me, Dom4 feels like a Ck2/Total War-esque type of strategy game, where you fight to expand your territory, spread your dominion (religion), and develop your nation. Where it really shines is its deep magical paths and unit diversity. I play the game with my second monitor open to the Dom4 mod inspector
where I can compare and contrast every item, spell, unit, and magic site in the game. With 25 nations in each time period, combined with the numerous magic paths one can decide to branch into, their are many many combinations of strategies and development. In other words, no two players may play the same nation the same way, they may play off different strengths depending on how they designed their pretender (leading god of their nation).
This game to me is an easy to play, tough to master - which opens up for hours and hours of gameplay. You can play against the AI who offer a fair challenge (albeit becoming predicatble as you play more - such is expected with strategy AI), and when you seek a higher challenge it offers both real time and play by email multiplayer. I didn't think I would enjoy the play by email system but it's really relaxing to have a few games going at once and getting to do a turn or two per day before and after work/school. I always look forward to downloading my turns and seeing how my wars turned out, what kind of events popped out, and coming up with a plan for the next turn. All the while trying to formulate long term magic goals that will keep me relevant into the late game.
In short, if you enjoy strategy, fantasy, mythology, or games such as Total war, Paradox strategy titles, or even the Civ series, do yourself a favour and give Dominions 4 a try.

Just finished the first part - clocking in at pretty much spot on 2 hours. I was fascinated to see what Telltale would do with a property that has such a huge following but is not known for its story content. I'm really glad I picked it up - they have done a fantastic job of creating a compelling story that feels woven into the world of Minecraft.
Like most TTG adventure titles, It's mostly dialogue choices, with a few short action sequences and the occasional "puzzle" (which should be fairly straightforward regardless of player age). The dialogue is pretty funny though, simple but effective - and there are plenty of good choices you have to make. If you have a love for Minecraft, then this is definitely worth a look.
Great if you're playing by yourself, but would also definitely be a great one to play if you have children who enjoy Minecraft and you want something you can experience together. Some of the choices and action prompts pop up pretty quickly though, so be prepared to make a few snap decisions! Luckily, any fast action moments are usually not too troublesome if you fail them.
With only one episode out right now, there's no guarantee of how this will turn out. But after finishing the first part, I can say that I definitely want to see where this is going next. I'll be eagerly anticipating the release of the next instalment!

While you may just see a Thumb Up, actually take into consideration on what I have to say about Rising Storm 2: Vietnam, because this recommendation may not come to everyone. Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is an enjoyable game. When you're grouped up with your friends, working together and understanding the mechanics of the game, it can be a blast. Wether you're playing it for the Role-play factor, or just looking for a solid tactical shooter, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam can deliver on some of the finest Team Based Multiplayer Action. It CAN.
I say it CAN, because Rising Storm 2: Vietnam doesn't always deliver. Getting the fun out of this game can be hit and miss. When It hits, it's an aboslute blast, but when it misses you'll be trying to figure out why you spent 25 bucks on a basically unfinished game. Rising Storm 2 is covered in bugs, basic issues with its game design and an overall lack of polish. As someone who clocked in multiple hours into the game's many betas, I can safely say that I can hardly tell the difference between such and the finished product. Tread lightly on your purchase for this game.
At the end of the day, the choice comes to you, are you willing to put up with what is basically an early access experience being marketed as a full release, are you willing to wait until its kinks are ironed out, or do you wish to wait until the game is truly in a finished state. For some (including myself) the experience here is worth buying in its current state. If that falls under you, and you do end up purchasing this game under its current condition, please help out the devolpers by staying active in the community and giving them feedback to help fix this game.

Ok, I'm going to take another stab at reviewing this, after about 100 hours of play.
First off, Stellaris is fun. Not just because it's the kind of game that teaches you to enjoy losing, but generally. The style, the atmosphere, it's all very warm, funny and exciting. Second of all, it's insanely hard. For starters, there is no "easy difficulty". Like, normal is supposed to be for losers, anyway, so newbies basically have to suck it up.
In general, whatever Paradox afficianados tell you, Stellaris is horribly unwelcoming to new players. The tutorial is... awful. I'm not telling you to turn it off, but you might as well turn it off. If you don't understand something, your best bet is to google the answer. Yes, really. I've actually, honest to God saw people referring someone to read Clauzewitz, if they want to get better at Stellaris. That sounds a bit extreme, but it give you an idea of just terribly unwelcoming Stellaris really is.
Having said that, I'm going to share a bunch of very basic rules of thumb, which should help a new player actually enjoy their first run. And no, not everyone finds losing enjoyable.
1. Minerals. Minerals minerals minerals. You require more of them. You need minerals to make ships, spaceports, buildings and more ships. If you're not working all the mineral-producing asteroids in your sector of space, you're not doing it right. You've also probably already lost.
2. Power. Mining stations, buildings and ships all consume power, but power-producing asteroids are few and far between. That means your planets need to focus on power almost exclusively, at least until you get your economy going. As the game progresses, your fleet will require an insane amount of power, so keep that in mind.
3.  Ships. You need a lot of them. Filling out (and overspilling) your capacity is a given, lest you're overrun by frustratingly huge fleets from the AI. Consequently, the biggest reason to expand to new planets is to build spaceports, which increase your fleet capacity. Also, try not to go over 40,000 "fleet strength". Why? No reason.
4. Don't expand too much too soon. See, what the game just straigth up hides from you, is that colonizing additional planets increases the cost of new tech and traditions (like culture from the Civ series. Traditions are important, by the way). This can be offset by constructing more science and "unity" (culture) buildings, but it's something to be aware of.
5. Frontier Outposts consume precious "influence", which you're always starved of, so use them very, very sparingly. Basically, at this point, just don't use them.
6. Mix a bunch of different ship hulls in your fleet. I won't get into specifics, but a ratio of 8:4:2:1 of smallest to largest hull sizes will take you a long way.
7. Shield piercing weapons suck. Once again, I won't get into specifics, but if you want to actually kill enemy ships, use something that's good against armor and bad against shields. Call it a superstition, if you want. Same with missiles and fighter craft. Don't ask why, just assume they're bad.
8. Make friends. It can be tempting to murder everyone if you've got the biggest guns around, but the AI in Stellaris is intelligent enough to rally against the player when they start winning. The solution, then, is to be a friendly and diplomatic empire most of the time and only attack people one at a time, if you can. Also, war crimes like indiscriminate purging and bombardement of civilian population can make you unpopular even with the other empires on the galactic stage, so it's a good idea to avoid them at first.
9. Wars are won by throwing your ball of ships at theirs, then capturing a bunch of planets with ground troops. That's supposed to change in the near future, but that's how you do it for now. Also, "vassalizing" an enemy empire is generally better than simply taking its planets, because you don't have to deal with all those unhappy aliens.
10. Play around with the menus. Particularly surprising is the vast amount of customization available in the "species", "policies" and "government" menus. If one or more "factions" in your empire is unhappy, chances are you need to toggle something in one of the above menus, somewhere. Just don't designate your primary species as livestock by accident.
Lastly, beware of Stellaris. Your starting galaxy is a vast and dangerous place, full of ancient empires and unknown horrors. If you don't know what something is, staying clear is always an excellent course of action. You can (and should) set the number of cheating "advanced" empires to 0, but there's much, much more where that came from.
If and only if you can manage all that and quite a bit more, Stellaris provides an immersive and very rewarding experience.

I've loved all of the Paradox games that I've played and Stellaris is no different. Other Paradox titles seem to have a much steeper learning curve compared to Stellaris, which makes it slightly more enjoyable for me because I'm horrible that the combat in all the other titles. The diversity in each campaign is awe-inspiring. You're able to create your own faction and play the game the way you want to, and all of the choices that you make impact the world for years in game time. The only problem I have with the game is the late game, which feels more like a chore rather than the in-depth, amazing experience that you have during the early-mid game. If you have played other Paradox titles and enjoyed them, then be sure to pick this up, and if you're looking at getting a new grand-strategy and haven't played any Paradox titles, try to find it on sale.

After 18 Hours of digging into Dominions 4 and playing through 5 different games , I can safely say this game did not come through for my inner strategy gamer.
Major Cons-
1- Cookie Cutter Strategies Included - There are a lot of spells but nations are so cookie cuttered into a particular set of paths that it is hard to develop more than a few strategies for a race. Unlike in games like Master of Magic where you can easily pick the spells you want to cast with your nation all the time to develop a theme or strategy that enhances the weak points or strengths of your race. Now, you can design your pretender to cast any spells you want. But this is a strategic game and your caster can only be in one place at one time and can usually only cast one of the big spells and then he/she/it is knocked unconscious. Its not very fun and does not make a lot of sense to me.
2- Low Strategic Value/Adaptability offered by units - As with spells, each race has a handful of units that are great at certain things but there was not a lot of strategic decision making offered by the units. After you get used to constructing a line of spearmen who can push back units or are fronted by trampling war elephants/cavalry, there is little to be done adapting to an opponent. I wished spells or different units could respond better to the how the game changes on the combat scene, but it does not offer any adaptibility.
3- The Strategy Game that makes you work - This is a big one for me. I don't mind researching unit stats and comparing them to each other. I really dont mind reading a 400 page manual to find out how each of the different nations function on a strategic level. But trying to figure out what spells you can and can't cast and trying to plan for it...and then just trying to see if it is even worth it because it feels like half of the spells are worthless in most situations ( aka, only affecting the weak♥♥♥♥♥caster with a melee damage buff...wtf...i guess this would be only for pretenders), is just frustrating.
So overall, I gave Dominions 4 a pretty fair shake. It has so much that would have been fun with a bit more tweaking and forethought, but the warfare is too one dimensional and cookie cutter.
Not recommended.

While you may just see a Thumb Up, actually take into consideration on what I have to say about Rising Storm 2: Vietnam, because this recommendation may not come to everyone. Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is an enjoyable game. When you're grouped up with your friends, working together and understanding the mechanics of the game, it can be a blast. Wether you're playing it for the Role-play factor, or just looking for a solid tactical shooter, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam can deliver on some of the finest Team Based Multiplayer Action. It CAN.
I say it CAN, because Rising Storm 2: Vietnam doesn't always deliver. Getting the fun out of this game can be hit and miss. When It hits, it's an aboslute blast, but when it misses you'll be trying to figure out why you spent 25 bucks on a basically unfinished game. Rising Storm 2 is covered in bugs, basic issues with its game design and an overall lack of polish. As someone who clocked in multiple hours into the game's many betas, I can safely say that I can hardly tell the difference between such and the finished product. Tread lightly on your purchase for this game.
At the end of the day, the choice comes to you, are you willing to put up with what is basically an early access experience being marketed as a full release, are you willing to wait until its kinks are ironed out, or do you wish to wait until the game is truly in a finished state. For some (including myself) the experience here is worth buying in its current state. If that falls under you, and you do end up purchasing this game under its current condition, please help out the devolpers by staying active in the community and giving them feedback to help fix this game.

Stellaris is a game for an aquired taste. Its a massive 4X real time space strategy game. Here are my thoughts on good and bad:
Pros
+Vast maps with a lot of starsystems to explore.
+Research is different than most games, and takes forever to complete.
+Different ways to form your empire/democracy. You can even be machines.
+You can upgrade and outfit your ships with new weapons and equipment.
+Good replayability
Cons
-Wars can be tedious due to a warscore system (basically limits how much you can conquer each war).
-Space combat is a big part of the game, but the fights themselves are more or less automatic.
-Lacks more options in deplomacy (also this part of the game needs an upgrade, though its cool you can make federations)
All in all, Stellaris is a game that has a slow phase and focuses a lot on exploration (at least at the beginning and mid game). You have to enjoy the "Grand campaign" style where it will take a long time to win, which I personally do. Although there are some negative things to be said, I still think its one of the better 4X space games out there right now.
I recommend it.

What I *really* love about Stellaris is how it piques the imagination. Any consumer of sci-fi will see the tropes sprinkled throughout the game and marvel at their digital manifestation. The scope for role-playing the galactic civilization of the far-flung corners of your imagination is huge.
Add on top of an already engaging base-game a massively productive modding scene, and the foundations are laid for many thousands of hours of absorbing play time.

This game looks and feels like a Flash game.  There is a definite beginning and end to the game, but it doesn't feel like a complete, compelling experience.  You can choose between two different civilizations to play as, but there is no real variety; it's the same thing each and every time.  Normally, there is a degree of randomness and variety in strategy games that doesn't seem to be present here.  While there are extra screens for managing things like diplomacy and science, turns play out on a screen that represents what your civilization is doing.  You have a certain population, and you use sliders to increase or decrease the number of people assigned to particular tasks.  Each task generates one more resources for your civilization, and new tasks are unlocked by building new "buildings".
So, aside from dipping briefly into other screens when needed, all you do is adjust resource production on the main screen with slide controls, and click end turn.  I'm not at all opposed to games that use a minimal style--my favorite strategy game is MO1.  But something about it just doesn't work here and I can't recommend it at all.
But, as with all games that have demos, I recommend you try it for yourself and see if you like it.  I ended up buying it because it was heavily discounted and I wanted to see if the game improved.  I don't hate it, but I don't particularly like it either.

Having played the excellent Saints Row: The Third and Saints Row IV, I decided to go back to the previous titles in the series.
Saints Row 1 for the Xbox 360 was just pure crap. hate, hate, hate. Avoid.
Then there is the flawed gem that is Saints Row 2.
Volition fixed up *alot* of the problems that was in Saints Row and added so much more.
Pity they did'nt remove the RPG Grind aspect that is the 'Earn Respect to play Story Missions' Aspect, but at least it is more fun to do it. I recommend you Grind until you hit Level 50 of Respect, you'll be good to last until the end of the game.
Up front, the PC version is Glitched and has problems. Installing Gentlemen Of The Row (
) *before* starting the game would help you alot in the long run. The game will still crash to the desktop at random long sessions, so save often. After the end of every mission. The Glitches do add some extra humour to the game, especially duri/ng the cutscenes. Check out my screenshots of the game in my steam screenshot archive to see a few.
Audio: Good use of sound effects, crap loads of recorded audio for the pedestrians.
The voice actor of Roman from Grand Theft Auto IV does some radio ads. He could be walking around somewhere too!
Graphics: It was made in 2008. Saints Row The Third came out in 2011. Massive difference. Despite that, it is still very servicible. I was not at all cringing while playing.
Controls: Passable with a keyboard and mouse, but much better using a controller. Thanks to the Gentlemen of the Row mod, it can change all ingame control prompts for the Xbox 360 gamepad (which is what I used) or the Playstation 3 gamepad.
Gameplay: In comparision to Saints Row The Third and Saints Row IV, I still found it to be enjoyable. Ok, i think most of you who read this review have already known how NieR:Automata™ is, but some of you may not now it just yet and so i can't skip the intro. NieR:Automata™ is a hack and slash open world japanese role playing game, surely all of you have already known how will it goes if it's open world game. You're going to run around like an idiot or goofing around, or running in circle while searching for something. But don't worry there's a incredible soundtrack to accompany your journey and sweep away your boredom. And IMO NieR is probably one of the best Hack and Slash game, it's a real Hack and Slash game unlike other JRPG like Tales Series, etc. This game is truly a masterpiece IMO but sadly the PC port's performance is surely not good for an AAA game which i will explain later.
So, what makes NieR different than other Hack and Slash games ? I think, it's the mechanism of the game, story, and the soundtrack. They are made so incredibly good, you probably have already heard about the soundtrack but what about the story ? The story consist of 5 total main story endings and probaby 21 endings which probably you don't want to see. The 1st two ending is similar but there's major difference and i recommend because i don't want to give any major spoilers.
+ You can listen to any of the song you've already heard in game. There's an object that'll play any music you have in the library if you're relaxing or if you're taking a short break or you just feel like listening to particular music.
+ Smooth camera move, it's just a camera move but it really boost the gameplay experience, you can even adjust the speed by your own self. It's very detailed and even such a pain to adjust though.
+ Beautiful soundtrack, it's just too beautiful and fits the game perfectly. It's making the story more and more sad than how it should've been. It'll throw away your boredom in the overworld too.
+ Great story even if it's a weird story, you'll probably think about it after you finish it since it's a weird story to begin with and don't expect to fully understand the story because the writer is weird to begin with.(LOL)
+ Alots of side quests, or maybe too many of them but fear not most of the quest place have already been marked in your map so it won't take too much time to look for it. And you can also experience a good story from the side quest itself.
+ Touching side story, there's a lot of side quests in Nier and it's probably such a pain to do it all but you have your reward if you're willing to do it such as soundtrack or a good story.
+ Too many weapons to look for, it can even be upgraded. I've given up on upgrading the weapons since it's not that easy to look for the materials. And it's hard to look for the weapon to begin with.
+ Detailed graphics and character's model, the world is soo beautiful and fascinating. Even bush is counted as an object, and it'll bother so often. The female android is supposed to be so pretty without the black thing in their face.
+ I don't know if i supposed to put it here, but i heard that people said that Nier is actually repetitive game but somehow there's always things that'll keep you from leaving the game before you actually finish it.
+ Nier will not take a long time to finish, though if you're planning to do most of the side quests (like me) you'll probably need about 40 hours for all the main ending.
- Noticed few of bugs inside the game, like when i killed the enemy in a corner of a building i can't pick up the item. And because of that i can't complete my quest and i have to load my game to make the enemy respawn the game regardless i don't mind
- Cutscene is capped in 30 FPS, i hate this one so much. I mean like why ? They could've make it better experience for us PC gamers with not capped it in 30 FPS. It could've been more beautiful.
- Screen setting change to window mode when i alt+tabbing, and always happen over and over again and the cursor won't dissapear from your screen.
- I heard there are alots of issues from people who bought NieR such as white screen but i didn't seem to experience any kinds of that. I'm using NVIDIA GTX1060 6GB.
- Not supporting 4K if you didn't use the FAR mod (Fix NieR Automata Resolution) by Kaldaien which you can found here
What is a good game in your opinion ? For me a good game is a game that'll make you think "i can't wait to go home to play this game." Nier is one of those game for me,
I grabbed NieR on summer sale since i don't really have alots of money that i can save to buy AAA games on full price because my country don't have high value currency. After 18 Hours of digging into Dominions 4 and playing through 5 different games , I can safely say this game did not come through for my inner strategy gamer.
Major Cons-
1- Cookie Cutter Strategies Included - There are a lot of spells but nations are so cookie cuttered into a particular set of paths that it is hard to develop more than a few strategies for a race. Unlike in games like Master of Magic where you can easily pick the spells you want to cast with your nation all the time to develop a theme or strategy that enhances the weak points or strengths of your race. Now, you can design your pretender to cast any spells you want. But this is a strategic game and your caster can only be in one place at one time and can usually only cast one of the big spells and then he/she/it is knocked unconscious. Its not very fun and does not make a lot of sense to me.
2- Low Strategic Value/Adaptability offered by units - As with spells, each race has a handful of units that are great at certain things but there was not a lot of strategic decision making offered by the units. After you get used to constructing a line of spearmen who can push back units or are fronted by trampling war elephants/cavalry, there is little to be done adapting to an opponent. I wished spells or different units could respond better to the how the game changes on the combat scene, but it does not offer any adaptibility.
3- The Strategy Game that makes you work - This is a big one for me. I don't mind researching unit stats and comparing them to each other. I really dont mind reading a 400 page manual to find out how each of the different nations function on a strategic level. But trying to figure out what spells you can and can't cast and trying to plan for it...and then just trying to see if it is even worth it because it feels like half of the spells are worthless in most situations ( aka, only affecting the weak♥♥♥♥♥caster with a melee damage buff...wtf...i guess this would be only for pretenders), is just frustrating.
So overall, I gave Dominions 4 a pretty fair shake. It has so much that would have been fun with a bit more tweaking and forethought, but the warfare is too one dimensional and cookie cutter.
Not recommended.

I find Dominions 4 to be fascinatingly intricate and polished, a credible result for 10+ years of dedicated evolution over four sequels, from what I've gathered. I've seen that in series before, yet somehow I'm still impressed here. Right after I got it, I told a friend of mine who spent about a year of his free time playing two humongous maps of Age of Wonders II--something I never expected [was a typo] when I gave it to him as his first brush with the genre--that my initial estimate puts Dominions 4 at about (AoW2)^2 in content. Personally, I relish a steep learning curve: grand strategy titles and deeply dynamic RPG character building systems have been particular pleasures down this line. Nevertheless, starting Dominions 4 I was surprised such as I haven't been in a long time to see I had underestimated how much I wouldn't know.
At first I was moderately impressed at the apparent scope of the thing, and I started to get burnt out on my course of study about the time I felt I could look at the nations lists with their dozens of choices and think I could describe the basic flavor for all of them. But then for the first time I looked at my first details about the magical and crafting systems and as ideas and dimensions began to click I was truly impressed like I had finally shifted the top layer of this giant package, and underneath it was still layers more good and integrated stuff!
The more I've dug up hour after hour of yet more complimentary game dynamics and worldbuilding flavor, the more I've thought I wish I had bought this game full price instead of on sale: all the more power to the developers if they're this kind of craftsmen.

Hi everyone, I do not normally take the time to actually write up a game review. After playing this game for a while, I must say not telling you all how great the game is would be ridiculous.
Intro:
Dominions 4 is a turn based strategy game created by a 2 man company Illwinter Game Design. The game places you in charge of one of MANY different nations in a struggle for global domination. The nation is lead by a powerful "pretender god" that you create prior to launching the game, who seeks to spread his/her dominion over the land. The developers based these factions around lore and culture of various peoples. A great example would be Mitlcan a tribal based kingdom that takes its roots from Aztec or another ancient Central or South American society. The nation has basic weapons but powerful magic that involves sacrificing blood slaves to use powerful blood magic against its enemies. There are also nations based around popular fiction such as the underwater nation Atlantis or Bandor Log who make you feel like the apes from "Planet of the Apes" etc. The developers release free updates to the game that include additional content! The manual is available to view online for free on their website just google it. For those who are interested you can even make your own maps to play on or write your own mods to use for the game. Free manual is available for modding & map design via developer website as well. The game does have an extremely steep learning curve as I have 253+ hours logged on steam playing mainly AI opponents, started playing with other players recently and I am being slaughtered. So I can honestly say its a deep and rewarding game you should try out. Beware it is one of those "I will just take one more turn...." kind of games and then next thing you know its 2am.
Pros:
*very deep game with unique nation selection across 3 eras
*unique units based on nations and independent provinces conquered
*very deep magic system that revolves around different types of mages who perform research to gain powerful spells
*8 paths of magic with over 800 spells! sorcery contains astral, blood, nature, and death magic. While elemental magic is fire,water,air and earth. Each magic path has a gem that fuels its artifacts and powerful spells except blood which uses blood slaves.
*Solid single player mode that lets you play a challenging AI but the game really shines in multiplayer that is usually played in a “play by email” format.
*Active community that create new maps and mods, active developers who patch bugs and release additional content for free
*the game is very replayable because of all the variety and the multiplayer aspect I could go on for days with the pros but I will call it here
Cons, for me these aren’t really a big deal so they don’t take away from my experience but if I had to pick things out that gamers may not enjoy it would be:
*graphics are a basic don’t expect any crazy animations or any cut scenes. One of the two devs does all the artwork a unit will have a regular animation and then an action animation that occurs when the unit attacks or casts a spell thats it.
*the map actually makes you feel like you are looking at a real life map for the most part
*combat is not real time you assign commands to your commanders and squads who will then perform those actions during combat, you will see the result of that after the fight has already been decided in a battle replay
As I stated I don’t actually mind any of the cons for me the game is great as designed. I hope you are scrolling up to the purchase button. I am interested in sharing more about this game because apparently I wrote up a short story as I ran out of room and had to really butcher the review. I will edit the review if I can host elsewhere. In the mean time check out this to learn more about the game
a brief tutorial by MarcusAureliusLP regarding pretender creation ( he has a lot of other longer content too you can find easily enough) or check the 300+ page manual on Illwinter Game Design’s website!

It's graphically primitive -- downright ugly, even.
The number of units, attributes, spells, and even the number of nations might be intimidating.
The AI isn't exactly good at managing all that complexity, so if you're playing well and don't handicap yourself it won't be a great challenge.
The developers are great at adding character and factions -- they love mythologies and it shows -- but sometimes not quite as good at maintaining balance.
However, there's a multiplayer scene and if you're not into MP (I'm not), you can treat it as a lovely magic-heavy sandbox with a ridiculous number of toys to play with.  There aren't too many games in which you can raise a Hydra, magically give it the ability to lead troops, and then make him the prophet of your faith; or to take a Hoburg (think Hobbit...), give him a magical item that makes him larger, and then give him boots to (literally) walk all over his enemies.    Or, say, for irony's sake summon an a powerful angel and equip him with weapons and armor gained only with the extensive sacrifice of virgins... if you want to play a drunk, demented (or both) god, this might amuse you.  I find outlandish prophets and strangely geared units funny, and I'd rather drink instead of methodically optimize my research and armies, so this is what I tend to do.
If you'd rather play it straight and less goofy, and you want competent opponents, then there's the multiplayer mode -- either via PBEM, or with one player hosting a server.
While the game doesn't support Workshop mode, it's quite moddable (sprites and text files) when it comes to adding new units or factions or modifying existing ones.  If you and your friends think that some spells are completely unacceptable, you could mod the game to make them inaccessible.   Too cheap units could be made more expensive.  And so forth.  Heck, if you wanted everybody to start with a single-use unit named "Nuclear Missile" that could teleport 10 provinces away and cast a kill-everything-on-battlefield spell but would vaporize after its first battle, you could -- you'd need to define the slay-all spell (presumably called "Explode" or "DEFCON 1"), create a unit with desired stats and a trait that makes it die after a battle, and rig it to autocast the spell when battle starts; and then you'd mod the starting forces for each faction to include the missile unit.  It'd be a rather strange game, but you could.
And so forth.

Short and sweet puzzle-platformer - the mechanics are built around one superb idea, and - quite a relief after several bad experiences - the controls are snappy and responsive.
The aim of the game is to navigate through various screens to get an important part of your spaceship. Beside walking and jumping, you have a teleport gun - it fires a blue projectile horizontally, and where it hits, there you'll be teleported. Teleportation maintains the momentum you have at the moment when the projectile hits - that opens up a boarload of navigation puzzle opportunities, which are thoroughly explored by the game designers.
The game has a cute 8-bit-ish soundtrack that you'll either love or hate - I happen to love it.

There's not much I can say about this game, since it's not just essentially, but LITERALLY a glorified flash-game, but I will make an effort at pointing out just how miserably bad it really is.
First of all, the gameplay. Wait... gameplay? I didn't even know this game HAD any gameplay! Yeah, no, to be serious, the essentially only thing you do in this game is to assign/reassign your villagers to different tasks. That's it. No, really, that's it!
Okay, sure, you can "research" some new "technologies", but unlike tech-trees in actual games such as Civilization or Endless Space, the ONLY thing the so-called "technology" in this game does is to raise the amount of villagers you can have, and how many villagers you can assign to specific tasks.
But frankly, that's about as substantial of an addition to the game's overall value as a single, paper-thin slice of cucumber is to a foot-long sub. In other words, none at all.
Then there's the fact that despite the seemingly "culture neutral" nature of the name, you can ONLY play as the greeks. No foolin'. And unlike certain other greek-centric games, like Master of Olympus: Zeus, you don't get to explore greek myth, culture, legends or hell, even architecture!
No, you pick between Spartans or Athenians, and then depending on which one you picked, you either prepare to go to war against literally every single foreign party you encounter, or ragequit to the main menu and restart as the Spartans after losing 80% of your population after the first raiding party when you're the Athenians.
The insanely poor balance between the two barely even functionally different "factions" you can play as is laughable at best, and borderline depression-inducingly tragic at worst. Spartans get an invaluable military bonus, and the Athenians get just about bugger-it-up-the-ärse-all by comparison.
Adding insult to insult and injury (that is, twice the insult to once the injury), the game has literally zero replayability. The game-world is STRICTLY pre-determined, down to what foreign parties you encounter, and their so-called "personalities".
If you can't have the mind-implodingly vast random-factor complexity of the Civilization series as a whole boasts, then that's fine, but really, if you're going to make us PAY for your shïtty game, then at LEAST give us ANY kind of incentive to play it for more than an hour, and then thank GabeN for the refund policy on Steam, simply because we could play better games literally for free on any flash-games site that's ever existed since before the words "Call of Duty" was any more than an actual military term. 0/10

This review is a little long, but clicking the 'read more' may really help you with deciding whether or not to spend your (hard earned) money on this.
I have played Minecraft for three years now and when I first heard rumors about this Story Mode game I was really excited! Today it got released and I played it for a little bit: I still am just as excited as I was before it's release!
This game is not Minecraft, really; it uses Minecraft as a layout for a story-telling game. "What do you mean?", you may ask. I mean that it's an episodic story brought to you through the game-mechanics of Minecraft. In a way that it could have also just been really different characters, even goats or 2D-Terraria characters, and really different items and ambiences, because it's about the story.
The fact that I like both Minecraft and story-based games made me buy this, not just my love for Minecraft. So keep in mind that when only one of those preferences applies to you, you may very well be disappointed by the game. Just like with any other Telltale Game.
Summary: it's a game combined with a story, without the story being directly related to the original game. Think about it, then decide whether to buy it or not ;)
