I was curious to see how Telltale would play with the Minecraft game mechanics to tell a story.
They do take a lot of freedom to twist the mechanics into something of their liking, but that's granted.
I liked what it turned out to be, and I think they've done especially well on the descision making in this title. Some descisions feel very heavy and make you want to come back to see what would've happened if you went down the other path.
But in retrospect, they are pointing this game at a pretty niche audience.
The game isn't for the younger Minecraft playerbase, since they would expect more action and freedom in a Minecraft world. But neither is it really for the point-and-click adventure fanatic cause the world of Minecraft is unknown to them and some of the logic used in the game would make no sence.
It's pointed at the older Minecraft players (such as myself) who can get all the references and understand that it's a different game altogether, but still enjoy it.
TL;DR:
For it's faults, it's still a nice Telltale game experience and I recommend it if you like Telltale storytelling and Minecraft.

I was on the fence about whether to get this game for awhile, partly because of the price and partly because of quality concerns, since obviously a lot of time wasn't spent on making the game graphically pretty. I purchased the game on sale, but after having played it I would recommend it even for full price to anyone who's looking for a deep, complex strategy game.
Dominions 4 plays like a highly advanced fantasy version of Civilization or similar turn-based games. That's not to say that it's super difficult to play - the basic mechanics are pretty simple once you get the hang of the somewhat odd control scheme where LMB is used for most things where you'd normally expect to use RMB (RMB is always used to get more info on something, instead of giving orders). I was able to feel somewhat competent without any tutorials, having only watched some brief gameplay on YouTube. However the game reveals layer after layer of complexity once you really start getting into it, and it definitely follows the "easy to play, hard to master" philosophy. There will be a learning curve once you get beyond the basics - the manual is almost 400 pages long.
So, what can you do in this game that makes it worth the time instead of just playing a Civilization?
* Choose a faction and a pretender god as its leader from just about any mythology and creature you can think of. Dragons, wizards, lizard men, frost giants, weird fungus monsters, sea serpents, cthulu, you name it.
* Recruit a general for every one of your armies, with his own name (given by you), stats, equipment, and experience.
* Separate your armies into formations and give them orders to follow in battle (you still don't need to micromanage the battles themselves; they play out between turns)
* Sacrifice virgins to your blood god and use the power to summon demons or forge magical artifacts.
* Spread your icy dominion to freeze over rivers so your armies can cross it.
* Call forth an army of undead and march it into the sea to surprise your enemy or control undersea territory.
* Cast a spell to plunge the entire world into utter darkness.
* March huge armies over all the land, then suddenly lose the game because no one believes in your god anymore (yeah, that happened to me).
So if you can get past the graphics (yeah, I know, it takes a lot to get past the graphics), you'll be rewarded with a rich, cerebral, highly replayable game in Dominions 4.

An incredibly deep turn-based strategy game with fascinating and deligtfully detailed game lore. A very steep early learning curve that once surmounted gives way to hundreds of hours of gameplay. Most intriguing and complicated magic system that I've ever seen in a strategy game.
As for cons, there are many. Single player AI is remarkably useless creation that in battle contends itself with throwing completely random selections troop at you, with no ability to plan strategies or conduct diplomacy. Make no mistake, Dominons 4 is a multiplayer game to the bone, and much of it's lasting appeal is directly in proportion to how much you enjoy scheming and devicing strategies for beating human players.
The multiplayer system itself is frankly archaic, requiring the hosting of an old-fashioned game server for other players to connect to and upload their turns to specific games. Individual matches might run for months at a time.
The magic system while complex, is daunting to master and requires memorization of the vast spell lists to properly use. There are numerous exploitable mechanics that are slow to get fixed, as well as a plethora of bugs.
Despite all it's flaws, Dominions 4 is still a true gem for turn-based strategy fans. It's quite unpolished and with decidedly indie production values, but with deep and rewarding mechanics.

Based mostly on the old CD ROM release, which contains the same WAD file as the Steam release.
Doom with a medival fantasy aesthetic. And I say that as a compliment. Weapons and their progression mirror those in Doom. Enemy types range from grunt types to almost minibosses and end level bosses. Stages have dynamic layouts and clever environmental puzzles. The medival fantasy motif allowed for some cool variations on a time tested formula.
Best played via ZDoom (or GZDoom), the way I've been playing Heretic and Hexen for years. ZDoom enables mouselook and modern FPS controls. GZDoom does the same, but also spruces up the graphics via OpenGL. Just go into your Steam folder*, copy the HERETIC.WAD file, paste it in your ZDoom/GZDoom folder, launch ZDoom/GZDoom, and enjoy.
*Program Files (x86)>Steam>steamapps>common>Heretic Shadow of the Serpent Riders>base>HERETIC.WAD
ZDoom and GZDoom can be found here:
and can be used on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

Essentially a reskin of DOOM in the best sense of the word, you play as an elf fighting an evil serpent-riding wizard hell-bent on destroying the world (for some reason).  Never-the-less, the game will still surprise you with its differences, such as usable items, interactive environments, and *GASP* the ability to look up and down!
The level design here is top notch, so kudos to Raven Software.  One of the strongest factors going for Heretic is its surprisingly impressive levels, both in terms of scope and functionality.
Though, one thing that I find slightly disappointing is the seemingly haphazard enemy selection.  There's golems (which look like mummies), gigantic skeletal warriors, small imps, serpent-men, minotaurs, wierd scorpion-like insects with axes for hands, bipedal lizards, something called a "weredragon", and a GIANT FLOATING SKULL....Whatever they seem to be, the game could've benefited from a more thematic assortment of enemies instead of the circus we have going on here.  Some of the sprite-work also appears to be rather rushed, namely the imps that infest nearly every level.  You might be thinking "that's a small nit-pick!" but if you compare the Imps in Heretic to the Lost Souls in DOOM, you can immediately tell that the imps were rushed.  Which brings to light another issue I have, where some enemies look "more" cartoony than others, like there were different sprite artists working on different enemies and they weren't communicating with one another, just trying to throw together an enemy and ship it out.
Overall, just a few things I noticed that chip away at the other-wise admirable attempt to cash-in on the Doom clone craze and coming out a LOT more successfully than its competition.

Stellaris is a game for an aquired taste. Its a massive 4X real time space strategy game. Here are my thoughts on good and bad:
Pros
+Vast maps with a lot of starsystems to explore.
+Research is different than most games, and takes forever to complete.
+Different ways to form your empire/democracy. You can even be machines.
+You can upgrade and outfit your ships with new weapons and equipment.
+Good replayability
Cons
-Wars can be tedious due to a warscore system (basically limits how much you can conquer each war).
-Space combat is a big part of the game, but the fights themselves are more or less automatic.
-Lacks more options in deplomacy (also this part of the game needs an upgrade, though its cool you can make federations)
All in all, Stellaris is a game that has a slow phase and focuses a lot on exploration (at least at the beginning and mid game). You have to enjoy the "Grand campaign" style where it will take a long time to win, which I personally do. Although there are some negative things to be said, I still think its one of the better 4X space games out there right now.
I recommend it.

What I *really* love about Stellaris is how it piques the imagination. Any consumer of sci-fi will see the tropes sprinkled throughout the game and marvel at their digital manifestation. The scope for role-playing the galactic civilization of the far-flung corners of your imagination is huge.
Add on top of an already engaging base-game a massively productive modding scene, and the foundations are laid for many thousands of hours of absorbing play time.

This is a small first impression review I got from playing the game for a couple of rounds.
-It looks okay. Not really a pretty game but nothing bad either.
-Guns feel alright, and bullets go where you aim them. No complaints there.
They reload very slow though, and grenades take forever too. But I suppose that was intended and it's not a bad thing.
-Some maps are good and fun, others are just too confusing to know where to go or where you're getting shot from.
-There are some teamwork options with squad spawns and VoiP, but no one seems to make much use of it.
Probably would be way more fun with some players that actually want to work together.
Could also use more interesting classes to stand out from all the other World War shooters.
-Gamemodes seem fine. Capture Controlpoint (Territory) played fine, and I enjoyed a similar mode (Supremacy) with non-locking points more.
-Enemies (and yourself) die in 1 good hit. Personally, not sure what to think of it.
If you spot someone and they don't spot you, you win. If not, you lose.
It doesn't allow for many exciting gunbattles because it's usually over before it starts.
Conclusion
It's a good game. No large complaints.
However, for me personally it didn't do anything special. It could use something to make it stand out.
I suppose the only special feature is the Supremacy mode and some tiny things like custom respawn locations.
I'd rate it a Grilled cheese sandwich.
It's OK as it is, but could use some bacon.

Most of the game is waiting for your profits to increase and buying things with it, but it goes up so quickly that most wait isn't too long. You rush through that progress in like a third of the time and it feels like when you start a game, all excited, and then when you get to the point where that particular excitement wears off, you can just renew it and make the game even better! It is very casual and has little strategy but its not meant to be a kickass game, just one you leave to play one in a while and it is very polished for what it is. It has 3 different sites for which you get seperate profits, those being the earth, moon, and mars, and each progress in different ways even if they seem the same initially.

A massive accomplishment in the gaming industry.
There are many things I liked about this game. Here's a few strong points: Accurate mapping, large degrees of micromanagement and lots of real events happening at the real times gave a bolder illusion of reality. It made me feel like I was a real ruler. I loved the cartooney graphics; when the models are on this scale they look really good. I enjoyed the variety of boosts and debuffs that you could have. The call the legions was great if you were Sparta (lots of generals so you can really take advantage of the 100k more units) and it was funny how on Easy you could use call the legions to get equal troops to the Romans and then overthrow them.
I couldn't find many bad things to say about this game, but they are big enough to make a point of: Real shame I couldn't play as a different city in Greece/Different country. Maybe open up a mod workshop so this is possible? The fact that I couldn't specify EXACTLY how many people I wanted doing a thing really annoyed me (Major OCD). The biggest nagging problem I found was that the Justinian Plague was REALLY confusing. For some reason sometimes things were unusable and sometimes they were and I think that because it's the least straightforward of the events it should have at least a LITTLE bit of prior instruction so you don't fail on your first time getting to that point in the game.
All in all though, great game, I'd rate 9.2/10 in it's current state, and 9.8/10 if the issues are fixed.

Saints Row 2 is the sequel to the first entry in the saga of Saints Row, You play the role of the Boss of the saints who just woke up from a coma after the events of the first game, and now needs to retake the city from new gangs and together with Johnny Gat rebuild the saints.
This game is classified as one of the worst pc ports ever, and they're kind of right, but with the help of mods it's playable, with some slow downs sometimes while driving, and a clear graphical downgrade, but other than that it's playable and definetly worth the purchase, sure the first game might not be in pc, but you can read the story somewhere else, anyways the important parts of the first game gets explained through the story, the betrayals and etc.
The three gangs you take on are Maero with the brotherhood, Akuji with the ronin and The brotherhood of Samedi each with different tactics of taking the city, and a different storyline for each, totaling around 15 misions per gang, and 5 more as epilogue , granting you several hours of playtime.
There's a ton of activities to do around the game to unlock secret weapons, unlimited ammo, unlimited sprint and other bonuses, some of them are insurance fraud you need to throw yourself into cars with crazy physics, septic avenger throw poop at houses and cars to cause property devaluation, races and more.
The main different between a sandbox game like GTA and Saint's Row 2 is the fact Saint's row 2 allows a lot of customization, sex, race, clothes,voices, more fun activities, crazy but fun storyline , like for example giving someone a tatoo with radioactive material, but also with some really sad moments through the story and good character development.
Game is easily worth the full price, or if you can wait get it during a sale or bundle.

Ever wanted to play a game set in one of the Frank Frazzeta paintings? Then look no further than Heretic. Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders is the first game in the Heretic & Hexen series, and along with ID software games, have been the main force of evolution in the first era of first person shooters. Each game from Heretic & Hexen series have introduced a design concept that all other FPS games have followed ever since. Heretic SotSR remains the most accessible and action-packed title in the series, set in a dark fantasy universe with 54 complex levels which will guarantee you 20 hours and more of pure hectic and frenetic fun.
You play as Corvus, one of the last members of the Elves, as theirs and human kingdoms are being annihilated by the overwhelming forces of the three Serpent Riders, ancient spellcasters that have evolved into forces of pure evil and destruction as they invade different realms while spreading corruption and chaos in their wake. Witnessing all this horror, Corvus decides to take matters into his hand and exact vengeance against the first and weakest of the three Serpent Riders, D’Sparil.
Heretic SotSR was the first game that introduced gibing based on elemental hazards such as stepping into fire or activating a squishing trap. All levels are sorted into 5 episodes, and each episode has one hidden bonus level. These levels have beautiful macabre and mystic 2D art as you traverse open fields, medieval villages, castles and dungeons while you are desperately trying to fight against many dangerous foes and followers of D’Sparil. Medieval weapons that you use are a bit of a knock-offs of Doom weapons, in a way they function and fire similar to Doom-marine’s pistol, shotgun, minigun etc, but they are all easy and fun to use, while some of them are better suited against certain types of enemies. Speaking of enemies, there are 16 distinct and horrifying enemies that will try to put you down: from flying Gargoyles that lunge at the players in for a slashing attack, slow and strong Golems that can cause massive damage if they get close enough, to Disciples that are very fast and use powerful magical ranged attacks, and Iron Liches as one of the most devastating enemies that hunt in groups. Prioritizing which type of the enemy to take out first is the key in wining every fight in Heretic. At the end of each episode, you’ll also meet deadly bosses, until you finally clash with D’Sparil itself. Heretic is also if not the first, then among the first FPS games that introduced inventory system with a dozen of powerful items that will aid you in combat, such as: Tome of Power that temporarily unlocks alternative attack of all the weapons, Quartz Flask that heal a small portion of health, or Mystic Urn that fully restores health when used, or saves player from imminent death when all health has been lost.
For every fan of fast and furious FPS games of the 90’s, Heretic is a must play: a wild dance of death and magic barrage against overwhelming hordes of enemies, set in the equally astonishing and dangerous fantasy realm – Heretic Shadow of the Serpent Riders will fill up your bloodlust and prepare you for the superior sequels of Hexen and Hexen II, where your skill and thinking will be put to the ultimate test. “”Sorsit!” “Soract!”

Doo- I mean heretic is a FPS that takes Doom and changes it into a fantasy style game. It retains solid shooting mechanics and the graphics are a little better but not by much(which is fine as I never felt doom was unplesant to look at anyway). I wouldn't be suprised if it uses the same coding from doom for some of the enemies and weapons(the pole weapons is the punch from doom, the axe armed enemies are the pig demon,etc.). It adds items to mix things up and they are a ton of fun to use ( I love the egg power as it turns enemies into chickens). The downside is your items are reduced to one from level to level no matter how much you have. I get why they did this, since building up nine invinciblity rings would kinda break the game, I think it's also to make you use the items instead of saving it for bosses. It's just disappointing when you have eight purple potions and you lose seven at the end, like it was a waste. Also like the first doom I was disapointed at repeated bosses in episode four and five.
If it sounds like I'm being critical, rest assured that was my last commplant. The great level design is there, the sound design is solid and the sound track is refreshingly diffrent from doom, and the enemies are still fun to fight(and the items add new ideas for attacks and methods for fighting enemies) and I love the fantasy feel. While I was a little disapointed it felt too much like doom(and less like it's own game) it's still doom and doom is a blast to play. It does do enough new to recommed it to any fan of shooters. All in all, go for it. It's great.

There's really not much to say that hasn't already been said about Skyrim, good or bad.
As far as gameplay goes, this is every bit as good as the original, with potentially smoother gameplay.
The only con right now that should make the greatest impact on buying this one or the original Legendary edition (complete with all DLCs), is that this one DOES NOT nearly have as much mod support as the original, with many mod authors who've created classic Skyrim mods either refusing to support the Special Edition or not yet doing so.
Some reviews point out that this release of Skyrim also hallmarked the newest venture for Bethesda: the Creation Club. Long story short, it monetizes mods by entering into independent contracts with mod authors, who are required to update their builds regularly with game updates. Ostensibly this is to ensure that these mods will always run with the base game and be of high quality, but the question remains why would you pay for any mod when you can either just not use them or get them for free?
If the Creation Club isn't a concern to you and you don't care about having a larger mod pool to choose from, consider this one. If you want to spend time hunting for the original Legendary edition (it's hidden now on Steam, but last I have seen is available as a key on other sites), I'd recommend that one more. You can probably find it for cheap.
Edited: Also, if I'm interpreting something correctly, Creation Club mods won't turn off achievements for either this or Fallout 4, whereas mods outside of the Creation Club will. This feels sketchy if you happen to like achievement hunting.

tldr;
A great team game, with an inconsistent, but often enjoyable, player experience.  A small community nowdays, but generally, welcoming and fun focused.  Buy it for a unique experience, especially if you can bring enough for a full crew of 4 or some multiple thereof.  When the crew clicks, it's often GREAT and when it doesn't it can be frustrating, boring, or just plain rage inducing.
full text;
I am coming at this as someone who put in ~20 hours 2 years ago, and one evening recently, which spurred me to write this.
Back then we normally ran in 4 person Crews to ensure those on our ship would work well (enough) together.  However, I have played on a number of random pug ships as well.
When you first start up, you will be restricted in what you can fly and do, but playing the game for a bit will get you out of this novice mode, and you will be a better player for it.  It is a reasonable way to make sure that most people in the later games at least know the basics.  The rest of this review focuses on the PVP after that time.
You get to choose 1 of 3 roles, Pilot, Gunner, or Engineer.
Pilot (Captain):  Amazing, but stressful.
You decide what ship and weaponry to bring to the battle.  How to confront the enemy, and when and where to engage.
You need to be able to multi-task, clearly communicating to both your Crew and the other Captain(s) on your team while  positioning your craft to ensure gun angles, get cover or flee when needed, and utilizing your tools at the right moments for the advantages and disadvantages they provide the ship.  Really, in all but the most extreme cases of crew preformance, the ships success and survival is in your hands.
When played with focus, against an equally skilled opponent, there are few other team games as demanding as the Pilot role in PVP for Guns of Icarus.
Gunner: Turret shooter with possibly little to do when not engaged in battle, but reasonably fun.
Although you need to balance your time focusing on gunning with other emergancy tasks, your most important job is to bring the right gun and ammo to the right target at the right time.  Communicating to the Captain if you are off angle is just as important as listening when they call out for a particular gun or angle to be covered.  Your influence on the outcome of a particular confrontation cannot be discounted, since, if nothing is shot, nothing explodes, but you opportunities to do so are at the mercy of your Pilot.
Engineer: Very busy role, very engaged, but not always the most visibly engaging.  Your game consists of either spotting the enemy, firing a gun, or, for the majority of the time, smacking the same components with the same items for the duration of the match.  Most of your actions will be almost pre-ordained by the pilot's actions.
While your influence on the ship is not to be understated; you can and will save the ship, most of the engineer's play time is spent focused on their own mini-game of timing hits and parkouring about the ship on the best repair route for the situation.  It is not unheard of for an engineer to spend the entire time focused on keeping their own ship in the air, jumping out of the catwalk, hoping from ledge to ledge over the open sky and saving the hull at the last second with a well placed mallet strike, but, missing out on the overall battle due their laser like inner focus.  Combine that with the ocassional poor Captain who will berate the engineer's performance for most the round as they pilot the ship between enemy ships, receiving full salvos from each against their already damaged hull, and you can have some very frustrating matches.
Overall the role is simultaniously fun due to the parkour and mini-successes of repairing, putting out fires, and buffing during a match, and least enjoyable, since it is almost entirely reactive.  There will be times your ship will explode without you ever getting a chance to do anything but fight fires and hit things with wrenches.  And no matter how well you repair, you cannot overcome poor Captain choices.
Community: Mixed, but can be really great.
Just like any other game, the community can be a mixed bag.  But that can have some profound effects on this game due to its team focus.  A bad Captain, not necessarialy inexpeienced or bad strategically, but one who either cannot or does not communicate with their crew effectively, or who just spends an entire match berating his crew, can cause an entire crew to abandon the game.  I have actually witnessed mutinies where crews will begin jumping over the sides like lemmings just to annoy a particularly irksome Captain.
Generally though, the community, as small as it is, is firendly, welcoming of new players, and mostly out for a good time.  If you have a horrible Captain, it does not take much to leave their ship or for them to leave you.
One thing to note, there are times, when matchmaker will simply seal your fate.  This seems to be a function of the number of players about nowdays.  But don't be disheartened, I have seen low level ships flatten higher level ones.  (It's not common, but it can happen)
Overall:
This is an AMAZING game if you want to play as a Pilot\Captain and experience a rather unique and deep strategy\co-op game.  For the other roles, it can be a fun game, but every round is a function of the quality of your Captain. Most are ok, some are horrible, and occasionally you'll find a great one.

This is a small first impression review I got from playing the game for a couple of rounds.
-It looks okay. Not really a pretty game but nothing bad either.
-Guns feel alright, and bullets go where you aim them. No complaints there.
They reload very slow though, and grenades take forever too. But I suppose that was intended and it's not a bad thing.
-Some maps are good and fun, others are just too confusing to know where to go or where you're getting shot from.
-There are some teamwork options with squad spawns and VoiP, but no one seems to make much use of it.
Probably would be way more fun with some players that actually want to work together.
Could also use more interesting classes to stand out from all the other World War shooters.
-Gamemodes seem fine. Capture Controlpoint (Territory) played fine, and I enjoyed a similar mode (Supremacy) with non-locking points more.
-Enemies (and yourself) die in 1 good hit. Personally, not sure what to think of it.
If you spot someone and they don't spot you, you win. If not, you lose.
It doesn't allow for many exciting gunbattles because it's usually over before it starts.
Conclusion
It's a good game. No large complaints.
However, for me personally it didn't do anything special. It could use something to make it stand out.
I suppose the only special feature is the Supremacy mode and some tiny things like custom respawn locations.
I'd rate it a Grilled cheese sandwich.
It's OK as it is, but could use some bacon.

This puzzle game is very similar to the Portal games, except that in Polarity, you don't have a portal gun, you have the option of changing your "polarity" from blue to red, and red to blue. You must use your polarity changing abilities to maneuver abstacles such as lasers, gates, bridges, and more. For example, depending on the color of a laser, you either can get through it, or you cannot. If it were a blue laser, you would have to change your polarity to blue to get through, and if it were red, you would have to change your polarity to red.
The story is a bit awkward, considering this game is an intricate puzzle game with blocks and jumping around, being a hacker trying to get data from a computer network is not a very fitting story.
Another thing I wanted to mention was that for me, personally, the pricetag of $15 is asking a bit too much, as I would say $10 or less is a more reasonable price, but since I picked this game up during the 2015 Summer Sale, I cannot complain because I paid 19 cents.
Overall, this is a great game, with puzzle elements similar to the Portal games, and other unique elements, but the price is asking a bit too much for what it is, and the story does not fit this game very well.
I would recommend this game to anyone who wouldn't mind selling two trading cards for this 19 cent game (when it is on sale).

Heretic is like Doom with magic. The gameplay is just as enthralling as ID's legendary game - it has wonderful level design, lots of demons to kill, secrets, secret levels, and a revolutionary inventory system (for the time). The gameplay is timeless - still good fun to play, and offer a great challenge for a seasoned old-school shooter fan (especially the last 2 chapters are hard as a gargoyle's turd). The weapons are similar to Doom's, but - I have to admit - they are less fun to use, because they are quite similar to each other, and lack that power I expect from them. For example the Firemace is pretty much useless. The best weapon is the Crossbow, which basically functions as a shotgun. Using a Tome of Power modifies your weapons' attacks, so that provides some variety.
If you like Doom and old-school shooters, give yourself a favor, and play this game.

I am giving this port a negative score. I hope you read that sentence correctly: this is a terrible PORT, so I do not condone paying for this.
Raven Software (the game's original developer) simply packaged the vanilla DOS distribution of the game with DOSbox, a DOS emulator. Because this game is emulated, it doesn't perform as well as its supposed to. The emulated musical renditions are unfaithful to what I heard when I used to play the game on a 100 MHz Windows 95 rig, and this sorry excuse for a Steam port includes none of the optional features that modernize and improve the game, like those found in free third-party launchers such as zDoom and The Doomsday Engine.
Sadly, all of id Software's DOS-based games received this sort of shoddy treatment when they were ported for digital distribution. Now that id Software is owned by Bethesda, I can't advocate buying anything associated with id Software anymore. (Raven developed this game, but id Software licensed the Doom engine to Raven.)
Heretic has always been one of my all-time favorite first person shooters. Raven Software made some tremendous improvements to the Doom engine when it made this game, but what impresses me more than the tech featured in this game is its atmosphere. Heretic's levels are more diverse than Doom's, and the excellent music and creepy chants from enemy warlocks (the Disciples of D'Sparil) make the experience of exploring these environments more immersive.
I find the game a lot more challenging than Doom, largely because of how the levels are designed and how ammo is distributed throughout them. The game is tough but fair, and does not hold your hand or bombard you with painfully obvious 'hints.'
You should play this game instead of Ziggurat if exploring compelling maps and uncovering secrets are things you value. If you like combat that feels exciting rather than tedious, you may enjoy this game more than HeXen, its sequel. (I sure do!)
Although it's difficult to play Heretic with others, the game's deathmatch mode has always been a blast. Playing against your buddies is especially fun since you may end up being transformed into a chicken. When that happens, you actually adopt the advantages and disadvantages of being in that form! However, I have always preferred playing classic FPS games in co-op mode rather than competitive mode, and Heretic is no exception to that preference.
If this were the 90s and Heretic was running natively the way it was meant to, I'd recommend the game in a heartbeat. I still recommend playing the game itself if you're willing to trouble yourself with downloading and setting up a modern launcher, but I don't advocate paying for this game. The port is flat-out lazy and undeserving of your money, and with Bethesda's takeover of id Software, it's doubtful that much (if any) of the money you spend will go to the developers who made this masterpiece. Bethesda is not a publisher I like to support any longer.
Normally I'd advocate buying older games on GOG for quality assurance. However, since Heretic's publisher 'mailed in' this digitally distributed port exactly as id Software did, you can't even count on the GOG port for an experience that is at least as good as the original when you boot the game immediately after installing it.
THE BOTTOM LINE: This bad (but functional) port is not worth your money, but the game itself is fantastic and should be enjoyed by every fan of old school first person shooters.

A fast, slick platformer about descending a tower made of randomly shuffled room-tiles. There’s enough room variety that it takes awhile to memorize them all, and when you’re going fast it’s still tricky to avoid making mistakes, and you will be going fast. This is one of the benefits of the game flow being downwards, although sometimes you’ll fly into spike pits at terminal velocity. Once you get it down, the game can be beaten in about 10 minutes without too much trouble, but there’s still plenty of challenge to the other modes if you’re looking for it.
I’m not a fan of how access to transdimensional leakage (a harder version of the tower with different bosses) is handled, having to grind out sets of pickups in a single run to get a ticket allowing a single attempt. It feels like a free-to-play system designed to pad out the game. Also, while there are several different melee, ranged and magic options, most options that change things aren't really
options. It would’ve been nice to see things that mix-up gameplay a bit more.
Anyway, it’s good.

Dom4 is basically the same system as Dom3 with some mechanical changes that you probably won't care about unless you have played both games a fair amount and some interface upgrades. The interface improvements do matter, and help to cut down the micromanagement inherent in the game, but there is still a fair amount of turn to turn management that you need to engage in which would be nice to automate. Perhaps the biggest thing to be aware of in this game is that singleplayer is very lacking. The game has a huge amount of depth, thousands of units, hundreds of items and spells; all of which the AI is unable to effectively employ. So if you get this game and intend to play any significant amount, look to get involved with multiplayer. Those are the game's primary flaws, for everything else Dominions delivers nicely. Each of the different nations plays differently from it's peers, and most have sereveral viable paths to pursue as the game developes. The game escalates from small numbers of spearmen fighting eachother to angels and dead gods slugging it out in a world where the sun has been snuffed out by magic. If you can look past the game's quirks, this is a fantastic product with amazing scope and detail. It's well worth your money.

Easy game to start playing. Make armies and take over the world. But hard to master. With a large list of spells and the creation of custom templates for your mages to follow this game can have a lot of thought put into the details. Mages can also spend a turn crafting items, casting tactical spells, or summoning monsters, ect.
Dominions 4 is a straight forward game with a lot of depth. I haven't tried the multiplayer, but I enjoy the SP experience a lot.

Hey you! Yeah, you there in front of the computer/phone/tablet, or whatever device you're using.  Are you a fan of Doom? Sure you are.  Doom is loved by many, and rightly so.  It was one of the most influential games of its time and still holds up extremely well today.  Why else would it be getting rereleased and even rebooted every decade or so?  What if I told you this game is basically Doom with a fantasy paintjob?
Yeah, because that's what it is, and I highly reccomend it.  But a quick warning; this game is a dinosaur by today's standards and the control scheme is rather, shall we say archaic and may be frustrating to modern  gamers.  But releif is available in the form of a little program called ZDoom.  This baby makes the game control like a modern shooter and even cleans up the graphics a bit.  And best of all, you can get it without spending a single penny, and without the headache of computer viruses.  Here's a quick guide to get it to work.
You need:
Unpacking softare (I reccomend 7-Zip as it's free, where as Winrar will eventually slam you up the butt with a paywall)
ZDoom: Found here.
1.) Download ZDoom
2.) Use your unpacking software to extract it into the Heretic Folder
3.) Copy contents from ZDoom folder into main folder.
4.) Find Dosbox.exe and rename it Dosboxbackup.exe.
5.) Find ZDoom.exe and rename it Dosbox.exe
And that's it, the game now controls like a modern shooter.  Once you've got that done, you can sit back and enjoy some fantasy bad guy blasting.  You are the Heretic, and you're out for blood.  The Serpant Riders have a nasty plan for Mankind, and your job is to stop it.  There is more to the story than that, but I don't want to give any spoliers, as you really should play this game if you're at all into Doom.
Your weapons include, but are not limited to, The Etheral Crossbow, The Dragonclaw, and the Hell Staff.  Weapons and Ammo are littered around each level and you'd best pick them up because evil can be around any corner.  The game plays in five episodes.  Finishing an episode will wrap up the current episode and give you a prelude into the next one.  Again, this is basically Doom with a fantasy vibe rather than a science fiction one.
The graphics are spot on for that old timey Doom feel, as is the music.  The only real complaint I have is that I can't figure out how to make the screen go Full screen. That aside, Heretic Shadow of The Serpant Riders is a hidden Gem and for five bucks, you can't go wrong.  Heck, you can get the whole series this game is in for ten bucks.  Four games for Ten bucks is a pretty hard offer to turn down.
In the end, I urge you to get Heretic if you are at all into Doom.  But yeah, get ZDoom and it'll smooth the controls out and make the game accessable to modern gamers.  Highly reccomended!

You know, it's tough, writing this as a negative.
Honest truth is, this game gave me the best feeling of being a small being in a grand universe, always feeling like the next corner of space we rounded would show us some unexpected wonder about the nature of things. This is the best existentialism game I've played except for maybe the Talos Principle, and this may be the best depiction of our lonely place in the great expanse that I've ever seen. But I cannot recommend it, as it stands.
What the game absolutely nails in its atmosphere, lore, and wonder, it largely betrays with the simple shell of a RTS model it chooses to employ. Did we not learn our lessons about doomstacks from Civilization IV? For the countless ways that this is the true spiritual successor to Civilization on a grander, space scale (talking to you, Beyond Earth), it's amazing they succumb to these simple flaws in designing a game that is, at the basic level, fun.
The management of your resources, colonies, research, and policies is spot-on, but just like in any multiplayer RTS, all serve as secondary (albeit important and highly necessary) elements to the combat. Most of the intricate and exciting early game land grabs and stage-setting for galactic domination ends up boiling down to a very limited number, or even just one, single space battle where the entirety of one civilization's fleet squares off against the enemy's. The tiny nuanced advantages in balanced fleet compositions (excluding if someone is WAY behind on research, of course) become irrelevant behind "the big number" of fleet power, and once one side starts losing, the snowball just continues into an utter stomp. You cannot control any individual tactics, no formations, it's basically just however the AI decides to use weaponry you've customized, and there rarely appears to be any viable strategy beyond piling every ship you own into a ball and either chasing their ball of ships across the galaxy (if you have a better combat number) or running while you try to amass a bigger ball (if you have a worse combat number).
The rudimentary nature almost akin to a cell phone game just feels so out of place in an otherwise nearly perfect game. It sinks the unique experience into a monotony in almost every match while you wade through the mid- to late-game. Until something is adjusted on these lines, I'm going to have to regrettably recommend against this game.

--- This Review is for Minecraft Story Mode - Episode 1 ---
Okay, Telltale outdid themselves again. Their flavor of the month this time is Minceraft.
The story is as simple as it goes - in the World of Minecraft there were once four brave heroes: A Building Master, A Mighty Warrior, A Demolitions Expert and A Redstone Engeneer. Their legend is passed down, of their adventures and of how they have slain an Enderdragon. But those heroes are no longer needed.
or... are they?
after what you might consider a Job gone Sour, amateur Builder Jesse (male or female, your pick. thanks ambigious name) and his friends are drawn into an Adventure to save their world from an all-consuming monster
The world itself is used quite well, using Monsters, basic concepts (like the crafting, combat,  the Monster Spawn mechanic and Block effects) of the world to craft a Story within the world. People have done so before, using books and signs as a Storytelling device, now Telltale gives the game its own flavor. It has recognition value, but not in the way Tales of the Borderlands, GoT or Wolf Among Us had, since all characters and story frame is a work by itself, but it still manages to keep you on the edge of your seat with it
the music is fitting, using a similar style of tunes used in the original game.
Basic knowledge of the Minecraft universe, namely the crafting system is needed for one Puzzle.There might be more in the future, but it helps to know how you can craft certain things.
Playtime for the first episode: around 90- 120 minutes, if kept up total play time around 10 hours
This game as of now does not have the typical telltale-style achievements.

Video Review:
Guns of Icarus is an older game now, having released in 2012. In it you play as either a pilot, engineer, or gunner, and run an airship in arena-based battles of up to four ships versus four ships in PvP or four ships versus endless-ish ships in PvE. With 74 hours into the game I think it’s safe to say I’ve played a lot of it over the years. Not as much as others, but more than most.
So gameplay wise you’ll be limited to one role mainly for the entirety of each match. As a pilot you’ll get to steer the ship, use abilities to do anything from speeding the ship up, leaving toxic gas in your wake, or a number of other things. You’ll likely also be in the captain role and get to give orders to either your AI crewmates or player partners who will hopefully listen to you. Occasionally you might go to repair something as well at leave no one at the helm as you can carry one tool for every role you are not and three for your selected role, which allows some capability for crossover and strategizing.
As a gunner you’ll be mainly working on the guns, obviously. You can load your guns with specific ammunition with various effects from incendiary, to heatsink, and even explosive. Of course you might have to do some repairing of your own gun or maybe even of the ship if things get so dire.
As an engineer you will be running around frantically trying to repair things as they blow up, get set on fire, or get shot up. You’ll be able to repair things faster, rebuild things faster, put out fires, buff guns, or even auto-repair things. Sometimes you’ll also be asked to do some gunning if there’s nothing to repair
All of these classes balance each other out really well since no one class can quite completely do the role of another. They also even have special abilities they can use. Engineers can sprint, gunners can reload faster, and captains can move the ship faster and more maneuverable all for a limited time. All in all the gameplay base here is really solid and makes for a really enjoyable experience already.
The graphics are charming and unique but certainly not revolutionary or even “good” for that matter even back in 2012 when the game was released. There’s not really any heavy level of production to this game. It received just enough to not be void or ridiculous, but most attention really went off to the gameplay. There aren’t many issues really. Some multi monitor issues depending on your exact setup but that’s not necessarily the game’s fault as far as I know. For example my friend didn’t have any issues with that, but I did. However we use very different monitors and he runs AMD whereas I run Nvidia and AMD is admittedly much better with multi-monitor frameworks.
You can fully customize your ships with color designs and ornaments and set up exactly what guns you want on it. Your only real limitations in that regard are the things available and the weapon slots you have on every ship. Ships all have different stats. Some are better than others in different situations and excel at doing very specific things sometimes. There’s entire metas on how to play certain types of ships. Although I learned the hard way that things that work in PvP aren’t necessarily going to work in PvE.
The AI in both PvE and PvP are pretty incompetent. They’re not very smart, are a nightmare if you are trying to solo run a ship (although my friend who runs solo constantly disagrees with me, but he only plays PvE), and they just are dumb and do things wrong and play about as bad as a brand new player would. Meaning you shouldn’t really get this unless you plan on playing with other people and I’ll mention more on that later. You can’t really put AI into PvP matches, nor can you have an AI pilot a ship when a player is present or in a PvP match. They can only do that in PvE for some reason.
The game itself gets an 7/10 from me here. It’s a very fun solid base. There’s some small issues with the game itself, but just small things. For what this game tried to be it certainly nailed it on the head. Although admittedly it’s not actually that much so it’s nothing that deserves anything higher than an 8 no matter how well it does it. But this isn’t the end of this review. The most important point has yet to be made and it’s pretty negative and basically why I bumped a point off the score I wanted to give it.
Now this is where things are going to split up between Online and Alliance because this game is marketed very strangely and impractically and I can only recommend buying one of these two.
To start, Online is the PvP only edition of the game. It is the original game and you can pick it up for a mere $5. That sounds like a great deal, right? Well just wait.
Alliance is the PvE expansion to the game. However, when you buy it you’re getting and paying for both the expansion AND the base game. It’s $15, meaning the price of the expansion is twice that of the original game. That’s a bit odd don’t you think? Well not so much.
Guns of Icarus had a very strong launch. Youtubers advertising it everywhere. Good marketing, good emails, and just solid work all around. It sold many copies and even successfully kickstarted an “adventure mode” which turned into Alliance (which is not even close to what adventure mode was supposed to be) and didn’t really receive any flak over it at all.
The huge issue here is that Guns of Icarus after a while had a very hard problem at maintaining its playerbase. Less than one month after its release there were over a thousand people playing it every day. At its peak there were nearly five thousand every day. This is in a game where you only really need eight people in one match for an optimal experience so these numbers are pretty good. After a while that number descended into only a few hundred every day and the daily peak was around four hundred. Still enjoyable, but harder to find a match given differences in skill level and all. Recently it’s gotten even worse. After the launch of PvE I think the developers just gave up trying to maintain a healthy PvP playerbase because now only a max of fifty to sixty people even play every day. The peak is about forty or fifty and during the night it will plummet down to ten people playing at once. And keep in mind this is across both PvE AND PvP. Ten people playing. A bare minimum PvP match without relying on AI needs eight players. A full one needs thirty two. That’s more people than you’ll even normally find online at this point. Because of this PvP is virtually nonexistent. You can’t find a match and if you can it’s small, uninhabited, and filled with AI.
So when it comes down to if I can recommend Guns of Icarus...this game that I adore and that I have dozens of hours of amazing memories on and and dozens more screenshots saved to steam for....It’s a yes and a no. If you’re looking at Guns of Icarus Online it’s a solid no. That’s JUST the PvP. You will waste a lot of time there finding a match in a nonexistent community. You’re paying $5 to not find any matches. Don’t do that.
When it comes to Guns of Icarus Alliance then I’m going to have to recommend it; especially if you can rope some friends (preferably 3 others) into playing it with you. But do note that you’ll be supporting a company that is simply not trying anymore and that is trying to milk what they know is the last leg of their game by charging three time more than the dead PvP mode by its lonesome, which they’re STILL SELLING even though you can’t find a match to begin with.
I love this game, but the team behind it sucks. Don’t buy it support them. Only buy Alliance if you want to fight cooperatively against AI. PvP is dead and it’s never coming back. Remember. Fifty player peaks. And it only gets worse from here.

Polarity in a sentence: Polarity is a first-person puzzle/platforming game where you, well, solve puzzle and... yeah.
That was Polarity in a sentence (And a half, I guess). Now, it's time for the real review.
Basic Info:
Polarity, greatly inspired by Portal, is a first-person puzzle platformer. You can play singleplayer or multiplayer. Either way, they're the same kind of puzzles.
List of Basic Uses:
-Cubes: Used to activate switches, platforms, laser walls, etc.
-Polarity: You switch your Polarity (Your color, some say) to jump onto colored platforms, or to get through a laser gate without dying.
-Gold Lasers, A.K.A. Color Changing Lasers: These are lasers that you can throw cubes into to change their color from either red to blue, or blue to red.
-Data: These are collected to unlock more levels throughout the game and eventually unlock the bonus stages. There are three per level.
Other Notes:
This game is completly Xbox 360 controller compatible without any configuration needed. There is also a split-screen multiplayer that has its own campaign.
Story:
Honestly, Polarity doesn't really have a story at all. However, you can peice together a basic story from what you're told.
You're a hacker trying to break into one of the greatest firewalls in the world, trying to collect data so you get your reward that was promised to you by an unknown person/thing - 10,000,000 Credits.
Gameplay:
Polarity has you jumping from platform to platform, switching your Polarity (Or, some may call, your color) and carrying and throwing cubes everywhere. What I'm trying to say is that you may have to get through a
laser gate, so you have to switch your polarity (Which, by default at the begining of every level, is
) to, obviously,
. That's different with platforms, however. With platforms, you must switch to the
color to get across, which leads to switching polarity in mid-air. What I'm trying to say is that your Polarity and ablility to work with cubes is all you need to beat the levels.
Polarity has 14 levels in singleplayer that are not too tough at all, but can actually be a bit fustrating for reasons such as "Crap, put the cube in the wrong spot - Oh, there it goes. Bye cube. Just gotta run back to the other side of the map again to get a new one..." Most of the levels are short, but every now and then, you'll notice repeating concepts in the levels. For exaple, you may have just completed a level where you had to through cubes into switches and now, you're throwing cubes into color changing lasers and then putting them in switches. May not
similar, but once you play, you'll know what I mean. That, however, is not too much of an issue.
Upon getting every Data Crystal in the singleplayer campaign, you unlock the 10 bonus levels. These levels are just
harder then the normal campaign, which is easy once you get the hang of how things work.
Difficulty... That's an issue. This game isn't hard by all means. It's just fustrating. Like in my example above, you can easily throw your cube the wrong way or just barely miss the button for it and *POOF*! It's gone. You'll have to go back and get a new one. Anyways, back to difficulty - It's too easy, in my opinion, to be a puzzle game.
too easy. The Data Crystals aren't even cleverly hidden at all. You can easily get all of those. You'll also find yourself breezing through this game. For example, if you have even the slightest bit of knowledge as to what you're doing, you can get through levels in 1-2 minutes each. The singleplayer campaign (Bonus levels included) may only take you about an hour and a half. That's how short and quick this game is.
Ah, multiplayer... I can't say that I LOVE it, but I like it. You and your buddy are robots (Sound familiar much?) and you must work together to solve puzzles similar to the normal puzzles, except this time, it's even harder. This time I mean it. It's not "I GIVE UP!" hard, it's just... Up there, I guess you could say. The Data Crystals can easily be passed without even knowing it, and they're hidden in better spots and actually take you a minute to get them. I would have to say that the multiplayer is better than the singleplayer just because you have a friend with you and you both get to slove the puzzles together.
Conclusion:
This is a first-person puzzle game that's highly inspired by Portal. Sure, it's not always fair, but it comes through for sure. I would just get this game while it's on sale, as you'll be glad that you didn't waste $5.00 on this. I'm not saying that this is a bad game, it's just I don't see it being worth $5.00. Not everyone looking for a good puzzle game will be satisfied fully, but I still love this game.
To conclude this review, I give Polarity a
. It could be better, and it wouldn't be that hard.

I picked this up because it looked fun from screenshots.I wasn't wrong.Pre-Civilization Marble Age is a rather simplistic turn based historical simulation game.It took me 90 minutes to go from Athens to being the Byzantine Empire and winning the game culturally.
The game is easy to learn and in a short amount of time you'll know what you are doing.Even if it is simplistic,it has depth and you can approach the gameplay differently.You can either be a diplomat,trader or a warmonger.
Diplomacy in this game was surprinsingly good.I didn't expect much from it,but it has enough options to make it interesting.Even if I was surprised by it,I found it lacking because it is way too easy to form an alliance,and the city states/civilizations don't have relations between themselves.
Trading is simple.You choose what you want to buy/sell and select the number of ships you want to allocate to that trade.
Battles are nothing special.It isn't like in CIV games where you control your army and so on.Your job is to build soldiers/make alliances and then attack someone.A window will pop up with the estimation of the fight and you can choose to flee or engange in battle.
What is fun about this game is the random scenarios that pop up.It's a historical game that respects the history.You play as either Sparta or Athens and you are faced with various challenges like natural disasters,plagues,Persian invasion,Roman territorial expansion,Hunnic invasion,Arab territorial expansion,various barbaric tribes invading and so on.
Once a scenario like that threatens your city/empire,you are given some choices and depending on your judgement,you will exit the crisis better or worse.
Graphics are caroonish and pleasing to the eye,the UI can be adjusted and the main menu is also lacking but good enough to get the job done.
Pre-Civilization Marble Age has some weaknesses in terms of diplomacy,replayability and balance(some civs,cities are absurdly strong when it comes to army)but even in its current state,I think it is worth a shot for the ones passionate about those kind of games.
I can see this game becoming very good with some updates,tweaks in terms of balance and even some DLCs.

Dominions 4 is a grand strategic game where you play as the god of one of the 77 nations available (spread out over three eras: Early, where magic is plentiful, technology is not, and giants (as well other magical beings) are common; Middle, the time of iron; and Late, time of steel and the ascendance of man.)
Each nation is fully fleshed out, based off of different myths, and has their own strengths, weaknesses, and quirks.
Gameplay is turn-based, with each turn representing one month. You queue up your orders (such as building troops, casting spells, moving, attacking, searching for magic sites, etc.) and, when you've got everything to your liking, you end the turn. Combat takes place simultaneously between turns. Armies are broken into individual soldiers, who are placed into squads. Each general has a command limit of how many men he can lead, and how many squads those can be broken into (although you can make more, at a hit to morale for all the troops under that general) and each squad can be given a formation and basic orders - such as "attack closest" or "fire at archers and keep distance". Your generals themselves can be given a list of 5 commands as well as an overall tactic - this is best used for mages, who you can instruct to cast specific spells.
There's research, with 7 different schools (conjuration, alteration, evocation, construction, enchantment, thaumaturgy, and blood magic), all of which offer a cornucopia of spells which are available to your mages, depending on which magic paths they are specialized in.
Generally speaking, the game can accommodate just about any number of players (up to 25-ish), and there's a huge number of user-made maps, as well as a random terrain generator which does a pretty good job.
There's a huge number of mods too, which can do anything from changing the cost of a spell all the way up to making entirely new nations.
Pros:
+ One of the deepest strategy games out today.
+ Battles can be huge, with potentially thousands of troops (each one an individual with its own stats) on either side.
+ Spells which can cause massive effects.
Cons:
- Interface can be intimidating to a new player.
- Old-school graphics: functional, but not pretty.
Overall:
+ If you're a fan of this genre, you should buy this game.
If you can get it for 10 dollars or less, it's worth it.

Dominions 4 can be primarily enjoyed in two separate ways.
The first is the single-player experience. I say experience, because the gameplay aspect can be lacking compared to other games that are primarily meant to be played single-player(script based combat, turns being resolved all in one go, no interaction with the AI. Stuff that has to be the way it is because it wouldn't work in a 3 month multiplayer game otherwise)
So why would you play Dominions 4 in single player? For the incredible amount of background lore, or fluff, the game has to offer. There are three separate Eras, each of which has it's own nations(29 for the Early era, 29 for Middle, 23 for Late Era). Now, the beauty of the nations is that each has a very detailed history, which is usually interlinked to other nations both within the era and outside the era.
For instance, the nation of Man(boring name, I know) comes to existance in the Middle Era. It's a nation of knights and witches that live deep in the woods. Quite basic stuff, but they are based on several nations from the Early era. In the Early era, there existed the nation of Marverni, a gallic tribal nation that spread out to the faery land of Tir'na'nog. The fae were driven out, and their magic was stolen by those who would become the witches of Man. The magic of these witches is very similar to that of the fae, but also has aspects of a nearby nation of sea giants that has since gone extinct(In gameplay terms, they share national spells and magic paths). With the fae magic, the witches created a holy order of wardens to protect themselves. During the Late Era, many drastic changes have happened. Magic has fled the lands of Man, and the witches have been replaced by a more secular class of mage-judges, who are some of the only ones that can work magic in the mystically drained land. The wardens of old have lost much of the power the witches had imbued them with, and have had to adapt their tactics in the changing world, turning to the use of crossbows from their old melee-only ways. Most of the nations change in a similar way to this, some die out completely with only remnants of their former nation diffused to other nations, and some new nations arise from nothingness, perhaps containing a smattering of elements from the Early Era, despite showing up in the Late Era.
On the other hand, there's the multiplayer. Where the gameplay was lacking in singleplayer, it's the opposite in multiplayer. It is incredibly deep and satisfying. With so many different nations and hundreds of spells(most of which have a purpose in the game. Though a handful are more or less useless, I think), the different possibilities are quite insane. Perhaps your army is composed of only flying troops, meaning you can fly around the world, striking where the enemy can't defend itself? Perhaps you have spells that can kill enemy commanders, which prevents them from flying around with their armies? Perhaps you have cast a spell of global repercussions which causes the world to be plunged to darkness, where the gold income of every place in the world plummets, unrest increases and battles are fought in pitch black darkness.(quite useful if you use a large amount of undead or you are a cave-dwelling troglodyte). Are your own national troops weak and useless? Well, you can make them more powerful with spells enchanting their strength, or perhaps giving all of them flight during battles, flaming arrows or turning them to mist. Suppose you wanted to summon creatures of legend such as manticores? Perhaps a dead hero you had was dear to you, well you can bring him back as a mummy that causes diseases to anyone nearby! Some may find it useful to craft an artifact sword that causes the temperature on the battlefield to raise, spontaneously combusting troops and causing them to tire out very quickly.  Does your nation lack archers? Why not craft magical bows that shoot a dozen arrows per shot and give a few of them to your commanders, instant ranged ability.
Just keep in mind, Dominions 4 is designed to be played as a slow paced multiplayer game, where you play a turn every few days, so a multiplayer game may last several months. Of course, a singleplayer game is much faster, but since the enemy lacks human ingeniuity, it's far less exciting to play against.

Heretic  is a pretty old game, and the lore isn't explained well in game, so understanind the story takes reading of the old manual and wiki pages. Gameplay wise, it is a fantasy flavored Doom - same sprite based graphics, same semi-primitive 3D Levels, similar weapons, same Midi-based music, same maze like level designs and secrets, well the same game engine. It isn't a "reskin of DOOM" though, it is it's own independent game in which I found pretty fun and has the same visceral enemy destruction and robust, but sometimes maze-like level design. Also, the items you recieve go into your inventory versus being used instantly, so you can save invincibility, invisibility, health potions, and even timed bombs for when you need it, but that also means you have to manage that inventory with scrolling and use keys. You also will find limited items that grant temporary flight for combat and exploration (though is only necessary for a few moments) and the Tome of Power (as mentioned in Heretic lore) that gives your weapons powerful alternate fire modes - which made the game really fun in big fights - more so than classic DOOMs in my opinion.
The start of some episodes are tough due to limited ammo and weapons, so expect to kite and bait enemies, and dodge them all together at times. I enjoyed my experience with the game, but I also found the ending to be underwhelming, which throws dozens of bosses from a previous episode and ends on a cliffhanger for Heretic 2, which is not easy to obtain (pricey on stores or via abandonware sites).
All these years later and this game is still a blast to play. Often overlooked due to the long shadow cast by Doom, it really is  worth every cent!

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

Polarity is a 3-D first person physics puzzle game with the core mechanic of switching "polarities" to progress through the level. In each level there are three data pieces located in hidden or hard-to-reach places that you must collect to finish the game. If you were a fan of the box-juggling of Portal, this game has plenty, as most levels requires you to carry, throw, and place boxes on buttons.
It's a fun little game whose biggest issue is the little. The game is fairly short, and I was able to beat the "story mode" in less than an hour, half of which was going back through the levels to collect all the "data" I missed due to tricky placement. New mechanics are barely added in this short amount of time, meaning each level feels roughly the same. The puzzles weren't challenging enough to help the length, and the story mode is barely a story. The game doesn't really use its core mechanic to its full potential, and it really seems like just a box-and-button puzzle game rather than something fresh and new. The aesthetic is nice.
If you do get this game, get it during one of its sale periods where it goes down to like 19 cents. I do recommend it because it is a nice puzzle game, but it's not all there.

The game's incredibly fast-paced gameplay is what really gets me to rate it a perfect 10. You know, it's tough, writing this as a negative.
Honest truth is, this game gave me the best feeling of being a small being in a grand universe, always feeling like the next corner of space we rounded would show us some unexpected wonder about the nature of things. This is the best existentialism game I've played except for maybe the Talos Principle, and this may be the best depiction of our lonely place in the great expanse that I've ever seen. But I cannot recommend it, as it stands.
What the game absolutely nails in its atmosphere, lore, and wonder, it largely betrays with the simple shell of a RTS model it chooses to employ. Did we not learn our lessons about doomstacks from Civilization IV? For the countless ways that this is the true spiritual successor to Civilization on a grander, space scale (talking to you, Beyond Earth), it's amazing they succumb to these simple flaws in designing a game that is, at the basic level, fun.
The management of your resources, colonies, research, and policies is spot-on, but just like in any multiplayer RTS, all serve as secondary (albeit important and highly necessary) elements to the combat. Most of the intricate and exciting early game land grabs and stage-setting for galactic domination ends up boiling down to a very limited number, or even just one, single space battle where the entirety of one civilization's fleet squares off against the enemy's. The tiny nuanced advantages in balanced fleet compositions (excluding if someone is WAY behind on research, of course) become irrelevant behind "the big number" of fleet power, and once one side starts losing, the snowball just continues into an utter stomp. You cannot control any individual tactics, no formations, it's basically just however the AI decides to use weaponry you've customized, and there rarely appears to be any viable strategy beyond piling every ship you own into a ball and either chasing their ball of ships across the galaxy (if you have a better combat number) or running while you try to amass a bigger ball (if you have a worse combat number).
The rudimentary nature almost akin to a cell phone game just feels so out of place in an otherwise nearly perfect game. It sinks the unique experience into a monotony in almost every match while you wade through the mid- to late-game. Until something is adjusted on these lines, I'm going to have to regrettably recommend against this game.

I discovered Dominions when it was Dom2.  That game was very hard to understand and play.  Dom3 was much, much better and Dom4 (in my opinion) is a modest improvement.  There is a lot to like about this game: building your god (I really like that part), discovering and using magic, and researching some of the over 800 spells.  Not to mention several dozen different nations to play with and each of those in THREE ages (i.e. different ages of the world).  I don't think it's possible to play the same game twice the same way; there's just too much diversity.
It's easy to take this game as a series of battles: win every battle, beat the other god(s) and you win the game.  Wrong!  It is about magic and if you don't utilize magic, you will lose.  That alone makes it a challenging game to understand and play, and win.  I really like that part of the game.
But here's the problem for me:  It is a massively detailed micro-manager game.  You have to check every thing in every  province, every turn, and usually every army (or part of an army) every turn, and anything and everything else in every part of the game and almost every part of the map -- every turn!  If you really, really like that in a game, this is one you must buy.  It is fun, and interesting, and deep and complex...but after a while I find it overwhelmingly tedious.
