I just finished this and. Wow. This game truly is a masterpiece. Every moment of the story is gripping, every second of the combat is enjoyable, and every last character is memorable. By the end of the game, every single spot on the map will remind you of a fantastic moment. The brilliant and creative mind of Yoko Taro and the fun and fast paced combat of Platinum Games make for an experience that will not soon be forgotten.

This is probably the greatest part. An emotional roller coaster that will have you question what it is to be human, while also pushing you forward to uncover every mystery. The game presents you with a fantastic opening right off the bat, only to get better as you play more. Not to mention, there are 5 endings. And by that, I don't mean everything is the same but the ending, I mean it is an entirely new experience that could have been a sequel. The first 2 playthroughs are the prologue, even though they are fantastic in their own right. However those fantastic experiences that already warrant a masterpiece are then absolutely demolished by the gripping story of the next three endings. Every caracter will make you care about them, and your actions will constantly make you question who really is in the right. Not to mention it all leads to (and this coming from someone who's played all three Witcher games, many Telltale games, and Life is Strange) the most difficult decision I have ever made in any game. Period. Also the sidequests are very good. They may seem like tedious fetch quests at first, but they always end on either an extremely somber or joyous note that will most likely make you feel something.
Of course gameplay would be good. This is Platinum Games we're talking about. Really though, this is just more evidence that Platinum is the king of gameplay, with every second being important. You will be gripping your controller in anticipation as you fight off a hoard of machines. This game brilliantly combines bullet hell, hack and slash, and shmup gameplay into one big beutiful package. Not to mention, the leveling system is great, allowiung you to remove parts of your hud to make room for upgrades if you want
Now, keep in mind this isn't as much of a positive as the past two but I do think it's worth noting. Honestly, there isn't much to do in the open world, but that doesn't warrant it a spot in the cons. The reason the open world is a pro, is because every single area holds emotional weight. Because of how the world is used, there is a major event everywhere, and just taking a walk to a quest or something will bring back great memories. This is one of the bonuses of the world being so small, since every spot has a place in your heart.
This game isn't afraid to step outside of the box. This game has top down shmup gameplay, twin stick gameplay, Space Invader esque gameplay, 3rd person hack and slah gameplay, bullet hell gameplay, and even side scrolling gameplay. But  most of you already know about the gameplay variety. However the game has even more variety than that. Variety in playthroughs is immense, with each one feeling like a different game. There is character variety and contrast. And overall, the game just likes to keep you on your feet.
Now where do I begin with this one. Every piece of music in this game helps set the tone perfectly, with the volume set to perfectly fit the type of gameplay you are experiencing. This is one of the only games I've seen credit multiple violinists in the credits. You will find yourself listening to some of these masterful tracks in your free time because they are so fantastic.
While I still prefer the PC version because of the multiple benefits, (Steam, graphics, etc) I do understand that it has problems. One big one is mouse and keyboard support. Serieously, coming form someone who prefers The Witcher 3 with keyboard and mouse, use a controller. Especially since, for some reason, dodging is set to double tap and you can't change it. Seriously. Especially in a game in which you dodge so much, that is just unnacceptable. However this problem goes away when you plug in a controller. Also, there's an awful resolution bug in which 1080p runs as 1080i in fullscreen, but there are many many mods to fix that. Also, this game isn't very well optimized.
Most of the game has a very gray color pallet, and while it does help set the mood, I feel some parts really need some more color. If you look around, you will find quite a few stretched textures, and often texture will pop in out of nowhere. And while this problem would be fixed by turning up draw distance, the graphical options are so limited there really isn't a way to do that.
This is beutiful masterpiece, and aside from a few technical issues, it would be a mistake not to pick this one up, even at full price. (This is my 2nd favorite game of all time)

You que up to join a match and if anyone in the 10 people don't click join that are qued it resets the que and can be up to another 5 min or longer waiting to join. Once you're finally in, if anyone does not pick a person to play as, it resets back to the beginning of your que and the wait starts all over. I had 20 minutes waiting to just join a game. This is rediculous who decided this was a valid way to conduct matchmaking. Thats not where it ends. There seems to be some issue while the match is going where it just freezes for a second and sends you back to the title screen. everything you just did all the time and energy you spend to win or contribute is gone. I understand this is in Beta, I understand it is free to play. I contributed $15 as well as the thousands of other people who play it every day. Invest some of that money into better servers and re-evalute the poorly thought matchmaking. This needs addressed as a top priority. My friends and I enjoy the game and the potential is sitting in the developers laps, they just need to spend a little more time on the keyboards and fix this. Until these issues are addressed, I can;t reccomend this game because it is a good game but I don't want others to be as frustrated as I am with it. If you can sit down and say yes I am willing to waste my day trying to play it only to freeze and have the server crash when you do get to play by all means play the game. I actually have over 1500 hours in the base game and decided I should write my review for Skyrim.
I may be biased since my first open world PC game was Morrowind, and I loved Oblivion as well.
I will keep my review short, but tl dr:
Skyrim is a beautiful game that you can mod almost any aspect of to suit your tastes. It is the most immersive game I ever played, sucks you in and makes you feel a part of the world. There are a few annoying bugs and glitches, and some quests and zones become repetitive, but the vast open world and interesting NPCs keep me playing for hours. The sheer number of quests and content outvalues the price tag.
Pros:
Vast open world
Great soundtrack
Immersive and well thought-out
Lots of content
Mods can add more content, make the game look stunning, and even spice things up when things get boring and repetitive
Many different playstyles
DRAGONS are cool
Many factions to join each with a unique and interesting storyline
You can buy houses and create a family
Many books in game that you can read and most are pretty interesting
Deep lore
Cons:
Bugs and glitches after 7 years :(
Combat is very simple and boring - unless you stealth :P
Most NPCs are forgettable
Quests sometimes get repetitive
Customization not as deep as Morrowing or Oblivion
Feels like there is more hand-holding, although that makes the learning curve less steep
AI is pretty dumb, both follower AI and enemy AI
Final conclusion: This is the best open world single player RPG I have ever played.

If any of you AAA whippersnappers have ever heard one of us old-schoolers groan about how FPS were way more fun in our day and wondered why we would say that, I urge you to give a game like Hexen a try. In this game, you won't have to spend 10 minutes going in and out of cover to shoot three enemies. Nor will you need to press 30 buttons just to be able to shoot and move at the same time. In this game, you go forward, kill♥♥♥♥♥♥ collect items and keys, and find the exit. Simple as. And did I mention you don't have to wait for a checkpoint, and you can just make your own by saving the game at any time from the in-game menu? Revolutionary!!!
(Really...it's like games have DEvolved in this regard over the years!)
Okay, so the graphics are bad by today's standards; for 1994, though, that WAS the standard, and Hexen pulls it off wonderfully. The sound, though, IS great even by modern standards, particularly the groaning and screeching of hidden enemies. The feeling of walking around a cleared room or courtyard HEARING these motherfreakers but not knowing when you're going to run across them provides significantly more tension than any Slender-style 'horror' game (really, if you've ever been in REAL woods at night, Slender shouldn't be the slightest bit scary to you.) And once you DO find them, they are some tough cookies, even at Level 2 difficulty (Level 2 or 3 is ideal for semi-experienced old-school FPS players wanting a challenging but not overtly stressful experience.)
What's more, this is the Shadow of the Serpent Riders edition, which means technically you are getting five games in one, as it contains all the commercially released 'episodes' of Hexen. With eight or so levels to plow through in each episode, this one is sure to keep you playing for a while.
In short, while it does feature outdated graphics and lack the rockin' soundtrack of the original PC Doom, Hexen does everything else extremely right. The setting is both ludicrous and original for the time, mixing two of geekdom's favourite genres (sci-fi and high fantasy), locations are remarkably detailed for 1994, there's plentiful items to collect and weapons to try out, the difficulty is balanced but not overtly easy, and sound design is great. It also expands on the traditional FPS formula of the day by adding light RPG elements, with collectible items that can help you at certain junctions. This does, however, bring up another minor flaw, as at no point in-game are you told what each item does - you'll have to resort to FAQ guides for that, unfortunately. Once you do figure out each item's use, however, they are actively helpful, sometimes rendering previously impossible levels or sections significantly more manageable, thereby actively influencing and enhancing the overall experience.
In short - if you're a graphics snob, require all your titles to be AAA quality, or are only in it for the trading cards, Hexen will not be for you. Anyone simply wanting an enjoyable retro first-person-shooting experience, however, can't go wrong with this one - especially if you manage to get it for pennies, like I did!
Final Rating: 8/10

Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders is a great game for classic Doom fans who are looking for more of the same shooting goodness in a new environment. You have a total of 5 Episodes in the game, each of them with 8 (+1 secret) intense levels of sweet monster destruction.
The gameplay is very similar to Doom 2, but with significant changes, such as Z-clipping (you can walk under and over enemies), ability to look up and down (though limited), and an inventory system that lets you keep items for later use instead of them activating on pick-up, removing the need to avoid walking over items in case you wanted to save them for later.
I played the game on Skill 4 (Thou art a smite-meister) and found the game to be a decent challenge, but felt that it could have done with slightly smaller quantities of ammunition. After the first level or two in each episode, I'd be practically swimming in ammunition no matter how wasteful I got.
I also played the game through the use of GZDoom due to being spoiled by modern day shooters and requiring mouselook (and the ability to use Steam overlay).
Overall, I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys classic FPS games and has yet to try this game out.

I first encountered Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders  as a shareware game, when we bought a new computer featuring Windows 3.11. Although Shareware (the first level, The Docks, was all that you could play) it was one of the games I enjoyed playing, although it regularly gave me frights, with monsters popping out from behind pillars, and only the unidirectional roars to tell me that they "might" be lurking around a corner.
I played it enough to warrant a full purchase via an unlock code, and the game proved to have a great deal of longevity. The stats at the end of each level, gave you feedback on no. of monsters killed, secrets discovered and items found. This lead to a great deal of replaying and backtracking to try and find each little hiding place.
I never really read the manual, and the plot is really inconsequential anyway, this is by no means a narrative driven game, suffice to say your elven race was slaughtered as they refused to believe in the deity of the "Serpent Riders" and were slaughtered as Heretics. You, the sole elven survivor are out to seek revenge.
Today it's legacy is questionable. The genre of Fantasy FPS, is non-existent, instead we have a modern warfare or sci-fi bias that the greater legacy games, Doom, and Quake popularized. Heretic is of course from the same  period. (It uses the Doom Engine). Yet has had far less overall impact on the trend of FPS fantasy, which is rather something of  a pity, as in an oversaturated market, this genre has potential. The only games that might have built from this core concept is of course Dark Messiah of Might and Magic (includes more brawling combat) and the recent Lichdom.
It has not aged well, the lack of resolution (it runs out of DosBox), poor textures and flickering lights may lead to eye strain, but the overall feel of the game is still enjoyable. It has none of the complexity and strategic gaming that later titles show, but it does sport excellent level design and exploration/puzzle mechanics, that aren't so common in modern FPS, as well as gothic interiors, and smooth gameplay.
(Definitely a game to settle down to with some Death Metal on the side!)

"Recommend" isn't a strong enough word for this one.  It's one of my top ten games of all time, and quite possibly one of my top three.
If you like massive TBS games, it's the massive-est--but the size isn't just bloat, it's gameplay.  There are dozens of nations to choose from, and each nation is starkly asymmetrical.  Many strategy games have multiple options for a starting nation that are different more in flavor than in overall strategy.  This game has multiple viable strategies to win, *per nation*.
The nations in question aren't just run-of-the-mill fantasy fare, either.  One of the two company founders is a religion professor, and the nations are based on a wide variety of historical and mythical traditions from around the world.  There's nothing else like it out there.
TL, DR: It's one-of-a-kind.

>thinking you can walk through other peoples lands without consequences
Marveni doesn't care that you're a coward who's being chased around by another nation- he cares that you just stole his gold, maybe gems, and forced him to deploy some people to take the province back.
Imagine if Napoleon Bonaparte showed up in your kitchen, drank all your milk, and informed that he would be occupying the couch for a month because he was scared of the British. Also, in this scenario, Napoleon Bonaparte is one of 7 people you need to kill to become God, and if left alive he will inevitably turn on you.

Dominions 4 probably presents the broadest array of distinct options I've ever seen in a strategy game, on top of a huge pile of mythologically inspired lore. And not just the western mythology stuff you've seen a million times either. You can summon a winged monkey-demon that wants to "gobble up the sun and plunge the world into an eternal slumber". He plunges the entire battlefield into darkness whenever he shows up. You can rain sacred flying jaguar demons on your enemies, free titans trapped in tartarus and nurse them back to health, and literally cause a zombie apocalypse. I've got a weakness for this kind of stuff, but the game is large enough you're bound to find a nation that appeals to you.
Not to say the game is without problems. The game's breadth makes it almost inaccessible, and as a game goes on, it increases your workload of fiddly micromanagement. Want to find errands for 30 wizards every turn? Dominions is the game for you. The game's mechanics are unnecessarily complex, and incompletely described in the long manual. The AI is almost non-existent, mostly useful for testing out tactics on the most basic level. The game is not especially balanced, and there are some awkward results of the game's committment to mythological versimilitude. (Women, across the board, have 1 less point of strength than men of the same group. Mechanically, this is largely insignificant, but it is still stupid.)
These problems are significant, and if you aren't entranced by Dominions 4's unique qualities, I don't recommend it. If you are entranced, this is, as far as I know, the only game of its kind.

Disclaimer: This is my personal feeling  (and pardon any rambling I may do here) about the game and various features in it, and is not meant as any kind of insult to those who are hard core fans of the game. Nor is it meant to particularly entice new comers to the game. While I clicked the yes button I really wish there was a "maybe" option as it is not for everyone.
Intro:
If you have played Dom 3 you may think you have played Dom 4 after starting it up. The interface is pretty much identical and much of the game is the same (with old school sensibilities about interface, so not much flash). However, many things that were fun for me, and perhaps too awesome (I don't think so but meh) were nerfed/toned down.
Items are no longer all that awesome if you focus and invest all your effort in forging. In fact they are barely worth the effort imho but you can still get some fun things out of them. Just don't expect them to be very effective. In particular the items that produced gems, no longer do so for all uses. They may give you something called "Temporary" spell gems which can be used in battle but not with rituals. And much of the skill enhancing items are either gone, nerfed or very much more expensive to make.
Id say you are better off not making items at all (as tempting as it may be when you realize that some items still seem fairly powerful.) If you do be prepared to be underwhelmed by the end result.
Spells & researching them were left largely untouched except for minor nerfs here and there to make them more balanced.
On Balance:
I will say I am not a proponent of fine tuning/balancing games. Particularly ones that are as successful already as the Dominions series is. However if you are going to do it, don't take away fun things unless you are adding in something to replace them. It is too easy to make a game all hard edges (and difficult even on easy mode, and forget the various coolnesses that may have attracted some people in the first place.) My $0.025 anyway.
Does Illwinter do this with this game? Yes and no. Some of the new strategic possibilities with disciples look fun. However,  the practice is tricky and is probably best suited for multiplayer. (Full disclosure: Which is something I have never done with any of the dominions games. I like playing 4x-likes solo/single player mode for the most part.)
I like and dislike the Thrones of Ascension mechanism. I like it because it allows you to play in a different manner than the old victory points system. And each throne adds something to the game though you may not enjoy all of the effects of controlling one. I dislike it because the AI at least on the non-cheating (impossible etc) modes does not seem to know how to properly exploit the thrones, only capturing one if it happens to be within easy grasp.
But since the whole goal of the game changes from "conquer your enemies  and make them cry (or turtle up if thats your strategy)" to: "conquer this tough independently held province and do it quickly to win before your opponents can mount their own campaigns against", it does not make sense for the AI to still go into conquer every territory mode (standard behavior).
Also once youve captured a throne you have to use it (with a prophet or your pretender) and make sure to hold it. Independants can and will recapture neglected provinces as inexplicable events. (You don't get to see troop movement or anything, as a warning first.) Which makes the game more and less interesting. More because you have to pay attention to defenses perhaps well inside your territory that you might otherwise neglect, and less because the same. Micromanagement is ever the bane of the 4x player. Yes it is important but it make the game drag to the point of wanting to go play tiddly winks or something else equally inane.
God Making:
Perhaps still the best part of the game is being able to set up the game in any way you like. Hard? Easy? Large? Small? Make your own maps. Make your own deity. Choose a form that is all combat or go with many schools of magic and master the arcane. Lots of choices is a good thing and you get a lot of that here.
Modding:
You can still mod it, though it seems that some of the modding rules have changed. And I would not begin that task unless you really want to see it through and have some actual ideas. Do it because you have a story you want added, not just to up the power level of some item, nation or diety. Or whatever but be warned that once you look under the hood you may feel less enthusiasm for the magic of the game ever after.
Graphics:
The graphics are unsurprisingly primative but adequate. Sprite based battles still look haphazard and may require some getting used to, to interpret properly. (Why DID that priest suddenly lose morale and run?? You may never really know...)
Overall:
The most disappointing thing for me is that as a solo game Dominions 4 has no real innovation, only small refinements on prior editions, which don't really rise to the expectations I had when I saw it was out. As they say: "Caveat Emptor" but I really expected more for some reason. Yes I bought it earlyish and didn't do my due dillegence (feh at brand loyalty) on checking other reviews but the product is what it is. Illwinter does not make bad games. So no matter how you feel about it, it will be a game to play not just one to sit on the shelf of buyer's remorse (Because steam never refunds you anything, ever.) You should still get fun out of it.
Buy it if you want a fantasy RPG-4x to play. It is challenging and the UI can be a little inscrutible at first but read the manual and you'll be fine. There is a community and sites to help you learn the strategy of the game. You may even be sucked into the multiplayer version or the modding community.

Don't be rebuked by the simplistic interface, behind it is a fascinating strategy game. There is a learning curve of course, especially if you want to master said interface (many advanced commands to ease your play are keyboard shortcuts).
But really what matter is the concept, if you like TBS games it's really worth trying it.

Polarity is like a simpler and shorter version of Portal, but that doesn't necessarily make it a bad game or a relentless copy of the game which obviously inspired it, as there are plenty of concepts and ideas that make this title stand on its own. To begin with, there are no actual portals, as the game relies on its blue-red polarity concept to solve puzzles, allowing you to change your polarity in order to pass obstacles and reach otherwise inaccessible areas. As that alone would become boring, companion cubes show up just at the right time to throw in the extra element that allows certain levels to present you with challenging puzzles, without over-complicating them to the point where you don't know what to do next. Cubes, just as yourself have polarities as well, however their polarity can only change in special areas, forcing you to use what you have at your disposal in order to solve puzzles, and since you can only summon a limited number of cubes, the solution will always pop up once you've exhausted all other options, making puzzles challenging, but not unsolvable. Unlike Portal, Polarity doesn't have a background story, and there is nothing to tie in one level to the next one, making your entire adventure feel without purpose, especially since the single player campaign can be finished in less than an hour.
The gameplay is simplistic and accessible to anyone, as it only requires basic character and camera movements and control buttons for switching polarity and interacting with cubes and other objects, but aside from that logic is the only tool you need in Polarity. Puzzles are challenging, but they never get to the point where they become hard or unsolvable without consulting a guide, mostly because the game will be over before the level design reaches that point. There are a lot of interesting features packed in the final levels, and there was definitely room for a lot more afterwards, but unfortunately none of those features reached their full potential, as the level design remains basic, even when there are more elements involved, as the solution will always be obvious once you take a look around you. The polarity switch is the game's greatest strength as it creates opportunities for clever and unique puzzles, but once again this feature never goes beyond that basic gate, making it feel unused in most cases. There are some interesting puzzles to have fun with, but even so it shouldn't take you longer than four minutes to solve each one, as you will always find the solution to each one once you've failed on your first attempt and realize the answer is the other way around.
The game looks okay for what it is, however even with the test chamber look inspired by Portal, there was room for a few details to differentiate one level from another, but in this case all the levels look similar and the only thing to set them apart one from another is the placement of the objects required to solve the puzzle. The visual effects are basic, and once again for what this game is, they do the job, even though in certain areas better effects would've made a difference in the sense of power the game tries to give you by interacting with its objects.
There are no voices in here since there is no background story, narration or characters, leaving the entire experience up to the level design and the puzzles, but the lack of such things only makes the game seem shorter than it already is. The sound effects are basic and repetitive, as you will still hear the same interaction sounds over and over again; the soundtrack is limited and even though it is in theme with what the game offers, you will eventually grow tired of hearing that same tune all the time.
Apart from the single player campaign, there is a Co-Op campaign which consists of a collection of levels designed for two players and a Bonus campaign which can be accessed once you've finished the main missions; all that added up and you've still got only 2-3 hours worth of content.
Polarity is a fun game to play if you fancy the genre, however don't expect this to have anything else to offer besides its gameplay concepts, and even with that in mind there is not much to play; after all, this is a 5€ title.

Heretic is possibly the most overrated game I know of. It's above average, good but far from great.
The main reason for this is simply put the level design. Possibly a fourth of my playtime consisted of aimlessly wandering around looking for what opened or what switch to push, a design choice decidedly "old-school", but nonetheless bad. DOOMs level design is infinitely better, because it will rarely (if ever) leave you scratching your head, wondering where to go next.
The weapons (with the exception of a few) are copies of weapons from DOOM, they just feel clunkier and are less satisfying to use. Enemies can usually also be correlated to some rough equivalent in DOOM, but most of them have been changed a little bit. The worst example of this is the Iron Lich (most similar to cacademons), whose whirlwind attack (depending on the situation) can be completely unfair, or completely useless. The best example of this are the Disciples of D'Sparil, who I can't even think of a correlation for in DOOM.
All that said, the art, music and sound in this game are all really great and create a forboding, dark and gothic atmosphere. If you're a fan of shooters from this era, you'd be a fool to miss Heretic. I would however recommend giving episode 4 and 5 a miss unless you're a masochist. They're not difficult in a fun way, it's just an excruciatingly slow grind of trial and error, possibly only surpassed by the likes of Final DOOM. If you don't like FPS of this era, this game has no chance of winning you over (I would recommend DOOM as a starter, it's still a great game).

TIP:
Use the Dosbox keymapper (CTRL+F1) to remap keys.
Default is arrow keys (not WASD) while left and right arrow are TURNING , not strafing, which is unlike newer shooters like Quake.
The defaults for strafing are comma and dot so just remap them to A and D.
Note that it also would affect the menu.
Also if you don't feel comfy with tiny windowed resolution (if you play windowed), navigate to the game folder in the Steam folder (just google or find for yourself where it sits) and edit heretic.conf to use windowresolution=800x600 or something similar. Heretic was the first licensed Doom engine game. And... it shows it's limitations at times. Both from a stylistic point of view and the technical side of things.
Doom was a lot of things, but above all else the game was very polished and it felt inspired. From it's soundtrack to it's enemy design, everything felt like it needed to be there. And it genuinely felt like the developers all had a central vision they shared for what the game eventually became.
Heretic on the other hand feels like it's stuck in Doom's shadow. The game mechanics feel far too similar to Doom and the aesthetic of the game, while impressive for the time did not age well. All of the weapons in Heretic feel more or less like reskins of Doom weapons. Apart from the graphics it feels like the same basic game but with a much less interesting aesthetic and soundtrack.
The things I appreciate Heretic more are for it's historical context like how it was one of the first FPS games to come bundled with online multiplayer support, how it had a very large custom map community and how it serves as a prequel to the HeXen series. But I really only recommend Heretic on it's own if you're a Doom fanatic such as myself, since I unfortunately see the game as very forgettable.

Ever wished Doom had a fantasy setting? Wish granted!
If you like retro shooters, you'll most likely enjoy this game.
You'll probably want to use a source port for it though.

"Heretic" is essentially a medieval fantasy version of "Doom" with a few minor (and major) improvements, such as the ability to aim/look up and down to a certain degree (there's no autoaim in this game, so mastering this skill is essential) and a basic inventory system, allowing you to carry several items which can help your progress. The original release featured 3 episodes, only one of which was playable as shareware. This is the expanded edition which was released commercially in stores following the success of "Doom". This new version gives you 2 additional episodes, bringing the total up to 5.
Graphics - bright, vivid and colourful, which is a stark contrast to the realistic and disquieting look of "Doom" - the level design is well done and the enemies, items and characters represent what they are meant to represent. With that said, it CAN get creepy and even scary at times, so this game hasn't completely lost its horror atmosphere genesis.
Sound - the musical score by Kevin Schilder is limited but at the same time varied in terms of atmosphere, mood and genre, ranging from enigmatic to hectic to ominous. Episodes 1 and 2 have their own music, while Episode 3 uses recycled tracks from the first two episodes except for two levels, which have their own unique musical pieces not heard in any other stage. The music from the last two episodes are the same as from the first two episodes, in the same running order. The sound effects are minimalistic and represent the most basic form of auditory feedback, while the enemies' noises can enhance or ruin the atmosphere, depending on your mood.
Gameplay - as mentioned above, the inventory system and the ability to look/aim up and down breathes new life into the ageing Doom engine. The overall play style is almost identical to that of "Doom" - find keys to unlock doors, shoot on sight and escape to the next level. One stage of each episode has two exits, one of which will take you to a secret level - you'll have to look hard for it. Using the inventory system is crucial to survival as certain items will work in your favour, while others will have humorous effects, making the game significantly easier. You will lose your inventory upon completion of a level, so don't be afraid to use away your items.
Presentation - you are greeted with a new version of the "Heretic" title screen upon starting the game. During the intermissions between levels, you are shown the time you took to beat the present level, amount of enemies killed on that level, items obtained and secrets discovered - a feature copied directly from "Doom". On the first three episodes, you are also shown a map indicating your progress from stage to stage - this feature is absent on the last two episodes, considering they were only included to make the game a commercial re-release (the original version was only available via mail-order).
Conclusion - the two extra episodes may or may not take your fancy since they add nothing new to the formula (I have mixed feelings about them myself) unless you want a new challenge (they were made for gamers who had mastered the original "Heretic" trilogy and wanted something harder), and it's a much more enjoyable game than "Doom" when you take in the extra features this game has to offer.
Final Score - 5 out of 5 stars.

Dominions 4 is an in-depth, involved, immersive game that harkens back to the good old days of turn-based fantasy empire gaming. Tasked with taking the place of the now absent creator of the universe, your character (known as a Pretender God) seeks to become the new, true God. You must build armies, research a huge range of spells, and vanquish rival Pretenders to claim the ultimate prize in creation.
I really, really like this game. It gives me a warm fuzzy feeling of nostalgia with the graphics, sound effects and just how much depth and substance is here. There's no glitz and dazzle with funky graphics to glamour you. Their are hundreds of spells in several different schools (such as Air, Earth, Fire, Water and darker paths like Death and Blood magic) which can be researched and used to advance your claim to Godhood. Your character can be anything from a wizened old crone, to a titan of the underworld, to a dragon, cyclops, divinely-created bull and many, many more things. This game is worth the price-tag, once you have this you don't need any other strategy games anymore, because this one has enough content to keep you going for a long time. It has a steep learning curve, so be prepared for that, but all the best games are the ones that take a while to get the hang of. Highly recommended to anyone who loves in-depth, fantasy turn-based strategy games.

For years i have been waiting for a solid multiplayer vietnam shooter (BF:V was allright though) and im glad that Tripwire delivered!
Weapons:
Basically, RS2:Vietnam plays the same as its predecessors but with more modern firearms. This means that every player has access to fullautomatic and semiauto weapons with even the most basic classes, making the gunplay much faster then before. As a nice throwback, the VC/NVA even has access to the good ol Mosin! The pump action shotgun and flamethrower from RS1 make their return in the form of their counterparts used in the cold war era, and the NVA/VC has access to the series' new double barreled shotguns. Fortunately, RS2:Vietnam does away with stat & weapon unlocks seen in the previous game, and offers all weapons and their variants from the get go, provided you selected the right class. The only unlocks are in the form of character looks, but doesnt change the way its played. (except US might confuse you for a VC/NVA guy faster if you run around with just your pants)
Gametypes:
The gamemodes were also changed up abit. The popular Territory mode makes a return, which consists of capturing or defending 1 or more capzones. When they are capped, the game moves on to the next (set of) objective(s) untill all the zones are captured, or the attacker runs out of time, or either team runs out of units. For some maps, RS2:Vietnam introduces the Suppremacy mode, which has all capzones readily available. However, capzones need to be connected if your team wants to score with them. A capzone can be sealed off if the enemy captures ground inbetween 2 zones of yours. Thus your team wont get any points from that capzone. As you can imagine, this gametype will cause more ambushes and can turn into a mess quickly if not coordinated properly. (for example, capturing your enemies first zone makes them pay hard if they dont get it back quick!)
Benefits per side:
No tanks (yet?) but RS2:Vietnam does offer new vehicles in the form of helicopters. These are all pilotable by certain playerclasses. There is the common "Huey" troop transport chopper, the scouting "Loach" (which can also dish out some bullethail punishment along the way) and the vicious "Cobra" attack helo, raining down hell on targets. As a infantry class unit, the game lets you spawn in a Huey, and this makes the Huey a very versatile tool for ambushes in Suppremacy. Aircraft are only available to the US (for now?) but the VC/NVA also have some of their own tricks up their sleeves. Like the Japanese army in Rising Storm 1, VC/NVA have the ability to place traps. Think about tripwires, landmines, punji traps... all of them are ideal for tunnels and tight places. Speaking of tunnels, the VC/NVA have the upper hand there, where aircraft cant spot/hit them. VC/NVA might carry less ammo in some cases, but are also free to use all their weapons in these tunnels, whereas the heavy geared US troops cannot, except for their handguns. VC/NVA also become invisible for reconplanes when staying still for a while, indicated by a "jungleleaves effect" at the edges of the screen. On the US side, squadmembers can spawn on their squadleaders, just like in previous entries. But the VC/NVA squadleaders have a different system. They dig tunnels, were squadmembers can spawn. This gives VC/NVA squadleaders the oppertunity to play more aggresively then their US counterparts, as long as they keep the tunnels up. The tunnels will stay untill certain objectives change, or the US flushes them out. Of course, firesupport also makes its return, with US getting the fearsome napalm and VC/NVA getting mixed artillery barrages. US also gets the "Spooky", which is a gunship loaded with miniguns that, much like the other forms of firesupport, lays down a killzone. In this case, with hails and hails of bullets. But like the recon plane and pilotable aircraft, these can be countered by the VC/NVA's air defense ability if timed well.
Rough edges:
The game however is abit rough around the edges. Trying to shoot over cover might make you hit the cover instead, and the bipod system really needs better detection for setting up. Supremacy can also be pretty messy REAL QUICK if your team does not have a good commander. My biggest gripe however is the amount of content. The maps are fun, but theres only 5, and 3 more which are reserved for small amounts of players. The lack of a campaign mode seen in the previous game also makes this a bit barebones at the moment, resulting in almost every map having US attack, and VC/NVA defend. However, Tripwire already added 3 new variants of existing maps and have 3 planned new weapons and along with the community, they will be adding more content in the future.
Now thats alot of text, but to sum it up:

Woah. So... lemme begin.
I have a lot to say about Loadout.
First.
HOLY MOLY A FREE GAME WITH NICE CARTOONY GRAPHICS AND A GIMMICK THAT WORKS!? AND DOESN'T HAVE MICROTRANSACTIONS EXCEPT FOR CHARACTER CUSTOMISATION?
Too awesome.
Second:
This game is pretty unique. Its graphics are cel-shaded cartoonyish, in a similar format and setting to Borderlands 1 and 2, and Loadout is a third person over the shoulder shooter. It's vaguely reminiscent of UT and other great arena games in terms of its damage, but where this game REALLY shines, is its unique gimmick of crafting your own weapons. I have barely scratched the surface, but pretty much every gun I've used or generated has been viable but not overpowered.
That said, Loadout suffers from a few things.
Given it is so early on, the bots in Loadout seem intolerably dumb while also having sixth senses and near-aimbot level accuracy - they stop to taunt after a kill, even if they are under fire from five directions, but if they catch you unawares you are utterly boned. They can hit you across the map with any hitscan weapon without trying, and their sniping skills are easily MLG level.
Coupled with the young community (in age and maturity both) you'll frequently be getting angry kids in chat, and people disconnecting mid game. That's not really the dev's fault, at least.
All told, it's a good fun game that I can recommend, as it's free, not microtransaction heavy like SOME other free steam games (looking at you, practically everything on that list) and is easy to pick up and set down.

I'm a bit speechless about this game... One things keeps coming to mind tough, and it's what another reviewer said: when you step away from this game, you keep playing it in your mind as if it's something real and urgent that you need to get back to and deal with. In one way that's not good when you have real life problems that need taking care of. On the other hand, that really says something about the depth and attention to detail of a game, not to mention the playablilty, mechanics, UI, graphics, music, sounds, all that — all of it is there in Stellaris. But so much more that I've never experienced in a game before. Exciting twists in the political sphere, unexpected events that set you back or force you to rethink your strategy, adapt to an ever-changing galaxy, fluxuating moods and opinions. You come into the game with certain ethics and politcal leanings, but later on you might need to let go of those and change your methods in order to survive and grow your empire.
Normally I would have reloaded a game several times to avoid a bad outcome or make a different choice. I tried that in this game only to find out there wasn't much I could do to avoid the consequences of my decisions. I had to learn to take the bad with the good. And now I find it more enjoyable to keep playing when things don't go your way. You are able to recover after different kinds of defeats. This is one of the most attractive aspects of the game. It's not over when you think it's over.
For example, war demands are limited and a hostile empire cannot take you over completely in one attempt (if you've grown large enough). A lost war is in principle only a lost battle. A period of cease-fire lets you rebuild what you have left and rethink your strategy. If you were vassalized or dominated, you can claim your independence when you are strong enough. But if that's not possible you can choose to fight for your idependence. Even if you are significantly weaker than your overlord, guerrilla tactics can still cause them to give in and cede territory. It's very well done! It's like the developers took all the nuances of our politically fragmented world and crammed them into Stellaris. This game would be very educational to students of history, politics or economics.
So I can really understand what that other reviewer meant. When you stop playing, you don't really stop. Your empire becomes a part of you. I don't recommend this game for people who love 4X-type games but lack self-control and discipline. XD

While I enjoyed the game for the most part, there were some issues about it that did not impact my enjoyement of the game.
First let's start with the positives.
Gosh! Let me just say that this game has an AMAZING sound track, wether you're trottling along in the desert, forest or city, there is a distinct sound for each area that is both original and familiar. With soothing melodies to the inspiring and assonant sounds, it is truly great.
The combat is fun, while a bit repetitive and heavily influenced by the level of the MC, it has enough diversity that it did not tire me for the entiry of the game.
As mentionned before, this game is very diversified in terms of location. Although it is weird that a dense forest is seperated from a dry desert by a little mountain range, the diffirent sights are there.
Story wise, it is very thoughtful and not damaging for those whom haven't played the previous Nier games. There are some nods here and there, but none that would impact the story.
(***Side note, there are multiple endings to the game that are accessible by the same way a NG+ works, so the first ending is just a taste of the actual story).
As for the characters... Let's just say that the japanese love for the female body is a full display here, for the lower part at least.
Here is now a bit about what I disliked.
The pc performance is not the best It could be, as it is a port. The frequent pop-ins where somewhat aggravating (Oh what a surprise! This tree gets more and more leaves as I get closer and closer!).
While the areas are diverse, I have the feeling that there are under utilised. With just a couple visits to each area at best, I would've prefered a less diverse but more dense set of territories to explore.
As for exploring, the game has a lot of invisible walls, I didn't mind them as much, but it is still something to point out as some places need noticibly longer detours even though a small cliff seperates the two area.
While the story could be enjoyed by many, I personnaly felt that the revelations that were told to the player did somewhat made the game for me a bit less enjoyable.
All and all, I enjoyed the game and I recommend people to play it.

I'm kind of saddened by this game. After the wonderful Armored Princess, Crossworlds, and North King's Bounty games, Legions comes in with not much changed graphically. What they have changed, though, is that it is now Free to Play. While I am fine with this in general, this is one of those F2P changes that feels wrong given what the game is about. In the past games, you could in theory stack your army with very powerful units (although a low number since your character level and thus "Leadership" is low) if you won early battles and knew where to recruit. Replacing this deep and interesting mechanic are paid "Starter Packs", which are not nearly as diverse or interesting as a custom crafted army, or you can buy Booster Packs or units with real money.
Even this state of affairs could have been remedied if I had some early access to a wide variety of units, some of which would be the higher tier units. This is simply not the case almost 10 hours into the game. I am stuck either rolling the 2-3 strongish units (even though my Leadership could support 6-7), or having to constantly spend gold on a very sparse selection of troops to replace heavy losses from crappy troops. I mean, I shouldn't have to buy Archers as my only replenishable ranged choice. At least open it up so I can recruit any low level archer.
I really hope the devs go back, do a proper update of the engine, and release a game for $20 and remove the game killing mechanics that support the F2P model. It just doesn't work for King's Bounty.
You're better off buying the earlier games.

I never played the first Saints Row. So jumping straight into Saints Row 2, I wasn't sure what to expect but one of my friends said it was amazing to play in 2 Player Mode.
He told me it was a Grand Theft Auto clone that was actually fun to play. Having just bounced off Grand Theft Auto 4 hard, I decided to give this a try and I can happily say this is one of the best 2 player games I've ever played both for the fun shooty shooty gameplay or the huge number of bugs that can take you completely by surprise.
The title screen didn't fill me with much hope. Music consisting of angry men telling me how much they love to "shoot up" their significant others and any people they seem to be on disagreeable terms with. My hopes started low. GameSpy didn't help matters either. Did people still have to forward ports in 2009?
But then wow... we got it working... and there is this huge unknown city to explore! with a friend! And we can run over old ladies in golf buggies!
The Grand Theft Auto'ness of the game shines through from the start. You start off having just recovered from the events of Saints Row 1. You get the chance to customize your character in a ludicrously huge number of ways and, after an escape from a prison island, are then free to explore this huge city. It is then your mission to rebuild the "Third Street Saints" by completing a number of increasingly dangerous missions, taking out rival gang members and running over old ladies in sports cars.
Luckily, you don't have to have played the first game to enjoy playing the second one. The plot of the first game is brought up frequently in conversation during the first few hours of the game though so if you haven't played the first, you can feel a bit left out of the loop at times.
Stillwater, the name of the city you have to take over, is full of opportunity for any low life street thug and you better get acquainted with them; Side missions such as drug trafficking, escorting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and the like will give you "Respect", the more respect you have, the further you can advance in the plot.
Some of these missions are fantastic. Insurance fraud is one of the best, which involves you and your friend diving in front of traffic in order to rack up money. The insane physics system the game has allows you to pull off some insane stunts too. There is no shortage of side missions to do in this city and all are well thought out and executed.
The side missions increase in difficulty as you complete them all the way up to Level 6 and you earn prizes for completing them which can be an incentive to do them.
The main plot is OK. If you are familiar with crime sandboxes like this one, you should know what to expect from this. The main place where the game shines is in its gameplay and the bugs that come along with it.
Bugs can range from simple physics bugs, falling through the world into a bottomless void, not being able to enter cars if too many people want to get into the same car, cutscene bugs and finishing missions and ending up half a mile in the ocean for no reason! They are just some of what can happen when playing (at least in co-op anyway, single player I haven't touched)
Just play this game with a friend over your preferred VOIP client of choice. This game is so much more entertaining when you do. It is worth the hassle of setting up. You'll get a good 40 hours of entertainment out of it.
This game has set my hopes up for Saints Row 3. Saints Row 2 is grounded enough but plays with tongue firmly in cheek. The seriousness of the characters contrast with the wackiness of the game world to create quite the experience. Just grab a friend and enjoy it.

Heretic: Shadow of the Serpent Riders is a fantasy First Person Shooter by Raven Software that came out in 1994 and uses Doom engine. Yes, it's Doom-like shooter set in fantasy. Awesome mix. Plus inventory.
Shadow of the Serpent Riders is a special patched release of a game that brings it to 1.3 version, thus adding two more additional episodes. No new game content like weapon or monsters or textures, just new levels. Think of Ultimate Doom.
Now, let's tip apart the way that game was handled on Steam. Well. At least they brought the most full version of the game here. And it uses DosBox, which is usually a good thing until you find out how badly id Software configures them for Steam.
The game will lag at full screen, so you want to go to game directory and edit heretic's conf file to make it use "opengl" for "output" setting.
Game's option like music device and controls is once again isn't easily accessed. On good side, they didn't remove Setup.exe this time around, unlike Doom games on Steam. So you have to open game directory, drag setup.exe onto dosbox.exe and then configure it as you want.
Storyline of a game is quite simple. Well, it has a lot of written in manual, but main idea and amount of plot in game is minimal.
Your hero is elven hero, who's name is Corvus. Elven race, guardians of the Pathoris world and keepers of Tome of Powers, were proclaimed as heretics, when Dragon Riders came to conquer this world. With two Dragon Riders leaving for the other worlds, the remaining Dragon Rider, D'Sparil, unleashes horde of monsters through portal after Elves manage to wipe out all of the human armies of the world. Most of the elves were killed, monsters took Tome of Powers for themselves and you are one of the lone survivors. Your journey will begin at the City of the Damned.
Somebody will get murdered in the end.
The additional episodes 4 and 5 have excuse plot of "portal didn't lead you to home, so enjoy the world destroyed by Dragon Riders and the home of D'Sparil".
Presentation-wise the game is quite awesome looking and sounding for it's time. Yes, Doom engine. But art-style-wise, Heretic presents the world that is dark fantasy yet very colorful, with great contrast. Setting is awesome, you get to wield a magical crossbow that is equalient to shotgun. While Episode 2 is a least interesting looking one, taking place in brown caves with lava, until it gets less dull with inclusion of ice in later level, Episode 3 brings an original setting of a underwater shrine and buildings. Even water in this game has that artsy look to it.
Music is great too. With medivel feel, it's not afraid to use modern instruments. Well, instruments of MIDI and Soundblaster. Most of them are melodic and catchy. Cathedral track will send chill down your spine for sure.
Gameplay itself is, surprise, Doom-like. You search and explore mazes at the running speed, finding keys and opening lcoked doors, pressing switches and discovering secret areas, shooting down monsters or rather rushing past them.
You will shoot down red flying gargolues, mummies, armor knights that throw axes at you, and dark wizards of D'Sparil, who will turn your blood cold with their backward speach that sounds like silly phrases. You will also deal with respawning "explosive barrel"-like things, will push yourself against streams of water and wind and will encounter bosses. Which are your standard FPS bosses. Being tough enemies that you will start encountering more often in later episodes. So not too amazing.
Though, unlike most FPS, it does do something good: There are no enemies who use hitscan against you. What it means is that any damage in the game can be avoided, giving it more arcade-like quality. If forget that it still makes you run over damaging acid like Doom does.
There are seven weapons of magical nature. Shotgun-like crossbow, Rocket Launcher-like Pheonix Rod, Plasma-gun-like Hellstaff. With most of them shooting projectiles, they feel slightly too similiar to each other in use. But thankfully, game introduces Tome of Power.
Tome of Power is a item power-up that you will find through levels. By using it through inventory you will power-up your weapons for a limited time. It doesn't just make them stronger, it also gives additional properity for them, making them even more amazing. For example, mace, the final weapon, stops sucking hard. Hellstaff will make a hot magic rain appear over where the projectile collided. Gaunlets, the game's chainsaw, will start to heal you as well.
Inventory is another addition to gameplay. You will get to collect various helpful items that you can use it anytime. It could be Hourglass who work as timed bomb and aren't much of use, or healing potion, or invincibility ring, or, as said, Tome of Power. Not related to inventory, you also will sometime find armor, but it's quite a rare thing.
There is one important thing to be said about inventory: When you move to the next level, you will retain only one quanity of each item. You will also lose item that allows you to fly around. I am pretty sure that it may sound like a bad thing for some players. But I think it was a good idea. Most of us are used to stockpile tons of items so we could rush bosses down. With system like that, you should feel free to actually have fun using additional items during normal gameplay, you will lose them for no good otherwise.
Last thing I should note is difficulty of additional episodes. Yes, episode 4 and 5 are harder. They are also more of same. And yes, the final level has eight Maloutaurs. But first levels of each of those two episodes deserve a special mention, as they will require you to think fast, use items effectively, avoid enemies you don't want to fight with in order to survive. It was really fresh challenge, at least on Normal difficulty. Got simpler after that though, as you gain more items in process.
But with all the positive things I said, I have to be honest, it didn't become favourite FPS. It's hard to explain why. But you see, the game just doesn't "click" like Doom does. It just doesn't. I am not sure what it lacks. There is something in game feel that it doesn't have. Perhaps there should have been more common enemies that die bloodily. Or maybe it's the projectiles nature of weapons not being comparable to shotgun and rocket launcher. But yes, it lacks something, hard to say.
Heretic is an awesome FPS and yes, it's a Doom clone. But it's an awesome Doom-clone, perhaps bettering Doom itself for some people.

I make it no secret that DOOM is my favorite game ever. I guess it's because it's the game I grow up with it and I find all the games of the series to be good. While I do love it, it's nice to see some people look at that game and not only make a good DOOM clone, but decided to add to it and make it better. So yes, I'm saying this is good already. Now let me explain as best I can.
Story
It's a 90's shooter so there not much to talk about. From the synopsis from the DOOM wiki, three sorcerers called the Serpent Riders came and people started to worship their awesomeness. except for the elves who find the powerful monsters very suspicious. When two of the riders left, the remaining one gets his cult to hunt them down. As the world gets destroyed, one man decides to stand up and kill the wizard. At least it's a fantasy setting and not with massive guns for a change.
Gameplay
It's DOOM with a few new things so lets talk about those: For starters you have an inventory to store items like health packs or invincibility rings, which allow to use them when you need to, unlike DOOM when it's used when you touch them. The weapons are mostly the same from DOOM except no shotgun or BFG, but one power-up called the Tome of Power allows you to use a secondary firing mode, such as turning your lightning gaulents into a life draining weapon or turning you chaingun equal into a weapon that shots multiple mines on impact. So we have a inventory and weapon modes. What else is new. Oh, you can FLY!! But it's only used to find secrets.
The enemies are also a step up from DOOM. These guys are designed to kill. We start with some flying imps and golems that just scratch you, then we meet guys that throw stuff, then ones that shot three balls at the same time and then the first guys start shooing fireballs, and so on. And that's not talking about the bosses which are a league of their own. These are some of the hardest bosses I've seen in a shooter and freak me out whenever I see some. Sure the Cyderdemon was cool but he's nothing compare to the Maulotaur with his giant hammer, fire attacks and charge attacks.
If there's any gripes I have with the game is that the levels have a pattern. What I mean is that it's yellow key, green key, blue key in any level in that order. This cause the levels to be dull after a while.
Presentation
Music is okay. there are some good tracks here, but they're nothing compare to anything from DOOM and start to sound the same after a while. The art design is mainly brown and grey but there's also a lot of blue, especially later in the game when we get to the underwater lair.Speaking of which, the Serpent Rider is everywhere. you constantly see his statues, his picture and symbol wherever you go.
Also, this is one of the goriest games I've played. Almost every enemies blows into tiny bits when kill. Sure other games have some prettying graphic kill animations but I could still recognize the corpse.
Verdict
It's a good DOOM clone with several improvements. If you love DOOM I recommended giving it a try.

I like this game a-lot. I think an enormous amount of work was put into the development of this game. This is really like Star Trex in so many ways but with more flavor, excitement and options.

However, even on normal if you put the A.I. up to 21 competitors, it does seem at times that more than dealing with two enemies at one time is too much or it was for me.
I felt compelled, that I had to always use cheats just to keep up and expand my empire in various ways.
I never felt I could take on so many enemies at once.
I am an older gamer now I suppose. I grew up with similar but an older collection of conquering games where you could gradually build up your forces and defend yourself against certain enemies while doing so and then carefully and strategically attack your enemies to get stronger or win.
This game unfortunately, with so many empires at once, You could be invovled with one enemy and multiple enemies attack you at once, taking out or destroying what took you a long time to build up in a very short period.
The A.I. though does finally bend if you do well enough, seems to take forever in some situations to give up.
One war my Confederation was in, went on for 100 years before the A.I. gave up and ceded my demands.
Again I only got so far with having to use cheats on a constant basis just to keep up, even having to make my ships invulnerable.
I get it in one way, this is the galaxy and if Humans and other alien lifeforms really did exist in an environment like this, very possible your country, star empire or Star federation could be blown to ashes or severely hurt and damaged by wars.
The thing is on normal with 21 competitors or even 15, it seems too much at times.
I wish there was an easy mode. I'm just someone who likes to take their time with things.
I am also someone who wants to explore other aspects of this game at times, without the constant threat of a war breaking out that I don't want part in.
One final note.  One of my Empires are purists. Meaning they are fungus like people who basically make sure most if not all of their planets are racially pure.
However something interesting happened. I placed a colony of my people on a arid world. Now my fungus people had been set to evolve from Continental worlds, so the colony I placed on this planet were not too pleased.
Then about 30-40 years later in the game, something happened, some members from that planet became a sup species of the same race, evolved to adapt to an arid environment and some of their traits I had placed at the start of the game for my race changed.
It said they looked different than other members from the original race I was playing with. Yet outside of new traits they had I didn't see it.
This was neat that your playing race can evolve. Really liked that idea. I wish though that if it said that these new members from this new sub species of the same race changed physically, I could actually see them change.
For example: My people originally look like greenish fungus individuals.
So this new arid variety maybe should then be able to change color or something, say a color fitting for the planet they have evolved from.
Other than that it is a very good game though.

If it wasn't clear by my number of hours played, I love this game and I highly recommend it. If you can get past a confusing UI and sprite graphics, you'll find a wonderfully complicated and strategic game that is also filled to the brim with competing mythologies in pursuit to rule over a world.
And that's just one of many viable strategies to win! You can also create massive communions of mages that use its weaker members' energy as fuel to power the rest into throwing out massive firestorms upon the enemy's heads. Or you can air-drop hundreds of magical elves riding ponies into every enemy province at the same time. Or even have your pretender god wish himself physical and magical mastery until no being in existance can stand up to the sheer power.
This is, through and through, a multiplayer game. Although there is single player which can be useful for trying out certain things, the focus is on playing the game with others. Communities for Dominions 4 multiplayer can be found on Desura's Dominions 4 forum, on dom4mods, and on Something Awful. I'm sure there are other communities as well. The only thing better than plunging the world into eternal darkness so your legions of undead can rule over the living,

Dominions 4 is a strategy game with no single-player campaign. It's all based around huge-scale single wars with the goal of becoming chief God, in single or multiplayer, that just escalate in scale as they go on. What starts with armies of dozens stabbing with swords and flinging basic magic spells like flickers of fire soon escalates into hundreds and thousands of troops clashing, with mythical beasts of various origins roaring and rampaging as ancient wizards call down great storms that rock nations.
The gameplay involves managing your nation. After designing your pretender God you choose what to recruit with recruitables divided between normal troops and commanders who can control different amounts of troops. It's a little more complicated with that but the game is easy to pick up. You then direct your commanders across a world map, taking over, reinforcing and just conquering the whole damn world.
There is a lot of variety in what you can play and how you can play. You choose from playing in the early ages, middle ages or late ages. The later the setting, the less magic there is in the world but the more advanced technology is. Playable nations come from a huge variety of influences. Some are historical, some mythological, some fictional and others more original. Only in this game can you play Three Kingdoms-era China battling a Lovecraftian army of horrors.
Overall, it's a very deep game but easy to pick up, with tons of content that any strategy fan should pick up!

After playing for about the 6th or 7th time with other factions I came to the realization that while the game is quite fun learning how it works and discovering all the options that are avalailable to you there are 2 key things that make this game falling a few steps short of greatness which I will point out later in this review. Now please note that this is my first Dominions title I've played and I have no prior knowledge or experience playing of any of the titles before it.
First off let me say what I like about this game, and there's quite a lot to enjoy in such a involving strategy game such as this, but a few I like to mention are the amount of content and spells that is within the package and how each nation plus god that you play as feel worlds different from each other, with different nations having access to a variety of different units and even their own spells, for instance the Bakemono nation in the middle age has their own racial summons to summon Oni onto the world map. Even after all that variety with approximately a dozen of different nations for each age and leaders you can choose from the game is won only by acquiring a number (chosen at the start of the game) of different thrones of ascension that are scattered throughout the map which can have quite a significant impact on all nations nearby once they are claimed by a player. I won't go into the specifics on how they do so now as it would take a whole summary of the game to explain details in the game that are prominent and quite arduous to understand (such as how dominion works and how your empires influence spreads). Let's just say that when you acquire these thrones, apart from giving you additional resources in the form of mana crystals, they can make the lands that are surrounding them more arid, temperate, hot, cold, or even unlucky just by having someone in control of them which can cause a huge impact on your playstyle or how you strategize about future moves. Another thing I like is that when I lost battles I felt that it was my own fault for not paying attention and not giving orders to a commander or a unit, or to forget putting my units in better defensive positions to deal with the enemies units, and while the combat is automated I still felt I had control on the outcome of each battle, which is not an easy thing to do for a strategy game that encapsulates so many different tactics and decisions to be made. The last thing I would like to mention about the pros of this game is that while this game may ultimately seem complex to many new players, in actuality it is a really simple strategy game to learn as your primary concerns are conquering lands and claiming the thrones of ascension, but the amount of choices that you have to achieve that goal are massive.
Now on to my opinions on the flaws of the game. The 2 greatest flaws this game has is the diplomacy aspect of the game and the balance of each nation. Now normally the balance of each nation wouldn't be an issue for me in a strategy game like this but considering the degree of difficulty that can scale based on the nations you play can be quite offputting ESPECIALLY for new players trying to grasp the concepts of the game. It took myself 3 failed games and numerous attempts at reading strategy guides to try and figure out what I was doing wrong to win as the yomi in the early age and after failing miserably I finally pursued playing another nation that apparently was much more powerful and won with relative ease without that much of any challenge minus a few times where I had left my lands undefended, or stupidly throwing all of my units in a nation's home base. But balance issues aside, the one thing that I absolutely wish that this game did a better job of is diplomacy, and while I haven't played a game with the Disciple mode (where one nation is a pretender god and other nations are that god's disciples) the game is primarily focused on combat and map positioning as opposed to diplomatic relations and tech trading. And while you can research a massive amount of spells it would seem that having the better units in the army trumps out any spell that you can research midway throughout the game . Now I may be wrong on this for later spells that are high-end, but for every instance that I've played the spells that are cast in combat usually are a minor thing to worry about as opposed to whoever has the better quality and quantity of troops in battle. There are no peace treaties that you can formulate with other nations and one is forced to solve every situation in the game militaristically by conquering their neighbors and fighting for the thrones of ascension , which can be fun for while, but it leaves something to be desired. For instance, after around the 100th turn of a game or so I will still have some of the same enemies that I have dealt with handily since the start of the game that are still pestering me, and it gets kinda worn and laborious to cycle between creating troops, sending troops, and defending. Although I have only played on a Normal difficulty setting, the A.I. doesn't actively try to win the game by going straight for thrones of ascension but rather conquer lesser defended provinces of the player which is a decent enough strategy, but I feel is not realistic enough because any human  player would immediately try to go for the victory points with as many units they have from the get go.
All in all Dominions 4 was worth my hard earned cash, as I have no gripes about the graphics (as I really don't care about how a game looks) or my experiences with the game and I do expect to play more of it in the future but probably on higher difficulty settings. But as I said at the beginning of this review, what stops this game from achieving greatness in my eyes is the fact that there are no diplomatic relations that you can have with the other nations and there are nations that are drastically better suited for winning the game than others.

I'm not gonna lie, Paladins is a game that is very similar to overwatch. With the rapid success of Overwatch, it is clear to see why people would try to mimic this game. Although the games are similar, they aren’t exactly the same. Like Overwatch, Paladins is an action packed first person shooter with various playable characters. The main difference would be that Paladins’ story focuses on a more medieval time era instead of the more futuristic and scientific one that Overwatch follows. It is clear that the developers(Hi-rez) wanted Paladins to be it’s own identity and not a comparison to something else. They focused on improving the aspects of the genre which Overwatch ignored. Doing so, paid off. Paladins offers a greater range of playstyles that the players can enjoy, AND, best of all, it’s completely free.

The matchmaking queue time are pretty quick and each game lasts around 15 minutes. With over 120 hours into the game in the past month, I think it’s safe to say that I’m pretty addicted to the game.
The developers are doing an amazing job at maintaining the game and providing the players with new content frequently. The fact that they’ve made such a great game for free, shows how much effort they’ve put into it. If you’re ever bored at home, and would like a quick game to invest a little bit of your time into daily, show Hi-Rez some love, and download Paladins.

Polarity is likely overrated, due to a massive number of people getting the game for 0.19USD and spamming reviews. However, I do feel the game is a reasonable purchase, especially at a discount of -50% or more. Gameplay is simple and enjoyable, while the game has many rough edges and limited content.
The biggest issue I can see is that the game is a sloppy Unity project. The launcher has limited resolution options, and the Steam overlay would ghost on the black borders. Level assets have cracks and seams, buggy lighting, and a major lack in refinement. Some puzzles can be broken by tricks, especially in co-op.
Co-op can be fully completed as one person flipping between keyboard and controller. Later co-op puzzles seemed to have extra cube-locks with no function, with no lines to show what platform was affected. Polarity has the hallmarks of the first game from a company, flawed but passionate.
I enjoyed the game enough to bother with co-op and put up with the sloppy level design to 100% the game. The current content is around 4 hours, with levels consistently taking 3-6 minutes to complete. I liked that timing and pacing, as I could play the game while waiting on friends or multiplayer queues. Puzzles were satisfying and reasonable, and only the cube transformation field (yellow particles) was confusing, with no introduction to even show it exists. The developers could make several improvements, but the game was quite enjoyable. The -96% sale was amazing, but I think the game is worth more than that. Polarity is a decent puzzle option to spend a little time thinking, but this gem is quite rough.
