I caught wind of this game really by accident while searching for something new to play. I have to say it must have been serendipity because this game is fantastic! It plays like a very complicated board game, which is why the graphics are not necessarily state of the art - but they don't need to be. What this game lacks in graphical horsepower it makes up for with brilliant game mechanics. The level of detail the designers put into each of the game mechanics and how they made a tremendous effort to ensure they each fit with the lore and setting of the game is amazing. For instance, a unit equipped with a spear can deflect incoming melee attacks from enemies equipped with a shorter melee weapon, such as a sword. Archers' arrows don't just hit or miss an enemy unit - they actually take into account the spread of the arrows over a target area.
The lore setting is also extremely unique. You are a pretender god vying to be the ONLY god. You can choose from a large number of deities each with their own special characteristics. Add on top of that about two dozen different civilizations you can match you deity up with...and on top of that there are three separate ages you can start from each with different environmental settings - you get the picture for the level of depth in this game.
Others have mentioned the user manual being a critical part of this game. It is. And yes it's long at about 400 pages, but about 300 pages of that are just reference tables for all the different units, spells, items, etc. I have to give the designers credit again here, because not only is this the most comprehensive user manual I have ever seen in a video game, but it's actually easy and fun to read! I've played other board games where the rulebook was a tenth the size but incredibly hard to read (I'm looking at you Republic of Rome!).
I definitely recommend this game for anyone that enjoys master strategy games like Europa Universalis and perhaps the Total War series. Probably the best way to describe this game is a healthy mixture of Civilization, Europa Universalis, Heroes of Might and Magic and Total War. The first hour or so I was a bit lost, but read the manual and you'll quickly pick up on the game mechanics and an appreciation for the level of depth and endless replayability of this game.
Don't let the basic graphics fool you, this is an addictive emersive gaming experience that I highly recommend. Turn-based strategy at it's finest.

First and foremost, while I heartily recommend this game, I must underline that this game is NOT for everyone.
First impressions for most people are horrible: the graphics are dated, the audio gets irritating after a short while and the user interface is one of the worst I've ever had to deal with - although there are few very welcome improvements over Dominions 3. Single player doesn't really offer much of a challenge either, once you understand the basics of the game. As a single player game, I would rate Dominions series as one of the worst I've ever played.
Where Dominions 4 shines though, is multiplayer. Despite the simplistic basics, it's easily one of the most complex MP games out there. The variety of nations is quite large, each era plays differently due to different units and varying access to magic paths and while there are obviously "generally accepted strategies" for each nation, each of them can be played in very varied ways depending on scales and pretender choice.
The game has very steep learning curve, but there is a wealth of information to be found quite easily - google is your friend here. I would personally recommend checking out some let's plays, playing single-player game until you grasp the basics and then try and find a newbie game to join on one of the forums (Desura's Dom4 forums worked fine for me).

There’s something untraditionally appealing about Out There Somewhere’s insubstantiality. It’s a very brief, straightforward experience, but rather than feeling shallow it uses its brevity to subvert the players expectations in interesting ways.
That arcade shooting segment at the start? That’s just a prelude to the platformer that takes up most of the game. That gun you’re carrying? It’s actually for teleporting you around instead of killing enemies. The huge world the game seems to be hinting at? In reality it’s a more classical one direction platformer. Out There Somewhere is full of little touches that seemed designed to throw you off course and surprise you with how things play out. They may come at the cost of making a lasting impression, but I feel like that wasn’t ever its prerogative.
Out There Somewhere also gets away with a lot more than most games could because of how strong its mechanics are, and how intrinsically they’re tied to level designs. The teleporter gun is largely your only tool throughout the game, and each screen is made to perfectly utilize it for platforming and puzzle solving (provided your reflexes are up for it). Eventually I was having to take into account bullet speed, character momentum, and environmental devices in order to navigate effectively. These additions are added quickly, but also scale the difficulty smoothly enough to where I almost didn’t realize how much more involved later levels were because the game had taught me how to play so well.
One could argue that Out There Somewhere is too short or simple or loose, and they wouldn’t be entirely wrong. The game often feels as if it’s holding on by a thread and some frustrating moments can be a lot more unpleasant due to how much of the overall game they encompass. But its length and careful scope feel so intentional and considered that I was willing to give it the benefit of the doubt and enjoy how it played with my expectations. I might not remember it a year or even a month from now, but as a condensed experiment in teleportation and unconventional design I don’t regret the journey.

A very good film about video games. But I want to briefly address some of the issues raised by negative reviewers of the film.
Anyone can see these are relatively good, and for the most part humble, people. People like Pugh of Stanley Parable and others question whether they really deserve this praise they are receiving. I will concede that a surprising number of them have pink hair. Not a fashion choice I'd go with but hey, incredibly I am capable of tolerating this.
Other than some questionably disparaging comments about Assassin's Creed in one interview, there is nothing in this film that is remotely attacking mainstream video game culture. Nothing. So where is the hatred coming from?
For all you pro-Gamergaters out there who feel the need to up-rate some of these disgusting reviews: This documentary goes for 93 minutes. It focuses on Zoe Quinn and Depression Quest for a total of less than 4 of them.
Guess what, you can read who's interviewed and the games they represent on this page. If you dislike these games, then why buy the film? Why bother? Both sides of this so-called debate shoot vitriol at each-other unnecessarily. Things don't get better by describing the whole indie culture as "incestuous", when that's obviously one of the most inane terms to describe a group of people who identify with each-others ambitions and goals.
I agree that the film isn't as well-structured as it could be. Other than following Davey Wreden around there isn't much narrative; though I liked when it came to PAX everyone who had already been interviewed in their own development places congregated there, which felt like the centre of the whole film.
I highly recommend this film to the people who looking at the title and info already THINK they will like this film. You will. Its a celebration of a culture of people making games for those who are looking for something different, interesting and personal.

Concerning my play time on Steam I watched the entire movie DRM-free from IndieGameStand so I am basing this review off the whole movie.
This movie is a fantastic and beautiful documentary covering the motivations, industry and process of Indie Games. There's a huge number of games represented and it covers game jams and awards for the personal journeys included more than the equally excellent (but slightly more personal) Indie Game the Movie. The soundtrack is great, the visual artistry is great and the sheer fun of watching it is outstanding. It'll make you feel good watching it and is quite frank about some of the slightly darker sides of making games in this day and age.

The subject of this film is not totally new to me, as I already saw different documentary films concerning game developers. It's still interesting to get an insight into the way this creators are working, the stress, the promotion of their games, why they do it...
But I liked this film because we've here some of the most important indie game developers I've heard of and which games I've played. I felt kind of emotional to hear the music of "The path" and happy to see the founders of Tale of tales, Christine Love and the others.
I get interested into games again because of all this new and diverse creation. And because I don't know anyone around me playing, this film was important to feel like being indirectly part of it.
Now I'm looking forward to watch the extra contents, it feels like there is more to see or say about what has been already introduced in the main film, concerning diversity, harassment of female developers, accessibility of tools and the joy to create and sharing it.

(Technical note: not even English subtitles on the extras. Please think of us foreign watchers!)
Got this for $1 and I guess I can recommend at this price, and because, well, it certainly isn't a waste of time.
However, while people in this documentary have interesting things to say, as a whole, the film is unfocused and largely unwilling to find a general message. It presents a group of unconnected people who are shown as if they're living together (?), and it mostly has footage that was shot years ago but doesn't care to add a "what happened next" section at the end... Is it because what happened next for most of the people featured wasn't so good? (Tale of Tales closing shop, Davey's depression, etc.)
Well, this is still part of an artist's journey, and the film denies us that.
In fact, I think the film's main goal is to encourage everyone to create games, and to do that it blissfully ignores the fact that 99.9% of all game developments, especially in indie, don't end well. Total impulse buy. The game was on sale for cheap and I didn't even finish reading the description. Probably not the best method of purchasing a game,, but I lucked out.
This is a puzzle game. Now, I normally don't play puzzle games, so I don't have the biggest library of game knowledge to compare this to, but it reminds me of a cross between Hitman Go and one of those flash games where you try to get the car out of a parking lot, or into a certain spot in a parking lot, etc.,. Each level is a static checkerboard, and pressing in any direction will send your character, the murderer, as far in that direction as he can possibly go. The result is that you have to shift your character around using the level layout in order to reach some harder to get to squares. The game teaches you the mechanics in the beginning tutorial and then gradually ramps up the difficulty as you progress, adding more enviromental factors and different types of NPCs.
It's a very addictive game in and of itself, but there is a lot of homage to slasher films in here. Aside from the puzzle play trial and error (and don't worry - you can use in-game currency that you collect to unlock hints or answers in case you get stuck), the longevity comes from trying to collect two things: death scenes and different murderers. Fair warning, it takes quite a lot of grinding to collect enough coins to unlock all of these things, and that would be my only gripe with this game: after a few levels, you unlock a coin grinder mini-game. While this is certainly helpful compared to playing through a stage and collected coins, I do feel it doesn't give you enough coins. Each successful scene in the mini-game nets you 10 coins. All killers are 1,000 coins, and the death scenes range from a couple hundred to 2,500. The mini-game becomes difficult by the late teens, meaning even if you are able to score 20, you're only getting 200 coins. It got to the point where I played the final deleted scene of the final movie (campaign) over and over because it routinely nets you nearly 300 coins.
Honestly, though, I think I stuck it out just to get all the steam achievements. That in and of itself is an accomplishment for the game, as I don't normally feel the need to play over and over for these.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun, and if you're a fan of these type of puzzle games, I don't think you can go wrong. At only $9, with my 30 hours put in, that's essentially 30 cents an hour. I've averaged the total length of time a mainstream action title nets me at 12 hours. At $60, that's $5/hr., so do I think you'll get your money's worth with this game? Yes, absolutely. Even if you don't feel the need to grind out unlockables, it'll still come in at a better value if you put even two hours into this game.

As puzzle games go, Slayaway Camp is an absolute success. You play as a whole host of slasher movie inspired killers whose goal is to slay camp counselors in a flurry of cutesy voxel art ultragore. The gameplay itself is very reminiscent of Hitman Go, where the killer must navigate the isometric levels by sliding in a series of logical moves that result in the murder of all victims, but one wrong move could lead to the killers demise or could lead to the level becoming unwinnable. If that happens, and it almost certainly will, a convenient and unlimited rewind a turn option is available, as well as the option to restart the level altogether. The game starts out easy, almost too easy, but as you progress the levels become fiendishly difficult, but always satisfying. New concepts, challenges and stipulations are added to the levels as they go, increasing their complexity and keeping the gameplay fresh. What's great though is that the developer included an option to skip levels or receive tips, which is excellent at preventing the game from becoming too frustrating when you inevitable hit a wall.
There's tons of great unlockables in the game to keep things interesting, such as new new killers and murder animations. The killers themselves are really fun by being direct homages to iconic movies and slasher tropes in general. I felt really incentivized to complete chapters because I was excited to see what movie the next chapter was gonna be a take on. And on that note, the design direction for the game is really stellar. It does such a great job at playing up the look and feel of 80's slasher movies from the character and level design to the VHS inspired chapter select menus. On top of that, the cute block shaped characters combined with the ultra gory death animations strikes a fantastic dissonance that makes this game stand out, and really highlights that the game doesn't take itself too seriously.
Finally, the pricing for the game is reasonable at just $9. If you are looking for a puzzle game with some character, Slayaway Camp might be just what you are looking for.

Nier: Automata is an action-RPG/shoot ‘em up (no, really) featuring ridiculously human robots fighting an endless war against machines created by aliens, in the hopes of defending the remnants of humanity from destruction.
Or is it?
Nier: Automata is a game full of plot twists, though some are rather predictable, as well as a number of big epic moments and a lot of attempts to pull on the player’s heartstrings, with varying degrees of success. Featuring three protagonists and almost two-dozen joke endings, as well as a couple of real ones, this is a game which goes on well past its welcome, and then some.
But I’m getting ahead of myself.
As an action RPG, this game has a fairly reasonable set of mechanics on the surface – you can run around shooting at enemies with your pod, a floating machine which follows you around, or cut them up in close combat with various weapons – spears, short swords, large swords, and gauntlets. Each class of weapon has its own attack pattern, and two of the characters can wield two weapons at the same time, allowing them to combo the weapons together, while the third character has a hacking ability which causes them to play a brief shoot-em-up game to deal their opponent damage.
Unfortunately, while these mechanics all sound well and good, it quickly becomes clear that the game doesn’t really work mechanically. The abundance of healing items means that you can pretty easily prevent your death by simply using them at will, and you get “plug-in chips” which can include various abilities to give yourself more hit points or regenerate by killing enemies, dealing damage, or simply standing around without taking damage. Given you can deal damage from range, it is pretty easy to kite most enemies around, and it is very easy to either be underleveled for the content (which makes it take a while to wear down enemies) or overlevelled (which trivializes the combat even more, though it is not actually all that hard to take down enemies even 20 levels above your own, though it is tedious to do so). There is a crafting system based on combining the plug-in chips into better versions of themselves, as well as upgrading the weapons and pods to deal more damage, and gathering the materials for such can become rather tedious, doubly so as you must upgrade all your weapons to the maximum level to face the optional (and hardest) boss in the game.
Alas, the game’s enemy variety leaves something to be desired; there’s maybe a couple dozen kinds of enemies in the game apart from bosses, but most of them are fundamentally either “stab you in close combat” or “shoot you from range”. Most of the machine lifeforms are slow and clunky, making for pretty samey combat and making it easy to simply run around kiting them and shooting them to death while avoiding their slow projectiles. By the first time you’ve beaten the game, you will likely be tired of the normal enemies, but don’t worry – you’ll get to fight them even more later on!
Because, you see, this game has an interesting definition of “beating” it. The first time you beat the game, it coyly encourages you to keep playing… at which point, you start the game over, except from the perspective of your sidekick character. This means that most of the content you experience will be the same, with only the beginning and end really differing, though you get even more tedious side-quests on his route (and the opportunity to finish up any you failed to finish the first time through).
Once you beat the game the second time through, and see
ending, the game ends with a screen seeming to promise a sequel… but it is not, it is actually the other two endings of the game, which you get through by playing through the game a third time, though this time, instead of replaying the first half of the game, instead you’re actually playing all-new content which you could only access by effectively playing the first half of the game twice. Joy.
If this game was nothing but the main story, and if it cut out a lot of the RPG mechanics, it would actually be a lot more interesting – the bosses are, on the whole, of fairly interesting design, and the core story is fairly decent, even if some of the characters you’re supposed to care about feel a bit underchracterized in the anime sort of way, where they suddenly get some focus right before they die. The second half of the game focuses half on a character who previously had gotten almost no focus at all, which feels kind of weird, and while by the end you do care about her, it ends up feeling less than tight in terms of writing. I would have liked to care a lot more about a lot of the characters, but they don’t get enough screen time for it, despite the game being well over 50 hours long, much of which is spent running around the world doing sidequests instead of advancing the main story, which is less than half of the game’s play time.
Sadly, you’re going to have to wade through a lot of junk to see all the diamonds in the rough here – and I just can’t say it is worth the time investment. I liked the beginning, I liked the middle, and I liked the end – but I didn’t like all the other stuff in the game, the various quests involving running around and doing things for people I don’t care about. If the game had focused those side quests on characterizing the main cast, it would have worked a lot better – but only a few actually serve such a function.
Overall, then, this isn’t something I can really recommend, but it isn’t because it is bad so much as that it doesn’t respect the player’s time. If you have time to burn, and are interested in something that is kind of artsy, this might be up your alley, and it is certainly a change from the usual fare in terms of game mechanics. But if you’re looking for a tight experience, you’re better off looking elsewhere.

This game is overhyped and I'll tell you why.
The concept is simple enough, you explore a series of rooms, kill a boss, move on to the next floor, and try not to die because that loses all your progress. But you'll die frequently, and not just early on. The enemy movements are erratic; some move randomly, some pursue you, some move randomly until they change their mind and try to pursue you...and your health is low. Not low for say, the start of a Zelda game. But it's low relative to how often you'll be unable to avoid the enemies due to randomness.
In fact, almost everything in the game is random, and the makers still decided they wanted to inflate the difficulty. So if shooting 4 ways in 13x7 room where the enemies prefer to move diagonally and the bosses fill 3x3 squares while spawning more enemies is too easy for you, you'll love all the obstacles that limit you more than them. You'll also love that most powerups are unexplained and a few will lower your stats. There ARE comprehensive guides, e.g.
but they can't predict when pills will help or hurt you, and there's no reason for the other information to not be given in-game, since it's only available in English. A small number of items actually do have a text pop-up briefly explaining what they do, so it's not like the idea of explaining things never occured to the devs. But they decided to make the pills a liability and the items with a set effect annoying, since there are dozens of each kind to look up. Seriously, look at a guide and ask yourself how much you'd be able to memorize without it turning into a chore.
If you roll the dice enough times, you'll get lucky and get items that are significantly helpful. But you'll still have a good chance at getting screwed over by the room layout and the behavior of enemies. I've seen people defend it on the grounds that you manage your resources within the confines of what you find on each floor, but that's secondary. Even pros can only get so far before lady luck kills them. For a game where death resets everything but unlocked characters, spending hundreds of hours running into that wall is frankly unreasonable.

NieR Automata is a very ambitious game that wouldn't work as another medium -- it needs to be a video game. It's an existential puzzle that is quite thought-provoking when all is said and done. I would tell my students to play it if the entire thing, including its multiple playthroughs, didn't take about 30+ hours.
The story really gets going once you pierce its seemingly familiar shell in those consequent playthroughs. It starts out as a fairly straight-forward cyberpunk narrative, but it evolves into much more -- in some odd ways delivering on the promise that Metal Gear Solid V never lived up to -- in the third playthrough. Automata has been praised a lot, and rightfully so, though I personally feel calling it a perfect experience is going way too far. While the meaninglessness found in the majority of the side-quests can technically be explained away by the game's own existential views, it doesn't make them any more fun. The same can be said for combat (and hacking), which turns slightly repetitive after a while. The gameplay systems are solid, but fairly superficial -- the game failed to get me to engage with a number of mechanics. There's also a fair bit of backtracking which, again, you could explain away with philosophy but ultimately feels tedious at times. In the end, though, you play this game for the narrative, and it's absolutely worth it. The PC port is abysmal, but the FaR mod magically fixes 99% of the problems. All in all, this is a very unique game that you should probably check out if you're into games pushing the limits of the medium.

I have to say, this game definitely deserves to be more popular than it is right now. It's one of the early examples of roguelite platformers inspired by Spelunky, but it is however definitely very unique and stands out in its own right.
First, it's extremely fast paced. Games like Spelunky or Rogue Legacy usually expect you to be slow and cautious - here, you also need to be observant, but you've got short time limit to find a timer pickup or you die- so you need to think on your feet, judging what is the fastest way to scale dangers ahead of you without getting hit. In fact, it's very arcade styled - winning the entire game shouldn't take longer than 15 minutes if you know what you're doing, but the game is extremely hard so you will spend hours practicing and learning your enemies to reach that point.
Second, it's very focused on action. Combat is meat of the gameplay, with a lot of depth to it - you are always equipped with three kinds of weapons and two special abilites (Zelda 2-like downstab and a jump spin attack) that let you approach any enemy encounter tactically. Platforming isn't too shabby either, since the game will require you to jump over spikes or swim through water, and you can wallslide, walljump, double jump (or even triple jump with the right item), super jump by crouching for a long time, crawl and glide.
Third interesting feature are unlockables. Unlike most roguelite games winning the game on Normal difficulty isn't that hard of a task and can be accomplished in 6-10 hours - but this isn't what the game is truly about. See, unlike most of these games there IS a pernament progression to this game - unlocking new stuff. You unlock bonuses that extend your timer or give your new lives, but most unlockables are new weapons. This is also where most depth of the game comes in - you have plenty of melee weapons to replace your standard katana, including a baseball bat, whip or lightsaber; instead of throwing shurken like most ninjas you can simply get a gun, a boomerang or even do a Hadouken from Street Fighter; and replace your bombs with molotov coctails or dynamite that allows you to blow up the terrain! All these weapons have unique properties that make them interesting choices in some situations. And of course you can mix things up with Chaos Mode that allows you to pick random weapons every session, requiring you to adapt to new situations.
Fourth unique things is level design - unlike most Roguelike games levels of the tower aren't completely randomly generated but tower is instead built from premade "blocks", combining best of both worlds - each playhtrough will still be unique and unpredictable, while game allows finely crafted and polished challenges and moments that only a human designer can create.
Of course, by its very nature this isn't a game you can sit down and play for hours, it's more suited to short sessions. But I assure you, the bite-sized frantic hard-as-nails (but never unfair) addictive action will keep you coming back everytime you need a coffee break. I should know, as of writing this I clocked over 30 hours just from these short sessions.
Is it worth its price? Being honest, I gotten more enjoyment out of this game than from Spelunky or Rogue Legacy, much more popular games, and it is over two times cheaper than them. It's not perfect - there are couple weird design decisions like Parachute bonus that slows you down when falling (a bane of speedrunners) - but you can literally count them on fingers of one hand.
If you like fast-paced arcade platformers, you will definitely fall in love with this game.
Oh! And if you want a glimpse of what you're getting yourself into, you can try the games predeccesor, House of Dead Ninjas, which is a fully free online flash game.

Dominions 4 is an awesome turn-based strategy game, somewhat combining province-based strategy games with Master of Magic and Warhammer Fantasy Battles. While it does have a somewhat clunky shell (e.g., UI controls via the keyboard that you actually need to read the manual for and/or watch other play), it is actually not too hard to learn, but has a lot of depth and provides the cliche "hard to master," especially when playing with/against others.

I have just as much fun reading the manual, either secretly at work, or before I go to bed, or perhaps with a whiskey in hand before a night out on the town, as I do playing the game....And, that is a good thing.  This is a labor of love; the essence of which drips from every poorly planned turn mocking my organizational and logistical talents.  I've played each incarnation of Dominions, though Dominions II most definitely stole my soul.  Luckily, I have a decent familial support group who pray on a daily basis for my errant ways to end.  After several seasons I have been called back into the material plane and, though my dominion fades, my black labrador prophet has has built temples of chew toys in my honor.  Now, with my triumphant and glorius return, alongside the enhanced multiplayer aspects of Dominions 4, the seat of the Pantokrator is most assuredly mine.

The game is great, but needs more maps atm. However people posting on here seem to forget the game just came out not long ago. Compared to Red Orchestra 2 it is much faster paced, but still holds to the core aspects of the game (though I feel the cover system was nerfed way to much. Its still there to an extent.) Currently after some map updates the game typically tends to be 4 maps played repeatedly. If your going to do a 2 hr trial of it, heres some suggestions so you wont get wrecked or kicked out by other players :
1.) Dont pick Commander. Its vital to the team to win and you need experience in the game to play it. If you choose it and are not doing it well, you'll likely get kicked. You also will likely get kicked if you don't have a microphone as Commander (even if you know what your doing) because people want their leader to communicate quickly.
2.) Dont pick Squad leader for much the same reasons, though it plays different and you don't require a mic for it.
3.) Explosions of any sort will very likely kill you if your not in cover (i.e. up against a wall, crouched behind a wall, etc.)
4.) Theres pullet penetration, use it.
5.) Aim, dont run and gun (unless your using a shotgun, and u need to be close with that).
6.) Theres friendly fire, and strict friendly fire rules. If you teamkill someone, say "sry" "sorry" etc in the chat. If your team-killed accidently then you should type "np" in the chat which will remove their team-kill penalty.
7.) Dont be a pilot, its very hard.
8.) Use your map with M and constantly be attacking the objectives, preferrably with your squad.
9.) Learn to ignore idiots on voice chat, theres too many to keep muting them :P
---
I also suggest playing Territories, and filter servers by players to find a nearly full 64 man game.
Hope this helps (b^_^)b

This is a bad game, and it has been broken for the first year after release.
On your first run, you will have fun exploring the galaxy and the game's mechanics, at least until you run into a game breaking bug or a dead-end event chain, of which there had been plenty even a year after Stellaris' release. The game as a whole is incredibly shallow. It does not have the light-hearted casual gaminess of traditional 4x games, and it does not build on PDS' rich history of Grand Strategy games. It wastes processing ressources on 3D ship models and star systems that have zero gameplay value. The combat system is controlled (no intersting status effects, only +X modifiers), technology progression is linear and micromanagement impossible - yet it manages to have been off-balance from the beginning to now. Planet development is nothing but meaningless busiwork. Diplomacy is a joke, at least compared to other Paradox titles. The generic, though sometimes interesting, lore is mechanically meaningless and is not connected in any way. And all empires play more or less the same way, no matter how much you customize them, simply because they share almost all of their mechanics (compare that to the diversity of CK2's religions and cultures!).

Great game, very polished, a new take on Space 4X by taking some inspiration from Grand Strategy games. Exploration is great, the internal politics of your empire are very cool, research is interesting and it has a lot of cool event chains that create emergent stories and add a nice flavor. It also has a huge scope - lots of stars and different species and very long game with many possibilities. This scope, however, is also its great failure: sometimes, there just isn't enough stuff to do in the mid or late game. Not all mechanics have the same complexity and depth - diplomacy is a bit lacking and wars can be a bit repetitive. It simply needs more content to live up to its promise, and while the DLC helps it isn't quite enough yet. The free patches have improved the base game a lot in terms of balance, UI, fixing problems and even adding some cool features, so it is already better than it was at launch (and I already had fun back then).
In short, the game is very good (compared to others in the category) but creates the expectations of something even bigger and better.

Which doesn't mean the menus ain't clunky, or some missions having multiple paths of wildly differing difficulties. This one still makes you feel the most like a clever assassin (along with, perhaps, Blood Money), if that's what you're after. If it's not, enjoy a shootout without health kits.
Oh and, if you haven't played this before, bear in mind this is a "serious" game. There ain't no butterflies and unicorns here; you'll be facing legions of corrupt politicians and their mistresses of the night, shady organizations, bizarre freak parties, petty crime ascending into organized crime, and other stuff you'd normally expect to read about in the newspapers, titled "Bad news".

If you liked Hitman: Blood Money, you will like this one. The systems are the same, but as a prequel, they are naturally MUCH less refined. That said, it's still a good game.
Go play Blood Money first; it's the superior game, but for a couple dollars, definately give this one a try.

It's kind of amazing how much depth can be put into a game with a cool concept and the will to do so.
The game it's a simple puzzle game with a horror "slasher flick" type of theme attached to it, the idea is that your character can move in four directions, left, right, up, down, only that your character won't stop unless there's something blocking it's path, alternatively there can be traps, cops field's of view, or simply getting stuck in between a couple of blocks are the things that can end your run.
The game also does sometimes without warning this cool "switch" of elements in the mechanics in some of the levels, (this ones presented as movies in vcr cassettes with cool covers and "previews" in the form of cutscenes always featuring different "killers" that you'll control during the remainer of the set of levels)
The idea in most cases is simply to stay alive and kill all civilians in a level, sounds a bit dark for a game with such a "cartoony" and "cute" aesthetic, but in reality the game, while keeping it's tongue'in cheek a bit with it's mixture of humor and violence can at times borderline in brutality, whenever you... "Take out" any of your... "Targets" the game has a chance of displaying a cutscene, at times one that can be reproduced by frightening people away from you leading them into traps (fires, holes in the ground, water tombs filled with cocodriles, etc...) altho in most cases it will simply reproduce a random cutscene of a massive set of dozens of them that are quite characteristic and that can be multiplied repeatedly by spending coins that you earn in-game.
At the end of each level (in a set of them) you can earn currency by completing a time event in a cutscene in which your character will be murdering an individual, then you'll earn "coins" that you can then spend either in more killers that you can select and use in the numerous of films/levels, or alternatively in more animations for the random executions that are displayed when murdering your "enemies".
The game for the most part it's quite self-explanatory, and it has an almost perfect learning curve, I would compare it to something like Hitman Go, but I feel, as much as I love that game, this game has it's own unique aspects in it's core game design that need to be shared, and for good reason, most of them, even after attempting a level multiple times, never really frustrated me as muchs as in other game's "personal" failures, could have, Hitman Go being a perfect example of this.
Instead the game offers a really cool "mechanic" to not call it "feature" that allows you to not only revert your mistakes resetting your position to the last movement you made, but also the ability to display handy tips for the shy price of just a couple of your in-game coins, if you still can't figure things out, after your second payment for tips, the solution for the level will be revealed.
Overall i'm really pleased as well as surprised by the ammount of quality, and content there is for this game, it's an actual fleshed out release, and even then, the game feels as just another small, maybe kind of try, and see how it is, during a sale, type of title, lost within the vast Steam store library of games, I feel as if it doesn't only deserves more attention, as much as it deserves much more significant exposure on the part of the "marketing deparment" in itself, altho maybe there's not much it can be done to promote core gameplay aspects of a game that appears rather "simplistic" at first and yet internally, profoundly, it helds an amazing ammount of passion, and heart.

In short, fun little Portal-wannabe game worth 0.19€ bought on sale.
That being said, the game has several problems:
- There are quite a few bugs, main issue there is clipping and disappearing cubes through floor or walls when not being careful (had this happening several times in coop). Other annoying bugs include auto dropping cubes when coop partner dies, random rotation of camera when using gamepad (Xbox 360 controller in my case) while pressing nothing and no end game screen for coop campaign  (there is normal "Next" button which does nothing so you don't know if it's broken or what's happening)
- Sadly the difficulty is almost none, all "puzzles" are very straight forward requiring almost no thought. I'd definitely wouldn't call it "demanding all of your wits and reflexes" as devs do.
- It's advertised as multi-player game but it only contains local coop (which wasn't problem for me but it might be for others). Included coop campaign isn't really coop for most of the parts, there are few moments where two players must interact with each other to finish the level but otherwise it's mostly one doing all of the work while the other is waiting for partner to open the road for him (being a burden in short).
- Both coop and single-player campaign takes only around an hour each.
This might sound like very negative review but in fact it really isn't. Thought there are issues with the game, they aren't game-braking. I still enjoyed playing coop with a friend and can only recommend it for this next-to-nothing price. However paying full price would most likely change how I perceived the game.

Polarity is a short and at times very easy puzzle game. It is in some ways comparable to portal, but without the portals. The main gameplay, at least, is similar to portal. You use cubes on pressure pads around each puzzle room, in an attempt to reach the exit. There is the added task of collecting data nodes, on the premise that you are a "hacker" stealing them from a vault. The story doesn't play too much into this except at the beginning and end of the game.
The puzzles themselves are fairly easy. There were a few that I had to think about solving, but most were solvable in less than 2 minutes. For reference: I was even able to complete the co-op levels as a single player, and the entire game to 100% [with all data nodes collected] within ~3 hours.
The music doesn't always play in this game, it fades in every now and then with a calming ambient piece. It is very nice, but I don't think there are many tracks that rotate. There isn't any voicing in this game, and beyond text that flashes on screen at the start of the game you are pretty much left to your own devices to figure things out. The graphics in this game are very nice. In some places the shadows look a bit odd, but mostly it looks nice. It has a sort of cell-shaded look, with textures that look fairly minimalistic.
To summarise this: Despite peoples insistence to compare this to portal, beyond some similar gameplay mechanics it isn't very similar at all. It isn't overly challenging, but if you want some simple first-person puzzles to wile away an afternoon, this is the game to go for.

You start off a few years after the events of Saints Row 1, the "Boss" being put in a comma after the attempted assassination on a boat. You find that a company "Ultor" has taken over the area that was Saints Row and that in your abstinence many new gangs have come to Stillwater and taken over parts of the city.

This game is roughly 7 years old, and even thought there are a few lower graphical moments it still holds up pretty well as a whole. If you want a saints row game or a realistic free roam game with fun activities, then I HIGHLY recommend that you consider this marvel of a video game.

I am a long-time Paradox fan, and I really want to love this game. The problem is it is a Paradox game in a long tradition of Paradox game that lag out terribly.
Whether it be the way the AI handles decision making, or the number of pops, or just the fact that the save game gets bigger and bigger... whether the cause lies in any of these things that I have read in numerous forums, once you reach mid-game it is likely to slow down to a crawl. In a game where new tech advances or settlements take months and years to reach, who has time for a day to last 5 seconds?
Here come the fanboys saying "it must be your hardware." It is not my hardware. The problem is the way the games are designed. I went through this with EU3 (which I still play) and HOI3 (which I had to eventually quit due to a lack of playability.)
Here are the positives. The game is beautiful, engaging, and different each time I play. I cannot say enough about the playability and replayability options. But if I cannot play a game with many different races in a huge 1000 star universe, without accepting a crawling rate of play, why offer the option?

Hitman: Contracts is the first good Hitman game in the series, in my opinion. It took what was good about the previous entries and improved them enough to make a great entry. It's not perfect by any means but I enjoyed my time playing it for sure. As far as story goes, it's as weak as every other entry and it's not the main focus of the game. Gameplay is the main focus and it has been improved greately over Hitman 2. The A.I is no longer unfairly overpowered but they still provide a real challenge, which is a perfect combo. Graphically speaking the game has aged somewhat ok. It's playable but you have to be the kind of person who enjoys old games, like me. This game is not perfect though. The only thing I was not a fan of was the level design in the second half of the game. In the first half, you have a few different levels in some different locations. After that, however, all of the levels seem to take place at night, in the rain, in Japan. I know that some of the later levels are "HD Remasters" of Codename 47 (never finished that one, so I don't know which ones) but it's easily half a game in a similar area. It gets old fast. I wish that they had changed it up a bit, changing some levels to daytime, some without rain, etc. That being said this game is still fun and a good entry in the Hitman franchise.

This might just be one of my favorite puzzle games of recent times. Something about the 80's horror movie vibe and voxel character gore has a lot of charm to it. In a way this is like the Broforce of puzzle games, and by that I mean, being able to play all of these classic villians, monsters, and creatures from your favorite horror films and slasher flicks instead of action movies. The humor of this game is spot on with the cheesiness of 80's slashers, and almost everything is a comedic homage to them or other well known horror movies.
The core gameplay is actually very simple, being only able to move in four directions, but trying to figure out ways to kill everyone on screen in a crude and bloody fashion, it is very addicting. It can be challenging, but never becomes too frustrating. There are several different death scenes when you kill someone, each character also has there own unique one. Something about watching these box-like characters violently murdering their victims is extremely satisfying, and humorous at times. Levels are grouped together in VHS quality worlds, each spoofing a bad B-rated slasher movie and their atrocious sequels. There's lots of unlockables to purchase with coins you earn after each level, or by playing a really fun minigame. You can buy more death scenes from the shop or more killers through the mystery box. There are a lot of characters to choose from and they seem to keep adding more, I don't think I've even unlocked them all yet. You can also use your hard earned coins to get some useful tips to beat a level if you get stuck.
I also want to point out how good the music is. It fits in so well, and the main theme song is so catchy. I had to buy the deluxe edition just for the soundtrack, and more specifically just for an mp3 of the main theme song. Only con is I wish there were more levels, there are tons already, also harder puzzles once you beat the game, but I just want more to quench my bloodlust.  Maybe we will get another DLC or hopefully a level editor in the future.

I'm a fan of the games and developers that are followed in the film, and I appreciate the mission of the documentary. I feel guilty because of the review bombing GameLoading is recieving, but the filmmakers asked for honest reviews.
GameLoading is a well-intentioned mess. There are excellent bits and pieces all throughout but the movie can't find a thread that logically or emotionally ties them together. It feels much longer than it is; creating an unfocused, scattershot pacing that never finds its footing.
I'm also not sure who this documentary is for? For an indie developer like me, its empty positive platitudes about the potential of games as a positive force is boring and patronizing.
There's not a lot of accessibility for people who play games as so much of the movie focuses on details of developer's day to day lives and development ideas. And it fails to be interesting to people who don't play games at all because no one in the film is speaking to them, and it's chock full of jargon and conventions that are foriegn to people outside the culutre.
It might work as something I can show my mom to make her feel good about my career choices.
I sometimes get the feeling that the subjects of the film are also being sometimes misrepresented. On twitter and elsewhere I know that these people's views on games are more interesting and nuanced than vague assertions that gaming and indie are just cool good things that are great. It seems that the filmmakers picked out the same kinds of empty happy soundbites from all the subjects without a consideration for a thesis or arc.
I'm glad the film was made because we can use some of its successes and failures and have something to look back on this period. The gender, sexuality and POC diversity is fairly strong. But next time, make a film that has something to say.

Here I am, once again writing a Steam review way past any reasonable sleeping hour. Having received Special Edition for free I admit that I might be a bit bias, but I'll try to keep this review as "Objective" as I can make it considering a lot of the aspects of Special Edition I'll be discussing are obviously somewhat subjective. My short personal opinion is that if you haven't already bought oldrim already it's well worth the money (especially on sale) and if you have it I believe it well worth migrating some time in the future.
I think this is the biggest topic being discussed currently within the community so I should get this out of the way first. Honestly, just as with Fallout 4, there just isn't enough here to give my full two cents about Creation Club. I think it's poorly implemented and Bethesda hasn't given a proper explanation of the services we actually get from this system which is my largest complaint towards Creation Club. With that out of the way I still believe Skyrim has one of the best modding experiance of any game to date. Special Edition is still awhile off from getting many mods from the original Skyrim ported over but those that have gotten updated are more than enough to fulfill one's desire to turn Skyrim into the game they want or just fix the stuff Bethesda should have done initially.
SSE isn't to the visual finesse offered by many games produced this generation of consoles or graphics cards nor is it to level of modded oldrim as this writing but I would be hard pressed to say this game is ugly. Special Edition can often be stunning to gawk at and while it has rough corners if you stare to close it can be amazing to look at when it wants you to. I also appreciate the lighting effects that Bethesda added in this game giving it some needed color in an otherwise drab color palette. Performance however is the most significant advantage over oldrim. Special Edition is by and far the best performing Bethesda title that I've played and is a massive improvement over the original which to this day I am unable to fully optimize.
Gameplay wise everything is standard affair if you already played Skyrim. You aren't getting any new vanilla content through this upgrade which is an honest shame because while the game is filled to the brim with content the game lacks variety in mission structure and the main story just isn't captivating or well written.
Skyrim Special Edition is a good addition to anyone who wants to get into the Elder Scrolls experiance but in a refined and polished condition for those who don't want pick into the systems brain and just want a plug and play Elder Scrolls title. While it disappointing that no new content was added and the depth from earlier TES games have been grinded down for mass market appeal it is still an experience that manages to fill a niche that few games really provide.

The 4th iteration of the Dominions series, it remains, as ever, a game for the hardcore multiplayer strategist. It is fantasy wargaming at its finest. Turn-based on the WE-GO system, in multiplayer this game will test your tactical and strategical skills as few others do, while juggling logistics based on an economy of ten to twelve primary resources, depending on how you count them. A plentitude of maps exist for the game and are available via mod-sites and, for those preferring randomness, it ships with a random map generator.
Sadly, the game is considerably better for multiplayer than singleplayer, as the AI is incapable of providing a challenge to any competent player: there are simply too many potential options to deal with in terms of magic; That said, a new player should expect dozens of hours of play before reaching a level where the AI can consistently be beaten on the highest difficulty setting and there's a live and vibrant multiplayer community for the game.

While I've only sunk in about 4 hours of playtime when I wrote this, I sank in about 2 - 3 hours studying the massive 295 page manual (half of it's just spell / unit statistics, so only 120 pages or so of reading). While the process of reading this manual was a bit oppressive and a rather large time investment just to start playing, from what I can see is there is a game with an incredible amount of depth and replayability.
Just from the start you get random worlds and the ability to craft your own "pretender" (basically a demigod) and then explore with the aim of conquering. There is espionage, assassinations, and management of your territories. Perhaps the only thing that's missing in my mind is diplomacy (it's a war game) but I for one never have really explored those aspects in games like this so nothing was really missing.
The difficulty of this title is steep, at least to someone like myself. What's good is that if you read the manual, you should be able to get several hours of playtime and experimentation before you start to get undermined by other nations. This gives you a good shot at your first playthrough to get a grasp on the basics before starting a hopefully more successful campaign.
The graphics are abhorrent, I won't lie, so if you need at least poor graphics to be satisfied I'd stay away. Graphics however are sacrificed for depth which to me, is far more important. There is so much complexity (but in a good way) to each aspect of the game: your towns (buildings, defense levels, dominion, etc.), the terrain, your soldiers (commanders, unit  types, formations, leadership, items), and a robust magic system as well.
I could go on, but I already fear that this review is a bit incoherent as there really is a lot to say about the game.
[B}TLDR[/B]
+Great Depth of Gameplay, incredible opportunities for strategy.
+Great Customization: Province Management, Commanders, Unit Types / Organization, Orders, etc.
+Very Replayable due to custom game modes.
+Tons of multiplayer options including classic favorites like Play By E-Mail and Hotseat
+Rich in Lore and Mythology based upon real life mythology.
+Tons of Unit Types, Spells, and Items
-Clunky UI, not reading / following the tutorial will make it very diffiuclt to get used to the controls.
-Incredibly huge manual (295 pages, of which 120 pages are essential reading) that you really must read if you don't want to spend many frustrating hours of trial and error.
-Absolutely hideous graphics, they really aren't good at all.

The game is purportedly very moddable and that's something I will explore as I get bored of the stock game as well!

As much as I may like the idea of the game, even after more than a year of post-release development, patches and payed DLC, the game still lacks sufficient amount of content. DLC is pretty much required to get any form of enjoyment from the game, since otherwise there will be hardly any mechanics more complex than collecting energy and minerals.
Utopia, despite what paradox may claim, is completely essential to the game in the same way that The Art of War is essential to EU4, without it there are is no assentation perks, no assentation paths, no megastructure, and no way to access all the features provided by Story Packs (Special Machine Empire Assentation Perks from Synthetic Dawn). The Megastructures have recently been buffed, but limited to one per type per empire, meaning that now the only way to sink excess resources is to build more fleet, but then then, the megastructures are not very interesting, simply granting science in case of the Nexus, Energy in case of the Dyson sphere, and unlimited sensor range in case of the Array (will cause immense lag). On the positive side, habitats added in the expansion allow for play a tall empire.
On the topic of Story Pack DLC, while Synthetic Dawn definitely added some content to the game, but ultimately machine empire unique government is exactly the same as the hivemind, except you cannot ascend the empire at all and instead get the ability to build machine worlds (if you have Utopia), and can get some additional trait points (if you have Utopia). The Leviathans ads some interesting stories to the game, but leviathans are rather "static", once you know the ship layout used to fight them and how much fleet power you need they become nothing more than a floating loot boxes.
The interactions with the AI Empires are limited to either trading excess resources with them creating a Federation, or declaring the war on them, no spying, no influencing the internal politics (sparking revolts like in EU4). Wars are just a drag, revolving around a single large fleet attempting to catch the enemy single large fleet and then sieging down the planets. Appallingly, player does not have any form of influence on the battles, you cannot tell the battleships to keep the distance, or to target specific enemy ships, just engage in battle, and occasionally emergency FTL out of it.
End game crises that are moved further and further into the late game as time progresses, which leads to the payer either being way to strong by the time the enemy arrives, or completely unprepared. If the crisis starts near your empire, and you are not yet a completely overwhelming force in the galaxy, you are done for. If it starts on the other edge of the galaxy, AI will hardly ever try to cooperate to defeat it without your involvement, and would much rather simply be defeated one by one.
All in all, Stellaris can definitely be a great game, but unfortunately it is not one yet, what it is in the current state (along with all the currently released DLC) is a foundation, which needs to be built upon, hopefully not in the form of Story Packs, that add slight variation of preexisting empires, but instead in form of new, player- involving systems, which will make the game more interactive and which will reward player initiative.
Suggestions:
Fleet Stances: Ability to give general commands to engaged fleets. (eg. “Ship Type” hold maximum distance; focus enemy “Ship Type”; “Ship Type” close the distance; etc.)
New Mega Structures/ Mega structure Interactions: Hostile AI appearing in the Science Nexus triggering a Localized Robotic Uprising Event within the Empire.  A hostile entity gaining access to your Sentry Array. Spiritualist empires being opposed to creation of Machine Worlds. etc.

Even though Hitman's first duo of releases had their share of problems, the series ended up finding success with gamers who couldn't get enough of dressing up in disguises and taking out contracted targets. The mystery surrounding protagonist Agent 47, and his cold, aloof nature is surprisingly alluring, in spite of the fact that he historically has very little dialogue, character development, and emotion. Two years after the release of Hitman 2: Silent Assassin comes Hitman: Contracts, a title that has had a mixed reception due to the fact that it rehashed some levels from Hitman: Codename 47.
At the very beginning of the game, Agent 47 is on a contract in Paris, where he is shot by an unknown assassin. Wounded and bleeding badly, he manages to return to his hotel room before he collapses into unconsciousness; as Agent 47 weaves in and out of near death, he reflects on his prior assignments, such as the escape from the cloning lab, and taking down a multitude of Triad members. Throughout the missions of the past, the player will be greeted with present day cutscenes of Agent 47 laying wounded in his hotel room; although the story isn't breathtaking by any means, it's enjoyable to experience the reimagined levels of Codename 47, some of which have multiple missions combined into one in this release.
Hitman: Contracts is the first game in the series where the developers really pumped up the blood and brutality; arguably, this release is the grittiest to date, and it's the first to feature violent deaths. From the very first mission, there are blood pools and smears all over the ground, and the second level takes place at an eerily strange party with a slaughterhouse theme; animal carcasses are hung everywhere, and the guests are dressed up in masquerade outfits. The dark, disturbing, almost psychological vibe carries on through the remainder of the game, and it helps that this is also the first Hitman title that has every mission take place at night. It should also be noted that only five missions from the original Hitman game are not featured in some way in Contracts.
The AI in this release is a lot better when compared to Codename 47 and Silent Assassin, you aren't spotted nearly as easily while wearing a disguise and it's easier to sneak up on enemies since they're not almost constantly looking behind them. Otherwise, there's not much difference in the overall gameplay and mechanics, that would come later. This title also features a slightly revamped HUD and inventory system that looks more sleek in comparison to its predecessors. Speaking in present day terms, this game also runs fine on current hardware and operating systems, unlike its two older counterparts. There's no need for any patches, FPS limiters, or .ini file modifications.
If you're new to the Hitman series, Contracts is a great place to start if you don't want to put up with trying to get Codename 47 and Silent Assassin to run properly. The game gives enough of a backstory to Agent 47 that newcomers won't feel too lost, although his true origin story isn't as detailed as it is in prior releases; to that degree, that's what watching YouTube playthroughs is for. Older fans of the series might not be so keen on replaying some previous contracts, but in the manner and detail of how they're remade makes it feel like you're playing brand new missions all over again. If you're down for the darkest, grittiest, and one of the most violent Hitman games, then Hitman: Contracts shouldn't be a game that you miss out on.

Hitman: Contracts is a remake of sorts of the first installment in the Hitman series, Codename 47.
This game made infinitely better the entire gameplay of the first and second installments, which sometimes missed proper instructions and/or had large empty maps.
With each mission given in this game, you are entirely free to choose your approach, either the Silent Assassin way which sometimes is hard but extremely gratifying, or the Rambo way entering the place guns blazing. The options are all scatered across the map, you only have to find the proper way to approach every situation. The freedom is still there. Do you want to snipe someone? There you go, take the sniper at the start. Want to take the Silent Assassin approach? Get close to your target by making him believe you're someone else. The challenges are there too. This is the first Hitman game to be done the right way. Sandbox style!
Obviously the graphics are outdated nowadays, but this game definitely has aged well, as it is as fun as it was when it first came out. After passing the entire game and all of its missions, sometimes I come back to play some Assassinations just to relax. That's how good this game is!
Anyway, just a heads up for all of you, if you're gonna play Blood Money too, the final mission in Contracts is tied to a mission of Blood Money, which makes the story more interesting!
Talking about the story, while some missions come back from the first game, there are a couple of Assassination Contracts which are entirely new to this game.
Anyway, final verdict 9/10, only because I played Blood Money and, hell... that's a 10/10.
Buy it, play it and don't regret it!

Nier:Automata is the sequel to the much appreciated yet fairly niche Nier. But through the involment of Platinum Games, this game was publicied much better and garnered way more attention than its predecessor. So alot of eyes were focused upon this game, but did it deliver on the overwhelming hype?
Yes. This game was my first game by the director Yoko Taro, and I have to say, I am impressed by his way of storytelling. He throws situations at you where you think you know how it will evolve, but then throws a curveball your way. There are tiny tidbits here and there game design wise that I do not agree with, but I get his standpoint. Other than that, the story is an amazing one. I would say it was good up until half-way through, which afterwards became a nonstop emotional ride.
As with any story-driven game, it needs good characters, which it has. Every single important character is given at least one arc of character development, even most of the sidequest givers.
The gameplay is amazing and action-packed, as expected of a Platinum Games game. At first I feared that it would become a button smasher a la Dynasty Warriors, but I was very pleased with the fact that the different weapons ingame have very different attributes and combo strings. On a relatively unrelated note, each weapon has a story attached to it. You learn more of it by upgrading said weapons. And even though there are more than 20 weapons ingame, all of them are in depth and white-knuckingly suspenseful. I dare to say some of them could even be a game on it self.
But there is a small issue I had, but it was not the games fault. I finished this game roughly 6 months after its release date, so people talking about it online were many. And of course, with it came spoilers. I was only spoiled in little sections here and there, but it led to the fact, that the game did not have as much of an impact on me as I would have thought, or hoped.
Yet overall, this game is definitely a mustbuy for everyone who wants a good story-driven game with amazing gameplay and characters. It is important to note that you do not have to have played the first game to fully enjoy this game. But the ones who do will be treated to many subtle and sometimes not-very-subtle easter eggs that will fill them with glee. I haven't but this game definitely was a huge incentive for me to do so. And to end this: Yes. You need this game in your life.
Also the age old question: 2B or A2? There are no wrong answers, only good ones.

If you are involved in the indie gaming, there won't be much new to learn (though I still did learn things I wasn't aware of before). I did enjoy the"feel good" moments - self-validation is always a nice feeling, isn't it?
As for newcomers, I've found it an excellent way to introduce them to the reasons I am so interested in the scene. It does do a nice job summing it all up, even while it's a little vague or nonspecific.
It's true that there is a certain formlessness to the film. And I agree there is some unbalanced camera time for some of the developers.
What you get out of this movie will likely depend on what you expect when going in.
Edit: I viewed this on the website before it was released on Steam, hence, at the time of this posting, "0.0 hours watched."

Still getting more out of this even on the third viewing.
Recommended for anyone who has an hour an a half to spend on learning about the people making indie games

Game Loading offers an informative glimpse into the world of Indie Gaming as it follows  a few different storylines.  The biggest thing that stood out for me aboutt his documentary was the focus on the human aspect of indie game development and how much these projects mean to their respective developers.  Each approach taken by the developers in this documentary is different, but they're all linked by a desire to create a good game that people will get enjoyment out of in ways that go beyond simply taking up time; enjoyment from a rich story to unique concepts to deeply emotional connection.  The Indie scene sets itself a part from AAA developers by being more in tune with a new generation of diverse gamers as well as by striving for unique concepts as opposed to rolling with a generic formula.
Finally, this documentary was as much about the Indie gaming scene as it was about telling you, the viewer, how you can start working on your own projects; from specific tools to use to development-pitfalls to avoid, the developers here seemed as interestd in empowering other people to start making games as they were in their own work.
If you're interested in gaming, at all, I would highly recommend that you check out this movie.  You won't be disappointed.

First the disclosure: I backed the kickstarter for enough to get the movie. ( I think it was around 10-15 euro)
I have seen this five times now (outside Steam), and it hasn't gotten old yet. I've been a gamer for a long time, and recently started learning game development as well. It is incredibly empowering to hear the stories of successful indie developers. The message I'm getting is that you don't have to be a superhuman to gamedev. You do need a drive for creating things, and the rest of the details you can learn as you go. And like John Romero says, you can start coding today. All the necessary tools are free now, which enables anyone with a computer to tell their stories via games. For me personally this realization has been huge.
There's something to be said about this movie being for a niche audience (indie game developers). While there is some truth to that certainly, my partner, who is a social worker, was also inspired by the independent and do-it-yourself attitudes of the interviewed people. I think she would like to have some of that in her field of work as well. So even if you don't have any interest in making games, I think you can still appreciate the passion with which these people work and relate that in whatever you are feeling strongly about.
The production values seem totally convincing to me, picture quality, camera work, sound and a great soundtrack all pass my inspection. I certainly feel like I got my money's worth out of the kickstarter and then some. I strongly recommend this to anyone who is into game development themselves. Still a good watch to anyone who has any kind of passion project going on. (And of course the friends and family of the above, to help understand them better :) )

As a fellow gamedev, films like this always part inspire and part depress me - wishing I was more successful with my own games and living the indie life 24/7 ;)
This is a seriously top-quality film and well worth checking out if you're interested in games development or have a friend/family member who is in/studying/interested in a career in games. Brings home the realities of the industry, but also highlights the passion which drives it and the diversity of products it produces - it's not all violence and "addicting" games to catch out kids with their parents' credit cards.
Well shot, great content, and really heartwarming. Love it!

GameLoading: Rise of the Indies represents a great snapshot of the indie game development scene at this very moment in time. If Indie Game: the Movie was a documentary about Sex Pistols, this would be a documentary about Punk Rock in the 70s. A realistic overview of the indie scene, spanning through different game events, different projects, and different aspects of game development.
NOTE:
The hour counter is at 0h because I watched GameLoading before having it on Steam.
Gameloading does a great job of highlighting some of the diverse members of the indie game development community and the kinds of experimental games they're making.

An entertaining documentary that provides a glimpse into the (often eccentric) people behind some of the most entertaining and interesting indie games. It focuses heavily on the machinations that influences these developers' art. Unexpectedly emotional - touching on personal loss and the unfortunate rise of misogyny and on-line abuse towards female, homosexual, and transgender people in and around the industry of game development.

King's Bounty: Legions comes from a long line of King Bounty games, which in turn come from an even longer line of King Bounty games, yeah crazy right?
King's bounty started life on the Amiga and was ported to several other home computers before morphing into the Heroes of Might and Magic series which still runs today. King's bounty was shelved, Heroes of Might & Magic lived on and Nival bought the rights to King's Bounty making their own series of games, similar to the original but with a modern take in terms of graphics and gameplay style.

I am new to the series, with that said I do enjoy this game. I've spent quite a few hours playing it and have bought some gems (I believe if you enjoy a free to play game its only right to buy some stuff).
Pros
-The game is fun and has a decent level of depth to the strategy and diverse content.
-You can let the ai play for you, which is great when you want to watch a movie and play the game at the same time.
-A multitude of deiffering monsters and soldiers to pick from.
-UI is easy to navigate and understand, except for the chat system.
-Units are very indepth with different abilities and counter classes.
Cons
-Adding friends is a pain and a chore, I made the mistake of signing up through my facebook, after trying for a few hours to find out how to add steam friends I couldn't figure it out.
(To fix this I would just do what normal games do and add friends through the game, then add a facebook friend option as a secondary method).
-the chat sytem is a pain, it constantly put me back into the sytem chatbox, only shows two boxes at a time which forces me to scroll to the clan chat. You can't talk in chat or clan chat while in a fight.
- Again I understand the p2w model and am not against it for the most part. But to keep your legendary and even "blue" units topped off at full strength you don't have many other options which will cause you to stall out at around level 20+.
(A solution I can see would be to allow players to save up items and use them along with a long cooldown to upgrade unit I.E a knight with several pieces of armor can be trained into a paladin, A swordsmen can be trained into a knight. this would give a deeper crafting system and not make players feel overly pressured into buying units with gems).
- the gems don't feel scaled stuff is a little expensive like a paladin costing 28 gems, thats fine if I was only buying one every couple levels but not when I need a new paladin every level.
This is just a brief review I'm sure I am missing a few points but over all I would recommend this game. If you have any questions please ask.

I went into this game with low expectations, since what I played of the first Saints Row was more-or-less a GTA clone. But I was really surprised at how awesome this game is. In the first hour of the game I witnessed a samurai ninja gang member run after and attack a female streaker who was running around taunting people, followed by a guy walking around in a hotdog costume. On top of this, I discover a song by my favorite band on one of the in game radio stations. At this point, this was already an awesome game and I enjoyed most of my time playing it.
In this game you play as the leader of the Saints, the same character from the first game, and you have to take over the city of Stilwater once again from three new gangs. Each gang had unique, well written generals and leaders, and the boss fights with them were quite interesting, though in some cases frustrating because of iffy controls. There was lots of humor in the game, some of it unintentional, but this really helped the game stand apart from the standard GTA formula.
I had few issues with the game apart from the two or three annoying bosses. Most of the cars are really bad to drive in, either slow, or bad handling. I stuck to a police car for most of the game. Fast, and turns well. I also had problems with checkpoints forcing me to redo entire missions after something like an apache helicopter appears out of nowhere and I can't avoid it and die. This gets annoying but overall, it didn't hurt the overall gameplay.
The best thing about this game is that it's fun. There's a lot of wacky stuff in here, like driving around in a septic truck and spraying houses and stuff to lower property values and whatnot. This game is unique and memorable, and I think I enjoyed the game more than GTA. And this is only the beginning. From what I've heard, the games just get wackier and more epic from this point, but this was an excellent starting point for me, since I can't really play the first Saints Row.
TL;DR
This game is fun, unique, the story is strong, and the characters are memorable. Play this game!

Guns of Icarus Online is a very fun online co-op/role-based game. It sets you in a dystopian, steampunk environment, as you and your crew man an Airship armed to the teeth. Hop in, find a good crew, and destroy your enemy!
Need-to-knows:
- Do all three role tutorials before starting. They are easy to figure out, but if you go into a game with no knowledge, your crew will most likely become annoyed with you.
- I find this game a lot of fun by yourself, but some may not. It is definitely more fun with friends, and this game has crews of four. If you can find 3 friends, its an absolute blast!
- This game has a built in push-to-talk system. If you can participate, it makes communication a lot easier. Know that a lot of users will use explicit language, but there is an audio setting just for it, you can turn it all the way down. There is even a way to completely disable it, so you won't accidentally active your audio.
- It has pretty advanced graphics. I have a good computer, but an old computer. Often some things such as the flamethrower will cause my frames to drop quite low.
- Each role can participate in other roles. Be prepared to adapt to many different scenarios.
- AIs aren't all that bad if you have one on your crew, as captain, f1 will put them at ease. F2 will set them to attack. F3 will set them to repair! Utilize them to the furthest extent.
- Faction can be changed, and it is not too important to the game. It is a lot of fun however!
Roles:
Engineer - Whack anything and everything, buff the engines, and keep the ship in the sky. A simple role, but a busy one.
Gunner - Use the various guns to shoot down enemies. It is easy to aim, but various ammos and guns are required to take down ships. Be sure to learn whats what, after a time you can find some combos that shred through ships.
Captain - Pilot the ship through thick and thin. Tell your crew what to do, play it safe and line up shots, or go in for a ram!
I'd reccomend doing some 1v0 practice rounds before playing this role, and generally becoming comfortable with the controls.
Ships:
There are various ships in the game for various reasons. Pyramidion is best for ramming. Squid is best for speed. Galleon is a tank. Goldfish is extremely powerful, but only with a good team.
I highly reccommend this game. All roles are fun, and even though its a seemingly basic game, it keeps me coming back for more!
My Experience:
- 26 hours in game.
- I'm mostly an engineer, who usually mans the gatling part-time. I have experience as captain though, and have recieved compliments as a pilot from veterans.
- I have 4 friends who own the game, as a group it can be an absolute blast, and be quite hilarious, too.
