I've put hundreds of hours into the Xbox 360 version, and was hoping to do the same with the PC version. Sadly this port is infamous for not running well even with mods like "gentlemen of the row".
Saint's Row 2 is considered by the core Saint's Row fan-base to be the best game in the franchise, and with good reason. Fun gameplay, tons of customization, an open world that feels alive, diverse characters, and a surprisingly good plot. Saint's Row 2 is great because unlike the new "Saint's Row" games the silliness is juxtaposed against a very realized world. The story is blends humor and drama perfectly, unlike the newer games in the franchise which attempt (for lack of better phrasing) "lolSOrandom" humor. That's not to say there isn't a lot of humor in this game, there is. But its never shoved in your face like it is in the newer entries of the series. Saint's Row 2 gives you an open world to do what you please in. Wanna play the game like a straitlaced sandbox action game? You can do that. Wanna play the game dressed as a hotdog using nothing but shock paddles as weapons? You can do that too. The game is as serious or as goofy as you choose to make it.
So, would i recommend Saint's Row 2? Yes, its one of my favorite games of all time and the last true Saint's Row game in the eyes of the core fan-base (myself included).
Would i recommend the PC port? That depends on the player. If you're willing to toy around with mods and settings go for it. It's not expensive anymore and when it works its wonderful.

You will struggle to find enemies, or get to objective, especially since respawns are so far away that you will spend most of the game trying to get into action and when you do, well suprise suprise - you get killed and have to repeat the process.

Sound have not seen improvement since beta (there are two types of sounds in game: screams and explosions 1 meter from you - even if you are at least 50 or more meters away, or the same screams etc. 1 mile away). I must add annoying sounds of speakers (at least you can mute them if I remember correctly).
Icons and overall HUD, are at best average (e.g.: too small icons, for beginners you sometimes don't know where to focus your attencion).
If you enjoyed red orchestra 2 and rising storm - live with those pleasent memories, as vietnam will only get you frustrated rather quickly.
For this price, game that still looks in many parts as beta, without proper patches, it's just not worth it.

Rising Storm two: Vietnam.
Let me start off by saying this game is not your average cod or counter strike.. you wont take 5-6 bullets before you die.. you will take one. and if you are lucky two, but have to get in cover bandaging for quite some time, so you will not bleed out, as your best freind is right in front of you and his brains are blown against the wall. or the enemy is just around the corner advancing.
Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is based in the Vietnam war, and forces the american army against the northern vietnamese in 64 player matches that can last anywhere from 10 minutes to an hour, depending on how each team plays. featuring a veriety of classes, each with unique roles and positions to play in the team, as well as your squad, you must coordinate with your team and squad to capture objectives. the better the teamwork, the higher the chances of victory.
This game is heavily immersive. from the stunning graphics and sounds to the intense combat supresstion as you go deaf and blind as bullets hit the wall or your buddy next to you. ear-peircing artillery shells blow your team to bits as an arm flies at you and lands at your feet. as your freind next to you is hit in the chest he falls to the floor bleeding out and he cries, moans and weeps. chokes on blood as he slowly dies. The horrifying screams of your entire squad being burned to death by a napalm strike. Youre in a helicopter and it is lit up with machine gun fire, and you see both pilots get hit and the helicopter falls, and crash lands. as you pull yourself out of the wreckage, and look behind you, everyone is dead. and you look up and for a split second you see a barrel in your face. and *Kink* the last sound you hear as the bullet enters your head, and nothing but black and silence.
Then there is the team play. A veriety of classes including a commander, each with their own guns, leads to a balanced team, which has to work together in order to win. The commander, the most inportant one of the team, calls in artilery strikes on locations designated by squad leaders. you communicate with your team and other players with voice chat in seperate channels, Vehicle, team, squad, and public, and coordinate attacks, defenses, and more.
However no game is perfect. like all other games this one has a flaw.
Bugs.

I've gotta be honest, When I first saw Stellaris, I believed it would be similar to the Civ series and Endless Legends. I was even excited about the possible Halo or Sci-Fi senarios as mods. While it might encompass the 4-X strategy model, I feel that it never executes it as perfect and as enjoyable as the Civ series
My main issue include, but are not limited to;
- Early game's boring: When survying systems or locating new territories, it never feels different from the start of your previous games. This isn't like Age of Empires II, where your start and stragety will vary depending on your location and the resources near you; it's more like "Well, I better get survying and wait for a habitable planet". When your given the chance to name planets and feel connected to them, they sure give no emotion to those other systems with about 3 minerals in them.
- Fleets ain't cutting it: After getting a good economy and wanting to invest it, it seems that it's mostly going into military. That's fine though, what I have an issue with is the combat.
Do you remember when the brilliant general Hannibal heroically won at the battle of Cannae with four times the enemy's numbers. Neither did I, because he was outnumbered about 1:10! So when I have pretty well upgrated ships flying into the forces of an "inferior" empire while being outnumbered 2:3 and losing, it's not really fun. I know if you increase the firerate of a fleet, it increases damage, but I feel that suggesting "numbers win" defeats the purpose of trying to upgrade an army and seeing your power increase in practice.
- AI is kinda broken: I'll admit that I would prefer to vs. a computer than a human. It's just to do with lag and my bad internet to be honest, but I got to admit, I don't like it. You remember that combat section? Yeah, it really digs into your economy when having that many ships, but somehow the AI seems to ALWAYS contains a larger fleet than me. hmmm.
I thought we got over this kinda of lazy programming stuff after the early RTS games of the 21st century and giving the AI resourse advantages (I was also playing on normal), but it seems some things never change.
And yeah, that's may subjective opinion about Stellaris. I guess 1 in 10,000 have bad service at MCdonalds and never come back, but I would like to get comments about how I could have a better time. It might be because I played the game wrong, but this isn't bloodborne or a Souls game (shoutout to HBomberGuy :) and I think I'm capable to not having to reasearch guides.

is a KILLER game (pun intended).
Alright, now that's out of the way... On to the real review.
This game is speed platforming at its finest. With a 30-second timer pushing you along, you really have to think fast to progress through the floors of the tower while killing enemies and replenishing the timer along the way. You have several tools in your arsenal: melee weapons, ranged weapons, and bombs all have their uses, and you also have magic spells to help out in a pinch. Melee and ranged weapons will be your main combat tools, because you have a limited number of bombs and magic to use. Some enemies will kill you before you can reach them with a melee attack, so you'll have to use a ranged attack to kill them. This adds an element of strategy, because you need to decide when to attack with which weapon. And as you progress, you will unlock other weapons to use beyond the standard katana, shuriken, and bombs. For example, I use "Death's Gleaming Scyth" for my melee weapon, which beheads all enemies, and "Scorpion's Hookshot" for my ranged weapon, which is essentially a deadly grappling hook. Bomb upgrades are a little harder to come by, so I just use the standard bomb for now. There are 11 melee weapons, 14 ranged weapons, and 12 bombs to choose from, plus 4 magic spells, for a total of 7,392 different weapon combinations to choose from. Add to that all the various item and weapon upgrades, such as adding extra lives or being able to carry more bombs, and you have quite an incentive to keep playing the game because there are just so many things to unlock.
Gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from a ninja game with a 30-second timer: hectic and fun. There are lots of different enemies to face, and they each act a little bit differently. Some will throw ranged attacks at you, others just run back and forth in an area, and many more. This makes playing the game a lot more interesting than just "melee attack anything that moves" because you'll need to be smart and know when to duck to avoid a ranged attack, how to counter enemies that can block your attacks if they see you coming, etc.
The physics in this game are perfect for a frantic platformer. Gravity must be higher in this world, because you fall really fast, which helps you progress more quickly but also makes it harder to plan for sneak attacks from above. You can also cling to walls or double jump to slow yourself down or reach higher places, which is a nice touch.
SHODN's music is great, very Oriental-feeling but with a nice upbeat tempo that reminds me a bit of "Kung Fu Fighting" by Carl Douglas. Perfect for a ninja beat-em-up (or in this case, cut-em-up).
Overall, this is one of my favorite modern platformers. It's fun and crazy, with enough strategy and variety to keep me interested and coming back for more. Definitely recommended for any fans of platforming games, or anyone who wants to kill lots of pixelated ninjas and die a lot. Because you will die A LOT, especially when you're first starting out and learning which enemies do what.

This game ... it is something special.
Not just because it does certain things that only a video game can do, or the way it's structured and the story is conveyed, but because it explores existential horror better than any other game, and is at the same time very beautiful, funny and human.
The world it's set in is a fantastical canvas for Yoko Taro to go batshit philosophical on you, and it's a joy to experience.
Oh, did I mentioned the soundtrack? It is easily one of the best video game OSTs out there, period. I was not familiar with Keiichi Okabe or Keigo Hoashi before Automata, but now just can't get enough of their music.
Don't get intimidated when you hear the game has 26 endings and requires multiple playthroughs. These are more like chapters in a book, and play very differently to provide unique points of view.

I've heard a lot about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the port is but I personally wasn't affected. Well, the resolution thingy sucks but there's FAR to fix that so no harm done.
And the game itself?
Story is beautiful, deep, soul-crashing at times and is one of the best storylines I've experienced in gaming for a while (last one was Witcher 3). Do yourself a favour and complete all three playthroughs - ending the game at the first one will rob you from the experience - first playthrough is merely very good, it's the third one where the real wonderful story is.
Gameplay is amazing, diverse and dynamic. You have your typical 3D hack-and-slash combat, you have bullet hell intermissions, you have sidescroller sections, you have top down sections, you have shoot-em-up sections, even visual novel sections at moments (thankfully quite short as I am not a fan of those). And the best thing is that's super fluid, interconnected and doesn't feel like forced diversification - it simply works.
This game is definitely a must-have and one of the best titles I've played.

Now I know what you might be thinking looking at the images and pictures and all. "What is this weaboo♥♥♥♥♥♥ How come people like it so much? Is it because they haven't played any other games?" Those are all valid questions and while the fanservice in this game is a little bit unnecessary, every single other aspect of this game outshines it by miles. Don't let that outfit on the cover turn you off from such an incredible experience, because everyone even those not fans of gaming have to play this. When I finished it for the first time I immediately started to write this review, because everyone needs to play this game at least before they die, it's really that good.
Think of a Hayao Miyazaki movie turned up to 200% in the form of a game, then you're probably gonna get something like this.
If you're a person who likes great gameplay, get this game. It combines real-time combat with panic and danger, especially with the high amount of damage that enemies do.
If you're a person who likes an unforgettable story, get this game. Yoko Taro showed how much of a master of storytelling he is in the previous NieR game and only proves it further in this entry in the now extremely popular series. The story is so utterly incredible that I counted two times where I have actually shed a few tears for a minute or so, and that is astounding for I have played games like Planescape: Torment, Final Fantasy 6 and 7, and many other great stories and have not gotten as emotional as I have in NieR: Automata. No other game has had me so emotionally connected to the story.
If you're a person who likes an incredible soundtrack that you will literally never get tired of, then get this game. Massive props to those who made the music in this game since it really is the best I have ever heard, as it immerses you into the game even more. I actually even listen to at least one piece of it every day ever since I finished the game for the first time.
This game has just about everything anyone could ever ask for. This game combines so many genres and elements from other games, integrated into the normal gameplay style perfectly.
The character design matches the character's personality and overall feel perfectly. I just can't emphasize how incredible this game is, for it will make so many other games I play in the future feel dull and a waste of time in comparison to the fun and emotions I had in NieR: Automata.
Of course, in order to have such a great time you have to at least beat ending B and beyond into E to get maximum joy, as I've seen people make the idiotic mistake of not playing past the first ending and never discovering the others, as playing just for Route A is not the way to go.
Trust me, this may seem like a waste of time judging by the images and the like but this game is so beautiful underneath that. This game has so many emotions that will pass through you as you play unlike any other game in ANY genre.
But don't get me wrong there is definitely not some refined aspects as well, albeit being small. For example this game can be very frustrating at points. If you die then you have to collect all the stuff your previous body had off it like upgrades and the like, but if you die before you do get your body back then you lose all of the upgrades and have to start all over again from square one. Thankfully that has never happened to me but for more inexperienced people it may prove so infuriating to the point of ragequitting, which is simply not fun.
Also Route B is repetitive, especially when it's practically the same as Route A which we just played through. This is the number one thing that turns people off from playing the game further to the end, and it's the biggest problem I have with this game. You'll know what I'm talking about if you've played it before. But honestly those two problems pale in comparison the rest of what this game offers.
Well anyway I don't want to drone on about how great this game is and bore you when you should instead be playing it right now experiencing it for yourselves, it really is an unforgettable journey that proves gaming is not simply a thing for children but for everyone.
Do note that this PC port is extremely buggy to the point of being completely unplayable to some people, so if you could I would reccomend getting the PS4 edition as it doesn't require for you to install the FAR mod which fixes a lot of stuff in the PC port. I didn't have to play with FAR since my rig can apparently run any bad PC port but be warned what you're getting into as I've seen people not even being able to so much as launch the game on startup.
A lot of people may think otherwise, but I do really think this is truly the best video game there is to date. Seriously, get this game and try it, and play it to the end. Don't just turn this game down by the cover, and don't watch the trailer either, it spoils too much. I'm telling you, this is an experience in gaming unlike any other. The ending credits is also a game unto itself.
This is a beautiful game, and I wish Yoko Taro a really good time in his life, he deserves it for making this. I also gotta thank videogamedunkey for introducing me to this game, it really has changed my view on not only gaming as a medium, but life in general.
Even at full price you won't regret getting this, in fact I feel slightly guilty not paying for it in the first place.

Polarity is a fairly simple 3D first-person puzzle platformer.  It's rather short; I beat the single player game in one sitting in an afternoon.  The game also contains a split-screen co-op mode and a set of bonus levels.
It lacks a lot of polish that makes similar puzzle games great: the menus are rather old looking, although the level select in the background is nice; there are a few clipping errors here and there, but nothing overt; the textures are a little flat, but there are is a nice shadow effect around the edges of things that make everything look a little bit nicer.
The single player puzzles are rather easy, and the co-op puzzles seem to be a bit harder.  However, it seems that the co-op mode has even less polish than the main game, with the cube spawn sites not even having the fancy model that the single player campaign uses.
I'd rate this game as a fairly good entry into the genre for someone who hasn't played much.  But for anyone looking for a well polished game or much of a challenge, it's best to look elsewhere.

Slayaway Camp is a puzzle game at its core.  It is an homage to slasher flicks of the 80s and early 90s in a puzzle game setting.  You play as a series of killers in different movies tasked with killing victims.  The catch is that you have to move in a direction until you hit a wall, object, or your victim.  If you move left, your character goes until he hits something.  So kill the victims and escape through the portal.  Simple.
But then the game starts throwing new mechanics into play.  As you progress through each scene/level, you will be introduced to different things.  Scenes which require you to finish within a certain number of turns, scenes that involve holes, mines, cops, and other objects that make your objective more difficult.
There are quite a number of levels.  I have gotten through the first 4 movies and still it seems I have much more to get through.  If you get stuck, the game offers you a hint.  For a price, you can get a hint or a step by step walkthrough of the level.  How does this work?  You gain coins after each level, which is used to unlock these kills.
I recommend this game to puzzle fans that enjoy horror flicks, or just want a different type of puzzler.

Saints Row 2 is a great game. If you haven't played the first one you should be ok (I never played the first one) the game does a good job telling you what happened, and I never felt lost story wise. However, there were some times when I felt that they referenced the first game, but it only felt like if my friends had an inside joke that I wasn't part of. Overall, the story was good, and I understood it. If you are coming at this after playing futer installments, you will notice that the tone is way different. It is much more serious and in many cases really brutal like when you are taking out key members of a rival gang. However, there is still tons of humor. Good examples being, driving around in a septic truck shooting sewage at houses to lower the property value, you and Pierce's arguments about which radio station to watch, the character interactions in general, and the news and advertisements that play on the radio. A thing that the game does really well at is the side missions. There is a huge variety of them from standard ones like stealing cars to the previously mentioned spraying buildings with sewage to lower the property value. Another thing that the game does well is the story progression. You have the freedom to really do what you want to do from the very begining. You can pick which gang mission you want to do, if you want to topple one before the other, or if you want to try to attack them all at the same time. However, my biggest problem is that there was a few more glitches than I would have liked, but I only had to restart once, and I crashed twice. Other than that the game was well designed, and all around a blast to play.

Stellaris is the kind of game you play when you want to focus more on the large scale aspect of galactic 4X.  In this you are the supreme ruler, but that does not mean you oversee the movements of every unit and track the building of every colony.
With a real-time-with-pause time system and a slick notifications interface you get to direct your civilization from it's first days of interstellar exploration up to it's domination or collapse.  Rather than playing with simple "racial bonuses" to differentiate various groups Stellaris has you playing with everything from cultural influence and governmental changes to genetic or technological modification.  You can create your own races like in may current galactic empire games, but the game also procedurally generates groups for you to encounter, preventing games from feeling like the same encounters time and again.
However, this is not the sort of game you play if you like to focus on micromanaging your troops/ships in battle.  Once units engage in conflicts you must sit back and watch, only having the right to call for retreat should you feel the tide turning against you.
In the end Stellaris has a dedicated developer regularly releasing new free content and updates along side paid deluxe DLC.  Their regular communication with their player community is commendable and their work to refine and improve on an innovative game makes it that much more enjoyable.  I highly suggest this game for anyone that enjoys games such as SimCity and who are ready to sit down and spend time really learning a game.  For players that prefer Starcraft style tactics you may want to watch some Youtube play videos of the current version so you can be sure of what you are getting ahead of time.

Hitman: Contracts is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Sqaure Enix and is the third game in the Hitman series. As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness
It puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed, the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
However, the game is not without its flaws. For a game nearly 10+ years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. Probably the biggest gripe however is the in-game saving option, which does not exist. If you are spotted in the middle of a mission or die, you will need to start the mission over. While not a big issue in the earlier missions, this can become extremely frustrating on the later missions where you need to navigate a huge mansion with tons of guards and one mis-step means you're killed and need to restart
However, Hitman: Contracts is a brilliant stealth game for its generation

Fun, well designed, and dated. Time was not kind to this one.
Enemy AI is basic, but mostly functional. They work on a distance/speed based detection system. If you run they can detect you faster, and if you get near them or, worst of all, bump them they'll leave a gooey wetspot where you stood.
The main issue i have with it is that you can't always tell if your in an area that you arent allowed to be in, until guards start swarming your position with machine guns.
Shooting is suprisingly well done. You really feel the impact your bullets have on their unsuspecting cranium, and it's only aided by the basic physics system that sends bodies flying when you shoot them. I highly recommend pulling duel pistols and spraying the level to the ground.
Level design is great as usual for this series, but unlike the levels in other games, they seem to like to stay in one setting a lot. You revisit the streets of hong kong a few too many times for my liking.
The other problem with a few of them is that they are way too big. Theres one level thats about a mile across, with objectives sprinkled in between. It will take most people about 20-30 minutes to finish just because they had to run from end to end, and if they mess up or run into someone in between, mission restart. Slightly alieviated by a save system on lower difficulties but good luck on anything higher.
Despite the wonky AI and the overly long levels, this is probably my 2nd favorite in the series, bested only by Blood Money. If you're willing to put up with early 2000s budget stealth mechanics, this is a must buy.
PS: If you play blood money before this one you will regret it. This one will feel incredibly dated in comparison and it may detract from your experience.

There is still no patch. But they released DLC and declare the good sales of the game on the PC. And they lie about working on it. This is not a driver problem, it's game problem, and modder already fixed main problems - just include it in game.
It's a very good game, but it's time to do something, at least this.
You can dislike as you want, but it's time to open your eyes and stop believing in their lies.

Negatives-
Pre-release quality game. I have experienced 2 problems with the game that aren't small. For me the game loads with a resolution bug that starts the game in a mode similar to when you alt-tab out of a game. The game isn't visible and in a pause state but it is running under task manager. Rendering the game unplayable. This was fixed using an unofficial patch called FAR mod, but some releases didn't play well with releases of the steam overlay so I found myself seeing this bug several times. The game at a number of noticeable points goes from super smooth to judder and back affecting play, there is no apparent complexity in the scenes when it occurs.
The game follows “for the sake of artistic vision practices” over “user friendliness practices”. This is great if you become a real fanboy of the game but it makes it frustrating to play the game casually. 3 examples.
1) The introduction has no save function but the rest of the game has a safe function.
Imagine spending hours waiting for the game to download. Then having to research how to get the game to run. Then dying 30 minutes in from getting lightly hit and getting stuck in a bugged hit loop and having to go back to the start. Then having to re fix the game so it runs the second time you play. Frustrating, uninteresting and no fun!
Some people don’t experience any of this but a sizeable number do. Then you get to read the fanboy comments on forums to try to work out what’s going on “This game runs perfect it’s your system” to try to find the occasional useful comment on how to get the FAR mod and how far you have to get to be able to save.
2) You can install chips that improve your defensive, attacking and general skill abilities. You have a limited number of space to install chips. You can combine two identical chips to make a better version of the chip but it takes up more space. You can get special versions of these chips that can take up less space that are rarer. Chip space can be upgraded in a store. However this is all implemented in the menu system with as little emphasis as everything else in the menu system such as music select. So expect to have to pay attention to every little thing in the game to not miss important parts of the game! Not easy with work and family commitments.
Finally you often have to complete side quests firsts to ensure that the story doesn’t advance over them. Which often meant that I had very little freedom of choice.
Design-
The game has about 30 endings. Well no it doesn’t. It has an introduction, 3 chapters, and a multiple choice ending, then around minor 25 cut short endings for fanboys. Why the 3 chapters are called endings I don’t know. It takes around 40 hours for one play through.
You play as 1 human shaped character at a time that fights its way around 1 town and surrounding area completing quests. You are equipped with a spam sword attack, spam dodge, jump, and an invincible flying box that shoots at enemies. The little flying box could complete the game better all by itself!
Easy mode can reduce some of the frustration in the game by allowing the installation of chips that automate some functions. Installing automated dodge ensures you cannot get stuck on a nasty boss. Installing automating the flying box reduces the multitasking and helps you to practice your own dodge and attack techniques.
Positives-
The story, artistic style, vision, emotion and depth is fantastic. The introduction was shallow, and the first chapter was OK, but the great part of the game is that it is layered like an onion and it kept letting you delve deeper and re-experience events with greater perspective. Absolutely brilliant right the way through to the furthest story ending possible. This ending includes a very unique sacrifice choice that let me walk away from the game with a new gaming experience. I’m not going to go into detail about the story, artistic style, vision, emotion and depth because that is what you should experience for yourself by playing. I’m only going to say that it was good enough for me to finish the game praising it to others and highly recommending it. Even with the frustrations I experienced playing it.

I'm not huge on puzzle games, so if I recommend one it's going to be something different. Puzzle game about mass murder good enough for you? Slayaway Camp mixes dark humor, varied design and an addictive unlocking system to make a great time waster. It also runs well on very low spec systems which is a big bonus.
Video review:

The Good: Almost everything, from the way its packed with refrences and jokes without being too in your face about them, to the fact that its a slasher movie game that actually has solid gameplay, to the fact that thanks to the addition of the N17 scenes that were not in the free online version meaning that I can keep playing after I finish the main game, to the over-the-top personalities of the slashers to the utter lack of pretentions. And you can earn lots and lots of different killers. It even will show you the solution to puzzles your stuck on for in-game money. The game engages in constant affectionate slasher movie parody without going so far it looks stupid or like it has a self-loathing complex.
The Bad: The way you grind coins actually requires reflexes, the hints are not as helpful as they could be. Also, the game's target demographic is very narrow, only people who have watched slasher movies before the era of self-awareness would get all the jokes. The game could use more options, like replacing the cats with dogs or deliberately bad picture and audio for that 'old vhs' feel. Also, its a trifle too counter-intuative at times how to solve some puzzles.
Overall, I give it a 9/10. I want more, but what is there is excellent. Only the lack content and sneaking supsicion the game is just an evil plan to get people who hate puzzle games to play a puzzle game keep me from giving it a perfect score.

I'm not normally a huge puzzler, but I do adore slasher movies, and this hits a lot of sweet spots for me thematically. It's hard to stay frustrated with even the most hellish of puzzles when the deaths are delightfully over-the-top and accompanied by an almost Mortal Kombat-eque "MURDERLICIOUS!"
The music is pleasantly ominous, and the recorded songs by GNÜ TRUNTION are a ton of fun. I've played the Faces of Killed 3 mini game over and over again just to keep Only the Strong Survive looping over the splatter noises.
If you like slasher horror tropes with your brain teasers, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's a really fun little game with a surprising amount of thought put into it.  10/10

Slayaway Camp is a simple, straightforward puzzle game where you play the killer in an 80s style slasher flick who has to navigate various traps and use the layout of the rooms you're in to efficiently murder your victims. Just like any good puzzle game, the game's mechanics start off super simple and get increasingly complex (as traps, stacking and scaring victims, and the authorities get involved) the further along you go making for some pretty serious head scratchers toward the end.
Lots of unlockable characters and even more unlockable death sequences (little animated bits that play during/between levels).
Enjoyed the puzzle mechanics and enjoyed the developer's genuine affection for 70s/80s slasher movies. For an under-$10 indie game, it has a ton of content (hundreds of puzzles) but if you want to just do the main "story" content, it won't take you more than 8-10 hours.
Only knocks on the game I would say are the Minecraft-y look which was initially a turnoff for me but that's probably a selling point for some people and there seemed to be too many levels where there was essentially one solution which made it very trial and error. Still... definitely recommended for fans of smart puzzle games and double recommended if you also enjoy the campiness (no pun intended) of old 80s slasher movies.

Fan of easy-to-learn yet challenging puzzle games? Sure!
Fan of gory slasher flicks from the 80's? Yeah! (But what does that have to do with anything?)
Would you like a game that mixed both? Wait..., WHAT!? :O
Slayaway Camp is a sliding puzzle game where you take control of the main hero (come on, everyone knows that the killers in those movies were the true heroes!) in each movie of the "Slayaway Camp" series. Each movie is made up by many set pieces (puzzles) where the goal is to slay all victims. It all starts simple enough, but each chapter introduces new mechanics that add quite a bit of challenges the farther you go. Fortunately the game offers the chance to skip troublesome levels, as well as offering some advice or a video showing you how to solve a particular puzzle in exchange of in-game money. (This is great, since it allows players of all skill levels to enjoy the game!)
The game's graphics are quite unique. Everything looks quite cute, until the blood starts flowing (be sure to check the game options to adjust everything to your liking as well as having a laugh!) The music definitely follows suit with moody and scary tunes, as well as a couple of 80's style hair-band rock tunes. I mean, you even get a horrid hippie-style song as the main theme in one of the game's most memorable puzzles! ;)
Controls are simple and easy to use, whether you are playing with a mouse or a gamepad. (Something to take into notice would be the fact that the mouse tends to override a gamepad's input while navegating the game's menus, but on the whole it is not a big deal)
Although the game can be played and enjoyed by pretty much anyone, the game is definitely geared to slasher flick fans who will have just as much fun locating all the references. Packed with plenty of content, the game is sure to bring you back for quite a while! :D

The first of the saints row games I played. It is best described as a sand-box game that lets you play a bat man style villian with out any pesky heroes getting in the way. Lots of fun, and grounded enough not to take itself to seriously.

Saints Row 2 is a great game. If you haven't played the first one you should be ok (I never played the first one) the game does a good job telling you what happened, and I never felt lost story wise. However, there were some times when I felt that they referenced the first game, but it only felt like if my friends had an inside joke that I wasn't part of. Overall, the story was good, and I understood it. If you are coming at this after playing futer installments, you will notice that the tone is way different. It is much more serious and in many cases really brutal like when you are taking out key members of a rival gang. However, there is still tons of humor. Good examples being, driving around in a septic truck shooting sewage at houses to lower the property value, you and Pierce's arguments about which radio station to watch, the character interactions in general, and the news and advertisements that play on the radio. A thing that the game does really well at is the side missions. There is a huge variety of them from standard ones like stealing cars to the previously mentioned spraying buildings with sewage to lower the property value. Another thing that the game does well is the story progression. You have the freedom to really do what you want to do from the very begining. You can pick which gang mission you want to do, if you want to topple one before the other, or if you want to try to attack them all at the same time. However, my biggest problem is that there was a few more glitches than I would have liked, but I only had to restart once, and I crashed twice. Other than that the game was well designed, and all around a blast to play.

Goddamn beautiful, a film obviously intended for a smaller subset of the game enthusiast audience but accessible nonetheless. Honestly, objectively, it's the sort of footage and presentation that would appeal most to someone who, like me, already knows even vaguely most of the faces and games mentioned within. If you like video games as an escape and do not particularly feel drawn to engaging with the medium in an artistic space or frame of mind, you're probably going to leave with a negative impression, because artistic and experimental "play" is mostly what this documentary is about. It brings a couple points of view into the blend, but the focal point of the whole film is GDC and the train jam leading up to it, culminating in a brief discussion of what goes into demoing an independent game at behemoth events like PAX. The developers it follows and the interviews in this film do more to sell the playful side of indie games creation than to document their processes, but ultimately what I took the most from when watching this movie was a genuine enthusiasm for creativity that made me want to make my own attempts. Not objective, not particularly informative, but more than a little bias-confirming and plenty fun.

There are essentially only three maps, two game modes that take place on those three maps, and no vehicles except for a couple of helicopters on one map that don't really play much of a role when it comes to the ground combat. This has resulted in a lot of players dropping the game pretty early on in it's lifecycle, and the game now has less players on average than Squad. It's pretty sad since this game could be a lot more interesting, especially if it felt more real.
Thus, my chief complaint is that the game just doesn't feel gritty and intense. It's too clean. Even burning an enemy alive with the flamethrower just isn't visceral. It certainly doesn't live up to the sometimes tramautic experience one could get from Red Orchestra 2. It's very bland, and doesn't seem to leave anyone wanting for more.
I hope to upgrade this review to a Recommend in the future, we'll see.

As much as I may like the idea of the game, even after more than a year of post-release development, patches and payed DLC, the game still lacks sufficient amount of content. DLC is pretty much required to get any form of enjoyment from the game, since otherwise there will be hardly any mechanics more complex than collecting energy and minerals.
Utopia, despite what paradox may claim, is completely essential to the game in the same way that The Art of War is essential to EU4, without it there are is no assentation perks, no assentation paths, no megastructure, and no way to access all the features provided by Story Packs (Special Machine Empire Assentation Perks from Synthetic Dawn). The Megastructures have recently been buffed, but limited to one per type per empire, meaning that now the only way to sink excess resources is to build more fleet, but then then, the megastructures are not very interesting, simply granting science in case of the Nexus, Energy in case of the Dyson sphere, and unlimited sensor range in case of the Array (will cause immense lag). On the positive side, habitats added in the expansion allow for play a tall empire.
On the topic of Story Pack DLC, while Synthetic Dawn definitely added some content to the game, but ultimately machine empire unique government is exactly the same as the hivemind, except you cannot ascend the empire at all and instead get the ability to build machine worlds (if you have Utopia), and can get some additional trait points (if you have Utopia). The Leviathans ads some interesting stories to the game, but leviathans are rather "static", once you know the ship layout used to fight them and how much fleet power you need they become nothing more than a floating loot boxes.
The interactions with the AI Empires are limited to either trading excess resources with them creating a Federation, or declaring the war on them, no spying, no influencing the internal politics (sparking revolts like in EU4). Wars are just a drag, revolving around a single large fleet attempting to catch the enemy single large fleet and then sieging down the planets. Appallingly, player does not have any form of influence on the battles, you cannot tell the battleships to keep the distance, or to target specific enemy ships, just engage in battle, and occasionally emergency FTL out of it.
End game crises that are moved further and further into the late game as time progresses, which leads to the payer either being way to strong by the time the enemy arrives, or completely unprepared. If the crisis starts near your empire, and you are not yet a completely overwhelming force in the galaxy, you are done for. If it starts on the other edge of the galaxy, AI will hardly ever try to cooperate to defeat it without your involvement, and would much rather simply be defeated one by one.
All in all, Stellaris can definitely be a great game, but unfortunately it is not one yet, what it is in the current state (along with all the currently released DLC) is a foundation, which needs to be built upon, hopefully not in the form of Story Packs, that add slight variation of preexisting empires, but instead in form of new, player- involving systems, which will make the game more interactive and which will reward player initiative.
Suggestions:
Fleet Stances: Ability to give general commands to engaged fleets. (eg. “Ship Type” hold maximum distance; focus enemy “Ship Type”; “Ship Type” close the distance; etc.)
New Mega Structures/ Mega structure Interactions: Hostile AI appearing in the Science Nexus triggering a Localized Robotic Uprising Event within the Empire.  A hostile entity gaining access to your Sentry Array. Spiritualist empires being opposed to creation of Machine Worlds. etc.

Alas, our beloved WWII FPS genre has fallen into obscurity after it was abandoned by AAA companies, such as EA and Activision. Of course we had Wolfenstein: The New Order but it was far from conveying the beauty of flying corpses disintegrated by mortar shells or thousands of young lives butchered by a single MG42 (it was a pretty solid FPS though, I definitely recommend it). Since then smaller companies are trying to fill the WWII FPS niche, some of them are pretty good (Red Orchestra 2), some of them are very promising (Day of Infamy), some of them are meh (Sniper Elite 2) and some of them are outright terrible (Uprising 44).
I have played one of the good ones, the Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm for 200 hours. While I had and still having great fun in them the core offerings of those two has gotten a little bit stale. I gave a break to come back to it later and the Steam page welcomed me with a great surprise. A new mod, one mod to bring them and in darkness bind them has appeared out of nowhere. I followed many mod projects for RO2, many of them failed and stopped or lost in development but this lovely mod has gotten itself out of the development hell for modders. I did not go into this with high expectations because it was just a community work but I was surprised as ♥♥♥♥. It surpassed any high expectations I could have. When it comes to modding I expect bugs (lots of them), glitching graphics etc. But my experience so far in this hasn't shown any of them. Apart from technicalities I almost cried with joy when I saw how the iconic map Carentan was made with absolute perfection (they should think about adding a front entrance to objective B though). All of the maps were beautiful and more or less balanced. Difficulties of some tough maps (such as Omaha Beach and Carentan) can be overcome through decent teamplay and I believe that's what the devs of this aimed for: more communication among the teams. Also the inclusion of new guns and classes are lovely. The rest is the classic RO2 formula and it was executed flawlessly.
I have some hopes for the future though, first of all some more maps even though it has around 15 maps if I'm not mistaken. Secondly, there should be more populated servers apart from one in Europe and one in US and finally, some textures look they have less resolution than the usual RO2 but I'm not sure about this. In the end I surely recommend you to give this a go if you enjoyed RO2/RS and I hope Tripwire will acquire these guys like they did with the devs of Rising Storm, polish this a little bit more and release it as a full expansion.
Very much thanks to the Kernow Interactive for making this work of passion and again I recommend you all to try this out, even buy RO2/RS to enjoy this.

Dom4 is the best and deepest turn based fantasy game ever made.  Why? There's 75+ different NATIONS to play with over 3 different eras.  Each nation has their own interesting history based on the dominions world and aren't just a fantasy ripoff of orcs, elves, etc.  There's an incredibly deep magic system with over 800 spells, 300 forgeable magic items and over 2000 units!  You can play single player, hotseat, play by email or multiplayer with up to 28 players including team games.  The game is also easily moddable and there's a big mod community.    With this many nations, spells, and units, this game is very complex and impossible to fully master.  It's an old school style game where you should actually read the manual (infact dominions 3 came with a 400 page manual).  This game is an acquired taste for the patient who enjoy gameplay over good graphics.  If you're a tabletop wargamer or enjoy the civ series you might like this. The graphics are sprite based but functional and the music is good. If you're on the fence about this game, Dominions 3 (which is similiar) has a free demo available for download. If you're a serious strategy gamer who cares about deep tactics and likes lots of possiblities instead of just rock, paper, scissors style of today's RTS games, you'll love Dominions.  It's one of my top 10 games of all time on any platform and the only game that I would say even comes close to comparing to it is Civ 5 with all DLC and expansions.  Even then, it's a tough call to say which I like more.  Dominions is responsible for more "oops it's 7 am, time for bed" than I care to admit. Give it a try (and read the manual and tutorial!)

Dominions is a pretty good strategy game with lots of variety and depth.  I started with Dominions 3, and now I've jumped in to 4.  I do notice some changes and some definite improvements including a bit more assistance with the micro managing.  It does show as an independent game, of course - the graphics and the manual leave plenty of room for improvement.  But it's hard to beat the variety and depth, and I don't think it's too hard to learn.
With the variety of maps, of win conditions, the three eras, the variety of nations, and the variety of gods, there's a lot of ability to customize how you play and cater to your preferences.
So far I've only played single player.  The AI does seem reasonably good, plenty of challenge there.  I can only imagine that being able to set up a multi-player game would be quite a lot of fun.

This is another incremental upgrade in the Dominions series.  There are Improved sprites, some minor interface improvements, some new items and spells etc.  Some of the game systems have been reworked.  The thrones are a nice addition and provides a more interesting and immersive path to victory rather than the gamey victory points system.  However there is still no AI diplomacy, which is a little disappointing.  The price is rather steep considering that, on the surface, there aren't that many changes.  If you're not a hard core fan of the series and don't have much money I'd recommend holding off until a sale.

This has easily become one of my favorite games ever, thanks mostly to an engaging, deep story set in a quirky lore-filled world teeming with things to discover. The combat mechanics are excellent and very satisfying, especially as you acquire more abilities. I absolutely loved the perspective and gameplay switches the game goes through in various areas and parts of quests; it adds an incredibly unique feel to the game you won't experience anywhere else. The soundtrack is a fantastic complement to the game, but also great for listening to separately.
The only real "negative" to this game is there are a decent amount of fetch/kill quests when you aren't running main story quests (it is an open world RPG after all). However, they're improved by being quirky, adding lore/background to the world, and still generally enjoyable due to the rest of the feature set. Don't let this discourage you though, because it's completely worth it to experience the story and world NieR:Automata has to offer.
NOTE: The DLC doesn't particularly add anything worthwhile for me, but the new colosseums gives players more interested in the combat a chance to challenge themselves. And the outfits are cute.

Grapchis are very good, if not the actual graphical quality, but the graphic design is top-notch. The soundtrack is amazing, so much so that I bought it separately and listen to it all the time. Regarding the port, I had one crash and no real performance issues, though I do think it necessary to install FAR on every machine.
Overall this game will be the ones I'll reminisce about and come back to in the years to come. I've never seen anything quite like NieR:Automata and am extremely glad I picked it up.
Oh, and, there is the fanservice. It's up to the individual player to form their own opinion of it, but it never got to the point of bothering me.

Slayaway Camp is a puzzle game at heart themed around a collection of slasher movies. Bringing those two elements together comes off well and enhances the core gameplay. It's a brain twister, literal and figurative.
The rules are easy to learn and new mechanics are introduced throughout the game at certain points. It's a nice little detail that the developers worked out a fitting way to implement mechanics that are in line with the actual theme of the movies. It only makes sense to have a shark scaring people into drowning or to put in portal tiles in a spacey sci-fi flick. The puzzles as such have the right amount of complexity with misleading arrangements and sometimes only one right solution. Because the level areas maintain a manageable size, the puzzles are never overwhelming but tricky.
While solving puzzles generally doesn't require external motivations, Slayaway Camp further awards the player with points to spend on a variety of unlockable death animations and random murder costumes. It's a minor treat but still I found myself in anticipation of which classic or unusual murder costume the game had in store next.
It's a puzzle game with an addictive gameplay and killer coating.

Really quite enjoyed this. If you've seen Indie Game: The Movie you know roughly what to expect - it's a documentary about making indie games, about what that means to people, about some of the reasons for doing so, and some of the challenges. But Gameloading is kind of more upbeat and community-focused, bit more of a whirlwind tour of a slice of the indie community rather than a close-up examination of a day-to-day process in the way IGTM followed Ed McMillen etc. Which is not to say there aren't a few "central" people - Davey Wreden working on The Stanley Parable and Robin Arnott on Soundself feature a lot - but it's not a "day in the life" kind of movie.
It's "light", I guess, might be the worst I could say if I were looking for problems. Some people might have a problem with that; might find it kind of insubstantial if they're already familiar with indie gaming culture and are looking for some kind of magic special insight. I didn't feel that way.  Gameloading isn't trying to be some deep and detailed analysis of how game development operates. It's just here's some people, here's this stuff they're doing and their explanations of why they love doing it, yay for that! It's a celebration of community and openness and trying new things, not a report, and there's nothing wrong with that. I've read comments calling the film kind of self-congratulatory fluff, but I can't really share that view. Even if I was of the mind that there was nothing here but a clique of hipsters patting each other on the back, I personally happen to think everyone depicted absolutely deserves a pat on the back, so...good on them?
I bought the bundle and I haven't watched any of the extra features yet; I'll come back and amend this when I have. Stellaris is the kind of game you play when you want to focus more on the large scale aspect of galactic 4X.  In this you are the supreme ruler, but that does not mean you oversee the movements of every unit and track the building of every colony.
With a real-time-with-pause time system and a slick notifications interface you get to direct your civilization from it's first days of interstellar exploration up to it's domination or collapse.  Rather than playing with simple "racial bonuses" to differentiate various groups Stellaris has you playing with everything from cultural influence and governmental changes to genetic or technological modification.  You can create your own races like in may current galactic empire games, but the game also procedurally generates groups for you to encounter, preventing games from feeling like the same encounters time and again.
However, this is not the sort of game you play if you like to focus on micromanaging your troops/ships in battle.  Once units engage in conflicts you must sit back and watch, only having the right to call for retreat should you feel the tide turning against you.
In the end Stellaris has a dedicated developer regularly releasing new free content and updates along side paid deluxe DLC.  Their regular communication with their player community is commendable and their work to refine and improve on an innovative game makes it that much more enjoyable.  I highly suggest this game for anyone that enjoys games such as SimCity and who are ready to sit down and spend time really learning a game.  For players that prefer Starcraft style tactics you may want to watch some Youtube play videos of the current version so you can be sure of what you are getting ahead of time.

This has easily become one of my favorite games ever, thanks mostly to an engaging, deep story set in a quirky lore-filled world teeming with things to discover. The combat mechanics are excellent and very satisfying, especially as you acquire more abilities. I absolutely loved the perspective and gameplay switches the game goes through in various areas and parts of quests; it adds an incredibly unique feel to the game you won't experience anywhere else. The soundtrack is a fantastic complement to the game, but also great for listening to separately.
The only real "negative" to this game is there are a decent amount of fetch/kill quests when you aren't running main story quests (it is an open world RPG after all). However, they're improved by being quirky, adding lore/background to the world, and still generally enjoyable due to the rest of the feature set. Don't let this discourage you though, because it's completely worth it to experience the story and world NieR:Automata has to offer.
NOTE: The DLC doesn't particularly add anything worthwhile for me, but the new colosseums gives players more interested in the combat a chance to challenge themselves. And the outfits are cute.

I've not finished all the movies/levels yet but I'm going to write this review anyway since I have faith that the quality won't drop off far enough for me to want to retract anything I say.
Slayway Camp is your basic block sliding puzzler but with a hell of a lot of character thrown in. Instead of sliding to press switches, or change coloured blocks, you're sliding around campgrounds, beaches, hospitals and more as a masked killer on the loose looking for victims.
If you're a fan of 80's slasher flicks this game will be right up your alley, it does homage to them (especially the Friday the 13th films) very well, down to the cheesy synth-rock ballads and the killer's refusal to hurt animals. Each level pack is given a trailer with increasingly forced puns and justifications for the killer to be killing....a lot like most slasher franchises of the 80's and 90's.
With each movie (set of levels) a new mechanic is added, such as environmental hazards, the previously mentioned animals, police officers which will arrest you if you enter their range, SWAT which have level-crossing lasers and will fire at will and more. With each new system put in place the levels become more and more strategic, having you need to take absolutely all risks into account before making a move.
Slayway Camp's star feature, in my opinion, are the levels where you're given a very tight amount of moves to kill all your victims and escape in. The game absolutely shines here, you can't mess up even once and it's incredibly satisfying once you figure out the perfect route to complete the level.
The only negatives I can think of are that the previous mentioned new mechanics are often given very, very easy levels to figure them out in - I understand why this was put in place but it is a little annoying that 2/13 of each level set's levels will be a total cakewalk, even on the later levels.
My only other 'criticism' of Slayway Camp is that it may be better purchased on mobile devices rather than on Steam as the UI is definitely more suited to a phone or tablet than it is for a desktop, and the design is definitely suited for 'pick up and play' style use, if that's what you're looking for in a game.
If you want to check it out before buying it you can play a couple of the level packs on Kongregate.

Slayaway Camp is a game about two things: sliding and gore. It provides a solid and well-balanced gameplay experience, but SC does have a couple annoying things that make it tedious. I also had my fill of this type of puzzle experience after several hours. Other players that stick with the game will find a good number of maps and victims to clear.
SC oozes b-movie horror vibes all over the place. It’s funny if you understand the references and tropes that the game parodies. Did I mention the blood? There’s plenty of bones and blood with all the victim slaying that one does. There are also different kinds of executions available to purchase to keep things fresh on the slaying front. You can play as different killers depending on the movie (set of levels tied by a theme) selected or any that you unlocked. Revisiting the movies to play the deleted scenes levels is recommended since more jokes are found there.
The blocky aesthetic works pretty well overall except for the close-ups when a cutscene execution is triggered. That’s when the game is at its worst graphically. The models don’t look very good at that distance, but the unique executions are fun to look at for the first few times. They do wear out their welcome after a while, but thankfully, you can skip them with the press of a button. The slow-motion executions that can trigger are a good time that result in an explosion of bits and pieces.
The gameplay is the strongest part of the whole sliding experience, partially due to the developer deftly handling the pacing of new obstacles and mechanics. The game starts off simple with your character sliding across the tiles without much to stop you. Over time, you’ll encounter pits, water, cats, mines, police officers, S.W.A.T., and more. They all contribute to a fun and challenging experience. I thought the idea with light switches was really neat because of how it changed victim/police behavior. When it comes to the tools available for figuring out the moves to make, you can easily restart the map, rewind, or fast forward your moves.
There’s also a system in place for buying hints and solutions. You can also skip levels instead if you don’t have the money (there’s an uninteresting mode you can play for gold which is comprised of quick time executions). I definitely bought a few solutions after coming to a complete standstill mentally.
So, if you like the GO series or sliding puzzles in general (not the tile ones), Slayaway Camp should provide slides for days. You’ll enjoy it much more if you’re familiar with the references, but the solid gameplay, over-the-top kills, and silliness in general put this game somewhere in between above average and good.

~For this Vietnam Veteran, far more than physical scars remain.~
The place was nice; that’s what I remember.
It was warm, it was comfortable. And it was “home”.
I liked it there.
I can recall the fire. They always made one—welcoming flames caged behind bars. I told them to let it free; they would not.
The place was nice.
There was no rain and this was odd. I had always been wet. But the place was nice.
Seventy-three days. That’s how long I used the fire. Those flickering colors were foreign to me. We weren’t allowed to see them before. They told us we must be like the night: Dark, silent, and unseen. None of us loved it, but They said it had to be.
I did not sleep in that nice place. When I would lie down, the walls fell over and I was back. There was no fire.
I needed those flames, I needed their warmth, their light.
The bed was too soft, I lay on the ground and there still was no fire.
In the air I could smell wetness and yet there was none.
I must have been restless because they came and spoke kind words to me. I liked it when they spoke. It  made up for the lack of flame.
They would ask me what was wrong and I would not reply. They asked if I had nightmares, and I suppose that I did.
But what could these nice people do? They could not help.
I told them I had nightmares, but I did not clarify further.
I did not tell them what happened when my eyes would finally close, what torment would besiege me as I lay upon the stone hard floor.
No, I did not tell them of the mares in the night.
When I feel myself slip away, the fire is gone and the walls vanish. The roof has also left and it lets in the water. When I leave the nice place. When it leaves me.
It’s moist and dark.
I don’t want to be back.
There is a thundering in the floor, which has become earth. Earth covered in grass, slick with rain.
My entire body is streaming with water. The singing crickets fall silent around me as the thundering in the ground becomes louder.
The earth trembles with its noise and now its source has come.
It has come for me and I am unable to stop its coming.
580,000 thundering mares surround me. Their iron shoes tear the grass and scar the dirt below.
I rise to greet them, for we are familiar. The herd and I.
They thunder and prance and I join them.
We have begun to run.
I am one of them. And though I remain the same, I can feel their speed, their surging bodies radiating with heat. So much heat that they steam in the darkness, only adding to the wet.
I can feel their breathing, every sharp intake of breath and rushed exhale. Their streaming manes and tails whip around them, and whip me.
We are one, but bound to be separate.
They take up a cry, a whole chorus of whinnies. And though I can see and feel their voices I am deaf to their calls.
The thundering roars in my useless ears.
I try to call to them, to speak, to yell out my plight.
But they do not hear me. They rush on, and I feel their power, their unthinking movements.
To feel their feeling is maddening, and I cannot share in their calling.
The rain has stopped and we are bathed in the rays of a new moon.
But a thick mist has moved in. It moves too fast.
There are eagles above it and though their eyes are keen, they do not heed us. They do not heed the herd, which still thunders.
The wings are wide and they soar without effort. But they are loud. Their feathers are loud.
And though I cannot hear them, the herd flinches at their soaring. But they do not change course. They remain the same surging group with only one thought between them: ahead.
The mist grows thicker and it stifles my lungs.
I am choking.
The mist is too thick, too fast.
I cannot see the herd, or hear their calls, but I feel their thundering.
The mist should be cool. Cool like the rain.
But it burns. Its fine droplets burn at my skin.
The thundering increases, and I know they are calling.
The burning mist still veils them but I know they are there.
They do not know where.
“I am behind the shroud, I am under it!”
But the mist has stopped my lungs, and no breath reaches my voice.
The grass below me is brittle, and I understand the mist has done it.
It is dead.
Am I?
No. I can feel the burning moisture.
The burning replaces my feeling of the herd and I cannot remain.
My legs are suddenly not running, and I am on the ground. The mist seems thicker, and it burns deeper.
It’s in my lungs, my heart, my very mind.
I am burning within.
No thundering is worse than this torture.
I want it to end; I want the burning to stop.
My fingers are clawing at my body in attempt to rid myself of the mist. But it closes in ever thicker and I sprawl on the ground.
The grass is still wet, but it is dead. It does not give my tormented body relief.
Eyes roll to show the whites and the mist devours. The dark mares and their thundering are still shaking the ground but I cannot follow them.
Now their thundering, and their trembling, is fading.
They are gone.
I am alone.
No fire. Just mist.
I lay there, burning in the mist and waiting for the herd to return. But they do not.
Though I wait. And wait.
Nothing.
And then, there it is, a soft padding and a hard flapping. I cannot hear them, but I feel. The burning is intense, but I still feel.
The padding and flapping is not the herd. I know who they are. They are the bearers of mist. Be they friend or foe matters not.
I will not allow them to bring burning wet. I will not die within. My thundering will return to me, though it made me deaf. Running will be restored to my legs.
The mares of the night left me behind, but I will not let them burn.
No carriers of mist will veil me.
But when a cool hand reaches toward me, I do not think about where it came from. I pay no heed to the sudden brightness, which is far too white for this new moon night. I do not remember or care to remember that I am in the night and the hand is from elsewhere. The night is vanishing and is replaced. The nice place?
There is too much white, and too many hands.
Kind words are spoken, but I do not hear them.
I hear and feel nothing but the thundering of my heart—so similar to that which I could not regain.
The burning wet will not harm my thundering mares of the night.
I lunge because the running has come back to my legs, but I do not hear the new calls because my ears can’t listen.
Red replaces the too much white, but then both are gone, swallowed by a deeper darkness than before.
Before I fall, I see a flicker.
The flame they never let the herd see.
But then I let the darkness consume me, and as I am lost within it, I fancy that I can hear a thundering.
580,001 are running in a new darkness, and I have joined them.
*Me after finishing my first time playing the game and finally exiting to desktop*

This film gives you a snapshot into the world of indie games, who's making them and why.
It was great getting a view into the lives of people who make many of the games I've played over the past few years, and learn more about the thought process behind them.
I'm a game maker and felt that this film also touched on lots of ideas that game creators are talking about at the moment. It will be fun to watch it again in a few years and see which questions we've all figured out, and which ones we're still pondering over.

The Indie Dev scene today is an adolescent on the brink of puberty, and this film captures it.
It is not an audiovisual masterpiece, polished and immaculate, but it is true.
It is raw, gross, whiny, spoiled and full of lust.
It will show you that this particular creative space attracts some of the most interesting and complex people in the world.
You will see weird and queer and different and unique. You will also see people like you.
You will understand the passion and love they have for what they do; the courage, the uncertainty.
You will feel... something.
That's all that matters.

This isn't a documentary about "how to be a game developer" or anything like that. It's a look at the culture and direction that current independent game development has, and what about that development appeals to people. Featuring a lot of interviews with people like Zoe Quinn, John Romero, Rami Ismail, and Christine Love, as well as footage from PAX, GDC, and Train Jam, it's a pretty wide look at what sorts of people are finding success (and sometimes failure) in games.
It also features a host of extra interviews with Mattie Brice, Nina Freeman, and more. Very well-polished - as a documentary, it's excellent in terms of visual and audio quality. It currently seems to be streaming-only, so if you're looking for a downloadable version, you'll need to find it elsewhere.
If you're interested in the more interesting people and games currently coming out of the indie games community, I'd give it a watch.

It's pretty good.
GameLoading offers a broader look at a wider cross-section of the independent games scene, a bit more relaxed and conversational and a bit less cinematic than similar docs.
It seems to assume a lot on the part of its audience, as if it was made more for the community itself than for others outside it. But it does highlight people scraping by (and failing) rather than just showing big successes, which is far more useful to people who aspire to make games, so that is in service to its audience.
If non-industry viewers can keep up, they'll see some interesting stuff come together, and maybe they'll come out of it thinking of games as something more complex.
Excellent and wide ranging look at variety of indie devs and their stories.

It would be difficult to talk about
without making comparisons to 2012's
, so I'll just go ahead and do that. Where that film took a focused look at three developers and the emotional struggles of launching a game,
takes a broader, more diverse look at the culture surrounding indie games, in particular those of the experimental/art/alt sort. The strongest narrative thread to be found here is the one following the development and launch of
, but the individual stories take a back seat to the larger discussion and exploration of why these games appeal to their developers and players, what function they serve in modern culture, and where they are going in the future. The tone is less dramatic doom-and-gloom than
; although there are some common themes of uncertainty and fear of failure, the resonating message is one of hope, excitement, and community.
assumes its viewer has some pre-existing knowledge of indie games and omits any fluffy stage-setting introductions (e.g., "Let's talk down to our audience about what an indie game is and how it's different from a AAA game") in favor of getting straight to the good stuff. The interviewees range from AAA industry veterans to indie heroes to up-and-coming developers you might not have heard of yet. The viewpoints and topics of discussion vary widely as well; it's interesting to hear so many different facets of gaming and development discussed with the love and attention they deserve.
If
is a film that I watch to feel commiseration with developers and the occasional hardships of game development,
is one that I see myself watching to remind myself how supportive and welcoming the community can be. It's easy to only see the negativity when observing games culture through the filter of a Twitter feed, so it's nice to see the positive elements represented in this way. This is a movie that makes me excited to keep making games.
If you have any interest in indie games or in taking a look behind the scenes of game development, I highly recommend
.
Full disclosure: I contributed to the Kickstarter campaign for this film.
