In some ways, it has a Sins of a Solar Empire sensation to it.
Except it has:
> More in depth diplomacy such as formal war demands and federations
> Government types (Egalitarian, spiritualist, imperialist, gestalt machine intelligence etc)
> Fairly customisable ships you can design and save with a huge variety of weapons
> Lots of anomalies, events, mini stories that keeps the game interesting throughout the course of your empire's history
> Large variety of races and species and selectable/editable gene traits (miners, migrants, communal, militarist, etc)
> Each NPC empire has their own personalities that makes it interesting galactic history an interesting cascade
> Extensive research card system (not really a tree)
> Different empire types and crisis events that makes late game challenging
When I bought it, I spent literally a whole weekend just playing this non-stop. So, for me it's pretty fun. Lots of things to keep you busy especially when you start.
Although, some down sides. Althought there's an enormous amount of content, I feel as though most typical players don't really try out some of the options the game has to offer - like myself, I played two games and both times, I preferred choosing Human species with an egalitarian xenophillic government type. I could be ruthless and enslave all other oppositions or play as a machine empire and exterminate all organic type - the game has these options but I don't feel compelled to do so. Such empires are excellent adversaries however. It's not really a negative, but I feel as though it's something worth mentioning.
On top of that, I feel as though very, very late game. The game is a bit boring, this is after you defeated any Awakened Empires (think Asgards from Stargate or Borgs from Star Trek) and the galactic crisis event (think invasion of Ori from stargate or Reapers from Mass Effect). Being all powerful is boring yah, but the marching journey through the stars to secure your empire's utopian destination is challenging and quite engaging.
All in all, I like this game and was worth my time and money, particularly if you enjoy science fiction games.

I'm not big on super detailed descriptions, so I'm going to keep this short and sweet, Cause simple is always the best policy.
In my opinion Stellaris, is an amazing game. I love the game, it’s got a lot of things I like in a game: empire building and management, army building and customization, and big maps to extend your empire across.
The space battles are impressive in my opinion, especially in late game when you have massive fleets beating the tar out of each other. Empire management is fun but not too overwhelming at times, unless you play like me and have 20 or so core sector systems under you control, cause I'm a monster. As well as a moding community that puts out a lot of pretty good stuff.
My only problem with the game is that the AI seems to cheat a bit, and when I say a bit I mean a lot. They can always see everything on the map (which is the first time I have every noticed it this much in an RTS, I know, I'm blind or something), but that’s not that big of a deal. The thing I can't stand is that the AI disregards the limitation the player is put under, Fleet Capacity and Core Sector Systems, and gets boosts to their economy. Which can quickly screw you over in the early game...and mid game sometimes. The game forces you to focus on Military, only way to survive the early game.
Then there is the End Game Crisis, the killer of all good games, very strong (sometimes OP in my opinion), but if you have a good enough game and plan well, manageable.
Other than that, the rest of the game is great, difficult at time and very, very......very frustrating. But, still a fun game to figure out and come up with new ideas on how to deal with what the next game will throw at you.
Very nice game, although rather expensive.

I wish I could reccomend this game, I really do. The concept is interesting and the game is very visually appealing, But the gameplay is lacking in many reagrds. First is the fact that despite giving players the illusion that there are many ways to play and every galactic empire can be different, gameplay always boils down to who has the biggest military the fastest even if you're playing as a pacifistic race. The second big problem, that is bad on it's own and veen worse when paired with the first, is how rediculously overpowered the AI are. Regardless of difficulty setting or turning off "advanced empires" the AI will almost always be better than you. AI empires don't seem to be even remotely bound by the same limitations as the player or any limitations at all for that matter, the game has just started and at least 2 empires control 10 times as much space as you do and have the military power to squash you like a bug a million times over. It's frustrating being Xenophilic Pacifists minding your own buisiness and suddenly having an AI empire vaporize hours worth of work in a matter of nanoseconds, despite difficulty as low as it can go and AI aggresiveness set to "low". The game being that unforgiving regardless of the settings makes it very hard to get used to the mechanics and get better, not only are you hard pressed to actually get better because you get steamrolled before you can learn anything, but you are dissuaded from even wanting to get better. The way I see it the only way to get better is to play one of a few select ways and play them exactly in a specific way, what's the point of all the game's choices if you don't actually have a choice how you want to play?

Have you ever wanted to form your own intergalactic empire that spans millions of lightyears? Have you ever looked at your weird mushroom pets and thought ‘why not make them space faring?’
Stellaris allows you to do all this and more! There’s so much good to say for this game that I’m struggling on where to start!
First I would just like to say that my PC set up isn’t the best and can’t handle some of the modern games out there at top quality without coming to a crawl but this game looks great and shows no lag for me on my end.  Even when I have massive space battles against pirates that are disrupting my mining operations of a sun it won’t lag.
I had two games going, one was a Bird Empire with a god Empress with a struggle against everyone to advance in the universe. The other (using console commands though) was a powerful robotic civilization that took over the planet they were built on by turning the original builders into mindless machines, consuming all life and bringing it into the collective.
You start out with just a planet, science ship, construction and a tiny fleet and go on from there with a helpful tutorial telling you how the game functions. Although if you’ve ever played something like CIV you’ll kind of understand how this game works. Although I should note that if you start with a game with the tutorial on you’ll get told about of things work every time you open a tab which can be kind of annoying.
The game has so much detail to it without being too complicated, they even allow you to set rights for different species, including making that annoying as hell Sloth Empire that destroyed all your ships as slaves! Take that you slow b****ds!...
On planets there are resources such as rich lands that make it so your farms grow more food for your people although if you’re a robot you don’t need food. There might be mineral deposits that make your mines produce more and on planets that you can’t populate such as gas giants you are able to put a mining station in orbit that constantly sucks in resources that you need to grow.

I appreciate the fact that this game is free, and that it is made by a very small team. However, sadly, I cannot say that it is a good game. To briefly summarize the game, RGBverse is an endless runner that has a combination of jumping challenges and some basic pattern challenges in the form of changing colors to fit the platform you are jumping on. There is a brief attempt of a story to the game, which while I'm not sure is needed, doesn't really hurt either. I believe that the concept of the game has potential, however the execution is very poor. I will say outright that I am generally bad at endless runners compared to many people, and they don't necessarily appeal to me as they might to some, however this game has no redeeming qualities compared to other "endless runners" that I have played.
The primary reason for my criticism of this game is the incredibly poor responsiveness from the game. This game has what I would call "artificial difficulty" due to this issue. This is because the response time of controls are slow enough compared to environmental hazards that you are guaranteed to die some of the time if you do not know a hazard is coming up, and there are several hazards like this. I believe that creating environmental hazards that force you to die the first time is bad design, as it does not present a real challenge to the player, and instead delivers an insult.
Along with the criticism of poor responsiveness, is inconsistent responsiveness. The game does not always seem to react to input with the same speed, or accuracy. More than once, I watched as the little ball I was "controlling" decided to continue jumping even though I wasn't touching the keyboard at all anymore. Sometimes you respawn stuck to the ground, unable to jump at all, which kills you in about a couple of seconds. After that, you can jump again, but little glitches seem to be all over in this game. Sometimes it lags a moment before switching colors. Other times it switches immediately. I had a boost pad shoot me straight down instead of forward like it should have. Combined with the artificial difficulty built into the game's design, this makes for a rather unpleasant experience.
The graphics of the game are passable, especially considering it's a free game, but they look very inconsistent. Some things look pretty good while others look unpolished and awful. This combined with what I would call uninspired effects and artistic design, make the game visually forgettable. It doesn't exactly look terrible, however its graphic flaws are significant enough that it doesn't really look that good either.
The music is rather bland and highly repetitive. I wouldn't expect anything more than that from such a small game, however there's nothing that sets it apart from anything else, making it entirely forgettable, much like the visuals. There is one consolation in the music though, and that is the fact that while it's repetitive, it isn't annoying, and it does not distract from the game at all. Many basic games fall prey to incredibly poor music choices, and even some bigger games do as well. RGBverse appears to do a good job avoiding that trap.
This game claims to be a challenge to reflexes and precision abilities, however that is not quite accurate. By creating input delay and making obstacles that cannot be avoided due to said input delay, the game removes all elements of reflex. It instead replaces those reflexes with learned patterns and timing, which may not even help you if the controls decide to fail at that moment. The game does challenge precision through this action, however once again, in failing to have consistent responsiveness, even precision won't always save you.
Overall the game ranges between painful to play and easy to forget. There are no standout qualities of this game, but many faults. If the graphics were more consistent, the music more defined or varied, and the controls responsive, this could be an entertaining game to some degree. In its current form however, it is poorly designed and poorly executed in nearly all of its attributes.

RGBVerse is a constant runner type game, in this case the runner of the game is a ball that goes along a track. At the end of the track is a giant portal like goal. Between you and the goal is quite a few openings in the track you have to jump over, platforms that may or may not be colored, a few projectile like obstacles, spikes, launch pads, and so on. Certain objects will be colored in this game, one or more of 3 distinct colors, Red, Green, and Blue. In order to land on these objects without dying you have to change to the same color of the object.
The premise of the game is rather simple to explain. Simple can be good, in this case the game itself is easy to understand, not having any unneeded complications. Generally speaking, the game looks fairly pretty too, it keeps to its created theme and visually there is nothing that breaks the game environment. The game’s art is fairly good, though parts of it can look fairly dull. Unfortunately, there is little praise I can give to the game beyond this.
The primary problem with this game is its controls, first in order to change to a specific color you have to hold the specific color that is needed for the platform. There is 3 different colors so something like that can’t be too complicated, yet I can’t help but feel that a toggle option would have improved this aspect of the game. Now you may be thinking that such a small problem could be too bad, and you would be right, if the problem was the lack of a toggle switch than that would be nothing. The problem lies with how the game handles input. To be blunt, there is a delay on ALL inputs. You want to jump? Press the space key and jump… bout a half second later. You want to change color? You better have pushed that button well before you needed to cause that is when I will notice it. The input delay that this game has is game breaking. Any bit of enjoyment one may have gotten out of this game is all but ruined by this delay.
There is 9 levels to this game, I have only played 2 of them. The game’s levels themselves are at least decently laid out, perhaps I would even call them well made if it wasn’t for how poorly the game handled. As the game is now it becomes nearly impossible to give the level design a fair critique.
To sum this game up, it is an endless runner with a decent (all be it, unoriginal) premise with absolutely terrible controls.

According to the website/Linkedin of Kyvos Studio, they're a company of three people, so I'd cut them some slack on making such an ambitious game, but my gamedev class required I write an honest review so I won't take that into account.
This is not a good game. The mechanics are well-used but still serviceable. I've played many games in middle school where you change your color to land on platforms or where you run constantly and avoid obstacles, so it had a chance at being worth the price of downloading it and putting it in your library.
The problems are the controls and the level design. First, the controls are very slow to respond which is a problem in a reflex-based game. The majority of my deaths (of which there were over 100 in the first level) were not from inexperience or learning curve, but because the ball wouldn't change color in time or I would jump as soon as I touched a platform because the jumping is programmed like a My First Unity Project. Speaking of fractions of a second, the turrets in the game seem designed to shoot at just the right time to kill you,. (It's actually just a lack of testing which would have immediately shown how rage-inducing it could be.) There were platforms too far away to drop down to but too near to jump to, unintuitive boost pads (go under them), and countless little points where you died not from challenge, but because very little effort was put into beta-testing.
And that's the real problem. They advertise this as a hard game for real gamers, but what they don't say is all the difficulty is in over-coming the bad game design. Yes, technically trying to play Red Light Green Light with Hellen Keller is hard, but not in a way that's fun.

Negatives-
Pre-release quality game. I have experienced 2 problems with the game that aren't small. For me the game loads with a resolution bug that starts the game in a mode similar to when you alt-tab out of a game. The game isn't visible and in a pause state but it is running under task manager. Rendering the game unplayable. This was fixed using an unofficial patch called FAR mod, but some releases didn't play well with releases of the steam overlay so I found myself seeing this bug several times. The game at a number of noticeable points goes from super smooth to judder and back affecting play, there is no apparent complexity in the scenes when it occurs.
The game follows “for the sake of artistic vision practices” over “user friendliness practices”. This is great if you become a real fanboy of the game but it makes it frustrating to play the game casually. 3 examples.
1) The introduction has no save function but the rest of the game has a safe function.
Imagine spending hours waiting for the game to download. Then having to research how to get the game to run. Then dying 30 minutes in from getting lightly hit and getting stuck in a bugged hit loop and having to go back to the start. Then having to re fix the game so it runs the second time you play. Frustrating, uninteresting and no fun!
Some people don’t experience any of this but a sizeable number do. Then you get to read the fanboy comments on forums to try to work out what’s going on “This game runs perfect it’s your system” to try to find the occasional useful comment on how to get the FAR mod and how far you have to get to be able to save.
2) You can install chips that improve your defensive, attacking and general skill abilities. You have a limited number of space to install chips. You can combine two identical chips to make a better version of the chip but it takes up more space. You can get special versions of these chips that can take up less space that are rarer. Chip space can be upgraded in a store. However this is all implemented in the menu system with as little emphasis as everything else in the menu system such as music select. So expect to have to pay attention to every little thing in the game to not miss important parts of the game! Not easy with work and family commitments.
Finally you often have to complete side quests firsts to ensure that the story doesn’t advance over them. Which often meant that I had very little freedom of choice.
Design-
The game has about 30 endings. Well no it doesn’t. It has an introduction, 3 chapters, and a multiple choice ending, then around minor 25 cut short endings for fanboys. Why the 3 chapters are called endings I don’t know. It takes around 40 hours for one play through.
You play as 1 human shaped character at a time that fights its way around 1 town and surrounding area completing quests. You are equipped with a spam sword attack, spam dodge, jump, and an invincible flying box that shoots at enemies. The little flying box could complete the game better all by itself!
Easy mode can reduce some of the frustration in the game by allowing the installation of chips that automate some functions. Installing automated dodge ensures you cannot get stuck on a nasty boss. Installing automating the flying box reduces the multitasking and helps you to practice your own dodge and attack techniques.
Positives-
The story, artistic style, vision, emotion and depth is fantastic. The introduction was shallow, and the first chapter was OK, but the great part of the game is that it is layered like an onion and it kept letting you delve deeper and re-experience events with greater perspective. Absolutely brilliant right the way through to the furthest story ending possible. This ending includes a very unique sacrifice choice that let me walk away from the game with a new gaming experience. I’m not going to go into detail about the story, artistic style, vision, emotion and depth because that is what you should experience for yourself by playing. I’m only going to say that it was good enough for me to finish the game praising it to others and highly recommending it. Even with the frustrations I experienced playing it.

Right. First thing to mention before anything. This game's port is not brilliant, I couldn't mantain a stable fps in a lot of game areas with a gtx 1060, and don't even think about getting this if you are packing an AMD gpu.
But even with its problems, I'm confident to say this game is nothing short of amazing, easily my GOTY.
This game is a hybrid between a typical Platinum Games spectacle fighter, a pseudo third-person shooter, a platformer, and a Galaga style bullethell shoot 'em up, all of that with some minor RPG mechanics like a leveling system.
At first glance it seems like a terrible idea to mix so many different genres, but NieR: Automata does it so well it all feels like one big cohesive game.
This game has a sort of perk system in the form of plug-in chips that can drop from enemies, and almost everything your character can do is determined by which chips he has equiped. It even includes things like UI elements (yes there is a chip that lets you access your HP bar). As the storage space for these chips is limited you can sacrifice things like your minimap to plug a chip that improves your damage output. As a fan of MGS i just love these little meta mechanics, and this game has quite a lot of them.
I'm not gonna spoil anything, since I think this game's story is something that HAS to be experienced, if you are interested in just the story, play the game on easy difficulty or something, but do NOT watch a playthrough, it's not the same thing by a mile.
This game's storytelling is nothing like anything I have ever seen on a AAA work before. You will not be watching lengthy cutscenes a la MGSIV in this game (it doesn't mean there isn't any cutscenes at all).
You will be fighting robots in a post apocalyptic Earth that hasn't seen the human presence in many millennia, it sounds like your everyday cliche Terminator story, but it's NOT AT ALL. This game raises some interesting questions about human nature, without feeling pretentious.
It has different endings, but not in the way you expect, and the true final ending is told in a way I don't think I've ever seen in any game EVER. It truly is a hidden gem.
In conclusion, I used to think Hideo Kojima was the sh!t, but now I just wanna know more about this Yoko Taro guy...

I don't want to sound over-hyped, so I'll just keep it simple. This game is cool. Sticking straight to the facts, this is a puzzle game that works through the filter of an 80's B-Horror film series! The movie shows up on a traditional video store shelf, complete with original VHS box art that you can flip around andd read the back of. For all those who grew up in the 80's, or at least were old enough to esperience the "Classic" horror movies of that time, THIS, is a really good throwback omajge to that whole genra. Especially now that Wes Craven has passed away, it feels like movies are going to start sucking. But this game allows you to play as "The Killer" !!!! Not another helpless victim. It comes along with an awesome sounding metal/rock esc music track, additional unlockable killer characters, unlockable fatalities, and up to at least 12 movies/campaigns!!!!

This movie is not Indie Game: The movie. I don't feel like it try's to be either. I also feel like this movie does not try to dive to deeply into one topic or antoher, but simply gives a narrative as to what is happening with indie games, Why indie developers do what they do and briefly talks about some of the hurdles, challanges, hardships and rewards that indie developers face. Where Indie Game was an in-depth character study of three dev teams and their struggles and triumphs, GameLoading is a snapshot of the second wave of indie game development. This is less about the specific developers, and more about the culture that connects the indie game scene. GameLoading is a celebration of the diversity of ideas and representations that indie games have an ability to portray, where they push the envelope in suject matter and mechanics.
Comparing GameLoading to Indie Game is unavoidable given their close proximity, but it's important to understand the team behind GameLoading have something very different to say.

I just finished watching it, although steam doesn't seem to properly show view time. A decent documentary. I found it extremely enjoyable to watch. If you want something to watch to learn "how" to do indie, this isn't what you're looking for; if you want something enjoyable to watch for an hour and a half, that is about the indie culture in games, and what games can mean, then this very well might be for you. It's well assembled technically and covers many things in and about games, from its content to its culture. It's also got some really spectacular pithy one-liners that I'll have to remember, like Don Daglow on interfaces.
It covers a broad spectrum of contemporary indies, while also drawing in the "big game development" experience of major figures like Don Daglow, or to have John Romero and Tom Hall relate how their development experience for eternal classics like DOOM was so very similar to the modern Indie experience. It also draws up the history of the industry, from the 70s to now; That history lesson is important, and all too often people forget about where we came from as a gaming community.
It covers the spectrum from the most hippie games imaginable like Soundself to bloody precision shooter indies like Nuclear Throne; this is a film that seeks to give a broad view about what indie is, what games are, and what they can mean. How they can be purely mechanical, technical experiences of challenge and mechanics-driven fun, or deeply impactful and human emotional experiences like That Dragon, Cancer, or Cart Life. It also touches on education, and organizations that are trying to teach children about code and creation and what the future generation can be like.
You'll see the words and thoughts of big names and small, and the diversity of opinion within games; overall, you'll see something that is ultimately very hopeful about what games can be.
Try not to be dissuaded by the salty baby tears of the gators swarming this space with negative reviews and insulting tags without actually watching the movie. This is something very much worth considering.

Like "The Blair Witch Project" before it, this movie by directors Anna Brady and Lester Francois is a horror film framed as a documentary.
The exposition begins with the filmmaker and protagonist arriving at a seemingly idyllic community in search of a story.  While the neon plumage and bizarre mating behaviors that prevail are unsettling, the people do seem pleasant and happy and friendly, at least at first.  Increasingly, it becomes clear that the language they speak only appears to be English.  In reality, their conversations are specious lunacy if not wholly unintelligible gibberish.  The audience is drawn inexorably to the conclusion that here the definitions of words are fluid and vague.  Evidence continues to mount until, after some detective work, we discover that this community exhibits total uniformity of thought.  The action climaxes with the filmmaker trapped and surrounded in a cultish society devoid of reason or purpose or joy.  Soon we reach the shocking final revelation: that $75 DLC which provides 2 additional pronouns to that twine game highlighting the struggles of rich college protestors fighting the evils of manspreading astronomers by blocking off the entrance to the non-gay bar that was rumored to have once served gamer clientele . . . was submitted to greenlight from your IP!
Ultimately, this movie is a rehash of well-worn tropes likely to bore anyone familiar with the horror genre.  I am particularly dismayed by the portrayal of women throughout as childish, unaccountable victims.  The use of hipster culture to signal an insane and credulous society is a cheap expository device that ruins much of the suspense.  In summary, this work is uninnovative, offensive trash.  0 bottles of Mountain Dew out of 10.
Disclosure: Mountain Dew is nasty.

If you've been following people in the indie dev community, and the gaming industry in general, some of what's documented here will already be familiar to you. But it's interesting to get a more personal look into the community, the creative process, how it affects people who spend years of their lives creating these things out of thin air, and what motivates them. It's used to send the message that anyone can make a game, and if they want to, they should. More, diverse people making games means more, diverse games, so that's a doubly good thing. Except for one thing this movie touches upon, marketing. More games, harder to get noticed.
Anyway, kind of going off on a tangent. My favorite thing about this movie is probably that they managed to document the very end of The Stanley Parable. Wreden fretting over last minute stuff and watching the game going live is fantastic. My overall takeaway from this movie is further respect for the passion and effort put into making games. I am now a little bit more happy and a little bit less of a cynical prick. And, you know, looking at recent/current events in gaming, that's quite important.

Hitman: Contracts is a fantastic game that offers so much for those interested in making dough and improving their wits by the means of organized crime and taking part in a series of stealth and murder.  The original suit and tie wearing assassin machine returns in this third installment of the ongoing Hitman franchise, which made its debut on November 2000.  This 2003 sequel does a better job delivering a smart stealth action game that requires those who can handle hardcore puzzle solving and in-plain-sight style stealth, while at the same time being creative.  There is no hand holding in this game, so get your thinking caps on.
In this game, you play as an infamous bald contract killer clone who is an urban legend to each of the countries he's visited when performing his assassinations.  Being under the radar for so many years had paid off for Mr. "47" that he seemed to be untouchable.  That is until a random unidentified person recognizes 47 and shoots him in the side.  Apparently, not everybody believes the lie about 47 being a myth.  And, this one guy managed to fill in some blanks and track him down.  He manages to get away and probably kill the guy who shot him.  However, he gets stuck hiding in a cheap nasty building that looks like an apartment complex.  As he's bleeding out he thinks about a bunch of his former contracts that he's completed over the years.
The player is put into those flashbacks until the final level of the game, which takes place in the present.  Meanwhile, in the present, before the end of the last level, 47 is stuck hiding in there while dozens of police officers, SWAT teams, and so on, surround the apartment complex, as well as 47's final target of the game.
This is the third game in the series. However, missions jump all over the place within 47's timeline.  In fact, the first level happens the second after Hitman: Codename 47 (the first game) ends.
Each level is rather huge and intimidating, while at the same time being open and approachable in a non-linear fashion.  47 can be stealthy and only kill his targets with no bodies found, no civilian casualties, and perform each hit with extreme precision.  Weapons and tools can be picked and brought into a level after completing it once, which allows the player to go beyond just using fiberwire and guns.  If the player were to look hard enough within a level, he might actually find some poison or bombs that could be used properly without any casualties.
The player will have a hard time progressing and unlocking anything useful if he or she does a poor job at not getting caught, or killing anybody that is not their target (this includes guards and other types of authority...especially civilians.)
I haven't had this much fun finding a good vantage point, opening my briefcase to assemble a sniper rifle, and then putting an extra set of holes into two guys' foreheads at the same time with the same bullet.
Speaking of bullets, if you play on harder difficulties, you're only allowed to shoot a certain amount of them to get the best possible score in the end of each mission.  This is to enhance the idea that 47 should not leave too much at the scene of each crime.  It's that kind of unneccessary damage that prevents the hit man from being the best there is.  So, make each shot count.  Or, don't shoot at all. You do not need to.
One feature that is reoccurring in all of the Hitman games is the ability to wear disguises.  This is done by going behind some guy in a non-populated area and sedating him with a knock-out drug.  If you kill him and he's not a target, your score goes down.  So, use sedative.
The player can take his clothes, whether it be the clothes of a body guard or an officer of the law, and then proceed to a part of the level that is not restricted to 47 in that particular set of clothing.  Getting to do things like this makes reaching the target a lot easier, as long as it is done properly.
Levels also allow environmental executions that can be performed onto particular targets.  There's this one target who's got a heart condition.  This man tends to go in and out of a sauna, and it just so happens you could turn up the heat in there and give the guy a heart attack that he'll never forget. That's what he gets for being a monster.
Aside from close ranged weapons like piano wire or sedative, and long ranged ones, such as the rifle, 47 can perform executions in a more creative fashion.  For example, the hit man could poison his target's drink or food.  Maybe, if the player is smart enough, 47 could place a bomb in the targets' vehicle.  If they were to be alerted, they'd all run to their limo, and then 47 could push the button, getting all of them at once the second before almost failing the mission.
--
The soundtrack in this game is absolutely, without a doubt, one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard in my entire life.  The combination of exploring each of the huge levels and the music that plays in the background is beyond satisfying.  This music perfectly captures the feeling of not just being some ordinary spy agent, but a hardcore contract killer who has no remorse for these cancers on society.
Jesper Kyd is the one responsible for this beautiful work of art.  I recommend listening to it.
The main characters of focus are 47, his handler (the one who contacts him and assigns his jobs) Diana Burnwood, and (to an extent) his targets. There is no main antagonist.  However, there is an antagonistic opposition at hand that does bring our main character and his handler into some trouble.  It's interesting to see how 47 handles things to make things work out for his agency, the ICA (International Contract Agency.)
The more I think about it, the story reminds me of a Tarantino film.  The levels/hits are out of order, the story goes back and forth between the present and past, and yet by the end there is a comprehensible story that makes perfect sense.
For a main character who apparently has no emotions, 47 is an incredibly well written and designed character.  His story in this game, and in the entire series, is one to admire.  His usual practice of keeping everything locked up inside without allowing anyone to see him feel is understandable once you witness his story from beginning to end.  He believes that it's what helps him carry out his contracts without fail.  But it always winds up being his admiration for the few he cares about that keeps him feeling alive.  That, and his admiration for the art that is professional assassinations.  For him, going on means wiping away the evil that's on earth one sicko at a time.
Eventually, after working with his handler for so long, there is this hidden emotional bond that brings the two together.  This entire game is mostly memories of the good times he had fullfilling his desire to wipe away the criminal underworld.  None of those memories would have been possible if it weren't for this same person who always gave him the job.  This particular game doesn't focus on the chemistry between the two main characters too much, believe it or not, but there's plenty of moments in the other games that show that both are willing to look out for one another no matter what.
In the game prior to this one, 47 was to rescue a friend of his: a man named Emilio Vittorio.  He was a priest trying to show 47 the light in being a good man, not a killer.  Ironically, 47 had to kill those responsible to get his friend back.
This is another one of those things that proves that 47 isn't a man without emotions.  He's just a guy that doesn't want his emotions to get the best of him.  It's one of the things that'll probably catch up to him in the long run, and cause him to snap when he loses someone he cares about.  And the last thing you want to do is cause the best killer in history to snap
That is one hell of a story, if you ask me.

This is going to be a pretty long read. I hate that steam only has a yes/no recommend button because it really does disservice to writing a review about a game where a lot of it is in the grey area and no black and white answer.... I have over 400 hours into this game so take a few minutes to read the whole thing.
I should start by talking about what I place a lot of my weight on during this review. I dont play with friends, we are all 23 and everyone has their own lives and its too much work getting ppl to play together for more than an hour. I keep it simple and play singleplayer because it lets you go at your own pace, esp in this game which is not a turn based but basically an RTS. I dont care about roleplaying either, I just want to do a quick customization, pick the starting options that matter (gov't and race traits) and hop into the game. I wont play some wierd "suboptimal" method just for role playing to make the game fun for myself, I paid around 75 bucks for the game and DLCs, why should I go out of my way to make the game fun rather than just expect it to be fun on its own? Another thing I dont give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about is graphics, as long as the game doesnt look like it was made before 2005, it doesnt matter to me as long as its core is strong and its fundamentally a fun game.
I care about AI the most. If the AI isnt challenging enough, the game turns boring for me quickly. The AI in this game is.... bad. I cant think of a softer word to describe it. There are 4 difficulty modes and either you steamroll the AI on easy and normal or youre pretty much are screwed and have to turtle for 20 hours before you can challenge the AI in harder and insane difficulty. Once you play 2 - 3 games, you quickly learn exactly what the AI does and the challenge really goes away.
The AI does not have any sense of zone control, it does not have any sense of predicting what other AI or the player will do. There is no long term strategy for them outside of sticking to their playstyle on a very high level sense of sticking to its government style. It doesnt adapt. The game itself doesnt have a lot of these different playstyle options that drastically change how you play the game, so regardless of who your neighbor is, every empire does the same thing where they rush their first colony and just continuously build fleets to either deter conflict or do mental math to see when it will attack you. A lot of the problem stems from species customization which just doesnt have many traits that change your play style, rather giving you small passive bonuses. (atleast for the AI to work with) Over the course of expansions, there have been some changes, I will get into that later. The difficulty is not about AI that becomes smarter, rather it is the same as normal difficulty but they have insane amounts of production bonuses. While this is not necessarily a bad thing, it makes the game much less interesting to play as regardless of difficulty level. For example in a normal playthrough empire X will have 10k fleet power, but in insane difficultly, because of production bonuses, they will do the same exact thing but have 40k fleet power.
Part of the problem of boring AI is that the galaxy is very bland geographically. There are small things like nebulae that slow down warping speed, but thats it. I only play hyper lanes because of this reason as it is one of the only option that gives some semblance of strategy when it comes to colony expansions, defense structures and choke points. Even this option is useless late game once you research certain tech that makes hyperlanes pretty much useless. Games like civ6 have mountains and hills and terrain that gives a variety of bonuses to combat and that makes each game feel a bit different and adds a layer of strategy.
Another extremely boring system right now is how war is waged. Right now, all you do is build 1 huge fleet up with all your ships and crash it against the enemies huge fleet with all their ship. Whoever comes out of that engagement the winner pretty much wins the whole war and its just a matter of time from there on to conquer planets to build up your warscore for the inevitable victory/defeat. There is no comeback mechanic, there is no strategic value in splitting up your fleets, defense stations are pretty much useless after the early/ mid game and are only there to slow down the enemy for a few seconds thats it. They recently got buffed but their main problem is that there is no good reason to have them. There is no supply line mechanic that stations can help extend, no refueling, no system patrolling.
The AI is extremely stupid in general during war as it will make decisions like sending in random ships to fight when its a guarenteed loss, ships will just wait out 80 percent of the war and losing half their territory before even doing anything sometimes.
Armies are tedious to manage as well, raising armies on planets and taking them and making them hover over a planet till they are ready to invade after which its just a numbers game of who wins.
Diplomacy is also severely lacking. There is no spying, no mercenaries, no way to incite uprising, no way to sabotage another empire from within, no way to disrupt trade deals, no complicated trading options outside of just 1 way give and take, no way to do 3 way deals, no way to entice a 3rd party to join wars in return for system or resources. No way to give partial information. It all runs on opinion modifiers that are very black and white.
Sectors (parts of your empire you can assign to the AI to control), while not as bad as before, are still stupid. You want to avoid using sectors at all costs if you are playing any empire that is even the slightest bit nuanced outside of KILL KILL MURDER KILL EVERYTHING as the sector has no idea what to build on which tile that the empire needs and what species to have on which tile.
Finally, THERE IS JUST SOOO MUCH MICROMANAGEMENT HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ The insane amounts of micromanagement required to properly assign correct scientists and pops to tiles and manually exploring and picking building to build makes you waste so much time on pause. I think a third of my playtime was spent on pause just micromanaging every 5 -10 years.
The end game is very boring and after a while you just wait on the end game crisis. While there are different flavors of the crisis, it all boils down to an empire spawning and killing everybody and you have to get together with all the other empires and beat them back. THere is no unique crisis that causes strife within the already existing empires. (Outside war of heaven which is part of the leviathan DLC)
I want to touch on some positives though after that rant lol.
The game looks good and it has some really good music. I have no problems there.
There are a lot of different options to customize your species looks and write backstories for them if that is what you are into.
The modding scene is alive and can help fix a few problems as well as enhance your gameplay.
It has a level of fun, especially in the early game when it comes to how you will expand and deal with your neighbors based on their type of playstyle. If you get lucky enough to spawn next to peaceful empires, you wont have to build up a fleet as early or quickly. If you have rivals you can get into defensive pacts to deter them. You can use frontier outposts to block off certain systems you dont want your neighbors to have. Unfortunately the galaxy fills up very quickly and by mid game a lot of these fluid relationships are set and strategic expansion methods fly out the window.
The tech tree is decent and the method of getting 3 random ones to choose from, while not optimal, does add a level of choice where you have to play your empire in a certain style. You could get unlucky and not get technology to add more energy buildings and this can hamper your sustain. (CONTINUED IN COMMENTS)

I bought this by impulse when I saw the price is around 20 cents. Decided to try it a bit and I instantly fell in love to the art style and music; it felt so nostalgic, like something from the NES era.
Out There Somewhere is a puzzle platformer game. The puzzle is on how you get to that side of the screen. To do it, you'll need to think, plan, and execute it with perfect timing which most of the time will require several tries to get it right. There are diverse mechanics in the game and it is combined in later areas to make challenging puzzles. What I really like is how the game made you understand the mechanic without long or complex tutorial. The game will just say "If you do X then Y." After that, the game will throw you a simple puzzle that revolve around that one mechanic. Some other time the game won't even tell anything; you just found yourself in a new area with some element you never see before. The area's goal is to make you familiar with a new gameplay mechanic without even telling you it's there. That is what other game needs to copy.
The game is rather short. I beat the story (not 100%) in under 1 hour (58 minutes to be exact). I was surprised when the credit rolls because I really really really want to play more. I'm really not sure whether I should recommend this or not.  I'd give it a 5/10.  Maybe that is just being generous.
I have to admit the gameplay was frequently fun, and it was very pretty... and I had plenty of fun ramming things to death as MOOSE CAVALRY...   at least when playing as 2B...
But the flaws really stand out. I'd score this a lot worse if it weren't for the fact that a lot of games these days can't even get the fun gameplay bit right.
The plot railroads HARD. It supposedly has different "routes", except there is only one storyline and just different perspectives on it, and if you deviate even slightly, it either gives a very whittled down Bad End... or it just blocks you via respawns, invisible walls and "but thou must" situations. Not even joking. There is NO CHOICE in this game. Not a whit. No freedom. You go where the plot tells you and so help you if you want to have any say in the matter.
As for what that plot is, that is railroaded so hard...  without giving too much away, it is completely senseless. One of the first sections of the game has 2B (a gynoid calling herself an android) telling 9S (an android) that "Emotions are Forbidden".  You'd expect her to take it seriously.  It doesn't take long for both characters to descend into throwing tantrums about all sorts of petty nonsense. This game fully champions the idea that being an uncontrolled mess of feelings like some unreserved 3-year-old is the correct and decent way to be...  with an extra side-helping of "emotions are the only correct justification for not killing things".
Besides that, there is also the way everything just gets bleak and depressing past a certain point... AND ALSO the Hacking mini-game... which is like the worst free-rotating shoot-em-up ever and was an absolute nightmare for me until I discovered that lock-on worked in combat.  There was far too much of the hacking mini-game.  Also expect to grind a lot for various reasons... It IS Japanese, afterall.
Frankly... I'd recommend the A route... and then suggest you just don't bother continuing after that. The rest is just a parade of disappointment, depression, boredom and annoyance.

RO2/RS is built around some basic, core principles. One of these is that to make up for there only being 64 players in a battle IRL featured at least hundreds, if not thousands, the maps are scaled down appropriately to make up for this. The weapons are designed around this, especially in regards to e.g. sounds and muzzle flashes.
Whilst the developers of this mod have created some beautiful player skins, they've neglected how the maps look (most are very dull and repetitive), and ultimately worst of all, not taken any care to scale them down to the relatively low player count previously mentioned. This results in huge, plain, open maps where most firefights are completely one sided affairs consisting of the defending side shooting at attacking players from so far away (~400m) that the game mechanics simply can't deal with. You rarely actually hear any gunfire when shot at, nor do you see muzzle flashes. And fairly obviously, huge maps with 32 vs. 32 players rarely result in any exciting combat. Instead the norm is a few random, brief engagements when one group of players stumble into an opposing group's crosshairs, and 9/10 are despatched of within seconds, barely knowing what happened.
I don't advocate firearms nuhuh.

Improvement over previous installment. Disciples and ascension of thrones brings new flavor to the game. One of the best indie games I've ever played and used countless of hours before this was released in Steam.
However this game isn't for everyone, so I recommend watching few let's plays or gameplay footage before buying. This isn't the cheapest indie game out there, but personally I would say it worth it when comparing to many other indie games in Steam at same price range.

Dominions 4 is just one of those games that sure, it doesn't have the amazing graphics of say Civilization or Europa Universalis but it makes up for that with a lot of depth, a ton of content and great replayability. The plotline for the game is fairly basic; Essentially each player is a godlike being called a Pretender, each controls a loyal nation and is battling to become the Pantokrator, or supreme god. To do this a pretender can either do it one of three ways; The first way is to conquer your enemies with vast armies which can take a long time depending on some of the maps, spreading your religion to the point it extinguishes the power of your rivals religion or the new victory condition for this installment, capturing the required number of Thrones of Ascension. Each throne grants you a special perk so to speak and also adds strategy to what provinces you conquer and when. Each nation exists in either one of three ages, sometimes all three. The sheer amount of units in this game is astounded and every single nation in the game is based on history, mythology or fantasy tropes (Although there are no stereotypical Elves or Dwarves at all really.) One of the best parts of the game is also the manual which not only contains information on how to play the game, but it also contains little bits of lore, developer commentary on the different nations and an entire roster of every unit in the game. It is even updated to consider in updates and patches. There is too much content for me to state in this review but the last thing I will say is this; If you enjoy turn based strategy games that give you that "One More Turn" mentality and you can look past the dated graphics then this game is well worth the $35 asking price.

Best turn based strategy to date. A hardcore game in every sense of the word, this is the perfect game for a micromanaging junkie. Watching the action of battles is suspenseful and fun, even relaxing considering you have no input while they take place. Every game is a new experience as there are near infinite strategies to pursue. While as of writing this review Dominions 4 lacks the mod library of Dominions 3, I'm sure in time content will be converted and new mods will be created. The only downside I can imagine to a fan of the genre would be the complete lack of diplomacy. Dominions 4 has added team games which help reduce the feeling of complete isolation. While the learning curve is steep, with the manual and some messing around I think most people will be successful in enjoying this game. 10/10

If you want a deep strategy game that takes you hours to learn, more hours to master, and countless hours of fun, buy this game. I also love the historical mythology flavor of all the units. I have spent hours in this game and the previous just reading descriptions of them!
Look past the graphics, it's all about the insanely deep strategic gameplay in a fantasy world.

This is, no kidding, the deepest strategy game you may ever buy on Steam. The manual - and yes, you will absolutely need to read the manual old school style - is 295 pages, with the tutorial being about 24 pages of text and images. It's a complex, fiddly game, with a very dedicated community of players. If you can get a good group together, multiplayer is fantastic.
I will warn you that the game's UI is obtuse as Hell and the graphics will really put your dedication to "gameplay over graphics" to the test. If you've never played a Dominions game, then be prepared to go down the rabbit hole of strategy.

The mechanics of the game have been done before but the style it is presented in, which is of an 80's slasher movie makes it standout. The animations are great and every blood splattered blocky death is done with humour and great animation. The puzzles, whilst some simple , some are not so obvious and sometime you kill the last person with a smile on your face thinking you have completed the level, only to find you are now stuck and can’t reach the exit, at which point you can use the rewind feature, that takes you back through your steps one at a time, allowing you to continue from any point in the level, this is animated like an old VHS tape rewinding. The way the puzzles are constructed and the need to position some victims in the level by such mechanics as scaring them in a certain direction, or getting their attention with a ringing phone, ensure that the way the puzzles are solved is in keeping with the theme of the slasher movie genre.

Hitman: Contracts
+ Hitman: Contracts provides players with a large number of assassination options. Dress as a chef and deliver a meal, then when you are out of sight hack your target to death with the meat cleaver you were carrying. Sabotage a fireplace in a mansion with gasoline to burn your target to death. Perhaps serving poisoned whiskey as the butler is your fancy? Disable metal detectors in a hotel security room to sneak your weapons past. There's lots of possibilities.
+ Like Hitman 2: Silent Assassin, the game has a good atmosphere and attention to detail. There are also some new missions to partake in, but some are repeated from previous titles (more on that in the con section). I loved "Murder at Beldingford Manor" - a giant palace home to beautiful courtyards, where you need to kill the owner. A big, open map with lots of entry points - a hedge maze trap door, front entrance and more. There's a few others that stand out, like "The Bjarkhov Bomb", where 47 must assassinate two Russian targets and detonate explosives on a nuclear submarine to sink it.
+ Enjoyable stealth and action combat make for an exciting experience.
~ Only about 8 hours of gameplay, slightly more of higher difficulties - but there is some replayability present which helps.
- The plotline is pretty much non-existent. Agent 47 has been shot by an unknown assassin in Paris and travels back to his apartment, delirious. He begins to drift in and out of consciousness, reminiscing about past assassinations which you will replay. In terms of new "story" content there is none. At the end of the game you'll get to control the fate of agent 47, but that's it.
- About half of the missions are re-makes from the first game in the series, Hitman: Codename 47. So for those who have finished that game, you're really offered 4-5 fresh assassination tasks which is a bit lacking.
- The freedom of choice for weapon loadout prior to assassinations is missing in Hitman: Contracts. You'll be given the standard ballers, silenced pistol, fiber wire and anaesthetic but that's it. Any other guns you want - you'll need to find throughout the level, and you can't collect them for use in the future either.
Overall Score: 7/10
Hitman: Contracts is a great game, but it loses points for blatant repetition of missions that already exist in the series. With a weak plot but nice gameplay a seven seems deserving. Be sure to grab it on sale.

When I first purchased this game I was really excited to play it. It is pretty deep and complicated, however, once you learn the basics and use the tutorial it is easy to get the flow and you start to appreciate all the complexity. When I say complex that does not mean you need to overly micromanage, I mean there is a lot of content and nuance to the game which you discover and master in a gradual manner. The way it progresses helps to everything unfold  so that it does not overwelm you too soon. As many have commented the early game is fun, you explore and build while learning a lot of things that make the game interesting. The problem is the middle game and the battle/war mechanics. It goes sort of like this, explore, discover, collect resources, encounter and trade with new alien races...rinse..repeat. There are some later game events but they are slow in developing. Then you find you are always outmatched in firepower so getting into an early war spells doom. Escpecially with a fallen empire which always impossibly outmatches you. They also taunt and insult you and there is little you can do about it. In addition other races are really standoffish and will not even enter into a non-aggression pact, there is always "no need." This makes insulting other aliens and conquering the galaxy through war almost impossible. Another bug for me is the influnence resource, it just does not accumulate fast enough or you never have enough. I really do not like using the "console" command to force feed resources but without giving yourself enough your civ can't even recuit staff. That aside everything else works well, the only thing missing is a little character. By that I mean there is not history or backstory, which makes it all a little vanilla. The new robot  DLC adds a lot of flavor to the game and playing as a synthetic race is interesting. But....if you have any passing interest in Star Trek then the New Horizons mod is a must. In fact try it even if you don't know anything about Star Trek. This mod which is freely available and turns a 7.5/10 game into a 10/10! It is an awesome mod which could easily be called Stellaris Star Trek Edition. It tranforms the game into an engrossing and well made epic. The sheer work put into it is amazing and it is free to boot. I would easily recommend you purchase Stellaris just for this mod. It is perahps one of the best Star Trek PC games ever. The ships, the alien races, the music and sounds and all the lore is included. Events are specifically taken from episodes from a variety of Star Trek TV and movie stories along with screen captures. All the alien races are there and finally you know who you can trust and ally with from the moment you meet them. Forming alliances are quicker and creating a Federation comes early in the game. Stellaris at its core is designed more for exploration and boldly going forth into the galaxy and this fits perfctly into the Human race of the game. I was tempted to play as a Klingon but the core game plays better as the Human faction. I am in the middle stages of the game and it is vastly more interesting then the vanilla Stellaris. I have not gone to war yet, but I have enough backup not to worry about any alien aggressors. Plus the anticipation of discovering all the Star Trek aliens and encountering varied and interesting events is awesome. My review is 10/10 if you play with this mod for sure!

Lots of gators in these waters. Being as tiresome as ever. Their negative reviews are all the usual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t rhetoric, but I didn't like this movie much either.
In a word, it's shallow. It doesn't provide any insight, understanding, or even any difficult-to-find information. It provides brief snapshots of a bunch of developers, a small bit of the usual trite advice about making indie games, and not much else. Most of the subject developers are already well-known - if you're into indie games at all, you'll probably already know most of what this documentary covers. This isn't a movie about the video game industry. So if that's what you're looking for then don't buy this. This is a movie about inspiring indie game developers.  There seems to be an uprising of content like this (content focused around independent game development) being promoted by companies like valve and unity. I guess you can say that they're probably only doing it for profits in the long run, but it's providing a huge opportunity for growth as a medium.
A little over a year ago game development wasn't really a big goal for me. I've always been really into to making meaningful art and doing that through video games has been something that's interested me almost the entirety of my life but I always thought that the technicalities of it would be too much for me. But people like Extra Credits, who produce so many videos about design theory, companies like unity that  have free and comprehensive tools and tutorials, and sites like stackexchange where you just have this huge community helping each other out, these things put those technicalities into the grasp of a common person.
And I think documentaries like this one, and Indie Game: The Movie serve to inspire people like me who maybe can't afford college because they couldn't get financial aid, and are developing a game in their spare time while working minimum wage at subway. Because it's such an exasperating process. Documentaries like this one make me feel like I have a shot at making something worthwhile and getting it out there. And I think that feeling is definitely essential if an Indie developer is actually going to follow through with their project.
Seeing this rated as having mixed reviews kind of makes me sad. Though when I read the negative reviews it sort of makes sense. The people saying this is bad are the same people who want to protect the "Gamer" identity and keep the game industry pretty much exclusively oriented for young adult males. So I guess if you're one of those people don't buy this. However if you're an aspiring developer you should definitely buy this, because it's stuff like this that might just keep you from giving up on a potentially incredible work of art.

Prefacing this review with the fact that I've written a handy guide here (
) to prove I've actually watched the content in case of any sync errors with steam showing 0.0 hours played.
Gameloading is a very frenetic, hard-to-watch documentary about a specific clique of game developers that identify as "indie," but are actually very interconnected with one another.
At a run time of 1:33 including the credits, this film skips between over 34 interviews, but spends only meaningful camera time on a select few. While industry veterans such as Jon Romero and Tom Hall are a welcome addition to provide their insight, they have less than 2 minutes of cumulative screentime in favor of a sea of pink-haired hipster 20-somethings complaining about how poor they are despite toting Macbooks across the U.S.(and in a few cases, the Atlantic). There's a clear narrative goal that is contradicted by the obvious facts and environments these globe-trotting trust funders inhabit.
What's worse is there's a call-out to Kickstarter backers in the credits, so on inspection the movie was backed there for over 100K, and they're STILL asking for $9 a head on Steam? Truly atrocious. I feel like I've learned nothing, was bombarded with unlikable negative personalities for 90 minutes, only to see them get rewarded with millions of dollars in the end for failing out of film school.
If you saw that Indie Game movie on Netflix, just save your money and watch it for free somewhere else eventually, it's as empty and pretentious a film as the Stanley Parable, but without the interactivity.

It's...it's not what you expect. Trust me.
This appeals to only a VERY VERY small minority. I mean I get it, I do. Though this isn't the type of movie that most gamers would like. They say they are gamers, but my mind screams that they're not. It's meant for the kind of audience that would throw  and splatter a bucket of off-branded rainbow paint on someone's porch without consent and call it "art." Get it? I'm putting this in a nicest way possible. Those are the kind of people they are shooting for. You know Doug's sister Judy from Nicktoon's Doug back in the day? That's the audience. Judy Funnie.
Look, if you use Twine, you're not a game developer. Just as a toddler is not a engineer just because his Fischer-Price toy makes him out to be. I played Depression Quest, it's boring. If I want to read a boring novel, I would read a Ayn Rand book. I believe it's still free as of today on Steam if you don't want to take my word for it. No, go ahead. Really.
The Pros?
Stanely Parable is pretty cool. That's really the only game they advertised that's passable as a game. I played it, it's unique for sure.
The production is pretty good. I'm sure they worked hard producing this sundance flick.

It's great seeing so many of the faces behind the games I love! Much of this was a recap of events in the indie scene that I'm familiar with, but I also learned about several game jams, trade shows, studios, and education groups. The message is: go make your own games now, no matter who you are.
I'm not sure what people who don't follow the scene would make of it. There's a lot of inside baseball and some of the personalities could seem very confusing without knowing their work ahead of time. For example Cart Life's creator is kind of creepy, but it totally makes sense when you know his game. At the same time they take time to explain the games they've made, so maybe it would work.
So, nice and mostly feel good. Very fractured because it interviews so many people, but it does a nice job of weaving them all into a single dialog.

A whole lot of production to say almost nothing of value. It's essentially a sequel to Indie Game The Movie, and more or less acts as a post-release advertisement for The Stanley Parable, Depression Quest, and a whole bunch of other gimmick software, all while fluffing the developers who made them. Also, Ben Kuchera is there for some reason that I can't quite discern, given his lacklustre-yet-storied career of games "journalism" and known-and-visible history of PR favouritism and hypocrisy.
Other reviewers are talking about the "effort" put into this, and the "insight" it provides you with. Effort for what? Insight into what? It's a sideways advertisement for an incestuous clique of developers receiving awards from their friends for experimentation, and waxing 60%-grade social-science final-assignment on the deep feels of developing a gimmick game.
Games made on a train ride by hipsters who can freely afford to globetrot while masquerading as poor people who are just scraping by. One of the spotlighted games is literally just a limited-feature music visualiser that uses live microphone input instead of an MP3. It's amazing, truly - but not for the reasons this movie thinks it is.
Lucky me, I didn't spend any of my own money on this. I sold a CSGO Lounge item to pay for it. But in the end, someone's money paid for me to watch this, and for that I'm deeply sorry.
Don't buy this. Don't watch this. It's barely even entertaining for free, and imparts no real knowledge upon the viewer regardless of how much they've paid to see it. This is a movie about the greatness of people, not the hardship of game development. Don't pretend it's anything but public relations.

I'm no Dominions veteran. I learned about Dom3 just a week before Dom4 came out but what I learned about it in that time was enough to buy this game for 30 euros on bloody Desura. And that was 1st time in years when I bought a game outside of Steam.
Are you getting bored by your 10th Crusader Kings' world conquest?
Have you conquered whole Europe as Palatinate in EU4 ironmode?
You wish Rome 2 was less graphic and actually some content?
Then Dominions 4 is clearly a game for you.
You can tell it's 10 years of constant development. With 70 different factions, thousands creatures and spells ou guys are in for a treat!
Single player and AI leave much to be desired but they are just a training ground for great multiplayer experience. There are few more gratifying things than fighting seasoned veterans of this title. Especially since community is very helpful and welcoming allowing you to survive learning curve with just a few broken limbs.
Dominions 4 multiplayer is like a chess. If chess had 3.000 diferent units instead of 7 and could be played with few dozens people.
And was cool.
And had dragons.
And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of spells.
If you are into all that just buy it. It has best $/content ratio you can find.

Extraordinary amount of content (75 factions, 2.5k units, hundreds of spells and items), in-depth mechanics with many unique ideas (like the combat system in which you can deploy your troops and give them scripted orders instead of having direct control over them, placing emphasis on careful planning and predicting enemy tactics), factions primarily based on historical nations and real-world mythology from all around the world (and lore being superbly represented by the mechanics: I'd go as far as saying Dominions has the best worldbuilding in video games), great multiplayer experience (simultaneous turns, works really well in play-by-e-mail format, typically played with machiavellian diplomacy), good modding-support...
I've personally been a fan since Dominions 2 (although I didn't pick up multiplayer until recently) and despite ridiculous pricing of the time (I think I paid $80 for both Dom2 and Dom3 when you include postage fees), it was worth every cent and then some. After all, in what other game can you have a deathmatch between Gods that lead nations such as Spanish Inquisition, Atlantian Eskimos, Man-eating Giant Jews, The Mongols, Undead Romans and the like? What other game allows you to have reality-altering magic or armed-to-the-teeth titans capable of wiping out armies single-handedly while remaining "balanced"?
Now, it should go without saying that Dominions 4 has low production value and it's not a stellar single player game. Some veteran players have also raised concerns about a couple of changes (like removal of reverse communions) that might end up hurting it in the long run (I don't dare to make a claim for either direction myself). However, as far as I can tell, Dominions 4 is still an upgrade over its predecessor, and even if some of the issues come to haunt it in the long run, there's only one game that even compares, and that's Dominions 3, a proven masterpiece. Dominions 4 is probably even better, and with the bulk of MP-games being made to it right now and improvements to single player being noticeable (even if not huge), it's the obvious choice if you want some Dominions action.

This game has you play as a killer and you can only go in full directions left right up or down.
Players have to kill all the victims and then exit via a portal, at the end of a level you get a bonus kill scene where you can earn some extra money to spend.
Money can be spent on unique fatality kills or unlock new killers too, you can also use money to get a hint for a puzzle or even get a full sequence on how to complete the puzzle too. Mind you, all of these are expensive so you'll have to pass a lot of puzzles in order to buy them, which keeps you playing.
As levels progress, new features are added. there will be victims you're not allowed to kill and there will be victims who can actually kill you. You also have traps, hazards and other objects which will alter the puzzle together.
Some puzzles are easy and some will get you quite frustrated. We're all different in how we think and solve puzzles in general so you'll always be challenged in some way and sometimes you'll blitz no problem.
I hope they can introduce some kind of workshop support for this game. I'm up to the NC-17 videos which provide some extremely challenging puzzles and being a colourful game too with its simple graphics, I'd say its a very enjoyable game.

Stellaris is a game I bought on a whim because I need something to pass the time and has turned into probably one of the most engaging, enjoyable, and memorable games I have played; that I have over 400 hours at the time of writing and still find myself drawn to it should be a testament to that.
This continued enjoyment of mine come from the continued effort and care that the developers have put into this game; with all the patches they launch that add new content and fix the games features what didn’t work, and most of the problems I had with the game when I bought it have been addressed.
The only real problem I have with Stellaris is some of the late game gameplay.
In most all of my play throughs I usually end up controlling a large portion of the galaxy but am locked in an endless stale mate or cold war with other empires with neither side having the strength to attack the other and have a chance at winning, leading to huge spanses of time where nothing really happens.
The second problem I have is with the end game crisis, an extremely powerful late game event that threatens all empires in the galaxy. My problem with the end game crisis isn’t the crisis itself, (infact think it does help to break those endgame stalemates) but is with how AI empires try to deal with them, which is to say poorly. In most cases it tends to be the player vs the crisis, and if the crisis spawns near your empire and/or you don’t have a strong fleet to begin with it tends to be game over right there. Though if you are playing with other people you have a much greater chance to deal with it, as you can actively work with them and not just hope that the AI empires actually do something helpful.
Either way I still highly recommend Stellaris.

This is a solid twitchy platformer to pick up and play for 10-20 minutes at a time. You descend a procedurally-generated tower while slashing enemies, jumping over spikes, and collecting items. The controls are super tight and fun to play with. There’s a short timer that you have to be constantly regenerating to stay alive, so you’re forced to move quickly and rely on your reflexes. Super House of Dead Ninjas is a well executed retro-styled precision platformer. The lightning fast combat and sensitive controls can seem a bit unwieldy at first, but they ultimately lead to a uniquely adrenaline-charged "ninja" feel that only hurtling through the levels at a breakneck speed can create. There is a wealth of unlocks as well, the only problem being that after showering the player with new weapons and upgrades during the first few hours of gameplay they slow to a mere trickle. Add to that the unusual order in which upgrades unlock, and you have a recipe for potentially unsatisfying progression.
Still, the meat of the gameplay is, like a fine steak, rare and delicious. Although the game suffers from "roguelike repetition" the randomly generated levels and enemies each present unique obstacles which push a player's reflexes to the maximum as they adjust on-the-fly. Gamers who love this genre will find Super House of Dead Ninjas to be a superb entry with many hours of replayability as they race to survive long enough for that elusive high score.
