A lot of people might just assume I never got around to it, or had some issue with it. That's not exactly false, but not quite true either. The honest reason is that I just usually can't get into these super-long single-player RPGs. I'm much more of an MMO kinda guy.
However I was watching a playthrough on YouTube and after a while of following this other person's adventure, I found myself increasingly wanting to begin my own; so, after six years I finally installed the new Special Edition and fired it up, dipping myself into this strange world.
Well hold on, that's not entirely true either...
First I had to install a mod just so the game properly supported my screen resolution. There are games from almost 20 years ago now that can support arbitrary screen resolutions. I still don't understand why every engine doesn't do this. Skyrim's "cutscenes" are all in-engine so this shouldn't really be a problem. Then I installed a character mod that polishes up the default faces a bit because egads are they ugly. They're still ugly, but less so, and I wear a mask anyway so ah well. At this point the only other mod I really will probably install is SKSE64 + SkyUI when that's finished because man those menus are terrible.
It's a game with a lot of problems, sure. There are NPCs that try to walk up vertical walls and gates, random items floating in the air, and last night I had to no-clip my way out of a bit of geometry that I could easily walk into but not back out of, but man do I find myself fascinated by the world now that I've finally trekked my way into it properly.
When I first tried it 6 years ago I found it kind of boring and impenetrable, but watching another person's story and choices I finally found the urge to push through and tackle it, and I'm really having a ball with no end in sight. Take note, publishers, this is why you support the Let's Play communities.

SUMMARY:  Buy it for the puzzles, keep playing it for the laughs.
TLDR:  I bought this game on a lark, expecting it to be more about splatter than puzzles.  Much to my surprise, however, there's a very good puzzle game in here under the simple cubist graphics and cheesy-just-to-be-cheesy farcing of the 1970s-80s ultra-campy slasher/splatter movies.  This is actually quite a legit sliding puzzle game and you get a couple hundred of them.  The puzzles get more and more complex as you go along, adding new elements that force you to devise new solutions and plan your moves well in advance.  But despite this, most puzzles are just the right size, not too long or too short.  It's just that instead of something like an elf picking up gems or whatever, it's a psycho killer painting the walls with blood and leaving body parts strewn about the floor.
The game's levels are called "movies", of which there are about 13.  Within each "movie",  there are 12-16 "scenes" which are the puzzles.  After completing a "movie", you unlock it's "deleted scenes", which are 5-7 additional and fairly challenging puzzles.  Each "movie" stars a different killer and introduces new puzzle features.  Usually the 1st 2 or 3 puzzles are very simple to make sure you understand the mechanics of the new features, but then you really have to start thinking.  Much of the solving process ultimately involves herding victims and arranging movable obstacles into specific places to let you not only kill all the victims but avoid traps and then reach the level's exit, all while avoiding police and not harming innocent animals.
Periodically, as you kill victims, short cut-scenes play showing a spoof of some classic slasher movie death scene. (you can click to skip these if you want).  A lot of the achievements revolve around unlocking new cut-scenes, which you do by buying them in the store.  You get a few coins for completing a puzzle, with a short, simple "click-at-the-right-time" thing to get a few more.  You can then spend these on a selection fo cut-scenes, which are called "gore packs".  You can also spend the coins on unlocking new random killers besides those who appear naturally in each "movie".  But none of this is essential to actually doing the puzzles, it's just a way to get into the whole splatter movie vibe plus collect achievements if you're into that.
Anyway, the puzzles are good and the presentation is funny.  Get it.

After the events of the first Saints Row, the 3rd Street Saints fell apart and 3 new gangs rolled in and took over Stilwater. Now you have to rebuild the Saints and take back your empire with help of Johnny from the first game, Pierce, Shaundi and Carlos. You can choose which gangs you want to take on in whatever order you want.
I love the customization. You can make so many different outfits with clothing from many different stores, like On The Rag, Impressions, and Let's pretend. The vehicle customization is great too, you can get spinners for your wheels, choose from a lot of different body mods and different colors and styles of paint, and tint your windows. You can choose what style in which you want for your cribs, too.
The city of Stilwater looks good and is fun to explore along with the ocean around it. The attention to detail is exquisite. You can take off and drive, or fly around and just explore for hours and find new things. There are a ton of easter eggs. I've devoted some time to just walking around the city by foot, and breathing in the environment.
Even after you finish the campaign, there are plenty of activities to keep you busy. My favorite is Insurance Fraud, where you throw yourself at cars to wrack up cash.
One thing I do not like about this game is, you have to have enough respect to do missions. I felt like this was a cheap way to make the campaign last longer. The campaign is long enough as is.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes open world crime games.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game made me have a lot of different feelings, but perhaps not one's they intended. After getting all 26 of the endings, completing all the sidequests and the dlc, I feel like I can give my most complete opinion.
I went in with a lot of expectations, after thoroughly enjoying Metal Gear Rising, and Bayonetta, and hearing all the praise around the game, I was excited. I'd also heard to play past the first ending, something I expected, as I'd played Drakengard before. The first few hours of the game gives a strong first impression, up until the
boss fight. I believe it's around this point where the game loses a lot of its direction. It's something I feel painful to say, as the game itself feels really nice to play.
The gameplay is something that I can deeply appreciate. Animations are stylish and smoothly transitions from offense and defense. I love dodging, and I don't mind the more limited move selection, as it places more focus on learning enemy patterns.
This is all thrown out the window, by the fact that the enemy's
provide any sort of challenge. Their levels also dont scale, as a fault of relying far too much on its "RPG" elements which diminishes going through on NG+. Many action games feel satisfying as its mechanics don't have to account for exp, especially since there's already a difficulty selection.
This is my biggest issue with Nier: Automata, its Action elements are held back drastically by the need to have shoe-horned in RPG mechanics. It doesn't meaningfully change how the game is played, it's just numbers. When it does, it makes the enemy a joke, or just kills you in one or two hits. The difficulty selection doesn't remedy this either, as the normal difficulty is far too easy, and on hard, it harshly punishes any mistake.
I could find those issues not that important if there were a good variety of enemy types and bosses. However, very egregiously, the game recycles many bossfights. (Major spoilers)
I have extremely mixed feelings about the story. I can feel the love and care put into the sidequests, joke endings and the archives, but I wish that same love was put into the main story. It does shine through occasionally after the Forest Kingdom, especially with some of the character development, but it never has the chance to go anywhere. The game just ends. The multiple endings feel cheap. Especially C and E. The text entries should enhance the story, not replace it.
With that said, the connections to the other Nier and Drakengard games make me want to play the other entries as well.
One thing I cannot complain about is the soundtrack. Absolutely phenomenal. Can't say enough good about it.
Although, even disregarding the optimization issues, I can't recommend. The game doesn't have enough opportunities to shine. Which is upsetting, since all of the pieces are there for an amazing experience.

Polarity is an overall very nice, Portal-like experience.
PROS:
- The puzzles are relatively simple, but engaging.
- The gameplay is good and makes you want to keep progressing through the levels.
- The minimalistic style is pleasant to look at.
- The music is very relaxing and a joy to listen to.
CONS:
- I found the sound effects to be so annoying that after the first level, I went into the options to see if I can lower their volume - for some reason you can only turn them on and off, and I was forced to do the latter. The game doesn't really lose much if you do, and you are able to fully immerse yourself in the music that way.
- Some of the level design choices aren't particularly fortunate, like how you can't always be sure where the platform you're standing on ends, or how deadly pits and normal ground are so hard to tell apart. Also, the chambers tend to be too dark and big sometimes.
- 2 or 3 levels require quickly changing the polarity mid-jump, which is a pain to accomplish sometimes.
- The singleplayer campaign is pretty short, and together with the bonus levels, it can be completed in about 3 hours. (I didn't try the coop one yet, so there's that...)
- The ending could offer something more satisfying than just a few lines of text...
CONCLUSION:
Definitely get it if it's on sale. Especially the one that lowers its price to laughable 20 cents.

Calling Polarity "The best puzzle/platformer since Portal" is a bit of a stretch, but nonetheless, it is a decent game. It suffers from lack of polish in a few areas, and has somewhat glitchy physics at times, but for the price it's a fun little puzzle game. I came into it expecting the puzzles to get more difficult as the game went on, and to some extent they did, but each level still only takes around 2-3 minutes at most.
Overall, a decent time killer if you need to waste an hour (or more if you have a co-op buddy). Good if you're looking for a laid-back puzzler, especially good for the sale price.  4/5.

Lastly the combat system is clunky at first but it become surprisingly fun and rewarding in terms of game strategy.
I played the whole game with a xbox one controller and had no bugs.
Ultimately i can't recomend this game enough for every fan of the tv show and rpg in general.

I remember when i first played this game about 10 years ago and i hired it from a video store for my Xbox i put it in and waited for it to load up i was then hit by the scene of Agent 47 sitting in that chair in the dark with lightning lighting up the room with his W2000 Sniper and this incredibly badass electronic theme music playing that this game was going to be awesome.
This game is truly fantastic Hitman Contracts always holds a special place for me being the game that introduced me to the series and to me it holds up very well against both its predecessor and its successor. The biggest thing to note with Hitman Contracts is the very different tone that this game brings from other games in the series it comes across as alot darker and really gets into the sinister side of the criminal underworld and the life of a Hitman like Agent 47.
In my opinion the greatest thing about Contracts is the amazing atmosphere this game achieves the setting is very gritty and in many ways the game comes across as almost moody but in a really good way because it allows you to immerse yourself in its storyline and keeps you on edge as you work your way through the game personally this kind of gaming experience is one of my favourites and this game does a fantastic job of doing this from start to finish.
The game achieves this by using some pretty basic things like flashbacks setting the missions at night and with lots of rain to give of a very dark atmosphere combine this with the once again outstanding soundtrack by composer Jesper Kyd gives you a winning formula from the start the soundtrack is quite different from the Orchestrals of Hitman 2 and instead comes at you with a very dark style of Electronic music that keeps you on your edge of your seat full of suspense as you go about the game with many tracks be darn right aerie and others being incredibly thrilling and excting.
In terms of gameplay it feels very similar to Hitman 2 but i am pleased to say that the AI isnt nearly as twitchy and hard to anticipate as in Hitman 2 which makes the gameplay smoother and makes more sense. While this game does not have as many missions as in Hitman 2 it does an incredible job of providing you with a massive amount of non linear style gameplay through the various missions alot of the maps are very large and you have so many ways to go about performing your hits and it can take a very long time trying to work out the best methods. So although the game isnt as long as Hitman 2 you still have plenty of replayability and things to explore in this game this game also has some of the most memorable missions in the Hitman series.
To sum up for this game i consider it to be everybit as good as Silent Assassin was which is impressive in itself given how its quite often hard to follow up a good game with a sequel that is as equally good the only real weakness i can say is that i wish it had as many missions as Hitman 2 but the missions it does have are fantastic and that really isnt a fatal flaw i just wanted to play more for longer. All in all my score for this game is the same as Hitman 2 a solid 7.5/10 and highly recommend it for the price a superb game indeed.

In a Steam universe full of buggy, broken AAA titles, abandoned Early Access games, and developers selling DLC for games they haven't even finished, it's so refreshing to see a game that does what it sets out to do almost perfectly.  Slayaway Camp is a slider puzzle game presented as a love letter to one of the greatest of all movie genres - the 80s Slasher film.  You play as one of a series of psychotic klllers that pay homage to a host of horror icons; mostly from 80s greats like Friday the 13th and Halloween, but with a bit of bleed-over into the 70s and 90s for good measure.  You slide around the environment, avoiding obstacles and slaughtering helpless teenagers until everyone is dead and you can make your way to the exit.
Each of the 10 scenarios is presented as an 80s-era movie on VHS tape, and consists of a dozen or so "scenes", with another 5 or 6 "deleted scenes" that are unlocked when you finish the main ones.  The puzzles range in difficulty, with some being actually quite hard, but hints are available if you need them.  Each movie gives you a new iconic killer to play, and more can be unlocked with coins you earn in-game.  You can also unlock a number of execution kills that randomly play through the course of the game.  It's not too difficult to gather enough coins for unlocks, but if you want to speed things along there's a separate mini-game that let's you grind out as much as you want.
I typically can't stand games with these sort of blocky, 8-bit "retro" graphics, but there's an exception to every rule and this one's it.  One of Slayaway Camp's greatest features is its sense of humor and tongue-in-cheek approach to the subject matter, and watching all these little teens being slaughtered in shockingly brutal ways ends up being quite hilarious when you see it in all its blocky, pixelated glory.   We get enough
brutality in other games - this game is about
brutality, and it succeeds at that brilliantly.  In fact, pretty much everything that Slayaway Camp tries to do, it does exceedingly well.  I haven't had this much genuine fun with a game in quite a while, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

The bottom line:
DO NOT buy this game; it crashes too often.  Go play Grand Theft Auto 3 or later, or else Saints Row IV instead.  It really is a fun game, but it is just too much hassle dealing with all the crashes and bugs.
The Good:
It's got a little bit of comedy, doesn't take itself too seriously the way Grand Theft Auto does.
When you die, you just go to the hospital.
When you get arrested you just go to the police station.
Side-missions are challenging but fun.
You will get a good variety of weapons to play with.
You get a good variety of vehicles to drive:  cars, pickups, trash trucks, tow trucks, police cars, motorcycles, SWAT van, even a hot dog and fries truck!
The Bad:
VERY MANY bugs that will cause the game to crash.
You need to manually save about every three minutes or risk losing everything in a crash.
You often need to repeat EVERYTHING since your last manual save due to a crash.
Driving physics could be better.  Most of the cars seem pretty slow and don't corner very well.
If you fail a mission (you die, you don't get a good enough score, your homie dies, or you don't get to the destination in time) then you have to repeat the whole thing; there are no checkpoints during missions.
You cannot visit your garage, gang customizer, or several other options during missions.
The Summary:
If you're at all familiar with the "GTA" games, this one is a lot like GTA 3.  It's set in a fictional city called Stillwater, Texas, which looks a lot more like part of Chicago or maybe San Diego than Texas.  It's a bunch of islands connected by bridges and let's face it there's not that much water in all of Texas.  The game has a very diverse population, both racially and economically/socially.  People you meet on the street are mostly random by-standers but there are also police, firefighters, EMT (ambulance drivers), pimps and "hos" and rival gang members.  Once you progress far enough into the game, you also will occasionally meet some friends from your own gang, the "Saints."
The game sends you on a series of missions to rebuild your gang.  After the events of the first Saint's Row game, your character (the gang boss) got blown up and wound up in prison and in a coma.  So you have to bust out of prison, recruit some new friends, buy new safe-houses, fight off four or five rival gangs for more territory, etc.  You also have to either avoid or fight the police if you commit crimes like murder, car theft, or holding up a liquor store.  The game has a number of side-quests that you can do, too.  These range from "cause a lot of property damage in two minutes" to "win a street race" to "kill lots of rival gang-bangers."
There are also things you can do to customize yourself.  You can shop at clothing, jewelry, tattoo, and plastic surgery shops to change your wardrobe, tattoos, and face.  You can also steal vehicles and keep them in your garage to use later.  Unfortunately, any damage done to the vehicle will STAY unless you take it to an auto shop and pay to get it fixed.  (Just like real life.)  You can also shop at liquor stores and burger joints to buy food and booze to restore your health (just in case you get into a mess of bullets).  And of course you can find a pretty good variety of weapons that you can swap when you visit your safe-house.  You get one "melee" weapon (baseball bat, hammer, pepper spray, taser, knife, sword, night-stick, etc.); one pistol or dual-wield pistol; one shotgun or dual-wield shotgun; one SMG or dual-wield; one assault rifle; one type of grenade; and one type of launcher (i.e. rockets).  Any time you pick up a new weapon in the city, it is automatically placed in storage at your safehouse as well as equipping it on you.  You can also buy new weapons at the gun shops if you can't find the one you want outside.

Ah, Loadout. Where does one begin with such a raucous, amazingly well made title? How about... download it now.
Let's start with the main appealing element of the game - weaponcrafting. It's a great aspect, and adds a dynamic never before explored by any kind of shooter - first or third person. Adding a sense of unique playstyle that no other game of said genre could pick up unless via copying it directly is a surefire way of selling your game to others, which Edge of Reality have managed to do, as the game has exploded with over 2 million users in the first few months of having a spot on the market.  Furthermore, the game feels like it has a great feeling of replayability, despite being a multiplayer only title, as you can make anything you choose to at any time, so long as you can fund it with the in game currency.
The in game currency also leads me on to my second point - is it Pay to Win? Certainly not. As many previous reviews have stated, the game is purely PLAY to win. You simply cannot buy one of the two in game currencies, blutes, which are used to make any weapon you wish that would lead you to victory in the focused teamfights across multiple gamemodes. The other currency, known as Spacebux, may be purchasable but is really used to both support the devs and satisfy your thirst for exclusive vanity. Despite what people say right now - you can't buy your way to victory, unless running around naked somehow gives you superhuman abilities.
The third reason I'd recommend this game to anyone is the team focused play, as I mentioned just earlier. Every game mode is team oriented - from organizing defending and offensive teams in Jackhammer, the capture the flag-esque mode that requires both organization and the sense to bash the enemy team senseless with the flag itself, to working together in Annihilation across all kinds of objectives, eventually finishing with a bang by destroying the opposing team's dropship, winning you the game. Any company can make a shooter - but why bother if it's not going to grow a competitive teamplay side and have people to keep it going?
In conclusion - download it anytime you like. Now is good. Later is good. But now is also good. Take your pick, pick your playstyle.

It's a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I can't stop playing it.  I guess it kind of scratches an itch I have for Dragon Age style RPGs, and the GOT twist is just enough to keep me interested.  It's still a bad game, though and I wouldn't recommend it to the majority of gamers. Let me explain exactly why :
The Graphics
Despite being released in 2012 the graphics are straight out of the late 90s early 2000s.  Obscenely low resolution textures, and chunky looking characters. I actually laughed when I saw that this was created with Unreal Engine 3.  It's an amateur effort, at best.
The Combat Balance
Enemies will slash you with their swords when you're miles away, and archers will shoot arrows that can hit you through walls. They attempted to ape the Dragon Age "Tactical Pause" system, but it just doesn't work, particularly if you are choosing to play as a ranged character.  You are forced to constantly quaff these health potions to stay in fighting shape, but they have limited charges and can only be replenished at merchants, so it's VERY easy to get yourself into a progress breaking state where there are just too many enemies to tank.  The enemy numbers and placement ASSUMES you have more health potions than you actually do.  It's garbage.
The World
Very little effort was made to bring the world to life.  Almost everything is a static backdrop that cannot be interacted with unless it is directly relevant to your current quest.  There are all kinds of areas that the level designers built that serve literally_no_purpose.  There aren't even any collectibles or loot stashes in them, just empty filler.  You quickly learn that exploration is pointless and that you should just bee-line for your main objective.
The Dialogue
Is atrocious.  With a few exceptions (Varys is quite good, and seems to be voiced by the actual actor who plays him) but other than that you get bargain bin voice acting that sounds like it could have been done by one of the programmers.  Much of the writing is also exposition heavy and assumes that the player knows nothing about the GOT lore, so it tries to ram it down your throat ad nauseum.  (Jeor Mormant repeatedly explains the tenets of the Night's Watch for a good 10 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes at the start of the game).
So with all that bad stuff, why am I still playing it?  There are a few good things.
The Character Progression
When you level up you can select new abilities from a branching tree,  increase your core attributes, and earn various traits that give you small buffs.  It's nothing revolutionary, but what's there is solid and reasonably enjoyable.  Trying to build a deadly water dancer or dual wielding wildling is pretty cool.
The Story
While the dialogue and character writing is terrible, the overarching plot points are quite good, and seem true to Martin's world. There is deadly sibling rivalry,  executions, and political intrigue.  It rarely rises above the level of "decent fan fiction", but it's good enough to keep you wondering how it will end.
GOT hype
Yeah, this is a thing.  It's cool to find a merchant selling the Red Viper's spear, or hear that you will get to have an audience with Cersei Lannister. If you're not a fan of the books or show you can cross this one off the list, but if you are, it'll make your inner fanboy tingle.
Soooo yeah.  Overall it's a bad game, but if you're a huge GOT nerd or you want a sad Dragon Age clone set in that universe it's good for a few hours of fun.

An amazing game that nobody plays, which hurts it because it's a team multiplayer game.  Guns of Icarus allows players to live out their steampunk fantasies as the crew of a combat dirigible, patrolling the skies in search of enemy airships like them.  The captain flies the ship, the gunners operate the turrets, and the engineers repair damage caused by enemy gunners.  However, there are not enough crew members to manage all parts of the ship, so players must constantly run here and there focusing only on what's essential at the moment.  This role-based crew-of-a-ship aspect really creates and emphasizes a great feeling of teamwork rarely found in multiplayer games, and each player's role makes them feel unique and essential to the team, rather than just another identical soldier in the army.
The game offers many different  airships to choose from, each one with a different physical layout that changes how it must be repaired and how its guns can be aimed.  The visuals of the game are beautiful and appropriately full of rust and brass, and the music is a blend of classical orchestra melodies and wartime drum cadences fitting of the setting.  Online matchmaking is a complete loss, though:  due to low playerbase queue times are sporadic and balancing skill levels on the team is nigh impossible.
The sum of the parts adds up to an amazing positive in Guns of Icarus all the same, so if you can bear struggling through long wait times to find a game, games half-full of AI crewmembers, or have enough friends to play together, the satisfaction of playing a a TRUE team game more than makes up for it.

You'll find plenty of people talking about Slayaway Camp's humorous setting, but let's talk gameplay. Slayaway Camp, at it's core, is the tried and true ice-sliding puzzle, where pressing a movement key pushes you as far as you can go in that direction. Your objective is to murder all the people (except the cops) by moving into them, then getting to a designated exit point.
Moving into a person kills them, but leaves you stationary, potentially leaving you in a row or column of the grid you couldn't otherwise access. So, the position of people becomes important. People will also run away from you if you occupy a square adjacent to them, or kill someone who is adjcent to them, and they will run in the opposite direction as far as they can go. So, we get, in addition to the ice sliding puzzle, a block pushing game, but one where the blocks can't directly be pushed! Often the trickiness in the puzzles arises from deftly manipulating the scared people into being in the exact position you want them to be. Although, some of the puzzles have a limited number of moves, so the challenge is in being efficient.
Slayaway Camp's learning curve is quite gentle. Over its hundreds of puzzles, it drips down several new mechanics, and always presents an easy puzzle or two that forces you to explore the implications of the new mechanic. The overall difficulty increases gradually, and it may take 60-90 minutes before a more seasoned puzzle game player begins to feel the challenge. But, rest assured, the puzzles do become challenging, and remain that way for the majority of this surprisingly lengthy game.
What's more, they are definitely the good kind of challenging. I rarely found myself wandering aimlessly to see what I could accomplish. My method for solving a new puzzle was to dive in and see what I could accomplish. Then the difficulties of the level would present itself (How can I get to the exit? How do I get that last teenager in the middle of the room? etc). More often than not, by working backwards from these difficulties, I could figure out a blueprint for what I needed to get done, and in what order. It was a fun, intellectual experience, rather than a frustrating experience of headbutting a brick wall until it cracks (although, some of the move-limited puzzles were more like this).
I highly recommend Slayaway Camp. It's extraordinary value, and the developers have clearly crafted it with both love and skill. Speaking of the developers, they are highly responsive both to bug reports and suggestions for future expansions. Do yourself a favour and pick it up.

=================================================================
This is a highly story driven and thematic game. As such, depending on how well you connect with the characters and atmosphere will highly impact what you think of the game. For me personally, I had little connection with the characters but felt the story was 'good enough' to at least get me through the entire game.
Elephant in the room, yes the game runs poorly. System specs: i5 4690K, 8 GB RAM, GTX 970 SLI. Yes, I installed the FAR mod and you should too. I managed to get the game running at 1440p with everything on low. I frequently had ~10 fps drop in combat and every so often when walking around. Even running at 1080p, I frequently encountered similar stuttering and frame drops. Occasional game freezes coupled with no auto-save resulted in an hour or two of lost progress.
I felt the characters were too cold and devoid of emotion most of the time. As such, they were really hard to root for. Obviously they are androids so of course they are not supposed to have much emotion. Whether you like this type of character will ultimately determine how the story impacts you.
Standard post-apocalyptic style. Generally, I’m not a fan of this type of atmosphere and this game did not change my mind. I felt the grey undertones / relatively empty areas made the environment boring. After a while I just ran straight for the bosses as I had no desire to linger.
AMAZING! Obviously something that’s subjective, but I really enjoyed it!
Huge fan of Devil May Cry and Bayonetta. As such the combat was a letdown. The depth just isn't there. In general, all you do is mash light attack or heavy attack and dodge when necessary. I have also played a few bullet hell games and found the bullet hell sections to be trivially easy. Therefore, I found the moment-to-moment gameplay below average. I pushed through to finish the story. Cool idea to merge weapon based combat and bullet hell elements though.
As mentioned, I wasn’t a fan of the atmosphere so the side quests were not contextualized well for me. Most of the side quests are pretty standard fetch, kill, escort missions so I passed on most side quests unless I was in the area for the main quest. Some were good, but on average, I was not impressed.
A little weak on the customization. Character customization revolves around chip upgrades which are generally pure stat upgrades. Since you cannot string together weapon combos, I didn’t really feel the need to experiment with different weapons and all of them felt pretty similar. (Sure a light sword and a brawler weapon have different animations but they only differ gameplay wise in their dps.) As such I spent the entire game with my choice light weapon and my choice heavy weapon. Pod upgrades, the machine that shoots bullets from over your shoulder, do change the gameplay significantly.

I initially had mixed feeling about this. I mostly liked it but there's some small problems like how many of the bosses are disappointingly easy (possibly I should have played on Hard instead of Normal but that takes away the lock-on ability and I still did have some troubles in later areas). There's a fair few quests and side quests that feel a bit like boring busy-work too.
But despite the shortcomings I have to say overall I loved it. The story is really interesting and the gameplay is the standard Platinum goodness, with some interesting twists in gameplay like the mix of bullet-hell gameplay.
It's worth noting that if you get to the first "ending" (ending A) and just left the game there, you might come off feeling a bit disappointed. But as it turns out that's only half of the game. Play through again for the second ending and then the third playthrough is where it gets really interesting. I know that sounds ridiculous but give it a chance and you'll see.

I don't quite know how to explain how awesome this game is, so have a chicken nugget recipe
Enjoy :)
Ingredients
1/2 cup all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon granulated garlic
Kosher salt and ground black pepper
2 boneless skinless chicken breasts, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 cup prepared breadcrumbs
1 large egg
1 cup vegetable oil
Directions
Place the flour in a resealable plastic bag and season with the garlic, 1 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Place the chicken pieces in the bag with the flour and toss to coat (work in batches). Transfer the breadcrumbs to a rimmed plate, season with salt and pepper and set aside.
Whisk the egg and 1 tablespoon water in a medium bowl. Remove a piece of chicken from the flour, dip in the egg mixture, then the breadcrumbs, gently pressing the crumbs into the chicken, and set on a clean plate. Repeat with the remaining pieces of chicken.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chicken pieces to the pan (work in batches if needed) and brown on each side, about 8 minutes total. Use a spatula to transfer the chicken nuggets to a paper-towel-lined plate. Salt while hot and serve.

What a fantastic platformer. It's fairly easy to learn and especially difficult to master. Even when you think you've gotten to a point where you can just plow through the floors as quickly as possible, the game says, "No," and hits you in the face with a hidden saw blade, or a flying enemy, or the challenge of the bosses each of the way through.
If I'm rating the game on a number scale, I'm probably going to give it in the range of 8-9 out of 10. But the game is not without its flaws. First, there's the hit box: it's inconsistent. Most of the time it's exactly as you'd expect. You swing your sword (or 'chuks, or whip) and you hit your target. But there are times where I see the weapon sprite contact with the enemy sprite and it does no damage. This happens enough for it to be an issue, but not so much that it's a game stopper.
The other big issue has to do with telegraphing. The enemies don't really do a good job of it, and you'll very easily find yourself dying or getting hit by the enemies and bosses because there's little to no indication of a telegraphed attack. Compound this with a double jump that's a little low and you'll find sometimes that you have to be perfect more often then you should need in some cases to proceed. (Edit: I just found the super jump after writing the review, so that makes some boss fights potentially a bit easier.)
Now these aren't really "big" issues in the normal sense; but in the context of the game, they can add up to some pretty frustrating moments.
All in all though, the game is a fantastic platformer with a super progression path and you should definitely check it out.

Incredible Dracula is the first time management game I've been compelled to rate poorly.  Considering the high production quality, you'd think that's a pretty tough thing to pull off; but when it comes to the genre, it's ALL about the gameplay.  The best titles are those that reward strategy and smart play, the worst will have you pulling your hair out from unending frustration.  Unfortunately, Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love is most definitely the latter.
There are a few things that a good time management game needs: responsive controls, the ability to chain tasks, and interesting level designs that allow for creative solutions.  Then there's the tuning which should be tight, but not so tight that absolute perfection is needed to achieve your goal.  This is where Dracula fails.  Early on, getting 3 stars on Multit-Click Mode (which is basically Expert in every other game) becomes rage inducing as the levels are not only long, but leave no room for error.  It may not be an issue on Casual Mode in which you have unlimited time, but I play these games to challenge myself.  Learning the levels, devising a strategy and nailing the execution is what makes time management games so enjoyable.  But when I'm following the in-game strategy guide to the T and still come up sorely short on time, there's something very, very wrong.
To make matters worse, restarting the level (which you'll end up doing several times) is bogged down with a forced tutorial that you have to click through every time it's replayed.  You can opt to skip it within the level itself, but then you're required to click through a large confirmation box for it. While this may sound like such a little thing, when you're focusing on figuring out a level, having to jump through hoops every time you restart is disruptive to the thought process.  The ability to turn tutorials completely off in the options would have greatly improved the experience and eased some of my frustrations, but it's conspicuously absent.
The story itself is unique but may be off-putting to some (Dracula is on the run from his overweight, ugly and lovesick admirer).  The graphics are pleasant enough, and the monster theme has some cute ideas, but nothing ultimately memorable.  The best part of the game is the soundtrack which features lovely classically-styled orchestral themes.  I could listen to it for hours, but forcing myself through more of the gameplay would have me suicidal by the end.
I really wanted to love Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love.  Alawar is one of my favorite casual game developers and they consistently put out great products, but I simply could not get past the insane difficulty and logistical annoyances.  While plenty of games in the genre are generic and uninspired, at least they provide enjoyable gameplay - that's not the case here.  I'll likely swap over to Casual Mode to 100% the achievements so I can move on.  No challenge, no strategy, just going through the motions to finish what I started.  Perhaps some of the problems were fixed in the sequel, but I'm not sure I'm willing to give it a chance after this disappointment.

While Incredible Dracula has a lot of good ideas and mechanics for a time management game, it is difficult to completely enjoy it with all the idle time and subpar level design all around.
Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love is an ambitious game. It falls into the more cartoonish Dracula depictions, where the count spends 45 levels trying to escape from a rather enthusiastic bride-to-be he met on an online dating service (plus 15 bonus levels where he tries to get his son to school somehow).
Since the chose genre is time management, escaping in this case means using his zombie-like servants to clear the road ahead for him. This is achieved by collecting five resource types, which are then either used to remove obstacles, or to craft various potions and constructs (or whatever the level may come up with).
Although this variety in mechanics shouldn’t make any game repetitive, Incredible Dracula somehow managed to slip up in this regard: level design feels bland. Even worse, if the player accidentally chose classic difficulty, the game removes the command queue, meaning no orders can be assigned beforehand; this gets incredibly annoying on later levels, where travel distances are so vast that players will spend most of the time waiting for the workers to return.
But, if you are a patient type, like time management games, and stick to Casual mode, then Incredible Dracula’s humour and game mechanics can entertain you for quite a good while.

Love on first sight.
This game is a bit like Civilization: Beyond Earth (Or other Civilization games), but instead of colonizing one world, you colonize a whole big universe full of different stars and planets. It's also real-time, not round-based, which I prefer I lot, especially in multiplayer.
The best 4x I have played yet, and I've played a lot of them. But I have to add, I also simply love space-themed game settings.
Pros:
- The feelings you get if you're attached to space-themed things are amazing. You'll feel like a star traveller. Like a conqueror. Like peacemaker. Like a federation builder.
- Huge fleet fights that control really easily and can be viewed on a very detailed level. Different ships have different parts they are composed of and different slots you can put researched tech in. Multiple weapon-types that have advantages and disadvantages over other weapon types, so fights get tactical a lot
- Building wide instead of tall not _that_ important. Even as a small empire, owning 2-3 planets only, you can get to high tech levels, improve your fleet and fight against your own freedom or team up with others. You can build tall, improving single buildings on your planets over time to improve resource output very well. Owning a lot of systems doesn't automatically make you a winner
- A diplomacy system like I have never seen before. I especially like the federation system, which also comes with a federation fleet and rotates the leader every few years which then has control over it. You have different kinds of aggression and peace pacts and you can't just interact how you want, diplomatic decisions revolve around the government type and traits of your species and your previous diplomatic relation to other empires on many levels
- A living environment. Leviathans, researchable stations (Infinity Machine etc.), Fallen Empires with huge technological advantage that awaken, huge crises in late-game that can turn the whole game around, pirates that threaten your stations, anomalies to research that can turn into whole quest chains. If you think you've seen it all, you'll be surprised in the next game.
- Background music that, together with the general athmosphere of the game, honestly gives me the chills. Maybe you know that moment in the Interstellar movie when he was in that 4th-dimension-thing in the end, combined with the background music? Exactly this.
- A research system that doesn't just let you follow your fixed tree endlessly. Every game turns out into different research paths, if you want it or not. Makes every game feel differently. The depth is also somewhat endless. I didn't reach a point in the game yet where I had less than 3 options to research for all 3 categories available, and I already fought crises and FEs
- A race/species system with a depth I've never seen before. You can fully customize any species to any possible point, give them specific traits. In the game, you can do migration with other empires or e.g. harbor regufees to get multiple species into your empire, each with differnt bonuses on e.g. mineral output or food output. Later on you can manipulte genes to remove negative traits of races or add new positive ones. This can be microoptimized on a really deep level.
- A sector system. If you're annoyed by managing all those planets yourself, put them in a sector. No, it doesn't work perfect, but good enough with room for improvement. The sector AI can focus on specific industries and generate resources for you.
- A deep story and a lot of quests. As soon as you are like 5 years in the game, you have like 20 spots blinking on your map, some outside your reachable stars, some far away or even in enemy borders. By time, you will research them and unlock a lot of different stuff, many of which is related to your specific race of government type. There's always something to do.
- The 3D is great. The stars look awesome, planets look awesome, ships look great, ship battles look like star wars movies.
- The UI is good. It wishes for only minor more customization options, but generally, it gives you what you need pretty quickly and the tool-tips are very detailed, mostly.
- Games can span multiple days (considering your play speed). You have been warned.
- A multiplayer that works well. I'll add to that below.
- As I've seen it, the game is actively developed and expanded.
- Moddable, with a lot of mods already existing (I think around 8000 last time I've looked)
- It leaves you time to think (Except if you're playing multiplayer on Fastest). Don't think you can't keep up. You can.
Of course no game is perfect, and even here, there is room for improvement.
Cons:
- If you start a 32-people multiplayer game, expect to be down to like 2-3 people in a maximum of 60 minutes. I know it's hard to solve, but it's still annoying. You will never reach a crisis in a public multiplayer game. Either everyone leaves before it happens and your game turns into an AI single-player game or...
- Corvette Rush (Zerg Rush analogy). It seems really easy in the game to quickly find the pacifist empires, build 30-50 corvettes, completely push your naval capacity over it's maximum, invade them and take them everything, leaving them with nothing. While you were building up minerals for pumping out your first colony, he just spams corvettes, comes and takes your new planet including your home world. Game over for you and he just saved 2 colony ships and minerals for buildings and mines. In many games you have no other choice than spamming corvettes the whole early game, with your crippled mining output, and somewhat try to defend yourself. And then, a bit later in the game, you see someone with 100 stars and a 8k fleet consisting of....300 corvettes. Their whole game literally revolved around pressing the "Corvette"-button as soon as it became available on any planet and quickly invading everyone. I do get that it's completely legal to play like this. But it's annoying. The game is laid out to be long, crises happen late, FEs awaken late, the actual fun happens really late. And still, most people push the game to be over after under an hour with you not even reaching any cool tech yet.
- Performance. It seems basically impossible to host a 1000 star game. Many people won't join because their PCs can't handle them. And then, even in a 600 star game, in the late game there will be lag. "Fastest" suddenly becomes "Normal Speed". Simply because it has to simulate so much things, huge fleets, thousands of buildings, resource output, calculate AI actions etc. that it becomes really slow. I have a really good PC. Not the best, but I can play most current games on full graphics fluently. This really has to be improved.
- Humanoids look horrible. There are very few actual good looking human 2D avatars you can create. This also includes some other races, which have too few customization options of which many look really bad. Some clothing looks really bad in comparison to the size of the heads etc. Male/female is basically just a different hairstyle. Some other species do look pretty cool, however, this is not a general problem. Mods can solve this.
- Why do I have to log in in the launcher every time again? It's pretty annoying. Keep me logged in. Or at least save my e-mail address and don't make me type it again every time.
- It's expensive. I got it on sale and it is worth every euro I've paid for it. It might even be worth its 70€ it costs normally, including a total of like 25€ to actually have every DLCs you need so that you get accepted in multiplayer games. But my friends won't buy it, since it's too expensive for them. Sad, but what can I do. I do feel that 70€ plus the money you basically _have_ to spend to fully enjoy the game is quite expensive. The game you get for it is pretty awesome, though. Never going to deny that.
- The sector AI gets better, but still needs a lot of improvement.
I recommend this game. It's great.

Stellaris is an interesting game by the same people who developed Cities:Skylines.  On the smallest size galaxy that I could generate, the amount of playing time required for a single game seems to me to be exhorbitant (I went with 200 stars, only 1 AI, and "normal" setting for difficulty).  While their approach (seemingly eternal effort required to finish a game) works well with pure simulation games of the Cities:Skylines variety, I find it far less suitable for a 4X game.
The wiki and the official webpage are rather unhelpful -- and this is an exceptionally complex game  A TRUE tutorial version, that would allow a player to learn on a smaller galaxy, along with a detailed technological tree (showing what CAN be developed, and what the prerequisites for various technologies are) would be helpful in learning how to play the game.  In fact, a "Stellaris for Dummies" manual would be really nice.  Why "spoil the fun of learning"?  Simple -- I have limited time for entertainment, and if I must "work" for weeks just to learn HOW to play the game, I grow tired and irritable.
I still plan on continuing with Stellaris, but ... I believe that the approach taken by the designers has resulted in a seriously flawed 4X game that COULD have been much better.  If a game takes 50-60 hours of play time to complete, it is not play, it is work.  By comparison, MASTER OF ORION (the new version) takes me 8-12 hours to play a simple game.  I was able to develop some fairly decent strategies there after playing four or five games -- with roughly the same amount of play time that I am currently estimating it will take me to finish my first game of Stellaris.
If one is willing to invest the necessary time, I believe that Stellaris could be entertaining for some -- but I cannot really recommend the game to the general run-of-the-mill 4X game player.  If Paradox adds an "abbreviated" game option, a massively accelerated research option, or some other game compression options, along with additional documentation and tutorial information, I will happily change my recommendation.
-----------------------------------------------------
Ok, I thought that I'd give this game a second chance.  With some of the advice taken from the one "Stellaris for Dummies" discussions, I changed my approach and played a second game.  The gaming time involved?  Roughly 28 hours of gaming.  I THOUGHT that I was holding my ow, but the one alien race competitor I allowed in the setup (and the 200 stars) was able to build a fleet nearly five times the size of mine (and I had a 2.1k offensive force, of mixed corvettes, destroyers and a couple of cruisers).
The aliens basically blew me away; no real chance to resist them.
Now, at the easiest setting, with minimal stars, taking roughly 28 hours to get ot the point where the game is hopelessly lost indicates to me, that this is a very poorly designed game.  Like a game of GO on a 300 x 300 array (instead of the standard 19 x 19 array), the amount of time to play one game goes up astronomically.
Now I have no problem with a "killer mode" but it SHOULD be possible to play what amounts to a "quickie" game, to learn the basics and some of the reasonable strategy in, say, six to eight hours.  As it is, trying to learn this game is like trying to learn chess by playing against a Grandmaster who isn't willing to teach you ANYTHING (and who has memorized the MCO - the Modern Chess Openings -- while you're not even permitted to know how to move the pieces except by experimentation and being told, "no, the rules don't allow that" when you fail to follow the unwritten rules).
I regard this game as a tremendous cheat, and if you want to play a GOOD 4x game, which you can "start easy" and ramp the difficulty up (from playable as a beginner to nightmare mode for eperts) then I'd recommend the new MASTER OF ORION instead.

Ok, so before everything else, a little about me: I'm not really strong at go, I played for two years and reached 12~13k on KGS, then I had to stop for two years to focus on studying. When I got back into go 2 months ago, I decided to train hard in order to "get my old 'strength' back". And that included playing against this bot once it was out.
This bot beats me everytime (of course), but it doesn't feel at all like I'm playing a 7d. My first game against it (unlimited time, 7d strength) was lost by 40.5 points in an even game (in case you're interested, here's the link:
). This is a bot that was supposed to give me 17 stones at the time, and it only beat me by 40.5 points.
In case you're wondering, no, I'm not 3d, I'm around 8k on OGS. So, either it isn't 7d /at all/, or it played slack moves once it knew it was ahead (like AlphaGo, maybe). I personnally think it's a mix of the two. On your everyday computer, I don't think it reaches 7d, unless you force it to do 10M playouts thanks to the analyze feature, but that would mean a looooot of time for each move.
The interface is also extremely old school. While it isn't ugly, it lacks game setting customization: you can only choose between predetermined main times and byo-yomis, the komi can't exceed 9.5 (so no reverse-komi handicap games), and you can only either choose between a set time for the bot to use or an unlimited time and setting a rank, so no option to "do at least X playouts per move). Funnily enough, if you put it on the "unlimited time, 7d rank", it almost never thinks about moves for more than a few seconds, but when you set it with a limited time per move, it thinks a lot more and usually plays "better" (as far as I can observe at my level, anyway).
All in all, it is very expensive, and only people who are really serious (and can afford the price) about learning go will even want to consider buying this.
However, I would still recommend this to those because of the analyze feature I mentionned earlier, you can make it analyze a position for as long as you want, and this way you can review games you played, see what moves it considers bad, and what it proposes instead. Playing games against it has also allowed me to progress a lot (because, at my level, it still is way better than me).
If you're patient, I'm sure a free strong enough engine with similar features will be out within 1~2 years, and by the time, (hopefully) CrazyStone Deep Learning version 2 with more customizable game settings and an even stronger engine.
I personnally hope V2 will be free for those who purshased the V1. In the meantime, I need to practice more :)
EDIT: I've run a series of games on OGS to test its strength, it settled at 2~3d with 10 seconds per move and high priority (on a i5-3210M @ 2.5GHz), so it is decently strong even on an average computer.

First things first – this game will not teach you the rules of Go.  If you’re a total beginner, this isn’t the game for you: there’s no tutorial, and the documentation is very basic, so if you’ve never played Go before, please check out some of the excellent resources available on the web first.  (One excellent place to start would be Reddit at /r/baduk – Baduk being the Korean name for the game.)
If you already know how to play, then the question you should ask is, is this game for you?
The obvious thing the game offers you is the AI.  Rated up to 7d, this is the most powerful commercially available Go AI, and can challenge all but the most skilled amateurs.  Its minimum setting of 13k, on the other hand, should match up pretty well against anyone with more than a handful of games’ experience.  In addition, the game supports handicaps up to 9 stones, and based on a couple of games, it does a good job of playing handicap Go (far from universal amongst Go AIs).
So while a player of almost any skill level can get a good game from Crazy Stone, all but the strongest could do the same against any number of cheaper or free AIs available.  Given that, why would you pay such a steep price for the best AI?
The reason is the item at the bottom of the features list:  the Analysis Engine.  Crazy Stone allows you to review and analyze games you’ve played against the computer as well as games from the major online Go servers (anything that can export a game record in standardized format).  For each move you can see Crazy Stone’s analysis – including the top 20 moves it considered and the relative value of each.  If you’re willing to put in the time to go through it, this is almost like being able to play a teaching game any time you want, having a 7d grade your moves.
For me, the Analysis Engine is worth the entire price of admission.  I’m roughly 1k-1d strength, so I usually know most of the moves that Crazy Stones evaluates, but going through the analysis gives me tons of food for thought about the differences between them.
Technical notes:  this program can use all the CPU you can give it.  I’m running this on a fairly beefy CPU i7-5930K, 6-core 3.5Ghz – looking at the Analysis Engine, this allows it to simulate about 10,000 games per second.  Generally speaking, it seems to take around 30,000 simulations to get a good analysis for a move, so about three seconds on this machine.  I also tried it on an i7-3770K, 4-core 3.5 GHz – 7,000 games/second, and an i7-4810MQ, 4-core 2.8 GHz laptop – 6,000 games/second.  So it seems like most 4-cores would need around five seconds of analysis time per move.  Unfortunately, I don’t have any duo-cores to try out, but you can probably figure on doubling that time to ten seconds.

Enjoy :)
Ingredients
1/2 cup all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon granulated garlic
Kosher salt and ground black pepper
2 boneless skinless chicken breasts, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 cup prepared breadcrumbs
1 large egg
1 cup vegetable oil
Directions
Place the flour in a resealable plastic bag and season with the garlic, 1 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Place the chicken pieces in the bag with the flour and toss to coat (work in batches). Transfer the breadcrumbs to a rimmed plate, season with salt and pepper and set aside.
Whisk the egg and 1 tablespoon water in a medium bowl. Remove a piece of chicken from the flour, dip in the egg mixture, then the breadcrumbs, gently pressing the crumbs into the chicken, and set on a clean plate. Repeat with the remaining pieces of chicken.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chicken pieces to the pan (work in batches if needed) and brown on each side, about 8 minutes total. Use a spatula to transfer the chicken nuggets to a paper-towel-lined plate. Salt while hot and serve.

Do you love slasher movies?  Slayaway Camp loves slasher movies.  This throwback to the slasher movies of the 80's absolutely does justice to the genre while simultaneously satirizing it to great appeal.  Instead of being a straight-up "survive the madman" horror game, this game spins that around to where you are a cute voxel murderer cheerfully plowing through scores of victims in the most over-the-top ways possible.  The puzzle mechanics, aesthetics, and extra content all blend together to create a unique slasher experience
Mechanics-wise, this is first an foremost a puzzle game.  You are a killer sliding around a puzzle map, navigating obstacles, avoiding cops, killing generic victims and escaping through your satanic portal (yes, you heard me correctly) to move on to the next puzzle.  Normally this would get old fast, but thankfully the game keeps things fresh by introducing different mechanics throughout the game.  This makes the game more interesting, not to mention vexingly harder, as you progress, especially when different mechanics start being combined to create some of the most difficult puzzles I have every seen.
However, the game doesn't explain very well how some of the mechanics work or affect other mechanics, like how lights affect the cops or telephones affect cats.  You will almost always die several times learning how the mechanics work before completing the puzzle.  For those that prefer this type of experiential learning, it won't matter.  But for those of us who prefer not being virtually set up for failure, it's annoying.
I would be remiss if I didn't mention the bonus game at the end of each puzzle.  You get to try and earn an extra kill by timing a button press to land your sliding marker in the "Kill Zone."  It's a neat little distraction, and it earns you coins to spend in the shop.  More on that later.
This game looks and sounds like bits were ripped out of every 80's slasher movie known to man and Frankensteined together.  While primarily based on Friday the 13th, you'll find nods to Jaws, The Ring, H.P. Lovecraft's work, and even Mars Attacks!  All of it brought to life effortlessly through the voxel-style art direction.  Even the menus are made up to look like those VHS video stores where one used to rent slasher movies from.
The soundtrack's pretty awesome, too.  Sure its got those stereotypical (and very well done) horror underscores, but it even remembers to include the cheesy 80's rock songs that accompany every slasher movie ending credits.
And the kills.  Oh my word, the kills.  Every kill imaginable (and previously unimaginable) is shown in glorious over-the-top fashion.  I have never laughed so hard at saxophone slayings or death-by-deep-fried-sugar.
There are two different types of unlockable extras - killers and kills.  Killers cost 1000 coins each (from winning those extra-kill mini games) while kills cost between 1000 and 2000 coins.  There is a large variety of kills you can pick from, but killers are earned by opening a "mystery box" and randomly winning a killer.  This irks me because I really wanted one of the killers (
) but as of yet haven't attained him.
My other minor gripe is that once you purchase a kill, you can't preview it in the store.  You have to either wait until it randomly appears in the game, or move over to the trophy shelf.  It just seems unnecessary to have the extra steps.  I dunno, maybe I'm just crazy.
There are other extras included, but I think I'll leave them for you to learn about on your own.
Definitely worth getting for any fan of puzzle games or 80's slasher flicks.  It's great in both regards and stands out heads above other puzzle games because of that seamless blend.

Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love Collector's Edition:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Our dear Count Dracula is looking for L.O.V.E. and enrols in a dating site on the Magical Internet on a quest to find the perfect other half! However, as he is new at this dating business, he quickly finds out that the photo display on a profile may not be the real deal. Well, put yourself in his coffin! He expected to date a beautiful lady Vampire, not a human princess who is looking to steal his freedom! That would be a shock if your name was Dracula! In any case, Count Dracula has 45 days to rescue the princess from unrequited love. That’s going to be b.l.o.o.d.y hard!
Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love Collector’s Edition is a Strategy / simulation type of game where you have to achieve one or several objectives in a minimum amount of time per level to claim three golden stars. Here, you will control count Dracula minions (or workers). They will have to pick up resources such as: food, logs of wood, stones, tools and money. These items will help you to repair run-down buildings like the famous hamburger place, “Blood Donald!” Also, the road will have plenty of obstacles to remove and it will cost you food every time you do so. Make sure you have plenty of this resource in your cape! You will have access to some special abilities -  to speed up building construction, remove obstacles – to speed up your minion movement or even stop the time for a little while, which will help you to earn your 3 golden stars at the end of each level. If you find a specific level too hard, you can refer to the strategy guide, which is really helpful and has great hints. In terms of modes, this game has three - Normal mode if you are an experienced player, Multi-click mode, which allows you to assign multiple tasks to your workers, and Relaxed mode, which does not have a time limit.
On top of that, you have to find and collect other items which are scattered within all levels. If you are like me, you probably hover over without noticing them, but look for gifts, black cats, portraits and statuettes.
I really like the graphics and animations. I especially like Rufus listening to music while standing behind a lawn mower (first level), very funny! You will use your mouse to give an order to your minions or to Count Dracula. The soundtrack is good and reflects the game very well.

Oftentimes, the first judgement players will make about a game is what its name is. Thus, when I heard of this game, called "Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love," I knew I had to play it. I expected a funny game and hoped for enjoyable gameplay. Much to my delight, it shot beyond both of those desires and kept me hooked for two days straight to finish all of the levels.
Let me be upfront here: I have never played a resource manager game. I tend to be awful at real-time strategy games, and there is indeed a time limit for ranking purposes. Thank goodness it does not result in game overs, or I would have gotten frustrated with it. Instead, I found it a lot of fun to piece together how to best beat the levels and gather a ton of resources. This was my first experience with the genre, and I could not have asked for a better introduction.
I planned to play Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love about five hours to write a solid review. Then it kept throwing new mechanics at me. I felt it was only fair to see them through for the most accurate review I could give. But I also admit that I was glad for the excuse, because I was hooked. I even plan on going back to try and get some better ranks in the levels. I had an absolute blast with this game, especially with it having legitimately good humor.
9/10. No really, I tried to find a justification for rating it lower than that and I couldn't. That's how much fun I had. If you do not absolutely loathe resource management games, get Incredible Dracula: Chasing Love. You won't be disappointed.

A fun and amusing resource and time management game with colorful detailed backgrounds. This game in places requires some well thought out strategy even in relaxed casual (not timed) mode.  The biographies/profiles of the characters are worth the read.
Storyline: Count Dracula decides to get modern and look for mate using an online dating system.  Having found "the perfect one" he goes to meet her only to discover she is nothing like her online profile. (That should be of no surprise! LOL) However, the Princess has matrimony on her mind and chases after Dracula, who runs away from her.
45 levels in the main game, 15 levels in the bonus chapter, and 3 modes, normal timed, relaxed (not timed), and timed multi-click (This is where the player can click on as many items as are available forming an item pick up cue).  What makes this game different for others is 1) interactive tabs for potions. crafting, and magic (3 each by game end), 2) clothing with a bonus ability attached (awarded during gameplay), and 3) powerups used for increasing supplies which upgrade during gameplay.  Late in the game there is a powerup upgrade that allows for upgrading all supply buildings at once (That is so nice and such a resource saver).  There are also "finds" that occur over the course of gameplay (main and bonus): princess statues (60, one per level), gift boxes (30, gives in-game 'stickers'), princess posters (6), and black cats (13).  Plus there are 3 extra 'secret' finds - death's scythe, alien, and sheep-king - found somewhere in the game. (Yes, I know where they are, and no, I am not telling, that would be a spoiler.)

Most, if not all, achievements can be earned during gameplay. (Note: Once a level is open the player can go back without having to play the entire game over).
Plays well and fast, the upgrades keep the gameplay fresh, the "finds" are a fun extra, and the storyline is amusing enough to keep the player interested.  Excellent game.  I highly recommend it.

Stellaris is the game Distant Worlds: Universe was hoping to grow up to be.
Okay I'm kidding!  I know it's a bit of a troll to say that.
But this does remind me to some degree of Distand Worlds, and of Galactic Civilizations, and also of Civilizations V (as far as the layers of different gameplay that show up).
Paradox published Stellaris, which had me worrying a little - "will this be like their other TBS games like Europa Universalis".  I was worried, because EU never hooked me - it seemed like this hodgepdge of options at any given moment that never felt natural or intuitive to me.  I really wanted to like EU, but for whatever reason it always felt strange when I tried to learn it.  Stellaris is nothing like that - maybe because they have a "Clippy" tutorial helper who does a pretty good job of introducing game conceps, with a quest interface to keep track of the several storylines that develop (some of them being tutorial quests if enabled).
What stands out in Stellaris is the leisurely pace at which the early game takes place - and even though it feels slow (and yes you can speed it up), even at the normal speed there's enough going on to stay engaged.  It's heavily "one more turn" only without the turns.
The mining operations become critical for having any speed of production, but each mine burns energy, and people will starve if you take them off the farms to work at power plants -- and your new alien neighbors really don't like you and they have a bigger fleet so... there's that too.
The immersion is REALLY FREAKING HIGH in this game - and one reason is because the graphics are gorgeous.  There's a simplicity in not too many choices to make at any given moment, and everything grows at a snail's pace, which makes the game not feel too harsh, sort of therapautic, while at the same time, there's a sense that "this is all going to get very very big the longer I stay with it."  And several parallel story threads are running as well - which prevents the whole glorious map from turning into a spreadsheet-fest - very well done.  I think this might be the most immersive of any space RTS or TBS I've seen yet.  What Civ has in familiarity of countries we've all heard of in history, Stellaris has in the unfolding lore being played out of various characters that show up on the map.  Also the artwork is meticulous.
The icing on the cake?  It plays just fine on my 2 year old laptop.  It might start to lag with too many ships eventually - but I haven't reached that point to say for sure.
I'd say check this out - absolutely if you like space and strategy.  This is the best game I've bought in several years - possibly to date.

This game is, mechanically, one of the best on Steam. It's great.
However, there is one overarching problem with it; A relatively small playerbase. This can result in high-ping games and half-full servers, which is a major blow to the game. The only way we can fix this problem is by playing the game. It's a good game, so it can't be that hard. I suppose this is due to a fairly rough initial learning curve.
Aside from the small playerbase and the resulting issues, this is a niche but very entertaining game. Let me break it down:
-This is a four-player coop, ignore any other category. If you loved the interplay and teamwork of working with a small team, such as playing Payday 2 or Left 4 Dead 2, then you should really look at Guns of Icarus. Teamwork is critical to the game and if that's what you love, you will love this game.
-Artwork.
The art alone is reason to buy the game. This game has the best artwork I've ever seen in any game. Ever. Hands down.
Music's bloody good too.
Graphics and animations are pretty average, but the sheer coolness of crewing the GoI warships willl guarantee you get your money's worth just exploring the game. I'm a big steampunk fan and aircraft buff, but I don't believe I'm very biased in this - take it from me, this is the best airship modelling in the world. Anything you thought of as cool before Guns of Icarus will probably need reevalution. I can't overstate how much this marriage of beautiful artwork and small-team squad gameplay thrills me.
-Balance. Though the game has a fairly steep initial learning curve, which will likely lead to you losing your first two or three matches due to not knowing how elements such as damage work in this game as opposed to many others will be a huge setback. If you take an hour or two to learn them, however, you can start playing competitively very quickly.
Senior players are actually rewarded for carrying rookies, and to further that cause you should find more experienced players very willing to teach you the basics and get you off the ground.
Heh.
But above all, atmosphere.
The game might seem to have skeletal lore, but it maintains within itself great self-consistency and keeps up the everpresent feeling of your own impermanence. The fast paces (often exceeding 100 k/h) of the airships and heavy damage taken constantly from a damage-centered gameplay dynamic serve to remind you at every second that you're riding not a modern airliner or a fireproofed helium blimp - these ships are slap-dash and falling apart around you, but this only serves to create a thrilling atmosphere in combat as parts go flying and clouds of smoke throw you into the shoes of a reckless young sailor with nothing left to lose, Not fighting for his life so much as throwing whatever he, his ship and his crew have left in the all-pervading pursuit of victory.
Look... If you do teamwork, super cool art, fire and explosions, or high-speed chases then just buy the game and thank me later.
The game would be better with an AAA budget behind it - mostly to advertise and expand the playerbase. But it's well worth buying as is.
