I haven't finished the game yet, but I love it so much I'll reccomend it anyway. The plot itself is fairly standard, androids vs machines in a war to protect the human race (as if that's a perfectly normal occurence, but you know what I mean) but it's the way it's told that makes it special.
The characters have depth and feel, the VA's suit them and the scriptwriting is both funny and moving. The world itself is presented incredibly, and the scenery of an abandoned earth city is very beautiful for one that has been bashed to bits by machines. There are 3 playable characters, each path with each character playing out differently, on top of the grand total of 26 endings to see, so there's a lot hidden for people like me who want to find them all. Plus - I'm only up to the second character - the combat for characters is different. The first 2B is attack oriented, while the second 9S allows you to hack opponents and play a short minigame in order to deal damage. I presume A2 will be slightly different again.
The combat itself is great fun. It's satisfying to watch enemies explode once defeated, and while you can get by with button mashing there are some intricacies like prefect dodges and counter attacking that are fun to pull off. There is a multitude of weapons of varying types to choose from and level, and although so far my fully upgraded weapons are of the same stats so there's not much difference other than appearance between weapons of the same type, you can chop and change between them during battle by setting them as weapon sets beforehand for a change of pace. Different types of weapons (eg. Sword, Greatsword, Spear) do play differently. Then to further customise combat, as an android you can equip yourself with Plugin Chips with different effects, like auto use heal items, recover hp when not hit, counter attacking, slow time on perfect dodge etc. Each of these chips can then be fused with chips of the same type and levelled up, increasing the effect they have.
Throw in side quests with funny/sad NPCs and outcomes, amazing soundtrack and flight suits (yes, flight suits for airbourne on rails shooter style combat) and you've got a great deal of fun. Will definitely be going back and playing Nier afterwards.

Coming from one who's favorite type of game is "4X Space Empire" I can recommend Stellaris above others. I have played the following related games:
Endless Space 1/2
Galactic Civilizations 3 w/ dlc
Civ 5 and Civ Beyond Earth
Sins of a Solar Empire
While I've enjoyed all of them (least of all ES and ES2), Stellaris is my favorite.
Compared to these other 4X titles, PROS ARE:
+Music. Or if you don't like it then you can use your own in-game
+Varied opponents. Some are pathetic pre-industrials, while others are so powerful it's a fools hope standing against them alone
+Tech. Whether you like the card system or not, I'd say it's done well and it adds variety to repeated plays
+Active Devs. They listen to the community. This game gets better and better.
+Living Empires. You can gene mod your pops/mod out your AI race. Terraform planets.
+Politics. AI doesn't flipflop from buddy to mortal enemy. What they do makes sense. A spiritualist empire hating your machine loving empire makes sense. Federations and vassals are cool. Internal political parties are a fun challenge to satisfy
+It pays to be an intergalactic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Slaves, extermination, eating newly conquered aliens...
+Tile Management. This is also good in GC3. Much more interactive and varied than CIV 5 and ES1/2.
+Overall balance. I'd say only CIV has as much balance here.
+AI is smart enough. No AI is perfect, but pretty good here.
+DLC. Well done yet not necessary.
+Fleet building. Good amount of useful/important choices. Maneuverable corvettes to draw fire, destroyers to screen missiles with point defense, battleships to hammer away at range, etc.
+Leaders
+Exploration. This is the best exporation game I've played hands down. The anomalies found are varied and interactive. They matter. You can push your luck or play it safe. Very cool stuff.
+UI
+Multiplayer works well
+Immersion. New advisor voices depending on ethos. You can't play completely out of character. Feels like a unique story each time.
+Great mods to change it up
As you can see there's a lot going for Stellaris. It ain't all perfect though. CONS:
-Stalemates. I've had a couple games where I was boxed in and the AI had so many defensive pacts with other empires that I dared not attack.
-Ground Wars. They are completely functional and work fine. But they are dry. Not a big deal since it's a small part of the game. Devs have said it's on their list of things to spice up eventually.
-Late game tedium. There can be a lot of clicking regarding your colonies and constructors. This is partially remedied through making self managing Sectors.
-Some bugs. But in my experience it's never been game breaking. They are being squashed though. Usually fixed within a couple weeks.
-Battles. While good, could be better in terms of more choice. Devs have expressed desire to work on it eventually. Better than GC3 and ES1/2 though in my opinion.

Militia is a unique turn-based strategy game with minimalist graphic design featuring many pictograms that might make this game look like a weird complex Chess variation. But that isn't true.
The gameplay follows the "Easy to learn, hard to master" scheme, as you'll learn almost everything about the gameplay mechanics in 10 minutes, then you are thrown into randomly generated levels. The challenge there is getting to the highest rank possible - every won game gets you closer to rank promotion, every lost game gets you farther.
Rank determines the difficulty of generated levels and provides a big challenge for everybody, as you'll have to keep a winrate better than 50%. While you'll be trying, you'll realize strategies and combos with specific units that you haven't thought before and... well, you'll get better.
There are two modes, light mode that is best for new players (but also provides a challenge) and dark mode, which was introduced later in Militia (
). Fighting both orcs and undead is really tough job, you'll often find yourself thinking your plan for some time, as there is no way back after you take your turn. There isn't an undo button, every mistake comes with a regret (and lose, and getting closer to losing your rank).
The whole presentation, from graphics to sounds, is simply awesome. Graphics are great for the game's intention, you'll just learn few pictograms, falling in love in it meanwhile. Militia is a big surprise for me, as it's simply great game. It features balanced difficulty and it's a pleasure to play for everybody who wants a casual strategy game, or for those who are alone and would like to play a board game.

NOTE: This review is only based on the No-Strum mode and aimed at people who have seen this game and are players of VSRGs like stepmania, osu!mania, o2jam, anything like that.
If like me you saw the introduction of the No-Strum mode and thought it was cool that there is a game like this on steam, be warned: the one fatal flaw with this game is that you cannot set a custom scroll speed, there are two options, "slow" and "fast", though IMO they should be renamed "slow" and "slow" cause that's what they really are to anybody who's even slightly compitent at any other game like this.
the second problem is the difficulty. I do want to say that this is only based on the official songs, as I'm sure once the community grows challenging charts will be available on the workshop. The expert mode is not that hard at all, if you've played any other VSRG for even a few months you will easily be able to 100% the expert charts, however like I said this is not really an issue I feel the dev should focus on as it's really up to the community to create harder charts. the steam acheivements are also very easy to obtain and I gained them all in around 3 hours and it only took that long because of the "clear 50 songs" achievement which takes the most time.
Another issue - No mods. not even the ability to speed up a song, I feel even if there were speed modifiers you could at least challenge yourself a bit with the built in charts, but no.
Another Issue that isn't really an issue more of a "I wish this feature was in this game", there is no timing judgements, only "hit" or "miss",  so there is no real accuracy meter in this game, the percentage it gives you at the end is just the amount of notes you hit, it doesn't go deeper than that. though like i said I don't really think this is an issue that needs to be fixed, more of something I'd like to see in the game.
Despite of all these flaws, I have actually grown to like the game in the short time I've played it.
I feel I've been harsh considering this is not supposed to be the kind of game I went into it thinking it was, at it's heart it's supposed to be more like guitar-hero than anything else and you should really consider that before rushing in to buy it.
The songs that come with the game are good, and the charts (although not as challenging as I'd like them to be) are mapped fairly well and the majority are honestly fun to play.
Honestly, if you're wondering if you should buy this game or not, it really depends what you're looking for in it.
If you're looking for a fun 5-key experience with nice songs, nice charts, and you're not really looking for a challenging experience. go for it, the game is genuinely fun.
However, if you're looking for a new VSRG to play to actually challenge you and maybe improve your 5k skills, I don't think this is the game for you, you could literally go play any other vsrg for free and get more challenge and improve your skill much faster.
So Overall, I would reccomend this game, but make sure it's what you're looking for, I bought this game thinking it was something it wasn't and initially didn't like it, but I've grown to like it for what it is. I'd like to restate that this whole review is based only on the No-Strum mode and all my points are aimed at VSRG players who are decent at their games. This review kinda turned into more of a "things i wish were in this game" but I think I made some valid points that would help others like me decide if they want to spend the money and buy this game or not.

At the start of my playthrough of Anodyne, this would have been a hesistant recommendation.
The first thing to note is that the game's claim to 'Zelda-lite' might be a bit misleading.
The game is less combat focused than you might think, and if you're looking for the depth of Link's Awakening's different items and enemies you won't find it here. I think in some ways Anodyne feels much more exploratory, like Yume Nikki.
You only have 1 weapon throughout the entire game, with a couple upgrades to make it better, but no tools like Zelda's mobility and combat altering roc's feather, hookshot, boots, etc.
The game's atmosphere is at most times surreal, putting you through areas like a cave filled with murmuring, growling people, a misty red land with giant walker-things, and an all black and white static town.
At this point I have to say how bad the game's story is.
The plot of Anodyne is unnecessarily convoluted to the point of making me not care about anything that's happening with Young, or the sage, or Briar, or any other character.
For such a surreal game, it trys so hard to tell you that the game is whimsical and not taking itself too seriously to the result of inane and annoying dialogue. Characters have nothing memorable or important to say, and none of the themes it hints at follow through in any detail.
Let's forget about the terrible story. Gameplay in Anodyne revolves around exploring the different areas and trying to find cards in treasure chests that will open up card gates, allowing you to get to new areas. You need 36 cards to open the gate to the final area of the game, and there are 37 cards total. How you do this is non-linear, with multiple areas becoming unlocked in the nexus for you to go back to once you've found their teleport points, and I like this option of several different paths and choices.
The combat and exploration are pretty good throughout if you don't mind some backtracking and repetition, and the atmosphere (when you're not talking to anyone) is usually great and backed up with solid graphics and a variety of good music.
So if this is just
overall, why would I bother recommending the game?
One thing:
After beating the game, you get full access to a tool that literally lets you break the game apart and travel out of bounds. I think this is one of the very best post-games I've ever played. It opens up more cards to find and very strange new places to explore with so much mystery and intrigue that I started looking at the game in a
. The one tool that lets you do this has to be one one of my favorite tools in all of gaming.
So, I would mostly recommend this one to fans of surreal exploration games like Yume Nikki, .flow, Space Funeral, etc.
But it's worth playing through this entire game just for the post-game - really.

Anodyne is an action game where you explore dungeons and defeat bosses. There are 6+ dungeons in the game. The "plus" referring to those dungeon-like areas without bosses.
Most (if not all) of the musics in this game give off the relaxing vibe. I really like the musics and they blend with the environments perfectly
The game uses 2D pixelated graphics. The areas look beautiful and the mappings are decent. The level designs are also good, except for some dungeon areas that are not "square shaped" which makes the map looks confusing with the area being connected to each other or not.
To be honest, i don't really get the story. At first, you're told to protect the Briar, and all you end up doing is going to dungeons for "training". There isn't much interactions for the story to clear it up (and i think the main story is only in the near beginning of the game and the near end of the game), although there are some facts written in the stones (which is scattered in the world) which holds some info of the game's setting.
The game will start by teaching you the controls. After you finish the tutorial, you'll be moved into an area called nexus, which is a gateway that lets you to teleport to all areas easily, provided that you have opened the portal. After you finish the first dungeon with a boss, you'll be able to finish the other major dungeons in any order that you want. However, i'm having some trouble in accessing these dungeons because i don't know how to reach to some places
until i move around between the areas a lot of times.
There isn't that many areas in the game, although i like how you can finish the dungeons in any order that you want. The bosses in the game isn't very hard either; i usually just keep on attacking the boss until it dies, without caring much about my HP (the bosses will usually die faster than me). The only exception for this is the last boss where you need to think a little to beat it. There is also one boss that's super easy that i don't really need to move in order to kill it
.
There are also some reaction based puzzles in the game. Some of them are quite easy, but some, especially in the
area is quite hard that you have to retry the puzzle several times if you're not that good. This makes it worse since you have to go through a long walk to the puzzle area again if you fail. There is also a ridiculous area where you have to wait for like 2h in order to get a secret (one of the collectables in the game). Luckily it's not required to beat the game.
If you play this game thinking because you want to play some Zelda-like games, then you have to stop. This game isn't really on the same genre. Sure, you have a weapon, a few health bars, and some dungeons to explore, but that's all there is to it. There isn't any puzzle in this game that requires you to think (most of them are reaction based), and you can only utilize your main weapon to kill enemies (there isn't any additional equips for you to use, except for some weapon upgrades that can help you kill enemies easily). Most bosses can be beaten in the same way; you don't even need to remember their attack pattern. But even without that, the game itself is enjoyable-
Except for the post game content. After the game introduces the last weapon upgrade, you basically can move everywhere, including to "glitched" areas that's not supposed to exist. This poses a problem when you end up having non walkable tiles on the other side of the screen and the screen where you came from, since you'll have no other choice except by teleporting to nexus and start over from scratch. Plus, you also need to spend a very long time by going through the glitched areas to find the secret items without using a guide. Just for a measurement, it too me ~4h to finish the game for the first time and it took around 2-4h to collect the other collectables. This is not including some secret collectables that can only be obtained with a glitch since i read somewhere that you'll lose all of your collectables if you collect it.
Speaking of collectables, there are some cards and secret items that you can collect in the area. The cards are usually easy to get since they are in the treasure chests. The secret items, on the other hand, might be hard to find since you'll have to explore to all possible glitched areas with your weapon upgrade in order to find the secret areas which has the secret items in it.
Pros:
- 6+ dungeons
- Collectables
- You can finish most dungeons in any order that you want
Cons:
- Most of the bosses are too easy to kill
- Annoying "puzzle" where you have to wait for hours just to get a secret item
- "Glitched" areas can be annoying if you want to explore the map

I cannot possibly give enough praise to this game. You want a short review? Buy it and experience the magnificence. Every component of this beautiful game is blended together so magnificently that it is the definitive interactive experience. No other game comes close. Acquire this game at any cost, and be prepared for the most intense emotional experience you can imagine. You think you know what’s going on? You have no idea until you start the third play through. Even calling them "play throughs" is deceptive, because there's only a single experience on your way to unlocking the major endings. Branching endings and playthroughs all weave together to create a single experience deeper then any other "choice" game. You have to play this game, for the glory of mankind.
Now for the longer review, where I try to make sense of the jumble of thoughts and experiences I had while playing Nier. Where can I even begin? How do you start describing an experience that changed the way you think? When describing something so unique, so insightful, I supposed you can only start by describing what makes Nier stand higher than any other game has dared to stand.
So I begin. No other game brought me sadness so great that I started sobbing uncontrollably. Even the most difficult games do not require you to carry the same burdens and handle the same hardships. While other games have touched on tragedy and loss, Nier handles the subjects so masterfully that even the best narrative experiences seem like children’s stories. Yet, for all the suffering I experienced while playing Nier, no other game has filled me with so much wonder that tears flowed down my face. Never have I experienced a game that touched me in such a personal way. Never have I experienced a game that helped me handle serious and deep issues I've been struggling with.
For me, Nier is a deeply personal experience, and I cannot think of another game that affected me in such a profound way. You, dear reader, may not have the same experience with Nier, but if you even come close to the experience I had, the value of this experience will be incomparable to any monetary cost.

A challenging puzzler with a wicked sense of humor and gratuitous voxel violence. The game screen can get a little busy and, as a result, all those chunky voxels can become a bit visually overwhelming in some of the levels where there are several different puzzle elements in play at once. Thankfully the game does let you zoom out from the default isometric view to an overhead camera that's much better for surveying the playfield and planning out your moves. Just don't forget to zoom back in to see all of the glorious violence!
And that's pretty much all I have to say about the game that could possibly be construed as negative. Slayaway is one of those rare games with such a tight focus on familiar premise and simple design that it's difficult to find fault with if you enjoy the genre. Some of the puzzles will give your noodle a proper thrashing, and the plethora of unlockables will keep slasher flick fans coming back for more. There's an impressive amount of content on offer here, especially considering the price.
I should note that the game is clearly designed with mobile platforms in mind, but this PC version is very well thought out to the point that you're not likely to even notice. The SE is reasonably priced and comes with some really cool extras including a few papercraft templates for Slayaway characters that I have every intention of putting together and displaying alongside my other game memorabilia.
Until Traveller's Tales decides it would be a great idea to make an M-rated Lego Friday the 13th game (which will sadly never happen), Slayaway Camp is about the best you could hope for. Murder has never been so hilariously adorable.

Overall: Guns of Icarus Online is a fantastic tactical, team based multiplayer game that indirectly forces people to use constant team work. ships are all unique and balanced with strengths and weaknesses, the scale of the battles at times are breath taking and working with a good crew and team feels great. costumes and paint jobs are the only thing you can buy, on top of that, they're nothing bank breaking. negatives being, getting into the game is tough, everything is confusing and without a helping hand from the crew, you wont know what to do, worst case you get barked at by yours or another pilot. player count is a concerning one, there are maybe under two hundred players at high point and under a hundred at low point on a normal day. once you get passed the git gud wall, the game is alot of fun.
Teamwork: constant communication and teamwork is critical to your team winning a match especially for pilots between other ships and the crew, without it, you are bound to fail to the other team if they have superior communication. now this can result in a glorious victory but the downside to this is not every pilot and crew member wants to talk (as long as crew follows orders, they're fine) so communicating information between eachother becomes very dificult and at some point someone messes up and gets someone killed. usually it's not a big issue as many experienced pilots know the critical nature of talking.
Ships: every ship in the game is unique, with stengths and weekness and a different way of handling them. one extreme example is the Galleon ship, heavy, slow but is a ♥♥♥♥♥ to take down with good engineers and is equipped with the most heavy weapons of any ship. on the other extreme is the Squid ship, fast, light, but is easily destroyed and only has three guns, none of them being heavy. in between are ships of different combos and many ways to adjust those ships to your play style.
Performance: this game is light and still looks great, I'm not saying that this game can run on Intel HD graphics with great framerate, trust me, I've tried, but it can run well on any modern graphics card, and processor.
Waitng: waiting in lobby is an issue for this game, as people normally want a full crew or atleast two crew members, not having to rely on the AI to do the work. you probably can imagine, you can't bark at an AI over voice chat and no pilot bothers with the speech system since their attention is needed for the on going battle. back to point, the man power needed to operate an effective ship requires people, and with lots of ships, you need lots of people, and finding people to join with the games player count can be time consuming. despite the long wait, the battles are usually well worth it and once you got a filled lobby, it will stay filled for a while.

After enjoying completing the game with 100% and just some cards left to collect, I decided to give this fine piece of software a review.
So what's this game anyway? Basically it's a platformer, with minor Shoot'em Up parts both at the beginning and the end of the game. Armed with a teleport gun and a space suit you control Captain Yuri on his journey to defeat the evil Grigori.
Simple control scheme: arrow keys and 3 others, Z X C by default, Europeans might want to swap Z with Y prior to starting. The game does have controller support, I used a keyboard though and had no problems.
Over the course of my several playthroughs and experiments I only encountered 1 or 2 minor bugs you wouldn't experience without specifically looking for it. Even if, none of them was game breaking. Otherwise it's got smooth and clean animations, perfect hitboxes and overall fair difficulty. There's no real tutorial but is streamlined on directs you perfectly through the mechanics, the growing complexity should be no problem for the average player.
If you want all achievements though, you're in for a tougher challenge, brace yourself and activate your thinker.
As for the design, it's an adorable small indie treasure, you won't get 10 hours of excitement but instead you'll get challenging fun packed into a small platformer. Nothing looks out of place, everything fits into this colourfully bright (but not bilindingly bright) small universe. Even the music is brilliant for such a small game, it's repetetive but it doesn't get boring, this way it's even fun waiting for the "delay" Achievement while doing something else. Only downside is there's no transition when the BGM changes but hey, it's not like that would hurt anyone
My first playthrough took me an hour and roughly 15 minutes, the only thing that really got on my nerves was clicking through Yuris messages on my playthroughs after the first one...
Bottom line: whatever you pay, it's a bargain

This here is a really well made little gem! It is so simple yet so good. The design is well made, and you will learn how to play it very easily thanks to the simple and intuitive tutorial.
It's basically somewhat similar to chess: you have a checkered board and different units with different movement patterns and abilities (same goes for the enemies). The difference is that you have very few units and all of them are placed in various positions of the board (don't know if randomly or with premade layouts). You can move/use ALL of your units 1 time and then it's the enemy's turn. The objective is to kill the "captains" of the enemy team and not necessarily all of it's units.
When one level is passed you will immediately start a new one, each one getting harder in difficulty, giving the player an increasing challenge. The game also immerses the player directly into the next level without having him click his way through various menu screens, keeping him engaged and willing to play that "one last level".
Going on with the levels you will also "unlock" different units, enemies and level layouts.
There are also 2 game modes with slightly different game mechanics, one of them a bit more complicated than the other one, both of them interesting.
Elegant and sober art keeps the look and feel so "clean" and swift.
I still haven't played much but I will certainly be playing it again. I suggest you support the developer and try this game out. You can see that he's put a lot of effort and thought into Militia and he deserves more players!
Well done! :D

Watch my video review here:
The game features two game modes with slightly different rules, but the primary objective being to eliminate the enemy captains (indicated with stars). Each level is randomized, with different friendly units and initial enemy positions. Similar to chess, every unit has specific movement and attack rules, so gameplay involves planning out where the enemies might move (their movements are randomized within the rules set) and where friendly units can attack. The game can get quite difficult, and losing a match knocks the difficult level down too far, requiring several successful campaigns to compensate. Still, Militia is an engaging, straightforward turn-based strategy game.

A charming, deceptively simple game. Easy to learn, difficult to master.
You pit three random player-controlled units against a much larger number of weaker enemies. You have trickier and more powerful options, but a single mistake means losing 1/3 of your firepower.
The game has an elegant tutorial and is very quick to learn.
Its ranking system accomplishes two difficult tasks at once: motivation to get better at the game, and an effective difficulty curve. You'll probably blast through the first few ranks easily, but soon you'll find yourself in challenging environments that push you to master the mechanics. I can confidently say this regardless of your skill level or aptitude for this sort of game.
Overall, a great buy for the price. You can play one of two distinct rulesets, either Light or Dark. Light offers much simpler mechanics, with units that jump and attack in easy-to-understand ways. Dark offers complicated individual pieces that do things like push other units, generate explosives, and warp across the edges of the board.
I am excited to see how many hours of play this game offers me.

This is a linear RPG, so it does lack the content that open world RPGs will have (for instance, maps are fairly small and there aren't many side quests). It also has a combat system that feels optimized for consoles. However, the game's story unfolds with a good, quick pace. The writing frequently cribs from the show, but while some passages are bad, the moments of great writing more than make up for it. Highly recommend to fans of GoT - moderately recommend to fans of RPGs.

Casual GoT fans = You'll notice some flaws, but the story and atmosphere are what you came for, right? You will more-than likely enjoy this game overall.
"Kinda-but-not-really-that-much" GoT fans = You should at least give this game a try if you enjoy RPGs... Keep in mind the storyline and characters are really the focus here.

--Terrible Workshop integration (More below)
---------TERRIBLE WORKSHOP INTEGRATION------------
OK. So one of the main features for this game was the workshop. The way I saw it before I bought the game was that people would put songs on the work shop that you could then download and play, Super easy and convenient. HOWEVER this is not the case. To play a song downloaded from the workshop you must already have that song downloaded on your computer. All you download is a "beatmap" that the person made for a song. So if you want say a song from Sonic, you would have to download it off the workshop (or create the beatmap yourself), then find the same exact version of the Sonic song they used to make there beatmap on the internet and download it, then import it into your game. So if you are looking to increase the low number of songs in this game with the workshop good luck, you have some tedious work ahead of you.
TLDR - Workshop is cumbersome and inconvenient, and should not be looked at as a feature for this game.
Buy this game if you love rythm games, if not wait until it goes on sale.

Slayaway Camp is a love letter to the 80's slasher movies presented in a gory voxel-puzzle game.
I'm pleasantly surprised with this game. I bought it on a whim just looking for something casual to play in-between bigger achievement hunting projects. I'm not the biggest puzzle game fan; it's not that I don't enjoy them, but I usually get bored trying to figure out the solution. I'm also not a huge fan of horror, although I'd classify this as horror-comedy. The game also does have a lot of voxelated gore; but there appears to be a slider that changes the amount of bloodshed and bones you see; with the option to increase or lower the amount.
The difficulty curve in this game has been fair, for the most part. The odd puzzle will present itself as a bit more tricky and involved than some before or even after; but they're usually solved fairly quickly. There's only one puzzle so far that had me stuck and ended up using a hint to help solve. After the game gives you a hint, it has an option to auto-solve the puzzle for you for a small amount of the skull tokens you use to buy Gore-Paks and skins for Skullface.
The game has a wide-variety of bonus kills and Gore-Pak kills. You get a free skin every movie you start; as well as being able to buy some through a Mystery Box feature. These skins (so far) also seem to have some skin-specific kills, and some levels also have level-specific kills. I can't say whether the Mystery Box skins have any skin specific kills yet as I've mostly been focusing on buying the Gore-Paks since some of them are more expensive.
This is a good puzzle game to pass the time with. There's a great amount of levels, as well as a solid amount of variety with new kills to witness, skins to see, movies to unlock that features different types of worlds, and new level hazards as you progress.
If you're a fan of puzzle games, horror, or just looking for something to pass the times with, this is a great buy. Even if you're not a huge fan of either, I'd still recommend giving this game a chance. If you're still unsure about the game, you could always check out the free version on Kongregate to help see if it would be something you enjoy.
I'm really digging this. Plenty of fun content for the price! A no brainer, pick it up if you like puzzle games and slasher flicks!

I received this game to play on stream and to review on my website. I went into this one hoping for the best but expecting the worst since a lot of these indy horror games are a huge let down. On top of that, I'm not a huge fan of puzzle games. With that said I have to say that this game brilliantly walks the line between a perfect homage to the 80's slasher genre of film and a cute puzzler that fans of puzzle games will love. Due to the art style of this game it will not run away more soft skinned puzzle fans, while being grizzly enough to entertain the horror fans. The fact that it's a puzzler was troubling but instead of frustrating me it brought out a weird OCD side of myself that kept me playing for hours. I'd totally suggest Slayaway Camp (as well as the DLC which I actually bought out of pocket) for any true slasher fan or puzzler fan out there.

Guns of Icarus is a game with a very cool premise but very bad execution; you play the role of either a gunner, engineer, or captain on a steampunk airship in a post-apocalyptic world, battling other airships in multiplayer modes like Skyball, Deathmatch, and other regurgitated online FPS modes. You and your crew of 4 must work together to keep your airship aloft and shoot down enemies, as your captain pilots it around the battlefield.
Airships are comprised of several key components; a main engine, 2 turning engines, a balloon pump, armor, an assortment of guns, and the hull. All except the hull can be repaired and buffed from the deck of the airship, while the hull serves as your overall HP; if the hull hits 0, you go boom. The armor protects the hull entirely as long as it is intact, so maintaining it is critical.
While the game is definitely fun and awe-inspiring for the first few moments, it quickly loses its splender about the 3rd game you get matched with level 30-40 players on the enemy team who all know what they're doing and are using the meta ships. Regardless how much effort you put it into each fight, the game hinges on knowing what to do and when to do it as well as good communication between the crew. While the game does have a decent in-game comms solution, there's no guarantee your crew (if you're lucky enough to get one) will respond, or even follow orders, and that's assuming they have some idea what they're doing. The high-level players, on the other hand, will all congregrate with their other high-level friends, and would rather seal-club you into the ground rather than help new players join the game... which is a bit sad considering it only has 200 people online on a Saturday afternoon-evening.
All in all, the game has potential, but poor matchmaking and sealclubbing ruin it.

Been playing this game for a few weeks.  It's a solid F2P game in the sense that the gameplay is entertaining, the netcode is solid, and you can have fun without spending any money.  My only real qualm is that sniping outclasses every other style of play.  It isn't difficult to one-shot enemies with a headshot after a few minutes practice, but to make matters worse, once you've upgraded your rifle a bit, you'll be taking over half of your enemies' HP just with a body shot.  To be honest you should be able to overpower most encounters just body-shotting your enemies down.  Most other weapons in the game tend to have either travel time, or a lengthy time to kill.  A hitscan weapon with 1-shot heashots and 2-shot bodyshots simply outclasses everything else.  Also bear in mind you get to carry two weapons in the game so can use any kind of weapon you'd want to supplement your sniping.  You're far from defenseless if somebody rushes you and gets in close.
That being said, it's kind of a moot point because it doesn't seem like that many people snipe at the moment-- but I'm sure that will change over time.  I don't think most people realize how powerful it is.  That being said, it's worth mentioning that the sniping in the game does feel pretty good and has a smooth arcady feel to it.
In conclusion,
game is fun, and a solid F2P experience-- but being realistic about the game's mechanics and the limitations of most weapon combinations, sniping is the only viable to play the game competitively.

When I was younger, I recall my friends taking their bikes out after school and riding to the local convenience store to buy candy and other life non-essentials. I was always fickle. I didn't like candy, but I loved lemonade. My friends would make fun of me, but when they would head off to have fun after school, I would set up my cardboard lemonade stand in front of my neighborhood and peddle my colored sugar water to what I once considered "well-established" families in minivans coming from at the end of the day.
It wasn't long before I hired a helping hand to manage a second lemonade stand down at the convenience store my friends would frequent. For kids, we were really raking in the dough. On my days off, I would treat my friends to candy at the store and they quickly realized how lucrative my lemonade stands were and I convinced them to run a stand for me, for a percentage of my profits.
Years later, I'd built a conglomerate. In addition to owning the most popular lemonade company in the world, with thousands of locations worldwide, I'd built a monopoly on the newspaper delivery industry (somehow still not replaced by digital content), car washes, pizza parlors and donut shops. I started to become overwhelmed with the amount of money pouring in and decided I needed a way to clear my mind, so I bought my first boat. It was a nice, quaint little yacht called 'Streets of Monaco'. I was sun bathing on the deck when it hit me - I was wasting my time with land based ventures. I needed to expand. I looked longingly out to sea and pondered only for a moment before telling my personal assistant to set up a deal - I wanted to buy a thousand shrimp trawlers.
Before I could blink, I now had control of the seas. Currently, my fleet's output accounts for 92% of the global catch. One day, researchers aboard one of my vessels over the Mariana Trench discovered a new species of shrimp and accredited me with the discovery for allowing them to accompany my ships out to sea free of charge. They honored me by naming the shrimp after me, and let me tell you, that was one tasty shrimp. Publicity from the discovery led to, though unnecessary, donations pouring in from global donors and research organizations.
Although I could afford everything a man could desire out-of-pocket at this point in my career, I took the money anyway because I'm a business man and I never pass up free money. I decided to put it to good us, however personal the reasons, and became a deep-sea innovator and pioneer, leading a team of myself (because I deserve all the credit) to the bottom of the sea. "Where," you ask? Well, to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, of course. It was there that I discovered hundreds of new species, a few of which held the cures for cancer, the common cold and stupidity. There was one fish, a very special fish, which I kept as a companion. In an instant, I became the most sensational man on the planet. I was on fire and quickly became bored once again. How was a man who single-handedly spearheaded exploration to the lowest point on Earth to be amused by Earthly trinkets and games any longer?
After paying off the U.S. debt and moving into the White House, it dawned on me that I was not a man who could be contained by governmental borders. Although I could easily buy my way anywhere, anytime, I decided I shouldn't have to - and bought the entire world. Why? Because I could. I was making money hand-over-fist. Faster than I could ever dream of spending it. I decided to expand my ventures, once again, and decided to make my first PR move. I bought every Hockey team. Period. Then I began to produce digital content. Movies, television shows, podcasts, you name it...
My name had become a common household name like Kleenex or Scotch tape. It was this familiarity and trust that led me to open my own bank. Logically, everyone immediately wanted to keep their money with me. As I was making so much money, there was no risk of ever going bankrupt. It wasn't long before I possessed 99.8% of all the money in the world. Now, then, what was a man to do? A man who literally owns the world. It was time for a new venture.
Similar to my previous desire to break the bonds of mortal divides, I soon yearned to be free of them altogether. I reluctantly partnered with former PayPal entrepreneur and Tesla Motors CEO Elon Musk, taking advantage of the trivial work and progress he had already done in space "exploration". Anything can be solved if you throw enough money at it. When it came time to depart on the company’s Maiden voyage, I became ill. The idea of space travel didn't turn my stomach, rather, it was Elon's musk. I had been forced to endure the odor long enough and, though I’m now ashamed to admit it, I sent him on a suicide mission. It wasn't long after his accident that I was able to successfully fix the “reliability issue” and become the first civilian to self-fund a trip to the moon, if that word could even be used to define my status anymore.
Upon my arrival in the terrestrial world, I immediately saw a market for new opportunities. It wasn’t long after constructing my moon base that things started to become dull and boring. Perhaps it was the loneliness, but one night while staring up at the blue marble, wondering how the poor souls on Earth were doing, I decided that in order to truly leave that life behind, I must also dispose of my Earthly companion. As there had only ever been one of my very special companion ever found, I didn’t want to simply set it free to have it die an ungraceful, lonely end, rather, I opted to eat my friend. It wasn’t until after I had taken the first bite that, much to my surprise, I realized this was no rare fish…
.
I was indifferent at first. I had never been very religious, personally. Although I didn’t finish my meal (it really didn’t taste that good), I did feel different. And I liked it. Something within me had changed. Suddenly, I was surrounded by more and more of these rare creatures and for some reason, they were attracted to me. By consuming angel, had I become some sort of angel magnet? To this day, I’m still not sure, but it was amazing. Year after year my revenues, though steadily flowing in, were climbing slower and slower. It seemed as if there was some sort of glass ceiling. Despite profits increasing at first, after a while though, the same thing happened. My growth seemed to slow once again. Becoming bored, I was lost in the recesses of space, my mind… Wondering where my next boost would come from. Then it was right in front of me. Like a light bulb turning on, I thought to myself “If by killing one of these angels my revenues were bolstered, then perhaps by killing another it will happen again…”
500 quattuorvigintillion angels later, I began to feel more like a battle-hardened, steel cold warrior instead of a motivated businessman. Remorselessly, day in and day out I slaughtered countless angels. The depths of my pockets became unfathomable, though I lost more and more of myself. The profits were a drug. I couldn’t stop. That is, until one day, I was faced by an angel whose face I recognized. It was my late wife. It was at that moment that I had realized what I had done (besides become the wealthiest, most important man in the universe). I had lost myself. That little boy with the lemonade stand, just trying to make enough money to buy some candy… For friends. Friends, I longer had any. Family... I never had children.
I remember… At first, having money was great. I was on top of the world. It was great, but I lost myself. Who I really am. Then the depression set in... Now I find myself back at home, on Earth, just being me. I live with my mother. My 5 o’clock shadow grows darker each day, my wife beater more stained. Stained with tears, sorrow. Sorrow, but not remorse. Now I just play AdVenture Capitalist, sorrowful that I can’t sacrifice angels faster.

Got that on sale, vaguely intrigued by its premises. Well, now that I just finished it I can say it truly is a diamond in the rough.
Why a diamond?
I'm a GOT Tv series fan (haven't read the books and I don't plan to, at least for now) and believe me, this game picks up all of saga's pace and spirit, bringing you a story which starts somewhat good and becomes even better and better as it unfolds before your eyes. You'll meet some of saga's main characters and you'll be hinted about others, but what matters is that Cyanide really crafted a very good story, with good dialogues and a good number of plot twists and secondary quests to keep you enticed. The two main characters, Alester the Red Priest and Mors the Black Crow, both have strong and complex personalities, and their backstories will intertwine in quite interesting ways.
Why rough?
Well, some players here hatefully despise its combat system. I don't. Sure, it isn't be the best around, but does its dirty job and it becomes rather intriguing once you get the grasp of it and once your characters acquire more abilities and powers. Characters animations and voices are...just meh. Could be better but also could be worse, nothing you couldn't stand. Ambients instead, unlike characters, are quite well designed.
Camera may give you some headaches during combat, especially when you'll have to fight in tiny areas against many enemies. Nothing too shameful , just mildly annoying every once in a while.
So, let's sum it: Do I recommend this game? Absolutely YES. Scratch under a layer of few and tiny drawbacks and you'll find a really worthy and fascinating story.
Even full price is not too much, but if you happen to see it on sale don't pass it over, BUY IT.

Militia keeps being compared to chess and I feel that's a rather short sited comparison. At the beginning of each round you are placed on a procedurally generated board with the objective of using your given pieces to clear the board of the 'Captain' pieces. The only real way that it's like chess is that any given piece has a specified move set.
This game is the almost the definition of "Easy to Learn, Hard to Master" the rules are always the same and in theory if you just think hard enough there's no way you can lose! However you always miss that one archer in the corner or that imp. It's strategy in its purest (and arguably best) form.
Whilst the game is local only it scales in difficulty with your ability. The more matches you win the higher your ranking the more difficult the scenarios. However if you fail a match you lose ranking and thus the difficulty decreases. Ideally this means that you slowly hone your skills and hit rank 10! (I'm still only at rank 5... it gets hard fast).
If that's not enough for you the game also includes the 'Dark World' Expansion which adds an entirely new mode. It features completely new pieces for you and the computer which allow for abilities that wrap around the board, create or detonate explosives and lots of other new abilities that make for an even tougher experience. This again comes with its own laddering system. It pretty much doubles the amount of content in the game.
Militia is a great game and one I'm likely to lose a fair amount of time to. It's simple yet compelling and likely appeals to a very wide audience including those who do not traditionally play games. The game is great on Steam but also maybe better as a portable game which is available on tablets. The developer also looks to be adding even more content in the future such as endless mode and time attack so it seems that I'll lose even more time to it.

This is a simple and engaging strategy game. It provides the satisfaction of chess-like mechanics with procedural generation to keep things fresh.

Militia was developed and published by BrainGoodGames. It was released on December 2nd, 2015 for £4.79. A review copy was provided for The Hidden Levels.
Militia is a “bite sized” turn based strategy game which heavily plays like the classic board game chess. The game is simply played with just a mouse and has no controller support. The game has nice contrast between the two competing sides and the ‘board’ on where it is played. No issues arose for me during my time playing Militia. The replay value is very high if you can learn and adapt to a more simple styled game. There are no difficulty options but the enemies get difficult with each level you complete.
What I enjoyed:
Easy to Learn – Within a few moments of playing I fully grasped the game controlling my troops with ease. There was a help screen in the game which I did not need
Ever changing challenge – The enemies adapt to you, the levels are randomized and the difficulty ever more increases keeping the challenge fresh.
Music  –  The music in the game is really outstanding and a real strong suit to the game. It really adds to the atmosphere. You could easily just leave the game running and enjoy the music.
What I disliked:
Price – The price at £4.79 seems steep for the type of game you’re getting.
No control of your units at the start – All the units are placed down randomly posing a greater challenge. I would like some control over where the troops would be placed though. I would also love to have control over what type of troop is gained.
Limited in turns – You only have a certain amount of turns to kill all troops before losing. You also are heavily outnumbered.
If you enjoy games like chess and have a great amount of patience for simple games, you could easily find yourself playing this game for long periods of time. The challenges keep rising and the randomization of the game keeps you on your toes. The game may not have a lot of depth but I fully enjoyed the simplicity and the easiness to grasp the game and rules. If you do love chess and any other styled game, this will be enjoyable.
Score: Wait for a sale

I picked up Anodyne as someone who grew up in the 80s and was looking for indie games inspired by the era. I'm a programmer by trade and have been planning an indie game of my own for several years now but wanted to find some titles  of a similar style to play through for inspiration and as a way to critique my own ideas. At first glance Anodyne seems overly simplistic and I wasn't sure if I'd like it but after giving it a few hours there is far more depth here than I expected and I'm truly enjoying it.
The devs for this game are huge fans of the original 8-bit and 16-bit Nintendo (and Super Nintendo) Entertainment Systems. The clues are everywhere in subtle and no so subtle ways, like the inclusion of a certain NPC who is heavily inspired by one of Nintendo's most memorable characters (no spoilers here).
Anodyne is heavily influenced by the original 8-bit and 16-bit Zelda games. From exploring dungeons and collecting power ups, to solving puzzles and revisiting areas to explore them further once your new items have unlocked new capabilities - Anodyne plays in a very familiar fashion. But while Anodyne may have been heavily influenced by Zelda the devs have definitely crafted a unique adventure of their own here.
I've not yet finished the game but I'm curious where the story is going. The dimensional gateways and certain story elements, such as the depth of dialogue between Young and some of the eccentric characters he meets along the way, as well as certain areas I've explored with unexpectedly dark subject matter suggests an ending with a bigger punch than I could have anticipated when I first purchased the game.
Summary: Anodyne is a surprising gem of a game with great music, classic retro-styled graphics, familiar (simple) gameplay mechanics, lots of beautiful and unique regions to explore, puzzles to solve and what appears to be some deep existential subject matter.

This is, without question, one of the most beautiful sendups of Link's Awakening available right now. What made that game appealing, both visually and sylistically, has all been brought into higher resolution, and with richer, more vivid colour palettes.
Worst comes to worst, if atmosphere and pixel art interest you, this game is worth your time.
But I can't promise that that time will be good.
The game is unpolished. Every jump I made had me sweating because I could never tell if the distance would be enough, and enemy encounters left some rooms feeling starved for space to dodge.
But the story may be the worst of it. At best, it feels confused. At worst, what major themes the story can be recognized to have make the narrative as a whole into a poorly executed attempt at self-reflection and escapism; leading to the story reward at the end of a frustrating dungeon being a critique the act of playing video games.
But maybe it's some post-modernist crap. I mean, I definitely wanted to take a break from it all and go outside, once I was done.

The game's very sweet, nostalgic, and creepy. It's not strictly linear, but it's also not *too* non-linear; you do have to backtrack at times, but not excesively as if you were playing a Metroid, plus you have convenient warp points. The mechanics are pretty simple while the story and art are the focus of the gameplay. It's a short game (I finished in under 8 hours and I'm a slow gamer), but it feels complete.
The only negative qualities I can think of, are 2 or 3 platforming puzzles that were a bit frustrating for me. Other than that, it's a great game.

An old favourite of mine on the PS2. When I saw this on sale for 99p, it was a must buy.
Apparently the levels in this game are a bunch of remakes of the missions from the first hitman game. (Hitman: Codename 47) Having never played that game though, I can't say how much they compare. Some fans of the series might see this as a cheap way of cashing in on a "new game", therefore being disapointed with Contracts. With this being my first Hitman game back in the day though, I was drawn in.
One of the first things you'll notice is the games dark, tense atmosphere, created through an excellent use of visuals and soundtrack. The lighting and shadow effects help to create a real intensity. Adding to that is the moody soundtrack which is right up there with one of the best featured in a game. (Credit to Jesper Kyd)
The gameplay/controls also feel really solid and familiar with the previous release. (Hitman 2: Silent Assasin) So if you've played that, the learning curve is easy to pick up quickly.
Sneaking around can be tricky but feels much more satisfying than just running and gunning. It's definitely recomended to play this game through stealth. The results are more rewarding and the game plays out much better if you choose this route. However, choosing the less subtle "mass murderer" kind of playthrough has a certain satisfying edge that you won't find playing more cautiously.
What makes the player coming back for more however is its lasting appeal and replayability. The ability to perform levels in different ways (stealth, action, multiple ways to assasinate targets etc.) is what makes this so.
Overall, a must buy for all Hitman fans. Plays and feels much like Hitman 2 but improves through its unique style and presentation. There are less levels in this game compared to its predecessor however, which may disapoint some fans.
The style of the game doesn't seem to have aged with time either. Only obvious difference being the games 2004 generation graphics. (which is forgivable)

This is my favorite game that I bought during the Summer Sale. Fast paced and challenging, with perfect controls! Controls can make or break a platformer and these are just great. You move and attack so quickly, but you feel in total control of your ninja the entire time.
You need very good reflexes for this game and the ability to watch a lot of things at the same time. Enemies can react VERY quickly to your character. Good thing the game has a great built in mechanic. When you kill a lot of enemies in a row, in quick succession, you will activate your Rage ability. You become invincible during this and kill everything in 1 hit, not counting bosses.
The game also has an awesome unlock system. I don't know the exact number, but somewhere around 75 different unlockable equipment, abilities and powerups are in the game. I really like this unlock system, because the better you do in the game, the better unlocks you will get access to for your next run. Expect to die a ton when first starting out, then when you start getting access to the upgraded equipment and things, you will get a lot further and eventually complete your first run through the tower.
This game can be beaten in around 4 minutes (go watch the speedrun on Youtube, it looks amazing)! The replay value is extremely high though. Lots of different modes to play, including a boss rush and speedrun mode. The unlockables will keep you busy for a long time. Leaderboards to try and improve your best times and scores. Not to mention the game is just extremely fun to play. With a very low price (pick up the great DLC also!), theres no reason not to get this game.

Surprisingly excellent game!
I am not a big JRPG fan, but I picked this up because of all the good reviewes and I am super glad I did!
The game-play is fantastic, fast paced, and very responsive; although it takes a bit to really get adjusted to the sensory overload. The game likes to challenge you by shifting game-play mechanics often (3D, 2D, and arial combat just to name a few) and yet it never feels disjoint. Also, the fact that you HAVE to do multiple playthroughs if you want to see the full story was actually quite interesting. And no, it really wasn't repetitive at all. Definitely an innovative game.
Lenghtwise, it is not super long but it's not short either (it took me 40 hours to see all the major endings and a couple secondary ones). But I skipped a few side quests and lots more short endindgs that could have exteneded that time.
The story was pretty good, but to be hoinest not earth-shattering and I felt there were some whos and whys left unexplained. I really came to care for these characters though. The side quests were hit or miss (but mostly miss).
Technically, I had no problems. I was able to open it in full screen and the game ran beautifully smooth (I do have a mid-high end pc though so maybe that helped). However, k+m conrols are absolutely HORRIBLE - you really need to play it with a controller.
All in all, a very good game; I highly reccomend it.

Review I had before OB 64:
Paladins: Champions of the realm is one of the best one of the best online first person champion based shooter game I have ever played and it is still in it's beta phase and that is saying something.
Paladins: Champions of the Realm is a free-to-play hero shooter video game developed and published by Hi-Rez Studios.
It is a game that takes place in another form of realm which is not earth which has different champions coming from all around the universe.
There are currently 3 types of gameplay (Seige, Onslaught and Payload) to play which are really awesome to play.
The game is in beta form and is constantly updating with new champions, maps, balance changes and many other features rolling out frequently.
The game already has 32+ active champions to choose form being from 4 classes: Frontline, damage, flank & support.
Each class will get experience point by doing their specific role. But you are not tied to doing that one specific thing which is great.
The best things I have seen Paladins do is not making any champion clunky or useless, if you can play a champion right, he will be good, even a support is not stuck with just healing or a frontline stuck with staying on the objective.
It is a Free-to-play game but it has microtransactions but I can say they did microtransactions right (almost). Microtransactions here are only for skin, emotes, sprays and other things which doesn't affect in gameplays. If you are good, you don't need to pay to win.
Champions have levels which doesn't boost any of their stats, so if your good you don't need to care about another persons level. Levels indicate how much a person has played with that champion.
The only bad thing about paladins is buying champions, cards, legendary cards which you can get with coins, essence or cystals. You can farm up coins, essence and even crystals (which can be bought with real world money.) which can effect your gameplay a little bit. But it's not that bad cause if you play enough (and it's not that much) you will have the ability to buy anything in the game which is good. But for my opinion, grinding essence is very tough for now.
Paladins being new to the genre an being still in beta form has already set it's flag on the Esports standards.
It has the potential to be one of the best champion based FPS games of all times and it is in constant development and getting better and better with time. The awesome thing about paladins is that it doesn't require a beast PC or a beast internet connection to run it. I don't have a graphics card on my PC or a broadband connection and play with a mobile connection and it runs decently. So a decent broadband connection and a decent PC and you are good to go. Champion skills are easy to understand but hard to master like any other game but it does it in a very good way.
As many players will say the game is a rip off of many other games, I will beg to deffer. This game was inspired by team fortress 2 concept but that's about it. It's like saying mario , limbo, sonic are ripoff game of each other because they are all side scrolling games. Paladins have unique champions with unique skillsets which unique gameplay mechanics.
The game let's you choose a character and let's you stick to that one character so team building is very essential because you cannot see the enemy teams picks (in casual) but it gets better when in game you can pick loadouts and items based on what you need to win the game.
Because the game is in beta and is constantly changind the game has many bugs but the developers react faster to fix this bugs which is another great thing about this game.

I recommend this game, but only for those who like to watch Game of Thrones. The reason is that this game makes you watch a lot: Cutscenes are numerous and long and make GoT feel like an animated interactive spin-off feature film. Also, in this combat system (that reminded me of Dragon Age: Origins), the player is mostly a passive observer of the auto-attacks, throwing in special moves and potions occasionally. For my play sessions, I took a bar of chocolate in order to keep busy when the "movie" continued between the interactive parts.
The world consists of a number of locations only connected by a fast travel map. They are not all corridors with only one way to move forward, especially King's Landing is relatively elaborate; coming from Skyrim and Fallout though, I felt it to be very limited. That said, the graphics and sound background of the winter scenery at the Wall and the different quarters of the capital are nice and atmospheric.
The character and the NPCs look good as well. The only problem here  is the use of a limited number of NPC models that are randomly distributed in the populated areas, and it is quite common that the same model appears several time at the same spot - it breaks the immersion a little if you visit a market and see the exact same person twice talking with himself on a regular basis.
The quality of the voice acting varies between mediocre and very good; fortunately the main characters are cast appropriately. The loot and equipment system, the classes and skill progression are not great, but functional. An innovative gameplay aspect is Mors' Warg ability to control his dog who can then follow traces, very similar to Geralt's hightened sense of smell in the Witcher 3. The best thing about this game are the plot twists, when you discover that characters (including one of the two protagonists) are not who he seemed at first.
My general verdict is that this is a decent game implemented in an interesting movie in the Game of Thrones universe and will mostly please fans of the series.

It's an endless cycle. Be careful

After playing through a few metroidvanias and other games with endless upgrades, Anodyne's simple gameplay was a breath of fresh air. You
find a handful of improvements for your weapon, but they're entirely optional. What's important is learning how to read enemies' attack patterns. Monsters in general are used sparingly, often as part of the carefully-crafted puzzles. They're part of the environment, rather than mere obstaclees; there's never a sense the developer is throwing enemies at you to arbitratily raise the difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty, the puzzles are exactly as hard as they should be. I only had to go looking for hints online twice in the entire game, yet I never felt like I wasn't being challenged. I can't compliment the level design enough.
While the gameplay is remniscent of classic Zelda, the writing and atmosphere reminded me of the bizarre dream exploration in Yume Nikki. Anodyne is an unusual story about relationships, and how far we're willing to go to hold on to people even when we know we can't always make them happy. At least, that's what I got out of it. It's cryptic at the best of times, but thankfully it's not just garbled nonsense. There are recurring themes and motifs that tie everything together, and what we see of the characters and their relationships is enough to stay invested over the course of the plot. Your mileage may vary, of course. Personally, I felt quite fulfilled by the ending.
TL;DR: Anyone who's willing to play along with the surrealism, or who's just in it for the puzzles, should pick up a copy of this game ASAP.

An old favourite of mine on the PS2. When I saw this on sale for 99p, it was a must buy.
Apparently the levels in this game are a bunch of remakes of the missions from the first hitman game. (Hitman: Codename 47) Having never played that game though, I can't say how much they compare. Some fans of the series might see this as a cheap way of cashing in on a "new game", therefore being disapointed with Contracts. With this being my first Hitman game back in the day though, I was drawn in.
One of the first things you'll notice is the games dark, tense atmosphere, created through an excellent use of visuals and soundtrack. The lighting and shadow effects help to create a real intensity. Adding to that is the moody soundtrack which is right up there with one of the best featured in a game. (Credit to Jesper Kyd)
The gameplay/controls also feel really solid and familiar with the previous release. (Hitman 2: Silent Assasin) So if you've played that, the learning curve is easy to pick up quickly.
Sneaking around can be tricky but feels much more satisfying than just running and gunning. It's definitely recomended to play this game through stealth. The results are more rewarding and the game plays out much better if you choose this route. However, choosing the less subtle "mass murderer" kind of playthrough has a certain satisfying edge that you won't find playing more cautiously.
What makes the player coming back for more however is its lasting appeal and replayability. The ability to perform levels in different ways (stealth, action, multiple ways to assasinate targets etc.) is what makes this so.
Overall, a must buy for all Hitman fans. Plays and feels much like Hitman 2 but improves through its unique style and presentation. There are less levels in this game compared to its predecessor however, which may disapoint some fans.
The style of the game doesn't seem to have aged with time either. Only obvious difference being the games 2004 generation graphics. (which is forgivable)

Fantastic solid FPS game, great for anybody that likes an authentic/hardcore experience.
Newcomers may suffer with the learning curve and map tactics, but you don't need to be exceptionally skilled at FPS games to enjoy this.
You have to think about where your running and what you do, because bullets are deadly, not like arcade FPS.

Rising Storm has always been a realistic shooter series. Vietnam is no different. If you have played the Arma series you will probably enjoy the dedication to war simulation, if however you are expecting a game like Call of Duty or Battlefield, prepare for a rude awakening to true simulated warfare.
Be a sneaky VC and place a trap on a forest track to surprise the G.I.
Burn out a village hut with a flame thrower as a Marine engineer.
Hide in bushes and bayonet the enemy as one wonders past.
Ride into the LZ on a Huey and pocket the rice fields with your M60.
As commander, Call in Artillery and send pink mist across the enemies lines.
Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is accurate, brutal, 64 Player Warfare.
A tip for any new player, take it slow. Don't be a leeroy. Listen to your commander / Squad Leader and most of all, play the objective! If you come into Rising storm with the correct expectations you will have an amazing time, if you come into it with the wrong interpretation you will end up aggravated.
The community is very active and loyal to the series. They can be very helpful but also rough on new players, especially if you refuse to follow those simply tips I mentioned. Be a team player and the team will be there for you.

I played “The Binding of Isaac” years ago on Xbox 360, and apparently I got it again for cheap in a Humble Bundle.
I can understand the joy of mastering a game, but the core gameplay of “The Binding of Isaac” just doesn’t draw me in.
Sometimes I’ll die on the first or second boss, other times I’ll defeat them. That major difference is almost entirely decided by “Did the right random item spawn beforehand?”
Boss fights are made easier if you go into their room with full health, but the close-quarters nature of the game means that you’re constantly getting hurt.
If I were a lot better at the game I would get used to these issues, but I don’t have very much fun playing it, so my skills will stay at an amateur level.
Plenty of difficult, good games have slaughtered me yet hooked me to play more and improve (Spelunky as another Roguelike, and Dark Souls), but The Binding of Isaac failed to do that.
The Binding of Isaac has a lot of strange items and secrets, but those aren’t worth the struggle and boredom IMO.

Do you like ARPGs, robots, great music, post-apocalyptic settings, existential dilemmas, and feeling sad? If so, then this game might be right up your alley. There's probably other reviews that detail the action and the story, so I won't touch on that. Instead, I will try and spread more awareness of the fact that this game requires replaying the main scenario to get the entire story.
For simplicity's sake, I will refer to the first half of the game as Act 1, and the second half of the game as Act 2.
An Act 1 playthrough with Character 1 will reveal much of the main plot of the first half of the game. To progress to Act 2, you will need to play through Act 1 again with Character 2. But do not despair, for seeing the main scenario through his eyes fills in gaps in the story and fleshes out many different characters' motivations, and includes additional interactions with other characters that don't occur on the first playthrough.
It is only when you've completed Act 1 with both characters can you progress on to Act 2, which is where most of the heavy stuff and happenings occur.
While Rebirth was better, I recommend you get this first.

Long story short, this game is an excellent game, and it's worth every penny.
Details:
STUFF I LIKE:
- Gameplay in general. I like the idea of flying these airships, I like the matching system, using the weapons is good, flying the ship has great controls, engineering is pretty intuitive, it just all works really well
- The teamwork specifically needs special mention. It's really great. It forces you to work with not only your crew, but your entire team. They made giving commands and orders really intuitive. Working together with your team and crew is awesome, and it makes you feel like an essential part of a team, which is something not a lot of games have.
- The aesthetics are great. I just like the way it looks. I'm not a huge steampunk fan, but this game really does it well.
- Character customization. This seems small, but being able to customize my character is a big deal to me, so I had to mention it. It's really good.
STUFF I DON'T LIKE:
- This is an issue that I guess can't really be avoided, but some of the players are hostile, and it makes them hard to work with. I know it shouldn't be a big deal, but it's really frustrating when someone won't cooperate on a game that relies heavily on cooperation.
- Leveling up. This is a personal issue, but it seems like you level up WAY too slowly. It just seems like it takes an awfully long time to make any real progress. Although, that may be a by product of my next point
- It takes a long time to play the game. A match usually won't start until it's mostly full, which is frustrating because filling a match can take a really long time when people are as impatient as they are. I don't know how the developers might fix this, but on the other hand, that's not really my job.
- It can be a little confusing. I know this isn't a big deal, but it took me a really long time to figure out how to use all the engineering tools and how all the different types of ammo worked. I feel like these could have been explained by the game a little better, but maybe that's just me.
Overall, in spite of its flaws, I think this game is worth it. It can be a little tough to get started, but once you get going, it really is a blast. If you've got some time to set aside for it, it's really a great game.

RXE is a really cool concept for people interested in building robots and programming (visual programming) them to do various tasks. This game is early access, and as such, my review may change over time. However, as it stands, I would not recommend this game, unless you plan to get in for the current low price and sit on it until they add more.
Currently, the game advertises “dozens of tools and parts.” While this is a true statement, it is a bit misleading. As of this writing, the game offers the following build components: 3 structural items, a computer, distance sensor, compass, servo motor, and a wheel for a total of 8 build items. And for programming it has 2 input nodes, 3 output nodes, 9 math operation nodes, and 4 miscellaneous nodes for a total of 18 programming nodes. Overall, this amounts to 27 “tools and parts,” which is indeed dozens, however this isn’t a very extensive list of “tools and parts” for building robots. So there are a very limited number of things you could do with this. To their credit, they are working on adding more content to the game and I am very excited to see this. There are several small bugs and errors you can see in the discussion forums as well, but these aren’t game breaking. So my only issue with this game is really the limited amount of content.
There are a few, in my opinion, crucial elements missing from this game. There is no programming node for if/then statements or other loops, there are no math functions for inequalities, and there is no way to use Boolean logic. This severely limits your ability to program the robots. I think these things are essential, and if added, I would gladly change my recommendation.
Finally, the tutorial and item (build and programming items) need detailed descriptions. As it is, the input and output values required by some sensors and items are extremely unclear. For example, without reading the discussion board, you would not know that a value of 5000 is the same as a value of 100 for the wheels, as the wheels have a range between 0-100. These items need to have detailed descriptions, and to their credit, they are working on (or maybe have put out by now) a fix for the descriptions, as the developer was notified about this in the discussion.
As it stands, this game is not worth the price tag. However, it may be worth getting now, as they plan to add more and raise the price as they do.
UPDATE: The developer got back to me very quickly regarding the issues I raised in the discussion board. They seem to be on top of things (already implemented some of the smaller fixes) and promised to add more items once the bugs are fixed! Overall, it is looking really good for this game. I still can't change my recommendation at the moment, but as soon as those items are in I would definitely recommend this game!!
