While i personally enjoyed a whole deal of this game during the beta stage of it, i cannot recommend this game right now.
Tripwire made a good attempt at the nowaday less appearing Vietnam War but they simply didn't hold up a candle to what they proposed at first.
Unlike the former installments, this game lacks alot of features, which one might be completly allright with should they not be as picky (Like me) but it simply can't be recommended out of one large reason of mine.
IT. DOSN'T. WORK.
As soon as they released Rising Storm II from the Beta stage, it was swarmed with the infamous Tripwire problem - connectivity. At first i thought it would be resolved within a small time, but it has not.
Allow me to explain - I've played Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm 1 and had the known issues of the game simply not letting you join a server, claiming you just can't out of a connectivity error or that it is full (despite having ten spots left) and the issue of you joining (at last) and spending roughly thirty seconds of the game only to notice the world dying infront of you. You can't do any actions (jumping over a fence, reloading etc), everyone is running into walls with invincible threadmills and you either stay there for the rest of the game until you disconnect or you chose to leave by your own.
This was for many years just something i had to fix by repairing Punkbuster each time prior to a game session with it. Pretty easy habbit if you fed up with it. As of now it's half-working without it last time i played a few months back.
However, all this persists in Rising Storm 2 and it has been since the mentioned launch update. They've thrown updates and patches and even themselves (after some time) thrown suggestions on how to work it but alas, i have not gotten it to work properly.
Some solutions i tried -
Re-installed the game, verified the game, removed beta documents, repaired it by removing and re-adding documents needed for connections.
And  lastly did  the punkbuster solution and (however with this new anti-cheat program) simply repaired and or installed it anew. But it did not help..it did not help.
I even tried to get a refund, dissapointed that i couldn't play the game i hyped so long for. But no, my playtime in the BETA counted as the actual playtime despite me only having actual post-launch gametime in the main menu or roughly five minutes in the actual game. Sucks dosn't it?
And to add more salt, Killing Floor 1 and 2 have these very same problems.
Tripwire may do good games in the long run, but they often are unplayable thanks to these issues and they fail to understand these past problems. I'd personally vouch for an indie-game company with no former game-developing experiences to make a better job at just that issue.
TL:DR - Fun if not content lacking game set in a demanded time-era that is unfortunatly haunted by it's parents past ghosts of game-breaking connection problems.
Please Tripwire, get a grip and be the game developers we want you to be, not the half-arsed ones!

Really enjoying my time in the various landscapes of ANODYNE: some pastoral and charming; others, creepy and surreal. Collecting cards makes the game feel like a scavenger hunt across the varied worlds. This is giving me a much more exciting reason to explore the beautiful maps in depth (especially since the plot so far is very very very very light).
Some dialogue and texts make me wonder if there is some sort of meta story going on, but if there is, I haven't quite discovered it.
I'd say this plays like YUMI NIKKI, but it's not as "out there" and there are also jumping puzzles and light combat that I'm finding enjoyable; nothing strenuous. You can't zone out, but this isn't Super Meat Boy, either! I enjoy the way the character moves through the screen, important for these 2D games!
But! I have a warning for parents or the sensitive: on the first day, I spent about 2 hours on the game and encountered no cursing. On my second day of playing, I was surprised to discover some R-rated language in the dialogue of some NPCs. Since the game so far had appeared extremely family-friendly (I mean, you're not even given a sword to fight with!), I was really thrown by that. It felt very out of place to me.
But so far that's my main complaint. Overall, this game scratches the right itch for me. Need to escape for a while but still be engaged and challenged? ANODYNE's a great place to visit!
* * *
Update: While I still recommend this game, the 2nd half turned tedious and frustrating for me. After I fought the boss, I tried the new ability out, and just got frustrated some more. Some would say that means I missed most of the game. Being a bit of a completionist, that bugs me, but not as much as playing more of the game would have. So...first half: great! Second half:...hmm. The "normal" playthrough of this game is a fairly typical puzzle-adventure with some cool mechanics. Although I found that part of the game fun and interesting as well, after the final boss is when it gets really good. In fact, if you want to do 100%, most of the game takes place after the final boss and it's like a completely different game from the "normal" playthrough. If you like games with minimal direction and a lot of exploration + discovering things for yourself, you'll love the endgame. It's like the ultimate collectathon.
In terms of story, there wasn't much. This is one of those games where the story is only hinted at and it's more about the setting and atmosphere. But it works. It's creepy, surreal, and quirky. I really liked the music and sound effects; they're slightly unsettling and really add to the atmosphere.

The game doesn't really begin until it ends. Until the ending, it seems like a bland Zelda-clone. After the ending, though, Anodyne drastically changes. I won't spoil it for you, but I'll say that even though I beat this game three years ago, I still can't forget it.

Long story short, this game is an excellent game, and it's worth every penny.
Details:
STUFF I LIKE:
- Gameplay in general. I like the idea of flying these airships, I like the matching system, using the weapons is good, flying the ship has great controls, engineering is pretty intuitive, it just all works really well
- The teamwork specifically needs special mention. It's really great. It forces you to work with not only your crew, but your entire team. They made giving commands and orders really intuitive. Working together with your team and crew is awesome, and it makes you feel like an essential part of a team, which is something not a lot of games have.
- The aesthetics are great. I just like the way it looks. I'm not a huge steampunk fan, but this game really does it well.
- Character customization. This seems small, but being able to customize my character is a big deal to me, so I had to mention it. It's really good.
STUFF I DON'T LIKE:
- This is an issue that I guess can't really be avoided, but some of the players are hostile, and it makes them hard to work with. I know it shouldn't be a big deal, but it's really frustrating when someone won't cooperate on a game that relies heavily on cooperation.
- Leveling up. This is a personal issue, but it seems like you level up WAY too slowly. It just seems like it takes an awfully long time to make any real progress. Although, that may be a by product of my next point
- It takes a long time to play the game. A match usually won't start until it's mostly full, which is frustrating because filling a match can take a really long time when people are as impatient as they are. I don't know how the developers might fix this, but on the other hand, that's not really my job.
- It can be a little confusing. I know this isn't a big deal, but it took me a really long time to figure out how to use all the engineering tools and how all the different types of ammo worked. I feel like these could have been explained by the game a little better, but maybe that's just me.
Overall, in spite of its flaws, I think this game is worth it. It can be a little tough to get started, but once you get going, it really is a blast. If you've got some time to set aside for it, it's really a great game.

Good idea, poor execution.
There is no actual fullscreen. You can only scale it up 2 or 3 times and then there is a giant black border around the entire game.
There is no automatic sound/monitor syncing, you have to exit out to the main menu, go into settings, and manually enter a number between -100 and 100, then go back into a level and try again.
The game uses prerecorded audio tracks rather than playing the notes live as they are pressed. Better for low-end computers, but it causes the gameplay to suffer. If you miss a note, the music continues to play, you just hear an annoying sound that the note was missed. It should not play the music if you miss the note.
, the music and the notes occasionally desync, because the notes were just placed there by someone who thinks that is where the music plays at, not EXACTLY where the music plays at.
There does not seem to be any progression, not even a tutorial. You can pick any song and the difficulty does not go up as you play the next song available. The next song is sometimes MUCH easier than the previous.
There probably should be 4 difficulty levels, not 3.
Difficulty level 1 would be 3 notes playable and few notes of the song show up.
Difficulty level 2 would be 4 notes playable.
Difficulty level 3 would be 5 notes playable.
Difficulty level 4 would be 5 notes playable and all the notes of the song show up.
That would be better for personal progression of getting better at the game. Those who have never played a music rythm game like this will most likely be overwhelmed by 4 notes at the current easiest difficulty.

This is a "puzzle platformer." While it also includes elements of a metroidvania (you collect 1 power-up to enable access to more of the zones, as well as a few health/ship powerups), I would prefer to compare the game to VVVVVV, Cave Story, and Portal 2.
The sounds and graphics are throwbacks to Nintendo/Super Nintendo era, which is more than adequate for a 2d "pixel-perfect" platformer. As you play you are slowly taught the many tricks to beating this game. However, excepting the gun upgrade, you can perform all of those tricks from the very beginning (and have to for some of the hidden treasures). There is a story, but it is intentionally ignorable. This game is about puzzle-platforming.
Play control is super-tight. Any errors made are completely your fault.
The biggest drawback to the game is its length. It is extremely short (a speedrun of the game should take you between 12-20 minutes). This isn't necessarily a negative--there are only so many ways to do the same kind of puzzle before it becomes tedious, and the game avoids that by not padding the game out.

Better than Silent Assassin, not as good as Blood Money.
Contracts is essentially a bunch of remakes of Codename 47 missions, but with a few new additions thrown in for good measure. There are few obvious paths, but most of the time there's nothing stopping you from taking the quick and easy way; run through the level, find the target, restart and plan your course of action then.
You have several tools at your disposal. Gone are the anaesthetic from Silent Assassin. Instead, you have an easy sedative with a needle; it's a one-use item, but it's effective at knocking out a civilian or guard who hasn't seen you.
There's no way to select a "load-out" or anything, unlike in Blood Money and Silent Assassin. You get very few "sophisticated" tools as well, and you're left to mostly come up with your own creative lures. You can, however, shoot out lights for distractions and cover.
But essentially? If you're played Silent Assassin, this is more of the same, but better. Same with Blood Money. It's really just a must-have for Hitman fans.

Anodyne is a good work of art. There's a great blend of tastes permeating this game's mechanics, and a lot of decisions the creative duo behind it made have given it a great soul. The puzzle solving is rewarding, the challenges aren't disrespectful of your time (excepting one particular platforming sequence in a later dungeon), and the combat doesn't reach outside of its bounds to achieve difficulty. All in all this game is a fantastic accomplishment, and a lot of fun.

Anodyne is like a bizarre, surrealist old-school Legend of Zelda game.
If you're looking for a game that expertly combines good old fashioned SNES style 2D top-down adventuring, collectibles, a little humor and more than a little spookiness, Anodyne certainly provides. Just don't expect to figure out what the hell is going on anytime soon.

I liked this game. It's a good Zelda-lite game. It's a tad harder than most 2D Zelda games, but it's also more forgiving with saves and checkpoints. The later platforming challenges were hard to execute from a precision standpoint, but overall I really enjoyed my time with it. The puzzles are about what you would expect from a Zelda game, even though they use drastically different mechanics. The game does a good job of teaching you as you go how the puzzles work so that when you come back to old areas you see answers to puzzles you didn't know were there. The soundtrack is really relaxing, even during Boss fights. Overall just a fun time with a fun game.
Great soundtrack and atmosphere. Gameplay leans more toward the puzzles and exploring than combat. I'm not a huge Zelda-type fan, but I really enjoyed this game.

I've never written a disclaimer like that before - intriguing right? The graphical content in this game mostly pertains to the methods in which the main characters perform their acts of life-ending showmanship. Even though the character models are all voxel-based (similar to Minecraft), there can be some really gruesome scenes throughout this horror fest. In fact, some of these death animations are so creatively macabre, the developers must have employed someone whose entire job was to think up of ways to commit murder in an artistic manner. Bees, nails, spikes, water, etc. You name it, Skullface and company can make it happen. Furthermore, these artists of death have found their way into Slayaway Camp, populated with an absurd amount of innocent teenagers. Channel your inner demon and help guide these fiends through multitudes of brain-tickling puzzles.
Now you might be thinking how a puzzle game might work with horror elements. I mean, helping Jason fill out a Sudoku puzzle isn't quite anything to write home about, and HOGs with a haunted house setting are a dime a dozen, so when Slayaway Camp decides to reform Sokoban style sliding puzzles into a means of expressing a "darkly comic homage to 80s trash horror", I am truly, and wholly interested. Blue Wizard Digital did not back down in finding a way to merge these two completely different genres, and their unique love-child is nothing but demented humor.
Even though Slayaway Camp is inspired from Sokoban, I find it more similar to the Pokémon Ice Gym/Team Rocket floor puzzles. Starting at a stationary origin, moving in any cardinal direction will initiate a slide, stopping only when the main character reaches a wall, an obstacle, or better yet, a soon-to-be-victim. Your goal in every level is to reach and murder all teenaged targets and escape through an exit. Various puzzle mechanics will be added into the lineup of stuff-to-avoid as you progress, making these sliding puzzles increasingly difficult down the line. Staying away from a SWAT member’s line of sight is manageable, but surround him with electric fences and I’ll have to think a bit. Drop in some cats, turn countdowns, or teleporters and I’ll be in deep trouble. Fortunately, an undo button provides the ability to go wild exploring path options, but the true life-savior lies within the hint and full-walkthrough system if things go south for too long. Knowing that the system is in place, the developers have crafted some hair-pulling, blood-pressure-raising, maniacally difficult puzzles. Towards the final levels of the last 2 films, the enormous amounts of feints, backtracking, and chaotic movement had me reaching for that help button more times than I’d like to admit.
Each level plays like a scene in a movie, filled with gut-wrenching murder cut-scenes and popular scary movie tropes. Beginning with a deep and cringy horror movie narration that would make the late Don LaFontaine proud, every videotape is set in a different stage. From the traditional camp grounds and hospitals, to the more unique work offices and scenic parks of New York City, Slayaway Camp really wants to be an equal opportunity murder campaign demonstrating that death is all around us, and fun to watch at that. With 10 movies and a bunch of deleted scenes, Slayaway Camp will most likely manage to satisfy your dormant cardinal need for bloodlust throughout its 200+ feature film puzzles. Even though slogging through so many puzzles can be a big stretch to perform in one sitting (which is why most puzzle games have a fantastic save & continue feature), Slayaway Camp varies its puzzles and environments enough that I was able to go through multiple videotapes at once without feeling bored or sick of the gameplay.
The developers' passion for slashing, killing, and reimagining cult horror films can be seen in the beautifully constructed, and well executed art design. I've never seen as much gore in a horror film as I have in Slayaway Camp, but the hyperbolic forms of murder can only be described as comically grim. From individual "murder-scenes," such as Skullface sliding a knife through a victim's eye, to unlockable death animations (victims roasting in fire) and iconic killer characters, Slayaway Camp just oozes with horror film recreation to a fanatical degree. In addition, small visual details, smooth gameplay, personalization options, customized intros and skippable transitions all lend a hand in heightening its polish and player engagement.
I’ve noticed that nearly all of Slayaway Camp’s levels are pretty small in nature. Even when it gets extremely complex, the designers have chosen to favor a claustrophobic environment over the alternatives. I definitely would have loved to see a large hanger like area split into various rooms with interconnecting mechanics, or perhaps a building with multiple floors. It’s a shame that the game’s scope was not as encompassing as it could have been. To be fair, Blue Wizard Digitial could have just went with a horror skinned puzzle game and left it at that. I am really glad they didn't, because their vision and love for slasher films set this game apart not only from other puzzle game competitors, but also horror game contemporaries too. The devs even managed to grab Mark Meer (Cdr. Shepard - Mass Effect) and Derek Mears (Jason - Friday the 13th) to take part in the fun.
I clocked in at around 7 hours to complete all 10 videotapes (Space Camp was freaking hard), which unlocked NC-17 and Deleted Scenes (levels) afterwards, including the fan-favorite censored shower scenes. Having only covered two-thirds of the available levels at this point, there is still so much left to see. If you are looking for a
dark-hearted experience to play this Halloween, or really any time of the year, make sure to pick up Slayaway Camp. If you need a little more convincing, the free edition of Slayaway Camp can be played on its official game page
. Note that the Steam version has
quality of life and progression differences, including coin drops and unlockables progress; however, the puzzles seem to be the same at a quick glance.

Slayaway Camp is a game that I didn't think I would ever see, a puzzle game mixed with the slasher horror genre.
For the most part I found Slayaway Camp to be a good game. I would classify it as a "sliding" puzzle game. In the game you move your character in a direction and they continue moving in that direction until they run into something. The basic gameplay in Slayaway Camp is figuring out how to more your character around the level killing all of the teens and making your way to the exit.
If you enjoy these type of puzzle games I think you will really enjoy Slayaway Camp. The puzzle design for the game is quite good. The game doesn't deviate too much from other games in the genre but it does a really good job at what it is. If you don't really care for these type of puzzle games though it probably won't be for you.
The theme/story of the game is spoofing 1980s horror slasher films. The game features different VHS tapes which are different movies in the Slayaway Camp series. Each VHS tape is a different set of levels. Slayaway Camp uses the different movies to make fun of this genre of horror movies. People who enjoy this genre of movies will probably really appreciate the game's story/theme.
Difficulty wise I would say that the game is moderately challenging. Quite a few of the levels you can figure out pretty quickly but you will run into the occasional puzzle that will take you some time to figure out. So far I have finished around half of the levels and have been playing around four hours. I would guess that the game will take seven to ten hours to complete.
I enjoyed my time with Slayaway Camp and if you like "sliding" puzzle games I think you will really enjoy Slayaway Camp as well. If you don't really care for these type of puzzle games though I don't think Slayaway Camp is going to be the game for you.

What is Guns of Icarus? Guns of Icarus is a game in which 4 players pick between three classes. A pilot, gunner, or engineer. The game revolves around a steampunk environment with flying ships. The ships all have parts that support the ship such as the Armor or the Balloon or each individual gun. There is a diverse cast of ships and guns that you can build a ship overall with. These ships create unique strategies and such overall and any of them can work if you have a good enough crew. Imagine each person on the ship being a piece of a engine, you put all four together and you have a fully working engine. Communication and teamwork is vital to this game, causing a overall better gameplay experience. If you love teamwork and friends THIS GAME IS A DEFINITE BUY.
Guns of Icarus is one of the best games i've played and will always be in my heart to be honest. Learning this game was simple and easy overall and learning new mechanics, experimenting with ship builds and such, and playing the game overall was just a amazing experience. The game looks very scenic and pretty. The map design overall is good. The upcoming Alliance DLC is going to be good and I can count on it to revive the game community. The community that is current is 600+ daily and it's no problem finding games. The community isn't toxic and is always ready to teach others.
Each ship is a wonderfully different strategy and each gun is important to the ship. Each class are all equally fun. The Gunner driving through with any weapon on the Captain's ship, ready to kill. The Pilot, piloting the ship choosing to keep his distance or ram into enemy ships causing havoc. Every ship is unique and will work if you have a adequate crew.
The Alliance DLC is adding so much more content and once they release that I know this game's community will go over the thousands and maybe go into the 10 thousands. It's going to add new guns, new ships, a CO-OP (4 player) campaign, factions, a faction gamemode, and a CO-OP PVE gamemode.

As a retro gaming fan, chiptune fan (including gameless originals by e.g. Disasterpeace, Anamanaguchi), and rhythm gaming fan (including GH/Rock Band), I feel like I'm squarely the target audience for this game.

For $10 I would've hoped they got licenses for at least one or two famous, memorable tunes, even if from indie games like Fez or VVVVVV, but nope, not as far as I can tell. (Although to be fair I stopped scrolling through after my fourth song because the game just felt boring already.)
If you're looking for rhythm on your PC, try Osu, which is free, unique, and fun. If you're looking for a Guitar Hero clone on PC you can try Frets on Fire which is also free, though I can't vouch for it personally. Just... whatever you do, you probably want to skip this game and keep your $10. Even on sale it's tough to recommend since the songs are boring and the controls feel unresponsive.

Note: The developer updated the game to address the two biggest complaints I had with this game. I have updated this review to reflect this.
I'll start off with the negative. Often when I read reviews about a game, I want to know what's wrong with it first and foremost, so that's what i'll provide.
This game has a few technical problems. There is only one lag compensation setting, forcing you to synch the game to line up visually or line up audibly, just like the original Guitar Hero game on the PS2. Guitar Hero 2, a game released in 2006, had a separate compensation value for the video and audio to account for each device having separate latencies. It's frustrating that a rhythm game released this year has overlooked a problem that its influences have already solved. Additionally, on Windows 10, closing the game crashes it. Some process related to the game remains open, causing steam to track additional playtime for it. If you're on the fence about keeping this game and are a part of the 30%+ people on Steam that use Windows 10, be aware that this bug may cause you to run over the 2 hour window for returns.
The interface isn't perfect. Many rhythm games will give you a preview of the song you've selected when you highlight it in the track list, but this game keeps playing the menu music for you. It can make it a little harder to find the songs you like.
On to what's good!
The developers read my review and took into consideration my feedback, as well as the feedback of others. A patch came out addressing some major issues within 36 hours of this review, which buys them a lot of respect in my book. It's a sign that they care and weren't just looking to dump a game on Steam and never touch it again, as some other Indie devs often do. To be perfectly honest, I am waiting for another patch or two before I personally re-invest in this title. But the soundtrack is quite nice (i've listened to it outside of the game), and reports from other users suggest that the changes to note timing have made the game much more fun to play. I think this warrants a purchase and would recommend this title if you like rhythm games and chiptunes.
I fully anticipate that i'll have to continue to update this review to reflect changes made by the developer. When I re-invest in the title myself, i'll be able to talk more objectively about what I enjoy in the game.

Hitman Contracts is the 3rd installment to the Hitman series, which features Agent 47 primarily reliving his past in flashbacks. Six of the twelve missions in Contracts are remastered versions of missions in Codename 47. Do not be discouraged by this fact, though. Hitman: Contracts will provide you with a unique, rich and thrilling experience. It is my personal favorite of the whole franchise.
The game takes place between two missions in Hitman: Blood Money (The sequel to Contracts). It's a bit tricky to understand and timelines have always been a bit obscure in the Hitman franchise. After getting shot by a corrupt chief of police, 47 escapes to a nearby motel where he goes into shock and experiences several flashbacks. You will wake up, eventually, to a
Hitman: Contracts is without a doubt the darkest and most atmospheric Hitman game to date. In terms of atmosphere and tension, Contracts hands down outshines Hitman: Absolution. The dark, rainy nights, during which many missions take place are intensified by the masterful soundtrack by Jesper Kyd (Assassin's Creed, Splinter Cell, Borderlands 2), which is the best soundtrack he's made in my opinion. Missions are not that easy without sneak-peeking at walkthroughs, and the mission "The Meat King's Party" is awesome, dark and to some audiences a bit disturbing as well.
Contracts is a great game. The missions are expansive and interesting. Unlike Blood Money, where a bald guy in a suit only really raised suspicion when entering someone's bedroom with a gun in hand, Contracts always keeps you on your toes. Looking at your tension meter basically makes the game a thriller, especially when being frisk searched. The tension in Contracts, at least in my opinion, is spot on. The tension in Hitman: Silent Assassin was far too unpredictable and in Blood Money it was more predictable than Sheridan phoning Hyacinth Bucket. Disguises are plentiful and there is a wide range of them to help you get to your targets.
Hitman: Contracts is thrilling and atmospheric with great replay value, an amazing soundtrack and interesting characters. My favorite moments from the game include..
1. Poisoning an English aristocrat by disguising myself as his butler
2. Exploring a hotel in Budapest disguised as a bell boy
3. Attempting to combat a triad leader and his bodyguard head on
All in all, considering the low price and the amount of awesome content you are getting, I really recommend giving it a try. The graphics are a bit outdated, but it's a 2004 game, after all. Also, a common mistake when playing a Hitman game (especially the first 3) is to look at walkthroughs on YouTube and whatnot. It's very rewarding to aim for the Silent Assassin (perfect) rating on a mission before checking out walkthroughs during your first time. Have fun with Hitman: Contracts!

Anodyne is an excersize is surrealism with a fairly well executed Zelda-style design. There is a story to be had here, one that you'll have to both look for and make assumptions to grasp. There are rooms filled with muttering duplicates without reason, and there is a circus deep inside a cave. Your weapon of choice? A broom.
It's engaging and exciting to see what oddities come your way throughout the game, and the aesthetics are sublime. Sound design is great, and while I'm not a huge fan of the vertical slice the game is framed in (nor some of the initial keybindings, but you can change that in the options), it creates a unique little space for one to explore and plenty of interesting perspective tricks that might not've been as effective were it presented differently.
The gameplay can be a bit stodgy, but the dungeon design never fails to stay interesting, and the odd urban aesthetics in the later stages craft a near eldritch experience in their odd familiarity, filled with abstract shadows that chase you and bizarre conversations. It borders on dadaism, honestly. The earlier dungeons fit more standard tropes, albeit with increasingly fascinating design. The puzzles are generally simple, and never made me pause for more than a few moments until the very last few on the main path. The collectables and their puzzles tend to be far more interesting, and the farther off the beaten path you go, the more complex they become. All for what amounts to cute car!
It's not life changing, but Anodyne captures a niche space phenomenally well. Give this little guy a shot if you haven't already. It's worth it just for the creative decisions alone.

I bought this game based on the stellar reviews of the art, music, and story--the three things I go for in a game. This game falls short in 2/3 categories.
Art: 6/10. The vistas in the cliffs were lovely, but many of the outdoor maps left something to be desired. You can design a pixellated tree and call it a tree, or you can design a pixellated tree and it will be freaking-beautiful-how-can-one-squeeze-that-much-detail-into-a-pixellated-tree sort of pixellated tree. So while I wasn't blown away, or even mildly wowed by the art, I love bit-style games, period. But they're difficult to bring to life unless paired with a solid, captivating story.
Story: 2/10. Anodyne drops you into the game without any back story, any context of the worlds you visit or creatures you speak to, any idea of what to do, any inkling of a purpose, not matter how you might search. "That's alright," I thought, "I like open world exploratory games. This'll be fun." The difference between an exploration game and Anodyne is that if you decide not to participate in the main quest line, it's assumed there are other quests around to pique your interest. Anodyne is not only devoid of a main quest line; it is devoid of any quests at all. The closest thing I found to a quest was a talking bear that asked me if I had any berries. The game is generally light on text, and those creatures that do speak to you have no information, useless or otherwise. (Edit: Okay, I lied. There is a main quest line in which a creepy mage person (can't tell if it's male or female) tells you that you must do something to save something, a quest which your characte blindly and wordlessly accepts. It happens so quickly and so casually that I can't even remember the specifics of it all.)
Music: 8/10. The music has been the saving grace of Anodyne. They did a fantastic job creating atmosphere and differentiating one map from another. Only one song was catchy enough to get stuck in my head, but I found all the music to be very enjoyable. (Applause!)
I've seen reviews that the controls were a bit clonky. I found them to be decent at best, tolerable at worst. My only complaint is that it's extremely tough to judge where a jump will land when one jumps north or south. The amount of times I died attempting to get a feel for it over some chasms in a cave is embarassing.
Overall, this game had a lot of potential for me but ended up being a disappointment. The lack of direction left me wandering in circles across several maps trying to figure out how to progress in the game, resulting in loss of interest. Kudos to the developers for creating a cool game, but their abstract method of storytelling (giving them the benefit of the doubt here) isn't going to be for everybody.

In 2011 Red Orchestra 2 presented two equally equipped sides, Germans and Russians relied on bolt action rifles. In 2013 Rising Storm picked up the Pacific theater of war and thus went into the direction of asymmetric warfare, reflecting on the different arsenal of the opposing sides: Yanks used modern semi-automatic weapons, Japs used antiquated bolt action rifles. In 2017 Rising Storm 2 Vietnam rotates into the world of automatic weapons on both sides and still introduces the highest level of asymmetry of the series to date.
Players are organized into roles and units. Roles are represented by classes, most of them are restricted to only a few slots, except for the Viet Rifleman and the US Grunt which can always be taken, and compared to the situational bolt action rifles attached to these roles in the previous installments, the AK47 and the M16 are more than capable of making an impact in any situation. The Squad Leader is not a class anymore, anyone that joined first or was promoted can be an SL regardless of the selected class, and gets allotted with certain SL equipments. Units are represented by squads, usually 5 squads of 6 men make up the platoon each side throws into battle. Infantry classes have similar counterparts on each side, sometimes only their name differs (like Sniper and Marksman), but there are also unique classes, like the northern RPG class which is primarily used against aerial targets, and its US counterpart is the Grenadier with the anti-infatnry grenade launcher. The US Combat Engineers are the only class in the entire game having access to flame throwers.
Squad-play is the name of the game, and it’s a make-or-break feature if played well. Squads can be customized, problematic members can be removed, desired players can be invited and joining can be restricted to ensure the squad performs properly. Squadmembers are meant to move and work together, and to encourage this, they receive an increased capture rate bonus inside objectives, and are less prone to enemy suppress when acting close together. This would be a no-brainer to exploit, but requires an experienced SL that is willing to coordinate and communicate the squads goals, and the squad members to cooperate and play along. Although squad-based gameplay is the strongest feature of the game, and if used well it’s absolutley rewarding to be a part of it, also the lack of squad-play can ruin a match. Renegate SLs and lone soldiers are ineffective, are more exposed to enemy fire and result in wasted tickets. Unfortunately many players act like this, and sometimes moving to another squad or even leaving the server is the only solution.
The mobility of the US is ensured by spawning on the SL and the ability to respawn in the transport helicopters that can drop whole squads into the back of the enemy. In contrast the Viets utilize surprise movements aided by the tunnels which allow them to reach far away objectives safely underground, and respawning through tunnel exits that the SLs can place anywhere on the map, except for the direct closeness of objectives.
Only the US have access to vehicles, and only to helicopters, the Viets have their own stone for these US scissors in form of their RPG class and the northern commanders AA Deployment ability which shoots down anything that flies above 75 meters. The complexity of flying the helicopters requires hours spent on the training ground before taking up a pilot role in the game, as an inexperienced Huey pilot can easily kill a whole squad, or the huge damage dealing potential of a Cobra gets wasted.
The classic Territory gametype is still the standard, where active objectives can be captured or held by having more men inside than the opposition. In Supremacy any objectives can be contested, but only those score points that are linked to the home base. These are the large-map gametypes for 64 players, where attacker and defender roles are swapped for Round 2. The small-map gametype is Skirmish, and is fit for 16 players along similar objective-based gameplay.
Even though a player has experience with the previous installments of the series, RS2V imposes a cruel learning curve on them, not to mention those that are completley new to the series. The challenge is not really to master the new weapons or learn every little portion of the maps, it will happen with time though. The key is to familiarize with the virtual jungle warfare. After spending the first few hours with rushing for the objectives alone and getting killed by invisible enemies, and dealing damage to teammates, it will be clear, that the initial approach must be reconsidered. You cannot risk to run standing, veteran players spend most of their time crouching from cover to cover and crawling in the dirt. Players hiding this way, easily take down the Rambo-wannabes. The game is slow paced, and „running through the jungle” never pays out instead of „using the jungle” to your advantage and punish the careless. The players have nothing to stop a speeding bullet, but they can use solid covers and carefully planned movements. Fragility and mortality are realistically emphasized, and the jungle environment makes you rightfully worried about who hides in the shadows or under the foliage. Players have to learn to rely on each other, to obey the rules of the game and the orders of the battlefield leaders. They have to be able to move as a unit, approach the target in the cover of laid down smoke, flank the defenders, get and stay inside the objective zones at all costs.
You want to know where you are, where your squadmates are, and that the movement you just saw in the distance was friend or foe, so you can open fire or throw a grenade in that direction. The game offers a handful of tools a player might need to decide if he can fire and avoid team killing. Experienced players don’t make a move without checking the minimap first. Certain skin colors, clothes and weapons can only be used by one of the sides. How a soldier holds his weapon while running helps to identify him. Paying attention to close range foregin battle chatter also reveals enemies.
A fair concept by the developers that the game doesn’t „reward” those that are able to pump more hours into the game than others, and doesn’t „penalize” those that can’t. The gained experience and the lack of it respectively helps and hurts these players enough, there is no need to enhance this effect gameplaywise. Anyone that enters any game any time, has the same assets and chances to play and perform well, regardless of level and K/D ratio, which don’t really matter and after advancing on the learning curve of the game, will be improved anyway.
Levelling up is connected however to character customization. After every five levelups, different helmets, shirts, fabric and accessoires are unlocked and can be equipped to the characters, which is not unique, still a very nice touch and effortlessly results in realistic variation of different looking soldiers on the battlefield. Greenhorns have their clean uniforms, veterans tend to look less formal and more functional.
The game obviously doesn’t target the widest audience possible, casual players might not have the patience to wait for their efforts come into fruition. The price is less than half of the so called A-titles, but this obviously doesn’t mean half value. Although the initial release could have been somewhat richer contentwise, the developers are promising new maps, vehicles and gametypes, which should be available for free, new cosmetic upgrades are planned for sale.
If you prefer tactical and cooperative gameplay, if you appriciate games with a carefully designed and succesfully implemented concept, if you are into authenticity and a fine line between realsim and fluent gameplay, if you want to support quality indie efforts, if you are looking for a game that won’t be abandoned after its new brother comes out next summer, you will stick to this game for years.

Do you like ARPGs, robots, great music, post-apocalyptic settings, existential dilemmas, and feeling sad? If so, then this game might be right up your alley. There's probably other reviews that detail the action and the story, so I won't touch on that. Instead, I will try and spread more awareness of the fact that this game requires replaying the main scenario to get the entire story.
For simplicity's sake, I will refer to the first half of the game as Act 1, and the second half of the game as Act 2.
An Act 1 playthrough with Character 1 will reveal much of the main plot of the first half of the game. To progress to Act 2, you will need to play through Act 1 again with Character 2. But do not despair, for seeing the main scenario through his eyes fills in gaps in the story and fleshes out many different characters' motivations, and includes additional interactions with other characters that don't occur on the first playthrough.
It is only when you've completed Act 1 with both characters can you progress on to Act 2, which is where most of the heavy stuff and happenings occur.

If GalCiv and Endless Space had a baby, it would be Stellaris.  There may have been some drinking involved beforehand, because its not entirely glitch-free.  Never the less, a very engaging 4X.
As with all Paradox titles, its taken me a few restarts to get going; oh, I've just encountered the Great Old Ones, I have a fleet of corvettes.  New game.  But it has a lower learning curve than most other Paradox games - notably Europa Universalis - and while 3 games into it I'm no closer to victory, neither am I loosing.  Much.  The feathery ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s spinward of my empire have been moving fleets around near my borders...
Like all Space 4X games, there have to be scifi references; I actually lost a science officer to a shuttle accident.  But unlike most of these sorts of games, Star Trek isnt the main reference point.  If anything, it looks like the devs took inspiration from Farscape, and because of that the universe of Stellaris is weirder and more violent than a Star Trek one.
Tactical battles leave something to be desired - the model seems to be SoD, you throw as many ships at the bads as you can and hope your expensive ships survive.  It does beat the rock/paper/scisors battles of Endless Space, and some positioning is important.  Mostly though, its throw a fleet at another fleet.
Graphics are alright - I'd like to see more differentiation on the ships; my battleships look identical to my carriers.  Same overall structure, but I'd like to see cosmetic differences so I can tell the damn things appart.  I prefer the well-drawn aliens to the well-animated cartoons of Civ6, but the planets lack a great deal of difference between them.
Overall, just the thing to satisfy a 4X space opera jones.
ADDENDUM:
This is why I wish Steam had a "meh" rating.  This is a good game...right up to the end.
Early game is great fun - exploring your solar system, the stars nearby, first contact, slowly upgrade your fleet to deal with those pesky space pirates...
Middle game is great fun - lots of very weird missions, a balancing game of resources, tech and explansion.  Negotiating with weird aliens, juggling factions.  Murder space slugs and energy blobs.
Late game.  So, Stellaris suffers from the late game doldrums that plague most 4X games, but the problem is that this isnt really a 4X.  Its a wargame that pretends there are other options.  You must be part of a Federation, or you're on the menue.  The computer seems to ignore fleet sizes, system defenses are useless, and there is no orbital defense - your planets is screwed if the enemy has at least one ship left.
But thats not the big, huge problem.  Because the actual end game is a deus ex machina - the Borg, or the Reavers, or what have you, show up - sometimes in the middle of your empire.  On the lowest setting, these hordes of space Mongols show up, still larger than any single fleet you or your allies posess, far more advanced, and burn through empires.  Battleships?  Cruisers?  Say goodbye to them, maybe you'll sink some Borg destroyers or frigates before your fleets vanish.  And worse, they dont take your planets - they burn them to the ground and salt the earth.  So that not only do you loose fleets, you loose the capacity to rebuild them.  And this was my experience on the easiest setting.  Default difficulty?  I was facing 10-1 fleet size, and my first encounter I didnt even penetrate the enemy's shields.
As far as I can tell, you either win a domination or diplomatic victory before the Great Old Ones show up, or you loose.  Everyone looses.  There is no culture or cash win, as far as I can tell, so this game is really a 2X game, with a focus on conquest.  So...a 1.5X.
Meh.

Cute little game thats a fusion of the various games it mentions in its blurb.  The music/graphics are very reminiscent of cave story, as are the very tight controls.  The main game is an exploratory metroidvania style, with a few secrets and some definite portalish puzzle solving.
The various elements gel very well together and the overall play was fun and engaging, while it lasted.  I'm not normally a 'time snob' but it definitely felt like the game was over all too soon.  Aiding that was the notion that there was never really a chance to go back and grab all those secrets you saw glimpses of earlier.  If you miss it, odds are, you missed it, and thats that.
I may actually do a second walkthrough enhanced run just to see what effects some of the last things i didn't do would have, but as it stands if you mostly just do forward progress you can probably beat it in just an hour or two.
(some kinda plus mode, or just some oportunity to 'turn back' at the end so you could finish collecting would have been appreciated).
As it stands though I did like it, and did have fun, and would reccomend it specifically to cave story fans who also like puzzle games because more than anything else this is a great fusion of those two styles.

Out There Somewhere is a 2D platformer with simple puzzle elements. Your mission is take out Grigor, but in the battle your ship was damaged and you crash land on an unknown planet. You have to find him on the planet and take him out for good. This is mostly done by platforming. The main mechanic to get used to is the use of a portal gun. You shoot it and when the projectile hits a solid target you will be teleported to that spot. You'll learn the ins and outs of how that works, along with interacting with different beams and other obstacles that will change the way your teleportation works. There's also a gun you can use as a weapon to fight off the planet's hostile inhabitants. This gun doesn't shoot very rapidly and it's a small bullet, but this only makes it all the more useful as you need to aim carefully and plan your shots. It's simple to grasp but will test your smarts and skills as you try to get the hidden upgrades. The graphics are pixelated and dark. The visuals, along with some cool synth music, make for a nice atmosphere to travel through. There's not a whole lot more to say. Not much story, just some simple mechanics and areas to clear. It's a nice little game.
There are some problems, though. All of them seem to stem from the game's legnth. It'll probably only take you 1-2 hours to beat it, and not much more for achievement hunters. That's fine story-wise, as there's not much there outside the premise. However, it seems like more could've been done with the mechanics that were set in place. More puzzles, more ideas with the mechanics, and just some more outside the box thinking. Having a longer game would also mean a larger world, with perhaps more items and powerups to collect. More bosses would've been good. There are two space shooting sections, but having more would've been nice as well. It's neat that those sections start and end the game to kind of tie it up in a nice little bow, but having more of them might make the playstyle feel a little more welcome. A map would've been nice too.
Overall, this is a lighter recommendation. The game is nice with simple mechanics and intresting atmosphere, but it's rather short and could use some fleshing out. Perhaps there will be another game by the developers in a similar fashion, or maybe even a sequel to expand upon these ideas, which have a lot of potential. What's here is good, and only taking a while to beat isn't bad, but this game FEELS short. It feels like this style of game should have more to it. Played Hitman Contracts in 2006 after playing Hitman 2 and was equally impressed with Contracts and it's many weapons and Missions that i went back and played Hitman Codename 47.

First time I played Hitman Contracts was on my Playstation 2 as a kid. I picked up Contracts on Steam during the summersale for a ridiculously cheap price and decided to revisit the game. It felt nostalgic to play it again, especially the first 3 missions.
The PC version suffers from a lot of problems on modern computers. If I stood inside a building, close to an exit I could see the snow coming through the house. When you go into steam overlay and back to the game again you get two mouse cursors which is a bit annoying. Hitman looks very outdated BUT there's HD mods online and probably other useful things you should look up before playing the game. However, if you are like me and want to experience the game just as it was before (without mods) you will run into some wierd glitches and graphical problems. It is a problem possible to overlook though.
Contracts have 12 missons. The maps are huge and on every mission theres a bunch of disguises, weapons and methods you can try out. It's like a sandbox where you run around and try out different things. After every mission you get a rank based on how well you did. I like that you can choose to shot everyone or be a silent assasin. Sometimes the movement is a bit clunky. For example there is no cover system and no good way of sneaking around doors, which can screw you over a few times. Other then that the controls for PC is okay.
If you can look past the graphical problems, if you're running the game on an old machine or if you have found a good HD mod for it, then I wouldn't hesitate. Especially if you are a fan of the other Hitman games or you're just curious to see how to golden age of stealth games looked like. This is a true classic.

This game loves to waste your time for no reason. There are other ways it wastes your time, but I've wasted enough time talking about it.

Quick Summary: Game of Thrones is a RPG taking place during the same time frame as the television show’s first season. The game’s story does not really intersect with the show but some recognizable characters appear. Honestly if you haven’t seen the show you might not understand what’s going on in the game very well.
You play 2 different characters on different quests, alternating who you control between chapters.  Mors Westford is a grizzled old veteran of the Night’s Watch, an ancient order of soldiers dedicated to defending the north from invaders. If you watch the Game of Thrones television show, you know that the Night’s Watch is mostly made up of a bunch of criminals who were given the choice: execution, or joining the Watch.  Because of this unsavory makeup, there are some ♥♥♥♥♥sons that get into all sorts of trouble, requiring badasses like Mors to keep them in line (usually means killing them). Mors’ main quest involves helping a mysterious young woman on the run from assassins with powerful friends.
Alester Sarwyck is a red priest of R'hllor (AKA the “Lord of Light”), returning to his ancestral home after 15 years self-imposed exile. His family’s lands are in disarray and his people are in nearly open rebellion without a strong leader. Alester’s main quest is to regain his title as lord of the Sarwyck house, and oust his ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ half-brother who has risen to power while Alester was away (a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in every sense of the word). Accomplishing this will require the blessing of Queen Cersei Lannister, drawing Alester into the political intrigues of the “Game of Thrones.”
The game is played in third person perspective, similar to Dragon Age 2, with a simplified combat/skill system and a mostly generic loot system. This is one of those games where all of the gear is predefined and similar (no random magical properties). You’re not going to find any ‘godly plate of the whale’ or ‘Windforce’ type items. There are a few items with special names, but the bonuses aren’t game breaking (+2% chance to dodge). Combat in the game usually involves pressing Space to “pause” and issuing commands, including drinking potions or using attack skills. There are a few starting classes to choose from, but Alester will always have his flame skills from being a red priest. Mors will have his dog to back him up (with its own set of skills).
Pros:
+The game’s story meshes with the television series. If you’ve watched the first season of the show you can get a little more background from the game, including insight on just how conniving some of the characters are.
+The game does take into account a lot of your “choices” both in conversation and decisions (like sparing people or executing them).
Cons:
-The combat system is very simple. There is some variation to the gameplay, such as controlling Mors’ dog, going around chomping people, but mostly you just take turns swinging swords at your enemies.
-As you progress through the game you will gather money (copper, silver, gold) but you will find that there’s really not much to spend your money on. Every city has merchants, but the things you can buy are so expensive that you’re better off just using the gear you look off of fallen enemies. The only thing you really need to buy are the various potions.
-The game has very little replayability. The character building doesn’t customize your character all that much, and combat has more luck than skill involved. I started a second playthrough after over 2 years and I just stopped playing after mopping up the Steam achievements I missed the first time.
Overall the game has a lot of room for improvement, but if you enjoy the television show or book series, you might find the game’s story interesting.  If you read all the various letters and history scrolls that you find in the game, it will take you well over 20 hours to finish.  Despite being an RPG with a pseudo ‘Open World,’ the game is very linear and you won’t be doing much overall exploring (except when you’re in an area for the first time looking for loot). Enemies do not respawn and you cannot grind for money or experience.

If you are a big Game of Thrones fan, you should enjoy the experience, but if you are just a random player - this game will disappoint.
The best thing here is the story. It occurs in the same time frame as GoT season 1. You will experience 2 different stories of 2 different men. Playing through 14 chapters you will learn all the background stories abound them. The characters are well fleshed out. The main story is well injected into a GoT world and you will even meet some familiar faces from the GoT tv series. Although not all of them will have a voice-over of the actors.
The action is very much the same as old-school RPG games, where you will command your character to attack, or to use a skill and they will do them in the order you've selected. I think this type of gameplay was a good choice for this kind of game. It's very similar to Dragon Age: Origins.
The skills are fun and all, but at the end of the game you will learn 95% of them, so no replayability value in this department.
The currency in this game is quite scarce, so don't waste all the hard earned money for an item you will eventually out level. Choose wisely.
And now - graphics. It actually sucks. The animations are mediocre. There are so many graphical bugs in the scripted scenes that's it's just mind blowing. You will see some random people walking through the walls, windows, wooden doors, fireplaces. You can get stuck in the corners if all your followers surround you and bam - you can do nothing about it.
Some characters have such strange voice acting. It's so funny in a not funny way.
Oh and the camera controls are the worst. If you want to look around, you have to hold the right mouse button. Even 15 year old games don't have this.
----
So, if you like Game of Thrones, try to forgive this game all of its flaws and enjoy the story. You will need about ~25-30h to complete this game, especially if you like to do side-quests.

WALL OF TEXT TIME!
I had no technical difficulties with playing the game. I assume most everyone with a positive review didn't either. So, chances are, the game will run fine for you. If not, Google is your friend.
Also, there are no spoilers in this review.
It makes the game less awesome when you know little details you shouldn't know yet. Avoid Googling anything about the game (except getting the game running) until you're done with the entire game. Where to obtain materials, how to do a quest, why something happens, outcomes of player decisions, just… don't. Chances are you'll see something that you shouldn't have. Anyway, on with the actual review.
----------
The game gives you just enough information to become invested in the story, while not giving away too much, keeping you guessing and maintaining suspense. Humor and cuteness in the right spots; seriousness and despair in the right spots. Perfect balance. Also, the story is incredibly dense, and absolutely no moment is wasted. Every action, every object, and every piece of dialogue has some reason behind it.
The game draws from many philosophical elements in our world. To get a fuller appreciation of the story, I recommend reading up a bit on existentialism and some religion stuff so you understand all the allusions/symbols in the game:
Each song perfectly captures and enhances the mood of each scenario. All of them are extremely memorable. I especially enjoyed the layered soundtrack that adds or subtracts elements from the song being played when you enter/exit combat or enter/exit different areas. It's such a great touch.
The gameplay combines third-person 3D hack-and-slash with bullet hell, and makes everything feel really satisfying. There’s not a lot to explain here if you know what both of those are. It’s good. There’s about 40-50 hours of gameplay in a full first playthrough.
I only have four minor issues with the gameplay. Minor enough such that I'm still willing to give it a 9/10. First, your character does not pivot when turning around, and they must walk in a tight arc. Occasionally it will result in "I didn't mean to do that" moments when you fall off platforms. The second is that your character loves ladders a bit too much. When you pass by a ladder, the character will grab onto it and stop moving. I feel like the distance at which this happens is a bit too big and you'll often find yourself interrupted by your character's infatuation with the metal rungs. The third issue is that you must double tap WASD to dodge/dash (on mouse/keyboard). You get used to it, but it becomes annoying when you're trying to make precise movements in bullet hell moments. Finally, you can’t really make tiny adjustments with the camera using the mouse to adjust your aim if you’re shooting far into the distance. Enemy lock in Normal difficulty on is useful and prevents this problem.
If you've read other reviews, many people say playing with mouse/keyboard is stupid, and you should be playing with a console controller. However, I used mouse/keyboard, and it worked perfectly fine for me once I adjusted the camera settings. If you want it to feel like WoW like I did, turn Rotation Speed and Pursuit Speed way up, and Auto Adjust way down. After I did that, everything felt fine.
Easily the most beautiful game I’ve played this decade. Granted, I haven’t played many high budget games recently, but this stuff is movie quality, I swear. I spent my first couple hours of gameplay just exploring and seeing things. It’s amazing.
Everything is good. EVERYTHING. You will probably be able to find little things you don’t like if you’re especially nitpicky, but I feel very strongly that this stuff will seem insignificant compared to how good everything is. Please buy this. It’s an amazing experience that I want everyone to have.

Like a good sequel should, Call of Duty: Ghosts doesn’t ignore the formula of fast, fluid gameplay that has made the series famous, but introduces a unique new premise, unprecedented player personalization, and sweeping changes that breathe new life into the multiplayer experience. It’s over-the-top and at times unnecessarily complex, but serves both current and next-generation consoles with ambitious new ideas and tremendous replay value.
Despite sharing a name with one of Modern Warfare’s best-known characters, Ghosts takes place in an entirely new Call of Duty universe set in the not-too-distant future. In a genre overwrought with antiquated Russian conflicts and ambiguous Middle Eastern terrorist threats, Ghosts takes on a refreshingly unique premise in which the threat comes not from the east, but the south: a federation of oil-rich South American nations rises to take over the hemisphere, pushing north and coming to blows with the U.S.
The prelude establishes a harrowing vision of a United States homeland that's broken but not beaten – not quite Red Dawn, but not Fallout 3, either. It’s a space not often explored by modern shooters, and its mood is heightened by missions set in a besieged Santa Monica and the wasted remains of San Diego, to the tune of an excellent, somber score from David Buckley (The Town, Metal Gear Solid 4). But ultimately, time on the poignant homefront is short lived as the story goes behind enemy lines in Caracas, the Andes mountains, and other exotic locales.
Those might lack to familiarity, but the variety of environments keeps the campaign fresh, not only in terms of visuals, but in gameplay as well. Instead of just fighting waves of enemies through a linear stage at ground level, you’ll find yourself rappelling down skyscrapers, flying helicopters, having firefights in space, commanding tanks, scuba diving through shipwrecks, playing as a dog, and evading shark attacks. Each requires new strategy, acute situational awareness, and – in the case of the space and water missions – special consideration for verticality and physics.
Of course, it wouldn’t be a Call of Duty game without elaborate setpieces, fierce shootouts, and tense stealth missions, and Ghosts delivers some of the most memorable experiences in the series. I felt genuine dread as the ground and buildings collapsed around me during orbital weapons strikes, the zero-gravity spectacle of the Federation’s space station ambush is awe-inspiring, and bursting through a highrise window as the entire building crumbles during the Federation Day mission is exhilarating.
But like previous CoDs, the story of Ghosts struggles to remain in focus amidst the fray of explosive cinematic moments and relentless firefights. Narrated loading sequences with stylized story animations push the campaign forward, but only last for one or two minutes before launching back into the action. It’s there, on the front lines, that much of the plot progression is presented and oftentimes lost.
It's by no means an achievement in dramatic storytelling — it's more about dumb fun — and it lacks the player-choice element introduced with Call of Duty: Black Ops II, but when given time to breathe Ghosts actually offers some interesting human drama. The story centers around two brothers, Logan and Hesh, their father Elias, and yes, their dog Reilly as they fight the Federation as part of the battered remnants of the U.S. military, and later as the elite Ghosts squad. The family ties, specifically the relationship between Logan and Hesh, made me care about the protagonists in a series that's habitually made its characters a dispensable commodity. The voice acting is decent overall, though there are periodic moments of cringe-worthy dialog, like one superfluous moment when Elias reveals he’s a member of the Ghosts. And then there’s Riley. Though the subject of many a meme at this point, Riley not only acts as a useful tool for recon and silently dispatching enemies, but is integral to several dramatic sequences, saving your character on more than one occasion.
The story stumbles in the second act when it strays away from the more evocative character focus in favor of a long stretch of back-to-back missions driven almost exclusively by guns-blazing combat. While not poorly done, this visually arresting, action-packed, but ultimately hollow middle stands in stark contrast to the effective first and final acts. On the bright side, that padded out my play time to roughly 10 hours, making this campaign one of the longest CoD single-player experiences.
The Verdict
Call of Duty: Ghosts isn't a reinvention of the franchise, but proves there's still room for innovation within its existing formula. Though at the risk of overcomplicating things at times, its robust multiplayer gameplay, surprisingly fun co-op modes, and lengthy, challenging, and varied campaign makes Ghosts one of the best Call of Duty games to date.

As someone who has an MP3 player full of chiptunes, this game immediately grabbed my interest. After doing a little digging around (there are only like... 3 youtube reviews; the game released today), I decided to take the plunge and purchase the game.
So what is it?
Chiptune Champion is a Guitar Hero clone that exclusively uses chiptunes for the tracks you play to. Being a kid from the 80s, the music definitely brought back memories of summer vacations spent on the NES and Gameboy. There's a wide selection of music to choose from the outset, and the ability to create your own tracks in the track editor or download tracks from the Steam Workshop gives this game the huge potential for massive replayability.
So that's the good part.
The bad part is the control scheme. What Chiptune Champion wants you to do is take your keyboard and hold it like a guitar. The 1-5 buttons are used for the "strings" while the enter and shift are used for the strum bar. Holy smokes is that unintuitive.
It took my wife asking me what I was doing to the keyboard to convince me to go down into the basement looking for one of my old Guitar Hero controllers. And surprisingly, it worked.
While there is no ability to use a guitar controller from inside the game, downloading a free program like JoyToKey will allow you to map the game's controls to the buttons on your guitar, making the control scheme infinitely better and nearly identical to playing Guitar Hero or Rockband.
So do I recommend the game? Yeah, but only if you have a guitar controller that is compatible with your PC. The game is pretty fun and the music is great. The controls could use a little work and hopefully the game will eventually support an in-game guitar control scheme instead of players needing to use a third party.

Story is either too hard to understand or poor. Whatever the reason is it makes it hard to keep track of what's going on. It could might as well have had no sense at all as the game is made in a dream-like style. It means it could have been just as abstract as the dream itself (which would make an interesting concept if it's true). The humor was nice, there were a few places where I had a good laugh.
Basically the game is about exploring, looking for collectibles, solving puzzles and fighting.
EXPLORING. The world is build of many different areas, areas are build of levels. Levels are screen-wide squares, you can see one level at the time and you move from level to level. The biggest problem here is lack of a proper map. Sure you have a symbolic map but it's just gray squares. It shows only how levels in the area you're actually in are connected, nothing more. It means you have to wander through the levels until you memorize what's where. It's important because it's an open world and you will have to come back to the same places a few times. Too much walking could make you feel a little bored.
COLLECTIBLES. In order to progress you have to find cards which will open the gates to the next areas or locked levels.
PUZZLES. Most of the puzzles are easy. However the game won't hold your hand and you'll have to learn everything yourself. Puzzles varies in different areas which is nice.
FIGHTING. There are different kinds of enemies and you have to adapt to their style of fighting. It's rather simple though. Also every boss has it's own style but they're not that difficult either. Your biggest enemy will be the controls. I've died so many times becuase my character didn't do what I wanted or because I've jumped into the hole.
It's very retro pixel art style so you have to be a fan of it to appreciate it. For sure diverse design of the areas is simply the greatest point of this game. Black and white town will always remain in my mind for its creepy and unique atmosphere.
Everything about this game is a love letter to the old consoles and so is the music. Again, you just have to be a fan to appreciate it. As far as I remember every area had its own, quite short music samples but nothing really remained in my head.

A lightweight adventure game inspired by the original Legend of Zelda. The main goal is find all of the cards located in treasure chests throughout the world and dungeons.
The overworld is mainly for exploring and has very little in the way of enemies. There are a few scattered environment puzzles. The dungeons have more enemies and puzzles.
The game is fairly non-linear, usually having quite a few different areas available to explore. Once you find enough cards you can open doors to new areas, giving you more options to explore.
There isn't much in the way of tools in the game, you mainly just look for cards and a few secret Easter eggs. There are a few upgrades for the weapon that can be found but that's about it.
At the very end of the game you're given a tool that lets you swap any two tiles, allowing you to actually remove walls and go through to screens you would never normally be able to get to. There are actually quite a few hidden areas with cards in them that are only accessible with this tool. This has a very "hacky" feel to it which I really thought added a new dimensionto the game after it's already been completed.
-Playtime-
The game is fairly short. Expect only 4-7 hours on a first play through, depending on how much backtracking you do. With the correct route the game can actually be completed in only about 2 hours.
-Achievements-
The big one here was to find 100% of the cards which requires you to go back through a lot of the areas with the tile swap tool. I enjoyed the treasure hunt of tracking down all the cards and having to use the swapper really added a different feel to it at the end. The other notable achievement is the speedrun, completing the game under 3 hours was actually fairly easy with the correct route.
Recommended on sale.

I can't recommend this game. It started off fantastic, with a heaping amount of fantastic pixel art, music, and generous dose of Zelda like gameplay, with a few funny little quips, and a slight smattering of (What I've heard of) Undertale, where not everything is quite as it seems, and not every "enemy" is actually an enemy. It falls apart beyond that however.
Essentially it goes as follows, Music, Pixel Art, Atmosphere get a 10/10. It's fantastic.
Gameplay... starts off strong, but a later mix of poor platforming and frankly irritating enemy types bring it down. 6.5/10
Story... there is none. It vaguely hints at some ideas and that's about it.
Buy it on sale, play until it irritates you/lose interest, and leave it. And only if you REALLY like Zelda-likes.
It starts off mysterious, and genuinely grips your curiousity, but through playing the game to completion... the best I can figure is that it's a sort of story (If you're willing to call it a story) about the human condition and certain feelings that people display. It's ridiculously bare bones, with only a VERY slight amount of text that actually makes you understand anything, and only about that specific topic. There's boss fights that don't actually seem to have any symbolism in their design (But I'm also awful at spotting symbolism) and when they die they say gibberish like "I'll always be with you." What the hell is that supposed to mean? Nothing is ever explained, shown or even hinting at something allowing you to make your own conclusion. In the beginning I was completely hooked, by the end I knew it couldn't really go anywhere, and at the end... I was left making that Jackie Chan "Huh? What?" face.
Speaking of bosses... these are some of the most... confusing bosses I've ever fought. A fair few I'm not even sure what I actually did/was supposed to do, and I beat the game. A lot of them are just plain annoying, some are underwhelming (In a game that really doesn't have any build up) and some are actually decent.
The final boss was the most confusing, with you trying to frantically figure out how in the hell to damage the damn thing while it's attacking you.
They also get to a point in level design where they have you start doing platforming... which goes horribly wrong about 90% of the time. Sometimes you jump, catch the edge, think your fine, then the game decides you catually didn't and tosses you down the hole. I honestly don't know why they included these sections, they're not fun, just aggravating.

Anodyne capitalizes on an oft-neglected area of nostalgia: handheld Zelda games. When I was growing up, one of my favorite games was Link's Awakening. I liked it more than the other Zeldas because of the unique dreamlike atmosphere it had. Anodyne copies the gameplay, and doubles down on the atmosphere to an astonishing degree. It's a truly unique specimen.
The gameplay is about what you'd expect. Walk around, solve puzzles, hit things with a melee weapon (In this case a broom, not a sword). It will feel particularly Zelda-y at first, but it begins to gain its own identity as time goes on. At first I considered the game's lack of items to be its biggest flaw, but on further consideration I think this is part of what gives it its identity. The limited number of options give the combat and puzzles a certain "purity" to them. There are no ways to "cheat," no easy way to win, just you and the challenge presented by the game. It's extra impressive since the difficulty curve is very smooth, and provides some genuine challenge by the end. Kudos to the level designers.
The game takes several notes from Links Awakening, but it is not the only card that Anodyne has to play. As you progress further into the game, more and more levels appear that are influenced by other games. There are levels that remind me of Earthbound, Last Survivor, LIMBO, and a lot of Yume Nikki. In fact, Anodyne's hopping between mysterious dream worlds with different art styles is eerily similar to Yume Nikki. A couple of level themes are even shared between the two. I found Yume Nikki's lack of gameplay very disappointing the first time I played it (I have since gained a greater appreciation), and Anodyne fixes essentially all the issues that I had with it. Calling it "Yume Nikki with story and gameplay" isn't quite correct, but it should give you a good idea of if this game would appeal to you. If you like Zelda, Yume Nikki, surreality, exploration, atmosphere, or just a well constructed game, I'd highly recommend it.

I have been trying to review Intake for quite a while now. It wasn't easy, because each time I decided I won't be playing this game anymore, I started it up for "the last time". I did that like 10 or 15 times already.
What is Intake?
It's a game about dubstep drugs. Yup. That's it. Drugs. And Dubstep.
How is that a good combo?
Well, Intake is a very simple in design game. You have to destroy colored pills. There are two colors, but you can only use one at a time. Two button game. Quick and easy. The difficult part begins when game throws hoards of those pills at your face in a split second. Did I mention flashbangs? Oh yeah, Intake has them. Lots of them at times. Hit one and your combo (and screen, and sanity, and flow) are gone.
Well, the more pills you hit without missing, the higher your combo, the higher your combo, the better your score. Combos grant you really weird power-ups as well.
It's nothing more than breaking pills, but oh boy, it's so satisfying. Dubstep in the background seem to be the best possible choice of music, tho I wish it wasn't
