I purchased this game as part of the Saints Row Ultimate Franchise Pack, which was on sale at the time for about $18.  I can honestly say this game has left me completely satisfied with my purchase, and despite having bought the bundle at the beginning of the summer, and played every day, it was at least a month before I even opened Saints Row 3 for the first time, because I was having so much fun playing Saints Row 2, and there is simply that much to do.  With 233.8 hours on record as of my review, I still am only at about 95-97% completion on my first and only playthrough, because it was simply too much fun screwing around.  Even after finishing the story missions, of which there are more than enough to make the game worth buying all by itself, there was still so much to do.
The controls took a bit of getting used to, but only at first.  After a short while, any oddities control-wise felt completely natural, which is far from always the case when talking about ported titles.  The only thing I could recommend a controller for would be the driving/piloting.  While driving ground vehicles, the WASD keys don't quite give you the best experience, but they work perfectly fine for it.  The main complaint I had about the game in general were the flight controls, which were awkward at first, but even after getting used to the layout, which wasn't that strange, it still lacked the ability to make small adjustments without losing control, unless you practice a lot. (I practiced a lot though, and mostly was able to work around it.) I got so accustomed to the keybindings in this game that I actually changed most of my SR3 keybindings to match (where they were different at least) because I found I honestly missed many of the default keybindings where they had been changed.  Still, using a console controller for the air vehicles is probably your best option, if nothing else.
The graphics are far from amazing by current standards, but considering the time the game was made, they're perfectly solid, and the water still looks more real than watch dogs (you actually have a wake in a boat! HOW ADVANCED!! Sorry had to. considering I got this game in a huge bundle for only 18 dollars, I am not only satisfied, I would gladly have paid $18 dollars for this game alone, if I evaluated the value of the game solely on the amount of fun I had playing it.  All in all, I fully recommend this game and hope others enjoy it as much as I have.

My expectations for the game were low, but it turned out to be one of the best RPGs I have ever played. And I've played quite a few.
It's impossible to escape comparisons to the first Witcher game, in good and bad. The game features set protagonists -- two of them, which you'll alternate controlling for the first 10 chapters, after which they'll adventure together -- and the role of the player is not so much to decide WHAT they do, but HOW they do it. This is a fairly rewarding affair, as each and every choice you make in dialogue is likely to have consequences. Often not large ones, but the game nonetheless does a very good job in acknowledging the player's choices.
The protagonists themselves stand out even in the fantasy world, Alester being an exiled noble turned Red Preist trying to reclaim his lands and Mors a skinchanger brother of the Night's Watch. Alester can use many abilities tied to fire, most notably revealing hidden passages and other secrets, while Mors is able to take control of his dog, who can then scout ahead or execute stealth kills. Both are well-written, and the player is given enough power over their behaviour for it not to feel as though the story is simply something one pokes along.
The story is of epic proportions. It took me nearly 60 hours to clear the game, though at the hardest difficulty I had to replay many a battle. This brings up one of my grievances with the game: Much too often, difficult battles would be preceded by long dialogue sequences which you'd then have to navigate through again if you died. Inexplicably, it's not possible to load a game during battle, even if it's clear you're going to lose, but are forced to exit to the title screen first.
The game isn't exactly small, but the few locations you can visit definitely start feeling cramped once you've ran through them a couple of times. Budget constraints are evident in virtually every aspect of the game, again very similarly to the first Witcher game. Another similarity is the very inconsistent quality of voice-acting. The protagonists are well-voiced, and the game even features some of the cast from the TV series, but most minor NPCs are Staruday morning cartoon quality.
There is a LOT of dialogue in the game, and that's what ate up most of my time playing the game. Unfortunately, a lot of that time was spent REplaying through dialogue, and not only due to the save mechanic cited above. The game employs a dialogue wheel, and each choice usually entails quite a bit of back-and-forth between the characters after the initial line. This often makes it difficult to predict what exactly will each choice make your character say and do. As yet another poor design trope, dialogue choices often inexplicably become unselectable unless you pick them in just the right order, and often it's simply impossible to ask a character all the questions you could without reloading, for no apparent purpose whatsoever.
There isn't a great deal of combat in the game, but what little there is is very clunky and unvaried. There is a definite tactical element, certainly, and at a high difficulty you're almost guaranteed to find yourself having to reload and try different strategies after the current one led to defeat. But every opponent is basically just a human of one of the six playable classes, with just their armour, weapon and health varying, so it quite quickly starts feeling like you're just going through the motions with each fight. By the time the game was over I was only too glad to be done with this aspect of the game.
Despite these problems, it's still a very good game. A gem in the rough, certainly, but a gem nonetheless. Definitely recommended for any lovers of story-driven RPGs. Quality of writing is high, and the story is even canonical, so here's your opportunity to add to the Game of Thrones mythos. :P

First of all: Although this game looks similar to some parts of Mirrors Edge and shares at least some gameplay concepts, it is NOT really like Mirrors Edge at all. Main concept is swinging through the levels, not running or climbing. So what you must learn and master is to use momentum when you chaining swings like Spiderman. There is also some wallrunning and wallbouncing quite regularly, but like I said, focus is on swinging. Controls are good, you get a good sense of your speed and momemtun when you play, which is necessary to calculate your jumps. Only "negative" thing to mention: You have to be pretty exact when you click on those midair anchor ball, and since your often moving at high speed, it can get difficult to hit those in the right moment. If you only click anywhere nearby, it is unforgiving and you fall to your death. Then again it is never unfair, only difficult, as you want to hit them exactly from the point farthest away if possible. As a help, checkpoints are numerous (basically on each platform you land on and sometimes even in the air) and there are help messages if you fail multiple times at one place.
Also, you can change your direction midair a little bit, that helps to be in control all of the time if you let go your swings at the correct moment.
When I first tried this game, I wasn't to impressed, as I expected a Mirrors Edge clone and was disappointed. I needed one or two stages to understand that it's really different from ME and to adapt to the mechanics. Then after each stage, I loved the game even more and couldn't stop playing. Gameplay is simply fun and addictive!
Each stage introduces a new gameplay element, so it doesn't get boring or too repetitive.
I finished the last level after nearly 5 hours (I would consider myself good at that kind of games) and if I hadn't other games to play in my library I would definitely go back and get those collectibles or do some speedruns. Maybe I will do sometimes in the future.
Short verdict: Nice physics-based platformer with polished and bugless gameplay, focusing on swinging. This game is really difficult at times (that's part of the fun!), but not unfair!
I recommend this to fans of platformers without fighting or enemies. It's all about controlling movement and getting to the end. You can do some decent speedrunning, if you like.

I am absolutely loving this game.  If the game interests you, then I highly recommend it; I hope more games like this are made.  I play a lot of the solitaire games, and here are the things I enjoy about Shadowhand:
IN RESPONSE TO SOME CRITICISMS...I want to emphasize...
I have some fun tools up my sleeve to spice things up in this game, but at the end of the day, this game does well as a solitaire game - it is a game of CHANCE.  It's a prettier version of me playing a deck of cards on my living room floor, with costumes and weapons and duels...but it's still a game of chance.
Now for the things I enjoy...
1) visually gorgeous - crisp, vibrant
2) story line - at 13 hours and several chapters in, the story is interesting, engaging and fun.  I love it!!
3) table design - card layouts vary, table design can change depending on the chapter theme and there are creative ways of creating challenges (example: find the lantern to unveil the group of cards, or find the torch to light the powderkeg to blow up a small group of cards, etc).  I appreciate when these exist in solitaire games and appreciate the variety and style in this game because they add variety and spice and aesthetic to solitaire games.
4) game play - I find the different tools/specialty cards useful and fun to use.  You get to purchase weapons/armor/misc items throughout the game.  I find the approach works very well - it's detailed enough to be interesting but not overcomplicated to get frustrating/boring or too complex to get involved with.  I love how your appearance changes based on what weapons and armor you are using at the time.  Also well done is with each card game, you can change your weapons and armor at the beginning - especially useful for duels.  Sometimes I replay a duel several times before I get a "perfect" rating; whenever I start a new hand (whether it's brand new or I'm replaying the hand) I can change my weapons/armor when I realize what things I need to boost up.  For example - playing a pirate, I can change a particular item that improves my defense against "sea" weapons.  Or if I'm dueling with someone who has a particular type of attack (like one that causes me to "bleed" over time, I can change my attire to help guard against bleeding.  I most especially enjoy using the specialty abilities - one favorite is I can change a card and have a 50% chance of the card changing to something in my favor (ie something i can use right away).  It adds a nice dynamic without it making it certain i win.  It's a fun tool, not a guaranteed to make me win the game.
5) solitaire game play - I LOVE that this game seems to not be artificially adjusted to make it easier/harder.  At the basic level, I find I will lose games or win games, but it truly feels like a game of chance.  Some solitaire games seem to be artificially easy, so much that I never use any special abilities or specialty cards because I don't need them.  This one doesn't do that.  On the other hand, it doesn't feel artificially hard either.  It's challenging without it being frustratingly easy or frustratingly hard.  It feels like a true game of solitaire - I have some fun tricks I can use, but at the end of the day, it's a game of chance.
6) misc - there are no timers or clocks  and I don't think there are any penalties for choosing to replay a hand, even continuously replaying it.  I usually replay until I get the "3 star perfect" rating and 13 hours in, I have not noticed any penalty.
7) music/sounds - love all the music and sounds throughout
THE BUG KING

Shadowhand is a high quality solitaire game with RPG elements (selecting abilities, armor, weapons and gear) that have a big impact on how your solitaire duels play out.
You play Lady Cornelia Darkmoor, posthumous daughter of a Duke.  She starts a carreer in highway robbery to help her best friend and to unravel the web of corruption gripping her community.
While a bit on the cheesy side, the story is well written and compelled me to keep playing this game daily until I finished it.  It took 16 hours to complete Normal mode, where you have the option to retry duels until you win and to continue on to the next chapter even if you have not satisfied all the chapter requirements.  This kept the story flowing and the encounters varied.  Good job devs!
Shadowhand is the best solitaire game that I've played on Steam (and I've played several).  Well worth the $15 price tag.  Keep 'em coming Grey Alien Games!

This game's core is a very simplistic card-counting game that I'm not sure it is possible to be either good or bad at. You pick from cards that are higher or lower and as long as you are even a little mathematically minded, you can plot whether or not to go up or down to get the highest combination. As a result, I grew bored. Maybe they add new elements to it later on that make it more like. . .  well, a game, but I played 3 levels without any introduction of skill-based mechanics. Often matches slow to a crawl when you have few cards available to choose between too.
The theming was great though. I genuinely enjoyed the dialogue and while I'm personally not a lesbian or even able to relate as I am not attracted to women, I applaud both the novelty of a twist on the old damsel-in-distress plot point and the inclusion. The art and choosing weapons and gear for my character also intrigued me, but if you find the main "game" portion of a game to lack any challenge because it seems both remedial and random, no amount of charm can redeem it. My suggestion to you all is to look for videos of the game being played to see if you think you'd find the card game fun before purchasing.

The real frustration is in the later chapters where some of the objectives can be nearly impossible. It really stinks to play through 6 of 8 hands only to realize you can't possibly meet the objectives.
Despite it's warts, this is still a good time and I've been compulsively playing it since I got it.

32 hours to do a playthrough, and feels much shorter.  That's a good thing.  This might be the first hack-n-slash after Kingdom Hearts that I'd play through again.  Combat is not so fun, but there is an option to have the game play the combat for you or merely assist you :D and it's worth it to do so.  Now here's the review:
I saw an interview with the main creator of the game which struck me.  He said that if he ever made a game that felt the same throughout its playtime, then he would have failed.  Nier:Automata does not stay the same.  It bends and twists the rules of most video games and introduces seemingly bland combat that actually introduces a surprising array of options for players to select.  If you chose, no 2 encounters would Be the same.  2B.  It easily transitions between a hack-n-slash, an art gallery, a deserted island, a philosophy textbook, a retro bullet-hell game, and a visual novel.  These transitions are wonderful for anyone who's bored with the humdrum flood of like-minded video games which offer nothing new.
Sience fiction that sucker-punches the player into a character-rich experience.  The music alone is good enough to buy an album.  This is more of a story than a simple video game.  The story's atmosphere is what many of us have been searching for.    Hopefully, it will lead more humans to question everything.

So many stories to tell.
If you liike 4x and space operas then Stellaris is for you. Yes, I have seen all the complaints about the games short comings-combat and mid game stagnation. After the last few patches this has been tweeked a bit but not completely fixed. There are some compelling mods that do fix the combat aspect if that is really going to affect your purchase.
The true sell of this game is the roleplaying and story telling aspect. The random event chains, the customization of your speices and empire, the ability to design your own ships and playstyle-its all top notch. Paying attention to the Story your empire creates is the most fun of this game. I don't start a game with the specific build to win-if you naked corvette spam or abuse the games mechanics you can easiliy outmanouver the ai. I start a game with a specific empire idea and try to roleplay the empire through the challenges the game throws at me- this always yields a 10/10 experience.
Even when I lose.
Ex: The most recent empire created was a race of pacifist space turtles. After a few years they formed the first federation which quickly dominated the Eastern Quadrent of the galaxy. Soon the space turtles ascended to become Psionic with a Immortal Chosen one who became their President (through election manipulation every couple years). The Psionic space turtles and the megacorporation Space Jellyfish became the 2 prominent Empires in the galaxy and in doing so made our Federation unchalleneged in Technological Advancments and Fleet power. Eventually this roused a Fallen Empire out of its slumber. Which in turn caused a war in heaven with a rival Fallen Empire. As species left the Federation left and right to join one side or the other the Space Turtles and Jellyfish formed a coalition with some of the younger races to stay neutral. This backfired and both empires declared war on our coalition. After a decade of war our coalition had pretty much destroyed one of the Fallen EMpires, but in doing so had worn our fleets down to dust. The surviving Fallen Empire had breached the boarder of the Space Turtle Empire and was burning towards the capital unchecked. Massing the fleet the coalition forces made one final stab towards the surviving Fallen Empire Homeworld in an attempt to take pressure off of the Turtles. It was a bloodbath, even Admiral Ackbar the Dragonslayer (yea you can kill space dragons with DLC) couldn't salvage it. After the war both races were a fraction of what they once were and were compleatly obliterated when the Unbidden arrived in the galaxy after rampent Jump Drive use. 10/10 would space turtle agian.
Best 4X space RTS since Distant Worlds.

If you like the stories of Westeros, then I would say that this is worth buying when on sale. The story in itself is very good, though the game is no where near as polished as it should be.
The combat can be clunky as whilst it isnt turn based (You assign skills in a slowed down real time), it can be very repetitive and there are often clipping issues where the characters will either occupy the same space or "vibrate" when they are standing half inside a wall. The system itself though is pretty easy to master once you understand the roles of each character (I always use Mors as a Landed knight and so he "tanks" whilst Alester can damage the enemy)
The quest system can be frustrating too if you are new to RPG's as if you miss a slight detail, you will pretty much fail the side quests. Most of the side quests can be completed over several chapters, but if you miss a specific pickup that starts the quest in the chapter where it has become available then you won't be able to complete the quest once you have moved on in the story. This can be awkward for achievment hunters.
I do wonder how this story would have turned out if it had been developed by a bigger studio, as it is clear that the writers have tried to keep everything in keeping with the lore of Westeros. It does kind of feel like this game was made by a company who snapped up the license before anyone else could and then they rushed to push out the game to cash in.
All of that being said, if you are a fan of Game of Thrones and old style RPG's then I would recommend you buy this just for one playthrough. If you arent happy with slow turn based combat and linear levels, then I simply would not. I would also say that this game is not worth the full price and you should wait until you see it on sale somewhere.

When people see Saints Row 2 they'll instantly think of Grand Theft Auto IV. It's inevitable. It moves similarly, the scenes have the same saturated lighting and there are several parallels that can be drawn between the gameplay of the two. Heck, the text is even color coded in a similar way for mission objectives. But, be warned, Saints Row 2 is most certainly not GTA.
Thankfully this is one imitator that turns out to be much more than a straight carbon copy. In fact, Saints Row 2 takes GTA's gameplay, turns it on its side and sends it rolling down a mountain filled with land mines, roving monster trucks and ninjas. Lots and lots of ninjas.
What does that translate to in terms of quality? A crazy good time. Or at least, what would have been a crazy good time if not for the game's poor coding on PC. For whatever reason the PC version absolutely chugs. Even on my Intel Core2Quad 2.4 GHz with 2GB RAM, an Nvidia GeForce 8800 GTX, and a Vista 32 operating system, the game ran between twenty and seven frames per second and had a host of other performance issues. In other words, it was nauseating and almost unplayable. The core gameplay is the same, but the general performance basically kills the experience.
Saints 2 picks up a few years after the events of the first. Your character has been in a prison hospital stuck in a coma since he (or she) was blown off of a yacht, thus badly burning his (or her) exterior. Luckily, that happens to open the door to the robust character customization. You can select from three female accents and three male accents as well as the usual huge array of physical traits. Plus, later in the game you'll earn new personalities, taunts, costumes and fighting styles. It's hilarious to strap the hot dog suit or the Borat bathing suit on your character and then watch some of the more dramatic cutscenes.
Of course, once you're done creating your evil concoction, it's time to bust out of prison, free your long-time running mate Johnny Gat and then build the Saints back into the prominent gang that they once were. That means reclaiming your old stomping grounds and getting a few lieutenants to govern your peons.
The beginning of Saints Row 2 is actually a bit more engaging than your typical open world game. There's not much of a tutorial and you aren't doing menial tasks like taking someone's girlfriend to eat and then back to her house. Instead, you're breaking out of prison, hopping on the back of a gunboat and going to town on some pursuing copters and police boats. Good times.
After you complete the first few tasks, the game really opens up. There's no unlocking of islands or other boroughs. Instead, the whole city of Stilwater is available to you from the get-go. And with that freedom comes a plethora of activities and diversions to try out. There's the all-new Trail Blazer and Septic Avenger or you can try out the analog stick-based sex mini-game. They're all just as fun and outrageous as the next.
It's in that ridiculous nature that Saints Row 2 would have really found its niche. Driving down the highway on a flaming ATV, exploding cars to extend your timer or throwing your limp body into oncoming traffic to rack up a medical bill are things that you just don't see in other videogames. Sadly in SR2 on PC these sequences are terribly marred by performance issues. SR2's activities are more outlandish than in the first game, but they're also more varied. There's still the more mundane racing and helicopter assault, but having the option of going outside the box is great.
Truly a wonderful game. Brings back a feeling lost in Grand Theft Auto over the years. Recommended to anyone who loves sandbox games.

I picked up this game on sale as filler to reach the $5 mark when making another purchase. It piqued my interest, being Super Hexagon-esque, but wasn't sure what to expect. What I got was a well crafted game with fast and smooth animations, snappy response, decent music, and (most importantly for this type of game) the ability to retry nearly instantly. I have a few nitpicks here and there, but ended up enjoying this game better than the other one I bought. Overall, a very enjoyable near-sighted bullet dodging simulator.
It uses six buttons, escape, spacebar and arrowkeys/WASD, can't get much easier than that. Hitting one is satisfying, as your pentagon responds quickly and nearly instantly. What's also neat, is this game supports controller. Pretty standard, left stick to move, A and B to navigate menus. But this leads into one of my qualms. Only the left stick can be used for navigation, not the right. I would have preferred being able to use my dominant hand for movement. Another aspect about controller is that it's easy to accidentally move to a corner rather than straight to the side, leading to an untimely restart. That comes across as more of a limitation of a controller interface, and of course, can be avoided if you use keyboard. I have a gripe about the keyboard as well, though. If using the standard three fingers on the movement keys, you will need to have one of those jump between keys, most probably UP and DOWN. That action makes it easy to slip up in those directions. Normally I wouldn't remotely consider this an issue, but since this game relies on millisecond precision, something as benign as jumping between rows can slip you up. It comes across as a bit of an imbalance, rather than intentional difficulty jump, as LEFT and RIGHT won't suffer from that.
Genre and selection is, in my opinion, perfect for this game. Fast-paced, electronic with some elements of chiptune, keep the blood pumping and usually go nicely with the difficulty. It looks like three different artists contributed music, Adhenoid, ForeverBound, and RollingFacade. The game starts out strong with a fantastic track.
by ForeverBound instantly became my favorite track in the game, followed by Adhenoid's
and
. RollingFacade contributed two tracks, but I didn't like either one.
works in the game, but I didn't find it to be anything exceptional. That's fine, I don't expect to like every track in a game.
is the oddball out. It's tempo is noticeably slower than all the others, and that might make sense if it were for the easiest difficulty, but it comes with the next step up. Slower tempo, mixed with continually faster speed, doesn't make for a good accompaniment.
RFLEX plays very similarly to Super Hexagon, as it's the same same vein of game. Start, dodge, restart. Good choice of clean and clear styling with no antialiasing or upscaling issues. The objects are either drawn vectors or very high resolution images. It has stylized scan lines and screen curvature, which you can even change the intensity of, like a CRT monitor. Nice bit of character to differentiate it from other similar styles. Everything is golden in the graphics department.
As for difficulty and progression, my experience has been good. The way each level seems to progress is that it starts slow and incrementally gets faster and faster until (I presume) it's humanly impossible to keep up, as opposed to Super Hexagon which seems to go a static speed for each minute. This means that it will get incredibly difficult to go for distance. My (current) personal best on the easiest difficulty for RFLEX is 88 seconds compared to around 5 minutes on Super Hexagon. At this time, the record for the easiest on RFLEX is about 170 seconds, so don't expect to be able to sit for a long (3+ minutes) single round. Transitions between levels goes pretty well, however something seems a little off with the last two. I find the second hardest difficulty to be the hardest. I've been able to get consistently further on the hardest than the preceeding difficulty. I don't know if this is frequent for others, but it's certainly not what seems to be intended.
This being said, difficulty between levels increases mostly fine. With each level, the blocks for each sequence are thrown from a variety of more directions and employ some other tricks to try to get you to slip up. There are some sneaky visual tricks up its sleeve, but lose potency with exposure, as any trick does. Also similar to Super Hexagon, is how the game handles each sequence of blocks. It picks from a random set of predetermined layouts and throws it at you from an arbitrary direction. This means that over time it's possible to memorize the sequence, basically guaranteeing that if you make it past the leading block, you'll make it past the remaining.
RFLEX presents a highly enjoyable experience in the same vein as Super Hexagon. It's a fast paced, retro styled, dodging game that's easily picked up, difficult to master, and lets you retry milliseconds after you inevitably fail. It has a few flaws, but gets the core gameplay completely right, making this game a great experience.

This is a game where a chapter is devoted to killing a batallion of IRS agents (yes). It is, after all, mostly a story about saving your fortune from miscreants, so might as well save it from the King as well, I suppose.
A game where bandit clothes give you superpowers (I'll get back to you when I get a hat that increases defense piercing by 25% and bleeding by 10%.) Where your avatar actually wears what you tell her to, which can be quite comical at the end game. Did you know fake beard could allow you to start duels first? Well, they're unsettling on a lady.
A game where a ship captain that smuggles goods between France and England is apparently a pirate. (What are pirates doing in the Channel? Is he a McFly chicken? And how was that place so dangerous that he'd lose an eye in it? Is he an ex-pirate who joined the bleedin' choir invisible?)
A game where the only stores around are a couple of your friends who occasionally meet you at the end of a chapter and never elsewhere. Cellphones didn't exist at the time, but chapter cuts did.
A game where the story started as a swashbuckling adventure, then quickly decided to drop that, and at some point we got to wonder, why the hell are we hiding our identity anyway? A story where in order to save your fortune, you don't hesitate to kill dozens of people who were just doing their job (I can't help but think of Stormtroopers here.)
The poor lady is in such a predicament, she can't even afford a pack of cards with figures in it. She only got cards 0 through 9. Yes she has zeros. Don't you? Or maybe it's just the author playing games on us. Just like he dropped the cosy noble love stories of 'Regency Solitaire' in favor of a life in shadow, he took risks, added strong RPG elements, dropped and replaced most of the rules that he devised long ago for Fairway Solitaire and were used by so many mindless clones. That's a good idea, but in the end it's 'only' a card game. Duels can be annoying, but in regular rounds, whatever your level, you can beat pretty much anything with good RNG. And failing miserably just because of bad RNG is as much of a problem here as it was in previous 'Pyramid Solitaire games with power-up' games of the genre.
In the end you start losing interest in the story, the writing that started gently lampooning 18th century conventions ends up being a boring pastiche full of cliché words and situations (the French-speaking parts made me cringe a little, nothing that can't be patched though, the anachronisms seem more problematic), few of the characters make sense, the cards are confusing to read (you'd think something would have be done to differentiate the 6 from the 9, eh..? Nope!), 'relaxing mode' (and perhaps others?) never tells you that you don't actually have to achieve the chapter goals (I ended up missing one by a small margin, and then the game just continued as if nothing happened), and I'd have more to say, but I realize that the more you love something, you more you'll criticize it for not being the perfection it could be. I suppose.
The graphics are superb, the UI (and overall UX) is adequate, the music is acceptable at best and thankfully disappears during gameplay, which at first is disorienting (why am I playing a game with only the howlind wind in the game's background?!), allowing you to play your own -- but not during duels for some reason, so you just end up cutting the music entirely from the game.
If you liked Regency Solitaire, you'll like this one as well, you'll probably even love it. If you liked Doom, you may also love it, I'm not judging. Personally I enjoy all kinds of games, so who am I to say what you'll like?

Solitaire game with light RPG elements in terms of equipment and character stat allocations. Playing through the various challenge levels takes you through the story of the titular Shadowhand. Shadowhand is a masked vigilante alias belonging to a 1770s era London noblewoman swept into criminal plots.
Played through the entire game on the hardest difficulty and unlocked all achievements. Let me tell you something, the highest difficulty is exactly what it claims to be - expect multiple restarts and quitting the game in frustration as I did. However, I kept coming back. Yes, many of the levels are extremely dependent on RNG, and many of the combat encounters on the hardest difficulty may feel unfair, but to be entirely honest I couldn't stop playing.
I got a new PS4 over the Christmas holiday, and instead of playing Persona 5, I needed to replay the 30 overkill challenge level over and over.
I got Pokemon Ultra Moon, and instead of diving in and selecting my Popplio, I needed to grind out the God-forsaken final 24 stars over 8 levels challenge on the final chapter.
I finished my Master's degree, and instead of taking a well-deserved break, I needed to 100% the achievements in freaking Shadowhand.
The hardest difficulty is hard, but damn it, once you've finally figured out what you're doing with the equipment, and  you actually understand how to optimize your gear selections, and when you finally take down that final level on the hardest difficulty, it feels earned.
Is Shadowhand on Very Hard the Dark Souls of Solitaire games?
I couldn't tell you. I play Solitaire games, do I look like the kind of girl who plays Dark Souls?
What I can tell you is that Shadowhand beat the hell out of me, it frustrated me, it kept me coming back, and when all was said and done, it was worth it. I had fun and got my 15 bucks worth.

This is a good game with many flaws. Some are minor, some may be pretty annoying, some are a matter of personal taste.
NieR: Automata is a pretty unique experience, its atmosphere, style and general feel being pretty different from basically everything. Despite that I'm not going to call this a masterpiece or even an amazing game. It's pretty great and pretty imperfect.
A detailed review with *minor spoilers* below.
I haven't run into any technical issues while playing NieR: Automata, so I can't comment on that and I'm not rating the technical aspect of the game.
This, I belive, is the strongest point of the game. It's a pretty unusual story that talks about many things. On the surface it's about the evolution of different types of artificial intelligence that gain consciousness and even an ability to feel. It speaks metaphorically about matters of uniqueness, personal experiences, memory, personality, love, life, and loss.
Nevertheless, the story is presented in a pretty convoluted manner. It's not told silently through environmental storytelling like, say, Dark Souls or RiME;  on the contrary, typically for Japanese storytelling, there's a lot of exposition. But the pacing and development are pretty weird. For example, you're told pretty early on that (minor spoiler) some of the machines (which are your enemy) disconnected themselves from the network and gained consciousness, as a result exhibiting unusual behavior like pacifism or religious faith. This doesn't really count as a "revelation" because it happens early in the story and isn't presented as something shocking. It's also hard to say whether this really goes anywhere. Rather than creating conflict and leading to resolution, this idea is more of a creative playground used to show how various groups of freed intelligences find various ways and reasons to live. Which is fine, but I'd call that lore rather than a story.
You'll have antagonists rising from nowhere and secrets that are never revealed, questions that are only asked and so on. You'll have to play the game many times (which is intended because you'll play as different characters) and dig a lot to make some sense of things. However, you'll certainly be surprised time and time again, so I can't help but call NieR's story impressive and unique.
Graphics is okay. It's nothing special. The image suffers from horrible texture LODs and pop in that makes buildings about 300 m from you look like they're from PS2 era. The world is rather plain and simplistically designed, there are few details and few really impressive places. In addition to that NieR is characterised by a rather dark, washed-out color palette, which, while gives the game a unique look, only emphasizes its plainness and poor graphics.
NieR: Automata tries to create a blend of a slasher game and a more traditional action-RPG. The result is a pretty smooth and deep gameplay that isn't too difficult to get into. You have two weapon slots, light and heavy, and you can equip any type of weapon in them (each weapon behaves differently depending on the slot it's being used in). There are no complex combos, just hitting with one weapon and then the other one (or separately; also holding down the attack button creates a separate effect). Your companion Pod acts as a moderately strong ranged weapon, akin to Devil May Cry's pistols, and you can find several such pods. There are also many skills with cooldown, but you can only bind and use only one simultaneously.
A pretty fun element is smooth transitions between 3D and 2D perspectives in some areas of the game as well as episodes where the game turns into a scroll shooter or a twin-stick shooter.
Combat is slick and fun but it gets repetitive. There aren't that many types of enemies, there aren't too many bosses. Chaging the difficulty doesn't make the game more fun; Hard is basically the same as Normal, you just receive more damage.
Also NieR has pretty atrocious targeting system. It
at all. In fact, the game acts as if it's something completely unnecessary, warning you that on Hard targeting is disabled completely. Which, frankly, doesn't really make sense, because a certain level of auto-targeting is a standard for all modern slashers and melee action games.
There are plug-in chips which act as passive buffs and can be found, combined and improved. They make you pretty strong, but upon death they're left on your body and you have only one chance to reclaim them (like souls in DS).
Using crafting materials you can also upgrade your weapons. However, there's little incentive to put much effort into that. Using your first sword you can go through the whole game. There's no clear way to predict which items are hard to locate and which ones are easy, and, more importantly, where to look for them. It's also very weird to see that items always spawn in fixed spots, and whenever you reload the game, new random items will spawn in the same spots. There are secret caches but they rarely provide anything special. Naturally, there are no such things as dungeons or rare monsters that would provide rare valuable materials. And while there are many weapons which look invariably cool, there isn't that much practical difference between them and they mostly affect enemies in the same manner.
The open world is a pretty sad sight. It's not terrible and has some things to surprise you with, but it's really small and unimpressive. In addition to that the navigation is made horrible by an abundance of invisible walls in the weirdest of places. While the fact that you can't fall from most ledges feels right (because that's true for most slasher games), it's annoying and disappointing that all those marvelous post-apocalyptic bombed buildings are just boxes: not only you can enter very few of those, you also can't go through any of the many holes, doors and windows in those buildings. The world geometry and navigation is mostly like something from PS2 era and it's very underwhelming.
Side quests are underwhelming as well. Each of them is unique and has a small story of its own, like in Witcher 3, but apart from that this comparison is not in NieR's favor. Despite having a story, these side quests are usually the regular mundane bring/kill tasks, and sometimes it's just basically "go and look at that". There are exceptions, but even those side quests which are wrapped into an interesting piece of a story are usually very mundane from the gameplay aspect. After doing just a few you probably won't want to do any more.
In other words, NieR: Automata feels like a regular slasher game with unnecessary crafting, item gathering and open world attached. It's not annoying but it also doesn't really bring anything into the game. Weapon upgrades could easily be ditched, and the number of weapons could be reduced in favor of making them more unique (just remember how fun it is to find each new weapon in Devil May Cry or Bayonetta; here it's like "meh, another spear"). The navigation around the world is pretty standard running or using fast travel. You can ride moose or boars but, just like many other elements, this feature seems disconnected from the rest of the game and is rarely of any use.
People praise this aspect a lot but I can't join in. Don't get me wrong, the music in the game is really great. However, I'm going to stand by this point:
. Never bind a song to a location. It gets old really fast.
Fun but repetitive. Pretty but plain. Surprising yet somewhat underwhelming. I'm still not done with 100% of the game so I can't judge it fully but I have a pretty good idea. Try NieR: Automata if you're looking for something different because it certainly is.

Keep in mind I'm not exactly fantastic at writing reviews but here I am going to try my best, its also spoiler free (in terms of concealing the mystery of the game).
I give this game a recommended score because for the most part I absoulutely loved this game. The first half or hell 3 quarters of this game are great, its slow paced & mysterious and filled with fantastic characters, I mean York alone may be one of my favourite video game protagonists of all time after playing this game. My favourite aspect of this game was living the day to day life of an FBI agent in a small country town tracking down a murderer, I'm aware this comparison is made alot (and rightly so) but it really felt like the Twin Peaks experience from the view of Dale Cooper, except we got to see Coopers day to day life.
The investigative aspect of this game, where you start your day off in the hotel with a coffee and breakfast, where you drive your car into Greenvale following up on leads and in the down time stop by the sheriffs station for lunch or hitting up possible suspects was fantastic, and I loved every minute of it. But to me this game has a fatal flaw. Towards the end Deadly Premontion became too much of a videogame.
By this I mean that on the approach towards the climax everything in this game became so, dumbed-down? You go from a slow detective mystery to fighting a huge ripped dude throwing giant axes at you, and are constantly bombarded by survival horror sections where you fight souls of the damned (or something akin to that). I mean, it just feels like such a different experience and personally, I dont enjoy it.
So now I will reveal the shocking truth, I havent finished this game, honestly because I couldnt bring myself to do it. I just found the action sequences so uninteresting, the little snippets of dialogue and story we get inbetween are fantastic as they are throughout the whole game but at this stage I honestly cannot bring myself to complete the game. Perhaps I will come back to it.
On another note, feel free to correct me on this all you Deadly P fans but I feel as if all the action and especially the survival horror aspects are more a problem of the studio as opposed to Swery (developer of the game), perhaps it was assumed that people wouldnt want a slow paced detective game and action scenes were shoe-horned into the production. To further elaborate on this it is for this reason that I am looking foward to Swerys next title The Good Life. From what we've seen it seems to play more like the slow paced detective mystery I love so much and perhaps without the studio pressure Swery will be able to follow his vision more clearly.
But who am I to say what Swerys vision is, on my final note I would like to say I still recomend this game even though this review largely focuses on what I dont like. I would buy the game even if I knew what happens towards the end because the slow-paced mystery experience early game is fantastic and the writing too is on the same level. As I've said York is a great character and Greenvale is charming and simultaneously dark and uncanny. Although alot of people compare this game to Twin Peaks, I really feel as if Deadly Premonition stands as its own product. Get this game but just understand what you may be getting yourself into if you dont like more action focused games (like me).

What I like:
It takes the best elements from all my favorite 4X games (Space Empires V, Star Ruler 2, Endless Space) and blends them together nicely. The diplomacy is deep enough without being distracting or confusing, where SR2's card system was neat, but I found that the whole system was a PITA to deal with, and I ended up either missing things or purposely ignoring them. The ship design is not quite what I would like; I would have liked something closer to SE5, but that's not to say it's bad, I rather like it. The way you can manage different species in your empire is awesome (Purge the filthy xeno scum!), and the recent addition of per-species rights is great.
What I don't like:
The AI. While it's consistent, it's pretty consistently stupid and non-helpful. My enemies are not much of a threat, and when they are, my allies are useless most of the time. Oh they declare war alright, as is required by a defensive pact, but damned if I'm gonna get any kind of assistance from them. My enemies, no matter who started the war, tend to just turtle in their capital while I stomp the rest of their empire to dust. To be fair, however, it has gotten better recently; my allies are only mostly useless.
Overall, I love this game. I feel like Paradox has really hit the nail on the head. And I love that I took a few months break (playing it constantly tends to get you burned out) from this game and I came back and it was even better.

Snap your mouse back and forth and destroy the falling pills with the coordinating colors before enough fall past you, and you die. 'Intake' takes the things that made 'Tetris' memorable and builds upon them, so you know it's good. And combining these characteristics along with the fast-paced soundtrack and upgrade system makes this game well worth the price.

I wouldn’t normally start a review talking about other people’s reviews of the same game, but I feel it’s important here as ether I’m missing the point with this game or I’m just not like the other people playing this game. I’ll talk more on this as we go through but just to say this game has received mainly positive reviews on Steam and that mine will not be so positive.
Welkin Road is something of a cross between Mirrors Edge and Spiderman, free running with some web slinging thrown in for fun . . . or lack thereof. Each level presents the player in a minimalistic world with nothing but skill and some gloves that allow you to swing in orbs dotted around to traverse the level. Being a huge Mirrors Edge fan I was very hopeful for this game, but I have to say I’m disappointed.
The looks are good, I’ve expressed in previous reviews how much I like this minimalistic approach with levels being composed of white and a single colour that some Indie games are using right now and here is no different. It looks good though I think unlike other games such as Absolute drift and Block ‘hood the first person view of Welkin Road really shows the flaws with this style. I still like it all the same and think Welkin Roads animation is really done well, while I wouldn’t call the game a looker it does look very ok.
The settings are pretty good offering enough tinkering for most to get the game running reasonably smooth, but the game offers no controller support. I normally wouldn’t mind this, especially in a first person game where I will normally opt for keyboard and mouse controls but in this game it has so much going on and the keyboard controls are so bad it really effects the experience. This could have been remedied simply by instead of placing imputes all over the keyboard simply combining them into one action button that would do it all. The game offers two modes currently, the standard campaign which is just about making it to the end of the level and of course speed run. I think there was room here for something more original, but I have little complaint all the same.
So on to the gameplay and this is for me where things go downhill, as I’ve already said the key layout isn’t the best but the game its self also works against you. You can jump off the same platform 100 times and the outcome seems random, sometimes you can latch on to an orb but others not, you can wall run but sometimes not. Now I know this is probably just as much user error as anything else but the game makes no effort to help you, there’s no leeway what so ever. I can already hear the cries of “Get Good” but this game makes Dark Souls look like a teddy bear, I honestly thought I was missing something or just being dumb but then I hit the Steam reviews and realized I wasn’t alone. Others were having the exact same issue but instead of like me finding this an issue many were happy about it as the game respawns you to the last platform you were on. Singing its praises as fun and happy they completed a level in 15 minutes! To me this game lacks accessibility and that really ruins the experience for me, I know I will never complete a level fault free on this game however hard I practice and that’s a big problem to me. I’m happy to put in the effort when a game rewards it or when I can see the mistakes I’m making are my own fault but Welkin Road doesn’t do this, Instead the errors I’m making are undetectable to myself and make me feel like the game is somehow cheating me. It’s just not fun and honestly had me nearly throwing my mouse at the wall in frustration.
All games need to have a learning curve and introduce you in to get you hooked, Welkin Road seems to lack this and while the majority of Steam review disagree with me I found this game more frustrating than fun. Not because I couldn’t complete the levels, with infinite retries that’s not an issue but because perfection eludes me and that’s a problem to me.
If your happy to fall to your death 100 times every level and not be sure it’s your fault check it out, but if not you might want to give it a miss.

Game Details:
Soaring amid the clouds, Welkin Road blends free running with grappling-hook-powered aerobatics, challenging you to reach the end of each level using only your wits and the abilities available to you. The road ahead will test your resolve, your concentration and your reflexes, forcing you to master your swings and movement as you learn new techniques to overcome the obstacles in the world… or plummet to your doom.
The gameplay is driven by two core components: grappling and parkour. Make use of the two grappling hooks to swing from point to point, creating momentum while using parkour-inspired movement to explore the world. Sprint, leap, balance, run on walls and hold on for dear life as you perform incredible, high-altitude, acrobatic stunts.
You have full control over the grappling hooks, as well as the direction, speed and timing of your swings. Master and blend all of these elements into fast, fluid and elegant runs. Challenge yourself further by competing against the clock and the time of other runners around the world.

For those of you who loved the original Mirror’s Edge and either refuse to have Origin on their system and don’t have a console you may be somewhat disappointed in the fact that it wont be coming to Steam. However, I’m happy to tell you that you don’t have to miss out on the excellence that is parkour on PC this year thanks to the outstanding Welkin Road that is currently in Steam Early Access and has been developed by the highly talented Gregor Panič.
Although the graphics and the overall look of the presentation are quite simplistic it’s in the actual gameplay that the game shines. It’s among the most challenging yet relaxing games that we’ve featured to date and I look forward to sinking my teeth into the game and actually learning how to really play and beat the game. The aim of the game is to use your parkour powers – that’s a full accompaniment of grappling hooks and your body – crawling, crouching, running, walking and jumping – your way from ledge to ledge and over a whole host of different types of barriers that present themselves in the most awkward and devilish of places.
I was a huge fan of the level design. The game is linear but it gives you just enough wiggle room to make it feel as though it is open enough that different strategies can come into effect. The biggest challenge in the game is to really understand the control scheme. Once you’ve learned the best way to control your character you’re pretty much set up to take the game by storm. Of course, the barriers and the obstacles aren’t very easy but most of the time it’s just learning and thinking about the best way to encounter them rather than them presenting as an impossible mountain to climb. Thankfully when you die you respawn quickly right at the obstacle that you succumbed to so you don’t have the annoying and aggravating problem of having to repeat content over and over again just to die at the obstacle that you failed to defeat the first time, rinse and repeat ad nauseam.
The game may be in early access but you can definitely forget about all of the demons that come with that tag. It’s been exceptionally well developed and continued support has come hard and fast. The few people that I know that have encountered problems with the game have had communication with the developer, Gregor, who has been extremely quick and super friendly to deal with. This is clearly a passion project for him and as much as he hopes to make it a financial success it is clear that the financial aspect of the product runs a distant second to his desire to release the best game possible.
If I were to criticize the game in any aspect it would be the lack of a narrative or story. I would like to see one implemented for the retail release of the game. A short back story and reason for the game’s existence would be fantastic otherwise it runs the dangers of becoming just another of the countless fun but lacking puzzle-esque games on Steam. Thankfully there are Steam achievements which currently satiate the thirst of the game being Steamified and I am hopeful that trading cards will either come with the game at retail launch or beforehand.
At $12.99 parkour fans are going to get their monies worth. If you’re not sure if the game is for you then wait but if you are interested in the game then you have the all clear to make that all important purchase decision.

Welkin Road consist of a campaign mode with eleven levels, and an “S” ranking system (like Resident Evil). Each of the eleven levels brings a new mechanic into the game, which adds variety to each level as the game progresses, since these new mechanics carry over into the later levels. The game is really simple in its premise. Players must sprint, walk, grapple, wall jump, and wall run from one checkpoint to the other: until they reach the pillar of light at the end that carries them to the next level. Since the setting of the game is on variously colored blocks that are raised high above clouds in the air, this might be what parkour heaven looks like?
Each new grappling mechanic is presented through varying colored orbs that hover throughout the level. Players must interact with these orbs through their grappling gloves (which look pretty slick to me), and manipulate their own momentum and movements to reach the next parts of the level. There is the most basic red orb (as an example), This orb is the first orb that players encounter since it is the first level. It simply sits in a predetermined position, making it easy to grapple to and swing around endlessly, or change the direction that you swing to land onto a platform on your side. Things get more complex quickly, with orbs like the blue orb, which run out of energy after about three seconds. This means grappling it for more than that time will result in you plummeting to your death. This introduction of varying mechanics is a great feature that keeps the levels progressively increasing in difficulty, and staying refreshing.
Welkin Road gives players access to all eleven levels from the start, so anyone feeling adventurous can hop right into the final level and punish themselves by trying to figure out all of the game's’ mechanics on their own. When players do play the campaign mode, they will progress from one level to the next, with tips offered at various puzzles or obstacles. These tips are optional in the game’s menu, but also only appear as a pop up message that players can activate, and read by clicking “F1” (by default). This was something I really enjoyed, since the game allowed me to first try to out various obstacles on my own. Only when I had died around ten times did I open the tips to get more insight into how to properly succeed.
There is speed run mode as well, where players can challenge themselves to race to the end of each level, once they have mastered the game’s mechanics, or even just for fun. Welkin Road also features secrets hidden throughout each level, the number of the secrets per level is listed when players starts the game, and is shown in the campaign menu screen.
Welkin Road’s mechanics function well, but the game does not feel perfect. The movements feel fluid when wall running, sprinting, and jumping. Wall jumping took a patch and some really good timing to nail though. There is a collision sound that plays when your player hits a wall, indicating when to press the spacebar to jump off of it. This threw off my timing more than anything, since it did not seem to be in perfect synchronization with when my character was actually touching the wall. Jumping upwards with wall jumps felt nearly impossible at some points of the levels as well, but the newest patch has made these motions much easier to complete. The physics of the grappling mechanic felt fluid as well, and stringing together jumps from one orb to another orb was manageable. My real issue was not the mechanics of the game but more so the level designs of certain obstacles. There were many jumps, or grappling sequences in the levels that took almost pixel perfect precision to complete. I loved the challenge of many of the obstacles, and figuring out solutions on my own. Yet  many obstacles required literal perfect timing across three or four jumps, which at times became frustrating more than anything. The game is far from unbeatable, but players should simply be ready to die plenty of times, and players should make sure their mouse settings are just right.
The game features a minimalist style, in both its art and music, which I found relaxing and undistracting. As mentioned before, each level occurs on white blocks mixed with a single color, which corresponds to the color orb of that level. The game is well optimized and lets players adjust the usual settings like contrast, brightness, bloom, resolution, and more. There is only music in the game’s menu but not while playing the actual levels. This was not an issue for me, I enjoy the atmosphere created by a game where you can hear the sound of the environment: especially atmospheric heavy games like Skyrim or Dishonored. Music does often enhance experiences however, so the same soft and soothing type of song in the menu would make the game more enjoyable for some.
Welkin Road lacks any narrative which for some may turn them off from the game. It was designed as a first person parkour, puzzle simulator and functions great at being just that. Adding these sort of mechanics into a full fledged game in the future would probably be a great asset, but for now, Welkin Road is entertaining, simple, yet a fun challenge.
Pros:
Minimalist Art Style
Fluid physics and player movements (slight improvements needed)
Clean graphics and good optimization
Relaxing Atmosphere
Developers active on Steam discussion page
Interesting, well implemented game mechanics
Well designed levels
Challenging
Cons
Game mechanics are not perfect
No in-game music (subjective)
Minimalist art style (subjective)
Misspelling of “collect” in campaign menu (minor but just something I noticed)
No narrative (subjective)

Game of Thrones is story driven role playing game set into action of the first season of a highly praised television series of the same name (or the novel by George R.R. Martin) If you are not familiar with neither the book nor the series, despair not. The game still offers an immersive story and enjoyable gameplay for you. Maybe it even sparks interest of yours to discover why it is so popular and give a chance to either the book or the series or even both.
The game starts on the northern part of the Seven kingdoms located on the continent called Westeros. On this very place the continent is divided by the 700 feet high wall built 8000 years ago and guarded by an antient order called Night's Watch. The first hero is Ser Mors Westford sworn brother of this order, a ranger able to track almost anyone with a help of his dog. One day a letter arrives with a special request for Mors about protecting a woman sent north. No reason just this, the letter was sent by an old friend of his and arrived with a bunch of soldiers dedicated to find her. Something is not right here and Mors was allowed to go for that girl and find out what is that all about.
The another character is a former southern nobleman Alester Sarwick who just arrived home for his father's funeral. After 15 years in exile in Essos, where he became a red priest of the Lord of Light, he came back to find his home in depression and poverty. This used to be a prosperious center, what could have happened. After finding out that his brother Gawen was disinherited and his sister Elyana has been betrothed to their half-brother Valarr, Alester makes an underlying decision to stay and help the things sort out.
As you've seen the story is divided in two parts, following acts of two characters which at the first look are separated by far distance and have nothing in common. However their past and future are bound together. How? I guess you will have to find out for yourself if you want to know more.
The story is the best part of the game. It has action, twists, heartbreaking moments, shortly everything you desire. In addition it is very detailed and can offer you closer look into this universe, its history, society, places or significant characters. It's achieved mainly through archives of Westeros which you can collect during gameplay and afterwards read in the Codex in the menu of the game.
Even though the dialogs offer you many options your choice doesn't really matter. Only once you have a choice which influences the end of the game. I've tried reaching both endings and the difference is only in the ending cutscene and last 2 minutes of the game. Exept this its the same, so I don't see any point in playing this game twice and trying different playstyles.
Since you can play for two characters in one fight you are able to control both and it's reached genuinely through quick switching between them and using their abilities during "slowed time". Being able to slow time in order to time attacks and maximize the efficiency is a gentle solution and enables finishing the game even on the hardest difficulty (as I did). It is entertaining, but as the game develops it's all the same again and again.
When we are talking about choosing capabilities, which you take in the abilities tree, choice doesn't really matter. You will be using only a few and most of them are useless to you. As usually you will get through with stun and damage ones. Skills improve your proficiency with particular weapons or effeciency of an armor you use, so easily you know what to pick. Another thing is that during gameplay you can obtain some traits improving your character, increasing hit chance or deflection for example, but only with a minor impact.
The last thing to mention here is the level cap. It can be reached only at the end of the game after you have finished everything possible in the game. So in conclusion only usefulness of reaching it is gaining a steam achievement.
The game plays out on a few locations of different sizes. As a whole this world is tiny and you can't miss much in it because you come back to every location so many times it is almost impossible unless some exceptions which are sealed after finishing a chapter.
During gameplay you can meet only few side quests in the advanced phase of the game. These will bring you again on the locations you have been before and most of these tasks are solved by tedious dialogues with different types of people or fighting which is then more tiresome than entertaining.
I would recommend this game only to those interested primarily in the story. This is a nice completion for fans of Game of Thrones, but as I have said before even others may find this game interesting and enjoyable.

Oddly enough, I was never in to Saints Row until the 4th.  The game left a lot of questions, a lot of backstory, so I figured the only way to get answers was to go back to the beginning, or as far as I could.
There doesn’t seem to be a Saints Row 1 on Steam, so Saints Row 2 will have to do.
The first thing to note is that the game is buggy as hell.  Right out of the gate the game didn’t work out of the box on Windows 7. I needed to download a special config file to get the window to open non-full screen.  After a lot of fiddling around I was able to get the game going, but anytime the game crashed while playing full screen I had to re-paste the config file in to the correct directory just to get the game to work.  Needless to say the game has issues, and let it be your warning.
I never really felt like the game was probably a good PC port.  I always felt like the controls are some how a bit lacking.  It feels like a console game that’s on a PC that was meant to be played with a gamepad.  The AI is generally horrible, and gives you that “I have to aim with a stick” feeling.  Driving is relatively easy, and not that great of variety as is in later sequels.
Lets cut to the brass tacks.  Do you like explosions?  Do you like violence?  Do you like shooting someone in the face and pushing them out the window of a very tall building?
You will run.  You will kill.  You will drive.  You… will spray sewage on the cops.  This is Saints Row 2.
The game in many ways is basically the same as the first.  There are different rival gangs that have taken over the city of Stillwater.  This use to be the Third Street Saints turf, but you have been in a comma for a long time after the ending of the first game.  With the help of your crew Gat (the bad♥♥♥♥♥, Pierce (the black homi), and Shandi (the crusty stoner girl) you will battle these gangs over many planned missions laid out with cinematics.  It’s hard to say the story is good, but it contains quite a few twists that do make it into later games.  All faction missions the same basic pattern.  Small missions leading up to boss fights for the head of each faction.  Most boss fights, albeit interesting, are actually pretty easy despite the fact they may not look so in the first place.
Combat is a 3rd person shooter style.  You’re able to loadout a variety of weapons to each of your main weapon slots.  Your main weapons include, melee, pistol, shotgun, smg, assault, special, and thrown.  You can recruit “homies” off the street that will fight will you.  They are basically cannon fodder, another homage to the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor AI.
There is a wide array of places to explore in Stillwater.  There are many side activities to do as well if you have the time and patience.  My initial play through consisted of ~22 hours of game play and that was basically doing what I had to get through the faction mission.  In order to do faction missions, you have to earn “respect”, and you do that mostly by doing side activities.  Once you get a level of respect you can then do a faction mission.  Rinse and repeat.  There is considerable amount of content I did not touch and did not explore.  I’d be confident in saying that you could easily double that time.
As is the Saints way, you can pimp yourself, your crib, your car, and your crew.  Want to be a giant hot dog?  No problem.  Want to be a guy wearing a thong?  OK, weird, but you can.   Want ninja gang members?  Sure. That’s the fun of Saints Row 2, its wacky without being TOO wacky.  Unlike the sequels it seems less playful and more grounded in reality.  There are no real crazy weapons or vehicles.
TLDR; Overall if you’ve played the sequels and are wondering about the back story I would say the game is worth the time.  I’d have a hard time saying the game is great, because it is not, but it was still a satisfying experience and for it’s time I think it was a solid effort.  It feels like a console port, has♥♥♥♥♥♥poor AI, and crashes like mad, yet is fun.

If it weren't for the mess of controls and general jankiness of the PC port, this would be amongst my favourite PC games of all time.  Regardless, Saints Row 2 offers an absolutely phenonemal open world with a bevy of entertaining things to do in it and an interesting storyline as well.  Saints Row 2 knows exactly what it wants to be: fun.  And that's exactly what it is.

The story is what makes this game click. It shows a world in which the characters are chaotic, weird, and insane but it keeps them real. There is a tragic scene which actually makes you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥for letting your partner down. The game makes you give a damn about your characters and makes you laugh because the saints are simply insane and counter intuitive to the "normal" world around them. The story consists of beating 3 gangs each of which involves starting♥♥♥♥♥♥with them, taking their hideouts, and murdering them all. After that, it’s the "take down the evil corporation" which seems cliché but they establish very clearly that the saints are not good people. In fact all the gangs are generically evil but they do the same evil crap as the Saints do and it helps characterize them.
The combat is pretty bad. In order to aim, you have to stop, press the v key and then press it again to stop aiming. They give you a lot of weapons. But dual wielding smgs and a RPG basically solve all the problems in the world. I literally hit the last boss with one grenade launcher and that was it. Mission over. You can pretty much have perfect aim with most of the guns (except shotgun) at any distance. The RPG would be best against helicopters but you have to predict where they go because they never get close enough to you to shoot them down. The frame drop during fighting doesn’t help either. There is a star rating but unless you start using the RPG or fire into a VERY crowded room, you will basically stay below 2-3 stars.
The graphics are OK (it’s a 2008 game) but the optimization is crap. I'm pretty sure I got way less than 30 fps and the game chuggs when you go from inside to the outside or when there are a lot of enemies. There was a mission on a boat where it was so slow I couldn’t even shoot anything. The ragdoll physics of when you hit the ground is laughably bad but the general physics isn't bad. When you first get into the cars, good luck with driving because they handle like pure♥♥♥♥♥♥ It takes a few hours before you get used to them and even then the fast cars are often out of control.
Now onto the game. To play the main activity, you have to do side missions and build up respect (the story purpose is to get money but it makes you do this even when you have money). Now some of the side activities are actually fun with you wanting to do them. However, there are a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of driving ones (see above) mostly one of each of the other ones. You have to do this EACH TIME AND IT'S ANNOYING AS HELL. It takes forever to actually get anywhere in the game. Also, you have to navigate between each of the missions, side missions, and gun store which is crap because the longer I have to spend on the road, the worse.
Overall, the game is good for the story. It's awesome for it. But the bugs and the terrible port are just horrible. Get it for a cheap price.

TL;DR
-Clever mash up of a rip roaring story about 18thC damsel who solves her own distresses with RPG characterisation and a card game/ solitaire combat mechanics
I came across Shadowhand via a preview on the site RPS not having heard of the developer or Regancy Solitaire nor even being familiar with RNG games (Random Number Generator.....I had to look it up too!)
Was struck firstly by the premise of the storyline, based in both a period of history and in characterisations that I find interesting.
However what made me order the title was the novel amalgam of storyline and combat mechanics, which appears to be one of only a handful in this type of genre.
The card gameplay is intuitive but has a certain depth to it, the RPG elements adds an additional tactical layer and at least until the mid game, the storyline and writing both evokes the period while keeping the action going.
Am now about 1/2 through the game, not for want of time (see my playtime) but rather a slightly OCD tendency to replay earlier chapters to build up consumables and special cards.
*Recommended for players interested in an unique RPG experience (suitable both for short and longer periods of gaming) in the surprisingly underutilised but very suitable game world of an 18thC female aristocrat!*

Half of the game is similar to Regency Solitaire: a mix of the solitaire card game and a puzzle. What sets Shadowhand apart is that it also adds combat. Playing cards reloads weapons and items, which you can use to damage your opponent or heal yourself. This is very exciting! Trashing an enemy with a massive combo attack or winning with only a few points of health left to spare makes a card game like this something else.
After battles, you can find/buy equipment, which helps you perform better against certain opponents. This is half the battle. Deciding on a good setup makes it so you have a chance, even when you pick some bad cards.
All in all, I think it's a very good game and I can't wait to see what Grey Alien does next.

PROS:

- Interesting story with a strong female protaganist
- Nice assortment of abilities, weapons and armor and uses for nearly all of them at one point or another
- Nice artwork
CONS:
- Some of the battles can be pretty rough
- Despite a rather in depth tutorial, there are still some things that are poorly explained like "Land" vs "Sea" vs no designation weapons.
All in all, I am really glad I took the chance and tried this game out. Like I said, it is outside the normal range of my games, but it truly won me over. A big thumbs up!

Its a RPG solitaire card game.  You can choose your gear loadouts, armor loadouts, skills, consumables and then play a solitarie like type of card game.  When you beat a chapter you get to place attribute points that impact the board when you play.
You get a card and must play 1 above or below that number until you cant, then you draw a card from a pile.  When the pile runs out the round ends or a new board is shuffledi n duels until someone wins.  There are times where you will need to replay a round a couple times as is the nature of card games, there is a random element to it.  Sometimes you get absolutely screwed and other times its a gimmie.  Your skills and consumables will allow you to tip the favor in your hands on the bad rounds.  Even with those though, sometimes a round isnt winable (nature of a card game).  Thankfully there is no penalty in retrying and you can do so as many times as you want until you beat the chapter goals.
Its quite addicting.  Its not overly complicated and the music is pretty good.  The story is entertaining albeit a bit cheesy at certain points its enough to ask you what happens next.
I do recommend this game and the developers are involved in the forums.  They will respond to almost any feedback/suggestions you have.

What I like:
It takes the best elements from all my favorite 4X games (Space Empires V, Star Ruler 2, Endless Space) and blends them together nicely. The diplomacy is deep enough without being distracting or confusing, where SR2's card system was neat, but I found that the whole system was a PITA to deal with, and I ended up either missing things or purposely ignoring them. The ship design is not quite what I would like; I would have liked something closer to SE5, but that's not to say it's bad, I rather like it. The way you can manage different species in your empire is awesome (Purge the filthy xeno scum!), and the recent addition of per-species rights is great.
What I don't like:
The AI. While it's consistent, it's pretty consistently stupid and non-helpful. My enemies are not much of a threat, and when they are, my allies are useless most of the time. Oh they declare war alright, as is required by a defensive pact, but damned if I'm gonna get any kind of assistance from them. My enemies, no matter who started the war, tend to just turtle in their capital while I stomp the rest of their empire to dust. To be fair, however, it has gotten better recently; my allies are only mostly useless.
Overall, I love this game. I feel like Paradox has really hit the nail on the head. And I love that I took a few months break (playing it constantly tends to get you burned out) from this game and I came back and it was even better.

Intake is a fun game. Click one mouse button to change color, click the other button to 'shoot'. Shatter glowing colored tablets to get points, and don't let any hit the bottom of the screen. At the end of each level, any pills still on screen turn into tiny bonus tabs you can shoot for more points. Your points at the end of the game are recycled into points that let you buy things like weird powerups, more music, more colors, and other modes.
It's trippy, it's fast paced, and requires twitchy clicking. It'll probably give me carpal tunnel by the end of the week.If you like pounding, dirty bass lines and bright neon-colored explosions with frantic shmup-like gameplay, this is a game for you.
Really the only downside is the default price(9.99 as of this writing). Worth considering waiting off for a sale but definitely worth playing and buying anyway. It's well-made, and plays well.

BugZy's Review: RFLEX - Geometry warfare!
The following is my opinion.
Enter the arcade world of RFLEX, where the only thing that will save your pentagonal character from ultimately colliding with what seem to be big black rectangles are the swift reflexes that you hope and pray to possess upon launching the game. Without them, you won’t last 10 seconds.
The game consists of a few basic elements, they are ‘dodge things,’ ‘don’t let things hit you’ and ‘move damn it, that thing is going to utterly destroy you.’ You use the arrow keys or a gamepad to move your pentagon out of the way of your lifeless enemies before they reach the end of their path, ending the round if they hit you.
When I started playing the game my first natural assumption was that the projectiles flew at my shape in a random order, but a few minutes in I realised that that was clearly not the case. There are patterns that you can predict in order to stand a chance at dodging your impending doom. It’s handy to know and has saved me several hundred times.
As you may predict based on what I have stated previously, the game is astonishingly challenging. After watching the trailer and maybe a few videos of gameplay, you may think ‘this looks pretty easy,’ but let me tell you, the game is a lot harder than it looks. There are five levels in RFLEX, they are Amusement, Challenge, Addiction, Lifestyle and Death Wish (the name scares me,) each with their own quirks and patterns and all very, very difficult.
If you would like to let everyone know you are amazing or are happy with telling the world you are terrible at the game, there are both global and friend leaderboards. Brag away!
The graphics are simple, just black on certain colours depending on what mode you have picked. Simple doesn’t mean bad though. Having the same colours every match makes it easy on the eyes as they aren’t constantly changing like in Super Hexagon (where you need the special glasses to prevent brain destroying migraines.)
You play the game to an awesome electronic soundtrack featuring ForeverBound, Valiant and RollingFacade. Oh and I couldn’t resist to mention that there is a drunk mode. It’s pretty self-explanatory and is a perfect simulation of being drunk whilst playing RFLEX.
Wesley is such a great guy that he has also added an epileptic friendly mode for those of you who suffer from photosensitive epilepsy and has stated that ‘if you are not satisfied with this option, and are unable to play this game, you are entitled to a refund.’
All in all, RFLEX is a great arcade game of dodge and if you have time to kill and a few dollars to spare, you should definitely check it out.
RFLEX has earned 9/10 wallabies.
